en: The transliteration emulates the Devanāgarī script;
therefore, word boundaries are generally not marked by spaces.
*Matsya-Purāṇa* 1.
May the lotus feet of Bhava, by whom the elephants of the quarters were cast down in the fury of his fierce and violent dance, exist for the destruction of all obstacles.

May the sound uttered from the mouth of Viṣṇu in his incarnation as the Fish protect you from misfortune—that sound which, when he was about to leap up from the netherworld (pātāla), caused the abodes of the sea-monsters to fall upward due to the impact of his tail, overturning the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and throwing it into disarray; and which, while pervading the entire circle of the earth, reached the ears of all. (Matsya Purāṇa 1.1)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).

Salutations to that self-existent one, who, though unborn, is known as Nārāyaṇa through the application of his creative acts; he who possesses the three qualities and is the source of the three Vedas. (Matsya Purāṇa 1.3)
At the conclusion of their long sacrificial session, the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest questioned Sūta, who was seated with one-pointed concentration, regarding the Dīrghasaṃhitā.
When the ancient, righteous, and charming stories had begun,
Śaunaka and the others greeted them again and again with delight.
O sinless one, those ancient accounts which were previously told to us by you—
we wish to hear them once again, for they are like nectar.
How did the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, create the world of moving and unmoving beings? And for what reason, O Blessed One, did Viṣṇu assume the form of a fish?
By what means did Bhava attain the state of Bhairava, and for what reason did the enemy of Tripura become the foe of cities?
For what cause did the bull-bannered god come to possess the skull-bowl?
O Sūta, explain all of this in detail and in due order;
for by your words, no satiety arises here, as if it were nectar.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, now listen to the entire Matsya Purāṇa, which is meritorious, purifying, and life-prolonging, as it was spoken by Gadādhara.
In ancient times, the patient King Manu, the son of the Sun, having performed extensive austerities and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, [attained his goal]. (Matsya Purāṇa 1.11)
In a certain region of Malaya, however, a hero endowed with all personal virtues,
who shared equally in both sorrow and joy, attained supreme yoga.
When a hundred thousand years had passed, the Lotus-seated Lord, being pleased, became the granter of boons to him and said, "Choose a boon. (Matsya Purāṇa 1.13)
Thus addressed, the king bowed to his grandfather and said:
"I desire from you one single, unsurpassed boon."
May I be capable of protecting the entire multitude of beings, both the stationary and the moving, when the dissolution of the world has arrived.
"So be it," said the Soul of the Universe, and he vanished right there;
a great rain of flowers, offered by the gods, fell from the sky.
Once, while he was performing the libations for his ancestors in the hermitage, a small fish along with some water fell upon his hands. (Matsya Purāṇa 1.17)
Seeing that form of a small fish,
the compassionate lord of the earth made an effort to protect it within the hollow of his hand.
In a single day and night, he became a fish sixteen digits in width, and he cried out, "Save me! Save me! (Matsya Purāṇa 1.19).
Taking him, he threw that water-dweller into a water-jar;
and there too, in a single night, he grew by three cubits.
Again, with cries of distress, that fish spoke to the son of the Thousand-rayed One:
"Save me! Save me! I have come to you for refuge."
Then the son of the Sun cast that fish into a well;
when the fish could no longer be contained even there, he cast it into a lake.
Thrown there, it expanded again to a size of one yojana;
even then, the wretched man cried out once more: "Save me! Save me, O best of kings! (Matsya Purāṇa 1.23)
Then, when it was cast by Manu into the Gaṅgā, it continued to grow;
thereupon, the lord of the earth cast it into the ocean.
When he had arrived, pervading the entire ocean, Manu, filled with fear, said: "Who are you, O Lord of Asuras?"
Or else, you are Vāsudeva; how could anyone else be like this?
To whom could a body equal to twenty thousand yojanas belong?
"You are known to me in the form of a fish; you distress me, O Keśava!
Hṛṣīkeśa, Lord of the World, Abode of the Universe—salutations be unto you! (Matsya Purāṇa 1.27)
Thus addressed, the Blessed One Janārdana, in the form of a fish, said, "Excellent, excellent! O sinless one, you have understood correctly."
O lord of the earth, in no long time at all, the earth—
with its mountains, forests, and groves— will be submerged in water.
"O Lord of the Earth, this boat has been constructed by the assembly of all the gods for the purpose of protecting the great multitude of living beings."

O you of noble vows, having placed within this [egg] all those beings who are born from sweat, from eggs, from sprouts, and those who are viviparous— protect them, for they are now without a protector.
O King, when the ship is struck by the winds at the end of the eon,
O Indra among kings, you shall then fasten it to this horn of mine.
Then, at the end of the dissolution, O Lord of the Earth, you shall become Prajāpati of all that is stationary and moving in the world.
Thus, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, you shall become an omniscient and steadfast king,
a sovereign of a Manvantara, and one worthy of worship by the gods.
Matsya Purāṇa 2: Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by him, Manu questioned Madhusūdana.
"O Blessed One, after how many years will the end of the intermediate period (antarakṣaya) occur?"
And how, O Protector, Madhusūdana, shall I protect all beings?
Or how shall there be for me a reunion with you once again?
Matsya said:
"From this day forward, a drought shall prevail upon the surface of the earth for more than a hundred years— a time of famine bringing misfortune."
Then, for the destruction of the feeble-minded beings, seven terrible rays will arise from the seven-horsed sun,
raining down blazing coals.
Even the submarine fire will undergo transformation at the end of the age;
so too the poison-fire from the netherworld, emitted from the mouth of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and the fire of the third eye arising from the forehead of Bhava.
O great sage, it will bring about a disturbance that consumes the three worlds;
thus, when the entire earth has been burnt until it resembles ashes, [the dissolution shall occur].
O scorcher of enemies, the sky will be heated by the heat;
thereafter, the world, together with its gods and stars, will go to destruction.
Saṃvarta, Bhīmanāda, Droṇa, Caṇḍa, Balāhaka,
Vidyutpatāka, and Śoṇa— these seven are the clouds of dissolution.
The oceans, having become agitated, will come together as one and, arising from the heat of fire, shall inundate the earth.
Taking hold of this boat of sensation, they will make these three worlds into a single ocean, gathering the seeds of sentient beings from every side.
O you of noble vows, having fastened the boat with the rope provided by me using the method of the cord,
restrain it at my horn, protected by my state as a fish.
O scorcher of enemies, you alone shall remain among the gods even when they have been consumed by fire;
I, along with Soma, Sūrya, Brahmā, and the four worlds, [shall likewise endure].
The holy river Narmadā, the great ṛṣi Mārkaṇḍeya,
Bhava, the Vedas, and the Purāṇas— [all] surrounded on every side by sacred sciences.
Together with you, this entire universe shall remain until the end of the intermediate period;
thus it shall be when the Cākṣuṣa interval has ended and the single ocean has arisen.
"O Lord of the Earth, I shall set forth the Vedas at the beginning of your creation.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there. (Matsya Purāṇa 2.15)
Manu also remained established in the yoga born of Vāsudeva’s grace,
practicing it until the dissolution of all beings, as previously indicated.
When the time as described had arrived, emerging from the mouth of Vāsudeva,
Janārdana then manifested in the form of a fish with horns.
The serpent,
who knew the dharma, drew all beings toward himself through yoga and, having placed them upon Manu, approached him in the form of a rope.
With a rope made of serpent-skin, he fastened the boat to the horn of the fish;
then, standing upon it, he prostrated himself before Janārdana.
When that dissolution of all beings had passed, the Purāṇa was proclaimed by the one reclining in Yoga in the form of a Fish, when questioned by Manu;
that I shall now proclaim—listen, O best of sages! (Matsya Purāṇa 2.20)
O twice-born ones, that very same account of creation and so forth which you previously asked me about,
Manu inquired of Keśava when all was one vast ocean.
Manu said: [Tell me] of the origin and the dissolution, as well as the lineages, the Manvantaras,
the history of those belonging to the lineages, and the detailed extent of the world.
He also taught the rules for the practice of giving, the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha),
the distinctions between the social classes and stages of life, as well as those known as sacrifices and works of public utility.
"You ought to explain in detail all that exists on earth, such as the installation of deities and whatever else there may be. (Matsya Purāṇa 2.24)
Matsya said:
At the end of the time of the great dissolution, this world was composed of darkness;
it was as if fast asleep, inconceivable, unknown, and devoid of defining characteristics.
The world—both the stationary and the moving—is unknowable and remains uncomprehended;
therefore, the Unmanifest Self-Existent One is the source of those who perform meritorious deeds.
Manifesting all this, the dispeller of darkness appeared—he who is beyond the senses, superior to the manifest, atomic yet greater than the great, and eternal;
known as Nārāyaṇa, he alone shone forth by himself. (Matsya Purāṇa 2.27)
He who, desiring to emit the manifold world, meditated upon his own body, first created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed.
That very [egg] became a vast cosmic egg composed of gold and silver,
possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns after a thousand years.
Having entered within, the self-born one of great splendor,
through his own power and by pervading that [universe], once again attained the state of Viṣṇu.
Within that, in ancient times, this Blessed One became the Sun;
and because he was the primordial being, Āditya became Brahmā while reciting the Veda.
He then made heaven and earth from the two halves of that egg;
he also created all the directions and the eternal sky in their midst.
At that time, Meru and the other principal mountains became its placenta (jarāyu),
while the mass of clouds, together with the circles of lightning, became the membrane (aulba) of the egg.
The rivers, as well as the Pitṛs and the Manus, were produced from the name of the egg (aṇḍa).
These seven oceans that exist also arise from within the waters;
they consist of salt, sugarcane juice, wine, and so forth, and are endowed with various jewels.
O subduer of enemies, that god Prajāpati became desirous of creating;
and from his splendor, Mārtaṇḍa was born there.
Because he was born from an egg that had died, he is remembered as Mārtaṇḍa;
that form of the Great-Souled One which consisted of the quality of rajas became the four-faced Lord, the Grandfather of the worlds.
Know that by whom this entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, was created—that great being is declared to be of the nature of *rajas*. (Matsya Purāṇa 2.37)
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 3:
Manu said: "Why did the Grandfather of the worlds attain the state of having four faces?"
But how did Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, create the worlds?
The Fish said:
First, the Grandfather of the immortals performed austerities;
then the Vedas appeared, along with their limbs (aṅgas), subsidiary limbs (upāṅgas), and the methods of recitation (padakrama).
In ancient times, Brahmā first remembered this Purāṇa, which is the foremost of all scriptures,
eternal, composed of sound, meritorious, and extending to a hundred crores of verses.
And immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths,
along with Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and the sciences, joined with the eight means of valid cognition (pramāṇas).
For him, who was devoted to the study of the Vedas and desirous of offspring, [the sons] were born from his mind;
because they were created by him from his mind (manas) as a prior creation, they are indeed called "Mānasas."
In the beginning there was Marīci; after him came the venerable sage Atri;
then Aṅgiras appeared, and immediately after that, Pulastya. (Matsya Purāṇa 3.6)
From him was born the one named Pulaha, and from him Kratu was born;
then Pracetas was his son, and Vasiṣṭha was born again.
In that same way, Bhṛgu became his son, and Nārada also appeared shortly thereafter;
Brahmā begot these ten sages as his mind-born sons.
Now I shall describe the physical [progeny] of Prajāpati, who was bereft of a mother:
from the right thumb, Dakṣa was born as Prajāpati.
From the space between her breasts Dharma emerged; from her heart the flower-weaponed god of love; from the middle of her brows arose Anger; and Greed was born from her lower lip.
From the intellect (buddhi) delusion arose; from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) pride was born;
from the throat came joy, O King, and death from the eyes.
Then Bharata, the son of Brahmā, emerged from the middle of the hand.
O King, these are the nine sons, and the tenth is a daughter;
she is renowned as Aṅgajā, the tenth daughter of Brahmā.

Manu said: Regarding that which was proclaimed—that delusion arose from the intellect (buddhi)—egoism (ahaṃkāra) and anger are recorded [as its products]; what, then, is called "intellect" (buddhi)? (Matsya Purāṇa 3.13)
The Fish said:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas).
The state of equilibrium among these is proclaimed as primordial nature (prakṛti). *Matsya Purāṇa* 3.14.
Some call it Pradhāna; others have sung of it as the Unmanifest (avyakta);
this very [principle] creates the progeny and transforms them.
From the qualities (guṇas) being agitated, three gods were born;
one single form divided into three portions: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
From the Pradhāna, which is subject to modification, the principle of Mahat is born;
it is called "Mahat" because from it the manifestation (khyāti) of the worlds always arises. (Matsya Purāṇa 3.17)
And from the Great Principle (mahat) arises ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), which increases pride;
from that, the five sense organs arise, which are under the control of the intellect (buddhi). Furthermore, other [organs] appear, which are under the control of action (karman). (Matsya Purāṇa 3.18)

The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose; and in due order, the anus, the generative organ, the hands and feet, and speech—this is the collection of the sense organs. (Matsya Purāṇa 3.19)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth are the [objects];
and excretion, pleasure, grasping, movement, and speech are their functions.
The mind is the eleventh among them, endowed with the qualities of action and intellect;
the wise consider its subtle sense-faculties to be its form.
Because the subtle elements (tanmātras) rest within it, the body is so designated;
and due to its union with the body, the individual soul (jīva) is also called "embodied" by the wise.
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings forth creation;
from the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), space (ākāśa) arose, whose nature consists of the quality of sound.
From the modification of space, wind arose, possessing the qualities of sound and touch;
and from the subtle element of touch within that wind, fire then manifested.

O King, through its transformation, that [subtle element] consisting of the three qualities became water, which possesses four qualities and is endowed with sound, touch, form, and taste, due to the modification of fire.
The earth, which consists primarily of the quality of taste, was produced from the subtle element of taste; however, it arose from the subtle element of smell and is endowed with five qualities.
That intellect (buddhi), which primarily possesses the quality of fragrance, is the most important;
the twenty-fifth principle, the Person (puruṣa), enjoys that which has been prepared by these [elements].
Even that individual soul (jīvātman) is said by the wise to be under the power of the Lord's will;
thus, in this human context, the body is declared to consist of twenty-six principles.
Sāṃkhya is so called because its nature consists of enumeration, and it is taught by Kapila and others;
having made this [system] the essence of reality, the Creator brought forth the world.
Having fixed the Sāvitrī in his heart for the purpose of creating the worlds, he remained steadfast;
then, as he was reciting it, she pierced through his stainless body.
He made one half female in form and the other half possessed the form of a man;
she is known as Śatarūpā and is also called Sāvitrī.
Then, O scorcher of foes, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, and Brahmāṇī likewise conceived their own daughters, born from their own bodies, as their offspring. (Matsya Purāṇa 3.32)
Upon seeing her, the Lord Prajāpati was distressed, struck by the arrows of desire, and exclaimed, "Oh, what beauty! Oh, what beauty! (Matsya Purāṇa 3.33).
Then those led by Vasiṣṭha cried out, "Sister!
But Brahmā saw nothing at all, except for the sight of her face.
"O, what beauty! O, what beauty! he said again and again;
then he gazed once more at her as she bowed low in salutation.
Then that woman of excellent complexion circumambulated her father,
desiring to behold his form as he felt ashamed before his sons.
Then a right face appeared there, with pale cheeks,
and subsequently a western face rose up, its lips quivering in wonder.
Afterwards, a fourth [face] appeared on his left, afflicted by the arrows of love;
then, due to that state of being tormented by desire, another [face] likewise arose for him.
As she was about to fly up, her form [was seen] due to the curiosity of looking;
by that [act], she performed most rigorous penance for the sake of creation.
All that perished through his desire for the union with his own daughter;
consequently, a fifth face appeared on that wise lord,
and the Lord covered that face with emerging matted locks.
Then Brahmā spoke to those sons born from his own self:
"Create offspring on all sides, including gods, asuras, and humans."
Having been addressed thus, they all then created various kinds of progeny;
and when they had departed for the sake of creation, [Brahmā beheld] this [Earth], bowed down in salutation.
The Soul of the Universe married the blameless Śatarūpā;
overcome by intense passion, the omnipresent Lord united with her.
The God, filled with modesty, dallied with her in the interior of a lotus-blossom palace.
For as long as a hundred divine years— as is the case for any other ordinary person—
after that, by the lapse of a great deal of time, Manu became her son.
He is known as Svāyambhuva; we have heard that he is called Virāj.
Because of the commonality of his form and qualities, he is designated as Adhipuruṣa.
There, the Vairājas were born— many of them who had praised their vows,
the highly fortunate sons of Svāyambhuva, seven groups of seven, and likewise others.
All those beginning with Svārociṣa were equal in nature to Brahmā;
likewise, those headed by Auttami, of whom you are now the seventh.
Matsya Purāṇa 4:
Manu said,
"O Lord, this arrival of your son is indeed most painful."
How did the Lotus-born One not incur any fault through this action?
O Lord, how did the mutual relationship of marriage come to exist among those of the same lineage?
Pray, sever my doubt regarding their offspring. (Matsya Purāṇa 4.2)
The Fish said:
This divine primordial creation arose from the quality of passion (rajas);
likewise, it possesses senses beyond the reach of the senses and bodies beyond the reach of the senses.
O King, she consists of divine splendor and arises from divine knowledge;
she cannot indeed be fully described by mortals with their eyes of flesh.
Just as serpents know the path of snakes, the sky of birds,
and the way of the divine ones— only those who are divine know it, not mere mortals.
For the gods do not bestow auspicious or inauspicious fruits based on what ought or ought not to be done;
therefore, O Indra among kings, it is not beneficial for men to deliberate upon that matter.
Furthermore, the four-faced Brahmā is the presiding deity of all the Vedas;
likewise, the Gāyatrī is declared to be his very limb.
They declare that pair to be either formless or embodied;
where the blessed Lord Viriñci is, there is the goddess Sarasvatī;
and wherever Bhāratī is, there indeed is Prajāpati.
Just as heat is never seen anywhere without its shadow,
even so Gāyatrī does not leave the side of Brahmā.
Brahmā is remembered as the mass of the Vedas, and Sāvitrī is established upon him;
therefore, O Lord, there would be no fault whatsoever in approaching Sāvitrī.
Nevertheless, in former times, Prajāpati Brahmā became bowed down with shame; because of his union with his own daughter, he cursed the flower-weaponed god of love.
"Since my mind has been agitated by you with your arrows through your act of overpowering me,
therefore Rudra shall soon reduce your body to ashes."
Then Kāmadeva propitiated the Four-faced One:
"O Giver of Honor, you ought not to curse me here without cause."
"O Four-faced One, I have been created by you in such a manner that I cause the agitation of the senses in all embodied beings. (Matsya Purāṇa 4.14)
"O Lord, you yourself previously stated that the mind of both women and men must always and everywhere be agitated with effort by me, without hesitation. (Matsya Purāṇa 4.15)
Therefore, O Lord, although I am innocent, I have been cursed by you in such a manner;
O Blessed One, grant me grace so that I may regain my own body once more.
Brahmā said:
When the Vaivasvata interval has arrived, there shall be a mortal named Rāma, born in the lineage of the Yādavas, who will rely upon my own essence and power. *Matsya Purāṇa* 4.17.
Having descended to earth, the destroyer of the Asuras will dwell in Dvārakā;
at that time, you shall become the son of his brother, who is equal to him.
Thus, having obtained a body and enjoyed all pleasures without exception,
he will then become the son of the king of Vatsa at the end of the Bharata dynasty.
Having attained sovereignty over the Vidyādharas and all manner of pleasures through righteousness until the dissolution of all beings, you shall come into my presence.
Thus, endowed with both curse and favor, the flower-weaponed god,
possessed of both grief and joy, departed as he had come.
Manu said:
Who was this one called Yadu, in whose lineage the birth of Kāma occurred?
And how was the flower-armed god [Kāma] burnt by Rudra? What then happened?
In the lineage of Bharata, who had what kind of progeny in ancient times?
Explain all of this from the very beginning, for I have a doubt. (Matsya Purāṇa 4.23)
The Fish said: She who was produced from half of his body, Gāyatrī, the expounder of Brahman; she who is the mother of Manu, the goddess Śatarūpā, possessed of a hundred faculties. *MatsP* 4.24.
Rati, Manas, Tapas, Buddhi, Mahat, Diś, and Sambhrama;
from her, Śatarūpā gave birth to these seven offspring.
Of those sons, Marīci and the others, who were the mind-born offspring of that wise one,
this world consisting of all knowledge belonged in ancient times.
Then he created Vāmadeva, who bears the excellent trident,
as well as the all-pervading Sanatkumāra, the progenitor even of the ancient ones.
The blessed Vāmadeva, however, created the twice-born from his mouth;
he created the kṣatriyas from his arms, and the vaiśyas and śūdras from his thighs and feet.
In the beginning, he created lightning, thunderbolts, clouds, red-hued flashes, and Indra’s rainbows; and after that, he created the Vedic meters and Parjanya.
Then the Lord of the hosts of those to be perfected (Sādhya-gaṇeśa) again created eighty-four crores of three-eyed beings who were free from old age and death.
Vāma created those immortals, but he was restrained by Brahmā:
"A creation such as this, devoid of old age and death, must not come to be. (Matsya Purāṇa 4.31)
That which consists of both the auspicious and the inauspicious is indeed praised as creation;
because he remained thus at the beginning of creation, he therefore became Sthāṇu (the Immovable).
The wise Svāyambhuva Manu, having performed very difficult austerities,
obtained as his wife one rich in beauty, known by the name Anantā.
Upon her, Manu begot Priyavrata and Uttānapāda;
and Dharmas daughter was the beautiful woman named Sūnṛtā. (Matsya Purāṇa 4.34)
From Uttānapāda, Mantharagāminī bore four sons:
Apasyati, Apasyant, Kīrtimant, and Dhruva.
In ancient times, Prajāpati Uttānapāda begot Dhruva upon Sūnṛtā after he had performed austerities for three thousand years.
Then, by the boon of Brahmā, he attained that divine and immovable station;
having placed Dhruva before him, the Seven Sages remain stationed there.
The maiden of Manu named Dhanyā gave birth to Śiṣṭa from Dhruva;
and Succhāyā, the daughter of Agni, bore sons to that Śiṣṭa.
That Ripuñjaya begot Kṛpa, Jaya, Vṛtta, Vṛka,
and Vṛkatejas upon Vīriṇī, the daughter of Brahmā.
Cakṣus begot Manu upon Vīraṇa’s daughter;
that Cākṣuṣa Manu was born of the royal maiden Naḍvalā.
Ūru begot ten heroic and sinless sons:
Pūru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk, and Havir.
Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, Sudyumna, and the unconquered Aparājita, with Abhimanyu as the tenth, were born of Naḍvalā. (Matsya Purāṇa 4.42)
From her thighs, the radiant Āgneyī gave birth to six sons:
Agni, Sumanas, Khyāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Gaya.
Sunīthā, the daughter of a Pitṛ, gave birth to Vena from Aṅga;
O Brahmins, they churned that unrighteous Vena,
and from his hand was born the one of great splendor named Pṛthu, who begot two sons.
Antardhāna begot Mārīca upon Śikhaṇḍinī.
From Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā, the daughter of Agni, gave birth to six sons:
Prācīnabarhis, Sāṅga, Yama, Śukra, Bala, and Śubha.
The venerable Prācīnabarhis was a great Prajāpati;
by him many Havirdhānas were brought forth as progeny.
Upon his wife Sāmudrī, who was of the same caste, the lord begot ten sons,
all of whom were named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery.
Protected by their ascetic power, the trees flourished everywhere in the world;
yet, at the command of the gods, O son of Ravi, Agni consumed them.
A daughter of Soma became his wife, renowned by the name Mārīṣā;
from them she gave birth to one son, Dakṣa, who was preeminent.
Immediately after Dakṣa, she gave birth to trees and all kinds of medicinal herbs,
as well as Soma’s daughter, the river Candravatī.
And of that Dakṣa, who was a portion of Soma, there were eighty crores [of daughters];
I shall describe their expansion as it is well-established in the world.
Some men had two feet, while others had many feet;
likewise, there were those with monkey-like faces, spike-eared ones, and those whose ears served as coverings for their heads.
Some had the faces of horses and bears, while others had the faces of lions; some had the faces of dogs and pigs, and others likewise had the faces of camels.
The righteous-souled Dakṣa produced all the various Mlecchas in great numbers;
having first created them by his mind, he subsequently begot women.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven, known as the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), to Soma;
from them, the entire world— including gods, asuras, humans, and others— came into being.
Matsya Purāṇa 5:
The sages said:
"Of the gods, the dānavas, the gandharvas, the uragas, and the rākṣasas..."
O Sūta, tell us in detail and exactly as it happened how [the world] originated.
Sūta said:
It is said that the creation of the ancestors occurred through volition, vision, and touch;
from Dakṣa Prācetasa onwards, creation arose from sexual union.
O twice-born ones, hear now exactly how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-existent One to "create progeny," performed that creation in the beginning.
But when the world did not attain growth through sexual union as he was creating the hosts of gods, sages, and serpents,
Dakṣa begot thousands of sons upon Pāñcajanī.
Seeing them assembled there, the illustrious Nārada, desiring to create various progeny, spoke to the Haryaśvas, the sons of Dakṣa.
"O best of sages, having ascertained everywhere the dimensions of the earth, both above and below, you may then proceed specifically with the work of creation."
Having heard those words of his, they departed in every direction;
even today they do not return, just as rivers do not return from the ocean.
When the Haryaśvas had perished,
the lord Prajāpati Dakṣa again begot a thousand sons by Vairiṇī alone.
Those Brahmins named Śabalas, who had assembled for the purpose of creation,
were addressed again by Nārada in the same manner as before.
Having ascertained the dimensions of the earth everywhere,
you shall then return and once again carry out creation in its various particulars.
They too then went by that very same path along which their brother had gone;
from that time forward, a younger brother who desires to follow his elder brother's path meets with suffering while searching for him; therefore, one should avoid such a course. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.11)
Then, after they had perished, Dakṣa, the Prajāpati born of the Pracetas, begot sixty daughters upon Vairiṇī.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two were given to the son of Bhṛgu, two to the wise Kṛśāśva, and likewise two to Aṅgiras; their names [shall be told] in detail.
Listen to the expansion of the progeny of the divine mothers from the beginning:
Marutvatī, Vasu, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, and Arundhatī. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.15)
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā—the beautiful Bhāminī—were declared to be the lawful wives [of Dakṣa]. Learn now of their sons. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.16)
From Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas;
from Marutvatī came the Marutvats, and likewise the Vasus from Vasu. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.17)
From Bhānu came the Bhānus; likewise, from Muhūrtā came the Muhūrtakas;
from Lambā came those named Ghoṣas; and Nāgavīthī was born from Yāmī.
Arundhatī was born from the surface of the earth;
Saṃkalpa was born of Saṃkalpā. Now learn of the creation of the Vasus.
Those radiant gods who pervade all directions are known as the Vasus;
learn now of their creation. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.20)
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.21)
The four sons of Āpa were Śānta, Daṇḍa, Śāmba, and Maṇivaktra; they were the officials in charge of protecting the sacrifice.
Kāla was the son of Dhruva, and Varcas was born from Soma;
Draviṇa and Havyavāha are both remembered as the two sons of Dharma. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.23)
Then Kalyāṇinī bore Prāṇa, Ramaṇa, and Śiśira;

Śivā likewise obtained from Anala two sons, Manojava and Avijñātagati, who possessed qualities almost equal to those of fire.
The son of Agni, Kumāra, was born in a thicket of reeds;
Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya were his younger brothers.
The offspring of the Kṛttikās is known as Kārttikeya;
the son of Pratyūṣa was the sage Vibhu, also named Devala;
and Viśvakarman, the Prajāpati and master craftsman, was the son of Prabhāsa.
He is remembered as the divine architect (Amaravardhaki) in relation to palaces, mansions, gardens, statues, ornaments, and the like, as well as tanks, groves, and wells.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, Raivata, Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Sureśvara; (Matsya Purāṇa 5.29).
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita—these are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the lords of the hosts. (Matsya Purāṇa 5.30)
The sons of these mind-born ones, who bear the excellent trident,
are considered to be eighty-four crores and are imperishable.
Those lords of the Gaṇas who provide protection in all directions,
along with their sons, grandsons, and daughters, are born from the womb of Surabhi.
In the sixth chapter of the Matsya Purāṇa, it is said: "I shall proclaim the sons and grandsons born to Kaśyapa from his wives:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, and likewise Surasā. (MatsP 6.1)
Surabhi, Vinatā, likewise Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, Viśvā, and Muni—learn now of their sons. (Matsya Purāṇa 6.2)
Those gods known as the Tuṣitas who existed during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu are remembered as these twelve Ādityas in the interval of Vaivasvata.
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Yama, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumat, and Viṣṇu as well; Matsya Purāṇa 6.4.
These twelve Ādityas, the thousand-rayed ones,
are remembered as the most excellent sons whom Aditi bore to Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
The sons of the sage Bhṛśāśva are remembered as the divine weapons;
O Brahmins, these are the hosts of gods throughout the various Manvantaras.
In every kalpa they arise and likewise dissolve;
thus we have heard that Diti obtained two sons from Kaśyapa.
Hiraṇyakaśipu and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa;
and from Hiraṇyakaśipu, four sons were likewise born.
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Saṃhlāda, and Hlāda;
and the long-lived son of Prahlāda, Śibi, and Bāṣkala.
Virocana was the fourth, and he obtained Bali as his son;
O twice-born ones, Bali had a hundred sons, of whom Bāṇa was the eldest.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Candra, Candrāṃśutāpana,
Nikumbhanābha, Gurvakṣa, Kukṣibhīma, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
There were many such [sons] as these, with Bāṇa as the eldest, all superior in virtue;
and there was Bāṇa, the thousand-armed, endowed with the entire collection of divine weapons.
In whose city the wielder of the trident dwells, gratified by his asceticism,
and who attained the state of Mahākāla, equal to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Hiraṇyākṣa had sons named Ulūka, Śakuni,
Bhūtasaṃtāpana, and likewise Mahānābha.
From these [ancestors], seventy-seven crores of sons and grandsons were born—
possessing great strength, massive bodies, diverse forms, and immense splendor.
Danu obtained from Kaśyapa a hundred sons, arrogant in their strength;
among them, the exceedingly powerful Vipracitti was the chief.
Dvimūrdhan and Śakuni, as well as Śaṅkuśirodhara, Ayomukha, Śambara, and likewise the one named Kapiśa. (Matsya Purāṇa 6.17)
Mārīci, Meghavān, Irā, Garbhaśiras,
Vidrāvaṇa, Ketu, Ketuvīrya, and Śatahrada.
Indrajit, Saptajit, and likewise Vajranābha; Ekacakra, Mahābāhu, Vajrākṣa, and Tāraka as well.
Asiloman, Puloman, Bindu, Bāṇa the great Asura,
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and others such as these were the sons of Danu.
Svarbhānu’s daughters were Prabhā and Śacī, the daughter of Puloman; likewise, Upadānavī was the daughter of Maya, as were Mandodarī and Kuhū.
Śarmiṣṭhā, Sundarī, and Candrā were the daughters of Vṛṣaparvan;
Pulomā and Kālakā were indeed the two daughters of Vaiśvānara.
In former times, there were sixty thousand Dānavas born to those two— Mahāsattva and Mārīca— who had many offspring and were husband and wife.
In ancient times, Mārīca begot the Paulomas and Kālakeyas,
who were indeed incapable of being slain by the immortals and resided in Hiraṇyapura.
Having obtained boons from the Four-faced One (Brahmā), they were slain by Vijaya;
Vipracitti, however, begot the Saiṃhikeyas upon Siṃhikā.
O Indra among kings, Hiraṇyakaśipu had thirteen nephews:
Vyaṃsa, Kalpa, Nala, and Vātāpi.
Ilvala and Namuci, Śvasṛpa and likewise Ajana, Naraka and Kālanābha, and also Saramāṇa.
Kālavīrya was renowned as the progenitor who increased the lineage of Danu;
the Nivātakavacas are recorded as the sons of the Daitya Saṃhrāda.
Those who were invincible to all the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, having taken refuge in Bharga, were slain by Arjuna on the field of battle. (Matsya Purāṇa 6.29)
Tāmrā gave birth to six daughters from the seed of Mārīca:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Gṛdhrikā, and Śuci.
Śukī gave birth to parrots and owls according to dharma;
likewise, Śyenī gave birth to hawks, and Bhāsī gave birth to ospreys.
Gṛdhrī gave birth to vultures, pigeons, doves, and other birds, as well as swans, cranes, curlews, and water-fowls. (Matsya Purāṇa 6.32)
Sugrīvī gave birth to goats, horses, rams, camels, and donkeys;
this lineage of Tāmra has been declared—now learn that which pertains to Vinatā.
Garuḍa is the lord of winged creatures, as is Aruṇa;
likewise, there is this daughter, Saudāmanī, who is renowned in the sky.
Both Sampāti and Jaṭāyu were the two sons of Aruṇa;
and Babhru, as well as the renowned Śīghraga, were the sons of Sampāti.
Jaṭāyuṣa’s sons were the renowned Karṇikāra, Śatagāmin, Sārasa, Rajjuvāla, and Bheruṇḍa. (Matsya Purāṇa 6.36)
The offspring of those birds—sons and grandsons—became infinite;
formerly, there were a thousand serpents born of Surasā.
O observer of noble vows, Kadrū had a thousand sons with a thousand heads;
among them, O subduer of enemies, twenty-six were renowned as the principal ones.
Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Śaṅkha, Airāvata, Kambala, Dhanañjaya, Mahānīla, Padma, Aśvatara, and Takṣaka. (Matsya Purāṇa 6.39)
Elāpattra, Mahāpadma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Balāhaka, Śaṅkhapāla, Mahāśaṅkha, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, and Śubhānana; // MatsP_6.40 //
Śaṅkuroma, Bahula, Vāmana,
Pāṇini, Kapila, Durmukha, and also Patañjali are remembered [as such].
The offspring of all these [snakes] became infinite;
for the most part, those who had previously been burnt in the palace of Janamejaya were reborn.
Krodhavaśā gave birth to a host of Rākṣasas named after herself;
a million of those fanged creatures met their destruction at the hands of Bhīmasena.
In the same way, Surabhi, who was firm in her vows, gave birth from Kaśyapa to the host of Rudras, as well as to cows, buffaloes, and excellent women.
The sage Ariṣṭā gave birth to many sages, as well as a multitude of Apsarases,
and likewise many Kinnaras and Gandharvas.
Irā gave birth to all grasses, trees, creepers, and shrubs;
Viśvā, however, produced Yakṣas and Rākṣasas by the millions.
Then Diti, the beloved of the immortals, gave birth to forty-nine Maruts from Kaśyapa; they were knowers of dharma and dear to all the gods.
Matsya Purāṇa 7:
The Sages said:
"How were the Maruts, the beloved sons of Diti, born?"
And why did they attain such supreme friendship with the gods, who were their rivals?
Sūta said:
Long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, when her sons and grandsons had been slain by Hari, she, afflicted with grief, went to the excellent world of mortals. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.2)
In the sacred field of Syamantapañcaka, on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī,
she performed severe penance, devoted solely to the propitiation of her husband.
Then Diti, the mother of the Daityas, being of virtuous vows, performed severe penance in the form of a seer,
subsisting on fruits and practicing the Cāndrāyaṇa and other austerities.
For more than a hundred years she remained overwhelmed by old age and grief;
then, having been tormented by her ascetic penance, she questioned Vasiṣṭha and the others.
"May you, sirs, tell me of a vow that destroys grief for one's son and bestows the fruit of good fortune both in this world and in the next."
Vasiṣṭha and the other sages spoke of the Madanadvādaśī vow, by the power of which she became free from grief for her son. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.7)
The sages said:
"O Sūta, we wish to hear about the Madanadvādaśī vow,
by which Diti obtained forty-nine sons once again."
Sūta said:
"That which was previously told by Vasiṣṭha and others concerning Diti in its excellent detail— learn that very same thing from me."
In the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth day,
one who is firm in his vows should place an unblemished jar filled with white rice.
Likewise, it should be provided with various fruits and accompanied by stalks of sugarcane;
it is covered with a pair of white cloths and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
One should place a copper vessel filled with various kinds of food and accompanied by gold according to one's means, along with molasses, upon that [image].
Above that, one should place a mango fruit resting upon a plantain leaf;
and to its left, one should place a piece of sugar.
Then one should offer incense and perfume, and cause songs and instrumental music to be performed;
in their absence, a man should tell stories of Kāma and Keśava.
One should bathe the image of Hari with fragrant water under the name "Kāma," and worship Madhusūdana with white flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.15)
Having worshipped the feet with the mantra "To Kāma," the shanks with "To Saubhāgyada," the thighs with "To Smara," and again the hips with "To Manmatha."
"To the one with a pure belly," [he worships] the belly of Hari; "To the bodiless one," the chest;
"To the lotus-faced one," the face; and "To the five-arrowed one," the arms.
"Salutation to the Soul of All"—with these words, one should worship Keśava on the crown [of the head].
Then, at dawn, one should present that water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.18)
One should devoutly feed the Brahmins while abstaining from salt oneself;
having eaten, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and recite this mantra: MatsP_7.19.
May the Blessed One Janārdana, who can assume any form at will and who is designated as the bliss within the hearts of all beings, be pleased with this.
By this procedure, one should perform the entire vow month after month;
fasting on the thirteenth day, one should worship the immutable Viṣṇu.
Having consumed a single fruit on the twelfth day, he should sleep upon the ground;
then, in the thirteenth month, [he should give] a cow together with a vessel of clarified butter.
One should give a bed equipped with all necessary furnishings to Anaṅga,
as well as a golden image of Kāmadeva and a white, milk-yielding cow.

Having honored a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments according to one's means, one should offer a bed, perfumes, and other such items, and utter the words: "May [the deity] be pleased. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.24)

The knower of dharma should perform the *homa* with white sesame seeds while reciting the names of the desired objects; likewise, he should do so with cow-derived sacrificial butter and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). (Matsya Purāṇa 7.25)
One should give food to the Brahmins, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
furthermore, one should give stalks of sugarcane and flower garlands according to one's ability. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.26)
Whoever performs this Madanadvādaśī according to this rite, being liberated from all sins, attains equality with Hari. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.27)
In this world, he enjoys excellent sons as the fruit of his good fortune—
he who has called to mind Smara, Viṣṇu, the blissful Self, the Great Lord.
"One who desires happiness should meditate upon the Lord, the progenitor of the body, in the form of Kāma.
Having heard this, Diti performed everything exactly as instructed.
Due to the greatness of her vow, Kaśyapa returned with supreme joy and once again made Karkaśā endowed with beauty and youth.
He invited her to choose boons; she then chose this boon:
a son of immeasurable splendor, capable of slaying Śakra.
"I choose the high-souled one, the destroyer of all the immortals," said Kaśyapa, addressing the powerful slayer of Indra with these words.
"I myself shall grant this here; however, O auspicious one, let this be done:
O lady of virtuous vows, let Āpastamba perform today the sacrifice for obtaining a son."
"Therefore, I shall conceive a fetus that will be the destroyer of Indra's enemy.
Then Āpastamba performed a sacrifice for the sake of a son, abounding in wealth.
And he offered oblations extensively, saying, "Become one whose enemy is Indra!
The gods rejoiced, while the Daityas and Dānavas turned their faces away in defeat.
Kaśyapa then deposited the embryo in Diti; he spoke to her again:
"O lady of beautiful countenance, you must indeed exert effort regarding this embryo."
O woman of excellent complexion, for one hundred years in this very forest of asceticism, you must not eat while pregnant, even when counting the days.
One should never remain nor travel at the roots of trees;
one should not sit upon household utensils, such as the pestle, the mortar, and so forth.
One should not plunge into water, one should avoid an empty house, one should not stand upon an anthill, nor should one become agitated in mind. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.39)
One should not scratch the ground with one's nails, nor with charcoal or ashes;
one should not remain constantly prone to sleep, and one should avoid excessive physical exertion.
One should not enter into husks, charcoal, ashes, bones, or skulls;
one should likewise avoid quarreling with people and the stretching of limbs.
One should not remain with disheveled hair, nor should one ever be impure;
one should never sleep with the head pointing north or west.
She should not be without clothing, nor agitated, nor have wet feet; she should not utter inauspicious speech, nor should she be excessively given to laughter.
She should constantly perform service to her husband, remaining intent on auspiciousness;
she should bathe with all medicinal herbs and with lukewarm water. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.44)
Having performed her protective rites and being well-adorned, she should remain intent on the worship of the site,
with a cheerful countenance, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband.
A woman who is charitable and virtuous should observe the *pārvaṇa* fast on the third lunar day, eating only at night;
this is the conduct for a woman, especially for one who is pregnant. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.46)
The son who may be born of her shall be endowed with increase in virtue and longevity;
otherwise, there is no doubt that she will suffer a miscarriage.
"Therefore, by this means, exert yourself toward this embryo.
May it be well with you; I shall depart. Thus addressed again by her, he replied, "So be it."
While all beings were looking on, she vanished right there;
thereafter, she established herself according to the ritual prescribed by Kaśyapa.
Then Indra, likewise terrified, approached the side of Diti;
having abandoned his celestial abode, he remained there, intent on serving her.
Seeking a vulnerability within Diti,
the subduer of Pāka became outwardly humble, composed, and possessed a serene countenance.
Not knowing that such an act was for his own welfare, he performed it;
consequently, at the end of a hundred years, it fell short by three days. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.52)
With a mind astonished by joy, she considered herself to have achieved her purpose;
without washing her feet, she fell asleep with her hair disheveled.
Overcome by the weight of sleep, with his head toward the west during the day, he lay somewhere;
then, finding an opportunity, the Lord of Śacī entered.
The lord of the thirty gods split that embryo into seven parts with his vajra;
from that, seven boys were born, possessing the brilliance of the sun.
Those seven boys, weeping, were restrained by the mountain-splitter;
yet as they wept once more, Hari split each one of them into seven pieces.
The slayer of Vṛtra indeed cut them again while remaining within that belly;
thus having become forty-nine, they wept bitterly.
Indra restrained me as I wept again and again;
thereupon the slayer of Vṛtra reflected, "What is this? (Matsya Purāṇa 7.58).
"By the greatness of which dharma have these been restored to life?
Having understood through the yoga of meditation the fruit of Madanadvādaśī," [he asked].
Surely this is now the fruition of the worship of Kṛṣṇa;
even when struck by a thunderbolt, they shall not meet with destruction.
"Since even a single one has attained multiplicity, and since they are fully capable of entering the belly [of Viṣṇu], these gods must surely be invulnerable; let them be so. (Matsya Purāṇa 7.61)
"Since you were told 'Do not weep' while staying within the womb yet continued to cry,
let those who are named Maruts become sharers in the sacrifice by that name."
Then the Lord of Gods, having propitiated Diti once more with the words "Forgive me," said:
"Adopting the principles of the science of statecraft (Arthaśāstra), this evil deed was committed by me."
Having made the host of Maruts equal to the gods, the lord of the immortals placed Diti along with her sons upon a celestial chariot and led them to heaven.
O twice-born ones, the Maruts were born from that [act] as partakers of sacrificial portions;
therefore, they did not reach unity with the Asuras, and thus they became beloved by the gods.
Matsya Purāṇa 8: The Sages said: "O Sūta, the primary creation which was described by you in detail—"
Tell us also of the secondary creations and who their respective presiding lords were.
Sūta said:
When Pṛthu was consecrated as the sovereign of the entire earth and became its ruler,
he then appointed the Moon as the lord of medicinal herbs, of sacrificial vows, and of ascetic penances.
He was the golden womb of the constellations, stars, twice-born, trees, shrubs, creepers, and their canopies;
likewise, he was Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, and Vaiśravaṇa, the sovereign of wealth and kings.
He made Viṣṇu the lord of the Ravis, Agni the lord of the Vasus,
Dakṣa the sovereign of the Prajāpatis, and Śakra the ruler of the Maruts.
Then [he appointed] Prahlāda as the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas, Yama as the lord of the Pitṛs,
and Śūlapāṇi as the king of the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Paśus, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, and Vetālas.
And he made the Snowy Mountain the lord of mountains, the ocean the lord of rivers and streams,
and Citraratha the lord of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kiṃnaras.
He appointed Vāsuki, the lord of nāgas of fierce prowess, as the sovereign of serpents,
and he made Takṣaka the lord of the elephants of the quarters, the great elephant named Airāvata.
He made Suparṇa the lord of winged creatures, and Uccaiḥśravas the king of horses;
he made the lion the king of beasts, the bull the king of cattle, and the Plakṣa tree the king of all forest trees.
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā) consecrated them once more as the lords of all the quarters;
he first consecrated the guardian of the eastern quarter by the name Sudharmā, the banner of his enemies.
Then the Lord, the sovereign of all, who is the womb of the cosmic egg, placed Śaṅkhapada, known as the name of the Lord of All, as the guardian of the south;
and he made Ketumān the lord of the western direction. (Matsya Purāṇa 8.10)
Prajāpati made Hiraṇyaroman the lord of the northern quarter, the son of a god;
even today, the lords of the quarters, burning their enemies, continue to protect the earth.
By these four, the king named Pṛthu was first consecrated on earth;
when the period known as Cākṣuṣa had passed and the one called Vaivasvata had begun again,
he became the lord of this world of moving and unmoving beings, the emblem of the lineage of the Solar dynasty.
Matsya Purāṇa 9: Sūta said:
Having heard this, Manu spoke again to Janārdana.
O Madhusūdana, tell me of the deeds of the former Manus.
The Fish said: O Indra among kings, [I shall describe] the Manvantaras, the life-stories of the Manus, the measure of time, and that creation in brief. *Matsya Purāṇa* 9.2.
Listen with a single mind and a tranquil soul, O son of Mārtaṇḍa:
in former times, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there were gods known as the Yāmas.
The seven sages of former times who are remembered as Marīci and the others, as well as Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Saha, and Savana; Matsya Purāṇa 9.4.
Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havya, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu—these ten were the progenitors of the lineage of this Svāyambhuva Manu. (Matsya Purāṇa 9.5)
Having performed these secondary creations at each dissolution, they departed for the supreme state.
This has been declared as the Svāyambhuva period; after this follows the Svārociṣa.
The four sons of Svārociṣa were equal in splendor to the gods:
Nabha, Nabhasya, Prasṛti, and Bhānu; they were increasers of his fame.
Datta, Niścyavana, Stamba, Prāṇa, Kaśyapa,
Aurva, and Bṛhaspati— these seven are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis).

While digging the earth in search of the horse, they were consumed by fire by Viṣṇu;
their son was Asamañjasa, who was renowned by the name Aṃśumat.
His son was Dilīpa; from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha, by whom the Gaṅgā, known as Bhāgīrathī, was brought down after performing austerities.
The son of Bhagīratha was renowned as Nābhāga;
from Nābhāga came Ambarīṣa, and from him was born Sindhudvīpa.
Tasya had a son named Ayutāyu; from him was born Ṛtuparṇa.
His son was Kalmāṣapāda, and from him Sarvakarman is remembered.
Anaraṇya was his son, and Nighna was his son;
both Anamitra and Raghu were born as kings from the two sons of Nighna.
Having performed that rite, the king became Anamitra and retired to the forest;
from Raghu was born Dilīpa, and likewise from Dilīpa was born Aja.
From Aja was born Dīrghabāhu, and from him came King Ajapāla;
from him was born Daśaratha, who had four sons.
All of them were of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, and among them Rāma was the eldest;
likewise, he was the destroyer of Rāvaṇa and the increaser of the lineage of the Raghus.
Vālmīki, the best of the Bhṛgus, composed his life story;
his two sons were Kuśa and Lava, who increased the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha was his son;
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and from him Nabha was born. (Matsya Purāṇa 12.52)
From Nabhas was born Puṇḍarīka, from whom Kṣemadhanvan is said to have descended;
his son was the heroic and powerful Devānīka.
The son of Ahīnagu was Sahasrāśva;
after him came Candrāvaloka, and from him Tārāpīḍa was born. (Matsya Purāṇa 12.54)
His son was Candragiri; from him came Bhānu, and from him Śrutāyu was born, who was slain in the Bhārata war.
In the lineage born of Kaśyapa, two Nalas alone became renowned:
likewise, the son of Vīrasena and the lord of men, the Naiṣadha.
These kings, who gave profuse sacrificial fees,
born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, have been proclaimed primarily in the dynasty of Vaivasvata.
Matsya Purāṇa 13:
Manu said,
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the supreme lineage of the ancestors."
And the status of being the deity of the śrāddha belongs to Ravi and especially to Soma. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.1)
Matsya said:
"Behold, I shall describe to you the supreme lineage of the ancestors.
In heaven there are seven groups of ancestors; three of them are formless."
Then there were four embodied ones, all of immeasurable splendor,
who were the formless hosts of ancestors belonging to the progenitor Vairāja.
Victorious are those hosts of gods known as the Vairājas,
and those who, having fallen from yoga, have attained the eternal worlds.
Furthermore, at the end of Brahmā’s day, those who expound the Veda are born again,
having regained that memory as well as the unsurpassed Yoga and Sāṃkhya.
Through yoga, they attain perfection from which rebirth is difficult to encounter;
therefore, those who give śrāddha offerings should bestow them only upon yogins. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.6)
The daughter of these [mountains] was considered the wife of Himavat;
Maināka was his heir, and Krauñca was his elder brother.
By Krauñca, the fourth island, Krauñcadvīpa, is remembered as being surrounded by clarified butter.
Then Menā gave birth to three daughters who were endowed with yoga:
Umā, Ekaparṇā, and Aparṇā, all of whom were devoted to rigorous vows.
One was given to Rudra, one to Śitikaṇṭha, and another to Jaigīṣavya;
all these young women were superior in asceticism in the world, having been bestowed by Himavān.
The sages said:
Why did the daughter of Dakṣa formerly burn herself by her own hand?
Likewise, how was the daughter of Himavat born upon the surface of the earth? (Matsya Purāṇa 13.10)
O Sūta, tell me in detail: what was said by the son of Brahmā, Dakṣa, to that daughter, the mother of the worlds, as she was withdrawing [herself]?
Sūta said:
When the sacrifice of Dakṣa had been prepared, with abundant gifts being distributed and the gods having been invited, Satī spoke to her father. *Matsya Purāṇa* 13.12.
"Father, for what reason was my husband not consecrated in this sacrifice?
To her, Dakṣa replied at the sacrifice: "The wielder of the trident [Śiva] is unfit for sacrifices. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.13)
"Since Rudra has acted as the bringer of this end, he shall therefore partake of inauspiciousness.
Then Satī became enraged, saying, "I shall cast off my body, which was born from you. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.14)
"You shall be the sole son of ten fathers;
and in your status as a Kṣatriya, you will meet your destruction through Rudra at the Aśvamedha sacrifice."
Having spoken thus and having resorted to yoga,
she then consumed herself with the splendor arising from her own body, while the gods, asuras, and kinnaras looked on.
"What is this? What is this? asked the hosts of Gandharvas and Guhyakas.
Then Dakṣa, approaching and bowing down in distress, spoke.
O Goddess, you are the mother of this world and the deity who bestows prosperity upon it;
out of a desire to show me favor, you have become my daughter.
"Nothing in the cosmic egg, including the moving and the unmoving, exists apart from you.
Show favor, O knower of dharma; you ought not to abandon me here."
The Goddess said: "Whatever has been undertaken must be accomplished by me; there is no doubt of this.
However, you, O wielder of the trident, must necessarily slay the sacrificer in the mortal world."
"For the sake of the creation of the world, you must perform penance in my presence with a serene mind;
you shall become a Prajāpati, fully capable of producing ten offspring."
"By a portion of myself, sixty women shall be born from your body;
performing penance in my presence, you shall attain supreme yoga. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.22)
Thus addressed, Dakṣa said: "O sinless one, at which various holy sites (tīrthas) am I to be seen by you, and by what names am I to be praised? (Matsya Purāṇa 13.23)
The Goddess said: "She is to be seen at all times among all beings everywhere on earth;
in all worlds, whatever exists is not devoid of me."
Nevertheless, I shall describe in accordance with reality those places where success is to be sought by those desiring accomplishment, or which are to be remembered by those desiring prosperity.
In Vārāṇasī she is Viśālākṣī; in Naimiṣa, Liṅgadhāriṇī; at Prayāga, the goddess Lalitā; at Gandhamādana, Kāmākṣī;
in Mānasa, she is named Kumudā; and likewise, Viśvakāyā in the sky. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.26)
In Gomanta she is named Gomatī; on Mount Mandara she is Kāmacāriṇī;
in Caitraratha she is Madotkaṭā; and in Hastināpura she is Jayantī. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.27)
Likewise, they know Gaurī to be in Kānyakubja, Rambhā on the Malaya mountain, Kīrtimatī in Ekāmbhaka, and Viśvā in Viśveśvara. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.28)
At Puṣkara she is Puruhūtā, at Kedāra she is Mārgadāyinī;
Nandā is on the ridge of the Himavat, and Bhadrakarṇikā is at Gokarṇa.
Bhavānī is at Sthāneśvara, Bilvapattrikā at Bilvala, Mādhavī by name at Śrīśaila, and likewise Bhadrā at Bhadreśvara. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.30)
Jayā is on Varāhaśaila, Kamalā in the abode of Kamala (the lotus), Rudrāṇī at Rudrakoṭi, and Kālī on Mount Kālañjara. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.31)
In Mahāliṅga she is Kapilā; in Markoṭa, Mukuṭeśvarī;
in Śālagrāma, Mahādevī; and in the Śivaliṅga, Jalapriyā. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.32)
In Māyāpurī she was Kumārī, likewise Lalitā in Saṃtāna;
she was Utpalākṣī in Sahasrākṣa and Mahotpalā in Kamalākṣa.
On the Gaṅgā she is named Maṅgalā; on the Puruṣottama, Vimilā; on the Vipāśā, Amoghākṣī; and on the Pāṭalā at Puṇḍravardhana.
Nārāyaṇī is on Supārśva, Bhadrasundarī on Vikūṭa; on Vipula she is named Vipulā, and on the Malaya mountain she is Kalyāṇī.
Koṭavī is at Koṭitīrtha, Sugandhā in the Mādhava forest, Trisaṃdhyā at Godāśrama, and Ratipriyā at Gaṅgādvāra. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.36)
Śivānandā is at Śivakuṇḍa, Nandinī on the bank of the Devikā, Rukmiṇī at Dvāravatī, and Rādhā in the forest of Vṛndāvana. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.37)
Devakī is in Mathurā, while Parameśvarī is in Pātāla;
likewise, Sītā is at Citrakūṭa, and Vindhyādhivāsinī is on the Vindhya mountains.
Ekavīrā was on the Sahya mountain, Candrikā in Hariścandra, Ramaṇā at Rāmatīrtha, and Mṛgāvatī on the Yamunā. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.39)
Mahālakṣmī is at Karavīra, the goddess Umā is at Vināyaka, Aroga is at Vaidyanātha, and Maheśvarī is at Mahākāla. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.40)
Abhayā is in the Uṣṇa tīrthas, Amṛtā is in the cave of the Vindhya, Māṇḍavī by name is in Māṇḍavya, and Svāhā is in the city of Māheśvara. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.41)
Pracaṇḍā is at Chāgalāṇḍa, Caṇḍikā at Makarandaka, Varārohā at Someśvara, and Puṣkarāvatī at Prabhāsa. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.42)
Devamātā is honored at the Sarasvatī, on the banks of the Pārāvāra;
the highly fortunate Mahābhāgā is at Mahālaya, and Piṅgaleśvarī is at the Payoṣṇī. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.43)
Siṃhikā is auspicious when the purification rites have been performed; Yaśaskarī is at Kārttikeya; Lolā is at Utpalāvartaka; and Subhadrā is at the confluence of the Śoṇa.
She is Lakṣmī in Siddhapura, Aṅganā in the hermitage of Bharata, Viśvamukhī in Jālandhara, and Tārā on Mount Kiṣkindha. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.45)
Puṣṭi is in the Devadāru forest, Medhā in the region of Kaśmīra,
Bhīmā the Goddess on the Himālaya, and likewise Puṣṭi at Viśveśvara.
At Kapālamocana there is purification; at Kāyāvarohaṇa, one's mother;
at Śaṅkhoddhāra, the sound named Dhvani; and likewise at Piṇḍāraka, Dhṛti.
Kālā is in the Candrabhāgā, Śivakāriṇī in the Acchoda, Amṛtā by name in the Veṇā, and likewise Urvaśī in the Badarī.
Oṣadhī is in Uttarakuru, Kuśodakā in Kuśadvīpa,
Manmathā on Hemakūṭa, and Satyavādinī on Mukuṭa.
She is to be worshipped in the Aśvattha tree, she is indeed the treasure in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
she is Gāyatrī at the mouth of the Veda, and Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva.
In the world of the gods she is Indrāṇī; in the mouths of Brahmās she is Sarasvatī;
in the orb of the sun she is named Prabhā; and among the Mothers she is considered to be Vaiṣṇavī.
Among virtuous women, Arundhatī is the foremost; among beautiful women, Tilottamā;
and in the hearts of all embodied beings, the power named Brahmakalā resides.
This supreme list of one hundred and eight names has been declared by way of summary;
this is also proclaimed as the one hundred and eight sacred fords (tīrthas). (Matsya Purāṇa 13.53)
Whoever should remember or even hear [this], is liberated from all sins;
that man who, having bathed in these sacred fords, beholds me.
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall dwell in the city of Śiva for a kalpa—
that man who spends his final moments among these [holy places] while intent upon me.
He who causes the eight hundred names to be heard in the presence of Śiva pierces through the abode of Brahmā and attains the station of Śaṅkara. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.56)
On the third or the eighth lunar day, a wise man becomes the father of many sons,
whether by giving gifts of cows or by performing ancestral rites (śrāddha) on every single day.
"By reciting this during the ritual of worshipping the gods, a learned man attains Brahman. Speaking thus, she there consumed herself by her own self.
In the course of time, Svāyambhuva Dakṣa became Prācetasa;
and the goddess Pārvatī became the bearer of half of Śiva’s body.
Born from the womb of Menā, Arundhatī—who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—attained the unsurpassed yoga by reciting this. (Matsya Purāṇa 13.60)
And Purūravas attained distinction in the world of royal sages;
Yayāti obtained the gain of sons, and Bhārgava the gain of wealth.
Likewise, other gods and daityas, as well as many brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas,
and śūdras, attained their desired perfection.
Wherever this remains written and is worshipped in the presence of the deity,
neither sorrow nor misfortune shall ever arise there.
Matsya Purāṇa 14: Sūta said:
There are worlds named Somapatha, where the sons of Mārīca dwell.
O God, the ancestors exist as gods, whom the gods fully sustain.
Where the sacrificers known as the Agniṣvāttas reside,
there is a river named Acchodā, who is their mind-born daughter.
And there is a lake named Acchoda, created by the ancestors in ancient times;
Acchodā performed divine austerities there for a thousand years.
The ancestors, being pleased, indeed arrived to bestow that boon;
they all assumed divine forms, adorned with celestial garlands and unguents.
All were young, powerful, and resembled the god whose weapon is the flower;
seeing her father named Amāvasu in their midst, she [was filled with longing] along with her female companions.
Afflicted by the god whose weapon is the flower and seeking a boon, that passionate woman chose union with him;
however, she fell from her yoga through that act of infidelity.
He did not touch the earth before; then he fell upon the surface of the ground on that lunar day (tithi) which was the new moon (amāvāsyā), against which he had formed no desire.
Because of his fortitude, she became renowned among the worlds as Amāvāsyā;
therefore, she is beloved by the ancestors, and [an offering] made on that day brings inexhaustible merit.
With her face cast downward, dejected and ashamed due to the depletion of her ascetic merit,
she entreated the ancestors in the city for the sake of restoring her own renown.
While she was lamenting with her parents, that ascetic woman was then addressed as follows, having foreseen the future purpose and your divine mission: MatsP_14.10.
The highly fortunate ones spoke these words with voices auspicious through their grace:
"Whatever is performed by the wise in heaven with a divine body," *Matsya Purāṇa* 14.11.
O woman of excellent complexion, that very person experiences the fruit of that karma;
actions bear fruit immediately in the state of divinity, and after death in the human state.
Therefore, my daughter, you shall obtain the fruit of your asceticism after death;
in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you will be born from the womb of a fish.
"Due to your transgression against the ancestors, you shall obtain a miserable lineage;
therefore, you will inevitably become the daughter of King Vasu."
Having become a maiden, you shall again attain your own worlds, which are difficult to reach;
and by the power of Parāśara, you shall obtain one son.
On the island abounding in jujube trees (Badarī), your son shall divide the single Veda into many parts for the infallible Bādarāyaṇa.
Śaṃtanu, the son of Samudrāṃśa and descendant of Puru, had two sons:
Vicitravīrya and King Citrāṅgada. (Matsya Purāṇa 14.17)
"Having given birth to these two sons as the *kṣetraja* offspring of that wise man,
you shall become the form of the *prauṣṭhapadī-aṣṭakā* in the world of the ancestors."
In this world she is known by the name Satyavatī, and likewise as Aṣṭakā in the world of the ancestors;
she constantly bestows long life and health, and grants the fruit of all desires. (Matsya Purāṇa 14.19)
In a future time, you shall become a river; through your merit and contentment, you will indeed become the most excellent of streams in the world, known by the name Acchodā.
Having spoken thus, that host vanished right there before them;
and she too obtained all that fruit which had been described previously.
Matsya Purāṇa 15: Sūta said:
"Furthermore, there are others of great splendor in heaven named the Vibhrājas."
There are the worlds called Barhiṣad, where the ancestors of virtuous conduct reside.
Where there are thousands of celestial chariots yoked with peacocks, and where the wish-fulfilling trees of *barhis* grass stand ready to grant their fruits; (Matsya Purāṇa 15.2)
Wherein the givers of ancestral offerings rejoice in halls of exaltation,
and whom the hosts of gods and asuras, and the throngs of gandharvas and apsarases [revere].
And the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas worship the deities in heaven;
likewise, the sons of Pulastya by the hundreds, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga, do so as well.
These high-souled and highly fortunate ones grant fearlessness to their devotees;
their daughter, Pīvarī, was born of their mind and is renowned in heaven.
The Yoginī, the mother of Yoga, performed most severe asceticism;
the Blessed One was pleased with her, and she chose a boon from Hari.
"O Lord, you who are pleased, grant me as a husband a man who is endowed with yoga, handsome, and has conquered his senses—grant me a husband who is the best among speakers. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.7)
The god said: "O lady of virtuous vows, when Śuka becomes the son of Vyāsa, you shall become the wife of that master of yoga."
And you shall have a daughter named Kṛtvi, who will become a yoginī;
she must then be given by you to the human lord of Pañcāla.
The mother of Brahmadatta is remembered as Yogasiddhā, and Gauḥ;
Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, Prabhu, and Śambhu will be your sons. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.10)
"Those great-souled and highly fortunate ones will go to the supreme state;
having produced them again through yoga, you shall attain liberation along with your subjects. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.11)
The sons of Vasiṣṭha are remembered as the Pitṛs in embodied form;
they are all known by the name Mānasa, and they are all embodiments of Dharma.
Those who give offerings at the śrāddha ceremony dwell in worlds that shine with light beyond the heavens; resplendent, they sport there. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.13)
If even those born from the earth dwell in celestial palaces where all desires are fulfilled,
how much more so the faithful givers who are Brahmins, full of devotion and endowed with ritual action?
Their daughter, named Gaurī, shines in the sky as a mental creation;
she is the beloved wife of Śukra and the increaser of the fame of the Sādhyas.
In the solar orb, there are worlds named Marīcigarbha,
where the Pitṛs known as the Haviṣmats, the sons of Aṅgiras, reside.
Those best of Kṣatriyas who offer Śrāddha at sacred fords (tīrtha) indeed become the ancestors of kings, bestowing the fruits of heaven and liberation. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.17)
The daughter of these [two], Yaśodā, renowned throughout the world,
was the excellent wife of Aṃśumat and the daughter-in-law of Pañcajana.
Then the mother of Dilīpa, the great-grandmother of Bhagīratha,
[attained] the worlds known as Kāmadughā, which bestow the fruit of the enjoyment of all desires.
Where the ancestors named Susvadhās reside, who are observers of excellent vows,
they are known in the worlds as the Ājyapas, the progeny of the patriarch Kardama.
The Vaiśyas, who are the heirs of Pulaha’s offspring, nourish them;
there, all those who perform the śrāddha rites behold [the ancestors] simultaneously.
Mothers, brothers, fathers, sisters, friends, relatives, and kinsmen—
even those seen over ten thousand lifetimes or experienced thousands of times— (he remembers).
The mental daughter of these [sages], renowned by the name Virajā, was the wife of Nahuṣa and likewise the mother of Yayāti. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.23)
Ekāṣṭakā subsequently went to the world of Brahmā;
these three groups have been described, and I shall now speak of the fourth. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.24)
But the worlds known as Mānasa are situated above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
their daughter is the famous Narmadā by name. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.25)
There dwell the eternal ancestors known as the Somapas;
they all bear the form of Dharma and are remembered as being beyond even Brahmā.
Having arisen through their own inherent power and attained the state of Brahman, those yogis,
having performed all the work of creation and so forth, now abide within the mind.
Their daughter was named Narmadā,
a river carrying water that flows toward the southern region and purifies all beings.
From them all the Manus have been fashioned as progenitors in the various creations;
knowing this, people perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) at all times, even in the absence of [specific] dharma.

Furthermore, in order to obtain from them once again the continuity of yoga through their grace, the ancestral rite (śrāddha) was specifically ordained at the beginning of the creation of the ancestors. (MatsP 15.30)
A silver vessel, or one adorned with silver, offered by all while placing the word *svadhā* first, always gratifies the ancestors. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.31)
A wise man should perform the rite of satiation for Agni, Soma, and Yama;
even in the absence of fire, he may do so by means of his breath or in water, O Brahmin.
The southwest direction is praised as the celestial abode of the ancestors, whether at the ear of a goat, the ear of a horse, in a cow-pen, or near a body of water. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.33)

The sacred thread worn over the right shoulder, water, sesame seeds, the left side of the body, darbha grass, meat, the pāṭhīna fish, cow’s milk, and sweet flavors [are required]. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.34)
Sword, iron, meat, honey, kuśa grass, śyāmāka grain, rice, barley, wild millet, mung beans, sugarcane, white flowers, and clarified butter; MatsP_15.35.

I shall now fully declare those things which are beloved and praised by the ancestors here at all times, as well as those which are detested and should be avoided during a śrāddha ceremony. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.36)
Masūra, śaṇa, niṣpāva, rājamāṣa, and kusumbha;
padma, bilva, arka, dhattūra, pāribhadra, and āṭarūṣaka. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.37)
Milk, as well as the milk of goats and sheep, kodrava, udāra, chickpeas, wood-apple, madhuka, and linseed, should not be offered in rites for the ancestors.
Even these should not be given to the ancestors by one who desires their welfare;
for he who gratifies the ancestors with devotion, they in turn gratify him. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.39)
The ancestors bestow nourishment, heaven, health, and the fruit of progeny;
furthermore, the rite for the ancestors is superior even to the rite for the gods.
And it is traditionally taught that the ancestors are the first source of nourishment for the deities;
they are quick to grant favor, free from anger, unarmed, and steadfast in their affection.
The ancestors, who are the deities of the past, are peaceful in nature, devoted to purity, always speaking kindly, affectionately attached to their devotees, and bestowers of happiness.
Ravi is remembered as the presiding lord over those who offer oblations, and he is the god of the Śrāddha rites.
All this has been narrated to you—the glorification of the lineage of the Pitṛs. It is meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, and should always be recited by men. (Matsya Purāṇa 15.43)
Matsya Purāṇa 16: Sūta said:
Having heard all this in its entirety, Manu questioned Keśava.
And the various times for the śrāddha ceremony, as well as the different types of śrāddha rites.
Which twice-born men are to be fed at śrāddha rites and which are to be avoided;
and at what portion of the day should one perform the śrāddha for the ancestors? (Matsya Purāṇa 16.2)
O Madhusūdana, to whom is it given, and how does the śrāddha go [to them]?
By what rite should it be performed, and how does it gratify those ancestors? (Matsya Purāṇa 16.3)
The Fish said: One should perform the śrāddha rite day after day with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.4)
The Śrāddha is said to be of three kinds: the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya).
Of these, I shall first describe the obligatory, which is devoid of the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana).
One should know that to be *adaiva* (without the gods); the *pārvaṇa* is prescribed for the *parvan* days.
O Lord of the Earth, listen now as the *pārvaṇa* is said to be of three kinds. *Matsya Purāṇa* 16.6.
O lord of men, hear now who those are who should be appointed at the Pārvaṇa rite:
one who maintains the five fires, a Snātaka, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, and one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas.
He should be a learned Vedic scholar, the son of a learned Vedic scholar, proficient in the words of the injunctions,
omniscient, a knower of the Vedas, a master of mantras, one who knows his lineage, and endowed with noble family.
One who knows the Purāṇas, knows the Dharma, is devoted to the study and recitation of the Vedas, is a devotee of Śiva, devoted to the ancestors, a devotee of the Sun, or a Vaiṣṇava; MatsP_16.9 //
One who is devoted to Brahman, a knower of yoga, tranquil, self-conquered, and virtuous—
such a person should diligently feed his daughter's son, as well as his friends and teachers.
He who drinks the sacrificial liquor, he who drinks from the maternal uncle's cup, he who is a kinsman, a priest, a teacher, or a Soma-drinker,
and whoever explains the sacred word or investigates the ritual— [these are the ones he slays].

One who knows the rules for the tones of the Sāman chants, the purifier even of those who purify the assembly, a singer of the Sāman, a celibate student, one endowed with the Vedas, and a knower of Brahman; MatsP_16.12.
Wherever these people eat at a śrāddha ceremony, that alone is as if it were the ultimate truth.
These are to be fed with effort; now learn from me those who are to be avoided. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.13)

One who has fallen from his caste, one accused of a crime, a eunuch, a slanderer, one with a physical deformity, those afflicted by disease, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, and those born of adultery (kuṇḍa and gola), as well as horse-keepers—[these are excluded]. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.14)
One who has superseded his elder brother in marriage, one whose soul is bound by vows, those who are negligent, insane, or cruel,
those who act like cats or like herons, the hypocritical, temple-priests (devalakas), and so forth.
Likewise, he [shall rule over] the ungrateful and the atheists, as well as those dwelling in the lands of the Mlecchas— Triśaṅku, Barbaras, Drāviḍas, Vītas, Draviḍas, and Koṅkaṇas.
One should avoid all those who bear sectarian marks (liṅgin), especially at the time of a śrāddha;
on the day before or the day after, one whose mind is disciplined should invite them.
For the ancestors, having become like the wind, approach those invited twice-born ones; they follow them as they move and attend upon them as they sit.
Having touched his right knee and thus invited you by me, he should announce the observance to the paternal kinsmen. *Matsya Purāṇa* 16.19.
"You and I, who perform the ancestral rites, must always be free from anger, devoted to purity, and observant of celibacy."
Having completed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), which is known as the libation (tarpaṇa),
one who maintains the sacred fires should always perform the Śrāddha rite called Piṇḍānvāhāryaka on the day of the new moon.
Having smeared a site that slopes toward the south with cow dung, one should perform the Śrāddha rite with devotion, either in a cow-pen or near a body of water. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.22)
One should offer the oblation to Agni and the *caru* for the ancestors using equal handfuls;
saying "I offer to the ancestors," one should place everything to the south. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.23)
Then, having performed the sprinkling of clarified butter, one should make three offerings (nirvāpa) in front;
these too should be made long and four finger-breadths wide.
One should fashion three ladles made of khadira wood and adorned with silver;
they should be one cubit in length, perfectly smooth, and have excellent tips shaped like hands.
