A water-pot, a bronze vessel, a stirring-ladle, sacrificial fuel and kuśa grass, sesame seeds, vessels, fine garments, perfumes, incense, and ointments; MatsP_16.26.
One should slowly bring everything from the right side while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
having thus placed all that on the ground in front of the house.
On a mandala smeared with cow dung and cow urine, one should worship it with unbroken rice grains and flowers while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya). Matsya Purāṇa 16.28.
Having greeted the brahmins again and again, he should wash their feet as they sit upon the prepared seats provided with darbha grass, according to the prescribed rule.
Having seated the Brahmins who have sipped water, he should address them with mantras:
two for the rite of the gods, three for the ancestral rite, and one for each of the two.
Even a lord should not perform an elaborate feast here;
rather, the wise man, having first honored the Brahmins with the *arghya* offering and other rites, should then feed them, beginning with those representing the gods.
Then, permitted by the Brahmins, the Brahmin should perform the rite in the fire according to the prescribed rule,
having placed the sacrificial oblation (caru) in a bronze vessel according to the procedure taught in his own Gṛhya-sūtra.
A wise man should perform the nourishing rite (āpyāyana) with the two fires, Agni and Soma;
or, for that best of the twice-born who maintains only a single fire, he should do so in the Dakṣiṇāgni or the Gārhapatya.

Having performed the sprinkling of water and other rites while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), everything thereafter must be performed by one who knows the rules while wearing it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).
And from that remainder of the sacrificial offering, having formed six balls of rice, he should then offer water with water-vessels containing sesame seeds using his left hand. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.35)
Having carefully bent his left knee, free from envy and provided with darbha grass,
he should diligently draw lines and perform the ritual sprinkling (avanejana) during the offerings.
Facing south, he should indeed place the ladle in his hand and, having placed each individual rice-ball (piṇḍa) upon all the darbha grasses in sequence, [perform the rite]. (MatsP 16.37)
Then, he should pour [the water] upon the Darbha grass while reciting the names and lineages;
he should wipe that hand upon those Darbha blades for the sake of the "partakers of the scrapings."
In the same manner, he should again perform the ritual rinsing (pratyavanejana) from that [water],
having paid homage to the six seasons with perfumes, incense, offerings, and so forth.
Having thus invoked all that with the Vedic mantras as prescribed,
for one who maintains a single sacred fire (ekāgni), there shall be only a single pouring of oblations and likewise a single ladle.

Then, having placed [the food] within [the space between the two sets of kuśa grass], he should give the food to his wives upon the kuśa grass; likewise, he should perform the invocation and the dismissal for the rice-balls and other offerings. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.41)
Then, having taken portions from all those morsels in due order,
a man should diligently cause those very brahmins to eat them first.
Because the twice-born consume that portion of food which has been set aside, it is called *anvāhāryaka*; therefore, [that rite] is performed at the waning of the moon.
Having first given water with sesame seeds and a *pavitra* grass ring into his hand, one should offer the tip of that rice-ball while saying, "May there be *svadhā* for these. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.44)
While describing [the ritual], one should always serve pure and sweet food;
remembering Nārāyaṇa Hari, one should avoid being overcome by anger. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.45)
Knowing them to be satisfied, he should then scatter food of all kinds; having taken up some of the food along with water, he should pour that water upon the ground. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.46)
Once they have sipped water, one should again offer water, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
one should perform the entire rite of pronouncing "svasti" over the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
One should conclude the rite with the gods at the beginning; otherwise, the śrāddha becomes fruitless.
Likewise, after dismissing the brahmins, one should circumambulate them clockwise.
Looking toward the southern direction, a man should pray to the ancestors:
"May our givers increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.49)
"May our faith not depart from us; may we have much to give;
may we have abundant food, and may we receive guests. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.50)
"May we have those who ask of us, and may we not have to ask anything of anyone;
may this be so"—this is declared to be the *anvāhārya* rite of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.51)
Just as it is said regarding the waning of the moon, so it is declared in other cases as well;
one should give the funeral cakes to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or even into fire or water.
Or he may scatter [the remaining food] before the foremost brahmins, or have birds peck at it;
meanwhile, the wife, endowed with humility, should eat the middle pinda.
"O ancestors, bestow here a fetus that increases our lineage;
let the remnant of the food remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.54)
Then, once the ancestral rites have been completed, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering;
thereafter, being tranquil, he should eat with his loved ones the food that has been offered to the ancestors.

Furthermore, one should avoid all of the following: eating again, traveling, riding in a vehicle, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and eating at a *śrāddha* or a *kṛcchrāddha*. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.56)

Avoiding recitation of the Vedas and quarreling, as well as sleeping during the day at all times, one should perform the *śrāddha* offering here according to this rule after having dismissed the guests. *Matsya Purāṇa* 16.57.
When the sun is situated in Virgo, Aquarius, or Taurus, and during all the dark fortnights,
wherever it may be that an offering is to be made after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
it should always be given by one who maintains the sacred fire according to this procedure. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.58)
Matsya Purāṇa 17: Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which was uttered by Viṣṇu.
The śrāddha known as Sādhāraṇa bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.1)
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the two junctions (yugma), and the ordinary transits of the sun;
on the new moon day, the eight days of the dark fortnight, and on the fifteenth days [of the lunar months]. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.2)
During the lunar mansions of Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī; when there is an encounter between a specific substance and a Brāhmaṇa;
during Gajacchāyā, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, and Vaidhṛti; and on the day [of these conjunctions]—MatsP 17.3.
The third day of Vaiśākha, the ninth of Kārttika, the fifteenth of Māgha, and the thirteenth of Nabhasya. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.4)
For these are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause what is given to become inexhaustible;
likewise, a wise person should offer the Śrāddha at the beginning of a Manvantara.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Aśvayuja, likewise the twelfth of Kārttika, the third of the month of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.6)
Indeed, the new moon day of Phālguna, as well as the eleventh of Pauṣa, the tenth of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh of the month of Māgha; MatsP_17.7 //
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Caitra, and the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha—
these are the beginnings of the Manvantaras, which cause what is given to become inexhaustible.
That seventh day of the month of Māgha, on which the Sun-god sits upon his chariot at the beginning of a Manvantara, is indeed known as Rathasaptamī.
A self-controlled man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years—this is a secret that the ancestors declare.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, during eclipses, as well as at festivals and the Mahālaya rites,
and at sacred fords, temples, cow-pens, and in houses adorned with lamps and gardens.

A wise person, with a disciplined mind, should offer the ancestral oblation (*śrāddha*) in secluded and well-smeared places; he should invite the Brahmins on the previous day and on the following day.

One should invite two for the rite to the gods and three for the rite to the ancestors, or one for each of the two; [these guests] should be endowed with virtue, conduct, and good qualities, and possessed of youth and beauty. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.13)
Even if he is very wealthy, he should feed [the guests] and not be attached to abundance;
having first provided seats, he should worship all the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers.
Having placed two vessels and a purifier made of *darbha* grass, one should pour water with the mantra "śaṃ no devī" and also barley grains with the mantra "yavo 'si. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.15)
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should place [the offering] toward the Vaiśvadeva;
having invoked [the Viśvedevas] with the two verses beginning "viśve devāsaḥ," one should scatter barley grains.
Having adorned [the vessel] with perfumes and flowers, one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra "yā divyā";
having worshipped with those two, one should commence the ancestral rite (*pitṛkārya*) that has been offered. (MatsP 17.17)
Having first provided a seat of darbha grass, one should fill three vessels;
having first fashioned the sky-purifiers (khapavitra), one should pour water with the mantra "śaṃ no devī".
One should prepare sesame seeds with the mantra "tilo 'si," and likewise offer perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
furthermore, the vessel should be made of wood or of leaves. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.19)
One should make a vessel for the ancestors either from lotus material or from substances produced in the ocean; it is said that a vessel for the ancestors may be made of gold or even of silver.
Even a conversation about silver, a sight of it, or its gift—whether by means of silver vessels or those adorned with silver—for these [is a cause of downfall]. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.21)
Even water given with faith conduces to inexhaustible merit;
likewise, for the ancestors, silver is considered appropriate for the arghya, the piṇḍa, the meal, and so forth. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.22)
Since it originated from the eye of Śiva, it is therefore dear to the ancestors;
one should avoid that inauspicious substance with effort during rites for the gods.
Having thus consecrated the vessels according to what is available and without envy, he,
holding darbha grass in his hand, should place them while reciting "yā divyā" and using the father's name and lineage.

Having been told by them again, "Perform [the rite] and we shall summon the ancestors," he should summon the ancestors with the two ṛg-verses beginning with "uśantas tvā" and "tathā yantu. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.25)
Having offered the arghya with the verse "yā divyā," he should then present the perfumes and other offerings;
first, having poured that water from his hand, he should offer the residual drops (saṃsrava) at the beginning.
Having placed it in the vessel for the ancestors, one should then set it upside down to the north;
having set it with the words, "Thou art the place for the ancestors," one should sprinkle water around it. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.27)
There too, free from envy, one should perform the fire-rite as before;
having brought food with both hands, one should serve it.
With a mind always perfectly tranquil, holding darbha grass in his hand,
he [should offer] food enriched with virtues, consisting especially of various kinds of soups, vegetables, and diverse edibles.
"Food accompanied by curd and milk, along with cow's ghee and sugar, satisfies all the ancestors for a month; so indeed said Keśava. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.30)
For two months with fish-meat, for three months with the meat of the deer, for four months with the meat of sheep, and for five months indeed with the meat of birds. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.31)
Likewise, the ancestors are satisfied for six months with the meat of a goat;
for seven months with the meat of a spotted deer, and for eight months with that of the ena deer.
They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boars and buffaloes, but for exactly eleven months by the flesh of hares, tortoises, and goats. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.33)
For a year they are satisfied by cow’s milk and milk-rice (pāyasa),
and for fifteen months by the meat of the Ruru deer.
With the meat of a rhinoceros, there is satisfaction for twelve years;
with kālaśāka vegetables and indeed with the meat of a rhinoceros, it is infinite.
Whatever cow’s milk mixed with honey, or rice-pudding with ghee,
is offered, the ancestors— the deities of old— declare that it is inexhaustible.
One should cause the recitation of the ancestral scriptures (svādhyāya), all the Purāṇas, and the various hymns (sūkta) dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Sun, and Rudra. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.37)
He [recited] the hymns dedicated to Indra, Agni, and Soma, which are purifying according to his own capacity,
as well as the Bṛhat, Rathantara, Jyeṣṭhasāman, and Rauhiṇa.
Likewise, the Śāntikādhyāya, the Madhubrāhmaṇa, and similarly the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa, as well as whatever else causes delight; MatsP_17.39.
O King, when those brahmins have finished eating, one should recite all of that [the Purāṇa] for them and for oneself near the meal. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.40)
Having collected food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water, one should cast it upon the ground in front of those who have finished eating. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.41)
May those living beings of my lineage who have been consumed by fire, as well as those who have not been consumed,
find satisfaction through what is given upon the earth and attain the supreme goal.

May this food given upon the earth for the satisfaction of those who have no mother, no father, no kinsman, no purity of lineage, and likewise no food— may it likewise lead to happiness in the worlds.

One who receives the scattered offerings (vikiro) upon the *darbha* grass should be the recipient of the remnants for those women of good family who have died without the sacraments (*asaṃskṛta*) or have been abandoned.
Knowing them to be satiated, one should likewise offer water once into the hand of the Brahmin on a smeared surface of the earth with cow dung, urine, and water. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.45)
Having carefully placed the darbha grass according to rule with its tips pointing southward,
one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) using food of all colors, just as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).

After first performing the ritual washing (avanejana), a person should offer perfumes, incense, and other such items by means of their name and lineage, having performed the secondary washing (pratyavanejana).
Then, having bent the left knee and with the right hand,
one should bring the ancestral offering (pitrya) clockwise and perform that rite according to the rules, holding darbha grass in the hand.
In the same manner, the wise man should perform the lighting of lamps and the worship with flowers;
then, after they have sipped water for purification (ācamana), he himself should sip water and offer water once to each.

Then, one should subsequently offer flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and water for imperishability (akṣayyodaka) along with sesame seeds, pronouncing the name and lineage [of the deceased], and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
One should give cows, land, gold, garments, and excellent beds—whatever is desired by the Brahmins, as well as for oneself and one's father. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.51)
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should offer satisfaction to the ancestors;
thereafter, he should perform the recitation of the *svadhā* for the ancestors and the offering of water to the Viśvedevas.
Having given his blessing, the wise man should receive [the gifts] from the twice-born while facing the east;
then, when addressed again by the twice-born, "May the ancestors be non-terrible," he should reply, "May they be so. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.53)
"May our lineage likewise increase," he said; and being thus addressed by them, he should further utter these words: "May our donors increase. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.54)

Having been told by them, "May these true blessings be so, may they be so," he should perform the recitation of auspiciousness (svastivācana) with devotion after lifting up the rice-balls (piṇḍas). (Matsya Purāṇa 17.55)
That remnant of the food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the bali-offering to the planets—such is the established rule of dharma.
The remnants of food that have fallen upon the ground belong to the honest and the faithful;
they declare this to be the ancestral portion for the class of servants.
O lord of men, this source of nourishment was created of old by the ancestors; it is always [efficacious] for women who have no sons as well as those who do.
Then, standing before them and taking hold of the water vessel,
he should dismiss them with the tip of a blade of kusha grass while reciting the mantra "vāje vāje."
Accompanied by his circle of kinsmen and joined by his sons and wife, he should perform a circumambulation outside, following [the deity] for eight steps.
Having returned, prostrated, and sprinkled water around the fire with the appropriate mantras, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as well as the daily bali offering. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.61)
Then, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, he should eat together with his guests, along with his servants, sons, and kinsmen, all that which has been partaken by the ancestors.
Even one who has not been initiated should perform this common Śrāddha on all festival days;
it is known as the "Common" Śrāddha and bestows the fruit of all desires. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.63)
Even one separated from his wife, even one staying abroad, and even a Śūdra who lacks the sacred mantras— a wise man should perform this [rite] according to this procedure with devotion.
The third is called the *ābhyudayika* or *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, performed on occasions of festive joy and abundance, such as sacrifices, weddings, and other auspicious ceremonies. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.65)
The mothers are to be honored first, and the fathers immediately after them; then, O King, the maternal grandfathers, and likewise the Viśvedevas. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.66)
Performing the rite of circumambulation, one facing east should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) accompanied by curd, unbroken rice, fruits, water, dūrvā grass, and kuśa grass.
Saying "It is complete," one should offer the respectful water (arghya) during the auspicious rite to each pair [of deities];
the twice-born should be honored in pairs with garments, gold, and other such gifts.
The purpose of the sesame seeds should be fulfilled with barley, preceded by the word "Nāndī";
and all auspicious things should be caused to be recited by the best of the twice-born.

In this same way, a Śūdra also, at all times even during an ordinary *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, should always perform the rite with uncooked food (*āmanna*) using the mantra of salutation (*namaskāra*). (Matsya Purāṇa 17.70)
"The Lord, the Master, has declared that a Śūdra should be preeminent in giving, because through giving, the attainment of all his desires comes about for him. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.71)
Matsya Purāṇa 18: Sūta said:
"I shall now describe the Ekoddiṣṭa rite as it was taught by Cakrapāṇi."
When the father has died, the sons must perform the funeral rites and observe the period of impurity (āśauca) just as they would for him.
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among Brāhmaṇas;
for Kṣatriyas it is twelve days, and for Vaiśyas it is indeed a fortnight.
For Śūdras, a month-long period of impurity is prescribed for those who are sapinda relations;
for one whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, it lasts one night, and beyond that, it is traditionally held to be three nights.
The same rule shall apply at all times for all castes even during birth;
likewise, after the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed.
One should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased for twelve days;
for that is said to be his provision for the journey, since it brings him great satisfaction. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.5)
Therefore, the deceased is not led to the city of the hungry ghosts for twelve days;
during those twelve days, he gazes upon his home, his son, and his wife.
Therefore, one should place milk in the open air for ten nights;
this serves to pacify all burning sensations and destroys the fatigue of travel.
Then, on the eleventh day, a Kṣatriya or one of the other castes should feed eleven Brahmins at the end of the period of impurity; he should feed an odd number of Brahmins. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.8)
On the second day, one should again perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite in the same manner,
according to the prescribed rule, omitting the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and excluding the portion for the gods (*daiva*).
One purifier, one offering of water (argha), and one rice-ball (piṇḍa) are prescribed;
after saying "May [the ancestors] be present," water with sesame seeds should be offered.
One should say "It is well-eaten" and scatter [the food]; at the dismissal, one should say "May you be pleased.
Here too, the remaining rites for the father should be performed by the knower of the Vedas as previously described.
By this procedure, one should perform everything every month;
on the second day after the end of the birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should provide a distinctive bed.
Likewise, having worshipped a golden man accompanied by fruit and clothing,
one should honor a brahmin couple with various ornaments and decorations.
One should perform the rite of releasing a bull, and an auspicious tawny cow should be given;
a water-pot, accompanied by various kinds of food and edibles, should also be offered.
O best of men, for as long as a year, one should perform the rites preceded by water and sesame seeds; then, when the year is complete, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony shall take place.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the deceased becomes a partaker of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha;
he is also fit for the rites preceding an increase [of prosperity], and from that point on, he becomes a householder. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.16)
In the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha, one should first employ the deities;
there, one should seat the ancestors separately and designate the deceased (*preta*) apart from them. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.17)
One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds for the purpose of the *argha* offering;
one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). (Matsya Purāṇa 18.18)

Having likewise mentally resolved upon this, the giver of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) should offer four balls while reciting the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ"; however, he should divide the last one into three parts.
Furthermore, for the fourth [birth], no further duty would ever arise;
thus, having attained the status of a father, he became entirely content.

After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, he attains the status of being among the Agniṣvātta ancestors and reaches the supreme nectar; therefore, [offerings] are not given to him [in the ordinary way]. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.21)
But it should be given to those very paternal uncles upon whom that funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) was established;
from then on, [it should be given] during the solstices (saṃkrānti), eclipses, and other festival days.
One should perform the *tri-piṇḍa* śrāddha on the anniversary of death during the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
he who performs it on the anniversary of death while abandoning the *ekoddiṣṭa* [format] [commits an error]. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.23)
Such a man shall always be a slayer of his father and a destroyer of his mother and brothers;
performing the *pārvaṇa* rite on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), that person sinks lower and lower into hell. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.24)
When [the ancestors] have departed, there would be a state of confusion among those who are closely related;
therefore, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite every year. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.25)
He who, free from envy, gives a water-pot along with food to a deceased person for as long as a year shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.

When one who knows the rules performs an *āmaśrāddha*, the giver of the śrāddha should then perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite with that [raw food] and offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) with that very same [food]. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.27)

When, in the course of time, the father shall attain the state beyond the three—through the three-fold *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite performed without remainder—then he shall be liberated from bondage. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.28)
Even one who is liberated attains a share in the *lepa* (smearings) through the cleansing with *kuśa* grass.
From the fourth ancestor onwards, those beginning with the father are the sharers of the *piṇḍas*;
the giver of the *piṇḍas* is the seventh among them. This is *sāpiṇḍya*, extending over seven generations. (Matsya Purāṇa 18.29)
Matsya Purāṇa 19:
The Sages said:
"How should the offerings for the ancestors (kavya) and the offerings for the gods (havya) be presented here by people?"
They go to those abodes situated in the world of the ancestors; who, then, is said here to be their attainer?

If a mortal twice-born man eats, or if an oblation is offered into the fire, how can that which is given by the *pretas*—who consist of both auspicious and inauspicious natures—be consumed? (Matsya Purāṇa 19.2)
Sūta said:
"They call the Vasus the fathers (pitṛs), the Rudras the grandfathers (pitāmahas), and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers (prapitāmahas); such is the Vedic revelation."
The names and lineages of the ancestors are what convey the offerings to the gods (havya) and to the ancestors (kavya);
the Śrāddha mantras and faith itself must be employed with extreme devotion.
Agniṣvātta and the others are established in their lordship over those who have passed into other states of existence, according to their names, lineages, times, and places. (Matsya Purāṇa 19.5)
These [ancestors] gratify living beings who have become their food, even if the deity has been born as a father due to the performance of auspicious deeds. (Matsya Purāṇa 19.6)
His food, having become nectar, follows him even in his divine state;
in the state of a Daitya it takes the form of enjoyments, and in the state of a beast it becomes grass.
The food of a śrāddha ceremony attends upon one even in the state of a serpent in the form of wind;
it becomes drink in the state of a yakṣa, and likewise meat in the state of a rākṣasa.
Likewise, in the state of being a Danuja, it becomes illusion; in the state of being a Preta, blood and water;
and in the state of being human, it becomes food, drink, and the essence of various enjoyments.
The power of pleasure is a beloved woman; the power of enjoyment is the capacity for eating;
the power of giving is the possession of wealth, as well as beauty and health. (Matsya Purāṇa 19.10)
Faith is said to be the flower, and union with Brahman is the fruit;
[it bestows] long life, sons, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and all forms of happiness.
The hosts of ancestors, being pleased, bestow even sovereignty upon men;
and it is heard that in ancient times the sons of Kauśika attained liberation—
having passed through five successive births, they reached the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Matsya Purāṇa 20: The Sages said: "How did those heirs of Kauśika attain that supreme yoga?"
How can there be the destruction of karma through five connections with births?
Sūta said:
There was a great ṛṣi named Kauśika, righteous in soul, at Kurukṣetra; learn now of his seven sons by name and by their deeds. *Matsya Purāṇa* 20.2.
Śvasṛpa, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, Kavi,
Vāgduṣṭa, and Pitṛvartin were then the disciples of Garga.
When their father had passed away, a severe famine befell them,
along with a great drought that struck fear into all the world.
"Having been sent by Garga and others to the forest, those whose wealth is their asceticism were guarding the milch-cow when they said:
'We, being greatly oppressed by hunger, shall eat this Kapilā cow. (Matsya Purāṇa 20.5)
While they were thus reflecting on their sin, the younger brother then spoke softly:
"If she must certainly be killed, let her be employed under the guise of a *śrāddha* ceremony."
"Employed in the ancestral rite (śrāddha), she will certainly protect us from sin.
Having been thus authorized by his younger brothers to follow the path of the ancestors, he acted accordingly. (Matsya Purāṇa 20.7)
Having partaken of that [food] again, he, being composed in meditation, performed the ancestral rite (śrāddha),
having assigned two brothers to the gods and three to the ancestors in due order.
Likewise, having made himself a guest, the giver of the śrāddha,
devoted to his ancestors, performed the śrāddha rite himself while reciting the mantras.
"Even without the cow, this calf has been offered to the Guru;
the cow was slain by a tiger—let this calf be accepted. (Matsya Purāṇa 20.10)
Thus was that cow devoured by those seven ascetics,
who, relying on Vedic power, were fearless in their cruel deed.
Then, drawn away by time, those hunters came to live in Dāśapura;
having attained the recollection of their former births, they were imbued with the feeling of being his fathers.
Because they had then performed even a cruel deed in the form of a *śrāddha* offering,
they were consequently born in the abode of hunters who commit cruel acts.
Due to the majesty of the ancestors, they were born with the power of recollecting their past lives;
then, through the yoga of detachment, they again undertook a fast unto death.
Seven deer, who remembered their past births, were born on Mount Kālañjara in the presence of Nīlakaṇṭha, having been moved by their state as ancestors.
There too, having renounced their vital breaths through knowledge and dispassion in accordance with dharma,
they were watched by the people as they underwent fasting unto death at the edge of the sacred ford.
O best of the twice-born, listen to all those seven yogins who were born as cakravāka birds on Lake Mānasa, both by name and by their deeds.
Sumanas, Kumuda, Śuddha, Chidradarśin,
Sunetraka, Sunetra, and Aṃśumat— these seven were masters who had reached the further shore of yoga.
Those three, having fallen from yoga and being of little intelligence, wandered about;
they saw him shining brilliantly in the garden, accompanied by women.
Sporting with various dispositions, possessed of great strength and prowess,
born of the Pāñcāla lineage, and endowed with abundant forces and vehicles.
Among those water-dwellers, there was one who desired sovereignty;
he was a brahmin devoted to his father, a performer of ancestral rites (śrāddha), and deeply affectionate toward his father. (Matsya Purāṇa 20.21)
O best of the twice-born, seeing two other ministers possessed of great forces and vehicles, they conceived the desire for the office of minister in that mortal realm.
Among them, those who were free from desire became the best of the twice-born;
however, there was one son of Vibhrāja known as Brahmadatta.
Likewise, both Kaṇḍarīka and Subālaka were the sons of ministers;
and Brahmadatta, having been consecrated by the learned priest Vipracitti, [ascended the throne].
At that time, the King of Pañcāla was valiant, learned in all the scriptures,
a knower of yoga, and one who understood the cries of all living beings.
That king had a beautiful wife, the daughter of Devala, renowned by the name Saṃnati, who was formerly known as Kapilā. (Matsya Purāṇa 20.26)
Because she was appointed to the ancestral rites, she became a speaker of the Veda;
together with her, that descendant of the Raghus ruled the kingdom.
Once, while in a garden with her,
that king saw a pair of insects agitated by a love-quarrel.
Enticing the female ant from all sides, the lover of the insect, his limbs tormented by the five arrows [of Kāma], spoke with a faltering voice: *matsya-purāṇa 20.29*
"There is no woman like you to be found anywhere in the world— a woman with a slender waist and broad hips, whose gait is directed toward a large chest."
She was golden-hued, possessed of beautiful hips, eloquent in speech, and sweetly smiling;
her eyes and lower lip were of excellent appearance, and she was fond of molasses and sugar.
"You shall eat only when I have eaten; likewise, you shall bathe only when I have bathed.
You shall be dejected when I am away on a journey, and tremble with fear even when I am angry. (Matsya Purāṇa 20.32)
"For what reason, O auspicious lady, do you stand with a face full of anger? Tell me.
She, however, spoke to him with indignation: "Why do you address me, you rogue? (Matsya Purāṇa 20.33)
"O lover, when the day had passed, you gave the powder for the sweetmeat to another woman, excluding me. (Matsya Purāṇa 20.34)
The ant said: "O woman of excellent complexion, because of my resemblance to you, I gave it to another;
O beautiful lady, you ought to forgive this one offense of mine."
"I shall never do such a thing again anywhere here, O lady of noble vows;
by this truth, I touch your feet—be gracious to me who am prostrate before you."
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, she then became gracious;
the female ant offered herself for the sake of deluding him.
Brahmadatta, too, having understood that entirely,
was filled with wonder due to his knowledge of the cries of all beings and through the grace of the wielder of the discus.
Matsya Purāṇa 21. The sages said:
"How did Brahmadatta come to know the cries of living beings on the surface of the earth?"
And that group of four cakravāka birds was born into whose family? 21.1.
The sages said: How did Brahmadatta come to know the cries of living beings on the surface of the earth?
And in whose lineage did those four cakravāka birds originate?
Sūta said:
They were born at that very time in that same city as the Cakrāhvayas,
the heirs of an aged Brahmin, who were Brahmins remembering their former births.
Dhṛtimat, Tattvadarśin, Vidyācaṇḍa, and Tapotsuka—
these were the sons of Sudaridra by name and by their actions.
Then the minds of those twice-born ones turned toward asceticism;
"We shall attain supreme perfection," said those best of the twice-born. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.4)
Then, having heard those words, Sudaridra, a man of great austerity, spoke with a piteous voice: "What is this, my sons? (Matsya Purāṇa 21.5)
"This is unrighteous," your father said to them, seeking to restrain them;
yet they abandoned their aged father, who was poor and living in the forest. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.6)
"What indeed will be the dharma here, or what will be our course upon your departure? They said, 'O father, you have devised a livelihood for us; tell us that. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.7)
"This wealth belongs to the king; he will give it to you in abundance—money and thousands of villages—to you as you recite at dawn. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.8)
Those who were the foremost Brahmins among the Kurus and the Jaṅgalas, those who were fishermen in Daśapura, and the deer in Kālañjara;
those seven cakravāka birds on Lake Mānasa—we are they, now perfected here.
Having spoken thus to their father, they went again to the forest for asceticism;
the aged king also went to the royal palace for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose.
In ancient times, the lord of Pañcāla named Anagha Vaibhrāja, desiring a son, [worshipped] Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods and the Sovereign. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.11)
Devoted to rigorous vows, he propitiated the Lord;
then, after a long time, Janārdana was pleased with him.
"Choose a boon, O King; may it be well with you—whatever is desired by your heart.
Thus addressed by the god, he chose this supreme boon: Matsya Purāṇa 21.13.
"O Lord of Gods, grant me a son of great strength and prowess, one who has mastered all the scriptures, who is righteous, and the supreme among yogis. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.14)
"Grant me a son born of yoga who knows the cries of all sentient beings.
"So be it," said the Supreme Lord, the Soul of the Universe, to him. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.15)
While all the gods were looking on, he vanished right there;
thereafter, he became his son, the powerful Brahmadatta.
Compassionate toward all beings, surpassing all beings in strength,
knowing the cries of all beings, he is the Lord of the lords of all beings.
With his mind intent on yoga, he followed the trail of the ants to the place where that pair of insects remained engaged in dalliance.
Then Saṃnati, seeing him laughing, was greatly amazed;
suspecting something in her mind, she questioned that lord of men.
Saṃnati said:
"O King, why did this excessive laughter occur so suddenly?
I do not know the cause of your mirth, since it was displayed by you at an improper time. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.20)
Sūta said:
The prince also spoke of the speech of the ant;
O fair-faced one, this laughter arose from those words of passion. *Matsya Purāṇa* 21.21.
"O lady of pure smiles, there was no other cause for this jest;
at that time, the goddess did not speak these words as a falsehood."
"I alone am laughed at today; I shall not live with you now.
How can a mortal understand the speech of ants without the gods? (Matsya Purāṇa 21.23)
"Therefore, I alone have been laughed at by you here; what could be more than this?
Then the king, having no reply and desiring to know the truth regarding that city of Hari, [remained silent].
Having undertaken a vow, he remained for seven nights free from sin;
then Hṛṣīkeśa spoke to him in a dream as he was wandering through the city at dawn.
"From the words of that aged brahmin, you shall know everything without exception";
having said this, Viṣṇu vanished, and then at dawn the king departed from the city.
As he was departing accompanied by his ministers and his wife, he beheld that elderly Brahmin approaching from ahead, speaking as he came. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.27)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "Those who were the foremost of Brahmins in Kurujāṅgala, the fishermen in Daśapura, and the deer in Kālañjara;
those seven cakravāka birds at Lake Mānasa—we are they, now perfected here."
Sūta said:
Having heard these words from the two of them, he then fell down in grief;
and both those excellent ministers attained the recollection of their former births.
And Bābhravya Subālaka, an author of the treatise on love (kāmaśāstra), was renowned in the worlds as Pāñcāla, a knower of all sciences. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.30)
Then Kaṇḍarīka, though righteous and an expounder of the Vedas and Śāstras,
having become a rememberer of his former births, fell down before them out of grief.
"Alas! We have fallen from yoga, bound by karma through desire!
Having lamented thus many times, those three who had reached the further shore of yoga—*Matsya Purāṇa* 21.32.
Having repeatedly rejoiced in the greatness of the śrāddha with wonder,
he then gave him wealth consisting of many villages.
Having dismissed that aged Brahmin who was filled with joy at the wealth,
the king [installed] his own son, who was endowed with the marks of royalty.
The king then consecrated the one named Viṣvaksena in the kingdom;
thereafter, all those foremost among yogins assembled at Mānasa.
Brahmadatta and the others there were devoted to their father and free from envy;
yet Saṃnati became fallen, for it was indeed caused by me. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.36)
"The king, however, saying 'So be it' and further expressing his approval, replied: 'All this fruit that is desired from the renunciation of the kingdom [shall be yours].'"
"By your grace, all this fruit has been obtained by me;
therefore, having established yourselves in yoga, all you forest-dwellers [should depart]. (Matsya Purāṇa 21.38)
Through the power of their asceticism, they attained the supreme state by means of the aperture of Brahmā;
likewise, [they attain] longevity, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and all forms of happiness.
O twice-born ones, when pleased, the grandfathers bestow sons and kingdoms upon men who recite this greatness of the ancestors and [the account] of Brahmadatta.
Whoever causes the twice-born to hear this, or hears it himself, or recites it,
is honored in the world of Brahmā for more than a hundred times ten million kalpas.
Matsya Purāṇa 22: The Sages said:
At what time does that śrāddha become one that yields infinite fruit?
At what part of the day should one who performs a Śrāddha ceremony perform it? And at which sacred fords (tīrthas) does a performed Śrāddha yield great fruit? (Matsya Purāṇa 22.1)
Sūta said:
When the afternoon has arrived and the constellations Abhijit and Rohiṇī have risen,
whatever is given at that time is declared to be inexhaustible.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe in brief by name those sacred fords (tīrthas) which are praised and beloved by the ancestors. *Matsya Purāṇa* 22.3.
The sacred ford of the ancestors named Gayā is auspicious and the best of all tīrthas;
there dwells the Lord of the gods of gods, the Grandfather himself.

In this regard, this verse was sung by the ancestors who desired their share: mātsyo rājā prajāpālo dātā bhāgārthino vayam / yathābhāgaṃ prayacchasva yathākālaṃ nareśvara // 6 // O King, protector of subjects, you are a giver; we are seekers of our shares. O lord of men, grant us our portion at the proper time.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or sets free a dark-colored bull.
Likewise, Vārāṇasī is meritorious and always beloved by the ancestors;
there, the presence of Avimukta bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, Vimaleśvara is dear to the ancestors and meritorious;
and Prayāga, the sacred ford of the ancestors, bestows the fruits of all desires. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.8)
The Lord Vaṭeśvara, however, together with Mādhava,
as well as Keśava, who lies in yogic sleep, always dwells there.
The merit of ten horse-sacrifices is found at Gaṅgādvāra,
and likewise at Nandā, Lalitā, and the auspicious holy site of Māyāpurī.
Likewise, there is the place named Mitrapada, and beyond that the excellent Kedāra;
they call it Gaṅgāsāgara, the auspicious site containing all holy fords (tīrtha).
Likewise, there is the sacred ford of Brahmasaras in the lake of the waters of the Śatadru;
and there is the sacred ford named Naimiṣa, which bestows the fruit of all sacred fords.
Where the eternal Gaṅgodbheda has arisen in the Gomatī,
there likewise is Yajñavarāha, the God of gods, and the wielder of the trident.
There is that golden gate where Hara, with eighteen arms, once stood;
there, in ancient times, the rim of Hari’s discus was shattered.
This is that Naimiṣa forest, frequented by all sacred fords;
there also is the vision of the God of gods, Vārāha.
He who departs with a purified soul shall go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa;
it is a place of great merit, where purification is accomplished and all sins are destroyed.
Where Janārdana himself resides as Nārasiṃha,
there is the sacred ford named Ikṣumatī, which is always beloved by the ancestors.
At the confluence where the ancestors always reside,
there is Kurukṣetra, which is greatly meritorious and endowed with all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Likewise, the holy Sarayū, saluted by all the gods,
and the river Irāvatī are similarly abodes of the sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha) of the ancestors.
The Yamunā, Devikā, Kālī, Candrabhāgā, Dṛṣadvatī,
the holy river Veṇumatī, and likewise the great Vetravatī.
For these rivers are beloved by the ancestors; at a śrāddha ceremony, they are considered to yield ten millionfold merit.
Jambūmārga is of great merit, where indeed the path [to heaven] is perceived.
Even today, O best of the twice-born, that Pitṛtīrtha, which bestows the fruits of all desires,
is renowned as Nīlakuṇḍa, a sacred ford for the ancestors.
Likewise, there is the meritorious Rudrasaras, as well as Lake Mānasa;
also the Mandākinī, the Acchodā, the Vipāśā, and the Sarasvatī.
Likewise, Pūrvamitra-pada, Vaidyanātha which yields great fruit, the Kṣiprā river, Mahākāla, and the auspicious Kālañjara; MatsP_22.23:2.
Vaṃśodbheda, Harodbheda, and Gaṅgodbheda, which yield great fruit;
Bhadreśvara, Viṣṇupada, and Narmadādvāra as well.
The great seers have declared that these ancestral pilgrimage sites (pitṛtīrthas), which remove all sins, are equal to the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.25)
Even by the mere remembrance of them, what need is there to speak of men who perform ancestral rites?
[These are] Oṃkāra, Pitṛtīrtha, the Kāverī, and the waters of the Kapilā. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.26)
And at the confluence of the Caṇḍavegā, as well as at Amarakaṇṭaka,
bathing and other rites performed shall yield a hundredfold more merit than at Kurukṣetra.
The famous Śukratīrtha and the supreme Someśvara Tīrtha are meritorious, removing all diseases and yielding a fruit greater than that of a hundred crores [of other rites]. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.28)

At a funeral rite, in giving, as well as in burnt offerings, in private Vedic study, and in the presence of water, there is the river named Kāyāvarohaṇa, as well as the Carmaṇvatī. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.29)
Likewise, there are Gomatī and Varaṇā, the supreme holy site of Auśanasa,
Bhairava, Bhṛgutuṅga, and the unsurpassed Gaurītīrtha.
Beyond that is the sacred ford named Vaināyaka, then Bhadreśvara,
as well as the one called Pāpahara, and the meritorious river Tapatī.
The Mūlatāpī, the Payoṣṇī, and likewise the confluence of the Payoṣṇī;
Mahābodhi, Pāṭalā, Nāgatīrtha, and Avantikā.
Likewise, the holy river Veṇā, as well as Mahāśāla,
Mahārudra, Mahāliṅga, and the auspicious river Daśārṇā.
The Śatarudrā and the Śatāhvā, as well as the supreme Viśvapada;
likewise the Aṅgāravāhikā, and those two rivers, the Śoṇa and the Gharghara.
The Kālikā river is meritorious, as is the Vitastā river;
these are praised as sacred bathing-places for the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha) for the purposes of ritual bathing and giving gifts.
The ancestral offering (śrāddha) given on these occasions is remembered as yielding infinite fruit.
These are Droṇī, Vāṭanadī, Dhārā, Sarit, and likewise Kṣīranadī. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.36)
Gokarṇa and Gajakarṇa, as well as Puruṣottama,
Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇatīrtha, and likewise the Sarasvatī at Arbuda.
The river named Maṇimatī, as well as Girikarṇikā,
the sacred ford Dhūtapāpa, and likewise the southern ocean.
By performing a Śrāddha at these sacred sites of the ancestors (pitṛtīrthas), one attains infinite merit;
the sacred site named Meghakara is Janārdana himself.
Where Viṣṇu, bearing the Śārṅga bow, is stationed at Mekhalā,
there likewise is the Mandodarī-tīrtha, the Campā-tīrtha, and the auspicious river Nadī.
Likewise Sāmalanātha, the Mahāśāla river, Cakravāka, Carmakoṭa, and the great Janmeśvara.
Arjuna, Tripura, and thereafter Siddheśvara;
Śrīśaila, the holy site of Śaṅkara, and thereafter Nārasiṃha. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.42)
Likewise, the meritorious Mahendra and that known as Śrīraṅga—
faithful offerings made at these places are also traditionally held to yield infinite fruit.
Indeed, even by the mere sight of them, these immediately remove sin:
the holy river Tuṅgabhadrā and likewise the Bhīmarathī river.
Bhīmeśvara, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Kāverī, the Kuḍmalā river,
and the river named Godāvarī— these are the Trisaṃdhyā, the most excellent sacred ford (tīrtha).
There is a sacred ford named Traiyambaka, honored by all holy places,
where the Blessed Lord Īśa himself resides as the three-eyed one.
O twice-born ones, a śrāddha performed at all these places yields millions upon millions of times the merit; even by the mere remembrance of them, sins are destroyed a hundredfold.
Śrīparṇī, Tāmraparṇī, and Jayā are unsurpassed holy places;
likewise, the sacred Matsyanadī and Śivadhāra as well.
And the famous Bhadratīrtha, the eternal Pampātīrtha,
the meritorious Rāmeśvara, as well as Elāpura and Alampuram.
And likewise famous as constituent parts [of the sacred field] are Āmardaka, Alambuṣa,
Āmrātakeśvara, and after that, Ekāmbhaka.
Govardhana, Hariścandra, Kṛpucandra, Pṛthūdaka,
Sahasrākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, and likewise the river Kadalī.
There also is the dwelling place of Rāma, as well as the meeting with the son of Sumitrā;
likewise Indrakīla, Mahānāda, and Priyamelaka.
These too are always highly recommended for the śrāddha ceremony, because the presence of all the gods is perceived within them. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.53)
A gift given to all of these yields more than a hundred crores [of merit];
likewise, the river Bāhudā is meritorious, as is the auspicious Siddhavana forest.
There is a sacred ford named Pāśupata and the auspicious river Pārvatikā;
a śrāddha offered at all of these yields a hundred times ten million-fold merit.
In that very place is Pitṛtīrtha, where the river Godāvarī flows with its waters entirely internal, joined by a thousand liṅgas.
That supreme tīrtha of Jamadagnya arrived there in due course;
it was there that the river Godāvarī was split asunder out of fear of Pratīka.
That sacred ford, known as Apsaroyuga,
is superior by hundreds of millions for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, for funeral rites (*śrāddha*), for fire-rituals (*agnikārya*), and for acts of charity.
Likewise, there is Sahasralinga and the supreme Raghaveshvara,
where the holy river Sendraphena flows, in which Indra fell in ancient times.
Having slain Namuci, Śakra attained heaven through asceticism;
a śrāddha offered there by men shall yield infinite fruit.
The sacred ford named Puṣkara, as well as Śālagrāma,
and the famous Somapāna, where the abode of Vaiśvānara is located.
The sacred ford named Sārasvata, as well as Svāmitīrtha,
the holy river Malandarā, the Kauśikī, and likewise the Candrikā.
The Vaidarbhā and the Vairā, the Payoṣṇī flowing eastward,
the holy Kāverī to the north, and likewise the Jālandhara mountain.
At these shraddha-tirthas, one obtains infinite merit from performing a shraddha;
likewise at Lohadanda and Citrakuta. (Matsya Purana 22.64)
The Vindhya-yoga, the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā, the Kubjābhra-tīrtha, and likewise the Urvaśī-pulina. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.65)
The Saṃsāramocana Tīrtha and likewise the Ṛṇamocana;
at these ancestral Tīrthas, one obtains infinite merit through the performance of Śrāddha.
Likewise Aṭṭahāsa, the Tīrtha, and Gautameśvara;
and also Vasiṣṭhatīrtha, and after that Hārīta.
Brahmāvarta, Kuśāvarta, Hayatīrtha,
as well as the famous Piṇḍāraka, and likewise Śaṅkhoddhāra.
Ghaṇṭeśvara, Bilvaka, and Nīlaparvata,
as well as Dharaṇītīrtha and likewise Rāmatīrtha.
And there is the famous Aśvatīrtha, which is infinite for those who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) and give gifts;
likewise, there is the holy ford named Vedaśiras and the river Oghavatī.
The sacred ford named Vasuprada, and likewise Chāgalāṇḍa—those who offer śrāddha at these places go to the supreme state. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.71)
Likewise, there is Badarītīrtha and Gaṇatīrtha,
as well as Jayanta, Vijaya, and likewise Śakratīrtha.
Likewise, there is the holy site of Śrīpati, as well as the Raivataka Tīrtha;
similarly, there is the Śāradā Tīrtha and likewise Bhadrakāleśvara.
At Vaikuṇṭhatīrtha, at the supreme Bhīmeśvara, or likewise at these other sites,
those who offer the śrāddha rite attain the highest goal.
The sacred ford named Mātṛgṛha, as well as Karavīrapura,
the famous Kuśeśaya, and Gaurīśikhara as well.
Likewise, there is the sacred ford of Nakuleśa, as well as Kardamāla;
similarly, there is Diṇḍipuṇyakara and Puṇḍarīkapura.
The Saptagodāvarī-tīrtha is the sovereign lord of all lords of sacred fords;
those desiring infinite fruit should offer the śrāddha there. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.77)
This summary of the sacred fords has been declared by me only in brief;
even the Lord of Speech himself would not be able to describe them in detail, much less a human being.
Truth is a sacred ford, compassion is a sacred ford, and the restraint of the senses is a sacred ford;
indeed, it is declared that for those of all castes and stages of life, even one's own home is a sacred ford.
That śrāddha which is performed at these sacred fords (tīrthas) is held to be ten million times more meritorious;
therefore, one should perform the śrāddha at a sacred ford with great effort. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.80)
The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the forenoon (saṃgava) is of the same duration;
midday should consist of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon follows thereafter. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.81)
The evening consists of three muhūrtas; one should not perform a śrāddha at that time.
That period is called Rākṣasī and is censured for all ritual acts.
The muhūrtas of the day are always known to be fifteen;
among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the time called *kutapa*.
Since the sun always becomes dim at midday,
therefore the commencement of that [rite] at that time is distinguished as yielding infinite fruit.
Midday, a sword, a vessel, as well as a Nepalese blanket, silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter’s son is remembered as the eighth. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.85)
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; because these eight cause torment (saṃtāpa) to such a person, they are therefore renowned as the *kutapas*.
The four muhūrtas that follow the Kutapa muhūrta,
making five muhūrtas in total, are considered the abode of the Svadhā offering.
"Kuśa grasses and black sesame seeds produced from the body of Viṣṇu are sufficient for the protection of the śrāddha; so say the dwellers of heaven. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.88)
Those residing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) who remain in the water should offer a handful of sesame-water with a single hand holding darbha grass; in this way, the śrāddha is especially distinguished.
At the time of performing the śrāddha, the offering is given with one hand;
however, the libation (tarpaṇa) must be given with both hands—this is the rule always remembered.
Sūta said:

Formerly, on Mount Malaya, there was recounted the meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging glorification of sacred fords (tīrthas) and ancestral rites (śrāddhas), which destroys all sins. *Matsya Purāṇa* 22.91.
The man who hears it or even recites it becomes illustrious.

And at the time of the śrāddha ceremony, those residing at sacred fords (tīrtha) should likewise recite it for the sake of pacifying all sins; it is the supreme destroyer of misfortune (alakṣmī). (Matsya Purāṇa 22.93)
The experts declare that this greatness of the Śrāddha rite is a purifier and a repository of glory; it removes the great sins of men and is honored even by Brahmā, the Sun, and Rudra.
Matsya Purāṇa 23. The sages said:
"How did Soma, who is learned in the scriptures, become the lord of the ancestors?"
And those kings who belonged to that lineage were increasers of their fame.
Sūta said:
In former times, at the beginning of the process of creation, Atri was commanded by Brahmā;
that lord then performed a supreme austerity for the sake of creation.
That Brahman which bestows bliss, which destroys the afflictions of the world, and which lies beyond the senses within Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra; MatsP_23.3 //
O Brahmins, that which brings about peace, possesses a peaceful mind, and resides within the inner eye, produces supreme bliss through its majesty and ascetic power.
Because the Lord of Umā was presided over by Umā herself,
upon seeing him, Soma became a child with only an eighth part remaining.
Then, from his two eyes, there flowed downward that light born of water,
illuminating the entire universe, including all things moving and stationary, with its moonlight-like radiance.
Desiring a son, they took up that abode in the form of women;
having become a fetus within their wombs, it remained there for three hundred years.
Then, being unable to sustain it, Āśā released the embryo;
thereafter, the Four-faced One took up that embryo and unified it.
Then the Lord Brahmā made that man young, equipped with all weapons,
and placed him upon a chariot drawn by a thousand horses and composed of the power of the Vedas.
Having brought the world to his own realm, that Grandfather was addressed there by the celestial sages: "May he be our lord. (Matsya Purāṇa 23.10)
The sages, gods, gandharvas, and likewise the medicinal herbs,
as well as Brahmā and the others, praised him with collections of mantras dedicated to the deity Soma.
As he was being praised, there arose an even greater manifestation of his splendor;
from the expansion of his brilliance, a multitude of divine medicinal herbs appeared upon the earth.
Therefore, its radiance is always greater at night;
for that reason, Soma became the lord of medicinal herbs and is also called the lord of the twice-born.
And this lunar orb, which is the essence of the abode of the Vedas,
waxes and wanes at all times during the bright and dark fortnights.
And Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave him twenty-seven daughters of great luster,
endowed with beauty and charm.
Then, for ten thousand times a thousand padmas,
the Moon performed austerities, solely intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu.
Then the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Supreme Self, Janārdana, being pleased, said to him, "Choose a boon. (MatsP 23.17)
Then Soma chose his boons: "I shall conquer the world of Śakra;
let those who enjoy [the fruits of their deeds] appear visibly in my palace. (Matsya Purāṇa 23.18)
"In the Rājasūya sacrifice, let the hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā be my officiating priests;
let Śiva, the wielder of the trident, be our protector against the Rākṣasas. (Matsya Purāṇa 23.19)
Having been told "So be it" by Viṣṇu, he undertook the Rājasūya sacrifice;
Atri was the Hotṛ, Bhṛgu the Adhvaryu, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) was the Udgātṛ.
Hari himself became his officiating priest (brahmán),
while Sanaka and the others are recorded as the assistant priests (sadasyas) in that Rājasūya ritual.
The Viśvedevas were the *camasādhvaryu* priests there; indeed, they numbered ten.
The three worlds were given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) by him to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). (Matsya Purāṇa 23.22)
Then, when the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) was completed, nine goddesses, their limbs tormented by the arrows of love and longing to behold his form, attended upon him.
Lakṣmī abandoned Nārāyaṇa, Sinīvālī abandoned Kardama, Dyuti abandoned Vibhāvasu, and likewise Tuṣṭi abandoned the imperishable Dhātṛ. (Matsya Purāṇa 23.24)
Prabhā left Prabhākara, Kuhū herself left Haviṣmān,
Kīrti left her husband Jayanta, and Vasu left Mārīca-Kaśyapa.
Then, having abandoned steadfastness, she drank the Nandī-soma;
at that time, Soma himself desired her as if she were his own.
Thus, when they had committed such an offense, their group of husbands was then unable to retaliate against that transgression with curses, weapons, or other means.
Nevertheless, the Moon shone while illuminating the ten directions;
having attained that sovereignty over the sages which was difficult to obtain,
he then achieved through asceticism the status of sole lord of the seven worlds.
Once, he saw her in a garden, adorned with many flower ornaments;
though her limbs were exceedingly delicate, she was weary from the weight of her broad hips and breasts even as she was breaking off flowers.

And that lord of the stars, afflicted by love, seized Tārā— the wife of the preceptor of the gods, whose long and beautiful eyes were as enchanting as the arrows of the bodiless god— by her hair on a secluded spot of ground.
She too, afflicted by love, took her pleasure with him, whose mind was captivated by the beauty of her form;
after sporting for a long time, the Moon then departed from there as well, taking Tārā with him to his own abode.
Even in his own home, he found no satisfaction amidst the arrival of pleasures, for he was devoted to Tārā;
meanwhile, Bṛhaspati, consumed by the fire of separation from her, became single-mindedly intent on meditation upon her.

The Lord of Speech was unable to cast a curse upon him, nor could he harm him by any means—neither with mantras, weapons, fire, nor poisons in their entirety; not even through various rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*) could he do him injury.
Then, tormented by the god of love for the sake of his wife, he begged Soma out of wretchedness;
yet, though thus entreated, Soma did not give Tārā, being bound by the noose of pleasure with Bṛhaspati.
When the Moon would not surrender her by any means, though entreated by Maheśvara, the four-faced Brahmā, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the world-protectors, Śiva then became overcome with anger.
Vāmadeva, who was renowned upon the earth and whose lotus-feet were worshipped by many Rudras—
then that Giriśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow, accompanied by his disciples and bound by the power of affection for Bṛhaspati, [arrived].

Taking up his bow Ājagava, the Enemy of Tripura, the Lord of Beings honored by the Siddhas, went forth for battle with Soma; his face was formidable with the fire of his third eye, which blazed with exceptional intensity.
Ganesha and the others, accompanied by twenty-six thousand Ganas, went along with them;
and the Lord of the Yakshas, joined by many hundreds of millions, followed those who were seated upon their chariots.
Accompanied by one hundred thousand Vetālas, Yakṣas, and Uragas, as well as one Padma and one Arbuda of Kiṃnaras,
and three million twelve hundred thousand chariots, Soma also went there with his wrath fully aroused.
Accompanied by the hosts of constellations, Daityas, and Asuras, and possessing increased splendor like Śanaiścara and Aṅgāraka,
the seven worlds likewise fell into fear, and the earth, containing its continents and oceans, trembled.
The wielder of the Pināka bow, having taken up a great fire of blazing weapons, advanced against Soma;
then there occurred that great battle between the two armies of Bhīṣaṇa and Bhīmasena.
Increasing as he brought about the destruction of all beings without exception, and appearing solely in the form of blazing sharp weapons and missiles,
the entire army of both sides met its end through those fierce and sharp arms as they struck one another.
Thus, blazing weapons fell, burning the heavens, the earth, and the netherworld;
out of anger, Rudra released the Brahmaśiras missile, and Soma likewise released the Soma-missile of unfailing power.
Then, due to the falling of those two [missiles], there was fear of the ocean, the earth, and the intermediate space;
even the Grandfather (Brahmā), beholding that pair of weapons increased for the destruction of the worlds, [was alarmed].
Then, having entered within, he somehow or other restrained [the gods] along with the deities:
"O Soma, why have you thus performed this deed which causes the destruction of people without cause?"

"O Soma, because you have waged such an exceedingly terrible war to abduct another's wife, you shall become a malefic planet among people; even though you are naturally pacified, you will surely remain so until the end of the white fortnight. Therefore, restore this wife to the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati); there is no dishonor in taking back what belongs to another. (Matsya Purāṇa 23.46)
Sūta said:
"So be it," replied the moon-crested Lord; having desisted from the battle and become pacified, Bṛhaspati took Tārā back and, filled with joy, returned to his own home along with Rudra.
Matsya Purāṇa 24: Sūta said:
Then, at the end of the year, [he appeared] resembling the twelve Ādityas.
Wearing divine yellow garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
Emerging from the belly of Tārā, the prince was like the moon;
he was wise, learned in all treatises on worldly affairs, and the originator of the science of elephant-lore.
That which is known as the *Gajavaidyaka* (Treatise on Elephant Medicine) belonging to the prince is so called because the prince Budha was considered the son of King Soma.
As soon as he was born, that powerful one conquered all splendors;
Brahmā and the other gods, together with the celestial rishis, arrived there.
Then, at the house of Bṛhaspati during the birth-rite festival,
all those gods asked Tārā, "By whom was this young boy born?"
Then, being ashamed, that beautiful woman said nothing at all to them; though questioned again and again, she remained bashful.
After a long time, he said, "Of Soma," and then the Moon took the son;
he gave him the name Budha and bestowed upon him sovereignty on the earth.
Then, having performed the consecration,
the omnipresent Lord Brahmā, accompanied by the Brahman-sages, bestowed upon him the status of equality with a householder and made him preeminent.
While all the gods were looking on, he vanished right there;
and in the womb of Ilā, Budha begot a most righteous son.
He who, by his own splendor, performed more than a hundred horse-sacrifices,
was renowned as Purūravas and was honored by all the worlds.
Having propitiated Janārdana on a delightful peak of the Himavat,
the king then attained sovereignty over the worlds as the lord of the seven continents.
By him, millions of Daityas, beginning with Keśin, were torn asunder;
Urvaśī, infatuated by his beauty, became his wife. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.12)
The earth with its seven islands, including its mountains, forests, and groves,
was protected by him, who desired the welfare of the entire world, through righteousness.
Fame was his chowrie-bearer and always his attendant;
then, by the grace of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods granted him half of his own throne.
He protected virtue, wealth, and pleasure equally and in accordance with righteousness;
in former times, virtue, wealth, and pleasure themselves came out of curiosity to behold him.
"How may those who desire to know his life-story see him equally for us?
Thinking thus, the king then offered them water for their hands and feet, as well as other honors, with devotion.
Having brought three divine seats adorned with gold, he sat down and then performed worship, which was even greater than that previously offered to Dharma.
Driven by desire and greed, they both went to the king and spoke with great anger;
Artha then uttered this curse upon him: "You shall meet your destruction through greed. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.18)
Kāma also said: "Your madness shall arise on Gandhamādana, by resorting to the Kumāra forest due to separation from Urvaśī."
Dharma also said: "O Indra among kings, you shall be long-lived and righteous;
your lineage shall endure as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars."
"May he attain increase by the hundreds and not go to ruin on this earth";
having spoken thus, they all vanished, and the king enjoyed that kingdom. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.21)
Day after day, that king of kings went to see the Lord of the Gods;
once, having mounted his chariot that travels through the southern sky, he departed.
Then, together with Arka, he saw Citralekhā being carried through the sky by Keśin, the lord of the Dānavas, as if she were Urvaśī herself.
Having conquered him in battle with various weapons in hand,
the son of Budha, seeking glory, discharged the Vāyavya weapon.
Likewise, Śakra, who had been thus utterly defeated by him in battle,
entered into friendship with the gods and gave Urvaśī to Indra.
From that time forward, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) attained friendship with him,
as well as a strength, vigor, fame, and splendor that surpassed all the worlds.
Being well-pleased, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Indra) said, "Let it be sung by Bharata," and she,
out of affection for Purūravas, sang that great deed.
He initiated the ceremony known as Lakṣmī-svayaṃvara, which was established by Bharata;
he then commanded Menakā, Urvaśī, and Rambhā, saying, "Dance! (Matsya Purāṇa 24.28).
There, Urvaśī, in the form of Lakṣmī, danced with rhythmic measure;
seeing Purūravas while she was dancing, she was overcome by desire.
Because all the dramatic performances previously taught by Bharata had been forgotten,
Bharata, out of anger at this separation from them on the earth, pronounced a curse.
"For fifty-five years you shall become a subtle creeper;
and Purūravas, too, shall experience the state of a piśāca in that very place."
Then Urvaśī, having gone to him, made him her husband for a long time;
and at the end of the curse, she [became the wife] of Bharata, the son of Budha.
He begot eight sons; learn their names:
Āyu, Dṛḍhāyu, Aśvāyu, Dhanāyu, Dhṛtimat, and Vasu.
Śucividya and Śatāyu were both endowed with divine strength and vigor;
Āyuṣa had two sons, Nahuṣa and likewise Vṛddhaśarmā.
Raji, Dambha, and Vipāpman were five heroic great chariot-warriors (mahārathas).
A hundred sons were born to Raji, renowned as the Rājeyas. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.35)
Raji propitiated the stainless Nārāyaṇa;
Viṣṇu, gratified by his ascetic penance, granted boons, O lord of the earth. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.36)
At that time, he was victorious over the gods, asuras, and humans;
then a war between the gods and asuras took place for three hundred years.
Between Prahlāda and Śakra, neither was victorious over the other;
then, questioned by the gods and asuras, the four-faced Lord spoke.
"Of these two, who shall be the victor? he asked. "Wherever Raji is," the king replied, "be you our ally for the sake of victory. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.39)
He said to the Daityas, "If I become your lord, then that is sufficient";
this was accepted by the Asuras, and likewise accepted by the Suras.
"Be our lord and destroy our enemies in battle.
Thereupon, all those who were otherwise invincible even to the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi) were destroyed.
The powerful Indra, pleased by his deed, granted him the status of a son;
then, having bestowed the kingdom upon Indra, Raji departed for ascetic penance.
Then, endowed with the power and virtues of asceticism, the sons of Raji forcibly seized Indra’s majesty, as well as his sacrificial share and his kingdom.
Then Śakra, deprived of his kingdom and oppressed by the sons of Raji, spoke dejectedly to Vācaspati: "I am being tormented by the sons of Raji."
"O Bṛhaspati, lord of intellect, I have no share in the sacrifice nor do I possess a kingdom; I have been conquered. Therefore, exert yourself on my behalf to secure the attainment of a kingdom."
Then Bṛhaspati made Śakra proud with power through the performance of rites for the pacification of planetary influences and through nourishing rituals.
Then Bṛhaspati, though a knower of the Vedas, went there and deluded the sons of Raji by adopting a Jaina doctrine that was outside the Vedic fold.
Having recognized them as being outside the Vedas and endowed with dialectical reasoning, the Lord of Intellect (Bṛhaspati) rendered those who had fallen away from the three Vedas [into heretics].
Śakra struck with his thunderbolt all those who were excluded from the dharma;
I shall now proclaim the seven righteous sons of Nahuṣa.
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Udbhava, Pāci,
Śaryāti, and Meghajāti— these seven were the increasers of the lineage.
Yati, even while still in his youth, became a yogi and a forest-dweller;
and Yayāti, always taking refuge solely in dharma, ruled the kingdom.
Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, was his wife,
as was Devayānī, the daughter of Bhārgava and a woman of virtuous vows.
Yayāti had five heirs; I shall name them:
Devayānī gave birth to a son, Yadu, and also to Turvasu.
Likewise, Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to the sons Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru;
among them, Yadu and Pūru became the increasers of their lineages.
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was a king of true prowess;
he protected the earth and performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.55)
Having always worshipped the ancestors and the gods with great devotion and self-restraint,
the unconquered Yayāti then conquered all his subjects.
Protecting his subjects with righteousness for eternal years, that king,
the son of Nahuṣa, reached a most terrible old age that destroys beauty.
Overcome by old age, that king, the monarch, spoke these words to his sons:
Yadu, Pūru, Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu.
"O sons, I desire to enjoy with young women the fickle pleasures of youth; please assist me. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.59)
To him, his elder son Yadu, born of Devayānī, said:
"You must perform assistance for us; what is the use of youth to you?"
Yayāti said to his sons: "Let my old age be accepted by you;
then, with your youth, I shall enjoy the objects of the senses."
"O sons, because of my long sacrificial sessions and the curse of the sage Uśanas, my purpose for desire has been frustrated; therefore, I remain unsatisfied. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.62)
"May he dispel this old age from you with his own body;
may I, becoming young through his fresh form, attain my desires. (Matsya Purāṇa 24.63)
Yadu and the others did not accept his old age;
we have heard that the royal seer cursed those four as follows.
Then Puru, the youngest of them and one whose valor was true, said to him:
"Do not give me your old age; instead, remain happy in your own youth through my new body."
"I shall take your old age and remain in the kingdom by your command.
Thus addressed, that royal sage, relying on the power of his asceticism, [consented].
Then, by means of the Paurava's age, the king transferred his old age to his high-souled son and himself assumed youth.
Then, having assumed the kingdom through Yayāti’s vital energy, Pūru ruled;
thereafter, at the end of a thousand years, the unconquered Yayāti [departed].
As if insatiable in his desires, he said to his son Pūru:
"Through you I possess a true heir; you are the son who shall perpetuate my lineage."
"This lineage shall attain renown in the world as the Paurava dynasty.
Then that tiger among kings, having consecrated Pūru upon the throne, [departed].
After a long time, he eventually succumbed to the law of time.
O best of sages, listen as I shall proclaim the lineage of Puru,
in which those Bharatas were born who increased the dynasty of Bharata.
Matsya Purāṇa 25:
The sages said,
"For what reason did the Paurava lineage attain preeminence upon the earth?"
Why does even the lineage of Yadu, the eldest, decline in prosperity?
O Sūta, relate in detail another account of Yayāti’s life,
for it is meritorious, conducive to long life, and worthy of being celebrated even by the gods.
Sūta said: In former times, Śatānīka asked Śaunaka about this very same great, meritorious, purifying, and life-prolonging account of Yayāti’s life.
Śatānīka said:
"Our ancestor Yayāti was the tenth from Prajāpati;
how did he obtain the daughter of Śukra, who is so exceedingly difficult to attain?"
O one whose wealth is asceticism, I desire to hear this in detail;
tell me in due order of the kings who maintained the lineage of Puru.
Śaunaka said:
There was once a royal sage named Yayāti, whose splendor was equal to that of the king of the gods;
how it was that Śukra and Vṛṣaparvan chose him as their son-in-law in the past.
I shall relate that to you as you ask, O best of kings:
the union of Devayānī with Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
A mutual rivalry indeed arose between the gods and the asuras for sovereignty over the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Then, desiring victory, the gods chose the sage Aṅgiras for the office of domestic priest for the sake of the sacrifice, while the others chose Kāvya Uśanas.
Those two brahmins were always in intense rivalry with one another;
there, the gods slew those Dānavas who had encountered them in battle.
Kāvya, relying on the power of his knowledge, brought them back to life;
then, having risen once more, they fought against the gods.
But those gods whom the Asuras slew at the forefront of the battle,
the noble-minded Bṛhaspati did not restore them to life.
For he did not know that science which the powerful Kāvya knew—the Saṃjīvanī; therefore, the gods fell into extreme despair.
Then the gods, agitated by fear of Kāvya Uśanas,
approached Kaca, the eldest son of Bṛhaspati, and spoke to him.
Favor us who honor you; grant us your supreme assistance regarding that lore which resides within this Brahmin of immeasurable splendor.
"O Śukra, bring her back quickly; you shall become a sharer in our portion.
That brahmin can be found by you in the presence of Vṛṣaparvan. (Matsya Purāṇa 25.16)
There he protects the Dānavas, but he does not protect those who are not Dānavas;
no one other than you is capable of propitiating him. (Matsya Purāṇa 25.17)
And Devayānī was the beloved daughter of that great-souled one;
no one else exists who is capable of propitiating her.
Through your virtue, courtesy, sweetness, conduct, and self-restraint,
when Devayānī is pleased, you will certainly obtain that knowledge.
Then, having been sent by the gods to the presence of Vṛṣaparvan, Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, said "So be it" and departed. (Matsya Purāṇa 25.20)
Having gone there quickly, O King, Kaca, honored by the gods,
approached Śukra in the city of the lord of the Asuras and, having prostrated before him, spoke these words.
"May your lordship accept me as a disciple—grandson of the seer Aṅgiras and the direct son of Bṛhaspati, renowned by the name Kaca. (Matsya Purāṇa 25.22)
"O supreme teacher, I shall practice the life of celibacy under you;
O Brahmin, grant me permission for a thousand years."
Śukra said: "O Kaca, a very warm welcome to you! I accept your words.
I shall honor you, who are worthy of honor; may Bṛhaspati be honored through you."
Śaunaka said: Kaca,
having replied "So be it," undertook that vow as instructed by Śukra Uśanas himself, the son of Kaśyapa.
O descendant of Bharata, he undertook the vow and observed its duration exactly as prescribed, thereby propitiating both his preceptor and Devayānī.
Constantly seeking to please her, who was within the range of his youth, the young man delighted Devayānī by singing, dancing, and playing musical instruments. (Matsya Purāṇa 25.27)
Cultivating the path of the gods, he gratified the daughter of Bhṛgu, who had reached the bloom of youth, with flowers, fruits, and various services.
Then Devayānī also, that beautiful woman, followed and attended upon that brahmin who was observing his restrictive vows in secret, singing along with him.
When the Dānavas perceived that Kaca had been practicing such intense vows for five hundred years, they then [acted against] him.
Seeing him tending the cows in the forest, they,
filled with indignation out of hatred for Bṛhaspati and solely for the sake of protecting their own cattle, killed him.
Having slaughtered them and cut them into pieces as small as sesame seeds, they gave them to the jackals;
thereafter, those cows returned to their own dwelling without a cowherd.

Seeing that the cows had returned from the forest without Kaca, Devayānī then spoke these words at the proper time to the descendant of Bhṛgu: mama priyasya kaccit tvaṃ na kiṃcid aparādhyasi / kutaḥ sa dīrghakeśānte kaco madvacanādiha // MatsP_25.34 // "O lady with long, beautiful hair, have you perhaps done something wrong to my beloved?
