for according to dharma, O beautiful one, the husband of a friend becomes one's own husband.
"You are worthy of worship by me and deserving of my respect; you are the most excellent and the eldest among the Brahmin women.
For the royal sage is even more worthy of my worship than you—do you not know that? (Matsya Purāṇa 32.22)
Śaunaka said: Having heard her words, Devayānī then spoke this:
"O King, I shall not dwell here today; you have done me a displeasure. (Matsya Purāṇa 32.23)
Seeing Śyāmā suddenly rise up with tearful eyes and quickly set out toward the presence of Kāvya, he was then deeply distressed.
The king followed behind her in great agitation, trying to appease her;
but she, her eyes bloodshot with anger, did not turn back.
Saying nothing at all to the king, her eyes filled with tears,
she soon arrived in the presence of Kāvya Uśanas.
Upon seeing her father, she saluted him and stood before him;
immediately thereafter, Yayāti honored the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Devayānī said:
"Dharma has been defeated by adharma; the world has turned upside down. Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, has overstepped all bounds."
"Three sons were begotten upon her by this King Yayāti;
but I have two sons, O dear one, born of me who am unfortunate—I tell you this."
O descendant of Bhrigu, this king is renowned as a knower of dharma;
yet he has transgressed the bounds of propriety, O Kavya—this I tell you.
Śukra said:
"O great king, you who know the dharma yet have committed an unrighteous act for the sake of pleasure—
for that reason, invincible old age shall soon overcome you."
Yayāti said:

"O Brahmin, that man who, though chosen by a woman, does not grant her the opportunity for conception when she requests it, is called a 'slayer of an embryo' (bhrūṇahan) here in this world by those who discourse on the Veda."
He who, when requested in private by a woman desiring intercourse during her fertile season and fit for approach,
does not unite with her according to dharma, is called a slayer of a Brahmin by the wise.
Having considered these reasons, O descendant of Bhṛgu,
I approached Śarmiṣṭhā, agitated by the fear of unrighteousness.
Śukra said:
"But you are not to be scrutinized by me; you are dependent on me, O King.
Among those whose conduct is false, there is no theft, O son of Nahuṣa."
Śaunaka said: Having been cursed by Uśanas out of anger, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa,
then immediately lost his former youth and was overtaken by old age.
Yayāti said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, I am not yet satiated with youth in the company of Devayānī. O Brahmin, show me favor; let this old age not enter me. (Matsya Purāṇa 32.37)
Śukra said:
"I do not speak this falsely; you have reached old age, O lord of the earth.
However, if you so desire, you may transfer this old age onto another. (Matsya Purāṇa 32.38)
Yayāti said:
"O Brahmin, let that son who gives me his youth become the heir to the kingdom, as well as the heir to merit and fame; may you grant your consent to this. (Matsya Purāṇa 32.39)
Śukra said: "O son of Nahuṣa, by meditating upon me in truth, you shall transfer your old age as you desire,
and you shall incur no sin."
Your son will grant you long life; he shall become a king, possessed of longevity, renown, and likewise many offspring.
Matsya Purāṇa 33:
Śaunaka said:
Having reached old age and having indeed returned to his own city, Yayāti—
The twice-born one spoke thus to his eldest and most excellent son, Yadu: Matsya Purāṇa 33.1.
Yayāti said:
"O dear one, old age, wrinkles, and grey hair have come upon me because of the curse of Kāvya Uśanas; yet I am not yet satiated with youth."
O Yadu, accept this evil along with old age;
with your youth, I shall enjoy the objects of the senses.
"When a full thousand years have passed, I shall give you my youth and take back my own sin along with old age. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.4)
"What Yadu said—
[he who was] white-bearded, dejected, made frail by old age,
his body covered in wrinkles, unsightly, weak, and emaciated."
In his youth, he was unable to accomplish his duties and was treated with contempt;
therefore, along with those who depend on him for their livelihood, I do not desire old age for him.
"O King, you have many sons who are dearer to you than I;
O knower of dharma, choose another son to take upon yourself this old age. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.7)
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth,
because of this sinful connection with your maternal uncle, your offspring shall be wicked."
"O Turvasu, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age;
O son, I would indeed enjoy the objects of the senses through your youth."
"When a full thousand years have passed, I shall indeed give back my youth;
in that same way, I shall take back my evil along with old age. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.10)
Turvasu said:
"O father, I do not desire old age, which destroys the enjoyment of desires,
brings an end to strength and beauty, and ruins the intellect."
Yayāti said: "O Turvasu,
since you, though born from my heart, do not grant me your youth,
therefore your progeny shall meet with total extinction."
"You will surely become a king over worlds that are mixed with the ways of thieves, those who act in a perverted manner, and those who feed on flesh. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.13)
"You shall prevail over those who are attached to the wives of their gurus, those who take pleasure in animal births, those barbarians who follow the ways of beasts, and those who are sinful."
Śaunaka said:
Having thus cursed his own son Turvasu, Yayāti spoke these words to Druhyu, the eldest son of Śarmiṣṭhā. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.15)
Yayāti said:
"O Druhyu, accept for a thousand years this old age of mine which destroys complexion and form, and give me your own youth."
"When a full thousand years have passed, I shall grant you youth, and I myself shall take back my own sin along with old age. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.17)
Druhyu said: "An old man enjoys neither kingdom, nor chariot, nor horse, nor woman; nor does passion arise in him. Therefore, I do not desire that old age for you. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.18)
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth,
therefore that beloved desire of yours shall never be fulfilled."
Where there will always be the movement of ships and floods,
there you, along with your lineage, shall obtain the title of "Arājya-bhoja."
Yayāti said:
"O Anu, accept my sin along with my old age;
for one thousand years, I would like to live with your youth."
Anu said:
"He who, though old, eats food like a child at the improper time, or like one who is impure,
and does not offer oblations to the fire at the proper time— that kind of old age I do not desire."
Yayāti said:
"Since you, who were born from my heart, do not grant me your youth, you shall therefore undergo the defect of old age that you have described. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.23)
Moreover, O Anu, your subjects who have reached youth will perish;
and you too shall likewise meet your end by leaping into fire. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.24)
Yayāti said: "O Pūru, take upon yourself my evil along with this old age;
you are my most beloved son, and you shall become the most excellent."
"O dear one, old age, wrinkles, and grey hair have come upon me because of the curse of Kāvya Uśanas; yet I am not yet satiated with youth. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.26)
"Indeed, for a short time I shall enjoy the objects of the senses through your lineage;
when a thousand years are complete, however, I shall return your youth and take back my own sin along with old age. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.27)
Śaunaka said:
Thus addressed, Pūru immediately replied to his father:
"O Great King, I shall do exactly as you have said; I will carry out your word."
"O King, I shall take upon myself your evil along with my old age;
take my youth from me and enjoy all desires as you wish. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.29)
"Concealed by old age, I have assumed your form and youth;
having given my youth to you, I shall wander according to my own will. (Matsya Purāṇa 33.30)
Yayāti said: "O Pūru, I am pleased with you, my child; I grant you this boon:
your progeny shall have all their desires fulfilled."
Matsya Purāṇa 34.
Śaunaka said:
Having been addressed thus, that royal sage remembered Kāvya, who is observer of great vows.
Then he transferred his old age into his high-souled son.
Then, with the youth of Puru, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa and best among men,
being filled with joy, enjoyed his beloved objects of sense.
According to his desire, according to his energy, according to the time, and according to what is pleasant—
that very king of kings indeed [should bestow] things not contrary to the Dharma, as each person deserves.
He gratified the gods with sacrifices, the ancestors with funeral rites,
the wretched with favors, and the best of the twice-born with their desired objects.
He [should protect] guests with food and drink, the Vaiśyas by means of protection,
the Śūdras through kindness, and the Dasyus by suppression.
And pleasing all his subjects according to righteousness as was fitting,
Yayāti protected them like a second Indra in person.
That king, possessing the prowess of a lion, being young and engaged in the objects of the senses,
lived in supreme happiness without violating the Dharma.
Having obtained those auspicious desires, the king, though satisfied, became weary;
at the end of a thousand years, that lord of men recalled his vow.
Having reflected upon this, that heroic king, who knew the divisions of time down to the smallest units,
and perceiving that the appointed time was fulfilled, spoke to his son Pūru.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon the earth—all that is not enough for even one person; realizing this, one should attain tranquility.
"O subduer of enemies, O son, I have enjoyed the objects of the senses according to my pleasure, my energy, and my desire during my youth. (Matsya Purāṇa 34.12)
"O Pūru, I am pleased; may prosperity be yours! Take back this youth of yours, and take this kingdom as well, for you are my son who has done what was pleasing to me."
Śaunaka said: At that time, King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, attained old age,
while Pūru regained his own youth once again.

When King Pūru, his youngest son, desired to be consecrated, the social orders, headed by the brahmins, spoke these words: matsya purāṇa 34.15 (196) The social orders, headed by the brahmins, spoke these words to King Pūru, his youngest son, who was desirous of being consecrated.
O Lord, how can you bypass Śukra’s grandson, the son of Devayānī,
who is the eldest, and bestow the kingdom upon Pūru?
Jadu was your eldest son, and Turvasu followed after him;
then there were Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā, as well as Anu and Pūru. (Matsya Purāṇa 34.17)
"How can the younger brother deserve the kingdom by bypassing the elder? We inform you of this; observe your own dharma. (Matsya Purāṇa 34.18)
Yayāti said: "Let all the social orders, headed by the Brāhmaṇas, hear my words:
for this reason, the kingdom must never be given by me to the eldest."
My eldest son Yadu has not obeyed my command;
he who is hostile toward his father is not considered a true son by the virtuous. (Matsya Purāṇa 34.20)

That son who carries out the words of his mother and father, who is beneficial and well-disposed toward them, and he who behaves toward his parents as a son should—such a one is truly a son. (Matsya Purāṇa 34.21)
Just as I was disregarded by Yadu,
so too was I treated with equal contempt by Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu.
My word was carried out by Pūru and especially honored;
he, my youngest heir, took upon himself my old age.
"That desire of mine has been fulfilled by Pūru, who took the form of my son;
and Śukra himself, Uśanas Kāvya, granted me this boon. (Matsya Purāṇa 34.24)
"That son who follows you shall be the king, the lord of the earth;
let your honors grant your assent: let Pūru be consecrated in the kingdom."
The subjects said:
"A son who is endowed with virtues and is always devoted to the welfare of his mother and father deserves all auspiciousness; even if he is the youngest, he is the master."
"This kingdom belongs to Arhan Pūru, who is dear to you and does what is pleasing to you;
because of Śukra’s boon, it is not possible to give a reply [to the contrary]. (Matsya Purāṇa 34.27)
Śaunaka said:
Having been thus addressed by the satisfied citizens and country-folk, the son of Nahuṣa then consecrated his own son, Pūru, in the kingdom. *Matsya Purāṇa* 34.28.
Having bestowed the kingdom upon Pūru, the king consecrated himself for forest life;
he departed from the city accompanied by brahmins and ascetics.
From Yadu were born the Yādavas; from Turvasu, the sons were the Yavanas;
the Bhojas were the sons of Druhyu; and from Anu came the Mleccha tribes.
The lineage of Puru is the Paurava dynasty, O King, in which you were born;
this kingdom has come down through the Kuru family for a thousand years.
Matsya Purāṇa 35:
Śaunaka said:
Thus did that king Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, [speak to] his desired son.
Having consecrated him in the kingdom, the sage joyfully became a forest-dweller.
Having dwelt in forest life in the company of brahmins,
subsisting on fruits and roots and self-controlled, he departed from here as if to heaven.
Having gone there, he dwelt in the celestial abode, joyful and happy;
after no great length of time, he was cast down again by Śakra.
"Helpless, fallen from heaven yet not having reached the surface of the earth, he remained suspended in mid-air; so have I heard. (Matsya Purāṇa 35.4)
From that very place, the powerful one went once again to heaven; so says the sacred tradition— that he did so after meeting with King Vasumān, Aṣṭaka,
Pratardana, and Śibi in an assembly.
Śatānīka said: "By what action did that lord of the earth reach heaven again,
and how, O Blessed One, was he cast down to the surface of the earth by Indra?"
"O Brahmin, I wish to hear all of this in its entirety and according to the truth as it is being told by you in the presence of the hosts of celestial sages."
For Yayāti, the lord of the earth, was equal to the king of the gods;
he was the enhancer of the Kuru lineage and possessed a splendor like that of the sun.
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear in its entirety, both here and in heaven, the account of that great-souled one of far-reaching fame and true renown.
Śaunaka said: "Behold, I shall relate to you the most excellent story of Yayāti,
which is meritorious in both heaven and here on earth, and which destroys all sins."
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, having consecrated his youngest son Pūru upon the throne,
then joyfully departed for the forest.
Having settled his sons, headed by Yadu, in the outlying regions,
that king dwelt for a long time in the forest, subsisting on fruits and roots.
Having conquered his self and subdued his anger, he gratified the ancestors and the gods,
and offered oblations into the fires according to the rules prescribed for the forest-dweller stage of life.
Constantly honoring guests with forest-grown offerings, the Lord,
adopting the practice of gleaning ears of grain, took his meals from the remnants of food.
For a full thousand years, the king maintained this conduct;
for three years he remained subsisting on water alone, with his speech and mind fully restrained.
Thereafter, he subsisted on air alone for a year without weariness,
and again for another year he performed austerities in the midst of five fires.
Standing on one foot for six months while subsisting only on air,
Puṇyakīrti thereafter ascended to heaven, pervading both heaven and earth.
Matsya-Purāṇa 36: Śaunaka said:
Having gone to heaven, that lord of kings dwelt in the abode of the gods.
He was worshipped by the thirty gods, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and likewise the Vasus.
Moving from the world of the gods to the world of Brahmā, that merit-performing master of his senses dwelt as a protector of the earth for a long time; so says the sacred tradition.
Once, that best of kings, Yayāti, having come to Śakra,
was questioned there by Śakra at the conclusion of their conversation, O lord of the earth.
Śakra said:
"O King, when that Pūru, having taken your old age upon himself, wandered about in the world, what did you say to him after handing over the kingdom? Tell me the truth here."
Yayāti said:
"With the approval of my subjects, I installed Pūru on the throne and spoke thus:
'This entire territory between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is yours.'"
"You are the king in the center of the earth; your brothers are the rulers at its borders."

One who is free from anger is superior to those who are angry; likewise, one who is patient is superior to one who is impatient. A human being is superior to non-humans, and in the same way, a wise man is superior to the ignorant.
When reviled, one should not revile in return; rather, one endures that very anger.
Such a person consumes the reviler and gains the reviler's merit.
One should not be a wounder of others, nor a speaker of cruel words; one should not take from another what belongs to an inferior.
One should not utter harsh speech, born of sinful greed, by which another might be agitated. ||| MatsP_36.8 |||
One should know that man who strikes the vital parts, who speaks harsh words, and who pierces people with the thorns of his speech,
as the most unfortunate among men— he carries Destruction (Nirṛti) fixed within his mouth.
One should be honored by the virtuous in front, and likewise protected by the virtuous from behind;
one should always endure the insults of the virtuous, guarding the conduct of the virtuous while being well-conducted oneself.
Word-arrows fly forth from the mouth; struck by them, one grieves for three days. They do not strike the vital organs of another; therefore, a wise man should not discharge them at others.
There is no such means of enchantment in the three worlds as there is for friendliness toward the worlds, generosity, and sweet speech.
Therefore, one should always speak kindly and never speak harshly;
one should honor those worthy of honor and should never utter a curse. (Matsya Purāṇa 36.13)
Matsya Purāṇa 37:
Indra said:
"O King, having completed all your duties, you have abandoned your home and gone to the forest."
O son of Nahuṣa, O Yayāti, I ask you about the truth: with whom are you equal in ascetic power?
Yayāti said:
"O Vāsava, among gods and humans, or among Gandharvas and great sages, I do not see anyone who is equal to myself in ascetic power."
Indra said:

"Since you disregarded those who were your equals, as well as those superior and inferior to you, being ignorant of their true power, therefore these worlds of yours are now finite; when your merit was exhausted, O King, you have fallen today."
Yayāti said: "O King of the Gods, if my worlds in Śakra’s realm have come to ruin due to my contempt for the celestial sages, Gandharvas, and men, then,
deprived of the world of the gods, I wish to fall into the midst of the virtuous."
Indra said:
"O King, you have fallen into the presence of the virtuous—those from whom, once fallen, one may regain a firm standing.
Knowing this, O Yayāti, you must never again despise those who are your equals or those who are superior."
Śaunaka said: Then,
seeing Yayāti falling from that meritorious world frequented by the king of the immortals, Aṣṭaka, the best of royal sages and protector of the ordinances of true dharma, spoke to him.
Aṣṭaka said: Who are you, a youth whose form is equal to Vāsava, blazing with your own splendor like fire;
falling from the sky like a towering cloud, appearing like the sun, the foremost among those who move through the heavens?

Having seen you falling from the path of the sun, immeasurable and possessing the splendor of Vaiśvānara and the sun, we are all utterly bewildered, wondering, "What indeed is this that is falling? as we reflect upon it.
And having seen you established on the path of the gods, possessing a splendor equal to that of Śakra, Arka, and Viṣṇu,
we have all come forth today to meet you, desiring to know about your descent from there.
Nor did those bold ones dare to question you first, nor do you ask us who we are;
therefore I ask you, O one of enviable form: to whom do you belong, and for what purpose have you come?
"Let your fear depart, and quickly cast off despondency and delusion, O you whose form is equal to the Lord of the Gods!
For even Śakra, the slayer of Bala, would not be able to endure you while you remain in the company of the virtuous."
O you who are like the king of the immortals, the virtuous are indeed the refuge for those fallen from happiness;
they, the lords of the moving and the unmoving, are ever united, and you are established among such worthy beings.
Fire is the master in heating; the earth is the master in receiving seeds;
the sun is the master through illumination; and a guest is the master of the virtuous.
Matsya Purāṇa 38:
Yayāti said,
"I am Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa and the father of Pūru, [fallen] due to my contempt for all beings."
I have been cast down from the world of the gods and Siddhas; fallen and possessing little merit, I am plummeting.
For I am indeed older than you in age; therefore, I do not offer a formal salutation to you.
Among the twice-born, he alone truly qualifies as an elder who is advanced in knowledge, austerity, or birth.
Aṣṭaka said:
"O King, you have indeed declared that you are superior to me in some way because of your age;
however, he who is truly wise and advanced through asceticism (*tapas*) is the one who is worthy of honor among the twice-born."
Yayāti said:
"They say that action contrary to [dharma] is sinful for those who abide therein; it leads downward to the world of the wicked.
The virtuous do not follow the unrighteous, provided that among them there is one who speaks against such conduct."
"I once possessed vast and great wealth; by striving, I was its master.
Having reflected thus and being intent on his own welfare, the wise man who conducts himself accordingly understands [the truth].
In the world of living beings, there are many diverse conditions dependent on fate, wherein one's power of action and authority are lost;
having encountered each of these, the wise man should not be distressed, considering through his own intelligence that destiny is all-powerful.
For a living being experiences either happiness or even suffering as dependent on destiny, not by its own power;
therefore, considering fate to be powerful, one should neither grieve nor ever rejoice.

The wise man should not suffer in sorrow nor rejoice in happiness; he should always conduct himself with equanimity, thinking that destiny is all-powerful, neither burning with grief nor ever rejoicing.
O Aṣṭaka, I am never bewildered by fear, nor is there any distress in my mind;
for I consider that I shall certainly become whatever the Creator ordains for me in this world. (Matsya Purāṇa 38.9)
For those born of moisture, those born from eggs, those that sprout from the earth, reptiles, worms, and fish in the water—
as well as stones, grass, and wood— all revert to their own original nature when their allotted time has ended.
Having realized that pleasure and pain are impermanent, why should I, O Aṣṭakā, indulge in distress?
What indeed should I do, and by doing what would I not suffer? Therefore, being vigilant, I shall avoid distress.

Śaunaka said: To King Yayāti, who was speaking thus, Aṣṭaka then questioned once more his maternal grandfather, who was endowed with every virtue, regarding exactly how he remained in the heavenly world.
Aṣṭaka said:

"O lord of kings, tell me truly and in its entirety, O King, which principal worlds were enjoyed by you, at what time, and in what manner; for you speak of dharma like one who possesses the knowledge of the field (kṣetrajña). (Matsya Purāṇa 38.13)
Yayāti said:

"I was once a king here, a sovereign of the whole earth; from there, I attained great and imperishable worlds. I dwelt there for a full thousand years, and from there I ascended to the supreme worlds."
Then, for a full thousand years, he dwelt in the beautiful city of Indra, which had a thousand gates and extended for a hundred yojanas; thereafter, he attained the supreme worlds.

Then, having attained the divine, undecaying world of Prajāpati, which is difficult even for the lords of the worlds to reach, I dwelt there for a full thousand years; thereafter, I ascended to the supreme worlds.
And having conquered the worlds, I dwelt at will in the abode of every god,
being honored by all the thirty deities, with a power and splendor equal to that of the lords.
Thus dwelling in the Nandana grove, able to assume any form at will, I spent ten million years wandering with the Apsarases, beholding the fragrant, flowering, and beautiful mountains.

While I was staying there, attached to divine pleasures, after a very great length of time had passed, a messenger of the gods of fierce appearance spoke to me with a voice raised three times in a loud, drawn-out tone: "Perish! (MatsP 38.19)
"This much alone is known to me, O lion among kings: thereafter, my merit exhausted, I fell from the Nandana grove;
and I heard the voices of the gods in the sky, lamenting out of compassion for me, O lord of men."
"Suddenly, Yayāti, though a doer of merit and of meritorious fame, falls when his merit is exhausted.
As I fall, I then said to them: 'How indeed may I fall into the midst of the virtuous?'"
Having been informed by them and having inspected this sacrificial ground of yours, I have come here;
I recognize the sacrificial ground indicated by the fragrance of the oblations, which is enveloped in a fringe of smoke.
Matsya Purāṇa 39:
Aṣṭaka said:
When, dwelling in the Nandana grove, capable of assuming any form at will, [he spent] ten million years;
For what reason did you abandon that foremost leader of the Kṛta Age and descend to this earth?
Yayāti said:
"Just as in this world a kinsman, a friend, or one's own kin is abandoned by men when their wealth is exhausted,
so too in heaven the hosts of gods moving in the sky immediately abandon a man whose merit is spent."

Aṣṭaka said: "How do they become those whose merit is exhausted? My mind is exceedingly bewildered in this matter. Of what kind are they, and to what abode do they go? Tell me that, for I consider you a knower of the field (kṣetravit). (Matsya Purāṇa 39.3)
Yayāti said:
"O lord of men, all those who lament fall into this earthly hell;
for the sake of being devoured by herons, jackals, and crows, they undergo manifold growth upon the earth."
Therefore, O lord of men, such wicked and censurable action in the world must be avoided.
All this has been explained to you, O King; tell me now further, what shall I say to you?
Aṣṭaka said:
When birds, vultures, blue-necked ones, and winged insects devour those [bodies], how do they become so, and how do they come to be? From you, I hear of the earthly hell. (Matsya Purāṇa 39.6)
Yayāti said: "After the body has perished, those whose karma is expanding manifest and wander upon the earth;
they fall into this earthly hell and do not look back for many series of years."
Sixty thousand and likewise eighty thousand years they fall through the sky;
as they descend, the terrible, earth-born Rākṣasas with sharp fangs drive them away.
Aṣṭaka said:
When those terrible, earth-born Rākṣasas with sharp fangs strike them as they fall, how do they come to be? How do they manifest? And having become such, how do they become embryos?
Yayāti said:
"The blood and semen, joined by the essence of the menstrual flow, immediately follow once emitted by the man;
then your *rajas* (ovum) is reached, and becoming an embryo, it enters therein. (Matsya Purāṇa 39.10)
They enter the trees and the plants, the waters, the wind, the earth, and the intermediate space;
indeed, all four-footed and two-footed beings likewise become embryos within these elemental states.
Aṣṭaka said:
Does he assume another body here while still in the womb, or does he go according to his own will?
Tell me, as I ask you out of doubt, how one enters this human birth. *Matsya Purāṇa* 39.12.
And by what does one obtain the body, the physical form, and so forth, as well as the eyes, ears, and consciousness?
O Father, explain all of this when asked, for everyone considers you to be the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña). (Matsya Purāṇa 39.13)
Yayāti said:
"The wind draws forth the seed, joined with the essence of the flower, from the womb during the season;
there, having been assigned its function by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), it gradually develops the embryo here."
Then, as soon as he is born and has assumed consciousness, he becomes a human being;
here, with his two ears he perceives sound, and indeed, with his eye he beholds form.

Know that in this body of the great-souled living being, there is an accumulation of eightfold [perceptions]: smell by the nose, taste by the tongue, touch by the skin, and divine state by the mind. (Matsya Purāṇa 39.16)
Aṣṭaka said:
When a man who has passed away is cremated, buried, or even cut up,
having become non-existent and met with destruction, by what means does he perceive himself again in the future?
Yayāti said:

"O lion among kings, having abandoned his vital breaths like one who has fallen asleep due to his state of dissolution, and having placed both his good and evil deeds before him, he leaves the body and assumes another womb according to his merit and demerit."
Those who perform meritorious deeds enter a meritorious womb; those who commit evil deeds go to an evil womb.
They become insects and winged creatures due to their sins—O Great-Souled One, I have no further desire to speak.
Quadrupeds, bipeds, and birds likewise become such as they are when they have entered the womb;
all this has indeed been fully explained. What more do you wish to ask, O lion among kings?
Aṣṭaka said:
"O Father, what indeed must a mortal do—by austerity or by knowledge—to obtain the highest recognition?
Being asked this by me, tell me everything as it truly is, so that he may gradually go to the auspicious worlds."
Yayāti said:

"Austerity, charity, tranquility, self-control, modesty, uprightness, and compassion for all beings—the virtuous declare these to be the seven great gates to the heavenly world for men. (Matsya Purāṇa 39.22)
The virtuous say that all these aforementioned practices, which have austerity as their primary essence,
perish through pride for men who are always overcome by darkness, even when they are being observed.
The man who, while studying, considers himself a scholar and destroys the reputation of another by means of his learning—
his worlds are finite, and that [learning] does not yield for him the fruit of Brahman.
Four types of actions are terrifying; when performed improperly, they bestow fear:
the fire-sacrifice of pride, the silence of pride, study out of pride, and sacrifice out of pride. (Matsya Purāṇa 39.25)
One who is being honored should not take joy, nor should one experience distress from being insulted;
for in this world, the virtuous honor the virtuous, while the wicked do not attain the understanding of the good.
"One should give," "one should sacrifice," "one should study"—thus have I heard from my teacher.
These are said to be the sources of fearlessness; they must never be abandoned. (Matsya Purāṇa 39.27)
By means of that ancient refuge which the wise, endowed with self-restraint, perceive within their minds, they attain union with the supreme good;
having attained it, they reach the highest peace both here and after death.
Matsya Purāṇa 40. Aṣṭaka said: "How does one who lives as a householder reach the gods? How does a mendicant? And how does one whose duty is that of a teacher?"
The forest-dweller, established upon the path of the virtuous, now brings forth many [virtues] within this world.
Yayāti said:
"The student who studies when called upon, who is diligent in the duties for his teacher, who rises before [his teacher] and goes to bed after him,
who is gentle, self-controlled, steadfast, vigilant, and devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, succeeds as a celibate student."
Having acquired wealth through righteous means, one should perform sacrifices, give gifts, and always feed guests;
and one should not take what is not given by others—this is the ancient secret doctrine (upaniṣad) for the householder.
Living by his own effort, turned away from vice, giving to others, and not causing pain to others—
such a sage attains the highest perfection, dwelling in the forest with his diet and activities restrained.
One who does not live by a craft, who is homeless and always has his senses conquered, who is liberated from everything,
who does not sleep under a roof, who desires little, and who wanders through various lands alone— he is a bhikṣu.
On whatever night people become delighted and, having conquered their desires, dwell in happiness,
on that very night the wise man, self-restrained, should strive to dwell in the forest.
A forest-dweller bestows his merit upon ten ancestors, ten descendants, as well as himself as the twenty-first;
yet, having abandoned his own bodily elements in the forest, he is truly liberated.
Aṣṭaka said: "How many divine sages (devamuni) are there, and how many types of silence (mauna) are there as well? Explain this to us, for we wish to hear it. (Matsya Purāṇa 40.8)
Yayāti said: "O lord of men, he who has a village behind him while dwelling in the forest,
or who has the forest before him while dwelling in the village— he shall be a sage."
Aṣṭaka said: How indeed does one dwelling in the forest have a village behind him?
Or how does one dwelling in a village have the forest behind him?
Yayāti said:
"A sage who dwells in the forest should not consume what belongs to the village;
for one living thus in the wilderness, the village remains behind his back."
Without fire and without a fixed dwelling, the sage should wander without a lineage;
he should desire only as much clothing as is required for a loincloth.
As long as one intends to sustain life, so long should one desire food;
for him who dwells thus in a village, the forest is already behind him.
But that sage who, having renounced desires and abandoned ritual action, remains with his senses conquered and observes the vow of silence— he shall attain perfection in this world.
Who would not deserve to worship him who has cleansed his teeth, trimmed his nails, is always bathed and adorned, and though dark-complexioned, is established in pure deeds?
When, emaciated by austerity, lean, and with his flesh, bones, and blood wasted away, the sage becomes free from the pairs of opposites and established in silence; // Matsya Purāṇa 40.16 //
Then, having conquered this world, he may also conquer the world beyond;
for when the sage seeks his food with his mouth like a cow,
then all that belongs to these worlds becomes fit for his immortality.
Matsya Purāṇa 41:
Aṣṭaka said: "Which of these two first attains harmony with the gods?"
O King, they both ran like the sun and the moon.
Yayāti said:

"Between those householders who have no fixed home and live according to their desires, and the mendicant who wanders even within a village while remaining self-restrained— the mendicant has attained the state of the former."
If one who has attained a long life that was otherwise unattainable should act with corruption, he would suffer for having done so;
therefore, he should thereafter perform severe penance.

O King, they say that what is cruel is indeed base; he who, with a mind intent on evil, practices dharma, is powerless in that regard. Such is straightforwardness, such is meditative concentration, and such is nobility.
Aṣṭaka said:
"By whom have you been sent here today, O King—you, a youth, wearing a garland, handsome and radiant?
From where have you come, and in which direction do you dwell, or is there perhaps some station of a king?"
Yayāti said:
"Having spoken thus to you, I, my merit exhausted, shall fall from the sky to this earthly hell upon the ground; therefore, O world-protectors of Brahmā, you must hasten."
"O King, since you have chosen a fall from a precipice in the presence of the virtuous, all those gathered here are indeed endowed with merit;
for this boon was obtained by me from Śakra, O lord of men, while I was about to fall to the surface of the earth."
Aṣṭaka said:
I ask you, as you are falling toward the precipice: O King, do the worlds exist for me here?
Whether they are situated in the intermediate space or in heaven, I consider you to be the knower of that dharma.
Yayāti said:
"O lion among kings, know this for certain: as many cattle, horses, wild animals, and birds as are ordained upon the earth, so many worlds shall be established for you in heaven."
Aṣṭaka said:

"I give those [worlds] to you; do not fall into the abyss! O Indra among kings, whatever worlds I possess in heaven, whether they reside in the intermediate space or in the sky—ascend to them quickly, for you are a slayer of enemies."
Yayāti said:
"O chief of kings, one like me, who is not a Brahmin yet possesses knowledge of the Veda, does not engage in the practice of accepting gifts.
O lord of men, I previously gave to the twice-born exactly what was always to be given."
A wretched man who is not a Brahmin should never live, even if he were the husband of a heroic Brahmin woman;
since I would now practice that which was never done before, seeking to know—what could be virtuous in that?
Pratardana said:
"I ask you, O one of desirable form:
if there are worlds for me—whether they be in the intermediate space or in heaven—and if they have been heard of, I consider you, the Knower of the Field, to be the authority regarding that dharma."
Yayāti said:
"O lord of men, there are many worlds where each is provided with seven hundred days;
dripping with honey and rich in ghee, they are free from sorrow, yet because they have an end, they wait for that [final limit]."
Pratardana said:
"O King, those worlds which are mine, I give them to you as you fall; let them indeed be yours.
Whether they are situated in the intermediate space or in heaven, ascend to them quickly, freed from delusion. (Matsya Purāṇa 41.15)
Yayāti said:
"Possessing equal splendor, being a king myself, I desire to perform righteous deeds for the welfare and security of the earth from another king.
Having encountered misfortune through the decree of fate, even a wise king should never commit a cruel act."
Reflecting upon the path consistent with dharma and observing the merit of asceticism, one should perform penance that brings renown;
for a king who possesses a mind fixed on dharma would never act as you have described toward a wretched man like me.
"Desiring to know what has not been done before by others, what good man would do it?
Matsya Purāṇa 42: Vasumān said, "O lord of men, O son of Aśvin, I ask you, Vasumān: does there exist for me a world in heaven?"
O Great-souled One, if you are celebrated in the intermediate space, I consider you to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of that dharma.
Yayāti said:
"The atmosphere, the earth, and the quarters of space, as well as the sun that blazes with its splendor— indeed,
as many worlds as these exist established in heaven, they shall wait for you when you have become [the king]."
Vasuman said to them:
"I give those [worlds] to you; do not fall upon me. Let those worlds which are mine indeed become yours.
O King, buy these even for a blade of grass, if your acceptance [of gifts] is truly considered defiled."
Yayāti said:
"O King, I do not recall ever having committed a falsehood or a sale, even in my childhood;
nor would I ever do what has never been done before by others, O seeker of wealth, for it is not right."
Vasuman said to him:
"O King, attain those worlds granted by me if you do not desire to purchase them;
I shall certainly not go to them, O lord of men—let all those worlds indeed be yours."
Śibi said:
"I ask you, O Śibi the son of Uśīnara: if there are worlds for me as well, dear father—whether they reside in the intermediate space or in heaven—I consider you to be a knower of that dharma."
Yayāti said:
"O King, O lord of men, you should not disregard me even with your speech or your heart, though you may wish to do so;
for by that [merit], infinite worlds—resplendent like lightning, resonant, and vast—stand established in heaven."
Śibi said:
"O King, if you do not desire to purchase them from me, then go to those worlds given by me;
for I shall not go to those worlds, my dear, once I have given them away, to which you yourself shall go."
Yayāti said:
"O god among men, since you possess power equal to Indra's and those worlds are infinite, I do not find delight today in anything given by another; therefore, I do not welcome your words."
Aṣṭaka said:
"O King, if you do not welcome us individually to those worlds, then we shall all go to hell after handing over those worlds to you. (Matsya Purāṇa 42.10)
Yayāti said:
"O virtuous ones who perceive truth and other such realities, speak that which is worthy of you;
however, I do not accept what was not done by me in the past."
"O lion among kings, that which was said by me while being free from desire does not exist here in that way;
rather, for this gift, whatever is appropriate, its fruit shall indeed be infinite."
Aṣṭaka said:
To whom do these five golden chariots belong that are seen here?
Being so lofty, they shine forth like blazing crests of fire. (Matsya Purāṇa 42.13)
Yayāti said: "These golden chariots of yours and mine shine here;
you must ascend them and go along with me. (Matsya Purāṇa 42.14)
Aṣṭaka said:
"Mount the chariot, O King, and travel through the sky;
we too shall follow when the time comes."
Yayāti said: "Now all must go together, since heaven has been won;
here is seen for you that dustless path leading to the abode of the gods."
Śaunaka said:
O King, having all mounted their chariots, those monarchs set forth; pervading heaven and earth through their righteousness, they shone as if ascending to the celestial realm. *Matsya Purāṇa* 42.17.
Aṣṭaka said:
"I thought that the high-souled Indra was my friend and would always be the first to come to me;
why then has this Śibi Auśīnara alone overtaken us all with such speed by means of his horses?"
Yayāti said:
"This son of Uśīnara, Śibi, who is blameless, gave away all his wealth to Devayānī; therefore, he is indeed superior to you all."

"Generosity, purity, truthfulness, non-violence, modesty, prosperity, forbearance, equanimity, and compassion—all these qualities shine, O Queen, because they abide in King Śibi of incomparable intelligence.
One who practices modesty maintains such conduct; therefore, Śibi is one who approaches others with his chariot. (Matsya Purāṇa 42.20)
Śaunaka said:
Then Aṣṭaka, out of curiosity, questioned his maternal grandfather, who was like Indra himself:
"O King, I ask you, tell me the truth: from where have you come, who are you, and how did you arrive here?"
For that which has been done by you, there is no other doer in this world besides you—whether a Brahmin or a Kshatriya.
Yayāti said:
"I am Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa and the father of Pūru; I was a sovereign ruler here on earth.
I speak this secret counsel to my own kin, for you are as clearly manifest to me as a maternal grandfather."
Having conquered this entire earth in its full prosperity, I gave it to the Brahmins;
then, having given many beautiful sacrificial horses, the gods became partakers of merit.
I gave this entire earth to the brahmins— this praiseworthy land filled with all kinds of food,
along with cows, gold, excellent wealth, and hundreds of horses and elephants by the billions.
By my truth, both heaven and the earth, as well as fire among men, blaze forth;
for never has a word been uttered by me in vain, since the virtuous honor truth.
"O Sādhu-aṣṭaka, I declare here the truth concerning Pratardana, Vasuman, and Śibi:
'All the gods, sages, and worlds are to be honored through truth'—this is my firm conviction.
Whoever among us should report everything we have conquered and all that has occurred exactly as it happened..."
Free from envy toward the twice-born and the sacred fires, may he attain the same world as us.
Śaunaka said:

Thus, O King, that great-souled Yayāti, whose deeds were most noble, having been rescued by his grandsons who were the best of friends, abandoned the earth and went to heaven, having pervaded the world with his merits. *Matsya Purāṇa* 42.28.
Thus has the entire life-story of Nahuṣa been related to you in detail and according to fact—
the lineage of which is renowned as Pauraveya, and in which you were born, O you who are like a lord of men.
Sūta said:
O Śaunaka, having heard this, King Śatānīka [addressed] him.
Filled with wonder and supreme joy, he shone like the full moon.
Then the king duly honored Śaunaka with jewels, cows, gold, and various kinds of garments. (Matsya Purāṇa 43.2)
Then, having accepted all the wealth sent by the king and having given it away to the Brahmins, Śaunaka vanished.
The sages said: "We wish to hear the lineage of Yayāti in detail;
please tell us how it was established in the world by his sons, Yadu and the others."
Sūta said:
Listen as I describe in detail and in proper sequence the lineage of Yadu, the eldest son of utmost splendor, as I speak it.
Yadu had five sons who were like the children of gods;
they were great chariot-warriors and mighty archers—learn of them by name.
Sahasrajit was the eldest; then came Kroṣṭu, Nīla, Antika, and Laghu.
The heir of Sahasrajit was the king named Śatajit.
The three heirs of Śatajiti were also of supreme renown:
Haihaya, Haya, and Veṇuhaya.
The heir of Haihaya was the celebrated Dharmanetra;
Kunti was the son of Dharmanetra, and Saṃhata was his son.
The heir of Saṃhata was the king named Mahiṣmān;
the son of Mahiṣmān was the powerful Rudraśreṇya.
In Vārāṇasī there was a king, as has already been told;
he was the son of Rudraśreṇya, a monarch named Durdama.
The wise and heroic son of Durda was named Kanaka;
Kanaka’s heirs were four, world-renowned.
Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, and likewise Kṛtavarmā, and Kṛtaujas was the fourth; from Kṛtavīrya was born Arjuna.
Born with a thousand arms as the sovereign of the seven continents,
that lord of the earth performed difficult austerities for ten thousand years.
Kārtavīrya propitiated Datta, the son of Atri;
O Supreme Person, he granted him four boons.
Previously, that best of kings had chosen a thousand arms, as well as the warding off of unrighteousness even by the virtuous whenever he practiced it. (Matsya Purāṇa 43.16)
Having conquered the earth through battle, its protection must be carried out through righteousness alone;
furthermore, for one engaged in combat, death itself may become a source of supreme merit.
Thus, by the power of his kṣatriya duty, he has conquered this entire earth— with its seven continents, its mountains,
and its surrounding seven oceans.
As that wise one desired it, a thousand arms indeed were born to him;
a chariot and a banner also came into being—thus we have heard. (Matsya Purāṇa 43.19)
It is heard that at that time, ten thousand unobstructed sacrifices were performed by that wise king across the various islands.
O great king, all his sacrifices were accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
all of them had sacrificial posts made of gold, and all of them had altars made of gold.
Adorned by all the gods who have arrived together, seated in celestial chariots,
they are eternally graced by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
At his sacrifice, the Gandharva Nārada likewise sang a song,
beholding the greatness of the royal sage Kārtavīrya.
Surely other Kṣatriyas will not attain the state of Kārtavīrya through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, or sacred learning.
For he, the yogi, wandering through the seven continents as one armed with a sword, a discus, a bow, and a chariot, beholds the thieves.
That lord of men became a universal monarch (cakravartin) for eighty-five thousand years, possessing an abundance of all kinds of jewels.
He himself became the protector of cattle, he indeed became the guardian of the field;
through his state of yoga, he became Arjuna, who was like the rain-god Parjanya in bringing down showers.
He who, with his thousand arms whose skin was hardened by the striking of bowstrings,
shone like the autumnal sun with its thousand rays.
This one of great splendor, having conquered the Naga Karkoṭaka’s son among men in Māhiṣmatī, established him there in that city.
This lord of the earth, overflowing with joy while merely playing, indeed encounters the force of the ocean's current as it flows upstream during the rainy season.
As he sports upon his forehead,
the Narmadā approaches, adorned with garlands of flowers, startled by the terror of his wave-like frowns.
With his thousand arms, he plunged into that great ocean and caused the Narmadā,
swollen by the rains and surging with violent currents, to flow upward.
When the great ocean is agitated by his thousand arms,
the great asuras dwelling in the netherworld become utterly motionless.
Where great whales and fish lie submerged in the vast Mahā-vīci hell,
where masses of foam are driven by the winds, and which is unbearable with whirlpools that cast one about.
He churned the ocean with his thousand arms,
while the gods, startled by the agitation caused by Mount Mandara, were apprehensive that the nectar might be lost.
Then the great serpents remain with their heads motionless,
like plantain groves at sunset, still in the absence of wind.
Having thus fixed an arrow upon the bowstring and discharged it with force, he bewildered Rāvaṇa along with his army in Laṅkā by means of five arrows.
Having conquered and bound him, he brought him to Māhiṣmatī and imprisoned him there;
then Pulastya went and pacified Arjuna.
He released the Rākṣasa descendant of Pulastya, who had been pacified here by Pulastya;
with his thousand arms, he produced the sound of bowstrings being struck.

Like the crashing of a thousand clouds at the end of an eon, or like the roar of a thunderbolt—oh, how great is the power of destiny, since this descendant of Bhṛgu has severed it! (Matsya Purāṇa 43.40)
That thousand of arms was indeed like a forest of golden palm trees,
where the powerful lord Apava, being enraged, cursed Arjuna.
"O Haihaya, because my forest has indeed been burnt down, though it was well-known to me,
therefore another shall take away the fruit of this difficult deed you have performed."
"First, that powerful ascetic Brāhmaṇa of the Bhṛgu lineage will swiftly sever your thousand arms and then slay you."
Sūta said:
At that time, death by the curse of that wise man befell Rāma;
however, this was also a boon previously chosen by the royal sage himself.
He had a hundred sons, five of whom were great chariot-warriors;
they were skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and possessed of great strength.
Śūrasena, Śūra, Dhṛṣṭa, and likewise Kroṣṭu,
Jayadhvaja the son of Vikartana, and Avanti, O lord of the people.
The son of Jayadhvaja was the exceedingly powerful Tālajaṅgha;
he had hundreds of sons who were known as the Tālajaṅghas.
Five clans of those high-souled Haihayas are renowned:
the Vītihotras, the Śāryātas, the Bhojas, and likewise the Āvantyas.
The Kuṇḍikeras were valiant, as were the Tālajaṅghas;
and also the son of Vītihotra, the heroic one named Ānarta. His son was Durjaya, the subduer of friends.
O Great King, while protecting his subjects with righteousness and sincerity,
there was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms.
That man who, having risen at dawn, recites the name of him by whom the earth as far as the ocean was conquered with his bow; // MatsP_43.51 //
There shall be no loss of wealth for him, and he recovers even what has been lost;
whoever here recounts the birth of the wise Kārtavīrya,
having his soul purified by the sacrifice, is glorified in the heavenly world.
Matsya Purāṇa 44: The sages said, "For what reason was that forest of the high-souled Āpava burned?"
O Sūta, tell me truly how Kārtavīrya displayed his prowess.
We have heard that this royal sage was the protector of his subjects;
how then, having been their protector, did he burn down that penance grove? (Matsya Purāṇa 44.2)
Sūta said:
The Sun-god, having approached Kārtavīrya in the form of a twice-born, said, "O Lord of Men, grant me a single satisfaction; I am the Sun. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.3)
The king said:
"O Blessed One, O Divākara, by what means is your satisfaction attained?
What kind of food should I offer, having performed the oblation, that I may provide for you? (Matsya Purāṇa 44.4)
Āditya said:
"O best among those who give food, grant me all that is stationary;
for by that I shall indeed be satisfied, O King, and that is my satisfaction."
Kārtavīrya said:
"O best of those who radiate heat, it is not possible for all immobile beings to be consumed by my splendor and strength; therefore, I bow down to you."
The Sun said:
"I am pleased with you; I give you inexhaustible arrows that face in every direction, which, when discharged, shall blaze forth, endowed as they are with my own splendor."
Possessed by my splendors, they shall wither the stationary beings;
having dried them up, they will reduce them to ashes, and by that, O lord of men, there will be satisfaction.
Sūta said:
Then the Sun-god gave those arrows to Arjuna;
with them, he consumed everything that came before him, both the stationary and all else.
Likewise, he [beheld] villages, hermitages, cowherd settlements, and cities;
delightful penance groves, forests, and pleasure gardens.
In this way, he first consumed the eastern quarter and then the entire southern one;
the earth was stripped of trees and grass, destroyed by his terrible splendor.
At that very time,
however, the great seer Āpava remained there, established in the water for ten thousand years.
When his vow was completed, the great ascetic of immense splendor arose;
that great sage beheld the hermitage consumed by Arjuna.
Out of anger, he cursed the royal sage as I have related to you;
now hear of the lineage of the royal sage Kroṣṭu, which is characterized by supreme prowess. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.14)
In whose lineage was born Viṣṇu, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan;
from Kroṣṭu himself was born the son Vṛjinīvat, a great chariot-warrior.
And the son of Vṛjinīvat was the very powerful one named Svāha;
O King, Svāha’s son was Ruṣaṅgu, the best among eloquent speakers.
Desiring offspring, Ruṣaṅgu indeed begot a son named Saumya;
Citra was his son, and Citraratha was his son, who was endowed with meritorious deeds.
Then a hero of the Caitraratha lineage was born, who gave away abundant sacrificial fees;
he became the renowned universal monarch known as Śaśabindu.
In this regard, this genealogical verse was sung concerning him in ancient times:
"Śaśabindu had a hundred sons, and from those hundred sons there arose yet another hundred. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.19)
The sons of Pṛthusāha were of great strength, wise, handsome, possessed of abundant wealth and splendor, and were the foremost among hundreds of such men.
Pṛthuśravas, Pṛthuyaśas, Pṛthudharma, Pṛthujaya,
Pṛthukīrti, and Pṛthumanas were the kings of the Śaśabindus.
And those who know the Purāṇas proclaim Pṛthuśravas to be the most excellent;
Suyajña was the son of Antara, and he was a performer of noble sacrifices.
But Uśanas, the most righteous of men, while protecting this earth for Suyajña,
performed one hundred horse-sacrifices.
O son, the scorcher of his enemies became patient;
his son was Marutta, the most excellent among royal sages.
The two sons of Marutta were Vīra and Kambalabarhiṣa;
the son of Kambalabarhiṣa was the learned Rukmakavaca.
Having slain his enemies who wore golden armor with various arrows, Rukmakavaca, the archer, obtained this earth.
On one occasion, during the Aśvamedha sacrifice, King Rukmakavaca, the slayer of enemy heroes, gave sacrificial fees to the Brāhmaṇas. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.27)
Five sons of great prowess were born to him, all wielders of the bow:
Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Parigha, and Hari.
The father established Parigha and Hari in Videha;
Rukmeṣu became king, and Pṛthurukma was his dependent.
Exiled from the kingdom by them, Jyāmagha then stayed at that hermitage;
while dwelling in the hermitage in a state of tranquility, he was enlightened by a brahmin.
Taking up his bow, the king, accompanied by his banner and chariot, went alone to another land along the Narmadā river, solely out of a desire for a livelihood.
Having gone to Mount Ṛkṣavat, he sat down after others had already eaten;
there, Jyāmagha’s wife, Caitrā, became pregnant.
The king lived without a son and did not take another wife;
he had a victory in battle, and there he obtained a daughter.
Out of fear, he said to his wife, "O lady of pure smiles, this is your daughter-in-law.
Thus addressed, she said to him, "Whose daughter-in-law is she? (Matsya Purāṇa 44.34)
The king said:
"She shall become the wife of whichever son is born to you.
Therefore, through fierce asceticism, she gave birth to a daughter.
The fortunate Caitrā, having reached maturity, gave birth to a son, Vidarbha;
and that wise king begot Kratha and Kaiśika upon his daughter-in-law, the princess,
and a third son, the most righteous Lomapāda.
In her, Vidarbha begot sons skilled in battle;
Manu was the son of Lomapāda, and he was the offspring of Jñāti.
Cidi was the son of Kaiśika; from him the royal lineages known as the Caidyas are said to have descended. Kratha, however, was the son of Vidarbha, and Kunti was his son.
From Kunti was born a son, the powerful Raṇadhṛṣṭa, who was bold in battle;
Dhṛṣṭa’s son was the righteous Nirvṛti, the slayer of enemy heroes.
He had one son named Vidūratha, who was the offspring of Nirvṛti.
Daśārha was his son, and Vyoma is recorded as his son. From Vyoma, the son of Dāśārha, the son Jīmūta is said to have been born.
Vimala was the son of Jīmūta; his son was Bhīmaratha;
and the son of Bhīmaratha is recorded as being Navaratha.
His son was Dṛḍharatha, and Śakuni was his son;
from him came Karambha, and Kārambhi’s son was Devarāta.
Devakṣatra became the king, the highly illustrious Daivarāti;
born like the offspring of a god, he was the delight of Devanakṣatra.
The son of Madhu was the highly resplendent Puruvasu;
from Puruvasu was born Purudvān, the best of men.
Then Jantu was born to Bhadrasenī, the princess of Vidarbha, by Purudvata;
and an Aikṣvākī woman became the wife of that Jantu, and by her he begot a son.
The Sātvata, endowed with goodness and the enhancer of the fame of the Sātvatas—
by understanding this creation of the high-souled Jyāmagha,
one becomes possessed of progeny and attains union with the wise King Soma.
Kauśalyā gave birth to sons endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva):
Bhajina, Bhajamāna, Divya, and Devāvṛdha, O King. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.47)
And Andhaka, Mahābhoja, Vṛṣṇi, and Yadunandana—
their four lineages, listen to them in detail.
From Bhajamāna and Sṛñjayī, who was a Bāhyakā, the Bāhyakas were born;
for Sṛñjaya had two daughters, and from them the Bāhyakas then arose.
His two wives, who were sisters, gave birth to many sons:
Nimi, Kṛmila, and Vṛṣṇi, the conqueror of enemy cities;
these were born to Bhajamāna by Sṛñjayī, the daughter of Bāhyaka.
In the sacrifice, he was the one who gladdened the gods, the king of his kinsmen, and the increaser of friends;
yet the king remained childless and performed supreme austerity, longing, "May I have a son endowed with all virtues. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.51)
Then, having joined the mantra, he touched the water of the Parṇāśā;
by that act of touching it, the river performed what was pleasing to him.
O King, because of his auspiciousness, that supreme river,
her soul overcome with anxiety, then reached a firm resolve.
"I do not find such a woman in whom a son like this might be born;
therefore, today I shall become ten thousand [women]. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.54)
Then, having become a young maiden and possessing a most excellent form, she made herself known to the king; he of great vows desired her.
Then, in her ninth month, that best of rivers gave birth to a son endowed with all virtues, Babhru, from King Devāvṛdha.
It is well known that those learned in the Purāṇas sing this in the genealogical accounts (anuvamśa),
extolling the virtues of the high-souled Devāvṛdha.
Just as we hear him from afar, so do we behold him when near:
Babhru, the best among men, equal to the gods who increase the divine power.
O King, sixty thousand and seventy-six ancestors of Babhru attained immortality through Devāvṛdha.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, a hero, devoted to the Brahmins, and firm in his vows;
he was handsome, possessed of great splendor, and likewise endowed with learning and valor.
Then Kaṅka’s daughter gave birth to four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śaśin, and Kambalabarhiṣa.
Kukura’s son was Vṛṣṇi, and Vṛṣṇi’s son was Dhṛti;
his son was Kapotaroman, and Taittiri was his offspring.
He had a son, a serpent named Nala, who was indeed wise;
by his name, that son is celebrated as Nandana-daradundubhi.
When that sacrifice had been fully extended, Punarvasu,
the most excellent of men, being well-born, performed an Aśvamedha for the sake of obtaining a son.
In the midst of that Atirātra sacrifice, he arose from the center of the assembly hall;
therefore, he was wise, skilled in ritual action, a performer of sacrifices, a donor, and possessed of abundant wealth.
O best of those who know the mother’s lore, it is said that he had a pair of children, a son and a daughter,
namely Āhuka and Āhukī, both of whom were renowned.
