There were indeed ten thousand chariots with a roar like thunderclouds;
yet there was no one there who spoke untruth, none who lacked splendor, none who had not performed sacrifice, and none who had not given a thousandfold.
"He was neither impure nor ignorant, for he was born among those who eat;
having received the sustenance of Āhuka—this indeed is what is said."
Āhuka also gave his sister Āhukī to the king of Avanti;
from Āhuka, the daughter of the King of Kāśī gave birth to two sons.
Devaka and Ugrasena were both equal to the offspring of gods;
from Devaka were born heroic sons who resembled the thirty deities.
Devavān, Anupadeva, Sudeva, and Devarakṣita—
these had seven sisters, and he gave them all to Vasudeva.
Devakī, Śrutadevī, Mitradevī, Yaśodharā, Śrīdevī, Satyadevī, and Sutāpī as the seventh—these were his wives. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.73)
Ugrasena had nine sons, of whom Kaṃsa was the eldest;
the others were Nyagrodha, Sunāman, Kaṅka, Śaṅku, and many more.
Ajabhū, Rāṣṭrapāla, Yuddhamuṣṭi, and Sumuṣṭida;
they had five sisters, namely Kaṃsā and Kaṃsavatī.
Sutantu, Rāṣṭrapālī, and Kaṅkā were excellent women;
Ugrasena, along with his offspring, was declared to have been born from a dog.
The son of Bhajamāna was Vidūratha, a preeminent chariot-warrior;
Rājādhideva was the son of Vidūratha, and he was a hero. (Matsya Purāṇa 44.77)
To Rājādhideva were born two sons equal to the gods,
Niyamavrata-pradhāna, Śoṇāśva, and Śvetavāhana.
The five sons of Śoṇāśva were heroes skilled in battle:
Śamī, Devaśarman, Nikuṇṭha, and Śakraśatrujit.
Śamiputra was the son of Pratikṣatra, and the son of Pratikṣatra was Pratikṣetra;
Bhoja was his son, and Hṛdīka was his son.
Hṛdīka had ten sons of terrible prowess;
Kṛtavarmā was the eldest among them, and Śatadhanvan was the middle one.
Devārha, Nābha, the mighty Bhīṣaṇa,
Ajāta, Vanajāta, Kanīyaka, and Karambhaka.
The learned Devārha was born as the son of Kambalabarhiṣ;
Asāmañja was his son, and Tamojāta was the son of that one.
The three valiant sons of Aja, who were of supreme fame—
Sudaṃṣṭra, Sunābha, and Kṛṣṇa— are considered the Andhakas.
The man who constantly recites this lineage of the Andhakas obtains for himself a vast lineage and becomes possessed of progeny.
Matsya Purāṇa 45:
Sūta said:
Gāndhārī and Mādrī both became wives of Vṛṣṇi.
Gāndhārī gave birth to Sumitra, the delighter of his friends.
Then Mādrī bore Yudhājit, Devamīḍhuṣa,
Anamitra, Śibi, and the fifth, Kṛtalakṣaṇa.
Anamitrasuta had a son named Nighna, and Nighna also had two sons:
the very heroic Prasena and Śaktisena; these were both of them.
The Syamantaka was the unsurpassed jewel-gem of Prasena;
indeed, that gem became the king of all jewels upon the earth.
Having placed that jewel upon his heart and being repeatedly entreated, Govinda did not obtain it; though he was capable, he did not seize it.
Once, while Prasena was out hunting adorned with that [ornament],
he heard a sound coming from a cave filled with a living creature.
Then, having entered the cave, Prasena indeed beheld the bear; likewise, the bear saw Prasena, and Prasenajit saw the bear as well.
Having killed Prasena, the bear then took that jewel;
but he was killed by him while remaining unseen within his cave at that time.
But having learned that Prasena had been killed, Govinda became suspicious:
"It is evident that Prasena was killed by Govinda for the sake of the jewel."
Prasena, adorned with a precious gem, had gone into the forest;
seeing him [the lion] slain by it, Govinda replied:
"I shall slay this man of evil conduct, for he has become an enemy to the Vṛṣṇis. (Matsya Purāṇa 45.10)
Then, after a long time, Govinda went out again on a hunt and by chance came to the vicinity of the cave. (Matsya Purāṇa 45.11)
Seeing that great noise, the powerful king of the bears let out a roar;
hearing that sound, Govinda entered with sword in hand and beheld Jāmbavat, the mighty king of the bears.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, his eyes bloodshot with anger, quickly and suddenly seized Jāmbavat, the lord of the bears.
Then the bear praised the Lord with Vaiṣṇava hymns;
thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, invited him to choose a boon.
Jāmbavān said:
"O Lord, I desire death at your hands by the blow of your discus;
and may this auspicious daughter of mine obtain you as her husband."
"O Lord, this jewel which I have obtained was acquired by me after killing Prasena."
Then, having slain Jāmbavanta with his discus,
the powerful and mighty-armed lord, having accomplished his task, took back the jewel along with the maiden.
He gave him [the jewel] to Satrājit in the assembly of all the Sātvatas;
by that false accusation, this Janārdana was deeply distressed.
Then all those Yādavas said to Vāsudeva:
"It was our conviction that Prasenajit had been killed by you."
The ten auspicious daughters of Kaikeya were the wives of Satrājit;
from them were born his one hundred and one renowned sons,
who were famous and possessed of great heroism, of whom Bhaṅgakāra was the eldest.
Then Vratavatī, previously born from that Bhaṅgakāra,
gave birth to three delicate daughters with lotus-like eyes.
Satyabhāmā, the best among women, observant of vows and firm in her resolve,
as well as Padmāvatī— these he gave to Kṛṣṇa.
Anamitra was born from Chitraka, the youngest son of Vṛṣṇi;
Satyaka was his son, and Sātyaki was his offspring.
Satyavān was the son of Yuyudhāna, who was the powerful grandson of Śini;
Asaṅga was the son of Yuyudhāna, and Dyumni was his son.
Dyumni’s son was Yugandhara; these are proclaimed as the descendants of Śini. Thus has the lineage of Anamitra, born of the Vṛṣṇi clan, been explained.
To Anamitra, the son of Yudhājit, was born Vīra on earth;
he had two other heroic sons, Vṛṣabha and Kṣatra.
Vṛṣabha took the daughter of the King of Kāśī as his wife;
from Jayantī, however, a splendid son named Jayanta was born.
From him was born Akrūra, who was always performing sacrifices, exceedingly heroic, learned in the scriptures, and fond of guests;
from Akrūra was born Sadāyajña, who was most liberal in his sacrificial gifts.
Akrūra obtained Ratnā, the daughter of Śaibya,
and begot upon her eleven sons of great strength.
Upalambha, Sadālambha, Vṛkala, and Vīrya;
Savīra, Sadāpakṣa, Śatrughna, and Vārimejaya.
Dharmabhṛt, Dharmavarman, and likewise Dhṛṣṭamāna—
all these became the Pratihotṛ priests, and they were born of Ratnā.
From Akrūra and Ugrasenā were born two sons who increased the lineage,
Devavān and Upadeva, who were like gods themselves.
And from Aśvinī were born the sons Pṛthu and Vipṛthu,
as well as Aśvatthāman, Subāhu, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa.
Vṛṣṭinemi, Sudharmā, as well as Śaryāti; Abhūmi, Varjabhūmi, Śramiṣṭha, and likewise Śravaṇa.
He who knows that this false accusation has been removed by Kṛṣṇa cannot, in turn,
be accused falsely by anyone.
Matsya Purāṇa 46:
Sūta said:
The daughter of Ikṣvāku gave birth to Śūra, who was renowned, wonderful, and praiseworthy.
From the heroic Pauruṣa, ten sons were born to Bhojā.
The mighty-armed Vasudeva was formerly Ānakadundubhi;
from him Devamīḍha was born, and from him, in turn, Devaśravas.
Anādhṛṣṭi, Śini, Nanda along with Sṛñjaya,
Śyāma, Śamīka, and Saṃyūpa were his sons, and he had five excellent wives.
Śrutakīrti, Pṛthā, Śrutādevī, Śrutaśravā,
and Rājādhidevī— these five were the mothers of heroes.
Kṛta begot a son, Sugrīva, from Śrutādevī;
and from Kaikeyī, named Śrutakīrti, that king begot Anuvrata.
To Śrutaśravas, the king of Cedi, Sunītha was born;
he was a frequent practitioner of dharma and became a crusher of his enemies.
Then, out of friendship, he gave his daughter to the aged Kuntibhoja;
thus was Pṛthā, the sister of Vasudeva, known as Kuntī.
That blameless woman was given by Vasudeva as a wife to Pāṇḍu;
for the sake of Pāṇḍu, she gave birth to sons of the gods who were great chariot-warriors.
From Dharma was born Yudhiṣṭhira; from Vāyu was born Vṛkodara;
and from Indra was born Dhanañjaya, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra.
We have heard that Nakula and Sahadeva were born of Mādravatī by the Aśvins, and they were endowed with beauty, good character, and virtue. (Matsya Purāṇa 46.10)
Rohiṇī, known as Pauravī, was indeed the wife of Ānakadundubhi;
she gave birth to his eldest son Rāma and his beloved son Sāraṇa.
Then, from Rohiṇī, there were born Durdama, Damana, Subhru, Piṇḍāraka, Mahāhanu, and two daughters with beautiful eyes named Citrā and Akṣī.
From Śauri and Devakī were born Suṣeṇa, Kīrtimān,
Udāsin, Bhadrasena, and likewise Ṛṣivāsa;
the sixth was Bhadravideha, and Kaṃsa slew them all.
On that first new moon of the rainy season which was to come,
the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the progenitor of beings, was born in the past.
Subhadrā, the sweet-spoken one, became his younger sister;
and from Devakī was born the highly energetic and illustrious Śūra.
Sahadeva begot Śauri, the upholder of the lineage, upon Tāmrā. Devarakṣitā obtained a son named Upāsaṅgadhara and an auspicious daughter; Kaṃsa caused her to be slain.
Vijaya, Rocamāna, Vardhamāna, and Devala—
all these great-souled ones were born of Upadevī.
And the high-souled Avagāha was born of Vṛkadevī;
from Vṛkadevī himself was born the one known by the name Nandaka.
O King, Devakī gave birth to her seventh son, Madana, who was highly fortunate, a seeker of truth, and unconquered in battles. (Matsya Purāṇa 46.19)
Formerly, while wandering in the forest in the monastery of the goddess Śraddhā,
Śauri begot an eldest son, Kauśika, upon a Vaiśya woman.
Sutanu and Ratharājī were the two wives of Śauri;
and Puṇḍra and Kapila were the two powerful sons of Vasudeva.
There was a Niṣāda named Jarā who was the foremost of archers;
Saubhadra and Bhava were also there, both being beings of great power.
The son of Devabhāga was known by the name Uddhava;
they call the first scholar the one born from Devaśravas.
The illustrious Aikṣvākī obtained a son from Anādhṛṣṭi;
from him was born Śatrughna, who was devoted to his ancestors and whose enemies were shaken off.
Being pleased with Karūṣā, who was childless, Kṛṣṇa granted her a son—
Sucandra, who was highly fortunate, heroic, and possessed of great strength.
These two sons of Jāmbavatī,
Cārudeṣṇa and Sāmba, are endowed with auspicious marks, heroic, and possessed of great strength.
Tantipāla and Tanti were both the sons of Nandana;
and the four sons of Śamīka were valiant and possessed of great strength:
Virāja, Dhanu, Śyāma, and Sṛñjaya.
Śyāma was childless, and Śamīka went to the forest;
loathing the status of a Bhoja, he attained the rank of a royal seer (rājarṣi).
The man who constantly recites or constantly hears this account of the birth and exaltation of Kṛṣṇa is liberated from all sins. (Matsya Purāṇa 46.29)
Matsya Purāṇa 47: Sūta said:
Now, the god Mahādeva was formerly Kṛṣṇa Prajāpati.
For the sake of dwelling [within], that Lord of Gods is born here among human beings.
Then, through the ascetic power of Vasudeva, the lotus-eyed one was born of Devakī with four arms, possessing a divine form and blazing with splendor.
Having beheld the Lord marked with the Śrīvatsa and endowed with divine characteristics, Vasudeva said to him: "O Lord, please withdraw this form."
"O Lord, I am afraid of Kaṃsa, and therefore I tell you this:
my sons have been slain by him—those eldest ones of terrible prowess. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.4)
Having heard Vasudeva’s words, Acyuta withdrew his form;
then, taking leave of Śauri, he led him to the house of Nandagopa.
Having given him [the child] to Nandagopa, he said, "Let him be protected.
Therefore, all prosperity shall belong to the Yādavas;
for this child, born of Devakī, shall slay Kaṃsa. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.6)
The sages said:
Who is this Vasudeva, and who is the illustrious Devakī? Who is this Nandagopa, and who is Yaśodā of the great vows?
She who gave birth to Viṣṇu, whom he addressed as "Father," she who conceived him as a fetus, and she who nurtured him— [to her I bow].
Sūta said:
Puruṣa was Kaśyapa, and Aditi is remembered as his beloved wife;
Kaśyapa was a portion of Brahmā, and likewise Aditi was a portion of the Earth.
Then the mighty-armed one fulfilled for Devakī all those desires that she had constantly cherished for her unborn, high-souled son.
Having descended to the earth and entered a human body, that god,
whose self is yoga, deluded all beings by means of his yogic power (yogamāyā).
When dharma had perished, the Lord Viṣṇu was born in the Vṛṣṇi clan to establish dharma and to bring about the destruction of the asuras.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Satyā the daughter of Nagnajit, Subhāmā, Śaibyā, Gāndhārī, and likewise Lakṣmaṇā. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.13)
Mitravindā, Queen Kālindī, as well as Jāmbavatī,
Suśīlā, Mādrī, Kauśalyā, and Vijayā—
these and others comprised sixteen thousand queens.
Rukmiṇī gave birth to sons who were skilled in battle:
the hero Cārudeṣṇa, who was brave in combat, and the mighty Pradyumna.
Sucāru, Bhadracāru, Sudeṣṇa, and Bhadra;
Paraśu, Cārugupta, Cārubhadra, and Sucāruka;
Cāruhāsa, the youngest [son], and likewise the daughter Cārumatī.
To Satyabhāmā were born Bhānu, Bhrāmara-tekṣaṇa, Rohita, Dīptimat, Tāmra, Cakra, and Jalandhama. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.17)
Four younger sisters were born to them;
and from Jāmbavatī was born a son, Sāmba, who graced the assembly.
Mitravān, Mitravinda, the excellent woman Mitravindā,
Mitrabāhu, and Sunītha were indeed the offspring of Nāgnajitī.
Understand that there were thousands of sons beginning with these;
that wise man had a hundred times one hundred thousand sons.
O best of the twice-born, it is likewise said that there were eighty thousand sons of Vāsudeva, and one hundred thousand sons in total.
The two sons of Upasaṅga were Vajra and Saṃkṣipta;
Bhūrīndrasena and Bhūri were both the sons of Gaveṣaṇa.
The heir of Pradyumna was Aniruddha, the most intelligent of men; he was born of Vaidarbhī and was irresistible in battle. His emblem was the deer.
From Kāśyā, the daughter of Supārśva, he obtained Sāmba and five other swift sons; these five heroes are celebrated as gods whose very nature is truth.
There were thirty million pre-eminent Yādavas of great soul,
along with six million who were heroic and possessed of great strength.
Indeed, all those of great prowess who were born here as portions of the gods,
as well as those mighty Asuras who were slain in the war between the gods and Asuras, [were reborn].
"Those who have arisen here among men and oppress all human beings— for their destruction, he has appeared in the Yadava lineage. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.27)
One hundred clans of the high-souled Yādavas—
all these clans shall indeed endure as long as the Vaiṣṇava dynasty exists.
Viṣṇu is their leader and is established in sovereignty;
all the Yādavas are said to abide by his command.
The sages said:
"The seven ṛṣis, Kubera, the yakṣa Māṇicara,
Śālaki, Nārada, as well as the perfected one Dhanvantari."
Why are Ādideva, Viṣṇu, and these deities remembered as being in groups? How many origins (sambhūti) are there? MatsP_47.31
How many other future manifestations will there be for that Great-Souled One?
And why is he born here when the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas have become peaceful?
Tell us who ask you: for what purpose has Viṣṇu, the best of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, been born again and again among human beings?
Sūta said: Having cast off his divine body, Viṣṇu is born here among human beings when the age has turned back and time has become slackened, O Lord.
During the conflicts between the gods and the asuras, the Lord Hari is born;
formerly, when the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was ruling over the three worlds.
And when the three worlds had been successively presided over by Bali,
there was a supreme friendship between the gods and the asuras.
Indeed, the world was completely filled with demons known as the Yugās and was exceedingly turbulent;
yet both the gods and the asuras remained equally obedient to their commands.
A great and most terrible conflict, fierce and destructive to both gods and asuras, arose for the purpose of crushing Bali. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.38)
Then, for the sake of the gods and asuras, and on account of Bhṛgu’s curse, he was born among humans here in order to establish the system of dharma.
The sages said:
"How did he himself come to engage in activity for the sake of the gods and asuras? Tell us who ask you about how that conflict between the gods and asuras occurred."
Sūta said:
On account of their inheritance, there were ten very terrible battles between them,
beginning with Varāha and ending with Śaṇḍa and Marka, as they are recorded.
Listen now to their names in brief as I intend to speak of them:
the first is Nārasiṃha, and the second is Vāmana.
The third was the Varāha [incarnation], and the fourth was the Amṛtamanthana;
the fifth conflict that arose was indeed the Tārakāmaya.
The sixth was indeed named Āḍībaka, the seventh was Atri-putra,
the eighth among them was named Andhaka, and the ninth was the slayer of Vṛtra.
Dhātṛ and Daśama, and after them Hālāhala is remembered;
the twelfth among them is the renowned Ghora, as well as Kolāhala.
In ancient times, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was struck down by the Man-lion (Nārasiṃha), and Bali was bound by Vāmana during his conquest of the three worlds.
Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by the gods in a hand-to-hand combat;
however, the ocean was split in two by the Boar with his tusk.
During the churning for the nectar of immortality, Prahlāda was defeated in battle by Indra;
however, Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was constantly intent upon slaying Indra.
But during the Tārakāmaya war, he was slain by Indra himself after displaying his prowess,
for he was unable to endure the entire host of gods together with their presiding deities.
All the Dānavas, Asuras, and Piśācas were slain by the Three-Eyed One in the battle with Andhaka throughout the three worlds.
Slain by the gods and humans, and likewise by the ancestors in every way,
the terrible Vṛtra was struck down in Hālāhala while he was engaged in combat with the Dānavas.
Then, by Mahendra with Viṣṇu as his ally, Vipracitti was turned back;
though he was a master of yoga concealed by illusion, he was slain upon his banner by Mahendra,
having entered the very form of that banner along with his younger brother.
Surrounded by the gods, Vṛṣa indeed conquered all the Daityas and Dānavas— both those who were restrained and those who were united— in the battle of Kolāhala.
At the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the sacrifice, Śaṇḍa and Marka were seen by the gods;
these were indeed the twelve battles that took place between the gods and the Asuras.
Causing the destruction of both gods and asuras, yet truly for the welfare of all creatures,
King Hiraṇyakaśipu shone for a billion years.
Having attained sovereignty over the three worlds, he ruled for seventy-two million, as well as eighty thousand additional years.
Furthermore, by way of succession, Bali was king for ten thousand years,
and again for sixty thousand, two hundred thousand, and twenty million years.
For as long as Bali held the authority of the kingdom,
for that same period Prahlāda indeed remained withdrawn from the asuras.
Those three Indrāstras were to be known as the most powerful among the Asuras;
once again, this entire world remained established under the Daityas for ten yugas.
This entire triple world was protected by Mahendra without agitation;
for ten yugas, moreover, it remained entirely free from rivals.
When that [Hiraṇyakaśipu] had been slain,
and by the turn of time the three worlds had come under the governance of Indra, the subduer of Pāka, Śukra then abandoned the asuras and went over to the gods.
When you had gone to the sacrifice for the gods, the sons of Diti challenged Kāvya, saying:
"Why have you abandoned our kingdom while we look on and gone back to the sacrifice? (Matsya Purāṇa 47.62)
"We are indeed unable to remain here; let us enter the netherworld (rasātala).
When they had spoken thus, he spoke to the dejected Daityas, consoling them with his voice: Matsya Purāṇa 47.63.
"Do not fear, O Asuras; I shall sustain you with my own splendor—both the mantras and the medicinal herbs, as well as the essences and whatever supreme wealth there may be."
All these [virtues] abide in me, while their foot remains indeed among the gods;
all of that I shall bestow upon you, for it was held by me for your sake.
Then the gods, seeing them surrounded by the wise Kāvya, consulted together, being fully aware and desiring to seize them.
"For this Kāvya forcibly turns all of us away from our purpose.
Let us depart quickly; let us go before he begins to teach."
"Having forcibly slain them, we shall cause the survivors to reach Pātāla.
Then the gods, becoming enraged, rushed toward the Dānavas.
Then, being struck down, they fled toward Kāvya himself;
thereupon Kāvya saw them being swiftly pursued by the gods.
Having withdrawn that protection through Kāvya, those gods, though previously oppressed by the Asuras,
saw Kāvya standing there and, free from fear, abandoned the Asuras.

Then Kāvya, having reflected upon those beneficial words of the Brahmins, spoke to them while recollecting their former conduct: tataḥ kāvyo 'nucintyātha brāhmaṇo vacanaṃ hitam / tānuvāca tataḥ kāvyaḥ pūrvaṃ vṛttamanusmaran // MatsP_47.71 //
The entire three worlds were seized from you by Vāmana with his three strides;
Bali was bound, Jambha was slain, and Virocana was struck down.
The great Asuras were slain by the gods in twelve battles;
for the most part, they were killed by various means, primarily those foremost among you.
"You are indeed still somewhat remaining; it is my opinion that there should be no more fighting.
Abide by the policy which I shall declare to you, until the turn of time. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.74)
"I shall go to Mahādeva for the sake of mantras that bring victory; then,
having obtained from the god Maheśvara those mantras that are irresistible,
we shall fight the gods again, and thereby you shall surely attain victory."
Then, having reached an agreement, those Asuras said to the gods:
"We have all laid down our weapons; we are without armor and without chariots."
"Having heard those words of Prahlāda, which were spoken in truth, they said: 'We shall practice austerities in the forest, clothed in bark garments.'"
Then the gods turned back, free from feverish anxiety and filled with joy;
when the Daityas had laid down their weapons, the deities desisted at that time.
Then Kāvya said to them: "For some time you shall remain humble, devoted to austerity, and waiting for the time that will accomplish your purpose. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.79)
"O Dānavas, wait for me while I remain in my father's hermitage";
having thus instructed the Asuras, Kāvya sought refuge with Mahādeva.
Śukra said:
"O God, I desire those mantras which do not exist with Bṛhaspati, for the defeat of the gods and for the victory of the Asuras. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.81)
Thus addressed, the god said: "O Bhārgava, perform this vow for a full thousand years: drinking the smoke of grain-chaff with your head hanging downwards;
if you do so, may it be well with you, then you shall obtain the mantras."
Saying "So be it," Śukra, the descendant of Bhṛgu, having received the permission, touched the feet of the god and spoke these words:
"O Lord, O Master, commanded by you today, I shall indeed observe the vow. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.83)
Then, dispatched by the God, Kuṇḍadhāra became his smoke-maker;
for when Śukra had departed for the sake of the Asuras,
he dwelt there with Maheśvara, practicing celibacy for the purpose of the mantra.
Having learned of that and perceiving the kingdom to have been entrusted [to him] by the Asuras according to political expediency,
the gods, filled with indignation at this vulnerability, then rushed toward them,
all armored and armed, led by Bṛhaspati.

Seeing the gods once again with weapons raised, the hosts of asuras suddenly sprang up in terror and spoke these words to them: matsya uvāca: matsya said: dṛṣṭvāsuragaṇā devān pragṛhītāyudhānpunaḥ / utpetuḥ sahasā te vai saṃtrastāstānvaco 'bruvan // MatsP_47.86 // Seeing the gods once again with weapons raised, the hosts of asuras suddenly sprang up in terror and spoke these words to them: matsya uvāca: matsya said: tato 'suragaṇāḥ kruddhā devān prati yayustadā / Then the hosts of asuras, filled with rage, rushed toward the gods. tataḥ samabhavadyuddhaṃ devānāṃ saha dānavaiḥ // MatsP_47.87 // Then a battle took place between the gods and the dānavas. śastrāstrairbahudhā muktairnighnatāmitaretaram / As they struck one another with various kinds of missiles and weapons, na ca sma kāścana vyathā babhūva tridivaukasām // MatsP_47.88 // not the slightest pain or distress arose among the inhabitants of heaven. te vadhyamānā balibhirasurairdevadānavāḥ / Being slaughtered by the powerful asuras, those gods and dānavas jagmurvidārayanto vai śaraistīkṣṇairmahābalāḥ // MatsP_47.89 // those mighty ones fled while piercing [the enemy] with sharp arrows. tato 'suragaṇā devān praharantaḥ punaḥ punaḥ / Then the hosts of asuras, striking the gods again and again, utpetuḥ sahasā te vai saṃtrastāstānvaco 'bruvan // MatsP_47.90 // suddenly sprang up in terror and spoke these words to them: bho bho suragaṇā yūyaṃ śṛṇudhvaṃ vacanaṃ mama / "O hosts of gods, listen to my words! yuddhaṃ na kurute yasmād bhavadbhiḥ saha no bhayāt // MatsP_47.91 //" Because he does not engage in battle with you out of fear. tato 'suragaṇāḥ kruddhā devān prati yayustadā / Then the hosts of asuras, filled with rage, rushed toward the gods. tataḥ samabhavadyuddhaṃ devānāṃ saha dānavaiḥ // MatsP_47.92 // Then a battle took place between the gods and the dānavas. śastrāstrairbahudhā muktairnighnatāmitaretaram / As they struck one another with various kinds of missiles and weapons, na ca sma kāścana vyathā babhūva tridivaukasām // MatsP_47.93 // not the slightest pain or distress arose among the inhabitants of heaven. te vadhyamānā balibhirasurairdevadānavāḥ / Being slaughtered by the powerful asuras, those gods and dānavas jagmurvidārayanto vai śaraistīkṣṇairmahābalāḥ // MatsP_47.94 // those mighty ones fled while piercing [the enemy] with sharp arrows. tato 'suragaṇā devān praharantaḥ punaḥ punaḥ / Then the hosts of asuras, striking the gods again and again, utpetuḥ sahasā te vai saṃtrastāstānvaco 'bruvan // MatsP_47.95 // suddenly sprang up in terror and spoke these words to them: bho bho suragaṇā yūyaṃ śṛṇudhvaṃ vacana
"When the weapons have been laid down, when safety has been granted, and when the preceptor has undertaken his vow,
you have indeed bestowed fearlessness upon us, yet you have arrived with the intent to kill."
"O gods, we are without a teacher; we stand here having abandoned our weapons, wearing rags and black antelope skins, inactive, and possessing nothing."
"We shall not be able to defeat even the gods in battle by any means whatsoever;
therefore, we shall seek refuge with the mother of Kāvya without fighting. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.89)
"We shall endure this hardship until our preceptor returns;
and once Śukra has withdrawn, we will fight, clad in armor and armed."
Having spoken thus, they then sought refuge with one another and with the mother of Kāvya;
being terrified, they did so, and she granted them freedom from fear.
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas! As long as you remain in my presence, there is no reason for you to be afraid."
Seeing that those asuras had been thus supported by her, the gods then attacked them with force, without considering their relative strength.
Then, seeing those asuras being oppressed by the gods, the goddess, filled with rage, said to the gods: "I shall deprive you of Indra. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.94)
Having gathered all the necessary materials, the goddess, rich in asceticism and firmly engaged in yoga, then approached Indra with great power and paralyzed him.
Then, seeing Indra thus paralyzed, the gods fled from there like mute men,
terrified upon seeing Indra brought under control.
When the hosts of gods had departed, Viṣṇu spoke to Śakra:
"Enter into me; may it be well with you; I shall lead you away, O best of gods."
Having been addressed thus, Purandara then entered Viṣṇu.
Seeing that he was protected by Viṣṇu, the goddess became enraged and spoke these words.
"O Maghavan, I shall burn you along with Viṣṇu by my power, while all beings look on; behold the strength of my asceticism! (Matsya Purāṇa 47.99)
Overpowered by her, those two gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, became [distressed].
How might we both be released? Viṣṇu spoke thus to Indra.
Indra said: "Kill her indeed, O Lord, before she consumes us both;
I am overwhelmed by her distinction, so kill her without delay. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.101)
Then Viṣṇu, having observed her and being beset by the distress of the potential slaughter of a woman,
meditated upon his discus and brought it forth for the sake of rescuing her.
Then Viṣṇu, acting with haste and filled with fear upon realizing what cruel deed that goddess intended to do,
took up his own weapon in anger and severed her head out of dread. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.103)
Seeing that terrible slaughter of his wife, Bhṛgu, the lord, became enraged;
then Viṣṇu was cursed by Bhṛgu on account of the killing of his wife.
"Since you, knowing the law, have caused a woman to be slain,
therefore you shall be reborn here among humans seven times."
Then, when dharma has been destroyed again and again by that curse,
he is born here among human beings for the sake of the welfare of the world.

Having addressed Viṣṇu and quickly taken that head, he then brought it to the body and, seizing it, spoke these words: matsya uvāca: kasmāt tvayā śiraśchinnaṃ mama putrasya bhūpate / etadākhyātumicchāmi tvattaḥ sarvaṃ yathātatham // MatsP_47.108 // The Fish said: "O King, why was the head of my son severed by you? I wish to hear all of this from you exactly as it happened. matsya uvāca: tataḥ sa rājā taṃ prāha matsyaṃ jātaṃ jalodbhavam / putraṃ me tvaṃ vijānīhi matsyarāja mahāmate // MatsP_47.109 // The Fish said: "Then that king spoke to the fish born from the water: 'O high-minded King of Fish, know me to be your son. matsya uvāca: ahaṃ te janako rājan nāmnā matsyo mahābala / tvāmahaṃ jñātumicchāmi tanme vyākhyātumarhasi // MatsP_47.110 // The Fish said: "O King, I am your father, a mighty fish by name; you ought to explain what must be done by you and me. matsya uvāca: putra me tvaṃ vijānīhi matsyarāja mahāmate / mayā tu yatkṛtaṃ karma tacchṛṇuṣva narādhipa // MatsP_47.116 // The Fish said: "O high-minded King of Fish, know me to be your son; O lord of men, listen to the deed performed by me. matsya uvāca: ahaṃ matsyo mahārāja tvāṃ putraṃ veda tattvataḥ / bhavatā ca mayā kāry
"O Goddess Viṣpūnā, you have been struck down; I shall restore you to life.
Then, joining his head to hers, he said, "Live! (MatsP 47.108).
If the entire Dharma has been known by me, or even practiced,
by that truth— provided that I speak the truth— may you live!
Then, having sprinkled her with cool water, he said, "Live! Thereupon, as soon as those words were uttered by him, the goddess was restored to life.
Then, seeing her as if she had just awakened from sleep, all beings cried out "Excellent!
Excellent! in every direction with their voices.
Thus was that goddess drawn back by Bhṛgu at that time, even as the gods looked on; it was indeed like a marvel.
The unperturbed Bhṛgu restored his wife to life once more;
and having seen this, Indra found no peace again due to the fear of Kāvya.
Then, while awake, Indra spoke these words to Jayantī: *Matsya Purāṇa 47.113*
Having reflected upon these words, the wise Indra, the subduer of Pāka, said to his daughter:
"This son of Kavi is indeed performing a terrible vow for the sake of his enemy;
therefore, O daughter, I have been greatly distressed by this intelligent man."
Go and attend upon him with tireless devotion, dispelling his fatigue through auspicious means and various services that are agreeable to his mind.
"O Kāvya, propitiate this twice-born man so that he may be satisfied.
Go; you have been given to him, so exert yourself for my sake. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.116)
Having been addressed thus, Jayantī accepted her father’s words and went to where he stood engaged in that formidable austerity.
Seeing him drinking the smoke of the grain-particles with his face turned downwards,
and being struck down by the Yakṣa Kuṇḍadhāra as he was falling, she [beheld him].
And seeing that Kāvya was being cast down,
standing there with his true form stilled by meditation, weak yet established in prosperity,
she then addressed Kāvya with the words exactly as they had been spoken by her father.
Praising him with agreeable words and speaking sweetly,
she attended to his limbs at the proper time with pleasant massages; thus,
in accordance with her observance of vows, she lived there for many years.
When that terrible smoke-vow was completed after a thousand years,
Bhava, being pleased, then offered a boon to Kāvya.
Mahādeva said:
"This vow has been performed by you alone and by no one else;
therefore, indeed, by means of your austerity, intelligence, sacred learning, and strength," *Matsya Purāṇa* 47.122.
And by your splendor alone, O Brahmin, descendant of Bhṛgu, you shall surpass all the gods; whatever is desired by you shall be attained. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.123)
"You shall attain all of that, but it must not be spoken of to anyone;
by that means, O best of the twice-born, you will become a conqueror of all."
Having granted these boons to that descendant of Bhṛgu,
Bhava further bestowed upon him the lordship over progeny, the lordship over wealth, and indeed invincibility.
Having obtained these boons, Kāvya’s hair stood on end with joy;
out of delight, a divine hymn manifested within him as he praised Maheśvara, the Blue-and-Red One (Nīlalohita), while remaining in a horizontal posture. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.126)
Śukra said:
"Homage be to the blue-throated one, the youngest, the most resplendent;
to the licking one, the son of Kavi, the calf, the lord of the food! *Matsya Purāṇa* 47.127.
Salutations to the one with matted hair, to the formidable one, to the one with tawny eyes, to the giver of boons,
to the one praised by all, to the one possessing sacred bathing places, to the God of gods, and to the impetuous one.
To the one with the crown-protrusion, the fair-faced, the multiform, the creator;
to the one whose seed is wealth, to Rudra, to the heat, to the one clothed in variegated garments.
To Hrasva, to Muktakeśa, to Senānī, and to Rohita;
to Kavi, to Rājavṛkṣa, and to Takṣakakrīḍana.
And to the thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, bestower of honey,
the excellent one of auspicious form, the white Puruṣa.
Salutations to Giriśa, to Arka, to the powerful one, and to Ājyapa;
to the well-satisfied, to the well-clothed, to the archer, and to Bhārgava.
To Niṣaṅgin, Tāra, Svakṣa, Kṣapaṇa,
Tāmra, Bhīma, Ugra, and Śiva.
To Mahādeva, to Śarva, and to Viśvarūpa-Śiva;
to Hiraṇya, to the Most Excellent, to the Eldest, and to the Middlemost.
O Lord of the Dwelling, salutations to Pināka, to Mukti, to Kevala,
to Mṛgavyādha, to Dakṣa, to Sthāṇu, and to Bhīṣaṇa.
To the one with many eyes, the bearer of burdens, the three-eyed one, and the Lord;
to the skull-bearer, the hero, Death, and the three-eyed god.
And to Babhru, Piśaṅga, Piṅgala, and Aruṇa; to Pinākin, Iṣumat, Citra, and Rohita.
To Dundubhya, to Ekapāda, to Aja, and to the giver of intelligence;
to the forest-dweller, to the householder, to the ascetic, and to the student.
To Sāṃkhya and Yoga, to the Pervasive One, to the Initiated,
to the Unstruck, to Śarva, to the Lord of the Fortunate, and to Yama.
To the one who is observant on the bank, to the great seer most devoted to sacred knowledge,
to the four-footed one, to the pure, to the protector, and to the swift-moving one.
To Śikhaṇḍin, to Karāla, to the fanged one, to the creator of the universe,
to the radiant, to the renowned, to the brilliantly shining, and to the one of excellent wisdom.
To the cruel, to the unchanging, to the terrifying, and to Śiva;
to the gentle, to the foremost, to the righteous, and to the auspicious.
To the one who is inviolable, the immortal, the eternal, and the everlasting;
to the active, the distinguished, the descendant of Bharata, and the witness.
To Kṣema, to Sahamāna, to Satya, and to Amṛta;
to the Maker, to Paraśu, and indeed to Śūlin, who possesses the divine eye.
To the drinker of Soma, the drinker of clarified butter, the drinker of smoke, and the drinker of heat;
to the pure one, to the one who clothes himself, to the newly born, and to Death.
To Piśitāśa, to Sarva, to Megha, and to Vidyuta;
to Vyāvṛtta, to Variṣṭha, to Bharita, and to Tarakṣu.
To Tripuraghna, to Tīrtha, to Avakra, and to Romaśa; to Tigmāyudha, to Vyākhyā, to Susiddha, and to Pulasti.
To Rocamāna, Caṇḍa, Sphīta, and Ṛṣabha;
to Vratī, Yuñjamāna, Śuci, and Ūrdhvaretas.
To the slayer of Asuras, to the slayer of evil, to the slayer of death, and to the one worthy of sacrifice;
to Kṛśānu, to the wise one, to the bearer of oblations, and to the stainless one.
To the destroyer of Rākṣasas, to the slayer of beasts, to the one free from obstacles, and to the one who breathes forth;
to the bewildered, to the great, and to the one difficult to traverse in the ocean.
And to Kṛṣṇa and Jayanta, the lord of the worlds,
to the one who is independent, the one who is to be pierced, and the one established in equanimity.
To Hiraṇyabāhu, to Vyāpta, to Mahat,
to Sukarman, to Prasahya, to Īśāna, and to Sucakṣus.
To Kṣipreṣu, to Sadaśva, to Śiva, and to the bestower of liberation;
to Kapila, to Piśaṅga, to Mahādeva, and to the wise one.
To Mahākāya, Dīpta, Rodana, and Sahāya;
to Dṛḍhadhanvin, Kavacin, Rathin, and Varūthin.
To Bhṛgunātha, to Śukra, to him who dwells in the abyss, to the Creator,
to the Unfailing, to the Tranquil, to the One of Excellent Wisdom, and to the Bull.
Homage be to you, O Blessed One, the All-pervading One who is clothed in animal skins;
homage to you, the Lord of beasts and the Lord of all beings.

Salutations to you, the essence of the *praṇava*, the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas; salutations to you, whose nature is *svāhā* and *svadhā*, and who are the very self of the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the essence of all mantras. *Matsya Purāṇa* 47.157.
Salutations to you, the self of action, who are Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhātṛ, and likewise Karta; who consist of sight and hearing; and who are the lord of the past, the future, and the present.
Salutations to you, the soul of the gods, who are indeed the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Asuras, Viṣṇu, and the Maruts.

Salutations to you, the self-existent and unborn one, who knows the ritual of Agni and Soma, who possesses the mantras and medicinal herbs for the sacrificial animal, who is indeed the primordial and first being,
and who is the Brahma-soul and the Lord of creatures.
Salutations to you, the self of all beings, who are the lord of the self, who are mastered by the self, who transcend all lords,
and who have become the limb of all living creatures.
Salutations to you, the self of Sāṃkhya, who are devoid of qualities yet the knower of qualities, who are both manifest and immortal, and who are the friend beyond all description.
Salutation to you, the soul of the worlds: to the earth, the intermediate space, the heavens, and the great realm; to Janas, Tapas, and Satya.
Salutations to you, the Unmanifest, the Great One, the source of the elements, and the sense-faculty;
salutations to you, the knower of the self, the distinct, and the soul of all.
Salutations to you, who are eternal, the mark of the Self, subtle, and indeed distinct from all else; salutations to you, the awakened one, the omnipresent lord, whose very nature is liberation.
Salutations to you in the three worlds; salutations to you beyond the three;

Thus addressed, having seen her with his divine eye, he said to her:

Seeing Kāvya returned having accomplished his purpose, all the sons of Diti,

Having perceived that opportunity, he too, urged by Indra,

Then, seeing them arrived, Bṛhaspati said:
"Welcome to those for whom I am the officiating priest; I have come for your benefit."
"I shall teach you the sciences that have been acquired by me.
Thereupon, with joyful minds, they approached him for the sake of learning.

"O Goddess of pure smiles, O virtuous lady with wide eyes of three colors and wandering glances, I am going to see those for whom I perform sacrifices. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.186)
Thus addressed, she said to him: "O observer of great vows, cherish those who are devoted to you.
This, O Brahmin, is the duty of the virtuous; I do not violate your dharma. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.187)

"Know me to be Kāvya; the all-pervading Lord Giriśa has been gratified by you.
Alas, you have all been deceived! Listen, O Dānavas! (Matsya Purāṇa 47.189)
Hearing him speak thus, they were then filled with agitation;
standing there, they gazed at both of them as they sat, utterly amazed.
Then, all of them being utterly bewildered, they did not understand anything at all;
while they were thus confounded, Kāvya then spoke to those Asuras.
"For I am your teacher, Kāvya; this Aṅgiras is the teacher of the gods.
Follow me, O Daityas, and abandon this Bṛhaspati! (Matsya Purāṇa 47.192)
Thus addressed by him, the Asuras looked at both of them;
however, the Asuras could perceive no distinction between those two.
Bṛhaspati, whose wealth is asceticism, spoke to them without agitation:
"O Daityas, I am Kāvya, your preceptor; this Bṛhaspati is merely in my form."
"O Asuras, this one is deluding you with my form!
Having heard him, they then gathered together and spoke. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.195)
"This lord has indeed ruled us constantly for ten years;
this twice-born man is our guru, yet he desires our downfall."
Then all those Dānavas, having prostrated and offered their congratulations, accepted his words; they were not deluded, owing to their long-standing practice [of discipline].
All those Asuras, their eyes bloodshot with rage, said to him:
"This man is our preceptor; go away, you are not our preceptor! (MatsP 47.198)
Whether he be of the lineage of Bhṛgu or Aṅgiras, this blessed one is our preceptor;
we abide under his command, so go forth at once, do not delay.
Having spoken thus, all the Asuras approached Bṛhaspati when they did not accept the great benefit spoken by Kāvya.
But Bhārgava was incensed by their arrogance, saying:
"O Dānavas, since you have been enlightened by me and yet do not resort to me."
"Therefore, having lost your senses, you shall surely meet with defeat.
Having spoken thus to them, Kāvya then departed as he had come.
Having learned that those Asuras had been cursed by Kāvya, Bṛhaspati,
having achieved his purpose, was then delighted and resumed his own form.
Having perceived through his intellect that the Asuras had been slain, he, having accomplished his purpose, vanished;
and when he had disappeared, the Dānavas became utterly bewildered.
Then they said to one another, "Alas, we have been deceived!
for they were struck by Aṅgiras from behind as well as from the front.
Deceived by his artifice regarding their respective objects,
they were dissatisfied; therefore, placing Prahlāda at their head, they quickly followed in the footsteps of Kāvya once again.
Then, having approached Kāvya, they stood before him with their faces cast down;
seeing them assembled once more, Kāvya spoke to his patrons.
"Since you do not rejoice in me after I have awakened you all, you have met with defeat because of that contempt. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.208)
To Śukra, who was speaking thus with a voice choked with tears, Prahlāda then said: "O Bhārgava, do not abandon us!"
O Bhārgava, favor those devotees who resort to you as their own refuge;
for while you were not seen, we were deluded by that preceptor of the gods.
You ought indeed to recognize these devotees with the eye of your long-accumulated asceticism.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, if you do not show us favor,
we shall enter the netherworld today, cursed by you.

Having understood the truth as it is, Kāvya, out of compassion and pity, being thus conciliated, restrained his anger and said to them: "You must not fear; you must not go to the netherworld (rasātala)."
"For those things that are destined to happen must necessarily come to pass while I am awake;

That consciousness which has been lost by you today, you shall regain;
and having conquered the gods, you shall likewise enter Pātāla once again.
And when the time for succession had arrived, Brahmā spoke thus:
"By my grace, the three worlds have been enjoyed by you with great power."
Having ascended to the heads of the gods, he remained there for ten complete ages known as *yugas*;
for such a length of time, Brahmā indeed exercised his sovereignty.
"O Sāvarṇika, your kingdom shall indeed be yours once again;
furthermore, your grandson Bali shall become the lord of the worlds. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.217)
Thus, indeed, was your grandson addressed by Viṣṇu himself in private;
when the worlds had been taken away by his word, various [reactions] truly arose within him.
Since all activities proceed from him and are directed by him,
therefore the Self-existent One, pleased with your conduct, has granted this to you.
"The Lord told me that Bali shall become the king of the gods;
therefore, he remains invisible to all beings, awaiting his time."
And another boon was granted to you by the Self-Existent One when he was pleased:
"Therefore, indeed, free from anxiety, you shall take your turn together with the asuras."
"O Lord, it was not possible for me to speak before you,
for I was forbidden by Brahmā, who knew that you would come to be."
"And these two disciples of mine are equal to Bṛhaspati;
they shall sustain all of you together with the gods."
Thus addressed by Kāvya of unwearied deeds, all the Asuras were delighted and went forth together with the high-souled Prahlāda.
Having heard the words spoken by Śukra that the outcome was inevitable,
yet still hoping for victory as Śukra had prophesied,
they all donned their armor, took up their weapons, and then challenged the gods.
Then, seeing the Asuras standing ready for battle,
all the gods, having gathered their equipment, fought them.
While that conflict between the gods and the asuras was thus proceeding for a hundred years, the asuras defeated the gods; thereupon, the gods indeed held a consultation.
"We shall summon those two by means of sacrifice; then we will defeat the Asuras.
Thereupon, the gods invited both Śaṇḍa and Marka.
And having summoned them at the sacrifice, they were told: "O twice-born ones, abandon the Asuras;
we shall honor you both once we have conquered the Dānavas. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.229)
When Śaṇḍa and Marka had thus made their agreement, as did the gods,
the deities then attained victory and the Dānavas were defeated.
Abandoned by Śaṇḍa and Marka, the Dānavas were likewise rendered powerless;
thus were the Daityas struck down in ancient times by the curse of Kāvya.
Overcome by the curse of Kāvya and deprived of all support,
they were driven away by the gods and entered the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Thus, from that time forward, the Dānavas were rendered devoid of effort by the gods through the hardship of Bhṛgu’s occasional curse.
When dharma had become lax, the Lord Viṣṇu was born again and again, establishing the order of dharma and bringing about the destruction of the asuras. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.234)
"Those Asuras who do not abide by the command of Prahlāda shall all be slayable by humans," the Lord declared. (Matsya Purāṇa 47.235)
In the Cākṣuṣa interval, Dharmā was born as a portion of Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, in the Vaivasvata interval, the gods performed the sacrifice.
Then, upon his manifestation, Brahmā indeed became the domestic priest when the fourth age had arrived and the gods had fallen into distress.
But at the end of the ocean, upon the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
during the second manifestation known as Narasiṃha, Rudra was indeed the family priest.
When the worlds were established in Bali during the seventh [cycle] of the Tretā-yuga,
for the sake of Vāmana, he acted with righteousness through his priest.
O twice-born ones, these three are known as his divine births;
now learn of the other seven human births which arose from curses.
In the first Tretā Yuga,
when one-fourth of Dharma had perished, Dattātreya appeared, preceded by Mārkaṇḍeya.
And in the Tretā age, on the fifteenth day of the month,
Māndhātā became a universal monarch (cakravartin), preceded by Uttanka.
In the nineteenth Tretā age, the all-pervading lord,
the son of Jamadagni, who brought about the end of all the Kṣatriyas, was the sixth [incarnation], preceded by Viśvāmitra.
In the twenty-fourth yuga, Rāma, the seventh son of Daśaratha, was born for the sake of Rāvaṇa, with Vasiṣṭha as his domestic priest.
In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu was born as Vedavyāsa from Parāśara,
preceded by Jātūkarṇya.
In order to establish the system of dharma and to bring about the destruction of the asuras,
the lotus-eyed Buddha was born as the ninth [incarnation] through his ascetic power,
preceded by Dvaipāyana, and possessing a form as beautiful as a god.
When that very age has declined and only its twilight remains,
Kalkī shall appear, preceded by Pārāśarya, as the son of Viṣṇuyaśas.
The tenth [incarnation] will be born as Bhāvya, preceded by Yājñavalkya;
he will [subdue] all beings who are paralyzed by ignorance and all heretics in every respect.
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Brahmins who had taken up their weapons.
Then, having utterly destroyed his enemies— the Śūdra kings who hate the Brahmins— he shall assume that very form.
Established in the twenty-fifth [yuga], Kalki, having accomplished his purpose, together with his army,
will personally purify the Śūdras as far as the edge of the ocean.
Having set his wheel in motion, that powerful one will bring about destruction,
having exterminated those śūdras who for the most part are unrighteous.
Then, at that time, Kalki, having accomplished his purpose along with his army,
will indeed personally bring prosperity to the subjects by means of him.
Deluded in this world, they will suddenly become angry with one another;
yet, having destroyed each other, they will be impelled by the destiny that is to come.
Then, after some time had passed, that god vanished;
and when the kings had perished, he then [reappeared] for the sake of gathering together the subjects.
But when the protection had ceased and they had struck one another in battle,
having killed each other, they were left without anyone to cry out for them and were deeply distressed.

Having abandoned cities and villages, they were free from possessions and regarded all things as equal; the duties of their stages of life (āśrama-dharma) had perished, and likewise, the system of social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) was lost.
At the end of the Yuga, houses will have pillars for their main supports, crossroads will have stakes of *śiva* trees for their foundations,
and women will have hair for their primary ornaments.
And those dwelling in the forests will have short bodies and short lifespans;
living by rivers and mountains, they will subsist on roots, leaves, and fruits.
Wearing rags, skins, and antelope hides, those people will resort to terrible confusion;
they will suffer from portents, possess meager wealth, and endure many afflictions.
Thus, having fallen into such hardship during that twilight period of time,
they shall then go to destruction along with the Kali age.
When that Kali Yuga had waned, the Kṛta Yuga then commenced;
thus has the conduct of the gods and asuras been correctly proclaimed.
In connection with the lineage of Yadu, I have briefly recounted the Vaiṣṇava glory;
now I shall proclaim that of Turvasu, as well as of Pūru, Druhyu, and Anu.
Matsya Purāṇa 48: Sūta said:
"The son of Turvasu was Garbha, and Gobhānu was his offspring."
The son of Gobhānu was the heroic Trisāri, who was unconquered.
Karaṃdhama was the son of Trisārin, and Bharata was his son;
Duṣyanta was the son of Paurava, and his son was indeed Akalmaṣa.
Thus, it is said that in ancient times, due to the curse of Yayāti regarding the transfer of his old age, Turvasu formerly entered the Paurava lineage. *Matsya Purāṇa* 48.3.
The heir of Duṣyanta was the king named Varūtha;
from Varūtha came Aṇḍīra, and Saṃdhāna was his son.
The Pāṇḍyas, the Keralas, the Colas, and likewise Karṇa—
their prosperous territories are known as the Pāṇḍyas, the Colas, and the Keralas.
Druhyu had two heroic sons, Setu and Ketu;
Setu’s son was Śaradvān, and Gandhāra was his son.
That great region of Gandhāra is known by his name;
its horses, born in the land of Āraṭṭa, are the best among steeds.
Dharma was the son of Gandhāraputra, and Ghṛta was his son;
from the learned Ghṛta was born Pracetas, who was his son.
The hundred sons of Pracetas were all kings;
they all became lords of the kingdoms of the Mlecchas and took refuge in the northern direction.
And Ano had three heroic sons who were supremely righteous:
Sabhānara, Cākṣuṣa, and likewise Parameṣu.
The son of Sabhānara was the learned King Kolāhala;
the son of Kolāhala was the righteous and renowned Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya had a son named Vīra, who was a conqueror of cities;
O great king, Janamejaya was the son of Puraṃjaya.
Mahāśāla was the son of the royal sage Janamejaya;
that king, equal to Indra, became established in great fame. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.13)
The son of that Mahāśāla, the righteous Mahāmanas,
was born as a universal monarch (cakravartin) who ruled over the seven continents.
But Mahāmanas begot two famous sons, both of whom were knowers of dharma: Uśīnara and Titikṣu.
The five wives of Uśīnara, born of royal sages,
were Bhṛśā, Kṛśā, Navā, Darśā, and the queen Dṛṣadvatī.
The sons born to them from Uśīnara were the upholders of the lineage;
through great asceticism, those righteous ones were born to the aged king.
Bhṛśā’s son was Nṛga, and Navā’s son was Nava. From Kṛśā was born Kṛśa, and from Darśā was born Suvrata.
Furthermore, the son of Dṛṣadvatī was King Śibi Auśīnara.
The sons of Śibi were four, world-renowned:
Pṛthudarbha, Suvīra, Kekaya, and Bhadraka.
Their prosperous territories were Kekaya, Bhadraka, Sauvīra, Paura, Nṛga, and likewise Kekaya. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.20)
Likewise, the city of Ambaṣṭhā belonged to Suvrata, while the city of Kṛśa was Vṛṣalā;
Navarāṣṭra belonged to Nava, but now hear about the progeny of Titikṣu.
The king renowned in the eastern direction was Titikṣu;
his son was Bṛhadratha, and Sena was the son of the latter.
From Sena was born Sutapas, and the son of Sutapas was Bali;
he was born into human form through his desire for progeny when his lineage had become extinct. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.23)
But that great yogi Bali, though bound with fetters by the Great-Souled One,
begot five royal sons born of his wife.
He begot Aṅga, Vaṅga, and likewise Suhma;
as well as Puṇḍra and Kaliṅga. That region is called Bāleya, O Lord, and the Bāleya Brāhmaṇas were the progenitors of his lineage.
And a boon was granted by the gratified Brahmā to the wise Bala:
the state of a great yogin and a lifespan equal to the duration of a kalpa.
Invincibility in battle, supreme intelligence regarding dharma,
the vision of the three periods of time, and likewise preeminence in procreation.
He is the lord who will establish incomparable victory in battle, the vision of the true meaning of dharma,
and the four fixed social orders (varṇas).
And their five heirs were the Vaṅgas, Aṅgas, Suhmakas, Puṇḍras, and Kaliṅgas; now learn of the lineage of Aṅga.
The sages said:
"How were the five sons of that great-souled Bali born?
What was the name of his queen who gave birth to them, and which rishi was their progenitor?"
And how were they produced by him? Tell that to us who ask;
and describe in its entirety his majesty and his power.
Sūta said:
Now, in ancient times, there was a learned ṛṣi known as Uśija;
that great-souled one had a wife named Mamata.
The younger brother of Uśijas, the highly effulgent Bṛhaspati, out of desire approached Mamata, the wife of his brother. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.33)
But Mamatā, the woman of excellent complexion, said to her husband’s younger brother, "I am pregnant with your elder brother's child; please desist. (MatsP 48.34)
But this fetus of mine, O illustrious Bṛhaspati, son of Uśij, born of my brother, might become enraged as he recites the Veda along with its auxiliary branches. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.35)
"Your seed is also infallible; therefore, you ought not to consort with me.
Since time has passed in this manner, O Lord, do as you see fit."
Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati, though possessed of great splendor and being a high-souled being, did not restrain his mind, for he was possessed by desire. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.37)
That righteous-souled one indeed united with her against his will;
but as he was emitting that seed, the embryo addressed him with these words.
O dear father, Lord of Speech, there is no possibility here for two [to coexist];
you are one whose seed is never in vain, and I have arrived here first.
Thus addressed, the venerable seer Bṛhaspati became enraged and cursed that son of his elder brother who was still in the womb. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.40)
"Since you have thus forbidden me even while remaining in the womb at such a time, therefore you shall enter into long-lasting darkness."
From that curse, a sage named Dīrghatamas was born;
from him was born Aṃśaja, who possessed great fame and was like Bṛhaspati in his splendor.
Then, with his vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), he lived in the hermitage of his brother;
there he heard the duties of the Saurabheyas from Vṛṣabha.
His brother was his paternal uncle, who then provided him with sustenance; while he was living with him, a bull arrived there by chance.
The son of Surabhi grazed upon the darbha grass brought for the sake of the sacrifice;
Dīrghatamas, however, seized that four-footed creature by its two horns.
Thus he was restrained, yet he did not move even a single step from his place;
then the bull said to him, "Release me, O best among the strong! (Matsya Purāṇa 48.46)
"O father, I have not encountered anywhere anyone as powerful as you;
nor indeed is there another equal to me in the reckoning of strength.
Release me, O father—and since I am pleased with you, choose a boon. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.47)
Thus addressed, he said to him: "Where will you go while I am alive?
I shall not release you, for you are a four-footed beast who tastes the property of others."
The bull said:
"O dear one, we possess neither sin nor theft;
likewise, for us there is no distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, nor between what is fit and unfit to be drunk."
For these many rules for bipeds are indeed recorded as the law for cattle;
they concern what should and should not be done, as well as the prohibition against approaching those who must not be approached.
Sūta said:
Having heard the dharma of cows, he was indeed bewildered;
having dismissed him, he propitiated the Lord of Cows by giving food, drink, and gifts according to his ability.
When he had departed after being propitiated, he, being devoted to that and intent upon it,
mentally undertook the duty of a cow, for he was indeed fixed in that and dedicated to it.
Then he approached the wife of Gautama’s younger brother;
perceiving her to be arrogant, he was unable to endure her, like a bull.
But considering divine dharma to be supreme, he approached his daughter-in-law;
however, she rebuked him, restrained him, and seized him firmly by both arms.
Having understood that matter which was destined to be so by virtue of her own greatness, she said to him:
"Having fallen into this reversal of fortune, you behave like an ox."

"You do not distinguish between those who may and may not be approached; seeking my daughter out of a bull's nature, I abandon you today for your wicked conduct—go now by the power of your own karma!"
"Having placed him in a wooden chest, cast him into the waters of the Gaṅgā;
for you are blind and old, and this ill-behaved man must be supported by you. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.57)
As he was being swept away with great force by the current,
the righteous Bali, son of Virocana, approached him and seized him.
In the inner apartments, he guarded him while satisfying him with various kinds of food and drink;
and being pleased, he indeed invited Bali to choose a boon.
And therefore, for the sake of a son, that bull among Dānavas chose a boon:
"O giver of honor, O illustrious one, you ought to procreate in my wife sons who know the truth of dharma and artha for the sake of our lineage."
Thus addressed, the powerful celestial sage replied, "So be it.
The king then sent his own wife, named Sudeṣṇā;
however, knowing him to be blind and aged, that queen did not go. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.61)
Then, that self-controlled seer sent a Śūdra woman who was his nurse’s daughter to the blind man;
through her, who was of Śūdra birth, he begot Kakṣīvat and others.
"The righteous-souled one begot the Śūdras," and so forth;
having seen Kakṣīvat and the others, King Bali spoke thus to him.
The King said:

[I seek those] who are proficient in the dharma of the sages, lords, exponents of Brahman, learned, having direct perception of dharma, intelligent, virtuous in conduct, and pure. *Matsya Purāṇa* 48.64.
"It is mine alone," Bali said to that Dīrghatamas;
the sage did not say anything to him, but replied, "It is indeed mine. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.65)
"O best of gods, O Bhavacchanda, those born from a Śūdra womb—
knowing me to be blind and old, Sudeṣṇā, your queen,
sent me, O King, to a Śūdra woman who was my nurse, out of contempt for me. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.66)
Then Bali propitiated that best of sages;
meanwhile, the Dānava Bali rebuked his wife Sudeṣṇā.
Having adorned her once more, he presented her to the Ṛṣi;
then Dīrghatamas accepted that queen who had acted in such a manner.

"Anoint me with curd mixed with salt and with licorice; lick me, O Goddess, without revulsion, from the soles of my feet to the top of my head. Then you shall obtain sons exactly as desired by your mind. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.69)
Then the goddess carried out all those words of his;
having reached his drinking place, the goddess avoided it at that time.
Then he said to her: "O auspicious one, since you have avoided [drinking] that which was offered, you shall give birth to a first-born son who is without drink. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.71)
Sudeṣṇā said:
"O highly fortunate one, you ought not to give me such a son as this.
Since you have been gratified by me to the best of my ability, O Lord, show me your favor. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.72)
Dīrghatamas said:
"O auspicious lady, this shall not happen otherwise than through your own transgression;
your son will certainly not grant you [the boon], but your grandson will indeed grant you the fruit."
"Without his downward breath (apāna), he will not attain the state of fitness;
therefore, having touched this in the belly among the limbs of Dīrghatamas," he spoke thus.
O lady of pure smiles, whatever has been consumed by them enters their limbs, yet not into the generative organ;
by that means they remain within the womb like the lord of stars on the full moon night.
There will be five princes who are like sons of gods;
they will be radiant, of excellent conduct, performers of sacrifices, and righteous.
Sūta said:
From that portion [of the seed], a son was born as the eldest to Sudeṣṇā;
he was Aṅga, as well as Kaliṅga, Puṇḍra, and likewise Suhma.
Vaṅgarāja—these five were the sons of Bali born of his wife;
thus these sons were likewise bestowed upon Bali by Dīrghatamas.
Then, having established those who had attained the status of Brahmins,
he indeed caused offspring to be born from human wombs.
Then Surabhi spoke these words to that Dīrghatamas:
"O Lord, because you have reflected and made the law of cows your authority."
O sinless one, I am pleased with you because of that singular devotion you have shown toward me;
therefore, having inhaled this long darkness, I shall surely dispel it for you.
"Likewise, this evil belonging to Bṛhaspati indeed dwells within you;
having smelled it, I drive away from you old age, death, and darkness."
As soon as he was smelled, that best of sages, Asita,
immediately became long-lived, possessed of a beautiful body, and endowed with sight.
When the darkness was dispelled by the rays of the sun, Gautama then became Kakṣīvān;
having gone from there with his father to Girivraja.
Having seen and touched his father, he indeed sat down for long-term austerity;
then, after a great length of time, he was purified by that penance.
Having shaken off his body born of a mother, the omnipresent Lord attained the state of a Brahmin;
then his father said to him, "Indeed, I have become a father through you."
O knower of dharma, I have achieved my purpose through that illustrious and virtuous son;
having liberated himself from there, he indeed attained the abode of Brahmā.
Having attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa, Kākṣīvat begot a thousand sons;
these sons of Kākṣīvat are remembered as the Kauṣmāṇḍas and the Gautamas.
Thus has this meeting of Dīrghatamas with Bali, the son of Virocana, been told to you, as well as the lineage of both.
Having been thus congratulated by his sons, the virtuous Bali, who was himself accomplished in purpose and veiled by his own yogic power (yogamāyā), spoke to those five sinless sons.
Invisible to all beings, that lord indeed awaits his time;
there, the king Dadhivāhana was the heir of Aṅga.
The son of Dadhivāhana was known as King Diviratha;
the offspring of Diviratha was the learned king Dharmaratha.
For on that mountain Viṣṇupada, that glorious Dharmaratha—
the Soma— was indeed drunk together with the high-souled King Śukra.
Now, it is said that Dharmaratha had a son named Citraratha;
his son was Satyaratha, and from him, it is said, came Daśaratha.
He was renowned as Lomapāda, and Śāntā was his daughter.
Then there was the heroic and highly illustrious son of Daśaratha, who possessed a fourfold army.
By the grace of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a son who increased his own lineage was born to Caturaṅga; he was known as Pṛthulākṣa.
The son of Pṛthulākṣa was indeed named Campa;
and the city of Campa belonged to Campa, which in former times was called Mālinī.
By the grace of Pūrṇabhadra, Haryaṅga became his son;
and from Vibhāṇḍaka at a sacrifice, Vāraṇa, the repeller of enemies, was born to him.
With mantras, he brought down that excellent vehicle to the earth;
it is said that Bhadraratha was born as the heir of Haryaṅga.
Then Bhadraratha had a son named Bṛhatkarman, a lord of men;
his son was Bṛhadbhānu, from whom was born the high-souled [Bṛhadratha]. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.100)
Bṛhadbhānu, the lord of kings, indeed begot a son named Jayadratha; from him came King Bṛhadratha.
From Bṛhadratha was born Janamejaya Viśvajit;
his heir was Aṅga, and from him King Karṇa was born.
Vṛṣasena was the son of Karṇa, and Pṛthusena was his son;
all these sons of Aṅga have been proclaimed by me as kings in detail and in their proper order. Now listen, O twice-born ones, to the lineage of Puru. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.103)
The sages said:
"How was Karṇa the son of a Sūta, and how was he the son of Aṅga?
We wish to hear this, for you are indeed exceedingly skillful."
Sūta said:
The son of Bṛhadbhānu was born as the king named Bṛhanmanas;
he had two wives, both of whom were daughters of Śibi.
And Yaśodevī and Satyā—listen to me regarding their lineage as well.
Yaśodevī gave birth to King Jayadratha;
and Satyā, the wife of Bṛhanmanas, bore the famous son named Vijaya.
Vijaya’s son was Bṛhatputra; his son was Bṛhadratha;
and Bṛhadratha’s son was the high-minded Satyakarman.
From Satyakarman came Adhiratha, who is known as the Sūta;
he was the one who took Karna under his care, and for that reason Karna is called the son of a Sūta.
All this regarding Karna has been related exactly as it was told. (Matsya Purāṇa 48.108)
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 49:
Sūta said:
"Pūru’s son was King Janamejaya, who possessed great splendor."
Prācīvat was his son, who established the eastern direction.
Prācītvata’s son was Manasyu;
likewise, the king named Pītāyudha was the son of Manasyu.
His heir was the lord of the earth named Dhundhu;
Dhundhu’s son was Bahuvidha, and Sampāti was his offspring.
Sampāti was the son of Raṃhovega, and Bhadrāśva was his son.
To Bhadrāśva, ten sons were born by Dhṛtā, the daughter of an Apsaras.
Auceyu, Hṛṣeyu, Kakṣeyu, Saneyuka,
Dhṛteyu, Vineyu, and Sthaleyu, O best of men.
Dharmeyu, Saṃnateyu, and Puṇyeyu—these were his ten sons.
Auceyu’s wife was named Urjvalanā, who was indeed the daughter of Takṣaka.
Upon her he begot Antināra, the lord of the earth;
and Antināra begot excellent sons of great intelligence upon Manasvinī.
Amūrtarayas was a hero, and Trivana was likewise righteous;
Gaurī was the third daughter, the auspicious mother of Māndhātṛ. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.8)
Ilīnā, however, was the daughter of Yama;
she gave birth to sons who were preeminent in the exposition of the Veda, for Ilīnā was indeed a bestower of auspiciousness.
Upadānavī obtained four sons from the son of Tila,
namely Ṛṣyaṇta, Duṣyanta, Pravīra, and Anagha.
From Duṣyanta, that universal monarch, was born Samitiṃjaya;
from him, by Śakuntalā, came Bharata, after whose name the Bhāratas are so called.
Regarding the son of Duṣyanta, an incorporeal voice spoke to the king:
"The mother is but a bellows; the son belongs to the father; he by whom one is begotten is indeed his own self."
"Support your son, Duṣyanta; do not despise Śakuntalā.
A son leads the progenitor from the abode of Yama after death;
you are the sower of this embryo—Śakuntalā has spoken the truth. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.13)
It is said that in ancient times, when the sons of Bharata had perished,
a great destruction was brought about by the wrath of their mothers toward their own sons.
Then, having been brought by the Maruts, that son of Bṛhaspati,
Bharadvāja, was transferred by the Maruts to Bharata.
The sages said:
"How was the highly effulgent Bharadvāja caused by the Maruts to transfer his seed for the sake of a son to Bharata? Tell us that exactly as it happened."
Sūta said:
While his wife was pregnant, that son of Uśij remained on earth;
seeing his brother’s wife, Bṛhaspati spoke to him. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.17)
"Adorn yourself well, O auspicious lady, and attend upon me for sexual union.
Thus addressed, she spoke to Bṛhaspati herself: Matsya Purāṇa 49.18: "Thus addressed, she spoke to him, to Bṛhaspati himself:"
This embryo has matured and speaks the Veda with its voice;
you too are one whose seed is unfailing, yet you thus revile the Dharma.
Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati himself said to her:
"O woman of excellent complexion, you must not instruct me in discipline."
Assailing her by force, he proceeded to violate her for sexual intercourse;
then the embryo spoke to Bṛhaspati as he was thus assailing her.
"O Bṛhaspati, I was indeed already established here; furthermore, you are one whose seed is never in vain. There is no room here for two. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.22)
Thus addressed by the embryo, he replied in anger:
"Since you forbid me at such a time as this, which is desired by all beings,
therefore you shall enter into long-lasting darkness."
Then, having restrained his desire out of joy for Bṛhaspati, that semen fell upon the earth;
having been withdrawn, it became a child.
Upon seeing that newborn boy, Mamata said to him:
"I shall indeed go to my own home; O Bṛhaspati, please take care of him."
Having spoken thus, she departed; and when she had gone, he too abandoned him.
Seeing that infant Bharadvāja abandoned by his mother and father, the Maruts, moved by compassion, took him up.
At that time, the powerful Bharata,
desiring a son, performed for many years sacrifices intended to procure offspring.
When that powerful sacrificer could not obtain a son,
he then performed the Marutsoma sacrifice for the sake of a son.
With that Marutsoma, those Maruts offered praise;
they indeed presented Bharadvāja to Bharata for the sake of obtaining a son.
The legitimate son of Bṛhaspati, the offspring of Aṅgiras’s son,
was transferred by the Maruts to Bharadvāja for the sake of Bharata.
But Bharata, having obtained Bharadvāja as his son, said: "O Lord, first you have accomplished your own welfare; I, too, have been fulfilled by you, O powerful one. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.31)
But when that birth of a son had previously proved futile,
the king Bharadvāja thereafter became known by the name Vitatha.

Therefore, from that Bharadvāja as well, there arose on earth Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas who were of dual lineage (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa) and of noble descent (kaulīna), and they are remembered as being of two kinds.
Then, when those two were proven false, Bharata went to heaven;
for the seer Bharadvāja, having consecrated his son, had indeed ascended to heaven.
The heir of Vitatha was the highly illustrious Bhuvamanyu;
he had four sons, equal to the great elements, who were all named Bhuvamanyus.
Bṛhatkṣatra was of great heroism, as was the heroic Nara and Garga;
Saṃkṛti was the son of Nara, and his son was Mahāyaśas.
Gurudhī and Rantideva are remembered as those two who were honored;
and from Garga, the learned Śibi was born as his heir.
Then the Śaibyās and the Gargas are recorded as twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas;
and the wise Urukṣava was the son of Āhārya.
His wife Viśālā, of great renown, gave birth to three sons:
Tryuṣaṇa, Puṣkari, and Kavi.
Indeed, these Urukshavas are remembered as having all attained the status of Brahmins;
these three great seers are declared to be the foremost among the Kavyas.
The Gargas, Saṃkṛtis, and Kāvyas were twice-born Kṣatriyas;
likewise, the Aṅgirasas, Dakṣas, and the land of Bṛhatkṣatra were gathered together.
The heir of Bṛhatkṣatra was indeed named Hastin;
by him this city, formerly called Gajasāhvaya, was built.
And Hastin had three heirs of supreme renown:
Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and likewise Purumīḍha.
Ajamīḍha had three wives who were the upholders of the Kuru lineage:
the renowned Nīlinī, Dhūminī, and Keśinī. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.44)
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, that man of great splendor begot upon them sons of divine luster; though he was aged, these righteous sons were born.
Through the grace of Bhāradvāja, hear from me their detailed account:
it is said that Kaṇva was born to Ājamīḍha by Keśinī. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.46)
His son was Medhātithi; from him the Kāṇvāyana twice-born ones descended. From Ajamīḍha, by his wife Bhūminī, the king Bṛhadanu was born. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.47)
From Bṛhadanu was born Bṛhanta; from Bṛhanta came Bṛhanmanas;
and the son of Bṛhanmanas was known as Bṛhaddhanus.
Bṛhaddhanu’s son was Bṛhadiṣu, whose son was Jayadratha;
Aśvajit was his son, and Senajit was his offspring.
Now, Senajit had four sons, world-renowned:
Rucirāśva, Kāvya, and King Dṛḍharatha.
Vatsa was the king Āvartaka, whose sons were the Parivatsakas;
the heir of Rucirāśva was the highly illustrious Pṛthusena.
From Pṛthusena was born Paura, and from Paura was born Nīpa;
Nīpa had one hundred sons of immeasurable splendor.
All those kings were known as the Nīpas;
among them was the illustrious founder of their lineage, the increaser of the fame of the Nīpas.
From Kāvya was born Samara, who was always fond of battle;
from Samara were born Pāra, Sampāra, and Sadaśva—these three.
Sons endowed with all virtues were indeed born, renowned throughout the earth;
Pāra’s son was Pṛthu, and from Pṛthu, Sukṛta was born.
Vibhrāja, endowed with all virtues, was born as his son;
and the heir of Vibhrāja was the powerful one named Aṇuha.
The highly illustrious Kṛtī, the son-in-law of Śuka, became the husband of Kṛtī;
the heir of Aṇuha was the lord of the earth, Brahmadatta.
His son was the highly illustrious Yugadatta, and Viṣvaksena;
Vibhrāja was born again through his well-performed deeds in this world.
Viṣvaksena’s son was indeed Udaksena;
his son was Bhallāṭa, and his son was Janamejaya.
For his sake, all the Nīpas were destroyed by Ugrāyudha.
The sages said:
Whose son was Ugrāyudha, and in whose lineage is he said to be?
For what reason were all those Nīpas destroyed by him?
Sūta said:
Ugrāyudha, a descendant of the Solar dynasty, performed austerities in Varāśrama;
having become as motionless as a pillar, Janamejaya attended upon him for eight thousand years.
Having promised him the kingdom, the Lord struck down the Nīpas;
he spoke various words of conciliation, yet they indeed struck both of them as well. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.62)
To those who had come seeking to kill him, he said: "Because I have not followed my word for the sake of protecting those who seek refuge, for that very reason I curse you thus."
"If I have performed any ascetic penance, let Yama lead all of you away.
Then, as they were being dragged along by Yama before him, he [spoke].
Overcome by supreme compassion, he said to Janamejaya:
"You ought to protect these heroes who have come here for my sake."
Janamejaya said:
"O sinful ones of wicked conduct, shall you become his servants?
Having been told "So be it" by Yama, the king then fought for a long time. (Matsya Purāṇa 49.66)
Having forcibly conquered those [demons] along with Yama and the terrible hellish diseases, he gave them to the Sage; that was like a marvel.
Yama, being pleased, then bestowed upon him the supreme knowledge of liberation;
having all performed what was appropriate, they departed for the imperishable Kṛṣṇa.
But those who adopt their conduct are not slain by untimely deaths;
they enjoy inexhaustible happiness both in this world and in the next.
From Ajamidha and Dhuminī was born the wise Yavinara;
his son was Dhritimat, and his son is recorded as Satyadhṛti.
Then the powerful Dṛḍhanemi was the son of Satyadhṛti.
The son of Dṛḍhanemi was the king named Sudharmā;
Sudharmā’s son was the powerful sovereign, Sārvabhauma.
Renowned as Sārvabhauma, he shone as the sole sovereign upon the earth;
in his great lineage was born Mahāpaurava, the delighter of the Pauravas.
The son of Mahāpaurava was known as King Rukmaratha;
then, the son of Rukmaratha was the monarch named Supārśva.
The son of Supārśva was also the righteous Sumati;
and from Sumati was born the virtuous King Saṃnatimat.
To that Saṃnatimat was born a great son named Kṛta;
he was a disciple of the high-souled Kauśalya Hiraṇyanābha.
Those by whom the Sāma-saṃhitās were indeed proclaimed in twenty-four ways are remembered here as the Prācyasāmanas, the chanters of the Sāman named Kārtas.
That Kārti, wielder of fierce weapons and the enhancer of the great Pauravas,
was he by whom the father of Pṛthuka was slain through his prowess.
The self-controlled great king named Nīla, the lord of the Pañcālas, was the heir of Ugrāyudha; he was the highly illustrious one known as Kṣema.
From Kṣema was born Sunītha, and from Sunītha came Nṛpaṃjaya;
from Nṛpaṃjaya was born Viratha—these are the Pauravas who have been praised.
Matsya Purāṇa 50: Sūta said: From Ajamīḍha and Nīlinī was born King Nīla.
Through the fierce austerity of Nīla, perfect tranquility arose.
From Suśānti was born Purujānu; from Purujānu came Pṛthu;
Pṛthu’s heir was Bhadrāśva. Now hear of the sons of Bhadrāśva.
Mudgala, Jaya, King Bṛhadiṣu, the valiant Javīnara, and Kapila as the fifth. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.3)
They know these five regions as the Pañcālas;
for we have heard that these are the protectors of the lands of the Pañcālas.
The descendants of Mudgala are the Maudgalyas, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas;
these Kaṇva-Mudgalas have indeed taken refuge in the faction of Aṅgiras.
To Mudgala was born a son, most devoted to Brahman and of great renown;
his son was Indrasena, and Vindhyāśva was his offspring.
