It is heard that from Vindhyāśva and Menakā a pair was born:
the royal sage Divodāsa and the illustrious Ahalyā. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.7)
Ahalyā gave birth to Śaradvat’s heir,
the best of sages named Śatānanda, who was himself a man of great asceticism.
His son was named Satyadhṛti, who had reached the further shore of the science of archery;
and from that righteous Satyadhṛti was born Śukra, whose seed was unfailing.
Having seen an Apsaras in the water, the semen of Satyadhṛti was discharged;
there, a pair was produced, brought forth in that very lake.
Then, while out on a hunt, King Śantanu saw him wading across that lake and, moved by compassion, he seized him.
These excellent Gautamas, the sons of Śaradvat, have been described;
hereafter, I shall indeed declare the progeny of Divodāsa.
The heir of Divodāsa was the most righteous King Mitrayu;
he was the foremost of the Maitrāyaṇas, and from him Maitreya is said to have descended.
These are the lineages of the ascetics; the Bhārgavas, however, are endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
And the king known as Caidyavara is remembered as the son of Maitreya.
Then, when the lineage had declined, the wise Sudās was born from the best of the Cedis, and his son Ajamīḍha was born again as Somaka.
When he was slain, Jantu, the son of Somaka, became the father of a hundred sons;
such was the lineage of the high-souled Ajamīḍha-Somaka.
But Ajamīḍha’s queen, Dhūminī, who increased the lineage with sons, performed difficult penance for a hundred years because she lacked a son. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.17)
Having duly and properly offered oblations into the fire and purified her food, she,
observing the great vow, went to sleep according to the ritual procedure for the Agnihotra.
In that Dhūmavarṇā, Ajamīḍha begot Ṛkṣa,
who was of the color of smoke and had a hundred elder brothers.
From Ṛkṣa was born Saṃvaraṇa, and from Saṃvaraṇa was born Kuru;
he, having gone beyond Prayāga, established Kurukṣetra.
Then, as the great king was being dragged for many years,
Śakra, being thus dragged, granted him a boon out of fear.
Kurukṣetra is remembered as both meritorious and delightful;
its lineage was very great, and it is after his name that they are called the Kauravas.
Kuru’s beloved sons were Sudhanvan, Jahnu,
the highly resplendent Parīkṣit, and Prajana, the crusher of enemies.
The heir of Sudhanvan was his son Cyavana, the best among the wise;
his son was King Cyavana, who knew the true essence of dharma and artha.
Cyavana’s son was Kṛmi, who was born from Ṛkṣa and was a man of great asceticism;
Kṛmi’s son was the very powerful and renowned lord Indrasama.
The heroic Vasu, the ruler of the Cedis, was a traveler of the intermediate space;
from that Caidyoparicara, Girikā bore seven sons.
The renowned Bṛhadratha was the great chariot-warrior and king of Magadha;
his sons were Pratyaśravas, Kuśa, and Harivāhana as the fourth.
Pañcama, Yajus, Matsya, and Kālī was the seventh;
the heir of Bṛhadratha was the renowned one named Kuśāgra.
And the son of Kuśāgra was the powerful one named Vṛṣabha;
the heir of Vṛṣabha was the king named Puṇyavat.
From him was born Puṇya, and from Puṇya came the king Satyadhṛti;
from that Dhanu was born his heir, and from him was born Sarva.
The son of Sarvasambhava was King Bṛhadratha;
two fragments were born to him, and he was joined together by Jarā.
Because he was joined together by Jarā, he is therefore known as Jarāsaṃdha;
Jarāsaṃdha, possessed of great strength, was the conqueror of all the kṣatriyas.
The son of Jarāsaṃdha was the powerful Sahadeva;
the son of Sahadeva was the illustrious Somavit, who was a man of great asceticism.
Śrutaśravas is proclaimed as the son of Soma and others among the Māgadhas;
Jahnu, however, begot a son named Suratha, a protector of the earth.
The heir of Suratha was the heroic King Vidūratha;
and the son of Vidūratha is remembered as Sārvabhauma.
From Sārvabhauma came Jayatsena, and Rucira was his son;
from Rucira came Bhauma, and from him Tvaritāyu was born.
Akrodhana was the son of Āyu; from that god he is known as Devātithi.
The heir of Devātithi was indeed Dakṣa.
From Bhīmasena came Dakṣa, and his son was Dilīpa;
Pratīpa was the son of Dilīpa, and he is remembered as having three sons.
Devāpi, Śantanu, and Vāhlīka—these were the three.
Of Vāhlīka, there were seven heirs, the kings who were the lords of the Vāhlīkas.
But Devāpi, being reviled by his subjects, became an ascetic.
The sages said:
"For what reason indeed was the lord of men reviled by the subjects?
What fault was proclaimed against the prince by the people?"
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, there was once a prince who suffered from leprosy; they did not honor him, for the duty toward the Kṣatriyas is indeed a matter for the gods."
I shall proclaim what is to come regarding Śantanu; listen to it.
Śaṃtanu became the king; he was indeed a learned and great physician.
And regarding this great physician, they cite here this verse: MatsP_50.42: "They say that the son of Śaṃtanu was a great physician."
Whomever he touches with his two hands—whether an aged man or even one who is diseased—he becomes young again; therefore, they know him as Śantanu.
Indeed, his name Śaṃtanu was proclaimed here by the subjects;
therefore, O King, Śaṃtanu chose the daughter of Jahnu as his wife.
In her, the lord begot a son named Devavrata;
meanwhile, Kālī, the daughter of the fisherman, gave birth to a son, Vicitravīrya.
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana begot a beloved son of Śantanu, who was tranquil in soul and stainless,
in the wife of Vicitravīrya.
She gave birth to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura;
and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, in turn, begot one hundred sons upon Gāndhārī.
Among them, Duryodhana was the foremost and indeed the lord of all the kṣatriyas;
likewise, Mādrī and Kuntī became the two wives of Pāṇḍu.
Five sons were born to Devadattā for the sake of Pāṇḍu;
Yudhiṣṭhira was born from Dharma, and Vṛkodara from Māruta.
From Indra was born Dhanañjaya, whose prowess was equal to that of Indra;
and from the two Aśvins, Mādrī gave birth to Nakula and Sahadeva. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.50)
These five sons were born to the Pāṇḍavas by Draupadī;
Draupadī bore Prativindhya, the eldest, from Yudhiṣṭhira.
From Bhīmasena was born Śrutasena; from Dhanañjaya, Śrutakīrti;
and from Sahadeva, the fourth, Śrutakarman, was born.
From Nakula, Śatānīka was born; these are proclaimed as the sons of Draupadī.
Beyond them, there were six other great chariot-warriors (mahāratha) who were the sons of Pāṇḍu.
From Bhīmasena was born a son, Ghaṭotkaca, by Hiḍimbā;
and from Bhīma, the son of Baladhara, Kāśī gave birth to a son named Sarvaga.
Mādrī gave birth to a son named Suhotra from Sahadeva,
while Niramitra was born to Nakula from Kareṇumatī, the princess of Cedi.
From Subhadrā, the charioteer Abhimanyu was born of Pārtha;
and Devakī likewise gave birth to a son, Yaudheya, from Yudhiṣṭhira.
Parīkṣit was the son of Abhimanyu, a conqueror of enemy cities;
Janamejaya was the son of Parīkṣit and was supremely righteous.
He indeed composed the Vājasaneyaka for Brahmā;
he was, it is said, cursed by the great seer Vaiśampāyana.
"O evil-minded one, these words of yours shall not stand upon this earth;
they shall remain in force for as long as you yourself shall remain in the world."
Having learned of the victory of the Kṣatriyas, from that time forward they all approached and stood before King Janamejaya.
From that time forward, due to the curse of the Kṣatriya sacrificer,
the officiating priests were entirely excluded from performing sacrifices from that point on in every respect.
Some [priests] of that high-souled Kṣatriya sacrificer,
having worshipped Prajāpati with the Paurṇamāsa oblation,
were then prevented from entering by Vaiśampāyana himself.
This Janamejaya, the son of Parīkṣit, was indeed of the Pūru lineage;
having performed the horse sacrifice twice, he was a great follower of the Vājasaneyaka school.
Having caused all that [Veda] to be promulgated by the seer Vājasaneya,
he went to the forest after being cursed during a dispute with the Brāhmaṇas.
From Janamejaya was born the powerful Śatānīka;
Janamejaya consecrated his son Śatānīka upon the throne. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.65)
Then, through the horse sacrifice, the heroic son of Śatānīka was born,
known by the name Adhisomakṛṣṇa, who is now the one of great renown.
While he was ruling, this kingdom was brought by you;
indeed, a long sacrificial session difficult to attain was held for three years at Puṣkara,
for two years at Kurukṣetra, and [one year] at the Dṛṣadvatī, O best of the twice-born.
The sages said:
"O Lomaharṣaṇa, we wish to hear about the future of living beings;
for that which has passed in the past has indeed been recounted by you."
I shall describe the lifespan and the names of those kings by whom the Kṣatriya power will be established and who will arise.
The duration of the Kṛta Yuga, as well as that of the Tretā and Dvāpara,
the measure of the Kali Yuga, the defects of the ages, and the decline of the ages.
O Lord, having calculated all of this—the measure of pleasure and pain, and the defects of the age—please tell it to us who ask. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.71)
Sūta said:
Just as it was previously described to me by Vyāsa of unwearied deeds—
concerning what is to come in the Kali Yuga and likewise the Manvantaras.
"Listen to me as I speak of all those yet to come;
hereafter I shall proclaim those kings who will exist. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.73)

I shall proclaim all those kings who will appear in the future, belonging to the auspicious lineage of Aida and Ikshvaku, as well as the lineage of Puru— in which that noble family of Aida and Ikshvaku will eventually come to an end. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.74)
After them, there will arise yet other kings—
Kṣatriyas, Pāraśavas, Śūdras, and others who are outcasts.
The Andhas, Śakas, Pulindas, Cūlikas, and Yavanas,
as well as the Kaivartas, Ābhiras, Śabaras, and others born of Mleccha stock—
I shall describe those kings in turn by their names. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.76)
And among these, King Adhisomakṛṣṇa is the first;
in his lineage I shall describe the kings who are to come, as they have been told.
But Adhisomakṛṣṇa’s son shall become the king, O monarch, when that city named after the Nāga has been swept away by the Gaṅgā. *Matsya Purāṇa* 50.78.
Having abandoned his desire to speak and wishing to depart, he will dwell in the city of Kauśāmbī;
he shall have eight sons of great strength and prowess.
Bhūri was his eldest son; Citraratha is recorded as his [son].
From Citraratha came Śucidrava, and from Śucidrava came Vṛṣṇimān.
From Vṛṣṇimat, there will be King Suṣeṇa, who shall be pure;
from that Suṣeṇa, a king named Sunītha will arise.
From King Sunītha shall come Nṛcakṣus, who will be of great renown;
and the heir of Nṛcakṣus will indeed be Sukhīvala.
Sukhīva’s son will also be King Pariṣṇava;
and Pariṣṇava’s son will be the king Sutapas.
Medhāvin will be his heir, without a doubt;
and Medhāvin’s son will also be Purañjaya.
Urva will be his son; his son will be Tigmātman;
from Tigma will come Bṛhadratha; and from Bṛhadratha, Vasudāman will be born.
From Vasudāman shall come Śatānīka, and from him Udayana;
and from Udayana shall arise the heroic King Vahīnara.
Vahīnara’s son will be Daṇḍapāṇi;
from Daṇḍapāṇi will come Niramitra, and from Niramitra, Kṣemaka.
Regarding this, this genealogical verse was sung by ancient Brahmins:
"The lineage, which is the source of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya orders and is honored by divine sages, shall come to an end in the Kali age upon reaching King Kṣemaka. (Matsya Purāṇa 50.88)
Thus has this lineage of the Pauravas been duly recounted here,
as well as that of the wise and high-souled Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu.
Matsya Purāṇa 51.
The Sages said:
O Sūta, which fires are always to be worshipped by the twice-born?
Now, describe them and their lineage in due order.
Sūta said:
He who was known as Agnibhīmānī, the mind-born son of Brahmā in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara— Svāhā gave birth to him.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and he who is remembered as Śuci Agni—
Pavamāna is produced by friction, while Vaidyuta is the son of Pāvaka.
The fire known as Śuci is said to belong to Sūrya, and those that are stationary are also so recorded;
for the fire born of Pavamāna is indeed called Havyavāha.
Pāvaka, Saharakṣas, Havyavāha, Mukha, Śuci,
and Agni— the carrier of oblations for the gods— were the first sons of Brahmā.
Together with Saharakṣas, those three fires belong to the three classes of gods;
their sons and grandsons likewise number forty.
I shall indeed declare them by name, according to their distinct divisions:
the first is the purifying worldly fire, which belongs to Brahmā.
The fire of the Brahmaudana was his son, the famous one named Bharata;
he, Vaiśvānara Havyavāha, died while carrying my oblation.
Then he died; his son was Mathita Puṣkarodadhi, who was the Atharvan fire known as the *laukika* (worldly) fire, and is called the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire).
From Bhṛgu was born Atharvan, and from Atharvan Aṅgiras is remembered;
his fire is indeed the extraordinary Dakṣiṇāgni, so it is traditionally taught.
Now, that which is Pavamāna is said to be the fire produced by friction;
and that is indeed remembered as the Gārhapatya fire, the first of Brahman.
Then he begot those two sons, Sāṃśapāyana and Āvasathya;
thereafter, the bearer of oblations (Havyavāhana)— who is indeed remembered by the twice-born as the presiding deity of the Āhavanīya fire— desired sixteen rivers.
The Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the Narmadā, and likewise the Yamunā;
the Godāvarī, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī.
The Vipāśā, the Kauśikī, the Śatadru, and likewise the Sarayū;
the Sītā, the Manasvinī, the Hrādinī, and the Pāvanā as well.
Having divided himself sixteenfold among them, he then dwelt separately within those celestial abodes according to his desire.
The *dhiṣṇyas* were established according to their own names, and the *dhiṣṇavas* were born from them;
because they were born within the *dhiṣṇyas*, they are therefore known as the *dhiṣṇavas*.

Thus, these sons of the river indeed took their places upon the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇya). Hear now which among them are to be moved about and which are to be attended. Vibhu and Pravāhaṇa were the Agnīdhra; the other hearths were situated there. (Matsya Purāṇa 51.17)
He dwells in his proper place at the commencement of an auspicious day;
hear now the sequence of the fires that are indescribable and irresistible.
Vāsava, Agni, and Kṛśānu, who is the second on the northern altar—
these eight sons of the Samrāḍ-Agni do the twice-born worship.
Parjanya is Pavamāna; he is seen as the second.
Pāvaka, Uṣṇa, and Samūhya are said to be the fire in the north.
For he is the preparer of the oblation who is not to be cleansed; he is manifested as the Śamitṛ (the immolator).
He is called the one with a hundred abodes, the light of excellent nectar, and the sovereign power of Rudra.
The light of Brahman (brahmajyotis), whose abode is the earth, is said to occupy the position of Brahman;
he is indeed to be approached as Ajaikapād, since he is Śālāmukha.
For Ahirbudhnya is indeed indescribable; the two [others], however, are on the outside and at the end, to the south.
These sons of everyone are traditionally held to be worthy of worship by the twice-born.
Next, I shall describe those eight sons who are to be honored;
for the son of Hautrī was Agni, and the son of Barhiṣ was Havyavāhana.
The praiseworthy Agni Pracetas was the second companion;
for the son of Agni, Viśvavedas, is called Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
The source of the waters is remembered as Svāmbhas; it is perceived by the name Setu.
Indeed, these sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇyas) are used by the twice-born to perform sacrifices with Soma.
Then, that fire which is named Pāvaka and which is called Yoga by the virtuous, is to be known as the Avabhṛtha; it is worshipped together with Varuṇa.
For he is the son of the Heart and of Fire; dwelling in the stomachs of men, he cooks their food. Possessing fury, this fire of the stomach is constantly known as Viddhāgni.
For the all-pervading fire, arising from mutual friction, burns the elements here;
the son of that wrathful fire is known as the terrible Saṃvartaka.
Drinking water, he dwells in the ocean at the mouth of the submarine fire;
the son of Samudravasī is known as Saharakṣa.
But Saharakṣas dwells in the houses of men for the sake of their desires;
his son is the fire Kravyād, who indeed devours dead men.
Thus these sons of the purifying fire Agni have been proclaimed by the twice-born;
thereafter, his sons were carried off from Sauvīrya by the Gandharvas and Asuras.
That fire which is produced by friction in the forest is Āpa;
the venerable one who is led forward at the animal sacrifice is named Āyu.
The son of Āyu was Mahimān, and from him was born Dahanas;
he is the presiding deity over the pākayajñas, who consumes the oblation offered into the fire.
He who consumes the *havya* and *kavya* offerings from all the worlds of the gods—
his son is indeed Agni, the wonderful and highly illustrious one.
Free from pride regarding expiations, he consumes the stolen oblation;
the heroic son of Adbhuta is remembered as a great portion of the gods.
From him was born Vividhāgni, whose son was the great poet (Mahākavi).
From Arkaja, the son of Vividhāgni, eight sons known as Agnis are recorded.
In the optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi), [the deities are] Abhīmānin, Rakṣohā, Ayatikṛt,
Surabhi, Vasumān, Nāda, Haryaśva, and Rukmavān.
The Pravargya and Kṣemavat—these eight are thus proclaimed;
for from Śucyagni comes this progeny, and there are fourteen fires in total.
Thus have these fires been described which were brought forth during the sacrifice;
they remained even when the creation had passed away, together with the Yāmas and the foremost of the gods.
In the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara, these were the presiding deities (abhimānins) over the fires here among all things, both sentient and insentient, that are to be distributed.
Those who were proud of their positions as Agnīdhra priests were formerly the Havyavāhanas;
they were those established in ritual duties such as the optional (kāmya) and occasional (naimittika) sacrifices.
In the past, when the previous Manvantara had passed away, these [beings], together with the Śukras and Yāmas,
were present along with those hosts of gods during the first interval of Manu.
These indeed are declared to be the wombs, known as the abodes of the Jātavedas,
to be known among the seven [Manvantaras] beginning with Svārociṣa and ending with Savarṇa.
Thus has been fully enumerated here the characteristic of the fires (jātavedas) throughout all the present and future Manvantaras.
In all the Manvantaras, the fires exist together with the present deities, serving various purposes through diverse forms.
"Then, those who are yet to come shall dwell together with the future gods.
Thus have I declared this accumulation of fires in due order, both in detail and in succession. What else do you wish to hear?
Matsya Purāṇa 52.
The sages said:
Now tell us that which Viṣṇu, when questioned, declared as the supreme and most excellent.
Therefore, now explain in detail the nature of dharma and adharma.
Sūta said: Thus, in that single ocean, Janārdana in the form of a fish [expounded] the entire extent of the primary creation and the secondary creation.
The Soul of the Universe spoke to Manu, the son of the Sun,
concerning the yoga of action and the Sāṃkhya system, exactly as they are and in full detail.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, O you of noble vows, we wish to hear the definition of *karmayoga*,
for there is nothing in this world that is unknown to you."
Sūta said: I shall now describe the yoga of action (karmayoga) as it was expounded by Viṣṇu;
for the yoga of action is indeed praised more highly than a thousand yogas of knowledge (jñānayoga).
Knowledge arises from the yoga of action; therefore, that is the supreme state.
Brahman arises from both action and knowledge, for there is no knowledge for one who is inactive.
Therefore, one whose self is disciplined in action attains the eternal reality;
the entire Veda is the root of dharma, as is the conduct of those who know it. (Matsya Purāṇa 52.7)
Eight personal qualities reside in him as the primary ones:
compassion toward all beings, patience, and protection of the afflicted. (Matsya Purāṇa 52.8)
O twice-born ones, in this world, Anasūyā was likewise pure both internally and externally;
she engaged in auspicious conduct and practices without any effort in her duties.
He felt no stinginess regarding his own possessions, even when he was in distress or had acquired them with great effort;
likewise, he was always free from longing for the wealth or the wives of others.
The eight qualities of the self have been proclaimed by the learned as belonging to the Purāṇa;
this very practice of action (kriyāyoga) is the means for accomplishing the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga).
Knowledge without the yoga of action is not seen here in anyone;
one should therefore diligently adhere to the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti.
One should always perform, day after day, sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the propitiation of the hosts of spirits and sages.
A wise man should worship the ṛṣis with the study of the Vedas according to the rules, the ancestors with śrāddha rites and gifts of food, and all beings with bali offerings. (Matsya Purāṇa 52.14)
These five sacrifices have been ordained for the removal of the five slaughtering grounds:
the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom.
A householder has five slaughterhouses; because of them, he does not go to heaven.
To destroy that sin, these five sacrifices have been proclaimed by me.
Even one who possesses the twenty-two and eight purificatory rites that have been proclaimed will not attain liberation if he is devoid of the qualities of the Self.
Therefore, endowed with the virtues of the self, one should perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti;
one should always act for the welfare of cows and Brahmins by means of wealth. *Matsya Purāṇa* 52.18.
One should worship Śiva—who is the very self of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, Rudra, and the Vasus—with cattle, land, gold, garments, perfumes, garlands, and water. (Matsya Purāṇa 52.19)
"By means of vows and fasts performed according to rule with faith and free from envy, [one attains Him].
He who is beyond the senses, peaceful, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal—Vāsudeva, whose form is the universe—from Him indeed have these beings originated. (MatsP 52.20)
Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, Mārtaṇḍa, and he whose vehicle is the bull;
likewise the eight Vasus, the eleven lords of the Gaṇas,
the guardians of the world, the ancestors, and the mothers.
These manifestations, comprising all things moving and unmoving, have been declared;
Brahmā and the others are the fourfold root, and the Unmanifest is remembered as their sovereign.
Oṃ Oṃ! By worshipping [this], one worships Brahmā, as well as Sūrya, Viṣṇu, or Śiva;
for due to their non-difference, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings becomes worshipped. (Matsya Purāṇa 52.23)
The supreme abode of Brahmā and the others, as well as the established state of all three, resides within the embodiment of the Veda; therefore, Pūṣan should be worshipped with great effort.

Therefore, having placed these [deities] at the forefront of the fire and the twice-born, a man should worship them with gifts, vows, fasts, recitations, burnt offerings, and so forth. (Matsya Purāṇa 52.25)

Thus, for one who is devoted to the yoga of action, who cherishes the Vedānta scriptures and the Smṛtis, and who always fears improper conduct, there is nothing whatsoever to be attained here in this world or in the world beyond. (Matsya Purāṇa 52.26)
Matsya Purāṇa 53: The Sages said:
"O Sūta, recount in detail and in due order the number of verses in the Purāṇas."
The entire dharma of giving, indeed, according to the rule and in proper sequence.
Sūta said:
Listen now to that which the Ancient Person, the Soul of the Universe, spoke to Manu in the Purāṇas of old. *Matsya Purāṇa* 53.2.
The Fish said:
"In ancient times, the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā as the first of all scriptures;
immediately thereafter, the Vedas emerged from his mouths."

O sinless one, in that previous kalpa, there was only a single Purāṇa, which was meritorious, the means for achieving the three goals of life (trivarga), and extended to a hundred crores [of verses]. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.4)
And when the worlds had been consumed by fire, I indeed assumed the form of a horse and [recovered] the four Vedas, the Purāṇa, and the extensive treatise on Nyāya.
Having taken up the Mīmāṃsā and the Dharmaśāstra,
I composed them once more in the form of a fish at the beginning of the Kalpa within the ocean of waters.

Having heard all this related by the one who had entered the water, the Four-faced One spoke to the sages and the gods: matsyapurāṇe tripañcāśattamo 'dhyāyaḥ // MatsP_53.7 // (The fifty-third chapter of the Matsya Purāṇa)
From that [Veda], O King, the manifestation of all the scriptures and the Purāṇa occurred;
however, seeing that the Purāṇa was not being grasped over time, [he acted accordingly].
Assuming the form of Vyāsa, I always withdraw [the Vedas] at every Dvāpara age, [restoring them] with a measure of four hundred thousand [verses].
Thus, having been divided into eighteen parts, it is made manifest in this world of mortals;
even today, in this world of the gods, its extent is one hundred crore verses.
Its meaning has been established here in brief as four hundred thousand [verses];
eighteen Purāṇas are currently spoken of here. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.11)
O best of sages, listen as I shall declare their names according to what was previously told by Brahmā to Marīci.
The *Brahma Purāṇa* is proclaimed to consist of thirty thousand verses;
he who, having written it down, should give it away together with a water-cow on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.13)
When this very world became a lotus made of gold,
the account based on that event is likewise called the Pādma by the wise;
that Pādma Purāṇa is said here to consist of fifty-five thousand verses.
Furthermore, he who gives that Purāṇa, accompanied by a golden lotus and sesame seeds in the month of Jyeṣṭha, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.15)
That which Parāśara has declared concerning all the duties with reference to the events of the Vārāha-kalpa, the wise know that indeed to be the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa].
Furthermore, he who gives [this] on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, accompanied by a cow of ghee, being purified in soul, attains the realm of Varuṇa;
the wise know its extent to be twenty-three thousand [yojanas]. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.17)

In connection with the Śvetakalpa, Dharmānvāyu spoke here of that which consists of the wind-element and is endowed with the majesty of Rudra; that Purāṇa is said here to consist of twenty-four thousand verses. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.18)
On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, that man who gives to a Brahmin householder a cow made of molasses accompanied by a bull,
being purified in soul, shall dwell in the world of Śiva for one kalpa.
That work in which the expansion of dharma is described with reference to the Gāyatrī,
and which includes the slaying of the asura Vṛtra, is called the Bhāgavata.
That which arises from the account of those best of men who lived in the middle of the Sārasvata Kalpa is called the Bhāgavata in the world.

Whoever, having written it down, should give it away together with a golden lion on the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, goes to the supreme goal. They declare that Purāṇa to consist of eighteen thousand verses. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.22)
In that [work], Nārada expounded the dharmas based on the Bṛhatkalpa;
consisting of twenty-five thousand verses, it is called the Nāradīya.
On the fifteenth day of the month of Āśvina, one should give [this] together with a cow; one attains the supreme perfection from which rebirth is difficult to obtain. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.24)
In this regard, concerning birds, the investigation of dharma and adharma was indeed explained by the sages who practice dharma in response to the questions of the Muni.
All that was related by Mārkaṇḍeya in detail is here called the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, consisting of nine thousand verses.
And he who, having prepared it, should give it along with a golden plough on the full moon day of Kārttika, shall partake in the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
That kalpa which concerns the account of Īśānaka,
as it was told by Agni to Vasiṣṭha, they call the Āgneya.
And having written this, whoever should give it along with a golden lotus on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa according to the prescribed rite, together with a sesame-cow; ||| MatsP_53.29 |||
And that [work], consisting of sixteen thousand [verses], bestows the fruit of all sacrifices;
the man who applies himself to it is then glorified in the heavenly world.
In this [work], the four-faced one, having taken as his subject the majesty of the Sun,
recounted the maintenance of the world within the context of the history of the Aghora-kalpa,
and described the characteristics of the multitude of living beings to Manu.
Fourteen thousand and five hundred [verses] will consist mostly of future events; that is what is called the *Bhaviṣya* here.
He who, free from envy, gives this on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa,
accompanied by a jar of molasses, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
And concerning the account of the Rathantara ritual manual, Sāvarṇi [expounded] the supreme majesty of Kṛṣṇa to Nārada. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.34)
That in which the exploits of Brahmavarāha are repeatedly described is called the *Brahmavaivarta*, consisting of eighteen thousand verses.
He who gives the Purāṇa of Brahmavaivarta on the auspicious full-moon day in the month of Māgha is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
There, situated in the midst of the emblem of fire (Agni-liṅga), the Lord Maheśvara spoke concerning the Agneya [Kalpa] for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
At the end of the kalpa, this Purāṇa called the Laiṅga was spoken by Brahmā himself.
He who bestows it on the full moon day of Phālguna, accompanied by a sesame-cow, attains equality with Śiva. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.38)
Furthermore, concerning the majesty of the Great Boar (Mahāvarāha),
that which was spoken by Viṣṇu to the Earth is here called the Vārāha [Kalpa].
O best of sages, by way of the account of Mānava,
that Purāṇa is said here to consist of twenty-four thousand verses.
Having fashioned a golden Garuḍa together with a sesame-cow,
one should give it to a Brahmin householders on the full moon day of the month of Madhu;
by the grace of Varāha, he attains the station of Viṣṇu.
In that [Kalpa], the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) expounded the dharmas pertaining to Maheśvara,
concerning the Tatpuruṣa [Kalpa], augmented by [his] deeds.
The Purāṇa named Skānda is said to consist of eighty-one thousand verses; thus it is proclaimed among mortals. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.43)
And he who, when the sun has entered Pisces, gives [a gift] after having it engraved with a golden trident, attains the state of Śiva.
Concerning the majesty of Trivikrama, the Four-faced One (Brahmā) expounded upon the three goals of life; that [work] is celebrated as the Vāmana Purāṇa.
He who gives away the auspicious Purāṇa consisting of ten thousand verses, which follows the Kūrma-kalpa, at the autumnal equinox, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Therein, Janārdana in the form of a tortoise recounted the majesty of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa in the netherworld (rasātala).
In connection with Indradyumna, eighteen thousand [verses] concerning the Lakṣmī-kalpa were [revealed] by him to the sages in the presence of Śakra.
The man who gives a tortoise, equipped with a golden tortoise, during the solstice,
shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Therein, at the beginning of the Kalpa, Janārdana, in the form of a fish, [gave] to Manu a description of Narasiṃha for the purpose of setting the Vedas in motion.
O lords of sages, know that which was spoken concerning the events of seven kalpas, extending over fourteen thousand [years], as the Mātsya Purāṇa.
On the equinox, he who gives [this gift] together with a golden fish and a cow,
by him the entire earth is considered to have been given.
And when, in the Gāruḍa Kalpa,
Kṛṣṇa spoke concerning the birth of Garuḍa from the cosmic egg, that is here called the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.

It is recited here that one who gives this single [chariot] consisting of eighteen thousand [parts], yoked with golden swans, attains preeminent success and a permanent residence in the world of Śiva. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.54)
Brahmā spoke again concerning the majesty of the Brahmāṇḍa;
that Brahmāṇḍa consists of twelve thousand verses with an additional two hundred.
And that Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, in which a detailed account of future kalpas is heard, was proclaimed by Brahmā.
The man who gives that [image] during the Vyatīpāta yoga, together with a pair of woolen cloths and a golden cow,
obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices;
and that gift, when accompanied by the golden cow, bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā.
This work of four hundred thousand verses was proclaimed by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds;
it was related by my father’s father, and by him it has been narrated to me, and now I have presented it to you.
For the benefit of the world here, this was condensed by the Supreme Rishi;
even today, it remains among the gods with an extent of one hundred crore verses.
I shall now proclaim the sub-divisions that are established in the world; therein,
where the description of Narasiṃha is told in the Padma Purāṇa,
that work consisting of eighteen thousand verses is here called the Nārasiṃha.
Where the greatness of Nandā is described by Kārttikeya,
that is celebrated by people as the Nandī Purāṇa.
O those who observe the vows of sages, that narrative which shall take place with Sāmba placed at its forefront is called "The Sāmba" in the world.
The wise know the Purāṇas to be the ancient [accounts] of the past Kalpa;
the sequence of the Purāṇas brings wealth, fame, and long life,
and therein the designation "Āditya" is also fully explained.
O best of the twice-born, know that whatever Purāṇa is taught as distinct from these eighteen has emerged from among them.

In the Purāṇas, it is traditionally held that there are five constituent parts; they are known as the account of creation, the secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manus, and the history of the descendants—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.65)
In the Purāṇa consisting of five sections, there is the majesty of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra, as well as that of the world, including its dissolution and creation.
In all the Purāṇas, dharma, artha, kāma, and even mokṣa are proclaimed here, as well as whatever fruit is contrary to them.
In the Sāttvika Purāṇas, they know the majesty of Hari to be predominant;
and in the Rājasa ones, the majesty of Brahmā is predominant.
In the same way, the majesty of Agni is proclaimed among those characterized by tamas, that of Śiva among those who are mixed,
and that of Sarasvatī and the ancestors among those characterized by rajas.

Having composed the eighteen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī produced the entire narrative known as the Bhārata, which was augmented by one hundred thousand verses and enriched with the meaning of the Vedas. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.70)
That supreme narrative of Rāma which was proclaimed by Vālmīki,
and that which was spoken by Brahmā in its extent of a hundred crores [of verses].
Having thus brought it to Nārada, and by him again to Vālmīki,
Vālmīki proclaimed throughout the worlds this means for achieving dharma, kāma, and artha;
thus, these five hundred thousand verses, including the supplementary portion, were made known in the mortal realm.
The wise know the Purāṇas to be the ancient accounts of the past Kalpa.
He who reads or even hears the sequence of the Purāṇas—which bestows wealth, fame, and long life—attains the supreme goal. (Matsya Purāṇa 53.73)
This is a purifier and a repository of glory; this is exceedingly dear to the ancestors;
this acts as nectar among the gods, and it is eternally the remover of sins for men.
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim in their entirety the duties of giving (*dānadharma*).
Those who are devoted to vows and fasts, as described here by Matsya.
In the dialogue between Mahādeva and the wise Nārada,
I shall relate exactly as it occurred that which accomplishes the goals of dharma, kama, and artha.
In ancient times, Nārada questioned Hara— who is seated upon the peak of Kailāsa,
who is the enemy of the Bodiless One (Kāma), and who has destroyed the limbs of the Bodiless One— as he bowed with humility.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, leader of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra!
[Grant us] the wealth of prosperity, health, beauty, long life, fortune, and good luck.
Or how can a man devoted to you or to Viṣṇu become united [with them]? || MatsP_54.4 ||
O God, please describe here some vow that bestows liberation in due course, even for a widow who may be endowed with all virtues and good fortune. (Matsya Purāṇa 54.5)
The Lord said: "O Brahmin, you have asked well; it brings benefit to all the worlds.
O Nārada, listen now to that vow which, though already heard by you, leads to peace."
One should duly perform the vow named Nakṣatrapuruṣa, which has Nārāyaṇa as its essence,
beginning with the feet and reciting the names of Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rule.
One should worship the image of Vāsudeva under the Mūla constellation and others;
having reached the month of Caitra, one should perform the recitation by Brāhmaṇas.
One should worship the root with "Salutation to Viśvadhara," the two feet and the two ankles in Rohiṇī with "to Ananta," the two shanks in Varadā, and the two knees in Vāśvi and Kumāra-Ṛkṣa.
The two thighs, [corresponding to] the pair of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, should be worshipped with "Salutation to Śiva";
and the penis, [corresponding to] the pair of Pūrvāphalgunī and Uttarāphalgunī, is to be worshipped with "Salutation to the Five-Arrowed One."
O Nārada, one should worship the waist of Viṣṇu under the Kṛttikās with the mantra "Salutation to Śārṅgadhara";
likewise, one should worship both sides under the two Bhādrapadas with "Salutation to the slayer of Keśin."

O Nārada, the two sides of the belly should be worshipped with "Salutation to Dāmodara" during the Revatī asterism; and likewise, the chest should be worshipped with "Salutation to Mādhava" during the Anurādhā asterism. (Matsya Purāṇa 54.12)
The back should be worshipped under Dhaniṣṭhā for the sake of destroying the flood of sins;
and under Viśākhā, the arms should be worshipped with the mantra: "Obeisance to the glorious Lord who holds the conch, discus, sword, and mace."

In the hand [of the deity], the Hasta nakṣatra is to be worshipped with "Obeisance to Madhusūdana"; for Kaiṭabhāri, the fore-parts of the fingers in Punarvasu are to be worshipped with "Obeisance to the Lord of the Sāmans."
On a day when the lunar mansion is Aśleṣā, one should worship the claws of the Fish-bodied Lord;
one should take refuge in the feet of the Tortoise; and on the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, Hari is to be worshipped in the throat.
Having duly worshipped the ears with "Salutation to Varāha," one should worship the face on the Puṣya day with "Salutation to Janārdana" and "Salutation to Nṛsiṃha, the slayer of the Dānavas."
Salutations again and again to the dwarf who was the cause;
O twice-born one, the tip of the teeth is to be worshipped during the Svātī asterism, while the face of Hari, the delighter of the Bhṛgus, is to be fully honored during the Vāruṇa asterism.
Homage be to Rāma; under the asterism Maghā, the nose of the joy of the Raghus is to be worshipped.
Under Mṛgaśiras, the eyes are to be worshipped; homage be to you, O Rāma, whose eyes roll about!
Salutation to the peaceful Buddha; the forehead of Murāri is most worthy of worship during the Citrā asterisms.
Having honored the head of Viṣṇu during the Bharaṇī asterisms, let there be salutation to the Lord of the Universe in the form of Kalki.
On the day of the Ārdrā asterism, the hair of Puruṣottama should be worshipped with the words "Salutations to you, O Hari.
On the days of the [other] asterisms, the best of the twice-born should be worshipped with devotion by one who has observed a fast.
When his vow is complete, he should give to one endowed with all virtues, possessed of eloquence, beauty, and good character, and a singer of the Sāman chants,
a golden [image] with broad, long arms, adorned with pearls, moonstones, and diamonds.

One should present to an eminent brahmin an image of Hari placed within a jar filled with water, together with a cloth and a cow, as well as a bed equipped with household utensils, vessels, and the like.
If there is anything whatsoever here that may be given, give it all to a twice-born for your own welfare;
O you who possess the forms of Hiraṇyagarbha, Acyuta, and Rudra, make our desires bear fruit!
One should give a golden image of Puruṣottama together with his consort and Lakṣmī,
along with a bed free from knots, while reciting the mantra.
Just as no affliction ever arises for the devotees of Viṣṇu, so too [they attain] beauty, health, and supreme devotion to Keśava. (Matsya Purāṇa 54.25)
O Janārdana, just as your bed is never empty of Lakṣmī,
may my bed also be never empty [of you], O Kṛṣṇa, in birth after birth.
Having thus offered all that— clothing, garlands, and ointments—
one should then dismiss the Brahmin who knows the Nakṣatrapuruṣa.
Having fasted on all lunar mansions, he should eat food free from oil and salt according to his ability, avoiding any stinginess regarding his wealth.
Having thus worshipped the Nakṣatra-puruṣa according to the prescribed rule,
one personally attains all desires and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed here or in the hereafter,
whether by oneself or by one's ancestors, all of that shall go to destruction.

Thus, O Lord of Beings, the best of men or a woman who recites or hears this with great devotion shall perform a vow that shatters the impurities of the Kali age and bestows upon men the fruit of all prosperity—this [vow] dedicated to Murāri. (Matsya Purāṇa 54.31)
Matsya Purāṇa 55:
Nārada said:
For one who is unable to observe fasts but desires that same fruit [of fasting], [there is this alternative].
Is this supreme vow [observed] due to a lack of practice or because of illness? MatsP_55.1 //
Īśvara said: For those who are unable even to fast, eating at night is prescribed;
hear now how that [practice] within this vow also becomes great and inexhaustible. *Matsya Purāṇa* 55.2.
The wise who know the Purāṇas declare the proper worship of Śaṅkara, known as the "Solar Reclining," according to the conjunctions of the lunar mansions.
When the seventh lunar day (saptamī) falls on a Sunday,
and it coincides with the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), that lunar day fulfills all desires.
One should worship the image of Umāmaheśvara with the names of the Sun,
since one who performs the worship of the Sun should also worship it upon the Śiva-linga.
O best of sages, no difference whatsoever is seen between the Lord of Umā and the Sun; therefore, one should worship Śambhu in the home.

One should offer salutation to Sūrya for the hands, to Arka for the feet, and to Puruṣottama for the ankles during the Citrā asterism; to Dhātṛ for the shanks during Svātī, and to Viśākha for the knees.
Likewise, under Anurādhā, one should worship the two thighs of the thousand-rayed Sun with "Obeisance";
under Jyeṣṭhā, the private parts with "Obeisance to Anaṅga"; and under Mūla, the hips with "Obeisance to Indra" and "Obeisance to Soma."
In the pair of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, [one should worship] the navel; "Salutation to Tvaṣṭṛ" and "to the seven-waved one" [are the mantras].
In Śravaṇa, [one worships] the belly for the "Sharp-rayed One" (Sūrya); in Dhaniṣṭhā, the back for the "Cutter" (Vikartana).
The eye-socket should be worshipped for the destruction of darkness during the lunar mansion of Jyeṣṭhā;
and during the two [asterisms] of Pūrvā and Uttarā Bhādrapadā, the two arms should be worshipped with the words, "Salutation to the fierce-rayed one."
O twice-born one, during the Revatī asterism, both hands should be worshipped for the Lord of the Sāmans;
likewise, during the Aśvinī asterism, the nails should be worshipped with the words, "Salutation to the one who bears the yoke of seven horses."
O Nārada, one should worship the throat with the mantra "Salutation to the Sun of fierce radiance" during the Bharaṇī asterism; the neck during the Kṛttikā asterism;
and the lower lip during the Rohiṇī asterism, which is presided over by the Lord of Lotuses (Brahmā). Thus, these [parts] are to be worshipped.
The teeth of Murāri on the head of the best of deer are to be worshipped; salutations to Hari!
Salutations to Savitṛ for the tongue, and the nose is to be worshipped in Śaṅkara and also in Punarvasu. (Matsya Purāṇa 55.13)
On the Puṣya asterism, he should offer his forehead to the Beloved of the Lotus; on Ārdrā, his locks of hair to the One who bears the body of the Vedas;
then on Āśleṣā, his crown to the Beloved of the Gods; and on Maghā, his two ears to the Lord of the Herd of Cows.
In the Pūrva-phalgunī constellations, the eyes of Śambhu are to be worshipped as most venerable for the sake of honoring cows and Brahmins;
then, in the Uttara-phalgunī constellation, the two eyebrows are to be worshipped with the mantra "To Viśveśvara."
Homage be to Him who holds the noose, the goad, the trident, the lotus, the skull-bowl, the serpent, the moon, and the bow;
homage to Śiva, the root cause of the destruction of Gajāsura, Anaṅga, Tripura, Andhaka, and others.

Having thus constantly worshipped the weapons and Śiva with the mantra "Salutation to Viśveśvara," one should eat here only that which is not prepared with oil or vegetables, is meatless, is free from alkaline salts, and is not the remains of what has already been eaten. (Matsya Purāṇa 55.17)
Having performed the night-rites in this manner, O twice-born one, one should again give, under the asterism Punarvasu,
a prastha of śāli rice and ghee in a vessel made of udumbara wood.
Having placed it in a vessel, he should present it along with gold to a Brahmin;
on the seventh [day], there should be a pair of garments, and this becomes even more so at the breaking of the fast.
When the fourteenth annual *pāraṇa* day of Nārada arrives, one should devoutly feed the Brahmins with molasses, milk, ghee, and other such offerings. (Matsya Purāṇa 55.20)
Having fashioned a golden lotus with eight petals and a pericarp, pure and measuring eight finger-breadths, and provided with petals made of rubies; MatsP_55.21.
Having prepared a distinctive bed, free from discordant knots, along with pillows for rest, a mattress, and fans; MatsP_55.22 //
She is endowed with vessels, sandals, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and a mirror;
she is also joined with ornaments, fruits, garments, and unguents.
Having placed that lotus upon it and adorned it with its qualities,
[he should give] a brown cow, well-behaved, yielding milk, and accompanied by a garment.

One should give away a cow with silver hooves, golden horns, accompanied by her calf and a bronze milking vessel, in the forenoon while reciting the mantra; and one should not step over her. (Matsya Purāṇa 55.25)
Just as your bed is never empty of splendor,
fortitude, glory, and delight, even so may all perfections be mine.
Just as the gods know no one other than you who is more excellent and sinless,
so do you lift me up from the entire ocean of saṃsāra and its suffering.
Then, having circumambulated [the deity] and prostrated, one should dismiss [him];
all that, including the bed, the cow, and so forth, should be led to the house of a twice-born man.

This vow of the moon-crested Lord must not be revealed to one who lacks moral conduct, nor to a hypocrite, nor to one corrupted by fallacious reasoning, nor to a slanderer, nor to one who subjects it to excessive censure. (Matsya Purāṇa 55.29)
This secret, which brings about the bliss of Śiva, should be told to one who is devoted and self-controlled;
those who know the Vedas declare this imperishable [teaching] to be for men even the destroyer of great sins.

Neither is one separated from kinsmen, sons, or wealth, nor does one fail to bring joy to the gods; neither does such a person encounter disease nor the suffering of grief—nor does this apply to the woman who performs [this rite] with supreme devotion. (Matsya Purāṇa 55.31)
This was performed in ancient times by Vasiṣṭha, Arjuna, Kubera, and Purandara;
by the mere recitation of it, all sins go to destruction—of this there is no doubt.
Whoever thus recites or hears this account of the Sun’s reclining shall become beloved of Indra;
and whoever performs this rite here brings even all his ancestors who have gone to hell back to heaven.
(Matsya Purāṇa 55.33)
The Blessed One said: Now I shall describe the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, which destroys all sins;
through it, peace, liberation, and especially victory come to men.
One should worship Śaṅkara in Mārgaśīrṣa, Śambhu in Pauṣa,
the god Maheśvara in Māgha, and Mahādeva in Phālguna.
In the month of Caitra, a person should likewise worship Sthāṇu; in Vaiśākha, he should worship Śiva;
in Jyeṣṭha, he should worship Paśupati; and in Āṣāḍha, he should worship Ugra.
One should worship Śarva in the month of Śrāvaṇa, likewise Tryambaka in Nabhasya, Hara in the month of Āśvayuja, and likewise Īśāna in Kārttika. (Matsya Purāṇa 56.4)
On all the eighth days of the dark fortnight, one who is capable, having fasted, should honor those devoted to Śiva with cattle, land, gold, and garments. (Matsya Purāṇa 56.5)
Having consumed cow urine, ghee, cow's milk, sesame seeds, barley water, kuśa grass water,
cow horn water, *uśīra*, *śirīṣa*, arka, bilva leaves,
curd, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should worship Śaṅkara at night. (MatsP 56.6)
The great seers know the aśvattha, the vaṭa, the udumbara, the plakṣa, the palāśa, and the jambu tree as the sixth.
In the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Āṣāḍha, one should eat a tooth-stick from each of these trees in turn, two for each month.
One should offer the arghya water to the God, and at the conclusion, one should give a black cow with black garments,
as well as curd-rice, a canopy, a banner, and chowries.
He should give water-pots filled with the five precious gems to the twice-born;
black cows, gold, and various garments.
However, if he is unable, he should give even a single cow according to his capacity.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; by doing so, one incurs sin.
By fasting on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, a man is honored by the gods for three hundred times seven kalpas and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (Matsya Purāṇa 56.11)
Matsya Purāṇa 57:
Nārada said:
A man endowed with long life, health, and the prosperity of his lineage shall become united with the royal family.
O Moon-crested One, please explain correctly that vow by which one may [attain this] in birth after birth. (Matsya Purāṇa 57.1)
The Blessed One said: "What you have asked is excellent; it has been well spoken and brings imperishable merit. I shall tell you a secret which those who know the Purāṇas understand."
In this world, there is an excellent vow called Rohiṇī-candra-śayana;
on that occasion, one should worship the image of Nārāyaṇa with the names of the Moon.
Whenever the fifteenth lunar day of the bright fortnight falls on a Monday, or when the constellation Rohiṇī occurs on the full moon day; MatsP_57.4 //
Then a man should perform his bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and white mustard seeds;
furthermore, the wise one should recite the mantra "Āpyāyasva" one hundred and eight times.
Even a Śūdra, through supreme devotion and avoiding conversation with heretics, [should say]: "Salutations again and again to Soma, the giver of boons, and to Viṣṇu. (Matsya Purāṇa 57.6)
Having performed his recitation and returned to his own abode, he should worship Madhusūdana with fruits and flowers while chanting the names beginning with "Soma."
One should worship with "Salutation be to Soma, the Peaceful" for the feet; with "To Anantadhāman" for the knees and shanks;
one should worship both thighs with "To Jalodara," and the penis with "To Anantabāhu."
Homage, repeated homage to the bestower of the pleasure of desire; the waist of the Moon is always to be worshipped.
Likewise, the belly is for Amṛtoda; the navel is for Śaśāṅka—homage is to be offered to it. (Matsya Purāṇa 57.9)
Homage be to the Moon; the face is to be worshipped, and the teeth are to be worshipped as the lords of the twice-born (brāhmaṇas).
Laughter is to be honored with homage to the Moon, and the lips to the one who is fond of the forest of night-lotuses.
And his nose was offered to the Lord who is the joy of forest herbs;
likewise, his two eyebrows were offered to the one who is the source of bliss, and his pair of lotus-like eyes to Śauri, whose hand is dark as a blue water-lily and who resembles the moon.
Salutation to him who is worshipped at all sacrifices; let the two ears be offered to the slayer of the Daityas;
the forehead to the beloved of the Ocean’s Daughter (Lakṣmī); and the hair on the head to the Lord of Suṣumṇā (the Sun). (Matsya Purāṇa 57.12)
Salutations to the head of Murāri, who bears the moon; salutations to the wearer of the crown, the Lord of the Universe.
O Lakṣmī, beloved of the lotus, named Rohiṇī, whose body is beautiful with the nectar of good fortune and happiness! MatsP_57.13 //

Having worshipped the Goddess, the consort of the Moon, with fragrant flowers, food offerings, incense, and other articles, he should then sleep on the ground; rising again, he should bathe and, provided with sacrificial food (haviṣya), give it to a Brahmin.
At dawn, a water-pot containing gold and water should be given with the words: "Salutation to the Destroyer of Sins.

Having consumed cow's urine and meatless food that is not alkaline—twenty-eight mouthfuls mixed with milk and ghee—one should fast, and after eating, listen for a moment to an ancient legend (itihāsa). MatsP_57.15 //
The *kadamba*, blue lotus, *ketaka*, jasmine, red lotus, and *śatapattrikā*; the *amlāna*, *kubjā*, and *sinduvāra* flowers;
furthermore, the *mallikā*, the white *karavīra* flower of Viṣṇu, and the *campaka* flower of the Moon should be offered. (Matsya Purāṇa 57.16)
In the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, one should always worship Hari with these [flowers] respectively;
in whichever month a vow or other rite occurs, one should worship Hari with the flowers appropriate to that month.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules for as long as a year,
at the conclusion of the vow, a man should give a bed provided with a mirror and household utensils.
Then, having caused a golden pair of Rohiṇī and the Moon to be made,
the Moon should be six finger-breadths in size and Rohiṇī four finger-breadths.
Adorned with eight pearls, covered with a white cloth and eye-veil,
and placed upon a jar of milk together with a bronze vessel containing unbroken rice grains,
one should offer it in the forenoon accompanied by rice, sugarcane, and fruit, while reciting the mantra.
Then, one should give a white cow with a golden face, provided with silver hooves,
along with garments, vessels, and a beautiful conch shell.
Having adorned a virtuous Brahmin couple with ornaments,
one should imagine that this Moon, in the form of a Brahmin, is accompanied by his wife.
Just as Rohiṇī, O Kṛṣṇa, does not depart, leaving her bed,
so may there be no separation between me and your glorious manifestations, you who are the very form of the Moon.
Just as you alone are the bestower of supreme bliss and liberation to all, may there always be for me devotion toward you, which is both worldly enjoyment and liberation—O Moon! (Matsya Purāṇa 57.24)
Thus, O sinless one, for one who fears saṃsāra and desires liberation, this is the unsurpassed means for securing beauty, health, and long life. (Matsya Purāṇa 57.25)
O Sage, this alone is always dear to the ancestors;
having become the sovereign of the three worlds for three hundred seven kalpas,
one attains the world of the Moon and, becoming lightning, is liberated.
Or a woman who observes the Rohiṇī-candra-śayana vow likewise attains that fruit, from which rebirth is difficult to obtain.
Whoever thus recites or hears this hymn of praise to the Slayer of Madhu through the glorification of the Moon,
and even one who merely directs their mind toward it, shall be honored by the hosts of immortals while residing in the abode of Śauri.
Matsya Purāṇa 58: Sūta said:
The son of the Sun spoke to Viṣṇu, who was situated within the reservoir of water.
Of tanks, groves, and wells, as well as of large ponds and lotus-pools.
O Lord of Gods, I ask about the ritual procedure in the temples of the deities; who are the officiating priests there, O Master, and what should the sacrificial altar be like? (Matsya Purāṇa 58.2)
The sacrificial fee, the time, the location, and the preceptor as well—
tell me truly what materials are prescribed for all of these.
The Fish said:

Listen, O mighty-armed King, to the rule regarding tanks and other such works, which is recited in the Purāṇas by those who proclaim the Vedas. This is the traditional history (itihāsa). *Matsya Purāṇa* 58.4.
Having obtained an auspicious, bright fortnight after the winter solstice has passed,
on a holy day declared by the Brahmins, he should perform the recitation for the Brahmins.
In a region sloping toward the northeast, near a lake,
one should prepare an auspicious altar four cubits in size, square-shaped, and facing the four directions.
Likewise, the pavilion should be sixteen cubits in size and have four openings;
and around the altar, there should be pits one *ratni* in depth, each with three tiers.
O Prince, the birth-canal (yoni) should be nine, seven, or five finger-breadths in length—not more—and it should be six or seven finger-breadths in width. (Matsya Purāṇa 58.8)
And there shall be seven pits, with triple-tiered raised ridges;
they should all be of the same color and provided with banners and flags.
One should cause these doors of the pavilion to be made in each direction from branches of the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa trees.
There, eight auspicious officiating priests (hotṛs) and likewise eight gatekeepers should be appointed;
furthermore, eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas should be made chanters (jāpaka).
Complete in all auspicious marks, a knower of mantras, with senses conquered,
and endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct— such a preeminent twice-born man shall be the domestic priest.
In each pit, there should be a water-pot, sacrificial implements,
a fan, two white chowries, and two very large copper vessels.

Then, the wise preceptor, having consecrated them with mantras, should scatter upon the ground sacrificial porridges (*caru*) of various colors, each dedicated to its respective deity. *Matsya Purāṇa* 58.14.
The sacrificial post (yūpa) should be three aratnis in measure and fashioned from a thorny tree;
or it may be equal in height to the sacrificer himself, and should be firmly established by one desiring prosperity.
Twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) adorned with golden ornaments should be appointed;
they should also be provided with golden earrings, armlets, and bracelets.
Likewise, one should honor the fingers, the purificatory grasses, and various garments equally for all; however, the preceptor should again be given double,
along with a bed and whatever is personally dear to oneself.

O lord of the people, having first procured all these— the tortoise and the crocodile made of gold, the fish and the drum of silver, the crab and the frog of copper, and the porpoise of iron— [one should proceed]. MatsP_58.18.
Wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents,
he was there bathed with waters containing all medicinal herbs by those who have mastered the Vedas.
The sacrificer, together with his wife and accompanied by his sons and grandsons,
having reached the western door, should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
Then, amidst auspicious sounds and the resonance of kettledrums,
the knower of reality should immediately draw the mandala with five colors.
Then there is the sixteen-spoked wheel, with a lotus at its center and four faces;
it is square on the outside, circular within, and most beautiful in the middle.
Having placed those [images] upon the altar, the wise one should then install all the planets and the lords of the worlds in their respective directions according to the mantras.
Relying upon the Vāruṇa mantra, the wise one should place the tortoise and the other [beings] in the center;
he should likewise install Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu in that very same place.
Having installed Vināyaka, as well as Kamalā and Ambikā,
he should then install the host of spirits for the sake of the peace of all the worlds.
Having thus performed the consecration (adhivāsana) provided with flowers, edible offerings, and fruits,
one should wrap those jars, which contain water within, with cloths.
Having adorned the door-keepers on all sides with flower perfumes, the teacher should worship them and say to them, "Recite! (Matsya Purāṇa 58.27).
Two Bahvṛcas should be stationed in the east, two knowers of the Yajus in the south,
two Sāmans in the west, and likewise two Atharvans in the north.
Facing north, the sacrificer should sit to the south;
he should then address the officiating priests once more, saying, "Sacrifice! (Matsya Purāṇa 58.29).
Having thus instructed all those reciters, saying, "Remain engaged in the recitation of the supreme mantra," that knower of mantras sprinkled water around the fire.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter and likewise sacrificial fuel-sticks with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa;
furthermore, the officiating priests must perform the fire-sacrifice on all sides using only those mantras dedicated to Varuṇa.
Having offered oblations according to the prescribed rule to the planets, as well as to Indra and Īśvara, to the Maruts, the world-protectors, and to Viśvakarman according to the rule; MatsP_58.32.
The Bahvṛcas shall separately recite from the east the Rātrisūkta, the Raudrasūkta, the Pāvamānasūkta, the Sumaṅgala, and the Puruṣasūkta. (Matsya Purāṇa 58.33)
The knower of the Yajurveda should recite with his right hand the mantras of the Śākra, Raudra, Saumya, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Jātavedasa, and Saura hymns.
The Vairāja, the Pauruṣa Sūkta, the Sauvarṇa, the Rudrasaṃhitā,
the Śaiśava, the Pañcanidhana, the Gāyatra, and the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
O King, the Sāman-singers, stationed at the western gate, should chant the Vāmadevya, the Bṛhat-sāman, the Raurava, the Sarathantara,
the Gavāṃ-vrata, the Kāṇva, the Rakṣoghna,
and likewise the Vayasa hymns.
And to the north, those of the Atharvaveda should recite the Śāntika and Pauṣṭika rites,
mentally taking refuge in the Lord Varuṇa, the deity.
On the previous day, having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during the night,
one should take earth from an elephant, a horse, a road, an anthill, a confluence,
a pond, a cow-pen, and likewise from a crossroads, and place it into the jars.
One should perform his ceremonial bath with yellow pigment (rocanā) together with white mustard seeds, fragrant substances, and guggulu resin, combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having performed each [rite] individually according to the prescribed rules with the great mantras,
one should thus pass the night through the ritual action joined with the proper procedure.
Then, when the clear dawn has arisen, one hundred cows,
or again sixty-eight, or fifty, or thirty-six, or even twenty-five, should be given to the Brahmins.

Then, at an auspicious and most beautiful moment in the zodiac, as proclaimed by the astrologer, accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas, by Gandharva melodies, and by various musical instruments once again— MatsP_58.42.
Having adorned her with golden ornaments, one should cause the cow to descend into the water;
O Lord of the People, she should then be given to a Brāhmaṇa who chants the Sāman hymns.
Then, having taken a golden vessel endowed with the five jewels,
and having placed within it all manner of sea-monsters, fish, and the like,
it was held by four Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
One should cause a cow, provided with water from a great river and accompanied by curds and unbroken grains,
to stand facing north in the midst of the water.
Having bathed her with the Atharvaṇa hymns, with the mantras "punarmām" and "ityatha," and with the verse "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he cast [the water] and returned to the pavilion.
Having worshipped there, one should offer a bali-oblation all around the lake;
furthermore, O best of sages, it should be offered as a burnt oblation for four days.
The fourth-day rite must be performed, and there too, O tiger among kings, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's ability; thereafter follows the offering of land to Varuṇa.
Having prepared the sacrificial vessels and the implements for the sacrifice,
and having given them equally to the officiating priests, he should then distribute the pavilion;
and he should present a golden vessel and a bed to the *sthāpaka*.
Then, one thousand Brahmins, or likewise eight hundred,
or fifty, or twenty, should be fed according to one's capacity;
thus is the rite for a tank described in the Purāṇas.
This same rule is prescribed for all wells and step-wells, as well as for lotus ponds,
and likewise for their consecrations.
There may be a distinction based on the mantra in the case of palaces and other such grounds;
however, this procedure was seen by the Self-Existent One as being performed with half [the scale] for those who are incapable,
provided that men do not practice stinginess regarding their wealth, even when the structures are small, like the single-fire rite.
When water remains during the rainy season, it is traditionally held to yield the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
that which remains during the autumn yields the aforementioned fruits;
and when it remains during the late winter and early spring, it yields the fruits of both the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices. (Matsya Purāṇa 58.53)
They say that water remaining in the spring season is equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice;
even in summer, water remaining there excels the Rājasūya.
O Great King, even he whose intellect is purified by the scriptures who performs these distinguished rites goes quickly to the abode of Rudra; being purified, he rejoices in heaven for many eons.
Having enjoyed many worlds, beginning with Mahattama, together with his wives for two parārdhas,
he further attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu through the fruit of that sacrifice.
Matsya Purāṇa 59:
The Sages said,
"O Sūta, describe in detail and according to the rules the ritual for trees."
By what rite should the wise perform the concluding ceremony (udyāpana) of the Pādapa-vrata?
And those worlds that are remembered—tell us about them now;
you ought to tell us everything regarding the fruit one obtains after death.
Sūta said:
O Lord of the World, having approached [the site], I shall describe the ritual for trees as well as for garden grounds, just like the ritual for tanks. *Matsya Purāṇa* 59.3.
The officiating priests, the sacrificial pavilion, and the ritual materials, as well as the preceptor of that same kind,
he should likewise honor the Brahmins with gold, garments, and unguents.
Having sprinkled the trees with water containing all medicinal herbs, adorned them with perfumes, decorated them with garlands, and wrapped them in garments.
The piercing of the ears for all [the children] should be performed with a golden needle;
likewise, collyrium should be applied with a golden probe.
One should have seven or eight fruits made of polished gold for each of all the trees; these should be consecrated upon the altar.
In this rite, guggulu incense is best; having placed them upon copper vessels, one should set them amidst the seven grains, adorned with cloths, perfumes, and ointments.
O lord of men, having placed water-pots upon all the trees, and having made offerings of oblations along with gold for them all without exception; MatsP_59.9.
According to their respective domains, learned twice-born men should specifically perform oblations for the world-protectors, Indra and the others, as well as for the Lord of the Forest.

Then, one should release from the midst of the trees a milch cow facing northward— clad in white garments, adorned with golden ornaments, possessing a bronze milking vessel, and distinguished by her two golden horns. *Matsya Purāṇa* 59.11.
Then, with the consecration mantra, accompanied by musical instruments, auspicious songs,
and the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas as well as those dedicated to Varuṇa,
the preeminent Brāhmaṇa should perform the ceremonial bath with those very jars. (Matsya Purāṇa 59.12)
Having bathed and likewise wearing white garments, the sacrificer,
being composed, should honor all those officiating priests with cows according to his means.
One should provide food with milk for four days, along with golden threads, bracelets, rings, sacred finger-guards, garments, beds, as well as household utensils and sandals. (Matsya Purāṇa 59.14)
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with mustard seeds, barley, and black sesame seeds;
sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) of *palāśa* wood are recommended, and on the fourth day there should likewise be a festival.
Furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given there as well, according to one's ability.
Whatever is most dear to oneself, that one should give without envy;
one should give double to the teacher, and having prostrated, one should dismiss him.
The wise man who performs the tree festival according to this rite attains all desires and enjoys infinite fruit.
O Indra among kings, even that man who establishes but a single tree shall dwell in heaven, O King, for as long as thirty thousand reigns of Indra.
One shall deliver as many men of the past and the future as there are trees;
one attains supreme perfection, from which a return to worldly existence is difficult to find.
The person who would constantly hear this, or even cause it to be heard,
shall be honored by the gods and exalted in the world of Brahmā.
The Fish Purāṇa (Matsya-Purāṇa), Chapter 60:
The Fish said:
"In the same way, I shall further describe another [rite] which bestows the fruit of all desires."
That which those who know the Purāṇas understand as the "Bed of Good Fortune" (Saubhāgya-śayana).
Formerly, when the worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Mahas, and the rest— had been consumed by fire,
the auspicious fortune of all beings became concentrated in one place;
having reached Vaikuṇṭha, it resided upon the chest of Viṣṇu.
Then, after a long time, O King, during another act of creation,
when the world was enveloped by ego-consciousness and endowed with both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
And when the rivalry between the Lotus-seated One and Kṛṣṇa had commenced,
an extremely terrifying flame of fire emerged in the form of a *liṅga*;
from the chest of Hari, heated by that [flame], it issued forth.
Residing upon the chest of Viṣṇu, it abides in his auspicious splendor;
thereafter, in the form of rasa, it reaches down to the surface of the earth.
That [elixir], which bestows beauty and charm, was cast into the sky by the wise son of Brahmā; Dakṣa drank it as soon as it was offered.
The great strength and splendor born of Dakṣa Parameṣṭhin remained as a residue that fell upon the earth and was divided into eight parts.
Then there arose among the people seven things that bestow good fortune:
sugarcane, the king of juices (sugar/molasses), flat beans, lentils, and grain.
Like cow's milk, safflower, and saffron, as well as salt as the eighth—likewise, this is called the "Eightfold Auspiciousness" (saubhāgyāṣṭaka). *Matsya Purāṇa* 60.9.
Furthermore, she who was drunk by the son of Brahmā, the knower of yoga and knowledge,
became his daughter, who is called Satī.
Because she surpassed all worlds in her gracefulness, she is called Lalitā;
the wielder of the Pināka bow married this Trailokyasundarī.
What may not a man or a woman obtain by worshiping with devotion that Goddess who consists of auspiciousness and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation? (MatsP 60.12)
Manu said:
O Janārdana, how is the propitiation of that Mother of the World performed?
O Lord of the World, tell me all of that procedure in its entirety. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.13)

Matsya said: O beloved of the people, having reached the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform a bath with sesame seeds on the third day of the bright fortnight during the forenoon. *Matsya Purāṇa* 60.14.
On that day, it is said, that goddess of excellent complexion was wedded by the Soul of the Universe with the mantras used for taking the hand in marriage.
Then, on the third lunar day, one should worship the Lord of Gods together with her,
using various kinds of fruits, incenses, lamps, and food offerings.
Having bathed the image with the five products of the cow as well as with scented water, one should worship Gaurī together with the Moon-crested Lord.
"Salutation be to Pāṭalā for the two feet of the goddess Śivā;
and having uttered 'To Śiva,' [one should worship] Jayā on the two ankles. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.18)

Having recited "Salutation to Triguṇa" for Rudra and "to Bhavānī" for the pair of shanks; "to Śivā" and "to Rudreśvarā" for the two knees; and having proclaimed "to Harikeśa," [one says] "salutation to the Giver of Boons" for the two thighs. (MatsP 60.19)
To Īśā he gave a worm; to the Goddess, Śaṅkara;
to the two sides of her belly, Koṭavī; and to the Trident-bearer, Śūlin.
One should worship Maṅgalā with "Salutation to you," and worship her belly;
one should worship Rudra, the Self of All, and the two breasts with "Salutation to Īśānī. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.21)
Likewise, one should worship the throat for Śiva, who is the self of the Vedas, and the neck for Rudrāṇī;
the two hands for the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśa), who is the slayer of Tripura, and for Anantā.

One should always worship Hara with the mantra "To Trilocana," his arms with "To Kālānalapriya," his ornaments with "To Saubhāgyabhavana," his face with "To Svāhā-Svadhā," and the wielder of the trident with "To Īśvara."
The two lips should be worshipped as Aśokamadhuvāsinī, who bestow prosperity;
likewise, Hara should be worshipped as Sthāṇu, and the smile as Candramukhapriyā.
Salutation to Ardhanārīśa for the face; salutation to Asitāṅga for the nose;
salutation to Ugra for the eyes; salutation to Lokeśa for the eyebrows. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.25)
One should worship the destroyer of the city for Śarva, and likewise the Ālakas for Vāsavī; then one should worship with "Obeisance to the Lord Śrīkaṇṭhā," and thereafter the hair of Śiva;
[one should worship] the head with "Obeisance to the All-Self (Sarvātman)" for her who has the form of Bhīma and Ugra.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, one should place before him the eight auspicious items:
ghee, flat beans, safflower, milk, and cumin.
Mercury, salt, and cumin— these eight,
because they bestow good fortune (saubhāgya), are therefore called the "Eightfold Saubhāgya."
Having thus reported all that before the two Śivas,
O subduer of enemies, one should again consume the water from a horn at night on the ground.
Again at dawn, having likewise performed his bath and recitations, being pure,
he should worship a Brahmin couple with garments, garlands, and ornaments.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa two golden feet endowed with the eight marks of good fortune, saying, "May Lalitā be pleased by this. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.31)
In this manner, for as long as a year, on the third lunar day, those desiring all prosperity should always perform the ritual with devotion according to the prescribed rules.
Listen to me regarding this specific distinction concerning the consumption [of the substances] and the mantra for the gift:
in the month of Caitra, one should offer water from a horn, and in Vaiśākha, cow dung.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the mandāraka flower is prescribed; in Śuci, the bilva leaf;
in Śrāvaṇa, one should consume curd; and in Nabhasya, water infused with kuśa grass.
In the month of Āśvayuja one should consume milk; in Kārttika, ghee mixed with curds;
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, cow urine; and in Pauṣa, one should consume clarified butter. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.35)
Likewise, one should offer black sesame seeds in Māgha and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in Phālguna;
[the goddesses are] Lalitā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Kumudā, and Śivā.
At the time of giving the gift, one should proclaim: "May Vāsudevī, Gaurī, Maṅgalā, Kamalā, Satī, and Umā be pleased. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.37)
The *mallikā*, *aśoka*, *kamala*, *kadamba*, *utpala*, *mālatī*, *kubjaka*, *karavīra*, *bāṇa*, and unfading *kuṅkuma* [are used]. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.38)
And the *sindhuvāra* is prescribed for all months in succession;
likewise the *japā*, the *kusumbha* flower, the *mālatī*, and the *śatapattrikā*. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.39)
Whatever flowers are available, including the *karavīra* which is always recommended—
a man who has thus observed the fast according to the rules for the duration of a year [attains the fruit].
Whether she be a married woman or a maiden, having worshipped Śiva with devotion, she should,
at the conclusion of the vow, give a bed equipped with all its furnishings.
Having established a golden image of Umāmaheśvara along with a bull and a cow upon a bed, one should then present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, according to one's ability, one should honor other couples with gifts of clothing and the like,
as well as offerings of grain, ornaments, cattle, and stores of wealth;
free from stinginess regarding one's means and devoid of pride, one should perform this worship.
He who properly performs this Saubhāgya-śayana-vrata attains all desires and reaches the ultimate state;
one should observe this vow by means of the renunciation of a single fruit. (Matsya Purāṇa 60.44)
O lord of men, he who desires to obtain fame, good fortune, health, beauty, long life, clothing, ornaments, and decorations month after month shall,
O King, never be deprived of these for three hundred and nine billion years.
He who performs the Saubhāgyaśayana-vrata for twelve years,
or for seven or eight, shall dwell properly in the abode of Śrīkaṇṭha, being honored by the immortals, for as long as thirty thousand kalpas.
O Lord of Men, whether it be a woman or even a maiden who performs [this],
she too, cherished by the grace of the Goddess, obtains that same fruit.
Whoever should even hear this, or should give it away, or should apply their mind to it,
shall also become a Vidyādhara and dwell for a long time in the heavenly world.
This was formerly desired here by Madana, and performed by Śatadhanu, the son of Kṛtavīrya;
