then it was done by Varuṇa or by Nandin—how much more so, O Lord of Men, for one who is born from them?
Matsya Purāṇa 61:
Nārada said:
"Then there are Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and Maharloka and Janaloka."
Austerity and truth—these seven are proclaimed as the worlds of the gods.
But how might there be sovereignty over all things by turns?
O Lord, O Destroyer of Cities, how may there be auspicious form, long life, good fortune, and abundant prosperity in this world?
Maheśvara said: "In former times, on the surface of the earth, Hutāśana (Agni), together with Māruta (Vāyu),
was commanded by Puruhūta (Indra) for the destruction of the enemies of the gods."
When those Dānavas had been consumed by him by the thousands,
O ascetic, Tāraka, Kamalākṣa, Kāladaṃṣṭra, Parāvasu,
and Virocana fled from the battle.
Having entered the ocean waters, they attempted to establish their dwellings;
but because they were impossible [to overcome], they were left alone by Agni and Māruta.
From that time forward, having oppressed the gods, humans, and all moving beings,
as well as all the sages, they enter the water once again.
In this manner, O Brahmin, for fifteen thousand years, those heroes, by virtue of their strength in that watery fortress, oppressed the three worlds.
Thereafter, the lord of the immortals finally commanded Fire and Wind:
"Let this ocean be dried up. (Matsya Purāṇa 61.8)
"Since this abode of Varuṇa is the refuge of our enemies,
therefore let him be brought to destruction by you two this very day."
Then both of them said to Śakra, the slayer of Śambara: "O Lord of the Gods, this destruction of Sāgara is unrighteous. (Matsya Purāṇa 61.10)
"O Purandara, since the destruction of a great multitude of living beings would occur, therefore we two shall not commit sin today."
O best of gods, even within a mere yojana of this [place], hundreds of millions of living beings dwell; how could it deserve destruction?
Thus addressed, the lord of the gods, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these words out of rage as if burning the fire itself. (Matsya Purāṇa 61.13)
The immortals never encounter the conjunction of merit and demerit anywhere;
this is especially true for you two, who abide in greatness.
"O Vibhāvasu, because you have transgressed my command and, like the Wind-god,
have undertaken the ascetic vows of non-violence and the rest, you have acted toward an enemy in a manner devoid of the treatises on dharma and artha."
Therefore, with a single body in the form of a sage among men,
your birth shall take place in the world together with Māruta.
And when, even in human form, the ocean shall be dried up by you, Agastya,
O Fire, then you shall attain the status of a god.
Thus, O ascetic, by Indra’s curse they both fell at that very moment to the surface of the earth,
obtaining birth from Kumbha with a single body.
Through the power of Mitra and Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha’s younger brother was born;
he became the sage Agastya, a man of fierce asceticism.
Nārada said: How was that sage born as the brother of Vasiṣṭha,
and how are Mitra and Varuṇa remembered as his parents?
O Destroyer of Cities, how could the birth of Agastya have occurred from a water-jar?
Īśvara said: In ancient times, on Mount Gandhamādana,
Viṣṇu, having become the son of Dharma, the Primeval Person, performed extensive austerities.
Fearing his asceticism, Śakra dispatched both Mādhava and Anaṅga, accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, to create obstacles for him.

When Hari was no longer agitated by song and instrumental music, nor by ointments for the body and the like, nor by desire and the month of Madhava, nor toward the objects of the senses; MatsP_61.23 //
Then the host of women, who were like honeyed wine of desire, fell into despondency;
thereupon, for their agitation, the foremost of men produced from his own thighs a woman capable of enchanting the inhabitants of the three worlds.
Agitated by her, Hari spoke to both of those best of gods in the presence of the deities and the Apsarases.
Hari said to the general assembly of the gods, "She is an Apsaras;
she shall become famous in the world by the name Urvaśī."
Then, having been summoned by Mitra who was filled with desire, Urvaśī was told,
"Delight me," and she replied, "So be it."
Moving through the sky in that same manner, the lotus-eyed woman proceeded slowly;
though held from behind by Varuṇa, she did not welcome Varuṇa.
"I was previously chosen by Mitra; today I am not your wife, O Lord," she said.
Varuṇa replied, "Having entrusted your heart to me, you may go. (Matsya Purāṇa 61.29)
When she had departed, Mitra said, "So be it," and then pronounced this curse upon her:
"Go to the world of mortals and [marry] the son of the daughter of Soma."
"Since you have followed this dharma by consorting with a courtesan, therefore your semen was cast into a water-jar by your friend Varuṇa;
from that, two most excellent sages were born. (Matsya Purāṇa 61.31)
In former times, one named Nimi was playing at dice with women;
in the midst of that, Vasiṣṭha, born of Brahmā, arrived there.
The sage cursed the king for failing to perform worship, saying, "May you become bodiless! Thereupon, the king also [cursed] that sage.
Their minds being as if emptied by their mutual curse,
they both went to Brahmā, the Lord of the World, in order to have the curse destroyed.
Then, by the command of Brahmā, Nimi settled within the eyes;
thus, O Nārada, there are the winks of the worlds for their rest.
Vasiṣṭha also appeared within that water-pot as before;
then, from it, there arose the most excellent of sages, Agastya, tranquil in soul, white-complexioned, four-armed, and bearing a rosary and a water-pot.
In a certain region of Malaya, however, according to the rules of the Vaikhānasas,
he performed extremely difficult austerities together with his wife, surrounded by Brahmins.
Then, after a long time,
seeing the world excessively oppressed by Tāraka, he drank up the abode of Varuṇa (the ocean) out of anger.
Then all the givers of boons, beginning with Śaṅkara, became his [benefactors];
both Brahmā and the Lord Viṣṇu went there to grant him a boon:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever is desired by you, O Sage. (MatsP 61.39)
Agastya said:
"For twenty-five billion Brahmās,
I shall remain as a celestial being in the path of the Southern Mountain."

dispel for me the impurity caused by the eclipse of the moon.
May that god Śaṅkara— the moon-bearer, wielder of the Pināka bow, and rider of the bull—
destroy the suffering born of a lunar eclipse.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving,
including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun— may they indeed burn away my sin.
Having been thus addressed, he should be consecrated by them with those jars endowed with auspicious qualities,
accompanied by the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with white garlands and unguents.
He should honor the Brahmins— who are his chosen deities— with gifts of clothing and cows.
Then one should inscribe these very mantras,
together with water-jars, upon a cloth-strip or upon a lotus, provided with the five jewels.
Those best of the twice-born should place it upon the head of the sacrificer;
then they should cause the time following the eclipse to pass.
Facing the east, having worshipped and bowed to his chosen deity,
and having performed the auspicious rite of *godāna* once the lunar eclipse has ended,
he should present that turban to a Brāhmaṇa who has already bathed. (Matsya Purāṇa 67.21)
Whoever performs the ritual bath for the planets according to this procedure shall suffer no affliction from the planets, nor shall there be any loss among their kinsmen.
One attains the supreme accomplishment from which return to worldly existence is difficult to find;
during a solar eclipse, one should always recite the name of the Sun within the mantras.
One should give an abundance of rubies and a very beautiful tawny cow to one's husband during lunar and solar eclipses.
The person who would constantly hear this, or even cause it to be heard,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śakra.
Matsya Purāṇa 68:
Nārada said:
What should be done when there is agitation and wonder? By what means is Alakṣmī destroyed?
And in rites such as the consecration for those whose children have died, what is desired?
The Blessed One said: "O you whose wealth is asceticism, sins committed in the past bear fruit in this life in the form of disease and misfortune, as well as through the slaughter of loved ones."
To counteract that, I shall describe the rite known as the "Seventh-Day Bath," which always brings about auspiciousness and destroys the afflictions of people. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.3)
Just as the death of children who drink milk is observed there,
so too does it occur for the elderly, the diseased, and even for those in the prime of youth.
For the sake of pacification, I shall describe therein the consecration for those whose children have died;
this very rite destroys the agitation of wonders and the delusion of the mind. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.5)
And, O ascetic, there will also be the Vārāha Kalpa when Vaivasvata is the supreme Manu.
And when the twenty-fifth age,
known as Kṛta, shall have arrived there, a heroic and powerful king named Kṛtavīrya will arise, who will increase the lineage of the Haihayas.
O Nārada, he shall rule over the entire earth with its seven continents for seventy-seven thousand years.
As soon as he is born, his hundred sons likewise shall meet their destruction through the curse of Cyavana.
And when he shall have a son named Sahasrabāhu—deer-eyed, illustrious, and endowed with the marks of a king. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.10)
O Nārada, having propitiated the thousand-rayed Sun with fasts, divine vows, and Vedic hymns, Kṛtavīrya will obtain this bath that is sufficient for the life of his son. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.11)
When questioned by Kṛtavīrya, the Sun-god will indeed speak this,
which pacifies all evils and eternally destroys all impurities.
Sūrya said:
"Enough with this great distress, O lord of men;
your son shall be long-lived, but he will be a destroyer of sins. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.13)
I shall describe the seventh-day bathing ceremony for the benefit of all the world, O Nārada: for a woman who has lost her children at birth, it should be performed in the seventh month;
alternatively, this entire rite is highly commended on the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
Having obtained the strength of the planets and stars and having performed the recitation by Brāhmaṇas,
a wise man should avoid the birth asterism and that lunar day for a child; likewise, this should apply to the rites for the elderly and the sick, as well as for others.
Then, on ground smeared with cow dung as if for a single fire,
one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) made of red *śāli* rice mixed with cow’s milk to Sūrya and Rudra, according to the prescribed ritual and with their respective mantras.
O Nārada, one should recite the seven-verse hymn dedicated to the deity Sūrya and likewise offer oblations of clarified butter with the Rudrasūkta for the sake of Rudra.
In this rite, fuel-sticks of both the arka and palāśa trees are likewise to be offered;
furthermore, a fire-oblation of one hundred and eight barley grains and black sesame seeds must be performed.
Having likewise offered oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* one hundred and eight times,
that wise man should perform an auspicious bath.
Having duly placed four beautiful jars in the corners by a Brahmin learned in the Vedas who holds darbha grass in his hand, (Matsya Purāṇa 68.20).
And furthermore, in the center, one should place a fifth jar, free from blemishes and adorned with curd and unbroken grains, consecrated with the Saptarca hymn.
One should fill [the vessels] with the water of a sour sacred site (tīrtha), provided with jewels;
they should all be endowed with all medicinal herbs and accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should surround them with the five gems, fruits, flowers, and cloths.

Having brought earth that is thoroughly purified from an elephant’s footprint, a horse’s path, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, a pond, or a cow-pen, one should place it upon all [the ritual sites].
And having taken the middle one from among the four jars containing jewels,
the Brahmin should there recite the mantras dedicated to Sūrya.
And here, seven women with unimpaired limbs, accompanied by Brahmins,
having been honored according to their means with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
should perform the consecration for those who have lost their children.
These are the consecration mantras:
"May this child have a long life, and may this beautiful woman have living sons!
May the Sun and the Moon, together with the circles of planets and constellations [grant this]."
May Śakra together with the world-protectors, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
and those other hosts of gods, always protect the young prince.
May Mitra, Śani, Agni, and whatever child-seizing spirits (bālagraha) exist anywhere,
cause affliction to the child alone, and never to the mother or the father.
Then, wearing white garments and accompanied by her husband,
she should worship the seven [sages] with devotion, and then the preceptor of women.
Then, one should have a golden image of Dharmarāja placed upon a copper vessel and present it to the preceptor.
In the same manner, free from any stinginess regarding wealth, one should honor the Brahmins with floods of garments, gold, and jewels, as well as with foods such as milk-rice mixed with ghee.
And after the preceptor has eaten, this sequence of mantras should be recited:
"May this child have a long life and be happy for a hundred years."
Whatever evil he possesses is cast into the submarine fire (vaḍavānala);
[so too are] Brahmā, Rudra, Vasu, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and Agni.
"May they all protect [us] from the wicked; may they always be granters of boons.
One should honor the guru while he speaks such words as these. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.34)
According to one's ability, one should give away a tawny cow, and having bowed, one should dismiss it;
likewise, having bowed to Ravi and Śaṅkara along with their offspring, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru).
One should eat the remnants of the oblation while saying, "Salutation be to Āditya.
This very practice is praised in cases of portents, agitation, and bad dreams.

Always avoiding the birth-day and birth-star of the performer, one should worship for the sake of peace on the seventh day of the bright fortnight; by doing this, one does not suffer. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.37)
By means of this practice of constant giving, the man became long-lived;
for ten thousand years, he ruled over this earth.
O best of the twice-born, having narrated this merit-bestowing, purifying, and life-prolonging ritual of bathing on the seventh lunar day dedicated to the Sun, the Sun-god vanished right there.
All this has been fully explained regarding the supreme bath on the seventh lunar day;
it pacifies all evils and is most beneficial for children.
One should seek health from the Sun, wealth from Fire, knowledge from Īśvara, and liberation from Janārdana. (Matsya Purāṇa 68.41)
This [rite] shall be the destroyer of great sins, supremely beneficial, and a promoter of strength for children;
the sages declare that even for one who hears it with undistracted mind, success is attained.
The Fish said:
Formerly, in the Rathantara Kalpa, [the Lord] was questioned by the high-souled one.
Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, was established on Mount Mandara by Brahmā himself.
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the Immortals, O God, how may men obtain health and infinite sovereignty through slight austerity, or else attain liberation? *Matsya Purāṇa* 69.2.
O Mahādeva, O Adhokṣaja, what is unknown to you through your grace?
Let even a small amount of austerity be said here to yield great fruit. (Matsya Purāṇa 69.3)
The Fish said: Thus questioned by Brahmā, the Soul of the Universe and Creator of the World,
the Lord of Umā spoke these words that bring delight to the mind.
Īśvara said:
When, after this twenty-third Kalpa of the Rathantara, the Vārāha Kalpa shall come again, during its auspicious Manvantara— Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 69.5.
When the seventh [Manu], known as Vaivasvata, had appeared as the creator of the seven worlds,
they say that likewise the twenty-eighth Yuga was named Dvāpara.
At the end of that [age], that Mahādeva Vāsudeva Janārdana,
Viṣṇu, will become threefold for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden.
Likewise, the sage Dvaipāyana, as well as Rauhiṇeya and Keśava;
Keśava, the crusher of the pride of Kaṃsa and others, is the destroyer of afflictions.

By my command, Tvaṣṭṛ shall likewise fashion for the Lord of the World, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, that city named Dvāravatī— which is now Kuśasthalī— endowed with divine power, as a dwelling place.
Once, while seated in that assembly hall, the one of immeasurable splendor was surrounded by his wives, the Vṛṣṇis, and kings who had bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
Surrounded by the Kurus, gods, and gandharvas, the slayer of Kaiṭabha [Vāsudeva] spoke as ancient discourses related to dharma were being recited.
At the conclusion of the discourse, the majestic one was questioned by Bhīmasena;
he is the one who reveals this secret of dharma that you have asked about.
O Brahmin, at that time Vṛkodara, the mighty son of Pāṇḍu, will become the performer and the promoter of this dharma. (Matsya Purāṇa 69.13)
That righteous-souled one, in whose belly the fire named Vṛka was placed by me as a carrier of oblations, became known as Vṛkodara because of that.
Intelligent and of a proud disposition, possessing the great strength of ten thousand elephants,
he will be undecaying, glorious, and as handsome as Kandarpa himself.
Even for one who is righteous but lacks the strength for fasting due to a severe digestive fire,
this vow is superior to all other vows, because of that [efficacy].
Vāsudeva, the soul of the universe and the teacher of the world,
will proclaim that which bestows the fruit of all sacrifices and destroys every sin without exception.
It is the pacifier of all evils without exception, worshipped by all the gods;
it is the most sacred among the sacred and the most auspicious among the auspicious;
it is the future of all that is yet to be and the most ancient of all the Purāṇas.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Bhārata, if you are unable to fast on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the twelfth lunar days, or even on other days or under other asterisms," *Matsya Purāṇa* 69.19.
Therefore, having fasted according to this rite on this auspicious lunar day which destroys all sins, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
When the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha arrives,
one should perform an anointing with ghee and carry out a bath with sesame seeds.
In the same manner, having worshipped Viṣṇu with the mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," one should worship the feet with "Kṛṣṇāya" and the head with "Namaḥ Sarvātmane."
"To Vaikuṇṭha," "to the one who bears the Śrīvatsa on his chest," "to the bearer of the conch," "likewise to the bearer of the discus," "to the bearer of the mace," and "to the giver of boons"—
in this manner, all the arms of Nārāyaṇa should be worshipped in succession.
"To Dāmodara" for the belly; "To Pañcaśara" for the penis;
"To Saubhāgyanātha" for the thighs; "To Bhūtadhārin" for the knees.
Salutation to Nīla in the shanks; salutation to Viśvasṛj in the feet. Salutation to Devī, salutation to Śānti, salutation to Lakṣmī, and salutation to Śrī.
Salutations to Puṣṭi, salutations to Tuṣṭi, to Dhṛṣṭi, and to Hṛṣṭi—salutations again and again!
Salutations to the Lord of Birds, the winged one with the speed of the wind;
one should constantly worship Garuḍa, the destroyer of poison.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, Umāpati,
and Vināyaka with perfumes, garlands, incense, and various kinds of edible offerings, [one should proceed].
Then, having consumed *kṛsarā* prepared with cow’s milk along with clarified butter while maintaining silence, the wise man should walk one hundred paces.
Having taken a tooth-stick made of *nyagrodha* wood or else of *khadira*, the wise man,
having sipped water, should clean his teeth while facing either the east or the north.
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) when the sun has set, he should say:
"Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa; I have come to you for refuge. (Matsya Purāṇa 69.30)
On the eleventh day, having fasted and worshipped Keśava,
and having remained awake throughout the entire night, one should likewise perform a bath with milk.
Having performed the fire-oblation with clarified butter along with the preeminent Brahmins,
O lotus-eyed one, one should partake of a meal of milk on the twelfth day.
"I shall perform this with self-restraint; may it be accomplished for me without obstacle.
Having spoken thus, he should sleep on the ground, listening once more to the recitation of historical narratives (itihāsa). *Matsya Purāṇa* 69.33.
O lord of the people, having heard this when morning has dawned, one should go to the river,
perform an ablution with clay in the same manner, and likewise avoid heretics.
Having performed the twilight devotions according to the rules and having offered libations to the ancestors,
he bowed down to Hṛṣīkeśa, the sole lord of the seven worlds.
O lord of the people, a wise man should devoutly have a pavilion constructed in front of the house; it should be ten or eight cubits in size.
O destroyer of enemies, one should construct an auspicious altar measuring four cubits,
and there one should install an archway (toraṇa) of the same measurement of four cubits.
Having placed the water-pot there, he should then worship the guardians of the directions. Then, standing upon a black antelope skin,
he should hold the entire night long the stream of water from the hole [of the pot] over his head.
In the same manner, one should cause a stream of milk to fall upon the head of Viṣṇu;
and there, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (aratni) in size, provided with three tiers (mekhalā).

Having fashioned that [image] with the vulva as its mouth, the Brahmins should then, according to the rites of a single fire, offer barley, clarified butter, and sesame seeds with mantras dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Having properly offered the Vaiṣṇava caru mixed with cow's milk,
one should indeed cause a stream of clarified butter to fall in drops the size of half a niṣpāva bean.
O one of great heroism, having placed thirteen water-pots provided with various kinds of food and adorned with white cloths; MatsP_69.42.
The oblation should be performed there by four Ṛgvedic priests facing north, using vessels made of udumbara wood and accompanied by the five precious gems.
Four [priests] devoted to the Yajurveda should recite the Rudra-japa,
while four Sāmavedins should cause the Vaiṣṇava Sāmans,
together with the Ariṣṭa-varga, to be chanted all around.
In this manner, one should honor those twelve Brahmins with garments, garlands, and ointments,
as well as with finger-rings, bracelets, and golden threads.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should provide garments and beds;
thus the night should be passed with the sounds of songs and auspicious music.
Furthermore, for the preceptor (upādhyāya), all of this is indeed double;
then, having risen at the clear dawn, [he performs] thirteen [rites].
O best of the Kurus, one should give cows that yield milk, are well-behaved, and are equipped with golden mouths, along with bronze milking vessels.
With silver hooves, adorned with cloths, and anointed with sandalwood paste,
they were then gratified by those [gods] with devotion through various kinds of food, both solid and soft.
Having honored all the Brahmins with various kinds of food,
and having himself eaten food that is free from pungent salt, he should dismiss them.
Having followed [the deity] for eight steps together with his son and wife,
let the Lord of Gods, Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, be pleased here.
Viṣṇu is in the heart of Śiva, and Śiva is in the heart of Viṣṇu;
as I see no difference between them, so may there be well-being for my life.
Having thus uttered these [mantras], the wise man should cause those jars, as well as cows, beds,
and garments, to reach the houses of all.
In the absence of many beds,
one should give even a single well-prepared bed to a twice-born man, provided with all necessary furnishings.
O tiger among men, he who desires abundant prosperity should pass that day by having the Itihāsas and Purāṇas recited. (Matsya Purāṇa 69.55)
Therefore, O Bhīmasena, relying upon your inner strength and free from envy,
properly observe this vow which I have spoken out of affection for you.
"O hero, this [vow] has been performed by you; it shall be known by your name.
This is indeed that auspicious Bhīmadvādaśī, which removes all sins and is celebrated under the name Kalyāṇinī in former kalpas. (Matsya Purāṇa 69.57)
O foremost among the great heroes, may you become the primordial creator in this Saukara Kalpa;
by whose mere remembrance of your fame one’s sins are entirely destroyed and one becomes the lord of the thirty gods.
And she who was the sovereign of the Apsarases, having been made a courtesan in other previous births,
is now that very Urvaśī in the vault of heaven out of extreme curiosity for the cowherd’s daughter.
Whether she was born of the lineage of Puloman or even born into the family of a Vaiśya, she became the daughter of Puloman and the wife of Indra;
yet even there, this Satyabhāmā is now my beloved, serving as her attendant.
Having previously bathed, he likewise entered that mandala consisting of light, which is the body of the Veda;
and on this auspicious lunar day, the thousand-rayed Vivasvat [shone] with a thousand streams.
This very same deed was performed by the Vasus, headed by Mahendra, as well as by the gods and the enemies of the gods;
yet its fruit cannot be fully described even if there were ten million tongues in one's mouth.
"The son of the Lord of the Yadavas shall proclaim this infinite [Purāṇa], which tears asunder the impurities of the Kali age;
for it is capable of uplifting all one's ancestors, even those who have gone to hell, right here in this world. (Matsya Purāṇa 69.63)

He who hears this *Aghavidāraṇa* with devotion, or recites it here for the sake of helping others, becomes a lord of men who enjoys all prosperity on every lunar day; O Four-faced One, he attains equality with you.
O sinless one, that twelfth day which was formerly known as Kalyāṇinī and is to be honored on the days of the month of Māgha,
shall henceforth be called Bhīmapūrvā by the son of Pāṇḍu, yielding infinite merit.
The Matsya Purāṇa (Chapter 70),
Brahmā said:
"I have heard in the Purāṇas about the origin of the social classes and stages of life."
O Blessed One, regarding the determination of the sacred law (*dharmaśāstra*) for those of good conduct,
I wish to hear in truth the proper conduct of courtesans.
Ishvara said:
"O Brahmā, born from the lotus, in that very age there will be sixteen thousand women belonging to Vāsudeva."
By them, in the spring season, on the bank of a lake filled with blooming white lotuses stirred by the wind, which was teeming with flocks of cuckoos and swarms of bees; (Matsya Purāṇa 70.3).
Adorned by those devoted to unrestrained drinking parties,
the illustrious one with eyes like a deer’s made Mālatī his crest-ornament.
Sāmba, the conqueror of enemy cities,
who was like Kandarpa himself in beauty and adorned with every ornament, proceeded by a nearby path.
When he is gazed upon with longing by those tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god of love,
the passion within them will increase toward him.

Then the Lord of the World, observing them from all sides with his eye of knowledge, will pronounce this curse upon them all: "Because you have committed such an act out of lustful desire behind my back, bandits shall carry you away. (Matsya Purāṇa 70.7)
Then, being propitiated by those women who were tormented by the curse, the divine wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Lord and creator of all beings, will speak as follows:
The infinite-souled one, who is dear to the brāhmaṇas, will instruct [the world] on how to become a slave of the ocean so as to bring about future prosperity and lead it across.
"The sage Dālbhya will tell you what vow must be observed;
that alone will be sufficient for your deliverance, even while you remain in servitude.
Having said this and embraced them, the Lord of Dvāravatī departed. (Matsya Purāṇa 70.10)
Then, after a long time, once the burden [of the earth] had been removed, and likewise when the Mausala [conflict] had ended and Keśava had ascended to heaven, Matsya Purāṇa 70.11.
When the lineage of Yadu was empty and Arjuna had been defeated by all the thieves,
Kṛṣṇa’s wives were carried off into the ocean to be enjoyed as slaves.
And while these women, tormented by misfortune, remain standing, O Four-faced One,
one whose soul is absorbed in yoga, named Dālbhya, a man of great asceticism, shall arrive.
Having honored him with the arghya offering and prostrating again and again,
they lamented profusely, their eyes clouded with tears.
Remembering their vast enjoyments— the divine garlands and ointments—
as well as their husband, the Lord of the worlds, who is infinite and unconquered.

Standing before the sage, the inhabitants of Dvārakā will ask this very question concerning that city of divine nature, its houses of various jewels, and all the youths who possess the forms of gods: *matsya-purāṇa* 70.16.
The women said: "O Blessed One, we have all been forcibly violated by bandits. Since we are falling away from our own duty, be our refuge in this matter. (Matsya Purāṇa 70.17)
"O Brahmin, you were previously instructed by the wise Keśava: 'Why have you, having entered into union with the Lord, come to the state of being courtesans? (Matsya Purāṇa 70.18)
"O ascetic rich in austerity, tell us that dharma which belongs even to courtesans;
therefore, that Caikitāyana Dālbhya shall speak concerning them. (Matsya Purāṇa 70.19)
Dālbhya said: "Formerly, during your sporting excursions and water-plays at Lake Mānasa,
Nārada approached all of you."
"All of you were formerly Apsarases, daughters of Hutāśana;
because you did not bow down out of arrogance, that knower of yoga was questioned by you:
'Instruct us how Nārāyaṇa might become our husband. (Matsya Purāṇa 70.21)
Therefore, the granting of boons to you and this curse occurred in the past because of the offering of two beds during the months of Madhu and Mādhava.
By the gift of golden utensils on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
her husband will surely become Nārāyaṇa in another birth.
"Because you asked me [this] out of envy for my beauty and good fortune, without having paid me homage, you shall quickly suffer separation from one another;
all of you will be carried off by thieves and shall attain the state of prostitutes."
"Thus, by the curse of Nārada, all of you have become courtesans, deluded by passion, even though you belong to the wise Keśava.
O beautiful women, listen now to what I shall say."
Dālbhya said:
Long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, when the Dānavas, Asuras, Daityas, and Rākṣasas had been slain by the gods by the hundreds here and there— *Matsya Purāṇa* 70.26.

The Lord of the Gods, the best among speakers, declared concerning all those thousands and hundreds of women— both those who had been formally married and those who had indeed been enjoyed by force: MatsP_70.27.
Indra said:
"Now, O fair-limbed ones, conduct yourselves according to the profession of courtesans in the king's palace, and likewise with devotion in the temples of the gods. (Matsya Purāṇa 70.28)
The kings will be equal to their lords, and their sons likewise;
and there shall be good fortune for all of them according to their capacity.
Whoever shall always come to your house taking a bride-price must be treated by you with funeral rites, except in the case of a hypocrite.
When an auspicious day for the deities and the ancestors has arrived,
one should give cows, land, gold, and grain according to one's ability;
and, O lady of beautiful hips, one should perform the rites and utter the words for the Brahmins.
Furthermore, I shall duly instruct you in another vow;
that, moreover, must be performed by all of you without hesitation.
Those who know the Vedas understand that this is sufficient for crossing over saṃsāra when the Hasta,
Puṣya, or Punarvasu nakṣatras fall on a Sunday.
A woman should properly perform a bath with all medicinal herbs;
then even the presence of the five-arrowed god (Kāma) will be attained.
She should worship the lotus-eyed Lord (Viṣṇu) by reciting the praises of Anaṅga.
Having worshipped the feet for the sake of desire, the shanks indeed for the cause of delusion,
the private organ for the treasure-house of Kandarpa, and the anus with "Salutation to Prītimat."
The navel to the Ocean of Bliss, likewise the belly to the Left-handed One (Vāma),
the heart to the Lord of the Heart, and the breasts to the Delighter.
He offered his left side to Vaikuṇṭha, who causes longing, and his right side to the flower-bowed one, the wielder of the flowery arrows, who brings joy to the mouth.
One should worship the crown of the God of gods with "To Mānasa," the hair on the head with "To Vilola," and all the limbs with "To Sarvātman."
Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful one, who bears the noose and the goad,
who wields the mace, who is clad in yellow garments, and who bears the conch and the discus.
Homage to Nārāyaṇa; homage to the self who is Kāmadeva; homage for the sake of all peace; homage to Prīti; homage to Rati; homage to Śrī.
"Salutations to Puṣṭi, salutations to Tuṣṭi, salutations to the fulfillment of all aims!
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign whose essence is Anaṅga, with perfumes, garlands, incense, and food offerings, the loving woman [should proceed]. (Matsya Purāṇa 70.41)
Then, having summoned Brahmā, the knower of dharma and master of the Vedas,
who was complete in all his limbs, he honored him with perfumes, flowers, worship, and other offerings.
She should give that Brahmin a *prastha* measure of śāli rice accompanied by a vessel of ghee, saying, "May Mādhava be pleased."
Perceiving that very best of the twice-born— who was provided with food according to his desire—
as being Kāmadeva himself for the sake of pleasure, she fixed him in her mind.

In the same manner, one should perform the invocation, worship, and the offering of golden trees and divine libations;
likewise, one should offer to the supporting mountains, the lakes, and the forest deities.
The fire-oblation, the vigil, and likewise the consecration of the world-protectors (lokapāla) should be performed as in the case of the mountain of grain; one should utter this mantra: MatsP_85.4.
Just as this Janārdana is the supreme Soul of all among the gods,
so is the Sāmaveda among the Vedas and Mahādeva among the yogins.
Just as the syllable Om is among all mantras and Pārvatī is among women,
so too is sugarcane juice always considered the most excellent of all juices.
Therefore, O Guḍaparvata, grant me supreme prosperity;
since you are the brother of the bestower of good fortune and the abode of Pārvatī, O Guḍaparvata, grant me peace.
He who gives a mountain made of jaggery according to this rite is honored by the Gandharvas and is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Then, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven islands,
endowed with long life and health, and unconquered by his enemies.
Matsya Purāṇa 86: The Lord said:
Now I shall describe the supreme Suvarṇācala, which removes all sins.
By the gift of which a human being goes to the abode of Brahmā.
The best [gift] consists of a thousand palas, the middling of five hundred;
the lowest is half of that. Likewise, even one of small means should give according to his ability, starting from one pala upwards, as much as he can, free from envy.
O bull among sages, one should arrange everything just as for the mountain of grain;
likewise, one should present the supporting mountains to the officiating priests.
Salutations to you, the seed of Brahman; salutations to you, whose womb is Brahman.
Since you bestow infinite fruit, therefore protect me, O mountain.
Since you are the offspring of Agni, and since you are meritorious, O Lord of the World,
therefore protect us, O best of mountains, in the form of the Golden Mountain.
Whoever gives a mountain of gold according to this rite goes to the supreme world of Brahmā, which causes bliss;
there he shall remain for a hundred kalpas, and thereafter he attains the highest goal.
Matsya-Purāṇa 87: The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the ritual for the mountain of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rules.
By the giving of which a man goes to the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, a mountain of sesame seeds weighing ten *droṇas* is declared the highest; five *droṇas* is considered middling; and three *droṇas* is proclaimed the lowest.
O bull among sages, as before, I shall duly proclaim the mantras for the gift of all the other mountains situated around the periphery. MatsP_87.3.
Since sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and mung beans were produced from the sweat of Viṣṇu's body during the slaying of Madhu, may they serve here for the sake of pacification.

Since sesame seeds alone provide protection for both the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), O Lord of Mountains, lift me up from worldly existence; O Tilācala, salutations be to you!
Having thus addressed [the deity], he who should give this unsurpassed mountain of sesame seeds indeed goes to the station of Viṣṇu, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
One attains long life and rejoices with sons and grandsons;
honored by the ancestors, gods, and gandharvas, one shall go to heaven. (Matsya Purāṇa 87.7)
Matsya-Purāṇa 88. Īśvara said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme Kārpāsācala.
By the giving of which a person constantly attains the supreme state.
Likewise, a mountain of cotton is considered excellent here if it consists of twenty *bhāras*;
ten are declared to be middling, while five are remembered as inferior.
One of modest means should give even a single *bhāra*, provided he is free from stinginess regarding his wealth.
O bull among sages, having prepared everything just as in the case of the mountain of grain, one should give these [gifts] when the night has turned to dawn and utter this: MatsP_88.3.
Since you alone are always the protection for the worlds here, O Karpāsādri, salutations to you; be the destroyer of the flood of sins.
Thus, whoever should offer this king of mountains made of cotton in the presence of Śarva shall dwell in the world of Rudra for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth.
Matsya-Purāṇa 89: The Lord said: Hereafter, I shall describe the unsurpassed mountain of ghee (ghṛtācala).
This divine splendor, consisting of nectar, destroys even the greatest of sins.
With twenty jars of ghee, the ghee-mountain should be the best;
with ten it is declared to be middling, and with five it is remembered as the lowest.
Even one who possesses little wealth should construct the supporting mountains here according to the prescribed rule using two [parts]; likewise, he should arrange them with a fourth part.
One should place bowls of polished rice upon jars;
they should be made closely joined and elevated, according to the prescribed rule and as is beautiful.
One should wrap it with white cloths and with sugarcane stalks, fruits, and so forth;
the remaining procedure here is recited as being the same as that for the mountain of grain.
Having first performed the acceptance [of the offering], as well as the fire-oblation and worship of the gods,
he should, when the night has turned to dawn, present that to the preceptor;
and with a tranquil mind, he should likewise present the supporting mountains to the officiating priests.
Since ghee has arisen from the union of nectar and fire, may Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe, whose radiance is ghee, be pleased by this offering.
Since Brahman, consisting of light, is known to reside within ghee,
therefore do you protect us incessantly in the form of a mountain of ghee.
By this rite, one should offer the unsurpassed mountain of ghee;
even one joined with great sins attains the world of Śaṅkara. (Matsya Purāṇa 89.9)
Mounted upon a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes, adorned with garlands of tinkling bells, and surrounded by Apsarases, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas,
he shall sport together with his ancestors until the dissolution of all beings.
Matsya Purāṇa 90. The Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the unsurpassed mountain of jewels.
A mountain made of a thousand pearls would be unsurpassed.
The middle [mountain range] is five hundred [yojanas], and the lowest is remembered as three hundred;
the peripheral mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas) should be on all sides at one-fourth [the size of the central mountain].
The wise should fashion Gandhamādana with *vajragomeda* stones to the east and *indranīla* stones to the south, joined with *padmarāga* gems.
To the west, one should place the Vimalācala mountain mixed with lapis lazuli and coral;
and to the north, one should arrange it with rubies and gold.
One should arrange everything here just as in the case of the mountain of grain;
likewise, one should perform the invocation for the golden trees and the deities.
Free from envy, one should worship with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings at dawn;
as before, one should address these mantras to the preceptor and the officiating priests.
When all the hosts of gods are established within all jewels,
and you are eternally composed of jewels, homage be to you, O ever-immovable one!
Since Hari always brings satisfaction through the gift of jewels,
therefore protect us, O Mountain, by the constant offering of jewels.
He who gives a mountain made of jewels according to this rite goes to the same world as Viṣṇu, honored by the lord of the immortals.
O lord of men, he shall dwell here for a full hundred kalpas,
endowed with beauty, health, and virtue, and become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed here or in the hereafter,
all of that goes to destruction, just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Matsya Purāṇa 91: The Lord said,
"Hereafter, I shall describe the unsurpassed Silver Mountain."
By the giving of which a man goes to the unsurpassed world of Soma.
The best silver mountain consists of ten thousand palas;
the middling is said to consist of five thousand, and the lowest is recorded as being half of that.
If one is unable [to do so], then one should have it made after twenty [cubits] according to one's capacity;
likewise, one should fashion the supporting mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas) with a quarter of that measure.
As before, fashioning Mount Mandara and the other mountains according to the prescribed rite from silver, the wise man should likewise worship the World-Guardians made of gold.
The buttocks here should be fashioned from gold for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Arka;
for all others, it should be silver, but everything else here is made of gold.
The remainder, however, such as the fire-oblation, the vigil, and so forth, should be performed as before;
then, at dawn, one should give a mountain of silver to the preceptor.

With darbha grass in hand and free from envy, one should give the supporting mountains to the officiating priests after honoring them with garments and ornaments, while reciting this mantra: MatsP_91.7: "Obeisance to you, O mountains, who support the earth; by your very sight, all sins are destroyed. You are the refuge of the world, the source of all jewels, and the abode of all medicinal herbs. May you grant me long life, health, prosperity, and the fulfillment of all desires. Since you are beloved by the ancestors, by the lords of elephants, and by Śiva,
therefore, O King, protect us from this ocean of worldly existence filled with sorrow.
Having made this declaration, the man who gives an excellent silver mountain obtains the fruit of the gift of ten thousand cows.
Worshipped by hosts of Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases,
that wise man shall dwell in the world of the gods until the dissolution of all beings.
Matsya Purāṇa 92: The Lord said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the most excellent Śarkarāśaila (sugar-mountain)."
By the giving of which Viṣṇu, the Sun, and Rudra are always gratified.
A great mountain (mahācala) should consist of eight loads of sugar for the best [type];
four loads are declared to be the middling, and two loads are remembered as the lowest.
A man possessing only a small amount of wealth should construct the Viṣkambha mountains with one-quarter of the weight or half-weight that he would otherwise use. (Matsya Purāṇa 92.3)
Having procured everything, including the nectar of the immortals, just as in the case of the mountain of grain,
one should likewise place three golden trees upon Mount Meru.
The Mandāra, the Pārijāta, and the third, the Kalpapādapa—
these three trees one should place upon the heads of all [the images].
The two rows of *hari-candana* trees should be planted on the eastern and western sides on all mountains, and especially so on the mountain of sugar (*śarkarācala*).
On Mount Mandara, Kāmadeva shall always face the west;
on the peak of Gandhamādana, Dhanada shall face the north.
On Vipulācala, Haṃsa, whose form is the Veda, shall face the east;
on Supārśva, Surabhi, made of gold, shall face the south.

This mountain, the essence of the nectar of good fortune, is filled with sugar;
therefore, O Lord of Mountains, may you always be a source of joy.
O Śarkarācala, you who arose from those droplets that fell to the earth while the gods were drinking nectar— protect us!
Since sugar has emerged from the center of the bow of the Mind-born (Kāmadeva), you are composed of that, O great mountain; protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra!
The man who gives a mountain of sugar according to this rite,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme state.
Resembling the moon, stars, and sun, he, impelled by Viṣṇu, should mount that vehicle together with his attendants and remain there.
Then, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents,
endowed with long life and health for as long as three arbudas of births.
One should provide food according to one's ability at all these mountains without envy;
everywhere, one should eat food that is not pungent or salty by his permission.
One should cause all the mountain-appurtenances to be conveyed to the abode of the Brāhmaṇas.
Īśvara said: In former times, during the Bṛhatkalpa, there was a lord of men named Dharmamūrti, a friend of Śakra, by whom thousands of Daityas were slain. (Matsya Purāṇa 92.17)
By whose splendor the moon, the sun, and other luminaries become shorn of their brilliance;
by whom hundreds of enemies are rendered unconquered;
and who, though a human, remains invincible while assuming any form at will. (Matsya Purāṇa 92.18)
His wife was named Bhānumatī, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds;
with her divine form like that of Lakṣmī, she surpassed the celestial beauties.
The king’s chief queen, dearer to him than his own life,
shone like the goddess Śrī in the midst of ten thousand women.
He was never released even by ten million kings. Once, while seated in his assembly hall, the king, overcome with wonder, questioned his domestic priest, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, by what dharma is my prosperity unsurpassed? And why is there always such vast and supreme splendor in my body?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
Formerly, there was a courtesan named Līlāvatī who was devoted to Śiva;
on the fourteenth lunar day, she gave a mountain of salt to her preceptor.
Together with golden trees and other such items, according to the prescribed rules and in the proper manner.
At that time, there was a goldsmith named Śauṇḍa who was a servant in Līlāvatī’s house; by him [the ornaments] were fashioned from that gold.
O King, the trees and the foremost of the gods, endowed with great beauty and filled with faith, performed their work without wages;
knowing it to be a duty of dharma, they did not accept anything at all. (Matsya Purāṇa 92.25)
And O King, golden celestial trees were kindled by his wife for the sake of service on the side of the mountain,
Līlāvatī.
Having performed service to their guru and other duties toward them with sincerity,
that courtesan Līlāvatī, even after a long time, [attained her goal].
O Nārada, having met the law of time through the application of her own karma, she was liberated from all sins and went to the abode of Śiva. (Matsya Purāṇa 92.28)
That goldsmith, though poor, was possessed of great nobility of character;
he did not take the price from the courtesan here at this time.
She who caused the trees of a goldsmith to be fashioned from gold and perfectly set ablaze has been born as the mistress of the seven islands, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns;
she is this Bhānumatī of yours.
Because of its blazing, a brilliant form has arisen for this sovereignty over the world;
for that preparatory rite was performed at night by the two [wives] who were not arrogant toward the mountain of salt.
And from that [merit], one attains invincibility in the worlds, as well as prosperity endowed with health and good fortune;
therefore, you too should here perform the ten types of mountain offerings, such as the Mountain of Grain (dhānyācala), according to the prescribed ritual.

Saying "So be it," that embodiment of Dharma respectfully accepted the words of Vasiṣṭha and gave away hundreds of grain-mountains and other gifts; then, being honored by the immortals, he departed for the world of Murāri.
Even one who is destitute may behold these with extreme devotion, or touch them when they are being offered by others;
and he who hears of them with devotion or bestows his mind upon them becomes free from stain and goes to heaven.
An evil dream comes to an end when recited by men who are the lords of mountains and who shatter the fear of worldly existence;
O bull among sages, what need is there for one whose mind is perfectly tranquil to make here the gift of all the kings of mountains?
Matsya Purāṇa 93: Sūta said:
In former times, Śaunaka questioned Vaiśampāyana as he was seated.
How is the rite for pacification and nourishment performed constantly for the attainment of all desires? MatsP_93.1 //
Vaiśampāyana said:
One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, should undertake the sacrifice to the planets;
likewise, one who desires growth, long life, or nourishment, or even one performing malevolent rites.
Listen as I declare to you that ritual procedure by which, O Brahmin, [this is accomplished]. MatsP_93.2 //
Having reviewed all the scriptures and condensed their voluminous extent,
I shall proclaim the pacification of planetary afflictions as enjoined by the Purāṇas and the Śruti.

On an auspicious day proclaimed by the Brahmins, having performed the recitation by the Brahmins and having established the planets and their presiding deities, one should commence the fire sacrifice (homa).
The sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña) is declared to be threefold by those learned in the Purāṇas and the Śrutis:
the first is the Ayutahoma, and after that comes the Lakṣahoma.
The third is the *koṭi-homa*, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
and the sacrifice to the nine planets (*navagraha-makha*) is prescribed with ten thousand oblations.
I shall now describe its ritual procedure as declared in the Purāṇas and the Śrutis:
to the northeast of the pit, one should prepare a space two vitastis in width.
One should prepare an altar, surrounded by two embankments, measuring one span in height,
square in shape, and facing north, for the installation of the deities.
Having performed the bringing forward of the fire, one should invoke the deities therein;
then, twenty-twelve (thirty-two) deities are to be established.
The Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter,
Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu— these are declared to be the planets that bring welfare to the world.
One should know Bhāskara (the Sun) to be in the center, Lohita (Mars) to the south,
Guru (Jupiter) to the north, and Budha (Mercury) to the northeast.
One should know Bhārgava to be in the east, Soma in the southeast;
one should know Śani in the west, and Rāhu in the southwest;
one should place Ketu in the northwest with white rice grains.
One should know Īśvara to belong to Bhāskara (the Sun), and likewise Umā to Śaśin (the Moon);
Skanda belongs to Aṅgāraka (Mars), and likewise Hari to Budha (Mercury).
One should know that Brahmā is the preceptor of Śukra, and the Lord of Śacī (Indra) is the preceptor of Saturn; likewise, Yama is the preceptor of Rāhu, and Kāla is the preceptor of Ketu.
To Ketu belongs Citragupta; and for all [the planets], the presiding deities are Agni, Water, Earth, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the goddess Indrāṇī.
Prajāpati, the serpents, and Brahmā are the presiding deities (pratyadhidevatās).
One should likewise invoke Vināyaka, Durgā, Vāyu, and Ākāśa, as well as the two Aśvin-kumāras, using the vyāhṛtis. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.16)
One should visualize the Sun as red, accompanied by Mars;
likewise, the Moon and Venus as white, Mercury and Jupiter as tawny, Mandara and Rāhu as black, and the host of Ketus as smoky. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.17)
Garments and flowers should be offered in the colors of the planets; here,
fragrant incense smoke should be provided, and above it,
a wise man should arrange a beautiful canopy adorned with fruits and flowers.
One should offer rice with jaggery to the Sun, milk-porridge with ghee to the Moon, wheat-cakes to Mars, and milk with *ṣaṣṭika* rice to Mercury. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.19)
One should offer curd-rice to Jīva and Śakra, ghee-rice to Śanaiścara,
kṛsarā and goat-meat to Rāhu,
and variegated rice to the Ketus; then one should worship them with all kinds of edible foods.
And to the northeast of that, [he should place] an object adorned with curd and unbroken rice,
covered with mango sprouts, and provided with a pair of fruits and garments.
One should place a flawless pitcher endowed with the five jewels and provided with the five types of grain, and therein one should install the deity Varuṇa.
All rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as oceans, lakes, elephants, horses, carriage-roads, anthills, confluences, ponds, and cow-pens; Matsya Purāṇa 93.23.
O best of Brahmins, the knower of dharma should bring earth mixed with all medicinal herbs and water, and place it there for the bathing of the sacrificer. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.24)
May all the oceans, rivers, lakes, and likewise the streams,
come to bring about the destruction of the sacrificer's misfortunes.
O best of sages, one should thus invoke these immortals; then one should commence the fire-oblation with clarified butter, barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth. *Matsya Purāṇa* 93.26.
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, then pippala, audumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in sequence. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.27)
For each [deity], one hundred and eight or indeed twenty-eight oblations should be offered,
combined with honey, clarified butter, and curd.
A wise person should always prepare fuel-sticks of the measure of a span, which are without roots, without branches, and without leaves, for all ritual acts.
Even for all the gods, one who knows the supreme truth should offer fuel-sticks individually and silently with each of their own respective mantras.
Furthermore, one should offer oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) and other items smeared with clarified butter;
having offered ten oblations with the mantras, one should then perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) with the vyāhṛtis.
The preeminent Brahmins, facing either northward or eastward,
should perform the sacrificial oblations (carus) for each respective deity, accompanied by the appropriate mantras.

Having properly offered those sacrificial oblations (carus), one should then perform the fire-sacrifice (homa); the twice-born man should perform the oblation to Sūrya with the hymn beginning "Ā kṛṣṇena. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.33)
One should offer oblations again to Soma with the mantra "āpyāyasva," and one should recite the mantra "agnirmūrdhā divaḥ" for Bhauma. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.34)
"O Agni Vivasvat, at the break of dawn," [is the mantra] for one who presses Soma;
"O Bṛhaspati, fly around with your chariot," is the opinion of the Guru. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.35)
The mantra "śukraṃ te anyat" is also declared for Śukra; furthermore, one should offer oblations to Śanaiścara with the mantra "śaṃ no devī. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.36)
The hymn beginning with "kayā naś citra ābhuvat" is declared for Rāhu;
one should also recite "ketuṃ kṛṇvan" for the pacification of the Ketus as well. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.37)
One should perform the bali-homa for Rudra with the mantra "ā vo rājā," for Umā with "āpo hi ṣṭha," and likewise for the Lord (Svāmin) with "syonā. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.38)

Then one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu with "This is Viṣṇu's," to the Lord (Iśa) with "Viṣṇu," to Svayambhū with "Him as the Lord," and to Indra with "Indra indeed is the deity. Thus one should sacrifice to Indra.
Likewise, this oblation "And this cow of Yama" is proclaimed;
the mantra "The Brahman was born from Time" is highly praised for Kāla.
Those who know the mantras understand that it is unknown even to Citragupta;
"We choose Agni as our messenger" is the mantra recited for Agni.
"ud uttamaṃ varuṇam" is proclaimed as the mantra for water;
"bhūmeḥ pṛthivyantarikṣam" is recited in the Vedas for the earth. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.42)
The verse beginning with "The Puruṣa of a thousand heads" is proclaimed for Viṣṇu;
the verse beginning with "O Indu, for Indra accompanied by the Maruts" is recited for Śakra.
One should perform the rite for the Goddess with the mantra "O fortunate one with upward-pointing leaves";
furthermore, the oblation to Prajāpati is traditionally known as "Prajāpati. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.44)
"Salutation be to the serpents"—this is declared as the mantra for the serpents;
"This is the Brahman among the officiating priests"—this is cited regarding the Brahman priest.
The mantra "vināyakasya cānūnam" is remembered by the wise;
"jātavedase sunavāma" is said to be the mantra of Durgā.
The mantra "ādit pratnasya retasaḥ" is proclaimed for Ākāśa, and the mantra "krāṇā śiśur mahīnām" is celebrated for Vāyu. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.47)
The mantra for the Aśvins is recited as "eṣo uṣā apūrvyā" (This is the unprecedented Dawn);
however, for the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should offer with "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ" (The head of heaven).

Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, with that very full water-pot, accompanied by the consecration mantra and auspicious songs and instrumental music, [the preceptor should sprinkle the king] facing the northeast.
O Brahmin, the bathing of the patron must be performed by four twice-born priests who possess unimpaired limbs and are adorned with golden garlands and wreaths.
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you;
may Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the omnipresent Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, grant you victory.
May Ākhaṇḍala, Agni, the Lord Yama, Nirṛti,
Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth, and Śiva,
together with Brahmā and Śeṣa— may these guardians of the quarters protect you.

Fame, Prosperity, Fortitude, Intelligence, Nourishment, Faith, Action, Thought, Wisdom, Modesty, Body, Peace, Contentment, and Prowess—these mothers, the lawful wives of Dharma, have assembled; may they consecrate you. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.53)
May the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus,
and Saturn— the planets— consecrate you, as well as Rāhu and Ketu, being fully gratified.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
the ṛṣis, munis, cows, and the divine mothers as well.
The wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, the hosts of apsarases, all missiles, all weapons, kings, and mounts; MatsP_93.56.
May medicinal herbs, gems, the divisions of time,
rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams—
may these all consecrate you for the fulfillment of every desire and purpose.
Then, wearing white garments and anointed with white perfumes,
he was bathed by the best of the twice-born with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances.
The sacrificer, together with his wife,
free from pride, should diligently honor the officiating priests with sacrificial fees.
One should give a tawny cow to the Sun, and likewise a conch-shell to the Moon;
one should give a red draft-ox to Mars, and a humped bull to Mercury.
One should give gold to Budha, yellow garments to Guru,
a white horse to the preceptor of the Daityas (Śukra), and a black cow to the son of the Sun (Sani).
One should give an iron [image] to Rāhu and an excellent goat to the Ketus;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be made equal in value to gold by the sacrificer.
Alternatively, cows adorned with gold should be given to all;
or one should give gold, or whatever else by which the Guru is pleased. All sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) must be given everywhere accompanied by the sacred mantra.
O Kapilā, you are worthy of worship by all the gods as Rohiṇī;
since you consist of the deities of sacred fords (tīrthas), therefore grant me peace.
O Śaṅkha, you are meritorious among merits and the most auspicious of all auspicious things;
since you are held by Viṣṇu, grant me peace.
You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the bringer of joy to the world; you are the foundation of the eightfold form [of Śiva]. Therefore, grant me peace.
You are the embryo within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden seed of the Fire-god;
since you bestow the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace.
Since this pair of yellow garments is dear to Vāsudeva,
by the gift of them to me, O Viṣṇu, grant me peace.
Since you are Viṣṇu in the form of a horse, born from the nectar of immortality,
and are eternally the vehicle of the moon and the sun, therefore grant me peace.
Since you are the entire earth, a cow resembling Keśava,
and the eternal remover of all sins, therefore grant me peace.
Since the laborious tasks involving the plow and other weapons are always under your control, therefore grant me peace.
Since you are established as a constituent part of all sacrifices and are the eternal vehicle of Vibhāvasu (Fire), therefore grant me peace.
Since the fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of cows,
may there be prosperity for me in this world and in the next.
"Since the bed of Keśava is never empty, may my own bed also be non-empty, granted [by you] in birth after birth. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.74)
Just as all the gods are established within all the jewels,
so may the gods grant me jewels through this gift of jewels.
Just as other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of land,
may peace come to me here from the gift of land.
Thus one should worship with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth,
using abundance of jewels, gold, and garments, as well as incense, garlands, and unguents.
Whoever performs the worship of the planets according to this rite attains all desires and is glorified in heaven after death. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.78)
But the wise man, having diligently worshipped that planet which constantly causes affliction to one of meager wealth, should also honor the remaining ones.
The planets, cows, kings, and especially Brahmins—when honored, they honor [the one who honors them]; when treated with contempt, they consume [him] utterly.
Just as armor serves as a defense against the strikes of arrows,
so too does propitiatory rite serve as a defense against the afflictions of fate.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should not perform [a rite] devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
for even a single [deity] is satisfied by a complete sacrificial fee. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.82)
This rite of ten thousand oblations (ayutahoma) is always employed in the sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha),
as well as in marriages, festivals, sacrifices, and rites such as consecrations.

O best of sages, this ten-thousand-fold oblation (ayutahoma) has been taught for the purpose of removing obstacles and for occasions of agitation or wonder; now hear from me about the hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma).

Since the wise know that the *lakṣahoma* leads to the attainment of all desires, it is truly beloved by the ancestors and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.85)
Having obtained the strength of the planets and stars and having performed the recitation by Brahmins,
the wise man should have a pavilion constructed to the northeast of the house.
Or on the ground of a temple of Rudra, one should construct a square measuring ten or eight cubits, facing north, according to the prescribed rule.
A wise person should diligently have the ground sloping toward the northeast;
having selected a site for the pavilion that inclines toward the north-east.
One should have a beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed, endowed with the proper characteristics as prescribed:
square on all sides, with a yoni-mouth and a girdle (mekhalā).
The girdle should be four finger-breadths in width and raised to the same height;
it should slope toward the east and north, being level on all sides.
The sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha) is prescribed for the sake of the peace of all the worlds.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is deficient or excessive in measurement brings about many fears;
therefore, a pacificatory pit (śāntikuṇḍa) is ordained to be perfectly complete.
The Svayambhū has declared that the Lakṣahoma is ten times this [in merit],
through the diligent offering of oblations as well as through sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Furthermore,
for a *lakṣa*-homa, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be two cubits wide and four cubits long, having a womb-shaped opening (*yonivaktra*) and three tiers (*mekhalā*).
And to its northeast, situated at a distance of three spans,
there is a square pond that is equal on all sides and slopes toward the northeast.
Viśvakarman has declared that the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for the installation of the deities should be raised to half the width of the base and surrounded by three embankments.
The first rampart is declared to be two finger-breadths in height;
above that, there are two further ramparts, each joined with a height of one finger-breadth.
The width of all [the lines] is said by the wise to be three finger-breadths.
The wall on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should likewise be ten finger-breadths high;
upon that, one should invoke the deities as before with flowers and rice grains.
O best of sages, all [the images], facing the sun and accompanied by their presiding and subordinate deities, should be installed; they must not face north nor have their backs turned away.
There, Garuḍa is to be worshipped with special honor by one desiring prosperity:
"Your body is the sound of the Sāman; you are the vehicle of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
You are eternally the destroyer of poison and evil; therefore, grant me peace. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.99)
Having addressed the pitcher as before, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in the same manner;
having offered a hundred thousand oblations, exceeding that number by the count of fuel-sticks,
one should then pour a stream of clarified butter from the pitcher into the fire.
Having fashioned a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) made of *audumbara* wood— moist, straight, free of hollows,
and one cubit in length— one should then properly pour a stream of clarified butter over the fire from above that ladle, positioned over the two pillars.
One should cause [the officiant] to recite the hymns dedicated to Agni, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Moon;
and one should have him chant the Mahāvaiśvānara Sāman and the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
The bathing of the sacrificer and the recitation of the *svastivācana* are to be performed as before;
likewise, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given separately by the sacrificer as previously prescribed.
O Brahmins, in the sacrifice for the nine planets, four priests who are knowers of the Vedas— free from desire and anger and possessed of peaceful minds— [should perform the rite].
Alternatively, two priests alone, who are peaceful and well-versed in the Vedas, should be employed for the ten-thousand-fold oblation; one should not become entangled in excessive elaboration.
And likewise, for the *lakṣahoma*, eighteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be appointed according to one's capacity; or else, four who are free from envy may be appointed.
O best of sages, in the Lakṣahoma, which is ten times greater than the sacrifice to the nine planets (Navagrahamakha),
one should give edible offerings and ornaments according to one's capacity.
One who is capable [should give] beds with their coverlets, golden bracelets, earrings, finger-rings, and neck-threads. *Matsya Purāṇa* 93.108.
A person should not perform a rite devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) through stinginess regarding wealth;
by failing to give out of greed or delusion, he brings about the ruin of his lineage. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.109)
One who desires prosperity should give food according to one's ability;
for if a person is deprived of food, it results in the consequence of a famine.
A sacrifice lacking food burns the kingdom; one lacking mantras burns the officiating priests;
and one lacking sacrificial fees burns the patron. There is no enemy equal to such a sacrifice.
Furthermore, a man with little wealth should never perform a Lakṣahoma sacrifice,
because conflict always causes distress during such a rite.
One should worship those very [Brāhmaṇas] with devotion, two or three according to the rule;
or one may worship even a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas with devotion and with diligent offerings of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), rather than many [if] one possesses little wealth.
A Lakṣahoma should be performed according to one's abundant means;
for by performing it according to the prescribed rules, one obtains all desires.
And he is honored in the world of Śiva by the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts for eight hundred kalpas; thereafter, he shall attain liberation.
He who, possessing a desire, should perform this Lakṣahoma according to the prescribed rule,
attains that very desire and enjoys the state of infinity.
One desiring a son obtains sons; one desiring wealth obtains wealth;
one desiring a wife obtains a beautiful wife; and a maiden obtains an auspicious husband.
One whose kingdom has been lost shall regain his kingdom; one who desires prosperity shall obtain prosperity. Whatever desire one prays for, that indeed becomes abundant.
But he who performs this without desire goes to the supreme Brahman.
The Svayambhū has declared that the Koṭihoma is a hundred times superior to this,
in terms of the oblations offered with diligence, the sacrificial fees, and the resulting fruit.
As before, the invocation and dismissal of the planetary deities are performed;
the same *homa* mantras are prescribed for eating and giving as well.
Now, learn from me this specific distinction regarding the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and the altar (*vedi*). *Matsya Purāṇa* 93.120.
For a *koṭi-homa*, the sacrificial pit should be four cubits square on all sides,
provided with both a womb (*yoni*) and two openings (*vaktra*), and it is said to have three girdles (*mekhalā*).
The first girdle should be made by the wise to be two finger-breadths high;
likewise, the second is proclaimed to be three finger-breadths high.
The third [line] is praised for being three finger-breadths in both height and width;
the width of the two preceding ones is likewise recommended as being two finger-breadths.
The yoni should be one *vitasti* in length and six or seven *aṅgulas* in width;
it should be raised like the back of a tortoise in the middle and elevated by one *aṅgula* at the sides. *Matsya Purāṇa* 93.124.
Likewise, it should be as long as an elephant’s trunk and provided with an opening;
this is declared to be the characteristic of the *yoni* in all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*).
Everywhere above the girdle, it should resemble an aśvattha leaf;
and for a koṭi-homa, the altar (vedī) should be four vitastis in height.
It is square on all sides and endowed with three embankments;
the dimensions of the embankments and the height of the altars are as previously described.
Likewise, the pavilion should be sixteen cubits in size and have four entrances;
and at the eastern gate, one should station a master of the Rigveda who has reached the further shore of the Veda.
Likewise, the wise man should station one who knows the Yajurveda in the south, one who knows the Sāmaveda in the west, and similarly, one who knows the Atharvaveda in the north.
Eight officiating priests (*homakas*) who are learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*) should be appointed;
thus there shall be twelve Brahmins, whom one should worship with devotion as before, using garments, garlands, ointments, clothes, ornaments, and decorations. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.130)
Facing north, the Bahvṛca priest sits to the east, reciting the Rātrisūkta, the Raudrasūkta, the Pāvamānī hymns, and other highly auspicious texts for the sake of peace.
At the southern gate, one should cause an excellent knower of the Yajurveda to recite the Śākta, Śākra, Saumya, Kauṣmāṇḍa, and Śānti hymns.

Furthermore, in the western direction, the singer of the Sāman hymns (Chandoga) should recite the Suparṇa, the Vairāja, the Āgneya, the Rudrasaṃhitā, and likewise the Jyeṣṭha and Śānti hymns during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
One who knows the Atharva-veda should also recite the Śāntisūkta, the Saura hymn, the auspicious Śākunaka,
the Pauṣṭika, and the Mahārājya, using the northern [branch].
O best of sages, in this rite, the oblation should be performed as before with either five or seven [mantras]; for the bathing and the giving, those very same mantras are to be used.
The ritual of the stream of wealth (vasordhārā) is especially distinguished in the Lakṣahoma;
whoever performs a Koṭihoma according to this procedure attains all desires and thereafter goes to the abode of Viṣṇu. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.136)
The man who recites or even hears these three sacrifices to the planets,
having his soul purified of all sins, goes to the abode of Indra.
Having performed eighteen thousand horse-sacrifices, O knower of dharma,
one obtains that fruit which one enjoys from the Kauṭi-homa.
Thousands of killings of Brahmins and hundreds of millions of killings of embryos are destroyed by the *koṭihoma* sacrifice, just as it was spoken by Śiva. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.139)
Having performed the sacrifice to the nine planets for rites of subjugation, malevolent magic, and likewise for eradication and so forth, one should then carry out the rites for specific desires.
Otherwise, no desired rite ever bears fruit for men;
therefore, one should first perform the procedure for ten thousand oblations.
The circular pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) as well as for the rite of subjugation (vaśya);
it should have three ridges (mekhalā), one opening, and measure one cubit (aratni) in width.
Palāśa fuel-sticks are recommended when combined with honey and gorocanā;
likewise, they should be sprinkled with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
One should offer oblations of bilva fruits and lotuses with honey and clarified butter ten thousand times; this has been declared by Svayambhū himself for all occasions.

In rites for subjugation (*vaśyakarman*), one who knows the Dharma should offer oblations of *bilva* and *padma* flowers with the mantra: "May the waters and herbs be friendly to us" (*sumitriyā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ*). (Matsya Purāṇa 93.145)
In this case, neither the ritual installation nor the consecration with the water-pot should be performed;
rather, having bathed with all medicinal herbs, the householder, clad in white flowers and garments, [should proceed].
One should honor the Brahmins with necklaces adorned with gold;
fine garments should be given, as well as white cows accompanied by gold.
One shall bring even all the forces of one's enemies under control;
this oblation, which destroys evil, turns even foes into friends. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.148)
For acts of incantation to cause enmity and for malevolent rites (abhicāra), a triangular pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed;
it should have two ridges (mekhalā), face toward the corners, and measure one cubit in every dimension.
Then the Brahmins, adorned with red garlands and unguents, wearing red turbans and clad in red garments, should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Provided with three vessels rich with fresh blood and wine,
and holding sacrificial fuel-sticks made from the bones of hawks and endowed with strength in their left hands,
those with disheveled hair, meditating on the misfortune of the enemy, should offer oblations. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.151)
"May they be ill-disposed toward him; likewise, *huṃ phaṭ*!"—having thus consecrated the razor with this mantra for the Śyena-rite of sorcery, [he should proceed].
Having fashioned an image of the enemy, one should cut it all around with a razor;
one should cast the fragments of that enemy-form into the fire just as they are.

At the conclusion of the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the planets, one who is constantly performing malevolent magic or likewise practicing incantations to cause enmity should not perform this very rite again.
This alone yields fruit for men in this world, not in the hereafter;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should perform rites for peace (śāntika) right here.
The man who performs the three graha-yajñas without desire attains the station of Viṣṇu, from which a return to this world is difficult to find.
The person who would constantly hear this or cause it to be heard shall suffer no affliction from malevolent planets, nor shall there be any loss of kinsmen.
Wherever these three planetary sacrifices are inscribed and remain in a house,
there shall be no affliction for children, nor disease, nor imprisonment.

The wise know the *koṭihoma* as that which bestows the fruit of all sacrifices without exception, destroys every sin without remainder, and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Matsya Purāṇa 93.159)
The best of gods have declared that the Lakṣahoma yields the fruit of an Aśvamedha;
likewise, the Navagrahamakha is remembered as being equal to a twelve-day sacrifice (Dvādaśāhamakha).

Thus has been described the consecration for the sacrifice to the gods, which removes all impurities and is the cause of festive joy. Whoever recites this in such a manner, or whoever hears it incidentally, shall overcome his enemies and be endowed with long life and health.
Matsya Purāṇa 94: Śiva said:
[He is] seated upon a lotus, with lotus-like hands, possessing a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus.
The Sun should always have seven horses, seven reins, and two arms.
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, with white horses and a white vehicle;
he has two arms, holds a mace in his hand, and bestows boons.
Wearing red garlands and garments, holding a spear, a trident, and a mace,
