the son of the Earth shall have four arms, white body hair, and be a bestower of boons.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, with a luster like that of the Karṇikāra flower,
holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, the wise Budha sits upon a lion and grants boons.
Likewise, the two preceptors of the gods and the Daityas, yellow and white in color, should be depicted with four arms,
holding staffs, granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should likewise be depicted with the luster of sapphire, holding a trident and a bow and arrow, bestowing boons, and mounted upon a vulture.
With a terrifying face, bearing a sword, shield, and trident, and granting boons,
Rāhu is praised here as seated upon a blue lion-throne.
All smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, and having deformed faces;
seated eternally upon vultures, these banners shall be granters of boons.
All the planets, which bring welfare to the world, should be depicted wearing crowns;
all of them should always be one hundred and eight in number, and each should be raised [in height] by its own finger-breadth.
Matsya Purāṇa 95.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, there is yet another thing that has been heard by me.
It is capable of yielding the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; you should please tell me about that further.
Thus addressed, Śambhu replied: "O Brahmin, this man has reached the further shore of the Vedic word; he is my equal in asceticism and in his mastery of the Purāṇas and the extensive Śruti."
O Nārada, from that time forth, this Dharma in the form of a bull shall be the leader of the Gaṇas named Nandin, and he will proclaim the doctrines of Maheśvara.
The Fish said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods vanished right there;
and Nārada, desiring to hear more, questioned Nandikeśvara.
"You have been commanded here by Śiva; speak the vow of Maheśvara."
Nandikeśvara said: Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall describe the Māheśvara vow, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Śivacaturdaśī.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, eating but a single meal, one should pray to You, the Lord of the Gods: "I have come to You for refuge."
Having fasted on the fourteenth day and having properly worshipped Śaṅkara, and having given a golden bull, I shall eat on the following day. (Matsya Purāṇa 95.7)

Having thus observed the vow and slept, the man, having risen in the morning and performed his ablutions and recitations, should thereafter worship Śaṅkara together with Umā with white lotuses, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
"Salutation to Śiva" for the feet; "Salutation to the Soul of All" for the head;
"To the Three-eyed One" for the eyes; "Salutation to Hari" for the forehead. (Matsya Purāṇa 95.9)
He should worship the face with "To Indumukha," the neck with "To Śrīkaṇṭha," the two ears with "To Sadyojāta," and the two arms with "To Vāmadeva."
One should worship the heart with "To Aghora-hṛdaya," the two breasts with "To Tatpuruṣa," and likewise the abdomen with "To Īśāna. (MatsP 95.11)
One should worship the two sides with "Salutation to Anantadharma," the waist with "Salutation to Jñānabhūta," and the two thighs with "Salutation to Anantavairāgyasiṃha. (MatsP 95.12)
The wise one should worship the knees with "Salutation to the Lord of Infinite Sovereignty," the shanks with "Salutation to Pradhāna," and the ankles with "Salutation to the Self of Space."
One should worship the hair and the back of the one whose self-form is the sky-haired Lord (Vyomakeśa);
one should also worship Pārvatī with the words, "Salutation to Puṣṭi, salutation to Tuṣṭi."

Then, one should present to a Brāhmaṇa a golden bull, accompanied by a water-pot, adorned with white garlands and garments, endowed with the five jewels, and provided with various kinds of edible foods.
"May Sadyojāta, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the God of gods, be pleased here.
Then, having summoned auspicious Brahmins, he should satisfy them with devotion;
and having consumed the *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter), he should sleep on the ground facing north. (Matsya Purāṇa 95.16)
Having worshipped the Brahmins on the fifteenth day, he should eat while maintaining silence;
likewise, he should perform all this on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. (Matsya Purāṇa 95.17)
On all fourteenth days, one should perform the worship as previously described;
however, those specific rites that occur in each month, learn them here in their proper order.
One should recite this in sequence during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa:
"Obeisance to you, Śaṅkara; obeisance to you, Karavīraka. (Matsya Purāṇa 95.19)
"Obeisance be to Tryambaka; after that, obeisance to Maheśvara.
Obeisance be to you, Mahādeva; and after that, obeisance to Sthāṇu. (Matsya Purāṇa 95.20)
Salutations to Paśupati, O Lord; salutations again to you, Śambhu.
Salutations to you, Supreme Bliss; salutations to the bearer of the crescent moon.
"Obeisance to Bhīma"—thus have I come to you for refuge.
Cow's urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass; MatsP_95.22 //
Then, the ritual consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), followed by bilva, camphor, agallochum, barley,
and black sesame seeds, is prescribed in due order according to the rules.
It is ordained that this consumption occurs once each month on the fourteenth day.
And with *mandāra* and *mālatī* flowers, as well as with *dhattūraka*,
*sinduvāra*, *aśoka*, *mallikā*, and *pāṭala* flowers.
On each of the fourteenth days, one should worship the Lord of Pārvatī with arka flowers, kadamba flowers, śatapatrī, and likewise with utpala lotuses.
Furthermore, when the month of Kārttika arrives, he should gratify the twice-born with various kinds of food, edibles, garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Having performed the ritual release of a blue bull according to the procedure prescribed in the Śruti,
a man [should offer] a golden image of Umā-Maheśvara along with a bull.
One should give a bed provided with eight pearls, covered with a white cloth and a veil, equipped with all necessary furnishings, and accompanied by a water-pot.
Furthermore, having placed it upon a copper vessel together with rice grains,
he should present it to a peaceful Brahmin who is devoted to the Vedic vows.
It should be given to one who knows the Jyeṣṭha-sāman, or to one who observes the Navaka-vrata;
it should be given to a learned Śrotriya who recognizes virtues, or to a teacher who knows the ultimate reality.
Having worshipped him who has no deficient limbs, who is gentle, who always brings about auspiciousness, and who is accompanied by his wife, with garments, garlands, and ornaments; MatsP_95.31.
When a guru is present, the gift should be given to the guru; in his absence, it should be given to a twice-born.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; by doing so, one falls low due to the fault.
The man who observes the Śiva-caturdaśī according to this rite obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. (Matsya Purāṇa 95.33)
Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed by one's fathers or brothers, whether in this world or the next, all of that shall go to destruction.

In this world, there shall be an inexhaustible increase in long life, health, lineage, and food; and in the next world, one attains the state of having four arms, lordship over the Gaṇas, and after dwelling in heaven for hundreds of millions of kalpas, one reaches the abode of Śambhu.
Neither Bṛhaspati, nor the Moon, nor even the Grandfather Brahmā is able to describe its infinite fruit;
neither is the host of Siddhas capable of it, nor am I, even if there were ten million tongues in my mouth.

He who recites, remembers, or even constantly listens to this [account] of Śiva’s fourteenth day—which liberates from all sins—becomes beloved by the immortals; even the millions of celestial nymphs praise that blameless man, so what need is there to mention him who always practices it? (Matsya Purāṇa 95.37)
Or whatever woman performs this with great devotion, having first taken leave of her husband, her sons, or her elders,
she too, by the grace of the Supreme Lord who wields the Pināka bow, attains the supreme state.
Matsya Purāṇa 96:
Nandikeśvara said:
"O Nārada, listen to the greatness of the renunciation of fruits that may arise."
That which is imperishable and supreme in the world, bestowing the fruit of all desires.

O Sage, one should begin this vow on the third, twelfth, eighth, or fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, after having performed the recitation for the Brahmins. (Matsya Purāṇa 96.2)
O best of sages, on other meritorious months as well,
one should feed the twice-born with milk-rice accompanied by sacrificial fees according to one's ability.
One should avoid the eighteen types of grain as well as other fruits and roots for one year, except for medicinal purposes; furthermore,
one should have an image of Rudra made of gold along with a bull and Dharmarāja.
The kūṣmāṇḍa, the mātuliṅga, the vārtāka, the panasa,
as well as the āmrātaka, the kapittha, the kaliṅga, and the vāluka.
Śrīphala, aśvattha, badara, jambīra, kadalīphala,
kāśmīra, and pomegranate— these sixteen, polished with time, [should be offered] according to one's capacity.
Radish, myrobalan, rose-apple, tamarind, karamarda, kaṅkola, cardamom, katuṇḍīra, karīra, kuṭaja, and śamī; MatsP_96.7.
One should have these sixteen fruits made of silver according to one's means: the udumbara, the coconut, the grape, and the two types of bṛhatī. (Matsya Purāṇa 96.8)
One should prepare copper, the fruit of the *tāla* tree, the fruit of the *agasti* tree,
the fruit of the *piṇḍāraka* and *aśmarya* trees, as well as the *sūraṇa* tuber.
The red yam tuber, the one called kanaka, the citron, the fruit of the variegated creeper, and likewise the fruit of the kūṭa-śālmalī tree; MatsP_96.10 //
A person should have these sixteen copper vessels made according to their means: [vessels] of mango, niṣpāva, madhuka, vaṭa, mudga, and paṭola. MatsP_96.11.
One should place two water-pots upon grain, covered with cloth;
thereafter, one should have a bed prepared, well-adorned with fine garments.

On an auspicious day, having performed worship, one should present [the gift]— equipped with three vessels of food, accompanied by Yama, Rudra, and a bull, and together with a cow— to a peaceful Brahmin who has a family and is accompanied by his wife. *Matsya Purāṇa* 96.13.
Just as tens of millions of immortals dwell within all fruits,
so may devotion to Śiva arise in me through the vow of renouncing all fruits.
Just as Śiva and Dharma always bestow infinite fruits,
may they both grant me boons by bestowing the fruits associated with them.
Just as there are always infinite rewards for those devoted to Śiva,
so may there be the attainment of infinite fruits in birth after birth.
Just as I perceive no difference between Śiva, Viṣṇu, Arka, and the Lotus-born,
so may Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe, be forever the bestower of auspiciousness upon me.
Having given all of that and having adorned [the recipient] with ornaments,
if one has the means, one should give a bed equipped with all its furnishings.
But one who is unable [to perform the full rite] should, according to the prescribed rule, offer only the aforementioned fruits,
as well as two golden images of Śiva together with water-pots.
Having given [the gift] to a Brahmin, he should eat while restraining his speech, avoiding oil;
furthermore, according to his ability, he should feed other twice-born men as much as he can.
Those who know the Vedas recognize this auspicious vow of renouncing all fruits as belonging to the Bhāgavatas, the Saura-Vaiṣṇava yogins. (Matsya Purāṇa 96.21)
O bull among the twice-born, women should also perform this according to their ability;
O best of sages, there is no other vow in this world or the next that yields such infinite fruit as this.
O best of sages, for as many thousands of eons as there are atoms in gold, silver, and copper when those fruits are ground into powder,
one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
This [work] shall always be for the livelihood of people among men, removing all their impurities;
even in other births, one does not experience the sorrow of separation from a son, and attains the abode cherished by the world of Indra.
Or whatever man of little wealth hears this, or recites it in temples and the dwellings of the righteous—
O Lord of Sages, his body freed from sins, he too shall reach that city of Murāri which brings joy to the great sages.
Matsya-Purāṇa 97:
Nārada said: That which brings about health for men and bestows infinite fruit—
O Nandīśa, tell us that vow which leads to the peace of mortals.
Nandikeśvara said:
That which is the abode of the Soul of the Universe, the supreme, eternal Brahman, exists in the world in three forms: as the sun, fire, and the moon. *Matsya Purāṇa* 97.2.
By worshipping Him, O Brahmin, a person always attains well-being;
therefore, one should always eat only at night on Sundays.
When the day of the Sun is conjoined with the Hasta constellation, then,
free from envy, one should observe a single meal on a Saturday.
Having fed the best of the twice-born at night on a Sunday,
[he should offer] a lotus made of red sandalwood paste together with twelve leaves.
Having drawn [the diagram], one should place Sūrya in the east with a salutation;
likewise, Divākara in the southeast, and Vivasvat thereafter.
One should place the god Bhaga in the southwest, Varuṇa on the western petal,
Mahendra likewise in the northwest, and Āditya in the north.
One should place Śānta in the northeastern quarter with a gesture of salutation;
then, one should place the horses of the Sun upon the eastern petal of the pericarp.
On the southern petal, one should place the one named Aryaman; on the western petal, Mārtaṇḍa;
on the northern petal, the god Ravi; and on the pericarp, Bhāskara.
One should offer an *arghya* oblation of red flowers and water, along with sesame seeds and red sandalwood, into that lotus; then one should recite this mantra: *MatsP_97.10*
You are the self of time, the self of all beings, the self of the Vedas, and the one whose face is everywhere;
since you possess the forms of Agni and Indra, protect us, O Maker of Day! (Matsya Purāṇa 97.11)
I praise Agni; salutations to you, O Maker of Light, for the sake of food and for strength. O Agni, come hither, O Giver of Boons; salutations to you, Lord of the luminaries.
Having offered the *arghya* and performed the ritual dismissal, one should eat at night without using oil.
At the end of the year, however, one should have a golden lotus and a two-armed male figure fashioned according to one's means. (Matsya Purāṇa 97.13)
One should give away a brown cow with golden horns, highly precious, with silver hooves and a bronze milking vessel, together with her calf;
having placed a lotus and a human figure upon a copper plate filled with molasses, one should present them as a gift.
Having worshipped the twice-born with red garments, garlands, and incense, and likewise with red [substances] and golden horns,

and having mentally envisioned the Puruṣa together with the lotus, one should give [the gift] to a man who has performed many vows and charities, who is of unimpaired form, who has conquered his senses, who maintains a family, and who is free from arrogance. (Matsya Purāṇa 97.15)
Homage, repeated homage, to the destroyer of evil, the soul of the universe, the one with seven horses;
to the storehouse of the essence of the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas, the ordainer, the boat for the ocean of existence, and the progenitor of the world.
The man who performs this practice here for one year according to this rule,
having his sins destroyed, ascends to the abode of the Sun, fanned by rows of waving chowries.

Having attained the destruction of his karma, the king was freed from sorrow, suffering, fear, and disease; endowed with immeasurable splendor, he became the lord of the seven islands again and again, possessing a body of dharma.

And she who, devoted to her husband, her elders, and the gods, performs day and night the rites prescribed by the Vedas—O Nārada, she too goes to the world of the Sun, which is worshipped by the lords of the immortals; of this there is no doubt.
The person who recites this, or hears it being recited, or even approves of its recitation,
shall be honored by the immortals while dwelling in the realm of Śakra, and shall reside eternally in heaven.
Matsya Purāṇa 98.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now I shall further describe the fruit of the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the Saṃkrānti festival.
That which is inexhaustible in the other world, bestowing the fruit of all desires.
One should observe the Saṃkrānti vow during either the solstices (ayana) or the equinoxes (viṣuva).
On the day preceding [the observance], one should eat only a single meal after first cleansing the teeth.
On the morning of the actual day of the Saṃkrānti, a bath with sesame seeds is prescribed. (Matsya Purāṇa 98.2)
At the sun's transit, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp upon the ground using sandalwood paste; therein, one should invoke the Sun.
One should place the Sun in the pericarp, and then Āditya to the east;
[one should say] "Obeisance to Uṣṇārcis" in the south, and "Obeisance to Ṛṅmaṇḍala."
One should bow to Savitṛ in the southwest (nairṛtya) and again to Tapana in the west (vāruṇa);
having placed Bhaga in the northwest (vāyavya), one should worship them again and again.
One should always place Mārtaṇḍa in the north and Viṣṇu in the northeast;
thereafter, one should worship them upon the sacrificial mound with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and edible offerings.
Having had a water-pot, a vessel of ghee, and a golden lotus fashioned according to one's ability, one should present them to a twice-born man.
One should offer arghya to the God upon the ground with sandalwood water and flowers, [saying]:
"Obeisance to the All-pervading One, whose form is the universe, whose abode is the universe, the Self-born;
obeisance to the Infinite, obeisance to the Creator, O Lord of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus! (Matsya Purāṇa 98.8).
By this method, one should perform everything month by month;
or else, at the end of the year, a man should perform it all twelve times over.
At the end of the year, having gratified the fire with ghee and milk-rice, as well as the best of the twice-born,
he should further offer twelve water-pots accompanied by cows, along with gems and golden lotuses.

One should give cows that yield milk, are virtuous in character, and are endowed with horns of gold and hooves of silver; eight or seven such cows, accompanied by bronze milking vessels, garlands, and garments—or even four if one is unable. One who is beset by poverty should offer at least a single tawny cow (kapilā) to an eminent Brāhmaṇa.
One should give the earth made of gold, including its remaining contents, or else one made of silver or copper;
if unable, having fashioned an image of flour, one should present it together with a golden sun.
A person should not practice stinginess regarding wealth in this matter; by doing so, he goes downward—of this there is no doubt. (Matsya Purāṇa 98.12)
O Nārada, for as long as this earth remains together with its seven oceans and its lordly mountains headed by Mahendra,
he shall be honored by all the hosts of Gandharvas upon the heights of heaven.
Then, having attained the exhaustion of his karma, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents, endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct;
at the beginning of creation, he shall possess a body free from defect, accompanied by his wife, and his feet shall be honored by a vast multitude of sons and descendants.
Whoever thus recites or hears with devotion this entire rite of merit for the sun's transit,
or even forms the intention to do so, shall be honored by the gods in the abode of the Lord of the Immortals.
Matsya Purāṇa 99.
Nandikeśvara said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the unsurpassed vow of Viṣṇu.
It is named Vibhūtidvādaśī, which is honored by all the gods.
In the months of Kārttika, Caitra, Vaiśākha, Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna,
or Āṣāḍha, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, a wise man who eats light food,
having performed the evening twilight rites, should undertake the religious observance (niyama).
"O Lord, having fasted on the eleventh day and worshipped Janārdana, I shall take my meal on the twelfth day together with a brahmin. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.3)
O Keśava, may that [undertaking] of mine proceed without obstacle and be fruitful;
and while sleeping at night, one should utter the words: "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa."
Then, having risen at dawn and performed his ablutions and recitations, being pure,
he should worship the Lotus-eyed One with white garlands and unguents.
"Salutation to Vibhūti for the feet; salutation to Aśoka for the knees;
'Salutation to Śiva' for the thighs; and 'Salutation to Viśvamūrti' for the hips. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.6)
"Salutation to Kandarpa for the penis; salutation to Āditya for the hands;
[salutation] to Dāmodara for the belly; and to Vāsudeva for the breasts. (MatsP 99.7)
"Salutation to Mādhava for the chest of Viṣṇu; salutation to the long-necked one for the throat;
salutation to Śrīdhara for the face; and salutation to Keśava for the hair," [said] Nārada. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.8)

One should worship with "To the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, obeisance" for the back; "To the Giver of Boons" for the two ears; by his own name for the one who holds the conch, discus, sword, mace, and lotus in his hands; and for the head, O Brahmin, one should worship with "Obeisance to the Soul of All. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.9)
Having fashioned a golden fish joined with a blue lotus according to his ability,
the wise man should place it before him together with a water-pot.
A vessel of molasses mixed with sesame seeds and wrapped in a white cloth;
one should keep a vigil at night with the recitation of ancient histories and other such stories. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.11)
When the night has turned to dawn, one should present to a brahmin householder the image of the God, together with a golden lotus and a water-pot.
O Lord, just as you are never deprived of all your sovereign splendors,
so may you lift me up from the mire of saṃsāra with its entirety of suffering.
O Sage, one should offer the forms of the ten incarnations in succession month by month—
Dattātreya and likewise Vyāsa accompanied by an *utpala* lotus—
and thus continue for as many years as one avoids heretics.
Having thus completed twelve Dvādaśīs according to one's ability,
at the end of the year, O best of sages, one should present to the preceptor a bed accompanied by a mountain of salt and a cow.
Being capable, one should give a village or a field provided with a dwelling, having duly honored the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and decorations. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.16)
Having fed other excellent brahmins as well according to his ability, he should satisfy them with gifts of clothing, cattle, heaps of jewels, and stores of wealth;
one of small means should perform this little by little, according to his capacity. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.17)
Furthermore, one who is extremely destitute but possesses devotion toward Mādhava should perform worship with flowers for two years according to the prescribed rite. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.18)
Whoever performs the Vibhūti-dvādaśī vow according to this rite shall be liberated from sin and deliver a hundred ancestors.
For a hundred thousand births, one shall not experience the fruit of sorrow;
neither disease, nor poverty, nor bondage shall befall him.
Furthermore, in birth after birth, he shall become a devotee of Viṣṇu or a devotee of Śiva. (Matsya Purāṇa 99.20)
O Brahmin, for as long as one hundred and eight thousand yugas may last, he shall dwell in heaven and then become a king once again.
Matsya Purāṇa 100.
Nandikeśvara said: In former times, during the Rathantara Kalpa, there was a king named Puṣpavāhana.
Renowned in the worlds by name, he was equal to the sun in splendor.
O Sage Nārada, by the four-faced Brahmā, who was pleased with his ascetic penance, a golden lotus was given that could travel wherever one desired. (Matsya Purāṇa 100.2)
Then the king, accompanied by all the people and the inhabitants of the city,
wandered at will through the continents and the world of the gods.
At the beginning of the kalpa, because that seventh island was inhabited by him and is honored in the world, it is called Puṣkaradvīpa.
Because the vehicle given to him by the god Brahmā was a lotus,
the gods and demons call him Puṣpavāhana (the Flower-Vehicle).
"By the power of his asceticism, there is nothing unattainable for him even throughout the three worlds as he dwells within the lotus of Brahmā.
And his wife, O Lord of Sages, was matchless, praised by thousands of women on all sides;
she was named Lāvaṇyavatī, and she was as beloved to Bhava as Pārvatī herself."
He had ten thousand sons who were righteous-souled and preeminent archers;
seeing all this of his own, the king was struck with wonder again and again.
Beholding the arrival of that foremost of sages, the son of Pracetas, he spoke these words: *Matsya Purāṇa 100.7*

"O Lord of Sages, why has this splendor—worthy of worship by gods, immortals, and mortals alike, surpassing all the celestial beauties, and born from me—become my wife? And why, O Indra among Munis, has the Creator, gratified by my meager penance, granted me this lotus-abode?"
Even when hundreds of millions of kings, accompanied by their ministers, elephants, throngs of chariots, and people, entered it, they were not perceived;
they vanished like the moon in the midst of the sky, surrounded by shimmering clusters of stars.

Therefore, O Pracetas, tell me what else—whether performed by one born from the womb of a mother, or by me, or by my sons, or even by her—is the cause for attaining the fruit of all religious duties (dharma) and so forth? May it be well. Tell me this entire matter.
Then the Sage, having perceived that extraordinary event caused by a powerful motive which had been concealed from the lord of the earth during his previous existence, declared:
"But your birth occurred in an exceedingly terrible hunter's clan; indeed, you too were born as one who committed sins day after day."
Furthermore, your body became a composite of male limbs, entirely covered by foul-smelling beings and serpents;
you had no friend, no son, no kinsman, no father, and neither sister nor mother was there to support you when you were thus accursed.
O Lord of the Earth, this woman, who was most beloved and ever devoted to you, turned her face away from you;
at one time, a most terrible drought occurred there for the sake of food.
Then, afflicted by hunger, he could not obtain any grain, fruit, meat, or other provisions.
Then he beheld a great lake, rich with lotuses and its banks surrounded by mud;
taking many lotuses from there, he went to the city named Vaidiśa.

Because you could not obtain their value, the entire city was traversed by you for the whole day; no buyer at all arose for the lotuses, and you became utterly exhausted and tormented by hunger. *Matsya Purāṇa* 100.15.
Seated alone with your wife in the courtyard of your palace,
you then heard a great sound of auspicious music during the night.
Accompanied by his wife, he went to where that auspicious sound arose;
there, in the center of the pavilion, he beheld the image of Viṣṇu.
The courtesan named Anaṅgavatī performed the Vibhūti-dvādaśī vow;
at its conclusion, she offered an excellent mountain of salt during the month of Māgha.
Having adorned Hṛṣīkeśa with a golden celestial tree, she offered it to her guru along with a bed provided with all necessary furnishings.
Upon seeing her, the two of them then reflected thus:
"What need have we for these lotuses? It would be better to adorn Viṣṇu with them."
Thus, O King, devotion arose at that time between the husband and wife;
through that connection, having worshipped Keśava as a mountain of salt, they honored the bed and the ground on all sides with heaps of flowers. (Matsya Purāṇa 100.21)
Then Anaṅgavatī, being pleased, commanded that three hundred pieces of gold and three hundred pieces of silver be given to them.
Because they were focused on many other beings, the two of them did not accept it;
however, Anaṅgavatī brought four kinds of food for them and said, "O King, let this be eaten. (MatsP 100.23)
"But even that has been renounced by us both; O fair-faced one, we shall indeed eat.
Through this incidental fasting of yours today, there will be happiness for us both."
"O you of firm vows, from birth these two have been most sinful and performers of evil deeds;
yet, O sinless one, through association with them, a small portion of dharma has remained within you. (Matsya Purāṇa 100.25)
Thus, they observed the vigil together, engaged in that very practice;
and at dawn, the bed along with the mountain of salt was bestowed.
Twelve villages, along with garments, ornaments, cows, and water-pots, should be given with devotion to the preceptor among the Brahmins.
And the food was shared equally with friends, companions, the poor, the blind, and the wretched;
and after honoring that hunter couple, they were dismissed.
O Lord of Men, that venerable one was born as a hunter together with his wife,
due to that heap of lotuses and not from the worship of Keśava.
O King, because of the greatness of that being, your entire sin has been destroyed and your palace at Puṣkara has been restored by means of little austerity.
O King of kings, Janārdana, appearing in the form of Brahmā with four faces, was born at his own will; the Lord of the World was well-pleased with you.
That courtesan Anaṅgavatī has now become the wife of Kāmadeva;
she has become a co-wife of Rati, who is known as Prīti,
the one who generates joy in the worlds and is worshipped by all the immortals.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, having abandoned that Puṣkara on the surface of the earth,
take refuge on the bank of the Gaṅgā and observe the Vibhūti-dvādaśī vow; O Indra among kings, you will certainly attain liberation.
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, that sage vanished right there;
and King Puṣpavāhana performed everything exactly as he had been instructed.
O Brahmin, one who practices this should observe the vow unbroken;
O Sage, one should somehow or other perform twelve Dvādaśīs with lotuses.
O sinless one, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins according to one's capacity;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for Keśava is pleased by devotion alone.
Thus, he who here reads or listens with devotion to this [work] which shatters the three-fold impurities of people,
and even grants his mind [to it], shall dwell in the world of the gods for hundreds of millions of years.
(Matsya-Purāṇa 100.37)
Nandikeśvara said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Vrata-Ṣaṣṭhī,
which was proclaimed by Rudra, divine, and the destroyer of great sins.
Having performed this for a year by night, one should give a golden discus and trident, along with two garments, to a Brahmin who maintains a household together with a cow.
Thereupon, having become Śiva himself, he rejoices in the world of Śiva along with us;
this is known as Devavrata, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
He who, for one year while eating but a single meal a day, gives a golden bull together with a cow made of sesame seeds to Śiva, goes to the abode of Śaṅkara;
this is known as the Rudra-vrata, which destroys both sin and sorrow. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.4)
He who, eating only on alternate nights, offers a golden blue lotus together with a vessel of sugar at the end of the year, accompanied by a bull,
attains the station of Viṣṇu; this is known as the Līlā-vrata.
During the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should avoid anointing his body with oil;
by giving food and utensils as a gift, he goes to the abode of Hari.
This vow, which brings joy to people and to men, is here called the Prīti-vrata. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.6)
Having avoided honey during the month of Madhu, he who gives curd, milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice,
along with fine garments and vessels filled with flavorful liquids, [attains great merit].
Having worshipped a Brahmin couple with the thought, "May Gaurī be pleased with me," this is known as the Gaurī-vrata, which bestows the world of Bhavānī.

He who, having observed the *nakta* fast on the thirteenth day of the month of Puṣya and again in the spring, should give a golden *aśoka* tree ten fingers in height, joined with sugarcane; ||| MatsP_101.9 ||| He shall dwell for twelve years in the abode of Kubera, surrounded by celestial nymphs, and at the end of that time, he shall attain the world of Brahmā. ||| MatsP_101.10 ||| Having performed this rite, one should give a golden *aśoka* tree, ten fingers in height, together with sugarcane, to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas. ||| MatsP_101.11 ||| By giving it according to the prescribed rule, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice; by giving it during the month of Caitra, one attains the world of the Apsarases. ||| MatsP_101.12 ||| One who gives a golden *aśoka* tree, ten fingers in height, together with sugarcane, to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, attains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. ||| MatsP_101.13 ||| By giving it during the month of Caitra, one attains the world of the Apsarases; by giving it during the month of Vaiśākha, one attains the world of the Sun. ||| MatsP_101.14 ||| By giving it during the month of Jyeṣṭha, one attains the world of Indra; by giving it during the month of Āṣāḍha, one attains the world of the Moon. ||| MatsP_101.15 ||| By giving it during the month of Śrāvaṇa, one attains the world of Varuṇa; by giving it during the month of Bhādrapada, one attains the world of Yama. ||| MatsP_101.16 ||| By giving it during the month of Āśvina, one attains the world of Vāyu; by giving it during the month of Kārttika, one attains the world of Agni. ||| MatsP_101.17 ||| By giving it during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one attains the world of Soma; by giving it during the month of Pauṣa, one attains the world of Viṣṇu. ||| MatsP_101.18 ||| By giving it during the month of Māgha, one attains the world of Rudra; by giving it during the month of Phālguna, one attains the world of Brahmā. ||| MatsP_101.19 ||| Thus, O best of Brāhmaṇas, I have described to you the entire procedure for the gift of the *aśoka* tree, which grants all desires. ||| MatsP_101.20 ||| One should give a golden *aśoka* tree, ten fingers in height, together with sugarcane, to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, according to the prescribed rule. ||| MatsP_101.21 ||| By giving it during the month of Caitra, one attains the world of the Apsarases; by giving it during the month of Vaiśākha, one attains the world of the Sun. ||| MatsP_101.22 ||| By giving it during the month of Jyeṣṭha, one attains the world of Indra; by giving it during the month of Āṣāḍha, one attains the world of the Moon. ||| MatsP_101.23 ||| By giving it during the month of Śrāvaṇa, one attains the world of Varuṇa; by giving it during the month of Bhādrapada, one attains the world of Yama. ||| MatsP_101.24 ||| By giving it during the month of Āśvina, one attains the world of Vāyu; by giving it during the month of Kārttika, one attains the world of Agni. ||| MatsP_101.25 ||| By
Having given [a gift] together with a garment to a Brahmin, saying "May Pradyumna be pleased," and remaining for a Kalpa at Viṣṇupada, a man shall become free from sorrow;
this is known as the Kāmavrata, which always destroys grief. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.10)
He who observes the vow beginning in Āṣāḍha should avoid cutting his nails and eating eggplant for four months, while providing jars filled with honey and clarified butter.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should present that golden [image] to a Brāhmaṇa;
he attains the world of Rudra—this is remembered as the Śiva-vrata.

He who avoids flowers during the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, and offers three flowers on the full moon of Phālguna, as well as gold according to his capacity, [attains the fruit]. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.13)
One should give [offerings] at the two periods of the day; may Śiva and Keśava be pleased.
Having given, one goes to the supreme state; this is known as the Saumya-vrata.
He who avoids salt on the third lunar day beginning with Phālguna,
at the conclusion of the vow, should give a bed and a house furnished with household utensils.
Having worshipped a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Bhavānī be pleased," one shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; this is called the Saubhāgya-vrata.
Then, having observed silence during the twilight, at the conclusion of the rite, he should present a jar of ghee, a pair of garments, sesame seeds, and a bell to a Brāhmaṇa. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.17)
One goes to the station of Sarasvatī, from which return is difficult to obtain;
this is known as Sārasvata, the bestower of beauty and knowledge. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.18)
Having worshipped Lakṣmī on the fifth lunar day, a man should observe a fast;
at the end of the year, he should give a golden lotus together with a cow.
He indeed becomes endowed with prosperity in birth after birth and attains the station of Viṣṇu;
this is the vow named Sampad, which eternally destroys all evil.
Having performed the smearing [of the ground] before Śambhu and Keśava,
one should further give a cow together with a water-pitcher for as long as a year.
For ten thousand births he shall be a king, and thereafter he shall go to the city of Śiva;
this is known as the Āyurvrata, which bestows all desires.
Having bowed down to the Aśvattha tree, the Sun, and the Gaṅgā in one place, a man, restrained in speech and free from envy, should observe a single meal a day for one year. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.23)
At the conclusion of the vow, one should honor a Brahmin couple accompanied by three cows and give a golden tree; he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
This is known as the Kīrtivratam, which bestows the fruits of prosperity and fame. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.24)
One should perform a ceremonial bath with clarified butter for either Śambhu or Keśava,
having prepared a circle of cow dung adorned with unbroken grains and beautiful flowers.

At the end of the year, one should give a golden lotus eight finger-breadths in size, accompanied by a sesame-cow; such a person is honored in the world of Śiva. This is then called the Sāma-vrata, intended for a singer of the Sāman hymns.
On the ninth day, having observed a single meal and having fed young girls according to one's ability, one should offer them a seat, a golden garment, and a cloth.
By giving a golden lion to a Brahmin, one shall go to the abode of Śiva;
for ten million births he shall be handsome and unconquered by enemies.
This is known as the Vīra-vrata, which bestows happiness upon women as well. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.28)
He who observes the milk-vow for fifteen years,
and at the conclusion of those years performs a *śrāddha* ceremony, should give five milch cows as a gift.
He who gives ochre-colored garments along with water-jars goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu and delivers a hundred ancestors;
at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings— this is remembered as the Pitṛvrata.
For four months beginning with Caitra, one should give water unasked;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-jar accompanied by food and clothing.
One who offers a vessel of sesame seeds and gold is honored in the world of Brahmā;
at the end of the kalpa, he certainly becomes a lord of the earth—this is declared to be the Ānanda-vrata.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of the Lord with the five nectars for one year,
at the end of the year, he should indeed again present a cow along with the five nectars.
By giving a conch shell to a Brahmin, one attains the state of Śaṅkara;
at the end of the kalpa, he becomes a king—this is remembered as the vow of steadfastness.
Having avoided meat throughout the year, a man should become a giver of a cow at the end of the year;
likewise, he should give a golden deer, and he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
This is called the vow of non-violence (ahiṃsā-vrata); by it, one becomes a lord of the earth at the end of a kalpa.
Having performed an ablution at dawn during the month of Māgha, one should honor a married couple by feeding them according to one's ability and adorning them with garlands, garments, and ornaments;
such a person shall dwell in the world of the Sun for a kalpa. This is known as the Sūryavrata. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.36)
During the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should bathe in the morning;
he should provide food for Brahmins and become a giver of cows on the full moon day of Kārttika.
He indeed goes to the station of Viṣṇu; this is the auspicious vow of Viṣṇu. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.37)
From one solstice until the next, one should avoid flowers and clarified butter;
at the end of that period, however, one should offer garlands of flowers together with a cow made of ghee.
Having given ghee and milk-rice to a Brahmin, one shall go to the state of Śiva;
this is called the vow of good conduct (*śīlavrata*), which bestows the fruits of virtue and health. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.39)
He who provides a lamp at the twilight hours should avoid using oil for a year;
at the end of that year, he should offer a lamp along with a golden discus and trident.
By giving a pair of garments to a Brahmin, one becomes radiant in this world and attains the realm of Rudra; this is known as the Dīptivrata.

Having consumed cow’s urine and barley-gruel on the third lunar day beginning with Kārttikī, one should observe the *nakta* fast for one year; at the end of the year, one should become a donor of cows. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.42)
One shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth;
this is known as the Rudra-vrata, which always brings about auspiciousness. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.43)
One should avoid perfumes and ointments during the month of Caitra; yet,
by giving a conch shell filled with fragrance and two white garments to a Brahmin,
one attains the realm of Varuṇa— this is remembered as a firm vow.
Having avoided flower-salt in the month of Vaiśākha and then become a giver of cows, one remains in the abode of Viṣṇu for a kalpa and becomes a king here on earth;
this is known as the Kānti-vrata, which bestows the fruits of beauty and fame. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.45)
Having fashioned a golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) together with a heap of sesame seeds,
one should become a donor of sesame for three days, having satiated the fire along with the twice-born (brāhmaṇas).
Having honored a Brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments, according to one's means, [one should say]:
"May the Soul of the Universe be pleased," provided it is at least three palas [in weight].
On an auspicious day, he who gives [this gift] attains the Supreme Brahman and is not born again;
this is known as the Brahma-vrata, which bestows the state of Nirvana. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.48)
He who gives a cow with two faces accompanied by abundant gold, and observes a vow of consuming only milk for one day, goes to the supreme state;
this is known as the *Dhenuvrata*, from which rebirth is difficult to attain. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.49)
Having observed the vow of subsisting on milk for three days, and having given a golden wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) weighing more than a pala,
along with rice according to one's capacity,
one goes to the abode of Brahmā; this is known as the Kalpa-vrata.
He who, having fasted for a month, gives a beautiful cow to a Brahmin attains the station of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Bhīmavrata.
Having fashioned a golden image of the earth weighing more than twenty palas, one should give it away;
by remaining for a day under a vow of subsisting on milk, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
This is declared to be the Dharāvratam, which follows one through seven hundred kalpas. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.52)
In the month of Māgha or Caitra, one should become a donor of a cow made of jaggery;
by observing the vow of jaggery on the third lunar day, one is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
This is known as the "Great Vow" (Mahāvrata), which brings about supreme bliss. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.53)
He who, fasting for a fortnight, gives two tawny cows to a Brahmin,
attains the world of Brahmā, which is well-honored by gods and asuras;
at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings— this is remembered as the Prabhāvrata.
One who eats only one meal a day for a year and gives food and a jar of water shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa; this is known as the Prāpti-vrata.
One who eats only at night on the eighth lunar days and gives a cow at the end of the year goes to the city of Indra;
this is called the Sugati-vrata.
He who gives fuel to a Brahmin during the four seasons beginning with the rainy season, and at the end gives a cow of clarified butter, goes to the Supreme Brahman;
this is the vow known as Vaiśvānara, which destroys all sins. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.57)
He who, eating only at night on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), should offer a discus,
shall at the end of the year obtain a golden image of Viṣṇu and reach the abode of Viṣṇu;
this is known as the Kṛṣṇa-vrata, by which one becomes a partaker of sovereignty at the end of the kalpa.
At the end of the year, one who has subsisted on milk-rice should give a pair of cows to a Brahmin;
he attains the world of Lakṣmī, for this is known as the Devī-vrata.
On the seventh lunar day, one should eat only at night and, at the conclusion of the year, give a milch cow;
one attains the world of the Sun—this is known as the Bhānu-vrata.
On the fourth lunar day, one who eats only at night should, at the end of the year, give a golden elephant;
this vow, named Vaināyaka, bestows the fruit of the world of Śiva. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.61)
He who, having renounced great fruits for four months,
should give golden ones together with a pair of cows to a twice-born man in the month of Kārttika—
this is called the *Phalavrata*, which bestows the fruit of the world of Viṣṇu.
And he who, fasting on the seventh day at the end of the year, should give a golden lotus and cows according to his ability, together with a vessel of gold and food—
this is known as the Saura-vrata, which bestows the fruit of the world of the Sun. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.63)
The man who, having completed twelve twelfth days (dvādaśīs) by means of fasting,
honors Brahmins with gifts of cows, clothing, and gold according to his capacity,
attains the supreme state; this is remembered as the Viṣṇu-vrata.
Having performed the ritual release of a bull on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should observe the practice of eating only at night;
this is remembered as the annual vow that leads to the attainment of the state of Śiva.
At the conclusion of the Kṛcchra penance, the giver of a cow should provide a meal according to his ability;
he attains the state of Śaṅkara among the Brahmins. This is the Prājāpatya vow. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.66)
One who eats only at night on the fourteenth day and bestows wealth in cattle at the end of the year attains the state of Śiva; this is the Traiyambaka vow.
Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of ghee to a twice-born man;
they call this the "Ghee Vow," which bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā.
One who sleeps in the open air during the rainy season and subsists on the milk of a milch cow at its end shall dwell eternally in the world of Śakra; this is known as the Indra-vrata.

The man who, on the third lunar day, eats food that has not been cooked by fire and gives a cow as a gift, goes to Śiva from whom a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to obtain; this vow is remembered as one that produces bliss for men in this world and leads to their ultimate welfare. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.70)
Having fasted, one who gives a golden chariot weighing more than two *palas* and yoked with a pair of horses shall dwell in heaven for a hundred *kalpas*;
at the end of the *kalpa*, he shall become a king of kings— this is remembered as the "Horse Vow" (*aśvavrata*).
In the same way, a man should give a golden chariot yoked with two elephants;
having fasted, he shall dwell in Satyaloka for a kalpa and then become a sovereign of the earth. This is remembered as the Karivrata.
Having completed the fast, one should become a giver of cows at the conclusion of the year;
one attains lordship over the Yakṣas—this is remembered as the Sukha-vrata.
Having stayed in the water during the night, one should become a giver of a cow at dawn;
he attains the world of Varuṇa—this is called the Varuṇa-vrata.
And he who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow should offer a golden moon;
this is declared to be the Candra-vrata, which bestows the fruit of the lunar world.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who practices the penance of the five fires in the evening and gifts a golden cow goes to heaven;
this is remembered as the Rudra-vrata on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
On the third lunar day, one should perform a single canopy in a temple of Śiva;
at the end of the year, the giver of a cow attains [the goal]; this is called the Bhavānī-vrata.
In the month of Māgha, one should wear wet clothes at night; on the seventh lunar day, one should be a giver of cows.
Having dwelt in heaven for a kalpa, one shall become a king here on earth; this is the Pavana vow.
Having fasted for three nights, one should give a beautiful mansion on the full moon day of Phālguna;
one attains the world of the Sun—this is known as the Dhāma-vrata.

By worshipping a married couple at the three junctions of the day while fasting and adorning them with ornaments, one obtains food, cattle, and liberation from this world through the Indravrata. (MatsP 101.80)
Having given a vessel of salt to a Brahmin on the second day of the bright fortnight, one who gives a cow at the end of the year goes to the abode of Śiva;
at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings—this is remembered as the Soma-vrata. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.81)
Having observed the vow of eating only one meal a day, he who gives a tawny cow at the conclusion of the year attains the station of Vaiśvānara; this is remembered as the Śiva-vrata.
On the tenth day, one should eat only a single meal, and at the conclusion of the vow, one should give ten cows.
One should also present the quarters of the world made of gold; such a person becomes the lord of the Brahmāṇḍa.
This is known as the Viśva-vrata, which destroys even the greatest sins. (Matsya Purāṇa 101.83)
Whoever should read or even hear this unsurpassed "Sixty Vows" shall become the lord of the Gandharvas for a hundred Manvantaras.

O Nārada, this meritorious Ṣaṣṭhīvratam, which benefits all people, has been described to you; I shall now proclaim another that you wish to hear. For what indeed remains unsaid among those things that are dear? 101.85.
Matsya Purāṇa 102.
Nandikeśvara said: "Purity and the purification of one's inner disposition do not exist without bathing."
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, bathing is prescribed at the outset.
One should perform the ritual bath with water that has either been drawn out or not drawn out;
the wise knower of mantras should designate the sacred site (*tīrtha*) using the root mantra.
"Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" is declared to be the root mantra. (Matsya Purāṇa 102.2)
With *darbha* grass in hand, having sipped water according to the rule, self-restrained and pure,
the wise man, having prepared a square area measuring four cubits on all sides, should invoke the Gaṅgā with these mantras: *matsp_102.3*
You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu; you belong to Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is your deity.
Protect us from that sin which begins at birth and ends with death. (Matsya Purāṇa 102.4)
"Three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrtha), O Jāhnavī, exist for you in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space," Vāyu declared.
Your name among the gods is indeed Nandinī, and also Nalinī;
you are Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Vihagā, Viśvakāyā, Amṛtā, and Śivā.
Vidyādharī, Supraśāntā, as well as Viśvaprasādinī,
Kṣemā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī.
One should recite these names of merit at the time of bathing;
there, the Gaṅgā that flows through the three paths becomes present.
Having consecrated water seven times with the mantra while joining the palms together, one should pour it over the head three, four, five, or seven times;
likewise, one should perform a bath with clay after addressing it according to the prescribed rule.
O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu;
O Clay, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me.
"You were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa, who has a hundred arms;
O Earth, you were granted by Brahmā and consecrated by Kaśyapa.
Having ascended upon my limbs, drive away all evil. (Matsya Purāṇa 102.11)
O Earth, grant us nourishment; everything is established upon you.
Homage to you, O you who are the source and the destroyer of all worlds, O lady of excellent vows! (Matsya Purāṇa 102.12)
Having bathed in this manner and thereafter performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules,
one should rise and put on two clean, white garments;
then, indeed, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the nourishment of the three worlds.
Gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
cruel serpents, suparṇas, trees, jackals, and birds.

Those living beings who have the wind as their support, those who have water as their support, those who move through space, those who are without support, and likewise those who are devoted to the Dharma— MatsP_102.15.
This water is given by me for their nourishment;
having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (kṛtopavītī), one should then offer it to the gods and subsequently wear it around the neck (nivītī).
One should satisfy humans with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the sages:
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana.
May Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha—
may they all always attain satisfaction through the water offered by me.

One should satisfy with water mixed with unbroken rice (akṣata) all the divine and brahminical sages: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. (Matsya Purāṇa 102.19)
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and bent the left knee to the ground:
"The Agniṣvātta, Saumya, Haviṣmat, and Uṣmapā [ancestors]..."
Likewise, the Sukālins, the Barhiṣads, and the other Vājyapas—
these ancestors should be gratified with devotion by means of water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste.
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.
"Salutations indeed to Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, Parameṣṭhin, Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta.
With darbha grass in hand, the wise man should satisfy the ancestors according to the prescribed rule. (Matsya Purāṇa 102.23)

Having gratified the ancestors and others by name and lineage, as well as the maternal grandfathers, according to the prescribed rule and with devotion, one should utter this mantra: Matsya Purāṇa 102.24.
May those who are not kinsmen, or those who were kinsmen in another birth,
as well as whoever desires [offerings] from us, all attain complete satisfaction.
Then, having sipped water according to the rule, one should draw a lotus in front;
with unbroken grains of rice accompanied by flowers, along with water and red sandalwood,
one should diligently offer the *arghya* oblation and recite the names of the Sun.
Salutations to you who have the form of Viṣṇu; salutations indeed to him whose face is Viṣṇu.
Salutations eternally to you, the thousand-rayed one, the embodiment of all splendor.
Salutations to you, O Śiva, Lord of All; salutations to you, O Compassionate One toward all.
Salutations be to you, O Sovereign of the World, adorned with divine sandalwood paste.
Obeisance to you in the lotus posture; obeisance to you adorned with earrings and armlets.
Obeisance to you, Lord of all worlds, who awakens the entire universe. *Matsya Purāṇa* 102.29.
O all-pervading one, you behold all good and evil deeds;
O God of Truth, homage be to you! Be gracious to me, O Bhāskara.

"O Divākara, homage be to you; O Prabhākara, homage be to you. Having thus paid obeisance to the Sun and having circumambulated him three times, and having touched a twice-born man, a cow, and gold, one should then proceed to the temple of Viṣṇu.
Matsya Purāṇa 103:
Nandikeśvara said:
Hereafter, I shall provide a detailed description of Prayāga.
That which was told by Mārkaṇḍeya in the past to the son of Pāṇḍu.
But when this had occurred in Bhārata and the son of Pṛthā had obtained the kingdom, in the meantime, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī— ||| MatsP_103.2 |||
Tormented by grief for his brother and reflecting upon it again and again,
King Suyodhana remained there as the commander of eleven armies.
Having tormented us many times, they have all gone to their destruction;
only five Pāṇḍavas remain, having taken refuge in Vāsudeva.
Having slain Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the mighty Karṇa,
as well as King Duryodhana together with his sons and brothers.
"All the kings have been slain, as well as all others who considered themselves heroes.
O Govinda, what use have we for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments, or even for life?"
Thinking, "Alas, what misery!", the king, overcome by dejection,
remained for a while motionless, devoid of energy, with his face cast downwards.
When the king regained consciousness, he reflected again and again:
"What is the proper application, what is the restraint, and what indeed is the sacred ford?"
By which I may quickly be released from the taint of great sins;
staying where, a man goes to the unsurpassed world of Viṣṇu.
How indeed shall I question Kṛṣṇa, by whom I have been brought to this state?
How shall I question Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose hundred sons have been slain?
"How can I question Vyāsa, by whom the destruction of my lineage was brought about?
Thus did Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira fall into despondency;
all the Pāṇḍavas wept, overwhelmed with grief for their brother.
And those great-souled ones who were gathered there, known as the Pāṇḍavas,
as well as Kuntī and Draupadī, and all those who had assembled there,
fell to the ground, weeping on every side.
In Vārāṇasī, Mārkaṇḍeya recognized Yudhiṣṭhira as he had fallen into a state of despondency, weeping and distressed.
In no long time at all, Mārkaṇḍeya, the great ascetic,
arrived at Hastināpura and stood at the king’s gate.
The gatekeeper, having seen him, quickly informed the king:
"This sage Mārkaṇḍeya stands at the door, desiring to see you. Thereupon, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) went to the door in haste. *Matsya Purāṇa* 103.15.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Welcome to you, O highly fortunate one; welcome to you, O great sage!
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my lineage has been delivered. (Matsya Purāṇa 103.16)
"O great sage, my ancestors are pleased today that you have been seen by me;
today my body is purified because of this vision of you. (Matsya Purāṇa 103.17)
Nandikeśvara said:
Having seated him upon the throne, the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira indeed honored that sage with the washing of his feet, worship, and other rites. *Matsya Purāṇa* 103.18.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya, being pleased and honored, said to that king:
"Tell me quickly, O King, for what reason were you weeping?
By what have you been overcome with distress? What is your affliction, and what is unpleasant to you? (Matsya Purāṇa 103.19)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, having learned all that occurred regarding our kingdom, you have fallen under the sway of anxiety."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed King, to that which is established in the duty of a Kṣatriya:
no evil is ever seen in a wise man while he is fighting in battle. (Matsya Purāṇa 103.21)
How much more so for a Kṣatriya, especially one following the duties of a king? Therefore, having made this firm in your heart, you should not contemplate evil.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, endowed with humility, bowed his head to the sage and asked about that which destroys all sins. (Matsya Purāṇa 103.23)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I ask you, O one of great wisdom, who constantly beholds the three worlds:
tell me in brief that by which one may be liberated from sin.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O mighty-armed king, to the account of the journey to Prayāga, which destroys all sins and is the most excellent for men of meritorious deeds.
Matsya Purāṇa 104:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear how things existed in the previous kalpa."
O Sage, it was related exactly as it is by Brahmā, the chief of the gods.
How do men travel to Prayāga, and what is it like there?
What is the destination for those who die there, and what is the fruit for those who bathe there? (Matsya Purāṇa 104.2)
Tell me, what is the fruit for those who dwell at Prayāga?
Explain all of this to me, for my curiosity is great. (Matsya Purāṇa 104.3)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O child, I shall tell you that which is most excellent therein and its fruit,
for it was heard by me in the past as it was being recounted to all the brahmins."
From Prayāga as far as the abode of Vāsuki’s lake,
including the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara and the Nāga Bahumūlaka—
this is the field of Prajāpati, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not subject to rebirth;
thereafter, the gods beginning with Brahmā assemble and provide protection.
And there are many other auspicious holy sites that remove all sins;
they cannot be fully described, O King, even in hundreds of years.
Nevertheless, I shall speak of the glorification of Prayāga in brief.
Sixty thousand bow-lengths protect the Jāhnavī;
the Sun, whose vehicle consists of seven horses, always protects the Yamunā.
Vāsava always protects Prayāga in particular,
while Hari, joined by the deities, protects the entire region.
Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, always protects that banyan tree;
indeed, the gods protect this auspicious place which removes all sins.
Enshrouded by unrighteousness, the world does not reach that state.
O lord of men, when your sin becomes very slight or even minuscule,
it all goes to destruction for one who remembers Prayāga.
By seeing that sacred ford (tīrtha), by even chanting its name,
or by touching its clay, a person is liberated from sin.
O Indra among kings, there are five pools, and in their midst flows the Jāhnavī;
at the entrance of Prayāga, sin is destroyed in that very instant.
Even a man who has committed evil deeds attains the supreme goal by remembering the Gaṅgā from as far as thousands of yojanas away. (Matsya Purāṇa 104.14)
By chanting its praises one is released from sin; by seeing it, one beholds auspicious things;
and by bathing in it and drinking its water, one purifies one's lineage unto the seventh generation.
Truthful in speech, having conquered anger, established in non-violence,
following the Dharma, knowing the reality, and devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
One who bathes between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is liberated from sin;
contemplating his desires in his mind, he obtains them in great abundance.
Then, having gone to Prayāga, which is protected by all the gods,
one should dwell there for a month practicing celibacy and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
thus, one obtains all desired objects wherever one is born.
The goddess Yamunā, the daughter of Tapa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
that highly fortunate river arrived there;
and there the god Maheśvara himself is eternally present.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Prayāga is a meritorious place difficult for humans to reach; yet having touched its waters, O Indra among kings,
the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas,
and cāraṇas dwell in the heavenly world.
Matsya Purāṇa 105:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga."
Having heard which, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
Prayāga is indeed declared to be the refuge for those who are distressed, impoverished, and resolute in their purpose; however, it must never be disclosed [to others].
Whether a man be afflicted by disease, distressed, or even aged,
he who gives up his life between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā [attains the highest goal].
With celestial chariots possessing the luster of blazing gold and resembling the sun,
that man sports in heaven amidst the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The preeminent sages declare that he obtains his desired objects;
he rejoices amidst auspicious signs, surrounded by excellent women and divine palaces made of every kind of jewel and filled with various banners.
Awakened by the sounds of singing and musical instruments,
he remains honored in heaven for as long as he does not remember his former birth.
Then, fallen from heaven, his merit exhausted and descended from the celestial realm,
he is born into a prosperous family filled with gold and jewels;
he remembers that very sacred site (tīrtha), and by that remembrance, he goes there.
Whether staying in one's own country, in the forest, in a foreign land, or at home,
whoever gives up their life while even merely remembering Prayāga attains the world of Brahmā; so say the preeminent sages.
In that world where the earth is made of gold and the trees bear the fruit of all desires,
he goes to that realm where ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas dwell.
Surrounded by thousands of women on the beautiful and auspicious bank of the Mandākinī,
he rejoices together with the sages through his well-performed deeds in this world.
He is worshipped in heaven by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and the deities;
then, having descended from that heavenly realm, he becomes the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
Then, by reflecting again and again upon auspicious deeds, one becomes virtuous and endowed with wealth in this world; of this there is no doubt.
Established in dharma and truth through action, mind, and speech,
he who bestows a cow between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā [attains great merit].
Whether it be gold, jewels, pearls, or any other possession,
if one uses them for one's own purpose, for ancestral rites, or even for the worship of the deities,
that sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes fruitful for him, and he shall duly obtain its merit.
Thus, a twice-born man should not accept gifts at sacred fords, in holy shrines, or at any such auspicious occasions; indeed, he should remain vigilant in all such matters.
He who gives away a milch cow that is tawny or pale-red in color, with horns tipped in gold, hooves in silver, a bronze milking vessel, and full of milk; MatsP_105.16 //

At Prayāga, having duly caused a learned Śrotriya—one who wears white garments, is tranquil, knows the Dharma, and has mastered the Vedas—to accept [the gift], [one should perform the rite]. *Matsya Purāṇa* 105.17.
That cow should be given to him at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
along with costly garments and various kinds of jewels.
O best of beings, for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on the body of that cow, one is honored in the heavenly world.
The cow in which he takes birth becomes his own;
by that deed, he does not behold that terrible hell,
but having reached the Northern Kurus, he rejoices for an imperishable time.
One should give a single milch cow in exchange for hundreds of thousands of cows;
such a single cow can deliver one's sons, wives, and servants. (Matsya Purāṇa 105.21)
Therefore, among all gifts, the gift of a cow is preeminent;

in a place that is difficult to traverse, treacherous, terrible, and the source of great sins, the cow alone provides protection. For this reason, she should be given to the most excellent of the twice-born.
Matsya Purāṇa 106:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In whatever manner you describe the majesty of Prayāga,"
In that very manner, I shall be liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
"O Blessed One, by what rite should those who have reached certainty in the Dharma proceed? O Great Sage, tell me that rite which has been prescribed for Prayāga."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, I shall describe to you the sequence of the rules for pilgrimage according to this rishi-ordained method, exactly as it was seen and heard.
Listen also to the fruit obtained by that man who, desiring to go on a pilgrimage to the sacred site of Prayāga, travels somewhere while mounted upon a bull. *Matsya Purāṇa* 106.4.
Indeed, that man becomes a fierce jackal dwelling in a terrible hell;
moreover, his ancestors do not accept the water offerings.
But he who would bathe his sons and young children, and likewise feed them,
should cause all such gifts to be given to Brahmins just as he would for himself.
If a man should go by vehicle out of greed for power or out of delusion, all that [merit] of his becomes fruitless; therefore, one should avoid using a vehicle.
He who gives his daughter in marriage according to the Ārṣa rite, as far as his means permit, in the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā; ||| MatsP_106.8 |||
By that deed, he does not see that terrible hell;
having gone to the Northern Kurus, he rejoices for an imperishable time.
He obtains sons and wives who are righteous and endowed with beauty.
In that place, one should perform acts of charity according to the extent of one's wealth;
by doing so, the fruit of the sacred ford increases, of this there is no doubt.
O Indra among kings, he shall abide in heaven until the dissolution of all beings.
He who, having reached the foot of a banyan tree, gives up his life,
transcends all worlds and goes to the world of Rudra.
There, those twelve Ādityas, supported by the Rudras, scorch;
they burn the entire world, yet the root of the banyan tree is not burned.
When the world has become a single ocean with the moon, sun, and earth destroyed,
Viṣṇu remains there indeed, performing sacrifices again and again.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas,
and cāraṇas always frequent that sacred ford at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to Prayāga while offering praise,
where Brahmā and the other gods, the ṛṣis, the siddhas, and the cāraṇas reside.
The world-protectors, the Sādhyas, and the ancestors esteemed by the world,
as well as the supreme ṛṣis headed by Sanatkumāra.
Likewise, the other celestial rishis headed by Aṅgiras, as well as the Nāgas, the Suparṇas, and those Siddhas who move through the sky; MatsP_106.17.
The oceans, rivers, mountains, nāgas, and vidyādharas,
as well as Hari accompanied by the Lord Prajāpati, were present there.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, O tiger among kings, the middle of the earth is known as Prayāga, renowned throughout the three worlds;
there is nothing more meritorious than that in the three worlds, O Bhārata. (Matsya Purāṇa 106.19)
By hearing of that sacred ford, by the mere chanting of its name,
or even by touching its clay, a person is liberated from sin.
Whoever, firm in their vows, performs an ablution there at the confluence,
obtains a fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
O dear one, your mind should not be turned away from going to Prayāga, neither by the words of the gods nor by the words of the world.
Ten thousand holy fords (tīrtha) and sixty crores of others— O descendant of Kuru, their presence is found right here.
The same destination that belongs to the wise man established in truth and disciplined in yoga is attained by one who gives up their life at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who have not reached Prayāga do not truly live in this world; they are cheated throughout the three worlds. (Matsya Purāṇa 106.25)
Having thus beheld that sacred ford, Prayāga, the supreme station,
one is liberated from all sins, just as the moon is freed from Rāhu.
At Vipula on the bank of the Yamunā are the two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara;
having bathed and drunk there, one is liberated from all sins.
Having gone there to the famous abode of Mahādeva,
a man delivers all ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Having performed the consecration, that man shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
he attains the heavenly world for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
On the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā, O Bhārata, there are the well-known Sāmudrakūpa and Pratiṣṭhāna, renowned throughout the three worlds.
If one who observes celibacy and has conquered anger stands for three nights,
his soul purified of all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
To the north of Pratiṣṭhāna and to the east of the Bhāgīrathī is the tīrtha named Haṃsaprapatana, renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Bhārata, by merely bathing there, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
for as long as the moon and the sun endure, so long is one glorified in heaven.
Listen also to the fruit obtained by one who gives up their life in the holy and vast Urvashiramana, which is as white as a swan.
O lord of men, for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years, he dwells in the heavenly world together with his ancestors.
O best of men, one shall always behold Urvaśī in the heavenly world;
O son, he is constantly honored by the ṛṣis, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Then, having fallen from heaven and descended from the celestial realm with his merit exhausted,
he obtains a hundred maidens who resemble Urvaśī.
He shall become the husband of many thousands of women in their midst,
and he shall be a lord of the earth, the enjoyer of ten thousand villages.
Awakened by the sound of girdles and anklets,
he enjoys vast pleasures and then returns once more to that sacred ford.
Constantly wearing white garments, self-restrained and with senses controlled,
one who eats but once a day for a month shall become a lord of the earth.
He obtains a hundred women adorned with golden ornaments and becomes a great lord of the earth upon this world as far as the oceans. (Matsya Purāṇa 106.41)
Endowed with wealth and grain, he becomes a constant giver;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, he attains that sacred ford once again.
Then, at the beautiful Sandhyāvatī, a student of sacred knowledge who has conquered his senses,
being pure and fasting, shall attain the world of Brahmā by performing the twilight devotions.
Whoever reaches Koṭitīrtha and gives up their life there is honored in the heavenly world for ten million thousand years.
Then, having fallen from heaven and descended from the celestial realm when his karma is exhausted,
he shall be born handsome in a family rich in gold, gems, and pearls.
Then, having gone to Bhogavatī, to the north of Vāsuki,
there shall be another sacred ford (tīrtha) named Daśāśvamedhaka.
A man who has performed the consecration shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
he becomes wealthy, handsome, capable, charitable, and righteous.
Whatever merit is found in the four Vedas, whatever merit is found in those who speak the truth,
and whatever dharma exists in non-violence— all that fruit is obtained simply by going [on pilgrimage].
The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever she is plunged into;
she is ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra where she meets the Vindhya.
Where the highly blessed Gaṅgā flows with its many holy fords and those whose wealth is asceticism, that place should be known as a field of perfection; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
She delivers mortals on earth, she delivers even the nāgas below, and she delivers the gods in heaven; for that reason, she is known as the "Three-pathed River" (Tripathagā).
As long as the bones of an embodied being remain in the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he shall become the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
[There is] the supreme among holy places (tīrthas) and the great river among rivers;
it bestows liberation upon all beings, even those who have committed great sins. (Matsya Purāṇa 106.53)
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, yet she is difficult to attain at three specific places:
at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having bathed there, they go to heaven; those who die there are not born again.
For all beings whose minds are afflicted by sin and who are seeking a refuge,
there is no destination equal to the Gaṅgā.
She is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things;
fallen from the head of Maheśvara, she is the auspicious remover of all sins.
In the Kṛta age, the sacred field of Naimiṣa is supreme; in the Tretā, Puṣkara;
in the Dvāpara, Kurukṣetra; but in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā is distinguished as the best.
One should resort to the Gaṅgā, and especially to Prayāga;
O King, in this terrible Kali age, no other remedy exists.
Matsya Purāṇa 107:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga."
Having heard which, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
There is a sacred ford named Mānasa on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā;
having fasted there for three nights, one shall obtain all desires. (Matsya Purāṇa 107.2)
Whatever fruit a man may obtain by the gift of cows, land, and gold, he obtains that same fruit simply by remembering that sacred ford again. (Matsya Purāṇa 107.3)
Whether without desire or with desire, whoever enters the Gaṅgā,
upon death attains heaven and does not see hell.
Awakened by the musical performances of hosts of apsarases,
he departs on a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes;
O Indra among kings, he enjoys heaven for many thousands of years.
Then, having fallen from heaven and descended from the celestial realm with his merit exhausted,
he is born into a vast family rich in gold, jewels, and pearls.
Sixty thousand sacred fords (tīrthas) and sixty crores of rivers will go to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā during the month of Māgha.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows,
that same fruit is obtained by bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
He who performs the Karṣāgni penance between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā shall indeed have no deficient limbs, be free from disease, and be endowed with all five senses. (Matsya Purāṇa 107.9)
As many as are the pores on the body of that embodied being,
for so many thousands of years is he honored in the heavenly world.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he shall become the lord of Jambūdvīpa;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, he remembers that sacred ford once again.
He who enters the water at the world-renowned confluence when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu shall be liberated from all sins.
He attains the world of Soma and rejoices together with Soma;
for sixty thousand years he is honored in the heavenly world. (Matsya Purāṇa 107.13)
And having fallen from this world of Śakra in heaven, which is frequented by gods, sages, and gandharvas,
O Indra among kings, he is born into a prosperous family.
But that man who, with his head downward and feet upward, drinks the flame, is honored in the heavenly world for hundreds of thousands of years. (Matsya Purāṇa 107.15)
O Indra among kings, that man who was an Agnihotrin, having fallen away from his state,
enjoys vast pleasures and then returns once more to that sacred ford.
