Listen now to the fruit that belongs even to him who, having cut up his own body, gives it to birds, and who is then devoured by those winged creatures. *Matsya Purāṇa* 107.17.
He is honored in the world of Soma for a hundred thousand years;
even when he falls from there, he becomes a righteous king.
Endowed with virtues, possessed of beauty, learned, and sweet-spoken,
he enjoys vast pleasures and then returns once more to that sacred ford.
On the northern bank of the Yamunā and to the south of Prayāga,
there is that supreme sacred site (tīrtha) known as Ṛṇapramocana.
Having stayed for one night and bathed there, one is liberated from all debts;
one attains the heavenly world and shall forever be free from debt. (Matsya Purāṇa 107.21)
Matsya Purāṇa 108:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Having heard this which has been proclaimed by you concerning Prayāga..."
Today my heart has become purified by the glorification of Prayāga.
O Blessed One, tell me what kind of fruit results from fasting unto death;
and what world does one attain who is purified of all sins?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, O Lord, to the fruit of fasting unto death at Prayāga;
a wise man who possesses faith and has conquered his senses attains it. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.3)
Even one who is not deficient in limb, is free from disease, and is endowed with the five senses,
gains the fruit of the horse sacrifice at every step as he proceeds.
O King, he shall deliver ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants;
he is liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme state. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.5)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, the great majesty of Dharma is indeed what you tell me;
by even a small effort, one attains many merits."
"By means of many horse-sacrifices performed here with excellent vows, [this is attained]. Cut through this doubt of mine, for my curiosity is indeed great. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.7)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O great hero, O King, to that which was spoken by the one born of Brahmā;
it was heard by me as it was being told previously in the presence of the ṛṣis.
The precinct of Prayāga extends five yojanas;
as soon as one enters that ground, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step.
A man who gives up his life saves all those seven past generations and fourteen future ones. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.10)
Knowing this, O Indra among kings, one should always be intent on service;
for those men who lack faith and whose minds are struck by sin do not reach that place, Prayāga, which is protected by the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
But for those who, out of affection or greed for wealth, have fallen under the sway of desire, how can they obtain the fruit of the sacred fords? How can there be the fruit of merit for them?
O Grandfather, tell me this: what is the fate of one who sells all kinds of goods, being ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done at Prayāga? *Matsya Purāṇa* 108.13.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, to this great secret that destroys all sins:
he who, with his senses restrained, should bathe at Prayāga for one month.
He is liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme state.
Now hear what the fruit is for those who betray trust at Prayāga:
one should bathe three times a day and subsist on alms;
after three months, he shall be liberated at Prayāga, without a doubt. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.15)
But he who, out of ignorance, undertakes a pilgrimage to sacred fords and the like in this world, becomes enriched with all his desires and is glorified in the heavenly realm;
he obtains an eternal abode, filled with wealth and grain. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.16)
Thus, one who is filled with knowledge always becomes a possessor of enjoyments;
by him, his fathers and great-grandfathers are delivered from hell.
O knower of truth, to you who follow the Dharma and inquire again and again,
I have fully explained this eternal secret for your benefit.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my lineage has been delivered.
O Sage, I am pleased and I am graced by the mere sight of you. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.19)
O righteous-souled one, by the sight of you I am indeed liberated from sin today;
O Blessed One, I now know myself to be cleansed of all impurity.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"By good fortune your birth has become fruitful; by good fortune your lineage has been delivered.
Through its recitation merit increases, and through hearing it, there is the destruction of sin."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O great sage, what is the merit of the Yamunā and what is its fruit?
Tell me all this exactly as it has been seen and heard.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The daughter of the Sun, the goddess renowned throughout the three worlds,
the highly fortunate Yamunā, is celebrated there as a river.
The Yamunā flows by the very same path as which the Gaṅgā has issued forth;
she destroys sin through her mere mention at a distance of thousands of yojanas.
Having bathed and drunk there at the Yamunā, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one gains merit by its glorification and beholds auspicious things upon seeing it. (Matsya Purāṇa 108.25)
Having bathed and drunk [the water] there, one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation;
he who gives up his life there attains the supreme goal.
The place known as Agnitīrtha is on the southern bank of the Yamunā;
to the west of Dharmarāja is the sacred site remembered as Naraka.
Having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not born again;
such are the thousands of sacred fords on the southern bank of the Yamunā.
To the north, I shall describe the sacred ford named Nirañjana belonging to the great-souled Āditya, where the gods together with Vāsava reside.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who indeed perform their twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) three times a day worship that sacred ford;
it is frequented by the gods and other divine beings.
Becoming devoted to faith, perform ablutions at sacred fords (tīrtha).
Many other sacred fords are also remembered as removing all sins;
having bathed in them, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
Both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are remembered as yielding equal fruits;
yet, solely by virtue of her seniority, the Gaṅgā is honored everywhere.
Act thus, O Kaunteya, to perform ablutions at all sacred fords;
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes in that very instant.
But he who, having risen at dawn, recites and hears this,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.
Matsya-Purāṇa 109:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"I have heard what was proclaimed by Brahmā in the Purāṇa concerning the origin of Brahmā."
Thousands, hundreds, and millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) are all meritorious and purifying, and are considered to grant the supreme goal.
Somatīrtha is greatly meritorious and the destroyer of great sins;
by merely bathing there, O King of kings, it delivers a hundred generations of men.
Therefore, one should perform a bath there with every possible effort. (Matsya Purāṇa 109.2)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Naimiṣa is sacred on earth, and Puṣkara is sacred in the intermediate space;
yet Kurukṣetra excels all three worlds."
Having abandoned all of those, why do you praise this one alone?
That which has been declared there is immeasurable, incredible, and unsurpassed.
Why do you praise the vast Dharma with such little effort, when there is the supreme divine state and enjoyments exactly as one desires?
Explain this doubt of mine according to what has been seen and heard. (Matsya Purāṇa 109.5)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should not speak what is unbelievable, even if it is something directly perceived,
to a man who lacks faith and whose mind is afflicted by sin.
For one who lacks faith, is impure, evil-minded, and has abandoned auspiciousness—all these are sinners; therefore, this which you have spoken was uttered by him.
Listen to the majesty of Prayāga exactly as it was seen and heard,
both directly perceived and indirectly known, and as it shall be set forth.
Just as other things are unseen, so too, having made the scripture— exactly as it was seen and heard—
the authoritative means of knowledge, one should apply oneself to yoga for the sake of the self.
Another person there may suffer and never attain yoga;
for men, yoga may be obtained only after thousands of other births.
Just as yoga may be attained by men through a thousand yogic practices,
so too does he who bestows all manner of jewels upon the Brāhmaṇas.
By that gift which has been given, a person does not attain union [with the divine];
however, for one who dies at Prayāga, all this comes to pass, and not otherwise.
I shall declare the primary cause; have faith in it, O Bhārata, so that Brahman may be seen everywhere within all beings. (Matsya Purāṇa 109.13)
Whatever exists in a Brāhmaṇa that is not of the nature of Brahman is said to be "non-Brāhmaṇic";
likewise, Brahman is worshipped everywhere within all beings.
Likewise, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a wise man should honor Prayāga among all the worlds; for the King of Tīrthas is truly honored, this is the very truth.
Even Brahmā constantly remembers Prayāga, the most excellent of sacred fords;
having reached the king of tīrthas, one need not seek anything else.
"For who, having attained the state of a god, would desire the state of a human?
By this very analogy, O Yudhiṣṭhira, you shall understand;
I have described it exactly as that which is most meritorious."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard what you have spoken, and I am struck with wonder again and again:
how is that attained through yoga, and how does residence in heaven come about through action?"
A donor indeed obtains enjoyments, as well as the cow which is the fruit of his action;
I ask about those actions by which the earth is further attained.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed King, to how one who performs what has been prescribed [attains] the earth, the cow, fire, the Brāhmaṇa, the scripture, gold, water, and women. *Matsya Purāṇa* 109.20.
"Prajāpati has declared that those lowest of men who revile their mother and father have no upward passage."
Thus, the attainment and abiding place of yoga is extremely difficult to reach;
yet those men who are doers of evil go to a terrible hell. *Matsya Purāṇa* 109.22.
He who steals an elephant, a horse, a cow, an ox, or gold such as jewels and pearls in the absence of the owner, and subsequently offers it as a gift; 109.23.
Those endowed with such actions do not go to heaven where the enjoyers dwell;
instead, they are cooked again in hell.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding yoga, dharma, and the giver—
whether it be true or false, whether it exists or does not exist—
I shall now proclaim their definitive explanation, just as the Sun himself declared it.
Matsya Purāṇa 110:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen once more, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga."
Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gotīrtha, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean.
Gaya, Caitraka, and indeed the confluence of the Ganges with the ocean—
these and many other meritorious mountain peaks.
"Ten thousand holy sites and thirty crores more are eternally situated at Prayāga; thus say the wise. (Matsya Purāṇa 110.3)
There are also three fire-pits, in the midst of which flows the Jāhnavī,
who has emerged from Prayāga and is honored by all sacred fords (tīrthas).
The daughter of Tapaṇa, the goddess Yamunā, renowned throughout the three worlds and the benefactress of the world, joined with the Gaṅgā.
O tiger among kings, the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is considered the hips of the earth; Prayāga is not worth even a sixteenth part of it.
Vāyu declared that there are three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrtha) in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space; all of that is known as the Jāhnavī.
Prayāga is the central seat, as are both Kambala and Aśvatara;
furthermore, this Bhogavatī is the sacrificial altar of Prajāpati.
There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Vedas and the sacrifices, having taken on embodied forms,
as well as the sages whose wealth is their austerity, wait upon Prajāpati.
The gods perform sacrifices with ritual rites, as do kings who bear the discus;
therefore, O Bhārata, there is nothing more meritorious than this in the three worlds.
O Lord, by its power it excels all other holy places;
ten thousand tīrthas and three crores more besides arise from it. (Matsya Purāṇa 110.11)
Wherever the highly blessed Gaṅgā flows, that region should be known as a place of asceticism,
a field of spiritual attainment, and endowed with the banks of the Gaṅgā.
One should understand this truth regarding the virtuous, oneself, friends, and the devoted disciple, and whisper it into their ear. (Matsya Purāṇa 110.13)
This is auspicious, this leads to heaven, this is truth, this is happiness;
this is merit, this is righteous, this is purifying, and the supreme dharma.
This secret of the great seers destroys all sins;
by studying it, even a twice-born man becomes stainless and attains heaven. (Matsya Purāṇa 110.15)
Whoever should constantly hear of this meritorious and eternally pure sacred site (tīrtha) attains the memory of past births and rejoices in the vault of heaven.
Those sacred fords are reached by the virtuous who follow the example of the wise;
bathe in the sacred fords, O Kauravya, and do not be of crooked mind.
O Lord, since you have questioned me properly, I have indeed related this to you:
all your fathers and likewise your grandfathers have been delivered.
Vows, charity, austerity, pilgrimage sites, all sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, yoga, Sāṃkhya, right conduct, and whatever other means for attaining knowledge there may be—
all these are not worth even a sixteenth part of Prayāga. (Matsya Purāṇa 110.19)

Thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, knowledge, yoga, and even the sacred ford (tīrtha) involve much affliction; yet by means of them, one attains the supreme goal. Knowledge arises at the three times of day, and one shall go to the heavenly world.
Matsya Purāṇa 111:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, how has all this regarding Prayāga been described?"
Tell us all of this, so that it may indeed deliver me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, for at Prayāga all this world is said to reside;
there dwell Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Īśāna—the imperishable Lord and the gods.
Brahmā creates all beings, both the stationary and the moving;
Viṣṇu, however, nourishes these very creatures in the world.
At the end of the kalpa, Rudra indeed withdraws that entire world;
yet at that time, the sacred site of Prayāga never perishes.
He who sees the Lord as the sovereign of all beings truly sees;
by this effort they abide [in Him] and attain the supreme goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me truly how this sacred tradition (śruti) remains established,
and for what reason the best of men remain [in their respective states].
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara dwell here at Prayāga.
I shall explain the reason for that; listen to the truth, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
The sacred precinct of Prayāga extends five yojanas;
deities remain there for its protection and to ward off evil deeds.
To the north of Pratiṣṭhāna, the Lord Brahmā resides in disguise;
there the Blessed One stands in the form of Veṇīmādhava.
The Supreme Lord, having become a banyan tree, remains as Māheśvara;
then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis,
constantly protect the maṇḍala to ward off evil deeds.
In that place, by offering oblations, one casts off one's own sin and does not behold hell;
thus Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are present at Prayāga.
The seven continents, the oceans,
and the mountains on the surface of the earth remain protecting [the world] until the dissolution of all beings.
And all those other many beings who remain there, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
they too have been fashioned by the three deities depending upon that earth.
"This field of Prajāpati is renowned as Prayāga;
it is indeed meritorious and purifying, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Rule your own kingdom, O Indra among kings, together with your brothers, O sinless one. (Matsya Purāṇa 111.14)
Matsya Purāṇa 112.
Nandikeśvara said:
Together with all his brothers and with his wife Draupadī...
Having paid homage to the Brahmins, he gratified his gurus and the gods.
Then Vāsudeva, Mādhava, also arrived at that very spot in an instant,
being honored by all the Pāṇḍavas together.
Together with Kṛṣṇa and all those high-souled ones,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was once again consecrated in his own kingdom.
In the meantime, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya,
having uttered "May it be well," returned to his hermitage in an instant.
The righteous Yudhiṣṭhira also lived together with his brothers;
then the high-minded son of Dharma, having bestowed great gifts, [departed].
The man who, having risen at dawn, recites this greatness and constantly remembers Prayāga, goes to the supreme state;
he is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Vāsudeva said:
"O great king, you must carry out my word as I speak it:
free from all anxiety, perform daily recitations and offer oblations at Prayāga."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, always remember Prayāga along with us;
O Indra among kings, you will yourself attain the heavenly world, of this there is no doubt. (Matsya Purāṇa 112.8)
The man who either follows after Prayāga or even dwells there,
having his soul purified of all sins, goes to the world of Rudra.
He who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is contented, self-controlled, pure,
and free from egoism, attains the fruit of the sacred fords.
He who is free from anger, truthful, a speaker of truth, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.
Sacrifices have been proclaimed by the seers and also by the gods in due order;
for sacrifices cannot be attained by one who is poor, O lord of the earth. (Matsya Purāṇa 112.12)
Sacrifices involving many implements and an extensive array of various materials are performed by kings and only occasionally by wealthy men.
O lord of men, Yudhiṣṭhira, learn now that rite which even the poor are able to perform, and which is equal in merit to the fruits of sacrifices. MatsP_112.14 //
O best of the Bharatas, this sacred pilgrimage to holy fords is the supreme secret of the seers; it is even more distinguished than sacrifices.
Ten thousand holy fords and thirty million rivers,
O bull of the Bharatas, will flow into the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha.
"Be at ease, O Great King; enjoy the kingdom free from thorns.
O Indra among kings, you shall see me again, especially while performing a sacrifice."
Nandikeśvara said:
Having spoken thus, that illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism vanished right there before King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, having bathed his limbs there together with his retinue,
the king attained supreme bliss according to the prescribed ritual.
Likewise, O celestial sage, you too should set out toward Prayāga;
by performing your ablutions there today, you will have fulfilled your purpose.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, Nandīśa vanished right there;
and Nārada likewise departed quickly toward Prayāga.
Having bathed there and performed recitations according to the prescribed rites,
and having given gifts to the foremost of the twice-born, he then departed for his own abode.
Matsya Purāṇa 113: The Sages said, "O Lord, how many continents, oceans, or mountains are there?"
And for how many years do they endure, and what rivers are recorded as being there?
The dimensions of the great elements, as well as the light of the world;
the sufficiency and the measure, and likewise the course of the moon and the sun.
Tell us all this in detail, O knower of reality;
we wish to hear everything that you have spoken. (Matsya Purāṇa 113.3)
Sūta said:
"The thousands of different islands and the seven [continents] contained within them— the entire world cannot indeed be described here in its entirety, even by proceeding step by step."
I shall, however, proclaim the seven [planets] together with the Moon and the Sun;
their dimensions are declared according to human reasoning.
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should be established through reasoning;
that which is beyond the primary elements is the characteristic of the inconceivable.
I shall describe Jambūdvīpa as it is for seven years; learn from me its extent and its circumference in yojanas.
The extent of this island is one hundred thousand yojanas;
it is filled with various provinces and diverse, auspicious cities.
It was crowded with perfected beings and celestial musicians, and adorned with mountains composed of all kinds of minerals and rising up like masses of rock.
And by means of rivers originating from the mountains on all sides,
these six mountain ranges of the regions (varṣaparvatas), which extend eastward and have great flanks, [are situated].
For he has plunged into both oceans, the eastern and the western;
and there are the Himavat, which is mostly snow, and the Hemakūṭa, which is golden.
The great mountain Niṣadha is also well-faced on all sides;
it is composed of the four castes, while Meru is remembered as being made of gold.
It extends twenty-four thousand [yojanas] in width in the four directions.
Circular in shape and proportion, square, well-proportioned,
equal in its sides through various colors, it is endowed with the qualities of Prajāpati.
Born from the navel-binding of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, he was white in color in the beginning; for that reason, his status as a Brāhmaṇa truly exists.
And because it is yellow on the south, it is held to have the status of a Vaiśya. Furthermore, being endowed with the Bhṛṅgipattrī and the Nabhā on the west,
its Śūdra status is established through the name, meaning, and function of Meru.
His left side was naturally red in color;
because of that, his status as a Kṣatriya was proclaimed—thus were the castes declared.
Nīla is made of lapis lazuli, Śveta is white, Pīta is golden,
Mayūrabarhavarṇa has the color of a peacock's tail, and that Śṛṅgavān is made of gold.
These are the kings of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the distance between them is said to be nine thousand [yojanas].
In the center, however, is the region named Ilāvṛta, which surrounds Mahāmeru;
it is twenty-four thousand yojanas in extent and is equal [in width] on all sides.
In its center stands Mount Mahāmeru, like a smokeless fire;
the southern half of the altar belongs to Meru, and likewise the northern half.
Regarding those seven regions here,
their mountain ranges extend for two thousand yojanas each from south to north.
The width of Jambūdvīpa is said to be their length;
these include the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains, as well as those others that are inferior.
Śveta, Hemakūṭa, Himavat, and Śṛṅgavān are proclaimed to be equal in measure to Jambūdvīpa; so too is Ṛṣabha.
Therefore, Hemakūṭa also decreases by a twelfth part;
Himavat decreases from that same [measure] by a twentieth part.
The great mountain Hemakūṭa is eighty-eight thousand [yojanas].
The Himavat mountain extends eighty [yojanas] from east to west;
its decrease and increase are proclaimed due to the circular shape of the continent.
Just as there is a division of the regions and the mountains, so it is described hereafter;
in their midst are the inhabited lands, which indeed constitute those seven regions.
Enveloped by those mountains with their treacherous precipices,
those seven [continents] are inaccessible to one another due to the various rivers that flow through them.
In all these regions dwell beings of various kinds;
this is the region of Himavat, renowned by the name Bhārata.
Beyond that is Hemakūṭa, which is known by the name Kimpuruṣa;
and beyond Hemakūṭa is Niṣadha, which is called Harivarṣa.
Beyond Harivarṣa, on the other side of Meru, lies Ilāvṛta; beyond Ilāvṛta is the well-known region named Ramyaka, situated by the Nīla mountain.
Beyond Ramyaka is the renowned Śveta, and beyond that is Hiraṇyaka;
and beyond Hiraṇyaka, Śṛṅgaśākaṃkura is recorded.
O celestial sage, it should be understood that when the sun is situated in the bow-shaped region to the south and north,
its four [regions] are long, while the middle one is Ilāvṛta.
To the east of Niṣadha, this southern half of the sacrificial altar is remembered;
but beyond it lies Ilāvṛta, which is the northern half of that altar.
Between those two, however, Meru is to be known, where Ilāvṛta is situated;
it lies to the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha.
To the north lies the great mountain named Mālyavat,
extending thirty-two thousand yojanas toward the western ocean.
Mālyavat is indeed one thousand [yojanas] long, extending as far as Nīla and Niṣadha;
likewise, the mountain Gandhamādana is said to be thirty-two [yojanas].
In the center of the two circular continents is Mount Meru, the golden mountain;
it is four-cornered and lofty, resembling the four castes in its colors.

He is multicolored on his sides; at the eastern end he is said to be white, his southern side is yellow, and his northern side is indeed red—thus he is endowed with these colors. (Matsya Purāṇa 113.38)
The divine Mount Meru shone like a king, surrounded by them,
possessing the luster of the young sun, like a fire without smoke.
It rises eighty-four thousand yojanas high;
it enters sixteen thousand yojanas below [the surface], and its width is twenty-eight thousand yojanas.
Its circumference all around is twice its width;
that mountain is most divine and endowed with celestial medicinal herbs.
Enveloped by all the worlds adorned with gold,
the hosts of gods, Gandharvas, Asuras,
and Rākṣasas rejoice everywhere on that king of mountains along with throngs of Apsarases.
That Meru is surrounded by the worlds that bring forth all beings,
within whose various sides these four regions are situated.
Bhadrāśva, Bhārata, and Ketumāla in the west,
as well as the Northern Kurus, which are the refuge for those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Likewise, there are the supporting mountains Mandara, Gandhamādana,
Vipula, and Supārśva, all adorned with every kind of jewel.
Aruṇoda, Mānasa, Sitoda, and that known as Bhadra—
above these are four lakes and forests.
Likewise, there is the Bhadrakadamba on Mount Gandhamādana;
the Jambū tree and the Aśvattha on Vipula, and furthermore, the Vaṭa tree.
On the western side of Gandhamādana, however, is Amaragaṇḍika;
it is thirty-two thousand yojanas in extent and equal on all sides.
There, those of auspicious deeds are renowned as the Ketumālas;
there all the Kālānalas are great beings of immense power.
And there are women with the luster of blue lotuses, beautiful and lovely to behold;
and there is a divine, great jackfruit tree (*panasa*) there, resplendent with its leaves.
Having drunk its fruit juice, they live for a full hundred years.
To the east of that Mālyavat mountain is the eastern Gaṇḍikā;
there also, it is said, there are thirty-two thousand and one hundred [yojanas].
There, Bhadrāśva is to be known as one whose mind is always joyful;
there also is the Bhadramāla forest and the great Kālāmra tree.
There, those men were white, great beings of immense strength;
the women had the hue of the kumuda lily, beautiful and lovely to behold.
The women possess the luster of the moon, the complexion of the moon, and faces resembling the full moon; their limbs are as cool as the moon, and they indeed have the fragrance of blue lotuses.
Their lifespan shall be ten thousand years, free from disease;
having drunk the juice of the Kālāmra fruit, they shall all remain in perpetual youth.
Sūta said:
Having thus spoken to the sages regarding the regions and their natural origins, Brahmā—who previously bestowed grace upon me—said, "What more shall I describe to you? *Matsya Purāṇa* 113.56.
Having heard these words of his, all those sages of rigid vows, filled with curiosity and endowed with joy, replied.
The sages said: "O Sage, you have fully described those two regions, the eastern and the western,
as well as all the northern varṣas and mountains."
"Tell us truly who those mountain-dwellers are.
Thus addressed by the sages, he spoke to them once again.
Sūta said:
Listen to those regions which were indeed previously mentioned by me—
those situated to the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha.
In that age known as Ramanaka, beings are indeed born;
there, men are born preeminent in pleasure, stainless,
endowed with pure lineage, and all are pleasing to behold.
And there too, there is a great banyan tree, a massive *rohiṇa*;
indeed, they subsist by drinking the juice of its fruit.
Those fortunate ones, the best among men, live for ten thousand years and ten hundred years, always joyful.
To the north of Śveta and on the southern side of Śṛṅga is the region named Hiraṇvat, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows.
Possessing great strength and great being, their minds are always joyful;
they are endowed with pure lineage, and all are pleasing to behold.
Those best of men live for a lifespan of eleven thousand years, plus fifteen hundred more.
In that region, there is a great lakuca tree providing shelter with its leaves;
by drinking the juice of its fruit, the people there sustain their lives.
The peaks of Mount Śṛṅgasāhva are indeed three great ones:
one there is endowed with jewels, one is possessed of gold,
and one consists of all kinds of gems and is adorned by the worlds.
To the north of this peak and at the edge of the ocean to the south lies Kuru; that excellent region is meritorious and frequented by the Siddhas.
There the trees bear honey-sweet fruit, and the rivers consist of divine nectar;
they produce garments and, through their fruits, ornaments as well.
There are some delightful trees that grant all desires, and others there called "milk-yielding" trees, which are likewise enchanting;
they constantly yield milk possessing the six flavors, which is like nectar.
The entire ground consists of jewels, fine as golden sand;
everywhere it is pleasant to the touch, and the auspicious breezes are silent.
Falling from the world of the gods, auspicious men are born there;
endowed with pure lineage, they all possess perpetual youth.
Couples are born there, and the women are like celestial nymphs;
they drink the milk of those milk-yielding trees, which is indeed like nectar.
A pair is born on the same day and grows up together;
they possess equal form and equal conduct, and indeed they die together.
Each one was devoted to the other, like a pair of cakravāka birds;
they were indeed free from illness, devoid of sorrow, and always joyful in mind.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
the Mahāsattvas live, and no other woman appears.
Sūta said:
"O knowers of the supreme dharma, such indeed is the natural state of the regions in the Bhārata age as it has been observed; what more shall I tell you?"
Thus were the Ṛṣis addressed by the wise son of the Sūta;
and upon hearing this further account, they questioned the son of the Sūta once more.
Matsya Purāṇa 114.
The sages said:
"Regarding this Bhārata-varṣa, in which [the Manus] beginning with Svāyambhuva [resided]..."
Only fourteen Manus brought about the creation of progeny.
O observer of noble vows, O best among speakers, we desire to know this from you; please speak further concerning the hearing of Uttara.
Having heard this from the sages, the Sūta,
the son of Lomaharṣaṇa and an expert in the Purāṇas, then spoke to those sages of purified souls.
Having investigated with his intellect and reflected upon it again and again in many ways,
he then related to them the hearing of the reply.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the subjects in this land of Bhārata;
because he supported (bharana) and caused to propagate (prajana) [the people], Manu is called Bharata.
And because it is described by etymological definitions, that land is remembered as Bhārata;
for it is indeed recorded as being heaven, liberation, and even the intermediate state.
Indeed, the ritual procedure for mortals is not ordained anywhere else on earth except for this land of Bhārata; learn now its nine divisions.
Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmraparṇa, Gabhastimān,
Nāgadvīpa, as well as Saumya, Gandharva, and Vāruṇa.
But this ninth continent among them is surrounded by the ocean;
this continent extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north.
Its length extends from Kumārī to the flowing Gaṅgā;
its width, both across and upwards, is exactly ten thousand [yojanas].
For this island is settled on all sides by Mlecchas at its borders;
the Yavanas and Kirātas dwell at its eastern and western extremities.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were established in their respective portions in the midst [of society], subsisting through sacrifices, military service, trade, and other such occupations.
This is their conventional practice, their mutual interaction, which—
concerned with dharma, artha, and kāma— is directed toward the specific duties of the social classes (varṇas).
In this world of humans, the engagement in the four stages of life, with the stage of the student as the fifth, according to the prescribed rule,
is for the sake of attaining heaven and liberation.
This land of Mānava, known as the continent of Tiryag-yāma,
he who conquers it in its entirety is proclaimed a universal monarch (samrāj).
O Emperor, this world is known as belonging to those who have conquered the intermediate space (antarikṣa);
that world is known as Svarāṭ; I shall describe it further in detail.
And in this great region, seven celebrated principal mountain ranges are found:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and Ṛkṣavat.
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas);
and thousands of other mountains are situated near them.
Beyond those, others known as the Abhijñātas were vast with variegated plateaus;
other than them, the Parijñātas were known to be short and lived among those who were short.
Interspersed with them, the noble people of the countryside and the Mlecchas everywhere drink from the many rivers—the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, and the Sarasvatī. (Matsya Purāṇa 114.20)
The Śatadru, Candrabhāgā, Yamunā, and Sarayū; likewise the Airāvatī, Vitastā, Viśālā, Devikā, and Kuhū.
The Gomatī, the Dhautapāpā, the Bāhudā, and the Dṛṣadvatī;
the Kauśikī is the third, as well as the Niścalā and the Gaṇḍakī.
The Ikṣu, Lauhitī, Vedasmṛti, Vetravatī, Vṛtraghnī, Sindhu, Parṇāśā, Narmadā, Kāverī, and likewise the Mahatī— these rivers have issued forth from the slopes of the Himavat. *Matsya Purāṇa* 114.23.
The Pārā, Dhanvatī, Veṇumatī,
Śiprā, Avantī, and Kuntī are known as the rivers that take refuge in the Pāriyātra mountains.
The Śoṇa and the great river Mahānadī, as well as the Nandanā, Sukṛśā, Kṣamā, Mandākinī, Daśārṇā, and likewise Citrakūṭā;
the Tamasā, Pippalī, Śyenī, and also Citrotpalā.
Vimalā, Cañcalā, Dhūtavāhinī,
Śuktimatī, Śunī, Lajjā, Mukuṭā, and Hrādikā—
these rivers of pure water, born from the Ṛṣyavan mountain, are auspicious.
The Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Kṣiprā, and the river Ṛṣabhā;
the Veṇā, Vaitaraṇī, Viśvamālā, and Kumudvatī. (Matsya Purāṇa 114.27)
Toya, Mahāgaurī, and likewise Durgamā-śilā—
all these, born from the foothills of the Vindhya, possess auspicious, cool waters.
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Vañjulā,
Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayogā, Vāhyā, and Kāverī—
these are the rivers of the southern region that flow forth from the foot of the Sahya mountain.
The Kṛtamālā, the Tāmraparṇī, the Puṣpajā, and the Utpalāvatī—
these rivers, all originating from the Malaya mountains, possess auspicious, cool waters.
Tribhāgā, Ṛṣikulyā, Ikṣudā, Tridivācalā,
Tāmraparṇī, Mūlī, Śaravā, and Vimalā—
all these daughters of Mahendra are renowned as those who move with auspicious grace.
Kāśikā, Sukumārī, Mandagā, Mandavāhinī,
Kṛpā, and Pāśinī— these indeed were the daughters of Śuktimat.
All these rivers, possessing meritorious waters, are auspicious; they flow everywhere toward the ocean.
They are all the mothers of the universe, removing all sins and bringing forth well-being.
Of those rivers and their tributaries there are hundreds and thousands;
along them dwell these Kurus, Pañcālas, Śālvas, and Jāṅgalas.
The Śūrasenas, the Bhadrakāras, the Bāhyas along with the Paṭaccaras,
the Matsyas, the Kirātas, the Kulyas, the Kuntalas, and the Kāśis and Kośalas.
The Āvantas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Mūkas along with the Andhakas—these are generally proclaimed to be the countries of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa). (Matsya Purāṇa 114.36)
And these two are situated adjacent to Sahya; there flows the river Godāvarī, which is the most delightful region on the entire earth.
There, for the sake of Rāma’s pleasure, were divine trees and celestial herbs from heaven, including those named Govardhana, Mandara, and Gandhamādana.
They were brought down by the sage Bharadvāja for the sake of his beloved;
consequently, that region became known as Puṣpavara, which was delightful to the mind.
The Vāhlīkas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Ābhīras, the Kālatoyakas, the Puraṃdhras, the Śūdras, the Pallavas, and the Attakhaṇḍikas; (Matsya Purāṇa 114.40)
The Gāndhāras, the Yavanas, the Sindhus, Sauvīras, and Madrakas; the Śakas, Druhyas, Pulindas, Pāradas, and Āramūrtikas.
The Rāmaṭhas, Kaṇṭakāras, Kaikeyas, and those known as Daśanāmas, as well as the Kṣatriya-settlers, Vaiśyas, and Śūdra families [were established there]. (Matsya Purāṇa 114.42)
The Atrayas, Bharadvājas, Prasthalas, Sadaserakas, Lampakas, Talagānas, and the Sainikas along with the Jāṅgalas—these are the northern countries;
now learn of the eastern countries. (Matsya Purāṇa 114.43)
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Madgurakas, those dwelling within the mountains and those outside the mountains; then the Plavaṃgas, Ātaṅgas, Yamakas, Mallavarṇakas,
Suhmas, Uttarās, Pravijayas, Mārgavas, and Geyamālavas.
The Prāgjyotiṣas, Puṇḍras, Videhas, Tāmraliptakas,
Śālvas, Māgadhas, and Gonardas are known as the eastern regions (janapadas).
Beyond them are other peoples dwelling in the southern region:
the Pāṇḍyas, the Keralas, the Colas, and likewise the Kulyas.
The Setukas, Sūtikas, Kupathas, Vājivāsikas, Navarāṣṭras, Māhiṣikas, and Kaliṅgas from all regions; MatsP_114.47 //
The Kārūṣas, along with the Eṣīkas, the Āṭavyas, and the Śabaras;
likewise the Pulindas, the Vindhyapuṣikas, the Vaidarbhas, together with the Daṇḍakas.
The Kulīyas, the Sirālās, the Rūpasas along with the Tāpasas, as well as the Taittirikas and all the Kāraskaras; (Matsya Purāṇa 114.49)
And those of Vāsikya, as well as others who dwell within the Narmadā,
the Bhārukacchas together with the Samāheyas, and likewise the Sārasvatas.
The Kācchīkas, the Saurāṣṭras, the Ānartas, along with the Arbudas—these are the westerners;
now hear who dwell in the Vindhya region.
The Mālavas, the Karūṣas, and the Mekalas together with the Utkalas;
the Auṇḍras, the Māṣas, the Daśārṇas, and the Bhojas along with the Kiṣkindhakas. (Matsya Purāṇa 114.52)
The Stośalas, the Kosalas, the Traipuras, and the Vaidiśas; likewise the Tumuras, the Tumbaras, and the Padgamas along with the Naiṣadhas.
The Arūpas, the Śauṇḍikeras, the Vītihotras, and the Avantayas—
these are the renowned regions inhabited on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains.
Therefore, I shall describe those regions situated on mountains,
as well as those who are without food, those who go everywhere, and those of evil paths and no paths at all.
The Kuthaprāvaraṇas, the Ūrṇādavas, the Samudgakas, the Trigartas, the Maṇḍalas, and the Kirātas along with the Āmaras; MatsP_114.56.
The sages have declared that there are four ages in the land of Bhārata:
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—this is the cycle of the four ages (caturyuga).
I shall describe their nature in its entirety further on.
The Fish said:
Having heard this, those sages, desiring to hear further, spoke again at length to Lomaharṣaṇi.
The sages said:
"Tell us truly about the region of Kimpuruṣa and likewise Harivarṣa, just as you have described Bhārata."
O best among the learned, tell us the extent of Jambūkhanda, as well as that of the other continents, their inhabitants, and their trees.
Thus questioned by the brahmins at that time according to their specific inquiries,
he spoke of what was seen by the seers and accepted in the Purāṇas.
Sūta said:
"O Brahmins, listen with undistracted attention to that which you wish to hear:
the region of Jambūvarṣa, known as Kimpuruṣa, which is like the great Nandana grove."
The lifespan in Kimpuruṣa is recorded as ten thousand years;
the humans born there possess the radiance of well-refined gold.
In the meritorious Varṣa of Kiṃpuruṣa, the Madhuvaha Plakṣa tree is said to exist;
all the Kiṃpuruṣas drink its supreme nectar.
For the men are free from disease and sorrow, always joyful in mind;
and both the men and women are said to be golden-hued, like celestial nymphs.
Beyond that, they declare Harivarṣa to be beyond Kiṃpuruṣa;
there, human beings are born resembling great silver.
Having all descended from the world of the gods, the men in Harivarṣa are of many forms in every respect,
and they all drink the auspicious juice of sugarcane.
Old age does not afflict them there; therefore, they live for a long time.
Their lifespan is proclaimed to be eleven thousand [years].
I have described that middle region by the name of Ilāvṛta;
there the sun does not scorch, nor do human beings perceive it.
The moon and the sun, along with the stars, were shrouded in darkness and obscured;
[the beings] possessed the luster of lotuses, the color of lotuses, and eyes resembling lotus petals.
And all the humans born there possess the fragrance of lotuses;
subsisting on the juice of the jambu fruit, they are motionless and sweetly scented.
Having descended from the world of the gods, all those best of men were clothed in garments of great silver;
they lived for thirteen thousand years.
Those who dwell in Ilāvṛta live for a lifespan of one year;
they are situated on the southern side of Meru and to the north of Niṣadha.
There is a great, eternal Jambū tree named Sudarśana,
endowed with perpetual flowers and fruits, and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
After that great lord of trees, Jambūdvīpa was named;
it is again a thousand yojanas in extent and divided into a hundred parts.
The height of that king of trees stands reaching up to the heavens;
its juice from the jambu fruits flows forth, becoming a river.
Having circumambulated Meru, they go again to the foot of the Jambu tree;
there, in Ilāvṛta, they always drink the juice of the Jambu fruit with great joy.
Having drunk the juice of the jambu fruit, neither old age afflicts them,
nor hunger, nor fatigue, nor likewise any such suffering.
Therein is produced the gold named Jāmbūnada, which serves as an ornament for the gods; it resembles the Indragopaka insect and is brilliantly radiant.
The juice of the fruits of all the rain-trees there is auspicious;
when it overflows, bright gold is produced, which serves as an ornament for the gods.
Their urine or feces, in all eight directions,
the earth— by the grace of the Lord— swallows up even those who are dead.
The Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Yakṣas—all these belong to Himavat;
however, on Hemakūṭa, the Gandharvas along with their hosts of Apsarases are to be known.
All the Nāgas—Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the rest—resort to it;
on Mahāmeru, the auspicious ones worthy of sacrifice sport with the Thirty-three.
In this mountain, joined with blue lapis lazuli, perfected Brahman-sages dwelt;
the White Mountain (Śveta) is said to belong to the Daityas and Dānavas.
Śṛṅgavān is the best of mountains, the place of reabsorption for the ancestors;
thus have these nine regions in Bhārata been described by me.
Even those things composed of the elements, which are mobile and stable,
are seen by gods and humans to undergo manifold growth;
it is impossible to enumerate them fully, yet they must be believed in by one who desires prosperity.
Matsya Purāṇa 115: Manu said, "O Janārdana, I have heard the life-story of Budha’s son."
The meritorious rite for the ancestral offerings (śrāddha), which destroys all sins, has been heard.
I have heard of the fruit of giving a cow that is about to calve, as well as the gift of a black antelope skin and likewise the ritual of releasing a bull. (Matsya Purāṇa 115.2)
O Keśava, having heard of the form of the son of Budha, the lord of men, curiosity has arisen in me; tell that to me as I ask you.
By what ripening of karma did that King Purūravas obtain such a form and also supreme good fortune?
Having abandoned with her whole being that king, she who was esteemed as Urvaśī, even though there were gods, the best in the three worlds, and Gandharvas who were delightful.
The Fish said: Listen to how, through the ripening of his karma, King Purūravas obtained such a form as well as supreme good fortune. *Matsya Purāṇa* 115.6.
In a former birth, he who was this King Purūravas was indeed known as Purūravas,
the sovereign of the Madra country.
In the lineage of Cākṣuṣa, during the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa,
there was a king who was indeed endowed with all the qualities of a ruler, though he alone was devoid of physical beauty.
The sages said:
"By what deed did Purūravas become the lord of Madra and a king, O son of Sūta? And by what deed did he become so handsome?"
Sūta said:
O Great King, in his previous birth, there was a preeminent twice-born man named Purūravas, who was a king on the bank of a river in a village of brahmins. *Matsya Purāṇa* 115.10.
But that king who was the lord of Madra, known by the name Purūravas—
he was that very Brahmin in that birth, O sinless one, on the twelfth lunar day.
Desiring sovereignty, he observed a fast and worshipped Janārdana;
having undertaken the fast, he performed his bath preceded by an oil massage.
Through the fruit of his fast, he obtained a kingdom among the Madras free from all thorns;
yet, by fasting while applying oil for anointing, he became devoid of beauty.
Therefore, O King, men who observe the fast should diligently avoid bathing preceded by the application of oil, for that is supreme in destroying one's beauty.
All this that occurred in his previous birth has been told to you;
now hear the account of that lord of the earth regarding his status as the ruler of the Madras.
Although that lord of the earth was endowed with all the qualities of a king,
he indeed lacked the affection of the people because of his lack of physical beauty.
Desiring a divine form, that lord of the Madras,
having resolved upon asceticism and entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, went to the Himavat mountain.
Accompanied only by his resolve, the highly illustrious one set out on foot to see the river at the edge of his own territory, which was the abode of holy fords.
He beheld the exceedingly beautiful woman renowned as Airāvatī.
Born from the snowy mountain, possessing the force of a great torrent, its waters were as cool as the rays of the moon.
The king beheld the river Tuhiṇayaśas, whose mass of golden hue was like frost.
Matsya Purāṇa 116: Sūta said:
He beheld the auspicious, divine, and holy river Haimavatī.
It was crowded with Gandharvas and was constantly frequented by Śakra.
On that day, it was always splashed with the rut of noble elephants and shone brilliantly on all sides,
appearing like a rainbow in its center.
King Purūravas beheld that city, which was filled with the refuge of ascetics, inhabited by great brahmins, and possessed a brilliance like that of refined gold.
Beholding it covered with rows of white swans and adorned with chowries of *kāśa* grass—
as if it were an anointed queen— he attained supreme joy among the virtuous.
It was meritorious, very cool, heart-pleasing, and increasing the joy of the mind;
it was endowed with waning and waxing, lovely, like another form of the Moon.
It possessed very cool and swift-flowing waters, was frequented by flocks of birds,
was the most excellent daughter of Himavat, and was adorned with dancing waves.
Its waters are as sweet as nectar; it is graced by ascetics, serving as a ladder for ascending to heaven and destroying all impurities.
The foremost queen of the ocean, served by hosts of great sages,
who arouses longing in all the world and is most enchanting.
Beneficial to the entire world and bestowing the path to heaven, its banks were crowded with herds of cows; it was delightful and free from moss.
Resounding with the cries of swans and cranes, adorned with lotuses, deep with whirlpools as its navel, and possessing large islands as its broad hips; MatsP_116.10 //
She has the luster of blue lotus eyes, a face like a full-blown lotus,
and wears garments of white foam; she is auspicious with lips like ruddy geese,
teeth like rows of cranes, and eyebrows like a school of darting fish.
She whose breasts were the lovely frontal globes of elephants born from her own waters,
who resounded with the anklets of swans, and who wore a series of bracelets made of lotus stalks.
O King, at the time of midday, hosts of apsarases, intoxicated by pride in their beauty and constantly followed by gandharvas, sport there.
She carried that auspicious saffron released by the apsarases,
fragrant with various colors produced from the trees growing on her own banks.
It was difficult to behold due to the solar disc reflected in the multitude of waves,
and it was adorned by its two banks which were scarred by the blows dealt by the lord of the gods.
The water of that river, joined with the ichor from Indra’s temples and the sandalwood paste from the breasts of celestial women,
is enjoyed by the bees.
The trees growing on its banks were adorned with fragrant flowers,
and they were filled with the humming of bees that were drawn away and agitated by the rustling sounds.
On whose banks deer, driven by passion, always find delight,
as do the sages of the penance groves, the gods, and the apsarases.
There they obtain women whose limbs are pure, who are honored by the gods, who abound in celestial splendor, and whose faces resemble the lotus and the moon.
She who always bears water, untroubled by hosts of gods,
by Pulinda tribes, by royal assemblies, and even by packs of tigers.
Beholding that city, which was like a drink of nectar for the virtuous, as pure as the starry sky, and which granted the desires of the righteous, the king proceeded onward.
Its delightful banks shine with various kinds of great trees and with *kāśa* grass growing on the shore, which is full and resembles the rays of the moon;
it is always frequented by various brahmins as well as by the gods.
She who always and swiftly effects the destruction of the entire flood of sins for her devotees;
she who is indeed followed by multitudes of rivers, and who is constantly followed by the lords of sages.

For she who protects men like her own sons, she who is constantly joined by masses of snow, she who is constantly attended by hosts of gods, and she who is indeed resorted to by people for their own welfare; MatsP_116.24 //
Though frequented by herds of lions and inhabited by throngs of elephants, though possessing continuous streams of water and filled with gold,
and though its coldness was intensified by the increasing heat of the sun’s rays, that river Śītā was beheld by the king, whose fame equaled that of the moon.
Matsya-Purāṇa 117: Sūta said:
Beholding the holy river, his fatigue was removed by its breeze.
As he was traveling, he beheld the great mountain Himavat.
It was surrounded by many white peaks scraping the sky,
and even without the movement of birds, it possessed the auspicious path of the Siddhas.
Surrounded on all sides by the great roar produced by the flow of rivers,
that delightful place of cool water was devoid of any other sound.
That lord of men beheld the auspicious mountain, which had dark-blue Devadāru forests for its lower garment and clouds for its upper robe.
In some places he has a turban made of white clouds and a crown of the moon and sun;
in other places all his limbs are smeared with snow, and in others he is mixed with minerals.
Its body was anointed with sandalwood and marked with the five-fingerprints,
providing coolness even in the heat of summer; though its rocky crevices were formidable,
it was here and there stamped by the feet of the Apsarases, reddened with lac.
In some places touched by the rays of the sun, in others shrouded in darkness,
and in some parts drinking great quantities of water through its formidable cavernous mouths.
In some places it was graced by hosts of Vidyādharas sporting about,
and in other places it was celebrated with songs by the principal groups of Kiṃnaras.
In some places, that place was adorned with divine flowers, such as those from the *saṃtānaka* tree, which had fallen from the drinking grounds of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
In some places, that delightful abode of the Gandharvas was strewn with beds from which flowers had been crushed, as if they had risen from sleep.
In some places it was adorned with dark green meadows where the winds had ceased,
and in others it was joined with flowers, exceedingly beautiful and auspicious.
That mountain, a refuge for ascetics and exceedingly difficult for those possessed by passion to attain,
was frequented by deer and featured great trees torn down by elephants.
Where, at the sound of the lion’s roar, no terrified and frantic cry is heard from the agitated herds of elephants, nor is any exhaustion seen.
Its banks were adorned with ascetics and groves,
and by the jewels produced therefrom, the three worlds were beautifully ornamented.
The mountain, which provides unfailing refuge and is constantly frequented by noble people, is itself unsurpassed and possesses an abundance of jewels; thus does the noble one behold it.
There, by means of their austerities, ascetics shall attain perfection;
by the mere sight of which all impurities are destroyed.
In various places, there were regions that provided constant satisfaction through waters flowing from great precipices, waterfalls, and other cascades, driven by the wind.
In some places, it was impassable even to the mind, with peaks smeared by water yet rising high, rendered treacherous by the constant heat of the sun.
It was adorned with regions resembling groves of bamboo poles, where the branches of great *devadāru* trees grew so densely together as to form a continuous mass.
It possessed great peaks like Himalayan umbrellas, with hundreds of waterfalls and torrents;
its waters were inaccessible except by sound, and its caves were blocked by snow.
Upon merely seeing that ground of beautiful hips, the majestic lord of the Madras wandered there filled with joy, and then reached a certain spot.
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 118:
Sūta said:
"In that very region of the lord of mountains, which is most delightful..."
Inaccessible to other humans, he arrived there through the power of destiny.
From that region flows the Airāvatī, the best of rivers;
and that region is dark as a cloud with numerous clusters of trees.
With *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, along with *karṇikāra* and *śāmalī*;
with *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *śirīṣa*, and *śiṃśapā* trees.
With *śleṣmātaka*, *āmalaka*, *harītakī*, and *vibhītaka* trees;
with *bhūrja*, *samuñjaka*, and *bāṇa* trees; and with *saptacchada* trees.
With great nimba trees, as well as nimba, nirguṇḍī, and haridru trees;
with great devadāru trees and likewise kāleyaka trees.
With *padmaka*, sandalwood, *bilva*, *kapittha*, red sandalwood,
*mātāmra*, *ariṣṭaka*, *akṣoṭa*, *abdaka*, and likewise with *arjuna* trees.
With *hastikarṇa*, *sumanasa*, and well-flowered *kovidāra* trees,
as well as with *prācīnāmalaka*, *dhanaka*, and *samarāṭaka* trees.
With dates, coconuts, priyāla, āmrātaka, and iṅguda;
with *tantumāla*, *dhava*, *bhavya*, as well as *kāśmīrī* and *parṇī*.
With nutmegs, betel nuts, *kaṭphala* fruits, cardamom pods, and *mandāra*, *kovidāra*, and *kiṃśuka* flowers and silken garments; // MatsP_118.9 //
With *yavāsa*, *śamī*, *parṇāsa*, *vetasa*, and *ambuvetasa*; with *raktātis*, *raṅga*, *nāraṅga*, *hiṅgu*, and *priyaṅgu*.
With red Aśoka trees, as well as Aśoka, Ākalla, and Avicāraka; with Mucukunda, Kunda, Āṭarūṣa, and Parūṣaka.
With *kirāta*, *kiṅkirāta*, *ketaka*, and *śvetaketaka* trees;
with *śobhāñjana*, *añjana*, and the excellent *kaliṅga* and *nikoṭaka* trees.
With excellent trees possessing beautiful golden garments, with seats, and with delightful mango trees shaped like the arrows of the God of Love; MatsP_118.13 //
With yellow jasmine and likewise white jasmine,
with *jāti* and *campaka-jāti*, and also with *tumbura* and *atumbura* flowers.
With *mocarī*, *locas*, *lakuca*, sesame flowers, and *kuśeśaya*,
as well as with excellent flower-garlands, *cavyaka*, and *kāmivallabha*.
And with *puṣpāṅkura*, *bakula*, *pāribhadra*, *haridraka*,
*dhārākadamba*, *kuṭaja*, *kadamba*, and *girikuṭaja* trees.
With jars of *ādityamustaka*, saffron, and *kāmavallabha* flowers, along with *kaṭphala*, jujube fruits, and *nīpa* trees, which were as brilliantly radiant as lamps; (Matsya Purāṇa 118.17).
With red groves of *pālī* trees, white pomegranates, *campaka* trees, *bandhūka* flowers, beautiful *subandhūka* flowers, and jasmine vines forming bowers; (Matsya Purāṇa 118.18).
With *pāṭala* flowers, *mallikā*, and *karavīraka*;
with *kurabaka*, *himavara*, *jambū*, and *nṛpajambū* trees.
With *bījapūra* fruits mixed with camphor, with heavy *aguru* trees, and with *bimba* and *pratibimba* flowers, as well as canopies of *saṃtānaka* blossoms; // MatsP_118.20 //
Likewise, with *guggulu* trees, *hintāla*, white *ikṣu* canes, *tṛṇaśūnya*, *karavīra*, *aśoka*, and *cakramardana* trees; MatsP_118.21 //
It was crowded with *pīlu*, *dhātaki*, and *ciribilva* trees,
as well as *tintiḍīka*, *lodhra*, *viḍaṅga*, and *kṣīrikā* trees.
Likewise, with aśmantaka, kāla, jambīra, śvaitakadruma,
bhallātaka, indrayava, and valguja— these are the means for accomplishing success.
And with *nāgakesara* trees, which are enchanting with their beautiful filaments;
with *karamarda*, *kāsamarda*, *ariṣṭaka*, and *variṣṭaka*;
with *rudrākṣa*, those produced from *drākṣā*, *saptāhva*, and *putrajīvaka*.
With *kaṅkolaka*, cloves (*lavaṅga*), cinnamon trees (*tvagdruma*), *pārijātaka* trees,
and spreading *pippalī* vines, as well as *nāgavallī* creepers, [they were arranged] in their respective parts.
Likewise, it was adorned with groves of *marīca* and *navamallikā*,
as well as with preeminent arbors of *mṛdvīkā* and arbors of *atimuktaka*.
With auspicious, fruit-bearing vines of trapuṣa and nartikā,
and in some places with vines of kūṣmāṇḍa and alābu.
With spreading vines of *cirbhiṭa*, with *paṭola* and *kāravella*,
with canopies of *karkoṭakī*, with eggplants, and with the fruits of the *bṛhatī*.
With thorns, radishes, various kinds of root-vegetables,
as well as white water-lilies, vidārī, rurūṭa, and sweet-thorned plants.
With *sabhāṇḍī*, *vidū*, *sāra*, *rājajambūka*, and *vāluka*,
as well as with all types of *suvarcalā* and likewise with *sarṣapa*.
With *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *chattrā*, and *aticchattrā*,
along with *kāsamardī*, *sahā*, *kandala*, and *kāṇḍaka*.
Likewise, with milk-vegetables, black vegetables, leguminous grains, and all other kinds of grain without exception; MatsP_118.29.
With various medicinal herbs,
O lord of men, which are indeed radiant, and which bestow long life, fame, and strength.
[These mantras] remove the fear of old age and death, destroy the fear of hunger,
produce good fortune, and are entirely manifold in number.
There, with bamboo creepers and likewise with hollow bamboos, with *kāśa* grasses and *śaśāṅkakāśa*, and also with thickets of reeds; ||| MatsP_118.32 |||
With lovely groves of *kuśa* grass, as well as delightful thickets of sugarcane,
and with varieties of auspicious and rare cotton plants.
And likewise, it was adorned with most excellent and captivating groves of plantain trees,
