According to dharma, it is double the size of each preceding one in terms of pleasure and wealth;
on the back of Hemakūṭa, that lake is remembered as belonging to the serpents.
From that [mountain] flows the Sarasvatī, which is indeed luminous;
for when it has plunged into both oceans, the eastern and the western, it shines forth.
On the excellent mountain Niṣadha, there is a lake named Viṣṇupada,
from which those [rivers] originate in front, flowing in accordance with the Gandharvas.
From the side of Meru flows forth the great lake Candraprabha,
and from it issues the holy river Jambū, after which the gold known as Jāmbūnada is named.
The lake Payoda was blue, while that [lake] Puṇḍarīka was white;
from that Puṇḍarīka and from Payoda, two daughters were born.
This lake was indeed remembered as Uttaramānasa;
and from it, Mṛgī and Mṛgakāntā were born as a pair.
In the land of the Kurus, there are famous lakes known by the name Jayā; they are crowded with lotuses and schools of fish, and numbering twelve, they resemble the ocean.
From them were born two rivers, Śāntī and Madhvī;
in those eight regions, beginning with Kimpuruṣa, the god does not rain.
Here the excellent rivers flow with waters bursting forth:
Balāhaka, Ṛṣabha, Cakra, and Maināka.
They are settled in every direction, submerged in the salt ocean:
the Candrakānta, the Droṇa, and the very great mountain mass.
Udgāyana, however, plunged into the great ocean in the north,
as did Cakra, Badhiraka, and likewise Nāradaparvata.
Pratīcīmāyata, Pratiṣṭhā, Mahodadhi, Jīmūta, Drāvaṇa, Maināka, and Candraparvata—these indeed [are the mountains]. // MatsP_121.75 //
Those great mountains extend toward the southern ocean between Mount Cakra and Mount Maināka, situated in the southern region of the sky.
There, that fire named Saṃvartaka drinks up that water;
it is the submarine fire, the ocean-dweller, known as Aurva or Vaḍavāmukha.
Thus, these four mountains, having entered the salt ocean in ancient times out of fear of Indra, remained there when their wings were being lopped off.
Their immersion is seen in the moon during both the bright and dark fortnights;
they are the divisions by which the land of Bhārata is proclaimed.
Those described here are seen elsewhere as being described differently;
among these, each successive region excels the preceding one in its qualities.
In those regions, living beings are endowed in their respective parts with health, lifespan, and the measure of existence, according to their nature, their desires, and their purpose.
All those various species indeed dwell within all of them;
thus, upholding this entire universe, the earth stands as this world.
Matsya Purāṇa 122. Sūta said:
I shall now describe here, according to the truth and with certainty, the island of Śākadvīpa.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe to you the continent of Śāka.
Its width is twice that of Jambūdvīpa;
its circumference all around is three times its width.
By that island, this salt-water ocean is enclosed;
there lie meritorious regions where people die only after a long time.
How much less could there be famine here in this land endowed with patience and splendor?
There too, there are seven auspicious mountains adorned with jewels.
In these [continents] beginning with Śākadvīpa, there are seven mountain ranges in each of the three [outer continents];
these boundary mountains (varṣaparvata) are situated straight and extended in every direction.
The great mountain ranges named Ratnākara and others rise equally in every direction, with a height equal to the extent of the continents.
The salt ocean and the milk ocean both extend as far as Śākadvīpa;
now I shall describe the seven divine great mountains within that island.
The first mountain, joined by celestial sages and gandharvas, is called Meru;
extending toward the east, it is the golden mountain named Udaya.
There, the clouds arise and depart for the sake of rain;
beyond that is another very great mountain called Jaladhāra.
That indeed is declared to be the Moon, endowed with all medicinal herbs;
from it, Vāsava constantly takes up the supreme water.
There, the mountain named Nārada was called Durgashaila, a great mass of rock;
there, in former times, two mountains arose, Nārada and Parvata.
To the west of that is a very great mountain named Śyāma,
where it is said these creatures formerly attained a dark (śyāma) complexion.
That very mountain named Dundubhi, resembling a dark cloud, was formerly called Śabdamṛtyu; on that mountain, Dundubhi was struck by the gods.
The Śālmala mountain, consisting of various kinds of jewel-garlands, forms its interior;
beyond it, another great mountain is known as Asta, made of silver.
He was indeed called Somaka by the gods because, in ancient times,
the nectar (amṛta) that had been collected and carried away by Garuḍa for the sake of his mother was [recovered] by him.
His other sons were known as Ambikeya and Sumanas;
Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by the Boar on that mountain.
Beyond Āmbikeya is the beautiful mountain Vibhrāja, frequented by all medicinal herbs; it is the great crystal mountain known as Sphāṭika.
Because the fire blazes forth (vibhrājate), he is remembered as Vibhrāja;
and because the wind blows here, he is called Keśava.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the years of those mountains;
listen to their names in due order and according to tradition.
The regions have two names each, just as the mountains do;
the region known as Jaladhārā is situated at the rising point of the Udaya mountain.
The first region is known by the name Gatabhaya;
the second is known as Sukumāra, belonging to Jaladhāra.
That very [period] is proclaimed as the Varṣa named Śaiśira;
it is also the Kaumāra of Nārada, which brings about the arising of happiness.
That region of the Śyāma mountain is known as Anīcaka;
that very same auspicious place is declared by the sages to be Ānandaka.
The auspicious region of Somaka is to be known as Kusumotkara;
that very same region designated by the name of Somaka is called Asita.
Maināka and Kṣemaka were made by him for the son of Ambikā;
Kesara was also known as Mahādruma,
and that very region was called Dhava, known by the name Vibhrāja.
The circumference and the dimensions—both breadth and length—of the continent are reckoned as equal to those of Jambūdvīpa; and in its center stands a lordly tree.
There is a great tree named Śāka; its offspring are the Mahānugas.
Within these dwell the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas together.
They dwell and take delight there, being seen together with them;
in that place are meritorious provinces inhabited by the four castes.
In those regions, there are exactly seven rivers in each varṣa that flow to the ocean;
they are all known as Gaṅgās by dual names and are traditionally classified as being of seven kinds.
The first is named Sukumārī; this auspicious river of Śiva’s waters is celebrated by the name Munitaptā.
Sukumārī, perfected through austerity, was the second by name; Nandā and Pāvanī were proclaimed as the third. *Matsya Purāṇa* 122.31.
The fourth is the Śibikā, which is further remembered as being of two kinds;
the fifth should be known as Ikṣu, and likewise again as Kuhū.
Veṇukā and Amṛtā are proclaimed as the sixth;
Sukṛtā and Gabhastī are proclaimed as the seventh. (Matsya Purāṇa 122.33)
These seven highly fortunate rivers, whose waters are auspicious, nourish every person dwelling in Śākadvīpa year after year.
And other rivers, streams, and lakes with abundant flowing waters join them,
from which Vāsava pours down rain.
Their names as well as their dimensions cannot be fully enumerated; they are all meritorious and the best of rivers.
Those people of the countryside always drink from those rivers with joy;
these are declared to be the Śāntabhayas, as well as the Pramodas and the Śivas.
Ānanda, Sukha, and Kṣemaka, together with nine others—
these seven renowned regions are endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life.
They shall all be healthy, strong, and free from death;
for them there shall be neither the aeon of decline (avasarpiṇī) nor likewise the aeon of increase (utsarpiṇī).
There is no state of the Yuga-periods established by the four ages anywhere there;
rather, a time equal to the Tretā-yuga prevails there.
In all five of these, beginning with Śākadvīpa,
it should be known that time is considered natural (svābhāvika) through the consideration of the region.
Among them, there was never any confusion whatsoever caused by caste or stage of life;
and because their dharma was never deviated from, the subjects were exclusively happy.
In them there is no deceit, nor greed, nor envy, nor malice; whence could there be fear?
No error exists in them; that indeed is known as their innate nature.
For them there is neither time, nor punishment, nor one who inflicts punishment;
knowing the Dharma, they protect one another by means of their own duty.
The very great island known as Kuśa is indeed circular,
surrounded by river waters and mountains resembling clouds.
And with various regions adorned with diverse jewels and corals,
as well as other delightful lands of manifold forms.
It is surrounded on all sides by trees endowed with flowers and fruits;
it possesses wealth and grain everywhere, is eternally provided with flowers and fruits, and is filled with all kinds of jewels.
Enclosed on all sides by all kinds of domestic and wild animals,
learn now of Kuśadvīpa in its proper sequence and in brief.
Now I shall describe the entirety of Kuśadvīpa, the third [continent];
the Ocean of Milk is surrounded on all sides by Kuśadvīpa.
Endowed with a breadth twice that of Śākadvīpa,
there too seven mountains should be known as sources of jewels.
Likewise, there are oceans of jewels and rivers; hear their names from me.
All of them have two names each, just as they do in Śākadvīpa.
The first mountain, resembling the sun, is named Kumuda;
that very same mountain is also called Vidrumoccaya.
There, the second mountain, renowned by the name Unnata, consists of peaks made of all minerals and is covered with networks of stone.
That very mountain is called Hemaparvata;
covered on all sides by peaks composed of yellow orpiment, it encompasses the entire island.
The third mountain is Balāhaka, consisting of natural collyrium;
that very mountain is also known by the name Dyutimān.
The fourth mountain is Droṇa, where on that great mountain there are medicinal herbs,
namely the Viśalyakaraṇī and the Mṛtasaṃjīvanī.
That very mountain, most greatly adorned, is called Puṣpavān;
Kaṅka is the fifth among them, a mountain named Sāravān.
Furthermore, that mountain was called Kuśeśaya;
it was endowed with divine flowers and fruits and possessed divine songs.
The sixth mountain there is Mahiṣa, resembling a cloud;
he is further proclaimed as the one renowned as Hari.
In that [lake] dwells the fire named Mahiṣa, who was born from the waters;
there is a seventh mountain there called Kakudmat, for it indeed speaks.
That very [mountain] is to be known as Mandara, auspicious and composed of all elements;
for the element *manda* is that which reveals the meaning of "fools" (*apām*). (Matsya Purāṇa 122.61)
And because he split the waters, he is called Mandara;
there, Vāsava himself guards many jewels.
Starting from Prajāpati and extending toward the subjects, he himself ordains [the distances];
the intervening distance between them is declared to be double [the preceding].
Thus these seven mountains have been described in Kuśadvīpa;
I shall now describe their seven regions according to their respective divisions.
The region of Kumuda is remembered as Śveta, and that is also known as Unnata;
the region of Unnata is to be known by the name Lohita.
The Veṇumaṇḍalaka is likewise proclaimed;
and for Balāhaka, it is Jīmūta, as well as Svairathākāra.
Droṇa’s son is remembered as Harika, and Lavaṇa is likewise mentioned; Kaṅka’s son is named Kakud, and he is also remembered as Dhṛtimat.
The region of Mahiṣa belongs to Mahiṣa, and furthermore, that of Prabhākara belongs to Kakudmin;
that famous region is named Kapila.
Learn now that these seven regions are likewise distinct and distinguished, as are their respective mountains and rivers. 122.69.
There too, it is traditionally held that there are exactly seven rivers in each region;
all of them bear two names and are all remembered as possessing meritorious waters.
The river named Dhūtapāpā is also known as Yoni;
the second is to be understood as Sītā, and she is indeed remembered as Niśā.
The third is to be known as Pavitrā, and that which is Vitṛṣṇā is the fourth; she is called Hlādinī and is remembered as Candrabhā.
Vidyut is declared the fifth and is visualized as white;
Puṇḍrā is to be known as the sixth, and Vibhāvarī follows after her.
The great seventh [tithi] is proclaimed, and this is further remembered as Dhṛti;
others have also arisen from these by the hundreds and thousands.
Those rivers flow toward where Vāsava sends rain;
thus has this configuration of Kuśadvīpa been described to you.
The eternal extent of that [Śākadvīpa] has been declared;
and Kuśadvīpa is surrounded by the ocean whose waters consist of the scum of clarified butter.
This very great island is surrounded on all sides like the moon;
it is considered to be twice the size of the Kṣīroda ocean, both in its breadth and its circumference.
Thereafter, I shall describe Krauñcadvīpa exactly as it is;
its extent is twice that of Kuśadvīpa.
The ocean of clarified butter is indeed surrounded by Krauñcadvīpa;
it is encompassed on all sides in a circular form, with a circumference equal to that of a wheel's rim.
On that island, the most excellent mountains are said to be Devana and Giri;
beyond Devana, moreover, is the mountain named Govinda.
Beyond Govinda, moreover, is the first mountain, Krauñca;
beyond Krauñca is Pāvanaka, and beyond Pāvanaka is Andhakāraka.
Beyond Andhakāra, moreover, is the mountain named Devāvṛt;
beyond Devāvṛta is the great mountain Puṇḍarīka.
These seven mountains of Krauñcadvīpa are composed of jewels;
each successive mountain range has a width double that of the preceding one.
I shall describe his years; listen now to them by name:
the region of Krauñca is Kuśala, and that of Vāmana is Manonuga.
After Manonuga comes Uṣṇa; he is also called the third.
After Uṣṇa comes Pāvanaka, and after Pāvanaka comes Andhakāraka.
Beyond the region of Andhakāraka is the region of the Munis;
and beyond the region of the Munis, it is said, lies Dundubhisvana.
Crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas, its people are for the most part fair-skinned and pure;
it is there that the auspicious rivers are heard to flow every year.
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Saṃdhyā, Rātri, Manojavā,
Khyāti, and Puṇḍarīkā— Gaṅgā is remembered as being sevenfold.
Thousands of other rivers flow alongside them;
those many rivers, possessing abundant water, join those [principal] rivers.
The natural disposition of those regions in their entirety and in due order cannot be described in detail even in hundreds of years.
The creation of living beings and their subsequent dissolution—having explained these, I shall hereafter proclaim the [creation] of Śālmaladvīpa; listen to it.
The island of Śālmala is twice the extent of Krauñcadvīpa;
it stands encircling the ocean whose waters are like the scum of curdled milk.
In those regions, the districts are meritorious and the people die only after a long time;
how then could there be famine, for they are endowed with patience and splendor?
The first mountain, resembling the sun, was named Sumanas;
the middle one was yellow, and beyond that was the mountain consisting of jars (Kumbhamaya).
The third mountain is named Sarvasukha, endowed with divine medicinal herbs; it is golden and resembles the wing of a bhr̥ṅga bee.
That excellent divine mountain is indeed named Sumahānrohit;
it is a pleasant and auspicious region, resulting in happiness and bringing forth prosperity.
The third is Rohita, renowned by the name Rohiṇa;
there Vāsava himself guards many jewels.
Beginning from Prajāpati, he himself, being pleased,
ordained that there no clouds rain there, nor is there such a thing as cold or heat.
In the three continents, there exists the livelihood of the social classes and stages of life;
there is neither Rāhu nor the moon, nor likewise envy, malice, or fear.
In that place, there are springs bursting forth from the mountains and mountain cascades;
their food, possessing the six flavors, is provided to them spontaneously.
Among them there is neither inferiority nor superiority, no greed, and no sense of possession;
those men possess health and strength, and are exclusively happy.
For thirty thousand years, they remained established in mental perfection,
possessing happiness, longevity, beauty, as well as the sovereignty of dharma.
This auspicious arrangement of the islands ending with Śālmala should be understood to apply everywhere across the three islands;
thus has the rule for the islands ending with Śālmala been explained.
The continent, however, is circular and surrounded like a wheel by the Suroda ocean, which is twice its size.
Matsya Purāṇa 123. Sūta said:
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall now describe Gomedaka, the sixth continent.
The ocean of sweet water, however, is surrounded by Gomedha.
The extent of that [continent] is twice the extent of Śālmaladvīpa;
in that island, two mountains are to be known as being situated.
The first mountain is named Sumanas, consisting of natural collyrium;
the second is named Kumuda, endowed with all medicinal herbs.
The glorious and vast mountain known as Śātakaumbhamaya is surrounded by the ocean of sugarcane juice, and it is likewise encircled by Gomedaka.
But by the sixth ocean, which is twice the size of the Suroda,
Dhātaki and Kumuda, the two sons of Havya, are very extensive.
The first continent, Saumana, is called Dhātakīkhaṇḍa;
indeed, that which belongs to the Dhātaki tree is known as the first of the first.
The region known as Gomeda is called Sarvasukha;
then, following Kumuda, the second [region] is Kumuda.
These two mountains are circular and remain the highest of all;
to the east of that island stands the mountain Sumanas.
With his feet extending eastward and westward as far as the ocean, he stands thus;
in the western half is Kumuda, who likewise stands in that very manner.
By these foothills of the mountains, that region is indeed divided in two;
the southern half of the island is called Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
To the north of that is Kumuda, the second excellent region;
these two districts are the extensive territories of Gomeda.
Hereafter, I shall describe the seventh and most excellent continent;
it is surrounded by a sea of sugarcane juice and is indeed twice the size of Gomedadvīpa.
The island Puṣkara stands encircling [the sea], surrounded by lotuses;
and the glorious great mountain Citrasānu is surrounded by Puṣkara.
On the eastern half of the island itself stands the great Citrasānu, adorned with various peaks made of jewels and produced from masses of stone.
It is circular with a thousand [yojanas] in circumference and twenty-seven in width;
that one of great strength is indeed twenty-four yojanas in height.
On the western side of the island, the Mānasa mountain stands encircling it,
situated near the shore like the rising moon in the east.
Rising fifty-five thousand yojanas high,
his son Mahāvīta was the protector of the western half.
The region on the eastern half of the mountain is likewise considered to be divided in two;
it is surrounded by the Puṣkara ocean of sweet water.
In extent and in circumference, it is twice that of Gomedaka;
there, human beings live for thirty thousand years.
No error exists for them; this is known as their natural state.
Established in mental perfection, they possess health and an abundance of happiness.
In all three continents, there was happiness, long life, and beauty;
among them, there was neither inferiority nor superiority, for they were equal in terms of vigor and form.
In that place there are neither the slain nor the slayer; likewise, there is no envy, no malice, and no fear;
nor is there greed, nor hypocrisy, nor hatred, nor possessiveness.
Neither truth nor falsehood existed among them, nor did dharma and adharma; likewise, there were no occupations for the castes and stages of life, such as cattle-rearing, trade, or agriculture.
The threefold knowledge, the science of government, service, and indeed punishment—
therein neither rain nor rivers exist, nor is there cold or heat.
The waters there are spring-fed and flow from mountain cascades;
their climate is equal to that of Uttarakuru, and time remains constant there at all times.
That entire period is one of happiness, free from the afflictions of old age;
such is the creation in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and likewise in Mahāvīta.
Thus the continents are surrounded by seven oceans;
each ocean that lies immediately adjacent to a continent is indeed equal in extent to that continent.
In this manner, the increase of the continents and oceans should be understood relative to one another;
and because of the overflowing of the waters, it is designated as "ocean" (samudra).
In the region called Ṛṣabha, the fourfold progeny flourish during the rains;
because the sages truly delight there, it is indeed called Varṣa for that reason.
When the moon rises in the east, the ocean always swells;
and when the dark fortnight wanes and the moon sets, it indeed diminishes.
For when the ocean is being filled, it is filled by its own self;
likewise, when it is diminishing, the depletion of the waters occurs within its own self.
Just as water itself blooms through its union with the rising moon,
so too does that ocean swell at the rising of the moon.
The waters increase and decrease, yet their essence remains neither deficient nor excessive,
during the rising and setting of the moon in the bright and dark fortnights.
The waxing and waning of the ocean correspond to the increase and decrease of the moon;
they say it amounts to five hundred and ten finger-breadths.
The increase and decrease of the waters of the oceans is observed during the lunar phases;
it is remembered as a *dvīpa* (island) because the waters flow around it twice, and it is remembered as an *udadhi* (ocean) because of its abundance of water.
They are called "mountains" (girayaḥ) because they have been swallowed up, and "peaks" (parvatāḥ) because of their connection of joints;
moreover, in Śākadvīpa there is a mountain named Śāka, and for that reason it is so called.
In Kuśadvīpa, there is a clump of kuśa grass in the center of the country;
in Krauñcadvīpa, there is a mountain named Krauñca, which is designated by that name.
In Śālmaladvīpa, that great tree Śālmali is worshipped;
in Gomeda, however, there is a mountain called Gomeda, and for that reason it is so named.
In Puṣkaradvīpa, he is known as Nyagrodha because he is like a lotus;
that portion of Brahmā, born from the Unmanifest, is worshipped by the great gods.
In that place dwells Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, together with the Sādhyas;
there the thirty-three gods worship him along with the great seers.
There that god is worshipped by the gods and the best of great seers;
and from Jambūdvīpa, various kinds of jewels proceed forth.
In all those continents, for the people there, [this occurred] gradually indeed through uprightness,
celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint.
In all those continents and in the regions (varṣas) as described, the measure of lifespan and health increases twofold after each [continent].
There, the subjects are protected by all those who are wise by nature,
and food is always spontaneously provided to them without effort.
There, those people eat that food of great potency which possesses the six tastes;
moreover, beyond Puṣkara stands a great [region] encircling it.
The ocean of sweet water, however, surrounded it on all sides;
and around that ocean of sweet water was a circular mountain range.
That which is both illuminated and unilluminated is called Lokāloka;
there, on one side, is light and on the other, it is without light beyond that point.
But the outer half of the earth, equal in extent to the world-system,
is cut off on all sides and covered by a vast expanse of water.
The waters, ten times greater than the earth, protect the earth on all sides;
and fire, ten times greater than the waters, sustains the waters from every direction.
Vāyu is ten times greater than Agni; established as the sustainer of light, Vāyu is circular and moves transversely, enveloping and supporting all beings.
Likewise, space, being ten times greater, supported the elements of air;
and the source of the elements (Ahaṃkāra), supporting space, was indeed ten times greater than that.
The Great Elements (mahābhūtas), which are ten times greater than the element of being (bhūta) and so forth, are supported by the principle of the Great (mahattattva);
for that mahattattva is itself supported by the infinite unmanifest (avyakta).
Through the relationship of container and contained, those modifications belong to the modified;
earth and the other elements are such modifications, and they are mutually limited.
They are indeed superior to one another and have entered into one another;
thus, having arisen from one another, they are supported by one another.
Because they entered one another, they attained stability;
for they were originally without distinction, yet became distinct through their mutual entry.
The elements beginning with earth and ending with air are indeed limited therein; beyond those elements, non-space (aloka) is traditionally held to exist on all sides.
For thus, in the light of the sky, all things are perceived as distinct on every side,
just as smaller vessels are seen contained within a large vessel.
They exist as mutually distinct through their mutual dependence;
for indeed, light exists in space, and yet distinctions are contained within it.
These principles have been established as mutually superior;
as long as these principles exist, so long is origination said to occur.
In this world, the refinement (saṃskāra) of living beings occurs indeed within the elements;
for without the elements being present here, the production of effects is not possible.
Therefore, the limited divisions are indeed remembered as being of the nature of effects;
yet those divisions, beginning with Mahat, are also of the nature of causes.
Thus, this configuration of the earth,
consisting of the seven continents and oceans, has been described by me according to its true nature, part by part.
Indeed, by way of its extent, its mandala, and its enumeration,
the universal form of Pradhāna is possessed of a single portion of measurement.
O King, this much of the arrangement has been fully revealed by me; this alone is to be heard regarding the arrangement. (Matsya Purāṇa 123.64)
Matsya Purāṇa 124: Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the course of the sun and the moon.
As long as these two, the sun and the moon, continue to shine; MatsP_124.1 //
The extent of the islands and oceans of the seven continents shines forth;
half of that extent belongs to the earth, while the remainder lies outside.
The extent of the surrounding region is where the moon and sun shine;
because of the measurement of that surrounding region, heaven is considered by the wise to be equal [in size] to Budha.
Because he travels toward the three worlds with commonality and without delay, and because he protects the earth through his radiance, the Sun is known as Ravi.
I shall declare again and again the measurement of the moon and the sun;
for because of its greatness, the word "mahat" (great) is indeed used in this sense.
Now, learn of the orb of the sun, which is equal in extent to the diameter of this Bhāratavarṣa, measured in yojanas.
The diameter of the mandala is nine thousand yojanas,
and its circumference in this mandala is three times its diameter.
The moon is twice the diameter and twice the circumference of the sun;
after this, I shall further describe the measurement of the earth in yojanas.
The extent of the mandala consisting of the seven continents and oceans has thus been calculated here according to its measurement in the Purāṇa.
I shall now declare that after due reflection, for those who possess self-conceit;
for those who possessed self-conceit in the past were indeed equal to those who exist here at present.
The gods have indeed surpassed other gods by their forms and even by their names;
therefore, I shall describe the surface of the earth together with the present-day gods.
The entire arrangement of the divine realm is indeed as it is now;
the whole earth is recorded as being five hundred million [yojanas] in extent.
And its measure is half that of Meru, each succeeding one being half the size of the preceding;
it is recorded that there is one crore [yojanas] from the center of Meru in every direction.
Likewise, the extent of half the earth is eighty-nine hundred thousand and fifty thousand [yojanas].
Understand now the extent of the earth's expanse in yojanas:
it is calculated to be three koṭis in width across the four directions.
Likewise, seventy-nine thousand [yojanas] are said to be the extent of the earth consisting of seven continents and oceans. (Matsya Purāṇa 124.16)
The circumference of the terrestrial mandala is three times its width;
it is recorded as being eleven crores of yojanas in calculation.
Likewise, those [continents] number three million seven hundred thousand;
this indeed is reckoned as the circle of the inner earth.
As far as the extent of the arrangement of the stars in the sky,
so far is the extent of the arrangement of the earth.

The region of Mahendra is vast, singular in its essence, meritorious, and adorned with gold;
it lies to the south of Meru and behind Lake Mānasa.
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, dwells in the city of Saṃyamana;
furthermore, on the summit of Mānasa, to the west of Meru.
There is a delightful city named Suṣā belonging even to the wise Varuṇa,
situated in the northern direction upon the very summit of Mount Meru and Lake Mānasa.
The night of Soma is equal even to the city of Mahendra;
however, on the ridge of the Mānasottara mountain, the world-protectors reside in the four directions.
Established for the sake of the orderly arrangement of dharma and for the protection of the world,
she stands above the world-protectors (Lokapālas) during the entire southern course of the sun.
Understand now the movement of the sun when it has reached its limit:
at the commencement of the southern course, the sun glides like a discharged arrow.
Taking up the circle of the luminaries, the Sun constantly revolves;
and when he is positioned in the middle of Amarāvatī, [he moves accordingly].
In the city of Saṃyamana belonging to Vaivasvata, the rising sun is seen;

When the sun rises at midday in the Vaivasvata Saṃyamana,
it is seen rising in the Suṣā and Vāruṇī regions.
When the sun is in Vibhāvarī, it is midnight; in Māhendrī, it is sunset;

the maker of day ascends in Amarāvatī, the city of Mahendra.
At midnight he sets in Saṃyamana, and at sunset in Vāruṇī;
that Sun traverses [the sky] very swiftly, like a whirling firebrand.
The sun moves among the wandering stars as it revolves;
thus it glides along the four sides, ending toward the south.
At sunrise and sunset he rises again and again;
in both the forenoon and the afternoon, he visits two temples of the gods each.
At midday, however, the sun falls [upon the world] with its very splendors and rays;

From this point onward, as the rays diminish, he goes to his setting;
indeed, his rising and setting are traditionally held to mark the beginning and the end [of the day].
Just as it shines in front, so too behind and on both sides;
wherever its rising is observed, that is traditionally known as its rising.
Where they go to their destruction, that is called their setting;
Mount Meru is to the north of all [the continents], and it lies to the south of Lokāloka.
Because of the great distance between the sun and this earth, its rays do not reach it; therefore, it is not seen at night.
When the sun stands there in the middle of Puṣkara, it is seen positioned above like the hundred-thousand-rayed one. (Matsya Purāṇa 124.40)
In a single muhūrta, he traverses a thirtieth part of the earth;
learn this calculation regarding thousands of yojanas.
It is recorded as being one hundred and thirty-one thousand [yojanas] full,
along with another fifty thousand and further increments.

During its northern course, it moves within the solar orbs;

Moving in the northern direction, he traverses one hundred and eighty mandalas;
he proceeds inward, passing through these mandalas.
Learn also the measurement of the maṇḍala in yojanas;

The sun indeed moves its orb from the navel by degrees, like the circumference of a potter’s wheel;

In the southern course, the sun revolves swiftly like a wheel;

Then the wheel revolves even more slowly than those two;

Wandering over the earth for thirty such muhūrtas constitutes one day and night; during both the forenoon and afternoon watches, it indeed revolves through the [lunar] mandalas.
During the sun's northern course, its motion is traditionally held to be slow by day;
however, during its night, the motion of the sun is indeed swift.

The root *loka* means "to see"; however, being without light is non-worldliness (*alokatā*).

Therefore, during the southern and northern solstices, the day increases and the night decreases;
the day swallows the night, and the night swallows the day.
The equinox is ordained as the interval between autumn and spring;
the world is said to extend to the end of light, and beyond the world is called non-light.
The world-protectors stand there in the middle of Lokāloka;
those four great-souled ones remain until the dissolution of all beings.
Sudhāmā, Vairāja, and the progenitor Kardama; Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Ketumān, and he who is Rājasa.
Free from duality, free from pride, free from sloth, and free from possessions,

That which lies to the north of Agastya’s peak and is frequented by divine sages is known as the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), situated outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There dwell the sages who desire offspring, who maintain the *agnihotra* sacrifice;

O Lord of the people, those who desire worldly existence undertake actions that initiate the elements as well as ritual aspirations; their path is the Southern one.
Furthermore, they establish your dharma again in every age through fervent austerity, through established boundaries, and through sacred learning.
Indeed, those who were born previously will be born in the houses of those born later,

Thus revolving, those eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders continue their existence until the dissolution of all beings.
Resorting to the southern path of the Sun until the dissolution of all beings,
this is the enumeration of those performers of ritual action who have betaken themselves to the cremation grounds.
It is indeed for the sake of worldly convention, by means of the production of beings,

In the Dvāpara ages here, the seven Ṛṣis were born as Prajauṣaṇi;

Having thus heard this divine narrative concerning the movements of the sun and the moon, as well as all the planets in their entirety, [the sages] spoke to Lomaharṣaṇa. (Matsya Purāṇa 125.1)

Sūta said:

That Śiśumāra who is situated among the fourteen constellations is Uttānapāda’s son; he is Dhruva, who stands as the central pivot in the sky.

The host of luminaries, which indeed revolves by the will of Dhruva,

Their divisions and conjunctions, as well as the determination of time;

The second is the Āvaha wind; those clouds are dependent upon it, extending from one yojana from here, even up to one and a half yojanas.
The release of rain from them is proclaimed as a torrential downpour;

The wings of those mountains— which could travel at will, were prosperous, and desired the destruction of living beings— were indeed severed by Śakra of great power.
Those great wings of yours, which hold the waters, are named Puṣkara;

Assuming various forms and possessing most terrible voices,

Smoke is the nourishment for all of them without distinction;

From that, clouds are produced; this place is known as being composed of clouds.

The Sun moves upon a shining, swiftly-gliding chariot equipped with a wheel that stands firm, having one felly, five spokes, three naves, made of gold, minute in size, possessing eight rims and a single tire.

The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and likewise the Anuṣṭubh;

indeed, it moves through those orbits with speed, unwinding them.

For this is indeed the station of those who pride themselves on their status throughout the past, future, and present Manvantaras. (Matsya Purāṇa 126.33)
Thus, those fourteen groups of seven indeed dwell in the sun;
they abide within these fourteen Manvantaras.
In summer, winter, and the rainy season, she emits heat, cold, and rain respectively,
day and night, in their proper order.
Turning back its rays day after day, it proceeds while thoroughly satisfying the gods, the ancestors, and human beings;
O gods, they drink [the water] during the waning of time according to the sequence of those days in both the bright and dark fortnights.
Within a month, that nectar of his becomes refined and is preserved within the rays for a bountiful rain;
all the Pitṛs drink that nectar, as do the gods and the gentle Kāvyas.
For by the sun, through the rays that have been increased and then raised once more, and by the rain poured down, the medicinal herbs grow;
and by means of these herbs, mortals conquer hunger with food.
By that [light], the gods are satisfied for half a month, and the ancestors for a month with nectar and *svadhā*;
by food, humans live incessantly; for the Sun, having resorted to it, sustains all that through his rays.
Thus, with its single wheel, the sun moves swiftly;
at the end of the day, it moves there by means of those horses that do not step upon one another.
Hari is carried away by his bay horses; then he drinks water in a thousand streams with those bay steeds;
and again he releases them—yet that Hari himself becomes bewildered by his bay horses.
Traversing day and night on his single-wheeled chariot,
he swiftly circles the seven continents and seven oceans with each of his seven [horses].
Then the chariot remained joined with those horses that possess the forms of meters;
they were capable of assuming any form at will, moving according to desire, and swift as thought.
With green, non-painful, tawny, and sovereign masters who discourse on Brahman,
the mandala is [established] externally and immediately thereafter according to the sequence of the days.
Yoked at the beginning of the kalpa, they flow until the dissolution of all beings;
enveloped by the Vālakhilyas, it revolves through nights and days.
Being praised by the great sages with their composed words,
he is served by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases with songs and dances.
Driven by the sunbeams as if by winged steeds,
the Lord of Day traverses the constellations situated along the celestial paths, and the Moon does likewise.
Likewise, its rays are known to undergo decrease and increase like those of the sun;
and the chariot of the moon should be understood as having three wheels and horses on both sides.
Born from the womb of the waters, the chariot is equipped with horses, a charioteer,
and three white wheels, yoked to the finest of white steeds.
In that chariot, yoked once for all with ten divine horses, unimpeded and swift as thought, they shall carry you until the end of the age.
Harnessed to that chariot are the white horse Cakṣuḥśravas and other steeds of a single color, possessing the luster of conch shells; they carry him along.
Aja, Tripatha, Vṛṣa, Vājī, Nara, Haya,
Aṃśumān, Saptadhātu, Haṃsa, and likewise Vyomamṛga.
Thus, by these names, the ten horses of the Moon carry the divine Moon until the end of the eon.
Surrounded by the gods and accompanied by the ancestors,
Soma proceeds when the sun has moved beyond the beginning of the bright fortnight of the moon.
The upper portion of the moon is filled up according to the sequence of days;
thereafter, the sun causes the consumed moon to expand again.
And for fifteen days, the Sun, filling it with a single ray,
bestowed a portion after portion day by day.
As he dissolves into the Suṣumṇā, his digits indeed increase during the bright fortnight;
therefore, they wane during the dark fortnight, while in the bright fortnight they are replenished.
Thus, by the solar energy, the body of the moon is nourished;
on the full-moon day, it appears bright with its orb completely full.
In this manner, Soma waxes during the bright fortnights day by day;
thereafter, from the second day until the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, he wanes.
The gods drink the essence of the waters, O Indu, which consists of pure sap and is composed of water— sweet, gentle, and like nectar.
Having been gathered for half a month by the splendor of the sun,
they attend upon Soma at the full moon (paurṇamāsī) when he has arrived for the purpose of being consumed as nectar.
For one night, at the beginning of the dark fortnight of the moon, the gods indeed dwell together with the ancestors and the ṛṣis while the moon is facing toward the sun.
For the supreme Self is diminished by the sequence of its being drunk away through its digits;
three hundred and thirty-three [years] are thus reduced by thirty-three.
"Thirty-three thousand gods indeed drink the Soma;
O Kṛṣṇā, while it is being thus drunk, those digits increase. (Matsya Purāṇa 126.64)
Those bright [fortnights] wane, while the dark ones indeed cause [them] to swell;
thus, by the sequence of days, it occurs for the yellow [fortnight] and also for the gods and the moon.
Having drunk for half a month, those gods go to the new moon;
and the ancestors approach the moon on the night of the new moon.
Then, when the moon has only a small portion of its fifteenth part remaining,
the ancestors [receive offerings] again in the afternoon on that final day of the fortnight.
The remaining digits that were left over drink the time for two *kalās* each;
that nectar was emitted from the rays on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
At the completion of half a month, those known as the Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas go forth after drinking the nectar.
And all those who are called the Kavyas among the Pitṛs are indeed the years;
O twice-born ones, they are remembered as the five-year cycles known as the Kavyas.
The Saumyas, the Sutapas, and likewise the Barhiṣads,
as well as the Agniṣvāttas— these three classes of twice-born ones are to be known as established in the creation of the Pitṛs.
When the fifteenth digit is being drunk by the ancestors,
until it is completely exhausted, that is indeed the fifteenth part.
Likewise, on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), his [the moon's] opposite [half] becomes full;
indeed, the waxing and waning of the moon occur at the beginning of the fortnights, with its death occurring on the sixteenth day.
Thus, those waning and waxing of the night-maker (niśākara) are caused by the sun.
Matsya Purāṇa 127: Sūta said:
I shall now further describe the chariot of Svarbhānu, the planet among the lunar mansions.
Now, the chariot of the son of Soma was indeed composed of light and radiant white.
He was yoked with ten bay horses, swift as the wind:
white, bay, dappled, dark-blue, dusky, and crimson.
Śveta, Harita, Pṛṣata, and Vṛṣṇi—these ten highly fortunate sons were born from Vāta and were all preeminent. (Matsya Purāṇa 127.3)
Then Bhaumaratha is also known as the eight-limbed golden chariot;
with eight red horses born of fire and bearing banners,
that Kumāra indeed moves in straight, curved, and winding paths.
Therefore, the learned Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods and a descendant of Aṅgiras,
moves about in a golden chariot drawn by white horses.
He who dwells for a year in a zodiac sign equipped with eight yoked horses and banners arisen from fire goes to his own direction by means of that [sign].
Bhārgava travels by means of that chariot, which possesses swift speed and is yoked to eight horses resembling fire and adorned with banners. *Matsya Purāṇa* 127.7.
Then Śanaiścara also, having mounted a chariot made of black iron, proceeds with his powerful horses that possess the speed of the wind; such is this Śani.
Just as Svarbhānu’s eight black horses, swift as the wind and well-harnessed,
carry his chariot composed of darkness.
Rāhu, whose abode is the sun, goes to the moon during the lunar nodes;
from the moon he goes to the sun at the end of those nodes, when the darkness has passed.
Then, Ketumān’s eight horses were as swift as the wind;
they had the color of straw-smoke, lean bodies, and were most formidable.
These vehicles of the planets have indeed been described by me along with their chariots;
they are all fastened to Dhruva and bound by cords of wind.
Being thus set in motion, they indeed carry [the world] according to their respective functions,
bound by invisible cords of wind called *vātarajjus*.
Bound by that [wind], the moon, sun, and planets revolve in the sky,
as does the host of luminaries including Dhruva, which follows after it.
Just as a boat on river water is carried along with the water,
so too shall the temples of the gods be carried by the force of the wind;
therefore, those which are held aloft in the sky are called "temples of the gods."
As many stars as there may be, so many are its rays;
all of them, fixed to Dhruva, revolve and cause [the world] to revolve.
Just as an oil-press wheel revolves when it is set in motion,
so too do the luminaries revolve in every direction, bound by the wind.
Driven by the wind-circles, they move like a whirling firebrand;
because they flow forth [from it], it is therefore known as the Pravaha.
Thus, bound to Dhruva, this host of luminaries revolves;
this Dhruva in the sky, consisting of stars, is said to be in the shape of a porpoise.
Whatever sin one commits during the day, one is released from it at night upon seeing her;
she is as many stars as there are situated within the body of the *śiśumāra*.
Having observed the years, one may live for that long or even longer,
provided one understands the form of the porpoise in its entirety through its various divisions.
Then, his upper jaw is to be known as Uttānapāda along with Sottara;
Yajña is to be known as the lower jaw, while Dharma is situated upon the head.
Nārāyaṇa is in the heart; the Sādhyas and the Aśvins are in the two front feet;
Varuṇa and Aryaman are in his two hind thighs.
The year is to be known as being in the penis, and Mitra is situated in the anus;
in the tail are Agni, Mahendra, Marīci, Kaśyapa, and Dhruva.
This pillar composed of stars neither sets nor rises;
nor do the lunar mansions, the moon, the sun, and the planets, together with the hosts of stars.
Facing its face, all of them, having become like wheels, remain in the sky;
presided over by Dhruva, they revolve clockwise around Dhruva alone.
They revolve around the best of gods, the fixed Dhruva, who stands as the central pivot in heaven;
among those descendants of Āgnīdhra and Kaśyapa, he is the supreme Dhruva.
Alone, he wanders within the interior summit of Meru,
taking up the circle of luminaries while facing downwards;
gazing upon Meru, he moves in a counter-clockwise direction.
Matsya Purāṇa 128. The sages said: "Everything that has been spoken by you has been heard by us in its entirety."
How did the celestial abodes come to be? Describe the luminaries once more.
Sūta said: I shall explain all this— the course of the sun and the moon,
as well as how the abodes of the gods belong to the sun and the moon.
At the dawning of the fire at night, by the power of Brahmā, whose source is unmanifest,
this world was indeed unevolved and enveloped in the darkness of night.
When this [universe], remaining as the four elements, was presided over by Brahmā,
the Blessed Self-existent One (Svayambhū) appeared there, the accomplisher of the true purpose of the principles of the world.
Wandering in the form of a firefly, he reflected upon manifestation,
knowing that at the beginning of the kalpa-time, fire had resorted to water and earth.
Having gathered together for the sake of manifestation, he became threefold once more;
that which is the cooker in this world, the king, is called Agni.
That which blazes as the sun is known as the pure fire (Śuci);
it is also the lightning-fire, the digestive fire (Jāṭhara), the lunar fire (Saumya), and the lightning-fire that has water for its fuel.
One fire is attained through splendors, while another is attained even without fuel;
that fire which has wood for its fuel is produced by friction, and it is extinguished by water.
The fire that is radiant and burning is indeed devoid of luster when it possesses the characteristics of Soma;
and that which is in the white mandala is without heat and does not shine.
When the sun sets, its solar radiance departs by one quarter and enters the fire at night;
therefore, the fire shines.
But when the sun has risen again, the heat of the fire enters the foot of the fire of light;
therefore, it burns during the day.
Luminosity and heat reside in the energy of the sun and fire;
through their mutual interpenetration, they nourish one another day and night.
When the sun rises again in the northern half of the earth, as well as in this southern half,
night enters the waters.
Therefore, the waters become copper-colored due to the entry of day and night;
when the sun has set, the day indeed enters the waters.
Therefore, at night, the waters are seen again as bright and shining;
by this sequential process, [the light reaches] both the southern and northern halves of the earth.
For at sunrise and sunset, the day and night enter the waters;
and that sun which blazes there drinks the waters with its rays.
This fire, however, has a thousand feet; it resembles a red jar, and it draws [substances] from all sides through a thousand channels.
From the rivers, oceans, lakes, and wells,
there issues forth through his thousand rays a flow of cool, rain, and warm water.
Of those, four hundred channels of variegated forms pour forth rain;
they are the Candanas, the Medhyas, the Ketanas, and likewise the Cetanās.
All the rays are immortal and life-sustaining, and they are the dispensers of rain; those thirty rays, arising from the frost, are known to be mutually connected.
All the rays of the sun are drunk up by the moon, the stars, and all the planets.
These are the Madhyās, as well as others— the Hlādinīs, the creators of snow,
the Śuklās, the Kakubhas, the Gāvas, and those which are the Viśvasṛts.
All thirty of those are known by name as the Śuklās, the emitters of heat;
for they all sustain humans, gods, and ancestors.
Constantly satisfying men with medicinal herbs, the ancestors with the svadhā offering, and all the gods with nectar; MatsP_128.23 //
In spring and summer, it heats gradually with three [seasons];
and likewise in the rainy season and autumn, it rains with four.
In the winter and the cool season, the shedding of frost occurs again for three months;
then, by means of the *svadhā* offering, he bestows strength upon the plants and nectar once more.
Just as the sun bestows immortality upon the three [Vedas] within the immortal,
so too does the thousandfold solar ray accomplish the welfare of the world.
Reaching its seasonal course, it divides again into a thousandfold;
thus is the white, radiant mandala known as the world. (Matsya Purāṇa 128.27)
The moon is the foundation and the very source of the constellations, planets, and soma;
all the constellations and planets are to be known as originating from the sun.
Suṣumnā is that solar ray which nourishes the waning moon;
she is the golden-haired one in the east, who indeed creates the source of the stars.
To the south, Viśvakarman indeed nourished Budha with his ray;
and he who was behind, known as Viśvāvasu, is remembered as Śukrayoni.
The ray named Saṃvardhana is the source of blood,
while the sixth ray, Aśvabhū, is indeed the source of Bṛhaspati.
Furthermore, the ray of the sun nourishes Śanaiścara;
because those [rays] do not diminish, they are known as *nakṣatra*.
These fields indeed approach the sun with its rays;
the sun takes possession of those fields, and from that they attain the state of being lunar mansions (nakṣatra).

For those of virtuous soul who have crossed from this world to that world, these [stars] are called *tārakā* because they cause crossing, and they are called *śuklikā* because of their whiteness. (Matsya Purāṇa 128.34)
Through the conjunction of his splendor with those of the divine and earthly lineages in every respect, he is called Āditya because of his scorching heat.
This verbal root *sravati* is declared to have the meaning of "flowing";
because he causes the radiance (*tejas*) to flow, he is therefore remembered as Savitṛ.
The root *cand*, meaning "to shine," is said to be the primary verbal root [for this name],
because it signifies whiteness, immortality, coolness, and refreshment.
In the divine, radiant, and moving orbs of the sun and moon—
composed of water and fire, white, auspicious, and resembling rounded jars— MatsP_128.38.
The Karmadevas dwell in all these places throughout all the Manvantaras, as do the sages, the suns, the planets, and so forth.
Those divine abodes are indeed known as "places" (sthānas);
Sūrya entered the solar place, and likewise Soma entered the lunar place.
Śukra entered Śaukra, the radiant sixteen-spoked station;
Bṛhaspati entered Bṛhattva, and Lohita entered Lohita.
Śanaiścara entered his own station, and likewise Śānaiścara;
Budha also entered the station of Budha, as did Svarbhānu into that of Bhānu.
All the stars and the constellations enter into these luminous bodies;
they are to be known as the dwellings of the gods for those of meritorious deeds.
These stations endure until the dissolution of all beings;
indeed, they are the abodes of the gods throughout all the Manvantaras.
Out of pride, those gods remain there again and again;
yet those who have passed away pass away with their predecessors, and those who are to be will exist together with the future gods.
The residents dwell together with the present gods;
the divine Sūrya Vivasvat is the eighth son of Aditi.
The radiant and righteous god Soma is remembered as a Vasu;
Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu and priest of the Asuras, is to be known as a Daitya.
Bṛhaspati, of great splendor, the preceptor of the gods and son of Aṅgiras, is known as Budha; he is the son of the Moon and is indeed called Manohara.
Śanaiścara, who is deformed, was born as the son of Vivasvat from Saṃjñā;
moreover, that youthful lord of the red [planets], Agni, was born from Vikeśī.
The daughters of Dakṣa, known by the names of the constellations, are recorded as having been born in the fields [of the moon].
Svarbhānu, the son of Siṃhikā, was an Asura who brought about the destruction of beings.
He is proclaimed as the presiding deity (abhimānin) over the moon, the sun, the planets, and the lunar mansions;
these have been declared as the locations, as well as the deities who reside therein.
It is white, like fire, divine, and like the thousand-rayed Vivasvat;
it is the abode of the thousand-rayed one, consisting of both water and light.
The source of hope for what is pleasing is situated in the house of the sun's rays;
Śukra has sixteen rays, and he is indeed the deity whose nature is water.
Lohita, however, has nine rays, and his station is indeed to be attained;
that of Vedhas, moreover, is twelve-rayed and yellow like turmeric.
The abode of Śani has eight rays; it is black, aged, and made of iron.
The station of Svarbhānu, however, is made of steel and is the dwelling place of those who torment living beings.
The stars are the abodes of those who have performed good deeds, while their rays are golden;
they are called *tārakā* because they enable one to cross over, and they are also called *tārakā* because of their whiteness.
The diameter of the sun is recorded as nine thousand yojanas;
its orb is three times that, which is the extent of the sun.
The diameter of the moon is recorded as being twice that of the sun;
its orb is recorded as being three times the breadth of the moon.
Above all, the stars are the mandalas that have been released;
they measure half a yojana in extent, while the other groups are smaller than them.
Having become equal [in size], Svarbhānu then glides beneath it,
having raised up the terrestrial shadow fashioned in the form of a circle.
The third station, created by Brahmā, consists of darkness;
departing from the Sun, he goes to the Moon during the lunar phases.
On the solar parvan days, he goes from Soma back to the Sun;
because he strikes [the sun] with his own radiance, he is remembered as Svarbhānu.
The diameter and circumference of Bhārgava are prescribed as being one-sixteenth part of those of the Moon; such is its measurement in yojanas.
Bṛhaspati is to be known as having one-quarter less than Bhārgava;
both Ketu and Vakra are recorded as having one-quarter less than Bṛhaspati.
The wise one should know that the dimensions of those two [the sun and moon] are each reduced by one-quarter;
indeed, those forms which exist here in embodied shapes as stars and constellations [are likewise diminished].
The forms of Mercury are equal in size to those of the Moon,
while the forms of the planets Tārā and the constellations (nakṣatras) are indeed smaller than one another.
Five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, two hundred, and one hundred;
these are the stars that have been assigned above all the mandalas.
They measure half a yojana each, and none is smaller than that;
moreover, those planets among them which are above and characterized by cruelty are [of that same size].
Saura, Aṅgiras, and Vakra are to be known as slow-moving;
below them, moreover, are four other great planets.
Soma, Sūrya, Budha, and Bhārgava are the swift-moving [planets];
and as many as there are nakṣatras, so many millions are the stars.
Indeed, of all the planets, the sun moves below them;
having made its orb broad, the moon moves above it.
The circle of constellations also extends upward from the Moon;
Mercury is above the constellations, and Venus is above Mercury.
Vakra is above Bhārgava; above Vakra is Bṛhaspati;
above him is Śanaiścara, situated above the Teacher of the Gods (Bṛhaspati).
Above Saturn, the constellation of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣimaṇḍala) is to be known;
above the Seven Sages is Dhruva, and within Dhruva is the entire celestial realm (tridiva).
Then, the distance between each successive planet above the circle of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) is two hundred thousand and one thousand yojanas.
The stars and the planets are situated one above the other;
and the planets, as well as the moon and the sun, exist in the sky with divine splendor.
And as they move according to a fixed order, the moon,
the sun, the planets, and the stars are joined with the lunar mansions, occupying their respective houses of depression and exaltation.
In both union and separation, living beings perceive one another simultaneously;
for they stand thus toward each other and are likewise joined with one another.
The wise should understand their conjunction without confusion;
such indeed is the arrangement of the earth and the luminaries. (Matsya Purāṇa 128.79)
Of the continents, the oceans, and likewise the mountains;
of the regions and the rivers, and indeed those who dwell within them.
Thus, this arrangement of the luminaries occurs solely by the power of the sun;
its revolution is within the space between them, and it is contracted toward the Pole Star.
Extending everywhere among them, it is elevated and circular in shape;
it was fashioned by the Lord for the purpose of worldly convention.
"At the beginning of the kalpa, this entire arrangement consisting of light was indeed established by the Self-existent One (Svayambhū) with prior intention."— Matsya Purāṇa 128.83.
The universal form of Pradhāna, which is known as its expansion,
cannot be accurately enumerated by anyone with the physical eye of a mortal man, even regarding the coming and going of the luminaries.
Matsya Purāṇa 129:
The Sages said:
"How did the Blessed One, Maheśvara, formerly attain the state of being the Foe of Cities (Purāri)?"
And how did the god burn it? Tell us that in detail.
Out of great respect, we all ask you again and again: O giver of honor, tell us how that Tripura, so difficult to assail and fashioned by the magic of Maya,
was consumed by the god with a single arrow.
Sūta said: Listen how the god Bhava shattered Tripura.
There was an asura named Maya, a great master of illusion and the progenitor of all illusions. *Matsya Purāṇa* 129.3.
Defeated in battle, he performed supreme austerity;
while he was thus practicing penance, O brahmins, two other Daityas [assisted him] out of favor.
Aiming for that very task, the powerful Vidyunmālī and the heroic one named Tāraka performed supreme penance. (Matsya Purāṇa 129.5)
Overwhelmed by Maya’s splendor, they stood at his side and blazed like the three worlds incarnate, or like the three fires.
Scorching the three worlds, those Dānavas performed austerities:
lying on beds of water during the winter, and likewise undergoing the five fires during the summer.
And likewise during the rainy season, they spent their dear lives in the open air,
subsisting on fruits, roots, flowers, and water.
Subsisting on various kinds of food, their bark garments were covered with mud;
they were submerged in both pure and impure mud and water-weeds.
Thereupon they became fleshless, emaciated, and covered with a network of veins;
by the power of their asceticism, [the world] was shaken as if by a mighty force.
The entire world became lusterless, and speech was uttered only faintly,
as the worlds were being consumed by those three fires of the Dānavas.
Before them, the Grandfather, the kinsman of the world, appeared;
then those who had committed the rash act spoke to him as he arrived suddenly.
The Daityas indeed praised their own grandfather;
then Brahmā addressed those Dānavas, who were blazing with the power of their asceticism.
Then, his eyes and face filled with joy, he said:
"O children, I have indeed come as a granter of boons to you, having been gratified by your ascetic penance."
"Let that which is desired be chosen, and let that which is longed for be spoken of.
Being addressed in this manner, they acknowledged their grandfather.
Viśvakarman Maya, his eyes wide with joy, said:
"O Lord, in former times, during the Tārakāmaya war between the gods and the Daityas..."
Defeated, struck, and even slain by the weapons of the gods, they fled, trembling with fear, due to their persistent enmity toward them.
Seeking refuge and seeking peace, we know of no refuge at all;
yet, by the power of your asceticism and likewise by my devotion, [I have found it]. (Matsya Purāṇa 129.18)
"I desire to build that fortress which is difficult even for the gods to overcome;
and within that triple fortress, O best of the accomplished, let it be made by me. (Matsya Purāṇa 129.19)
Of the curses of those dwelling on the earth and those born of the water, of the splendors of sages, of the weapons of the gods, and of the gods themselves and Prajāpati; 129.20.
"May Tripura be inviolable, if that is dear to you," Viśvakarman was thus addressed by Viśvakarman at that time.
Laughing, he spoke these words to Maya, the lord of the Daitya hosts:
"O Dānava, there is no such thing as immortality for one of wicked conduct. (MatsP 129.22)
"Therefore, let the construction of a fortress be undertaken even at this very moment.
Having heard these words of the Grandfather (Brahmā), the Dānava Maya did exactly so.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke again to Brahmā, the lotus-born: "He who might utterly consume that fortress with a single arrow discharged but once—" *Matsya Purāṇa* 129.24.
"In battle, he shall slay even those who are otherwise unslayable; he shall remain as the survivor.
Having said, "So be it," the divine Grandfather [Brahmā] addressed Maya.

Just as an object obtained in a dream vanishes upon waking, so too did he disappear right there when the Grandfather had departed; and once the Grandfather was gone, the Daityas lost their splendor, like that of the moon eclipsed by Rāhu.
By virtue of the boon they had received and through their ascetic power, those exceedingly mighty ones shone forth;
that highly intelligent Dānava Maya, moreover, was the best among the bulls [of his race].
Then he reflected: "I have resolved to make it impregnable;
how indeed can this Tripura made by me become truly unassailable? (Matsya Purāṇa 129.28)
That divine city shall dwell under my protection and not by others;
of this there is no doubt, for that city cannot be destroyed even by a single arrow of his.
The gods must likewise provide for me the deliberation of counsel;
let each of the cities, moreover, have an extent of one hundred yojanas.
Their width shall each be one hundred yojanas,
and through conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, their ancient construction will come to pass.
And under the conjunction of Puṣya, they shall meet one another in heaven;
whoever shall obtain those [weapons] when they are joined with the conjunction of Puṣya, [he shall succeed].
In ancient times, he will slay hundreds with a single blow—
one made of iron upon the surface of the earth, and one made of silver in the sky.
Above the silver [city], however, there shall be a golden city;
thus, joined by these three cities, it shall become Tripura,
difficult to assail with intervals of a hundred yojanas in width.
It was resplendent with watchtowers, mechanical engines, and *śataghnī* weapons, along with wheels, spikes, stones, and shakers;
its gates were like Mount Mandara and Meru, and it shone brilliantly with the peaks of its ramparts.

Who indeed, other than the one Blessed One with three eyes, would be capable of destroying Tripura, which was protected by Maya known as Satāraka and also guarded by Taḍinmālin? (Matsya Purāṇa 129.36)
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 130:
Sūta said:
Thus filled with anxiety, the Daitya [reflected] upon that which arises from the power of divine means.
He constructed the triple city, a fortress traversed by the movement of thought.
By this path there is a rampart; here and there are gate-towers (gopura);
here is a turret-gate (aṭṭālakadvāra), and here is a turret-gate-tower (aṭṭālagopura).
"Let there also be a broad royal highway for you here, as well as main streets,
side streets, crossroads, and even squares."
This is the location of the inner apartments and here is the abode of Rudra;
indeed, there are waterfalls, ponds, large oblong tanks, and lakes here as well.
There are groves and assembly halls there, as well as gardens;
and there is a charming exit for the Dānavas at this place.
Thus did he, the knower of ancient lore, conceive in his mind;
we have heard that the city was created by Maya as the "Tripura" (the triple city).
As for that city made of black iron which was constructed by Maya,
the lord named Tāraka dwelt there as its established sovereign.
As for that city made of silver, resembling the full moon,
the lord there was Vidyunmālī, like a cloud garlanded with lightning.
And as for the city presided over by Suvarṇa, which had been built by Maya,
Maya himself went there as its sovereign lord.
The city of Tāraka is there at a distance of one hundred yojanas,
and the city of Vidyunmālin is also at an interval of one hundred yojanas.
In former times, that great city of Maya, which resembled Mount Meru,
was [constructed] by Maya in a mere moment through the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism.
The Daitya Maya constructed Tripura just as Trinetra [Śiva] fashioned the Puṣpaka chariot; for wherever Maya went while building the city from one city to another, [he left it behind].
In those very places, there are praised abodes belonging to Varuṇa himself,
made of gold, silver, and iron, by the hundreds and thousands.
The cities of the enemies of the immortals shine, adorned with jewels,
graced by hundreds of palaces, and towering with gabled chambers.
All these shall be accessible for enjoyment by everyone, transcending all worlds,
and provided with gardens, ponds, wells, and lotus-lakes.
There were groves of Aśoka trees filled with the songs of cuckoos,
as well as vast picture galleries and excellent four-winged mansions.
Seven, eight, and ten stories high, they were honored by Maya,
adorned with many banners and flags, and decorated with garlands and wreaths.
Resounding with the tinkling of networks of bells, fragrant and vast,
they were well-joined, plastered, and provided with flowers and offerings.
The dark clouds of sacrificial smoke and the full water-jars,
appearing as if they were covering the sky, resembled rows of swans.
In the city of Tripura, the houses arranged in rows shine as if they are laughing at the splendor of the moon with their hanging strings of pearls.
With *mallikā*, jasmine, and other flowers, scented with perfumes and incense,
he was constantly gratified by the equal pleasures of the five senses, as if by virtuous men.
In that Tripura, the ramparts, resembling mountain fortifications, were marked with gold, silver, iron, and the like, as well as with gems, jewels, and collyrium.
In each of those cities, hundreds upon hundreds of gate-towers,
adorned with banners and flags, are seen like mountain peaks.
Even the cities of Tripura were delightful with the sound of anklets,
and the maidens' quarters there possessed a splendor exceeding that of heaven.
With pleasure groves and monasteries, with ponds, banyan trees, and crossroads;
with lakes and rivers, as well as forests and parks.
The exits from Tripura were graced with divine enjoyments and various jewels in abundance; they were made beautiful with heaps of flowers,
and their moats were made a hundred fathoms deep by those who ward off illusions.
Having heard of that supreme construction of the fortress made by Maya, whose deeds and prowess were marvelous,
thousands of the sons of Diti— the enemies of the king of the gods— arrived there, possessing infinite valor.
Then Tripura became filled with those Asuras— who crushed their arrogant enemies, who were Janārdanas [in prowess], and who resembled mountain-elephants—
just as the sky was once filled by the cloud-givers with abundant waters.
Matsya-Purāṇa 131. Sūta said:
When the three citadels had been constructed as a fortress by Maya, the architect of the Asuras,
That fortress fell into a state of peril due to the gods and asuras who were bound by enmity.
Accompanied by their wives and sons, armed and resembling the God of Death,
they joyfully entered the houses assigned to them by me.
Like many lions in a forest or crocodiles in the ocean,
they were like a body composed of many joined parts through their wrath and extreme harshness.
In that same way, that city of Tripura, occupied by powerful enemies of the gods,
became crowded and filled with hundreds of millions of Daityas.
Emerging even from the netherworld (pātāla), the abode of the Dānavas,
those who resembled clouds and subsisted upon the mountains came forth to attend upon him.
Whatever desire anyone might long for, once they have attained it by taking refuge in Tripura,
Maya provides that very thing there through his power of illusion.
In the evenings accompanied by the moon, in lakes filled with lotuses, in groves with mango trees, and in the forests of those whose wealth is asceticism; 131.7.
With handsome limbs, their bodies smeared with sandalwood paste like rutting elephants,
they wore polished ornaments and garments, and were adorned with bright garlands and unguents.
The Dānavas constantly took delight with their beloved women, who were skilled in pleasing acts and gave rise to gestures of amorous allure, and they remained truly joyful.
Rejoicing in the place created by Maya, the great Asuras themselves set their minds upon wealth, dharma, and pleasure.
For those enemies of the gods who were joined with Tripura,
time passed happily in Tripura, just as it does for those dwelling in heaven.
Sons served their fathers and wives likewise served their husbands;
moreover, quarrels ceased and abundant affection prevailed.
Even though he was powerful, unrighteousness did not afflict those residing in the three cities,
for the sons of Diti were worshipping Hara in the sanctuary of Tripura.
The sounds of "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*) resounded, along with Vedic chants of benediction,
as well as the sounds of flutes and lutes mingled with the tinkling of their own anklets.
And the laughter of excellent women, which agitates the mind,
is constantly heard in Tripura as the lords of the Dānavas take their pleasure.
As they were worshipping the gods and bowing down to the Brahmins,
a great length of time passed while they recited mantras for the sake of dharma, artha, and kāma.
Then Alakṣmī and Asūyā, as well as Tṛṣ and Bubhukṣā,
along with Kali and Kalaha, entered Tripura together.
Having entered Tripura at the time of twilight, those formidable and terrible beings dwelt together,
just as diseases take up residence within bodies.
All these [demons], entering the interior of Tripura by means of Māyā,
were seen by him in a dream as terrifying Dānavas entering [the city].
And when the thousand-rayed sun, the maker of auspicious light, had risen,
Maya entered the assembly hall like a cloud approaching two suns.
Seated upon a delightful throne adorned with gold, resembling the peak of Mount Meru,
they were like rain-clouds resting upon the summit of the Golden Mountain.
On both sides sat the two Dānavas named Tāraka and Vidyunmālī at the side of Maya,
like two young elephants beside a bull elephant.
Then all the enemies of the gods, the Dānavas who were the foes of the deities, having been pierced deeply in the field of battle, sat down with their anger unabated.

When they had all sat down and were comfortably seated, Maya, the creator of illusions, spoke thus to the Dānavas: matsya uvāca: evaṃ bruvati vai maye dānavāste samantataḥ / praṇipatya mayamūcurhṛṣṭāḥ prāñjalayastadā // MatsP_131.25 // The Fish said: While Maya was speaking thus, those Dānavas, having prostrated themselves before Maya, then spoke with joy and palms joined in reverence. dānavā ūcuḥ: bhobhoḥ paritrātumarhasi asmānsarvānprapannān bhavān / tvaṃ hi naḥ paramo devaḥ kṛcchreṣvapi gatistathā // MatsP_131.26 // The Dānavas said: O sir, you ought to protect us all who have sought refuge in you; for you are our supreme deity and likewise our refuge even in times of distress. matsya uvāca: evamukte tu taiḥ sarvairmayo māyāvinaṃ tadā / abravīt prahasan vākyaṃ dānavāṃstān samantataḥ // MatsP_131.27 // The Fish said: When they had all spoken thus, Maya then addressed those illusory Dānavas, laughing as he spoke these words to them on all sides. maya uvāca: bhobhoḥ śṛṇuta madvākyaṃ dānavāḥ prītimānvaham / yuṣmākaṃ ca hitārthāya yadbravīmi nibodhata // MatsP_131.28 // Maya said: O Dānavas, listen to my words; I am full of affection for you, so understand what I say for the sake of your welfare. matsya uvāca: evamukte tu te sarve mayaṃ procuḥ prahṛṣṭavat / bhagavañchrotumicchāmastattvaṃ brūhi mahāmate // MatsP_131.29 // The Fish said: When this was said, they all replied to Maya with great joy: "O Blessed One, we wish to hear it; tell us the truth, O high-minded one!
