"O sky-dwellers, O you whose voices resound through the sky, O sons of Dākṣāyaṇī!
Listen, for this terrifying dream has been seen by me."
There were four women and three mortal men who brought fear;
with mouths ablaze from the fire of their anger, they entered [the city] of the destroyer of Tripura.
Having entered the city in their wrath, those of incomparable prowess entered the bodies [of the inhabitants],
becoming many-bodied beings.
And this city of Tripura, together with its houses and you all, has been submerged in the waters of the ocean by the darkness.
A beautiful woman, naked, mounted upon an owl and likewise upon a donkey; laughing with women and kissing a man, as does a woman;
the man has a tilaka of sesame seeds, four legs, and three eyes.
By whom that young woman was driven away and I myself was awakened;
such a young woman, so terrifying, has been seen by me.
"O sons of Diti, such a dream as this has indeed been seen;
for how could it have been seen but to bring hardship upon the Asuras? (Matsya Purāṇa 131.31)
If I am a king worthy of you, and if you know what is beneficial, listen with attentive minds; you ought not to be displeased.
Having abandoned desire, envy, anger, and malice,
abide in truth, self-restraint, dharma, and the teaching of the Sage.
Let propitiatory rites be performed and let Maheśvara be worshipped, so that this dream may indeed come to an end. (Matsya Purāṇa 131.34)
"Surely Rudra, the three-eyed god of gods, is incensed with us,
since these future events are being seen by us here in Tripura, O Asuras."
Avoiding strife and cultivating uprightness,
await the dawning of sleep and likewise the dawning of time.
Having heard these words spoken by me, "The sons of Dākṣāyaṇī," they were seen to be possessed by states of anger and envy, and thus destined for destruction.
Perceiving their own destruction and pervaded by misfortune,
they looked at one another right there with eyes filled with rage.
Then the Dānavas residing in Tripura, overwhelmed by fate,
abandoned truth and righteousness and set about performing improper deeds.
They hate the meritorious Brahmins and do not honor the deities;
they do not respect their gurus and even provoke one another to anger.
They engage in quarrels and mock their own duties;
they revile one another, speaking only of "I. (Matsya Purāṇa 131.41)
They speak loudly to their elders, yet when honored they do not address them;
suddenly their eyes fill with tears, and they become restless. (Matsya Purāṇa 131.42)
They eat curd-mixed barley, milk, and wood-apples during the nights; they sleep there while remaining covered and in a state of impurity from their food.
Having urinated, they perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) without having washed their feet;
devoid of proper conduct regarding purity, they lie down upon their beds.
They shrink back out of fear, just as a mouse does before cats;
having approached their own wives in secret, these shameless men are not purified.
Having formerly been well-behaved, they have now fallen into wickedness;
the inhabitants of Tripura harass both the gods and those whose wealth is their asceticism.
Though they were restrained by Maya,
those seekers of strife, doing only what was displeasing to the brahmins, met with their destruction.
The Vaibhrāja forest, as well as Nandana and the Caitraratha grove, the Aśoka and Varāśoka, and also Sarvartuka; MatsP_131.48 //
Following the will of the former gods, they become enraged and destroy heaven— the abode of the deities— as well as the forests rich in asceticism.
With its temples and hermitages laid waste, and its gods, brahmins, and priests shattered,
the world was overrun by the wicked followers of the King of the Immortals, like a field of grain beset by swarms of locusts.
Matsya-Purāṇa 132. Sūta said:
When the Dānavas were devoid of virtue, corrupted, and evil-minded...
While the worlds were being destroyed and the forests of those whose wealth was asceticism [were likewise perishing].
When those creatures dwelling in the sky let out lion-like roars and became terrified,
the three worlds were bewildered by fear and plunged into a darkness as thick as a forest.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Pitṛs, and the hosts of Maruts,
being terrified, came for refuge to Brahmā, the Great-Grandfather.
They approached Brahmā, who was seated upon that golden lotus;
together they bowed to him who has five faces and four countenances and spoke.
"O sinless one, the Dānavas residing in Tripura, though well-protected by you, are harassing us here as if we were mere servants; therefore, please give us your command."
O Grandfather, just as swans depart at the arrival of the clouds, or as deer flee from the fear of a lion,
so indeed do we wander out of fear of the Dānavas.
O sinless one, because they were being led astray by the Dānavas, the names of their sons as well as those of their wives were forgotten.
The dwellings of the gods are shattered and hermitages are destroyed;
these acts are perpetrated by the Dānavas, who are blinded by the delusion of their own hair-like senses, and they wander about [in chaos].
If you do not swiftly protect the world from the dānavas who have fled in haste,
this universe will be despoiled by them, becoming devoid of gods and devoid of human hermitages.
Thus addressed by the thirty gods, the Lord Pitāmaha, whose lotus-born origin is his source,
replied to the thirty gods including Indra, he whose face is like the moon.
O gods, O best among the wise, this end has now arrived for that boon which was granted by me out of fear, as I previously declared, O deities.
And that triple city, which is their abode, O bulls among the gods,
must be destroyed by the release of a single arrow, not by showers of arrows.
And among you, O bulls among the gods, I do not see anyone who could destroy that city along with its Dānavas with a single blow. (Matsya Purāṇa 132.13)
Tripura cannot be destroyed by an arrow with little power,
except by Mahādeva, the Great Lord and Prajāpati, after he has been invoked once.
Therefore, if you and others together entreat the god Hara, the destroyer of the sacrifice, he will slay Tripura.
The obstruction of the cities was made for a hundred yojanas each,
such that they were indeed destroyed by Bhava with a single blow,
all occurring in a single moment under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism.
Then, addressed by the distressed gods who said,
"We shall go," the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived at the assembly of Bhava along with them.
They behold that Lord, the master of the past and the future, Giriśa, the wielder of the trident,
together with Umā and the high-souled Nandin.
The god who is unborn and the color of fire, whose eyes resemble a sacrificial fire-pit,
who possesses the brilliance of a thousand fires and suns, and who is adorned with the hue of fire.

Then, having approached that unborn god Nīlalohita— the Lord of Cows (Gopati), Śambhu, the bestower of boons, and the husband of Pārvatī— they praised him, whose body was marked by the beauty of the moon's phases and whose face was more serene than the moon.
The gods said:
"Salutations to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the giver of boons;
to the eternal Lord of Creatures, to the fierce one, and to the one with matted hair."
Salutations to Mahādeva, to Bhīma, to Tryambaka, and to Śānti;
salutations to Īśāna, the destroyer of fear, and to the slayer of Andhaka.
To the blue-necked one, the formidable, the creator praised by the creator,
to the slayer of the enemies of Kumāra, and to the progenitor of Kumāra.
To the deep red one, to the smoke-colored one, to the excellent one, and to the throttler;
to the one with the eternal blue crest, to the trident-bearer, and to the one who reclines in the divine.
To the serpent-like one, the three-eyed one, whose seed is golden wealth,
to the inconceivable husband of Ambikā, and to him who is praised by all the gods.
To the one whose banner is the bull, to the shaven-headed, to the one with matted hair, to the celibate student,
to the one performing austerities in the water, to the devotee of Brahman, and to the unconquered.
Salutations be to the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe, who stands pervading all;
salutations to the one of divine form, the source of divine Śambhu.
To him who is approachable, desirable, worthy of praise, and always worthy of worship;
to him who is ever compassionate toward his devotees and grants whatever is desired by their minds.
Matsya-Purāṇa 133: Sūta said:
"The Lord Maheśvara was being praised by the gods, beginning with Brahmā."
He said this to Prajāpati: "Where is the great fear of the gods? (Matsya Purāṇa 133.1)
"O gods, welcome to you! Speak what is in your minds;
I shall grant it at once, for there is nothing that I cannot give to you."
"O bulls among the gods, I shall surely bring you great welfare;
for I am performing a most formidable and supreme austerity. (Matsya Purāṇa 133.3)
"Those who are hostile to you are hostile to me; they are wretched and of wretched prowess. Their destruction must be accomplished, as must your own prosperity. (Matsya Purāṇa 133.4)
Thus addressed by the god with affection, all those deities, including Brahmā, being worthy of their respective shares, spoke to the highly fortunate Rudra.
"O Blessed One, those Asuras of fierce prowess performed terrible austerities;
being struck down by them, we have come to you for refuge."
I am the son of Diti named Maya, fond of quarreling with the Three-Eyed One;
by me was that fortress of Tripura constructed, with its white gate-towers.
Taking refuge in that impregnable city, O Mahādeva, the Dānavas, rendered fearless by their boon, oppress us as if we were servants without a master.
The gardens, such as Nandana and others, were destroyed,
and all the excellent Apsarases, beginning with Rambhā, were carried off by the Danujas.
O Maheśvara, Indra’s riding elephants— Kumuda, Añjana, Vāmana, Airāvata, and the others— were also carried away from the gods.
And those horses, the leaders of Indra’s chariot, who had been carried off by the Asuras and were born among the Dānavas,
became suitable steeds for the chariots.
"The chariots, the elephants, the women, and whatever wealth we possess have all been carried away by the Daityas; our very lives are now in doubt. (Matsya Purāṇa 133.12)
Thus addressed by the gods headed by Śakra, the three-eyed Lord of the Gods,
the boon-granter whose vehicle is the bull, spoke to the deities.
"O gods, let your great fear of the Dānavas depart;
I shall burn that Tripura. Let that which I say be done. (Matsya Purāṇa 133.14)
"If you desire that I burn that city along with Māna, then prepare for me a suitable chariot; why do you sit idle? (Matsya Purāṇa 133.15)
Thus addressed by the sky-clad one, those gods, together with the Grandfather,
said "So be it" to Mahādeva and fashioned an excellent chariot.
The earth was the two poles, both Rudra and his attendant were the two side-pieces,
Meru was the seat, and Mandara was the axle.
The lords fashioned the moon and the sun with wheels of gold and silver, as well as both fortnights—
the dark fortnight and the bright fortnight.
The gods, led by Brahmā, made the two wheel-rims;
the two primary wings were the mechanical contrivances, and these deities were the mechanisms themselves.
It was encircled by the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara,
as well as Bhārgava, Aṅgiras, Budha, and Aṅgāraka.
Likewise, Śanaiścara and all those most excellent gods made the sky their beautiful-formed chariot-fender for him.
It was fashioned with two tongues and three eyes,
made of gold, and adorned with jewels, pearls, and sapphires, as well as by the eight-faced gods.
The Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, Irāvatī,
Vitastā, Vipāśā, Yamunā, and likewise the Gaṇḍakī.
The Sarasvatī, the Devikā, and likewise the Sarayū—
all these excellent rivers were designated by the name "Veṇu" on the chariot.
And those *nāgas* who were the Dhṛtarāṣṭras were made into the nature of courtesans;
as were those born in the lineage of Vāsuki and those born in the family of Raivata.
Those serpents, full of pride and possessing unimpaired bodies, stood there having become arrows within their quivers,
with beautiful faces of various species.
Surasā, Saramā, Kadrū, Vinatā, and Śuci;
Tṛṣā, Bubhukṣā, Sarvogrā, Mṛtyu, and likewise Sarvaśamā.
The killing of Brahmins, the killing of cows, and the killing of children— these terrors to the people,
having become maces and spears, then rushed toward the divine chariot.
In that age, it was the Kṛta Yuga; the four classes of people were engaged in the performance of the Cāturhotra rites, and they were playful, adorned with golden earrings.
That great yoke, resembling a yoke itself, was fixed upon the head of the chariot and bound by the powerful serpent Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The Ṛgveda, the Sāmaveda, and likewise the other, the Yajurveda—these four Vedas themselves became the four horses. (Matsya Purāṇa 133.31)
Whatever gifts there were, preceded by the gift of food,
those became the ornaments for those horses by the thousands.
Padmadvaya, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya—
these nāgas indeed became the binders of the horses' manes.
Those mantra-rites, sacrifices, and ritual acts originate from the syllable Oṃ;
likewise do remedies for calamities, animal sacrifices, and offerings.
These sacrificial threads were upon that auspicious world-chariot,
adorned by thousands of gems, pearls, and corals.
The goad was the syllable *oṃ*, and its tip was the *vaṣaṭ* call;
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and the auspicious Anumati were the traces of the horses,
serving as their harnesses and fastenings.
Then there were black, yellow, white, and madder-red banners, as well as pure white ones, all fluttering in the wind.
The bow was formed by the six seasons, and it became the year;
moreover, Ambikā became its firm, undecaying string.
For the Blessed Lord Rudra is Time (Kāla), and they know him to be the Year;
therefore Umā became Kālarātri, the decay that is the bowstring.
That arrow, by which the three-eyed Lord burnt Tripura along with its inhabitants,
became composed of the three deities Viṣṇu, Soma, and Agni.
For his mouth became Agni, and Soma, the dispeller of darkness, became the arrow;
the conjunction of all energies was his impetus, and he who holds the wheel of the chariot was Tejas.
And for the sake of increasing his vigor, Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas,
released his exceedingly potent poison in order that his splendor might dwell within him.

Having fashioned a celestial chariot through their divine power, the gods approached the Lord of the World and spoke these words: matsyapurāṇe trayastriṃśaduttaraśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ // 133.43 // (Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-Three)
"This chariot has been prepared by us for you, O enemy of the Dānavas, to conquer and protect against calamities the gods led by Indra. (Matsya Purāṇa 133.44)
Having praised that supreme chariot of the three worlds, which was shaped like the peak of Mount Meru, Śaṅkara said "Excellent! to the gods and beheld the chariot.
Having repeatedly beheld the chariot and exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent!
again and again, the Lord of the Immortals himself spoke to the gods, including Indra.
"O best of beings, let a charioteer be appointed quickly, one whose skill in the equipment of a chariot is equal to this chariot which has been prepared by you."
Having spoken thus, the gods, as if pierced by arrows by the God of Gods, fell into great anxiety, saying, "What is to be done? (Matsya Purāṇa 133.48).
Who indeed could be a god equal to Mahādeva, except for the god whose weapon is the discus? Even he has taken refuge in his arrow.
Like bulls yoked to a burden, as if colliding with mountains, all the gods sighed and asked, "How can this be? *Matsya Purāṇa* 133.50.
Among the gods, the God of Gods said to those who stood at the head of the Lord of the World,
"I am the charioteer," and having spoken thus, the elder brother then took up the horses.
Then, seeing Brahmā— who held a goad in his hand— acting as the charioteer, the gods together with the gandharvas let out a great lion’s roar.
The Blessed One, the Lord of the Universe, Hara, seeing that the Grandfather was indeed seated upon the chariot, said, "O charioteer, you are my equal," and ascended the chariot.
When the god indeed mounts his chariot, the horses, distressed by the weight of Hara,
fall upon the ground on their knees, and even the dust is swallowed up as if in a single mouthful.
Then the god, seeing those Vedas being seized by the fearless demons out of fear,
rescued his distressed ancestors, just as a virtuous son rescues his suffering parents.
Then there arose once more the roar of lions and the terrifying clatter of chariots;
and the cry of "Victory! from the gods became like the sound of the ocean.
Then the self-existent Lord, the bestower of boons, taking up his goad which consists of the syllable Om,
proceeded toward the horses at full speed after consecrating them with mantras.
As if swallowing the sky and as if plundering the earth,
they exhaled from their mouths like hissing serpents.
Urged on by Svayambhū and by the matted-haired Kapardin who was himself urged on,
those swift horses gallop like the winds at the time of universal destruction.
Upon the erection of the banner, the bull Nandin, by the will of Śiva, stood treading upon the unsurpassed banner-pole.
The two gods Bhārgava and Aṅgiras, holding staffs in their hands and possessing the brilliance of the sun,
protect the two wheels of Rudra’s chariot, desiring to do what is pleasing to him.
And the Blessed Lord Śeṣa, the serpent Ananta, the end-maker of his enemies,
with a spear in hand, protects the chariot and the bed of Brahmā at that time.
Yama swiftly mounted his exceedingly fierce buffalo,
the Lord of Wealth his serpent, and the Lord of the Gods his elephant.
Mounting his father’s boon-bestowing chariot, which resembled that of Yuga and was adorned with a peacock and a hundred moons, Guha appeared like a warbling kinnara.
And the illustrious Nandīśvara, radiant and wielding his trident,
followed behind and at both sides like the Destroyer of the World.
And the attendants, possessing the hue of fire and resembling mountains ablaze with flames,
followed Śarva’s chariot like crocodiles following the great ocean.
Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Kratu, Pulastya, Pulaha—those rich in asceticism;
Marīci, Atri, the venerable Aṅgiras, and the great sages headed by Parāśara and Agastya.
They praised Hara, the unconquered and unborn, with excellent words and diverse ornaments;
his chariot, together with the golden mountain, moved through the triple city like a winged mountain in the sky.

Resembling clouds with the roar of elephants and thundering with the sound of water-laden rain-clouds, the hosts of Pramathas, filled with their own pride, surrounded the chariot protected by the gods and advanced. Like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, exceedingly swollen and teeming with crocodiles, whales, and timingilas; MatsP_133.69.
Indeed, that most radiant and excellent chariot proceeded with a sound like the falling of a thunderbolt or the roar of a rain-cloud.
Matsya Purāṇa 134: Sūta said:
While that divine chariot was being honored by the worlds, the Lord remained stationed upon the chariot.
While the Pramathas roared fiercely and cried out, "Excellent! (sādhu).
While the great bull bellowed with a voice like the sound of the Lord, while the brahmins were crying out "Victory!", and while the horses were likewise neighing; *Matsya Purāṇa* 134.2.
Rising from the field of battle, the powerful divine sage Nārada,
who resembled the moon in splendor, quickly arrived at the city of Tripura.
"An ominous portent has certainly appeared among the Daityas in Tripura;
and here the blessed Nārada, whose wealth is asceticism, has manifested."
Seeing Nārada, who appeared like a rain-cloud, all the Dānavas gathered together and rose up, uttering words of salutation.
And with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and the honey-mixture,
those lords worshipped Nārada, just as Vāsava worships Brahmā.
Having accepted their worship,
that Nārada, worthy of honor and rich in asceticism, sat comfortably upon an excellent golden throne.
While Nārada, born of Nārada, was seated comfortably,
the lord of the Dānavas sat down together with the Dānavas, each according to his rank.
Then, seeing Nārada seated, the great Asura Maya, delighted, with his hair standing on end and his eyes wide, spoke these words: *matsyapurāṇa 134.9*
O Nārada, knower of the present, tell us why this portentous event occurs in our city as it never does anywhere else.
Terrifying dreams are seen, and banners are shattered;
even without wind, the flagstaff falls thus to the earth. (Matsya Purāṇa 134.11)

The watchtowers, along with their banners and gate-towers, began to dance; and terrifying voices were heard in the city crying out, "Kill! Kill!"* *The critical edition reads *hiṃsata hiṃsata*. I have translated it as an imperative for the sake of clarity in this context. However, the original text may reflect a different reading. I have provided the most standard interpretation. If you prefer a literal rendering of the Sanskrit, please let me know. I will provide the literal version below. The watchtowers, together with their banners and gate-towers, began to dance; and terrifying cries of "Kill! Kill! were heard in the city.
“O Nārada, I do not fear even the gods led by Indra,
except for the one, the boon-granting Sthāṇu, Hara, who bestows fearlessness upon his devotees.”
O Blessed One, O Sinless One, there is nothing unknown to you regarding portents;
you know the future and the past in their true essence.
O Nārada, best of sages, this source of fear for us has been indicated by portents; tell it to me, who have sought refuge in you.
Thus addressed by that Maya, Nārada, who is free from all ailment, [replied].
Nārada said:
Listen, O Dānava, to the truth of how portents come to pass.
The verbal root *dhṛ* is taught in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*) and also in the sense of "greatness" (*māhātmya*).
And because it is maintained with greatness, this is defined as Dharma.
That dharma which brings about what is desired is taught by the teachers;
the other, which has undesirable results, is not taught by the teachers.
Those who know the Vedas understand that it is taught that his destruction is certain if he goes from a wrong path to a [right] path, or from a right path to a wrong one. *Matsya Purāṇa* 134.19.
Mounted upon an unrighteous chariot together with these intoxicated Dānavas,
you provide assistance to those who act as enemies of the gods.
Thus, these and other such portents,
as well as omens foreboding destruction, are seen among the Dānavas.
This Rudra, having mounted his chariot composed of the great worlds,
comes to destroy Tripura, O Maya, as well as you and the other asuras.
Therefore, O giver of honor, you should always take refuge in Maheśvara, who possesses great majesty;
together with your son and the Dānavas, you shall attain him.
Having thus reported the great danger that had arisen for the Dānavas,
the god returned once more to the station of the Lord of Gods.
When the sage Nārada had departed, Maya, the leader of the Dānavas, spoke thus to the Dānavas, who were esteemed for their heroism: "O Dānavas... (Matsya Purāṇa 134.25).
"You are heroes, you have sons, and you have fulfilled your duties, O Dānavas!
Fight together with the gods; we too must act, for there is cause for fear."
"Having conquered, we shall all become members of the assembly of the immortals;
and having slain the gods along with Indra, we asuras shall enjoy the worlds."
And likewise, stay upon the watchtowers with weapons in hand;
clad in armor and ready for battle, remain there with your arms raised.
"And these three cities, O Dānavas, shall remain in their respective places; they shall become impregnable cities. (Matsya Purāṇa 134.29)
Likewise, those heroic deities who have come here are indeed known to you;
they must be warded off with effort, or else pierced with arrows.
Having spoken these words to the sons of Danu for the purpose of warding off the host of gods,
King Maya suddenly entered that city of Tripura, where the hearts of the young women were despondent.
Then, having honored Bhava with eloquent words— the one whose nature is as pure as silver,
the sky-clad one, the God of gods who destroyed the bodies of Madana, Ārya, and Andhaka— he sought refuge in him.
The three-eyed Lord did not indeed perceive that we had approached him seeking the state of fearlessness;
therefore, the Moon-crested One granted what was desired, and that Dānava indeed became free from fear.
Matsya Purāṇa 135.
Sūta said:
Then, in the midst of the battle, Nārada again approached the army of the gods.
And having arrived from Tripura, he himself took his seat in the assembly hall.
That region, renowned as Ilāvṛta, is extensive in both breadth and length;
there the sacrifice of Bali took place, and there Bali was bound.
That which is renowned throughout the three worlds as the birthplace of the gods,
where marriages, sacrifices, and rites such as the birth-ceremony and others are performed.
There, where the activities of the gods and the giving away of their daughters took place,
Bhava always took his delight with his companions, attendants, and hosts.
Where the world-protectors always stood as if on Mount Meru, Maheśvara—
whose eyes were honey-tawny and who was adorned with the crescent moon—
spoke to the lord of the gods and to the leaders of his hosts.
"O Vāsava, this triple city of your enemies is visible before you,
adorned with celestial chariots, banners, and standards."
This is the account that has been told, which, like fire, causes intense burning;
these people, resembling mountains, wear earrings and crowns.
The Dānavas stand upon the walls, gate-towers, and watchtowers, and at the ends of the enclosures;
these Danujas, with distorted faces, resemble clouds.
The Daityas, bearing weapons and desiring victory, go forth from the city.
Therefore, you, together with hundreds of gods, accompanied by allies and bearing excellent weapons,
along with my powerful servants, slay the great asuras.
And I, standing in my excellent chariot as steady as a mountain,
shall remain before the city, seeking its vulnerability for the sake of your victory.
"But when the city stands in a state of unity through conjunction with the Puṣya asterism,
then, O Vāsava, I shall consume it with a single arrow."
Thus addressed by the Blessed Lord Rudra here on earth,
the lord of the gods set out to conquer Tripura, surrounded by that army.
Accompanied by those hosts of divine attendants who had mounted their chariots and were terrifying [the enemy],
they roared like lions and rose up like clouds.
At that sound, the Dānavas from Tripura, eager for battle,
sprang up and rushed through the sky with their weapons toward the lords of the Gaṇas.
Others, resembling clouds, produced sounds like thundering clouds;
exultant, they played musical instruments accompanied by lion-like roars.
The lion’s roar of the gods and the great sound of all their musical instruments were swallowed up by the shouts of the Daityas, like the moon by the clouds.
Just as the ocean swells at the rising of the moon on the full-moon day,
so did Tripura arise, filled with great Asuras of terrifying form.
Others, having climbed onto the watchtowers on the city walls and even at the gate-towers, began shouting threats as they moved about.
Wearing golden garlands, those heroes with their hands and garments radiant with light—
some of those Danujas roar like clouds intoxicated by rainwater.
Running hither and thither with their garments disheveled, some who had taken refuge in their homes asked one another, "What is this? (Matsya Purāṇa 135.21)
"Why do I not know this? Indeed, my knowledge has vanished.
You shall know it in the next [birth], for the time ahead is vast. (Matsya Purāṇa 135.22)
He too, Pṛthvīsāra, mounted upon his lion-chariot, remains afflicting Tripura like a manifest disease afflicting the body. (Matsya Purāṇa 135.23)
"Let him who is he, be he; what concern is it when there is such a commotion?
Come, take up your weapon; where will my questioning lead? (MatsP 135.24)
Thus, having struck one another and speaking in succession,
those Dānavas residing in Tripura then approached and questioned him.
In the city named Tārakākhya, the Daityas, led by the one named Tāraka,
rushed out in anger like great serpents from their hole.
But as those Daityas were rushing forth, they were blocked by the leaders of the Pramatha hosts,
just as lordly elephants are held back by the leaders of lion-packs.
Then, as they were filled with pride, their forms blazed like those of proud fires, like fires being blown by a bellows.
Then, drawing their massive bows that produced terrifying sounds on all sides,
they struck one another with arrows that consume life.
Seeing the attendants with faces as terrifying as cats and deer, and with distorted countenances,
the Dānavas laughed aloud at their excellence of form.
Drawn by arms shaped like iron clubs, the arrows from the bows entered the armor of the warriors like birds entering ponds.
"You are dead! Where indeed will you go? We shall slay you; turn back!"—having spoken such harsh words to the foremost of the attendants, the Dānavas [attacked]. (Matsya Purāṇa 135.32)
With sharp arrows, they pierced the Daityas and Dānavas like the rays of the sun piercing the clouds;
likewise, the Pramathas— lion-eyed and possessing the prowess and stride of lions—
shattered them with fragments of rocks, boulders, and trees.
That entire city shone intensely, crowded with Dānavas, like the sky filled with clouds or swarming with swans.
With their bows drawn, the lords of the Daityas create a storm of arrows,
like clouds marked with rainbows creating a gloomy day.
Being struck repeatedly by arrows, those lords of the Gaṇas produced a flow from their bodies,
like mountains discharging veins of gold ore.
Likewise, the Daityas, struck by trees, rocks, vajras, spears, clubs, and axes,
are pulverized like bits of glass shattered by a diamond.
Just as the ocean swells at the rising of the moon on the full-moon day,
so did Tripura become filled with great asuras of terrifying form.
"This one named Tāraka is victorious," thus the Daityas proclaimed;
"Indra is victorious and Rudra as well," so did the lords of the Gaṇas declare.
In that ocean of an army, the warriors were warded off and pierced by arrows;
they cried out like water-bearing clouds at the time of the rains.
With severed arms and heads, with banners and white parasols,
the battlefield was terrifying, filled with flesh and blood.
Then, having suddenly leaped into the sky to the height of a palm tree, they struck them firmly with excellent weapons;
first the Dānavas fell, and likewise the Pramathas.
The Siddhas, the Apsarases, and the Cāraṇas moving through the sky, delighted by his firm blows, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (Matsya Purāṇa 135.43).
And likewise, unstruck celestial drums resounded in the sky,
roaring with the sound of clouds like enraged śarabhas.
Those Daityas entered that triple city with angry faces, like rivers entering the lord of the oceans, or like serpents entering an anthill.
In that city called Tārakā, the heroic gods fell on all sides with their weapons, like winged mountains.
In Tripura, the lords of the Gaṇas fought with a third part [of their forces];
Vidyunmālī and Maya were submerged in the battle like trees.
That lord of the Daityas, Vidyunmālī, possessing a splendor like that of the king of mountains,
seized a terrible iron club and struck Nandin.
Struck firmly with a club by the lord of the Dānavas, Nandī whirled about,
clearly resembling Nārāyaṇa in his manifestation as Madhu in ancient times.
When Nandīśvara had departed for that place, the leaders of the Gaṇas,
renowned for their prowess and filled with fury, rushed toward the Asura Vidyunmālin.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Mahākāla were his attendants;
then, with arrows, he struck all those leaders of the Gaṇas who possessed the forms of Gaṇapas.
Again and again he pierced the great lords of the Gaṇas;
having pierced them one after another, he roared loudly like a rain-cloud in the sky.
At the sound of his attack, Nandin, who possessed the splendor of the sun,
recognized him and then rushed toward Vidyunmālin.
Then he hurled at the Dānava, whose limbs resembled a diamond, that blazing thunderbolt given by Rudra, which possessed a radiance equal to a flaming fire.
Then that terrifying thunderbolt, released from the arm of Nandin and adorned with pearls,
fell upon the chest of the Daitya.
Struck by the thunderbolt, that Daitya, whose body was as firm as a diamond,
fell down like a mountain struck by Indra’s thunderbolt.
Seeing the lord of the Daityas slain by Nandin, the delighter of his lineage,
the Dānavas cried out and the leaders of the Gaṇas fled.
Provoked by anger at the suffering caused when Vidyunmālin was struck down,
they released a great rain of trees and mountains, just as clouds pour forth rain.
Oppressed by those heavy mountains, the lords of the Gaṇas did not know what ought to be done, like unrighteous men who are being saluted.
Then the glorious and powerful chief of the asuras, named Tāraka, shone forth,
assuming a form equal to that of the young mountains.
With their heads split open and their faces marked by severed feet,
the leaders of the hosts shone like serpents being warded off by mantras.
Being struck by Māya with the power of his illusion,
the lords of the Gaṇas wander about like birds in a cage, uttering many cries.
By her, the illustrious and powerful chief of the Asuras named Tāraka consumed the entire army like fire consumes dry fuel.
Then the Gaṇas were warded off by showers of arrows from the one named Tāraka;
struck down by the illusions and shafts of Māyā,
the lords of the Gaṇas became distressed like trees with rotten roots.
Furthermore, fire falls upon the planets, the seizing spirits, serpents,
the lords of mountains, lions, tigers, trees, and the sṛmara and varṇaka deer.
By the power of his illusion, Maya casts down even śarabhas, eight-legged creatures, water, and wind upon his enemies.
Those lords of the Gaṇas, being utterly deluded by the illusion of Maya known as Tāraka, became helpless;
they were unable to move even with their minds, just as the senses are restrained by a sage when their objects have been withdrawn.
Afflicted by great waters, fire, and the like, along with elephants, serpents, lions, tigers, bears, hyenas,
and rākṣasas, they were deluded by darkness like those seeking a firm footing in the midst of the ocean.
While the lords of the Gaṇas were being crushed and the non-gods were roaring aloud,
the foremost of the gods, armed with their weapons, entered the enemy's force to protect it.
Yama, armed with a mace; Varuṇa and Bhāskara likewise; Kumāra, accompanied by ten million immortals;
and Śakra himself, the preeminent among the gods of the celestial realm, riding upon the white elephant and holding a thunderbolt in his hand.
Then that Lord of Cōḍa, his son Divākara, Sāntaka, and the three-eyed Lord of great splendor—
these, arrogant with pride, entered the army of their enemies which was protected by powerful forces.
Just as a forest is by a proud lordly elephant, just as the sky is by the sun accompanied by clouds,
and just as a herd of cattle in the wilderness is by lions, so was that army assailed by the gods.
Then the attendants of Balarāma, distressed by the blows dealt to the wretched Dānavas, broke through their force;
for Hari, like the sun with its own light and full of heat, [dispels] the most terrible darkness of men.
He caused the night-watches to cease, just as the moon always dispels the accumulated darkness of the night;
then, when the power of the darkness was withdrawn and the power of the weapon was increasing.
For a moment, a great roar of lions was let out by the world-protectors of the quarters and the leaders of the Gaṇas;
[the enemies] were shattered in battle—deformed, miserable, with their heads severed and their bodies filled with arrows.
The other gods, pierced by the best of gods, sink like lordly elephants in the mud;
Vajrapāṇi with his terrible thunderbolt, and Mayūraketu with his spear.
By means of his fierce staff, Dharmarāja is the guardian of the waters; by means of his fierce noose, he is the king of the Yakṣas;
and by means of his trident, his vigor, and his splendor, he is Kāla and Sukeśa.
Those lords of the Gaṇas, resembling gods and radiant like fires sprinkled with the final oblation,
destroy the hosts of Danu’s sons just as falling thunderbolts of Indra.
Having pierced with an arrow the son of Tāraka— that Asura named Tāraka— who was protected by the gods, the son of Umā, the excellent deity Kumāra, he addressed him.
Having struck the hero, I shall indeed enter the city joined by the forces of the lord of the Daityas;
and having obtained rest that restores my vigor, I will once again wage war against those who have submitted.
For we, our limbs mangled by the wounds of weapons, our arms, banners, armor, and mounts shattered—
desiring victory and appearing victorious— are the lords of the hosts and the supreme rulers of the worlds.
Having heard these words of Maya in heaven, the one named Tāraka— whose eyes were like blood and who longed for battle—
quickly entered Tripura with the sons of Diti and the sons of Aditi, whose joy was increased by the prospect of war.
Then the army of Hara shone forth, accompanied by conchs, kettledrums, and bherīs, and resounding with lion-like roars;
followed by Maya, it appeared like a deep and formidable cave echoing with the cries of lions.
*Matsya-Purāṇa* 135.83. *Matsya-Purāṇa* 136.1.
Sūta said:
Having struck him, Maya, the master of illusion and bull among the Dānavas, quickly entered Tripura like a dark cloud entering the sky. *Matsya Purāṇa* 136.1.
Sighing long and hot, he looked upon the Dānavas standing in their midst and meditated like a second Kāla when the destruction of the world has arrived.
Even Indra was afraid when he stood before him, desiring battle;
and that highly illustrious Vidyunmālī has also met his death.
Indeed, there is no city equal to this Tripura in terms of its impregnability;
yet even for that city, this misfortune has arrived—for nowhere is fortification the ultimate cause [of security].
Everything, whether difficult or more difficult, is under the power of Time alone;
when Time is enraged, how will there be protection for us from Time today?
Whatever strength exists in any of the three worlds among all living beings, all that is under the sway of Time; such is the ordinance of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Who indeed could possess mastery over this immeasurable Self that cannot be sustained?
Who would be capable of leaping across it, except for the god Maheśvara?
I fear neither Indra, nor Yama, nor Varuṇa, nor the Lord of Wealth;
for that Maheśvara, the master of these gods, is invincible.
Whatever fruit belongs to sovereignty and whatever fruit belongs to lordship,
that I shall show you today, as far as the heroes extend in every direction.
"I shall create a pond filled with the water of immortality and excellent life-restoring herbs;
then the Daityas will live on by means of those supreme medicinal plants that restore life. (Matsya Purāṇa 136.10)
Having reflected thus, the powerful Maya, the best among those skilled in illusion,
created by means of his magic a pond, just as the Grandfather [Brahmā] created Rambhā.
Two yojanas long and one full yojana wide,
it was equipped with stairways for ascending and was as variegated in form as a story.
It was filled with the finest water, which was like the rays of the moon— polished, fragrant as nectar, and full of excellence, like a woman endowed with every virtue.
It was covered with blue lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses, as well as with *kādamba* flowers,
and surrounded by formidable enclosures possessing the brilliance of the moon and the sun.
It was filled with birds of beautiful golden luster and sweet songs,
appearing like seekers of their desires, and resembling a friction-stick for producing the life-force of living beings.
Having created that pond like Maheśvara creating the Gaṅgā,
Maya first washed Vidyunmālin in it.
That mighty Daitya, the enemy of the gods, having been submerged in the pond,
rose up instantly like a fire kindled by fuel or as if offered into the sacrificial flame.
Having joined his palms in reverence to Maya, he was saluted by the one named Tāraka; then, rising up, Vidyunmālī addressed these words to Maya.
"Where is Nandin, surrounded by Rudra and the Pramathas and Jambukas?
Let us crush our enemies in battle; for what compassion can we have toward their bodies? (Matsya Purāṇa 136.19)
"Either by attending upon Rudra we shall become all-powerful,
or, slain by them in battle, we shall become food for Yama."

Having heard these forceful words of Maya, the great asura Vidyunmālin embraced him with moist eyes and spoke this: MatsP_136.21: "Having heard these forceful words of Maya, the great asura Vidyunmālin embraced him with moist eyes and spoke this."
"O Vidyunmālin, my kingdom is desired by me, not my life, without you, O mighty-armed one; what need have I for anything else, O great Asura? (Matsya Purāṇa 136.22)
O Lord, this pond consisting of great nectar was created by means of illusions for the sake of the slain Dānavas and Daityas, to increase their life-force.
"By good fortune, O Daitya, I see you returned here from the realm of Yama;
having been seized by misfortune and calamity, we shall today enjoy a great treasure."

"Now the Dānavas, free from fear, are fighting with the Pramathas;
a pond created by Maya will restore the slain to life."
Then that terrifying drum, resembling the agitated ocean, being struck,
resounded loudly again and again with a roar like that of hell.
Hearing the terrible roar of the kettledrums, resembling the rumbling of gathering clouds,
the asuras, eager for battle, quickly descended from Tripura.
With bracelets of iron, silver, and gold adorned with jewels,
and with earrings, necklaces, and even towering crowns fastened [upon them].
For the Kāśīs, of firm prowess, having taken up their weapons, were like smoky fires that never cease and blaze forth.
Like dancers performing, like thundering clouds, like elephants with trunks raised high, and like lions free from fear; (Matsya Purāṇa 136.31).
Deep like lakes and scorching like suns,
those lords of the Daityas terrified the great army like trees.
The Pramathas, full of enthusiasm and capable of flying like Garuḍa, also rushed forward,
eager for battle, against the Dānavas— the enemies of the Dānavas.
Urged on by Bala, Nandīśvara, and the Dānavas known as Tāraka,
the Pramathas joined together and waged war.
With swords resembling the moon, with spears tawny as fire,
and with arrows released with great force, they struck one another.
The forms of the arrows being discharged and the swords being brought down were like great meteors falling from the sky.
With their hearts pierced by the Śaktis,
the Pramatha-asuras cry out like those struck down mercilessly, as if submerged in the hells.
Adorned with golden earrings and crowned with magnificent diadems,
heads fell upon the earth like mountain peaks collapsing at the end of an eon.
Severed by battle-axes, spears, swords, and iron clubs,
those who resembled the finest of elephants fell upon the surface of the earth.
The Pramathas, roaring with terrifying cries, suddenly shouted for joy;
others, perfected beings, accomplished the wondrous art of battle-music.
"You are powerful, O Pramatha; you appear arrogant, O Dānava!"—thus did the elephants at the front of the battle cry out these words.
Struck by iron clubs by the Dānavas, some followers of Śaṅkara vomited blood from their mouths like mountains spewing molten gold ore.
In the battle, the Asuras, the enemies of the gods, were struck down even more severely by the Pramathas with iron arrows,
as well as by trees and mountain peaks.
Then other preeminent Dānavas, urged by the Dānava Maya, lifted up those slain Daityas and threw them into a pond.
And they too, having reached the pond, rose up with radiant bodies like the immortals in the heavenly world, adorned with excellent forms, ornaments, and garments.
Then some Dānavas, having regained their lives by being cast into the pond,
slapped their arms, let out lion-like roars, and likewise rushed forward, O Asuras.
"O Dānavas, advance against these Pramathas! Why do you stand still?
For even though you are slain, the well shall restore you to life again."
Having heard these words, Śaṅkukarṇa, who resembled a leader of the foremost [demons],
quickly approached the Lord of the Gods and spoke these words.
"O Lord, these asuras have indeed been slain again and again by the Pramathas;
yet they rise up once more, terrible as grain drenched with water."
In this city, it is said, there is a pond filled with water whose essence is the nectar of immortality;
whenever the Dānavas are struck down and cast therein, they come back to life.
While Śaṅkukarṇa was thus addressing the god Maheśvara,
most terrible portents indeed occurred within the army of the Dānavas.
Named Tāraka, with most terrifying eyes and a gaping mouth like that of a lion,
he rushed in great fury toward the chariot of Mahādeva.
In Tripura, a most terrible roar of kettledrums and conchs resounded;
seeing the god upon the chariot of the gods, the Dānavas rushed forth.
An earthquake occurred there, and the chariot with a hundred parts sank into the earth;
seeing this, Rudra and the self-born Grandfather Brahmā were filled with agitation.
Accompanied by those two most excellent gods, that best of chariots reached a place without support and sank down, like a virtuous man [without a patron].
When the elements are exhausted, that chariot becomes slack like a body in summer, or like water in a small amount; it is as if its lubrication has been disturbed.
Leaping from his chariot,
the self-born one of great vital power lifted up the excellent chariot, which resembled the three worlds, as it was sinking.
Then, emerging from the arrow, Janārdana, clad in yellow garments,
assumed the great form of a bull and seized the unassailable chariot.
Like a great chariot-warrior, he, seizing the three worlds with his two tusks, carries them ready as if they were a chariot; just as one who upholds a lineage carries that lineage.
The lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, like a winged king of mountains,
then rushed toward the god Brahmā and slew him.
Struck by those called Tārakās, Brahmā laid down his goad upon the pole of the chariot and blazed forth repeatedly, exhaling breath from his mouth.
There, for the sake of worshipping the one named Tāraka, a great and terrifying roar, resembling the rumbling of clouds, was raised by the Daityas and the Dānavas.

Then, in that great battle, Keśava— whose hands were like chariot wheels and whose form was like a bull, worshipped by the lord of bulls— having crushed the entire host of the sons of Diti, entered the city of Tripura.
The preceptor of the gods drank that entire mass of water, shimmering with rain-clouds and rich with blooming white, blue, and red lotuses,
just as the sun consumes the dense darkness of night accumulated over time.
Having drunk from the pond of the lords of the asuras, Janārdana, the mighty-armed one clad in yellow garments,
entered the Śara forest while roaring aloud.
Then the Asuras, struck by the lords of the terrifying hosts, became rivers of blood increased by their wounds;
they were turned away from the battle by those with fearsome faces who were intent on applying their strategic maneuvers, just as men are driven back by those dedicated to the execution of policy.
Tāraka by name and Taḍinmālin, pursued by the Pramathas along with Maya, retreated to the city; afflicted by arrows, they fled like bodies carried away at the onset of a windstorm.
In battle, the lords of the Gaṇas— Mahendra, Nandīśvara, and Ṣaṇmukha— displaying their rising pride,
roared loudly and laughed with intoxication, saying, "May we conquer along with the moon and the other guardians of the quarters!"
Matsya Purāṇa 137: Sūta said:
"In that battle, those enemies of the gods, the inhabitants of Tripura, were shattered by the Pramathas."
Terrified, they entered the city whose gateways had been shattered by the Pramathas.
Like serpents with decayed fangs, like bulls with broken horns,
like birds deprived of their wings, and like rivers whose waters have run dry.
The Daityas, whose faces were disfigured by the gods, became as if dead; they were despondent and asked, "What is to be done? (Matsya Purāṇa 137.3).
Then Maya, the supreme lord of the Daityas, whose face was like a lotus, spoke to those dejected ones.
Having waged terrible battles with the Pramathas and the gods, and having likewise gratified the Pramathas and the immortals in combat; (Matsya Purāṇa 137.5)
O Daityas, you who first entered the city and later, oppressed by force and severely tormented by the Pramathas, fled in terror.
"Clearly, something unpleasant is being done by the gods; there is no doubt about this, since these highly fortunate ones are entering the forest of the mountain."
Oh, how great is the power of Time! Oh, how difficult Time is to conquer, since even such an impregnable fortress has come under siege!
While I was thus contending, roaring like a thundercloud,
the Daityas became lusterless, like the planets at the rising of the moon.
Then the guardians of the lake approached him from the sky like clouds at the end of time;
standing with palms joined in reverence, they addressed Maya, who resembled Yama himself.
That pond of yours which was created, filled with the essence of nectar, hidden,
and crowded with groves of blue lotuses and lotuses swarming with bees.
"O leader of the Daityas, that woman, who was yellow in color, has now been seen by someone in the form of a bull; that pond appears like a woman who is dead. (Matsya Purāṇa 137.12)

Having heard the words of Vāpīpāla, that lord of the Dānavas, Maya, repeatedly saying "Alas!", spoke thus to the sons of Diti: matsyapurāṇe saptatriṃśaduttaraśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ // 137 // MatsP_137.13 // (End of Chapter 137 of the Matsya Purāṇa)
"If this pond created by the power of my illusion had been drunk by me, we would have perished without a doubt; the city of Tripura would have gone to the Dānavas."
He restores to life by means of the deities those Daityas who have been slain again and again;
indeed, it is as if a well has been drunk from by the one clad in yellow garments.
Who else, other than Viṣṇu— the unconquered wielder of the mace— will drink from this pond of nectar-water that is hidden by my illusory power?
Even among the Daityas, there is nothing on earth that remains unknown to him;
yet, in matters where my own skill is recognized, it has not been chosen by the wise.
"This region is level and beautiful, yet it is devoid of trees and lacks even a mountain;
having been filled with fresh water, the hosts of Maruts are afflicting us."
If you all think, "Standing upon the edge of the ocean, we can endure the great force of the Pramathas, which is like a gale," [then consider this]. *Matsya Purāṇa* 137.19.
And during that deluge of the ocean,
the undertakings of these beings will become devoid of energy, as they are obstructed by the paths of chariots.
For those fighting, those slaying their enemies, those who are terrified, and those who are fleeing,
the ocean, resembling the sky, will be our refuge.
Having spoken thus, Maya, the Daitya and lord of the Daityas,
then went swiftly with Tripura to the ocean, the kinsman of rivers.
Deep as the water in the ocean, he leapt up toward the excellent city;
the ancient cities themselves, along with their gate-towers and ornaments, remained standing there.
When Tripura had departed, the three-eyed enemy of Tripura spoke these words to the Grandfather (Brahmā), who was skilled in the doctrines of the Vedas.
"O Grandfather, we are indeed greatly afraid of the Dānavas, O Blessed One;
for those Dānavas have taken refuge in the vast ocean."
"O Grandfather, take the chariot quickly to that very place where those Dānavas have gone with Tripura."
Then, having let out a lion’s roar, the gods, joyful and armed with weapons, surrounded that divine chariot and proceeded toward the western ocean.
Then, surrounding Bhava, the destroyer of existence, who is the teacher of both gods and non-gods,
they went swiftly, roaring, toward the ocean, the abode of the Dānavas.

Then, beholding Tripura adorned with beautiful banners and resounding with the blare of kettledrums, drums, and conchs, the deities of various forces roared like clouds. Even in the city of the foremost of the immortals, there arose a terrible tumult from the rumbling of clouds and the beating of mṛdaṅga drums.
It was mingled with the roar of the sons of Danu, resembling the ocean agitated by a counter-tide.
Then Bhuvanapati, the refuge of the gods, having attained a firm resolve, set out on a hunt for his enemy;
for the lord of the hosts of deities, suddenly beholding his foe within the triple city, spoke to Śakra.
O Lord of the hosts of the thirty gods, listen to this: the Dānavas have entered the abode of Tripura;
I shall destroy them along with Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Ṣaṇmukha, together with their own attendants.
"Go to the ocean, for it was there that the cities stood when he had already struck down the enemy's forces;
for Bhava, mounted upon his excellent chariot, went to the sea, being capable of destroying Tripura once again."
Thus deliberating, the sons of Diti stationed themselves above the salt ocean;
they assailed Tripura along with the lord of the Dānavas with showers of arrows, maces, and thunderbolts.
O best among the foremost of gods, I too shall mount an excellent chariot and follow behind you;
O sinless one, I shall provide for your welfare by countering those who are intent on slaying the chief of the Asuras.
Thus urged by the words of Bhava, Hari, whose body possessed a thousand eyes,
rose up and went forth with the desire to destroy Tripura, his lotus-eyes wide open.
Matsya Purāṇa 138.
Sūta said:
Then Maghavan, the lord of the immortals, [set out] to slay those Asuras.
All the world-protectors and all the guardians of the hosts departed in every direction.
Then all the lords, being delighted, leaped up into the sky;
moving through the air, they shone like winged mountains.
They set out to destroy that city, like diseases attacking the body;
sounding their conchs, kettledrums, cymbals,
and drums, the gods were seen by the inhabitants of Tripura.
Saying, "Hara has arrived," those mighty great Asuras fell into extreme agitation,
like oceans during a cataclysm.
Hearing the sound of the celestial drums, the Dānavas of fearsome appearance roared and played various musical instruments in great numbers.
With their vigor further aroused,
those former gods and the [new] gods, having committed offenses against one another, began slaughtering each other.
Even amidst mutual abuse, as they tore each other's bodies apart,
an incomparable battle ensued, resounding with the noise of their blows.
They were like suns emerging from the clouds, like blazing fires,
like the lords of serpents pronouncing blessings, like birds wheeling in flight;
they were like the great mountains trembling, like rain-clouds thundering.
Like tigers yawning, like clouds thundering,
and like oceans agitated by surging waves of increasing crests, they were stirred.
The great heroes among the Pramathas and the exceedingly powerful Dānavas fought on,
remaining as immovable as thunderbolts against mighty mountains.
The sounds of the drawn bows were terrible,
like the roar of clouds driven by the wind in the sky at the end of time.
And they said: "Do not fear in battle! Where will you go? For you are already dead.
Strike quickly; I stand here—come and show your manliness! (Matsya Purāṇa 138.12)
"Seize! Cut! Break! Eat! Kill!
Tear asunder!"—having thus shouted to one another, they departed for the abode of Yama.
Some were deprived of their swords, some were cut down by battle-axes,
some were crushed by mallets, and some were struck down by arms.
Some Dānavas, resembling flowers upon arrows, were slain by spears while others were torn apart by pikes; like mountains with their forests,
they fell into the waters of the ocean teeming with fearsome crocodiles and timingilas.
As the lifeless asuras fell with their limbs still firmly bound,
a sound arose upon the ocean like the roar of water-laden clouds.
At that sound, the sea-monsters, crocodiles, timis, and timingilas,
intoxicated by the scent of blood, agitated the great ocean.
Engaging in mutual strife, those beings of terrifying form wandered about,
devouring the blood of the Dānavas.
The sea-monsters swallowed the Daityas— along with their charioteers, weapons, horses, and garments and ornaments— while putting to flight the creatures that move in the water.
Just as the conflict between the Asuras and the Pramathas proceeds,
so too did the water-dwellers engage in battle in the sky and in the waters.
Just as the Pramathas roam about together with the Daityas, so too do the Timis and Nakras wander;
and just as they cut one another down, so too do they cry out when their bodies are torn apart.

In an instant, the region of the ocean was turned into one with blood-red waters and surging waves by the gods and asuras, along with crocodiles and timingilas, whose gaping wounds were streaming with the marrow of their limbs.
First, Śakra, joined by the great force of the immortals, stood pressing against the vast gate of Tripura, which resembled a great mountain of clouds, with his own mighty army.
Likewise, that younger brother of Hara, Skanda— whose complexion was like the rising sun and refined gold—
then ascended the city gate, like the setting sun descending upon the peak of the Asta mountain.
Yama, the lord of wealth, and the god [Varuṇa], equipped with the staff and holding the noose as his excellent weapon—
these two blocked the western gate of that city belonging to the enemy of the gods.
The three-eyed Lord Rudra, the enemy of Dakṣa, possessing the splendor of ten thousand suns, stood blocking that southern gate of the enemy’s city with his radiant celestial chariot.
The lofty mansions with their gate-towers, golden and radiant as Mount Kailāsa or the moon,
were occupied by the Pramathas who appeared joyful, like clouds raining down stones amidst the celestial lights.
Uprooting and repeatedly uprooting their houses, along with their mountain ranges and sacrificial altars,
and hurling them again and again into the midst of the ocean, the Pramathas, resembling dark clouds, roared aloud.
And the houses, colored red and joined with all the forests, containing groves of *aśoka* trees and *kokila* birds—O Lord, "Father! Son! "Brother! "Beloved!
"Dear one!"—while these houses were being torn down, the women uttered various ignoble cries.
When that city was facing the destruction of its wives, sons, and lives as the battle raged intensely,
the great Asuras— the lords of the Gaṇas, possessing a speed like the ocean and overcome with wrath— advanced against them.

There, a most terrible battle commenced, characterized by deep-seated enmity, involving axes, stone slabs, tridents, and excellent, unshakable vajras, which utterly destroyed the bodies that served as their dwellings.
As the gods and dānavas rushed at one another, contending and striking each other down,
a roar arose like that of the oceans at the end of a cosmic age.
Constantly vomiting blood from their wounds, their faces flushed with rage and roaring in many ways,
those lords of the Gaṇas and the foremost of the Asuras fought while emitting a great clamor.

The roads in the city, once strewn with red mud and variegated with gold bricks and shattered crystal, have in a mere moment been made easy to traverse; yet they remain terrifying, with severed heads, feet, and hands scattered about.
But he named Tāraka, his eyes clouded with rage, remained hidden along with his trees and mountains in the midst of battle;
at that very moment, the excellent gateway was blocked by Bhava of wondrous prowess, who desired to protect it.

There, that being of great and wondrous heroism, having struck down the spirits who had come to the ramparts, moved about with his senses free from pride; then, having emerged from the city, he let out a terrible roar.
Then he, resembling the best of Daityas and a mountain, like an elephant in rut, though restrained, desired to seize Rudra’s chariot; he surged forward like the ocean overflowing its shores.
Śeṣa, Sudhanvan, the god Giriśa, and he who is the four-faced one— along with the three-eyed one—
having encountered the one named Tāraka in battle, were agitated like oceans by the force of the wind.
The remaining Śiva, along with Pitāmaha and Īśa, being violently shaken in that chariot situated in the sky,
his joints shattered under the force, cried out and uttered terrible roars.
But Bhava, having placed one foot upon the back of the horse of the Ṛgveda and the other upon the bull,
stood there with his bow and arrow raised, observing the union of that city.
Then, as the horse and the bull stepped upon Bhava,
their chests and tusks were struck by the wielder of the trident as he pressed down upon them.
From that time forward, the udders and teeth of horses as well as those of cows became obscured;
by that [act], they attained invisibility.
Named Tāraka, with terrifying eyes and fierce, blood-red inner glances,
he was firmly restrained by Nandin, the delighter of his lineage, in the presence of Rudra.
With his sharp axe, that Nandin carved the lord of the Dānavas,
just as a carpenter carves sandalwood that yields fragrance.
Struck by the battle-axe like a śarabha struck by a mountain, the heroic lord of the Gaṇas named Tāraka drew his sword and fled. (Matsya Purāṇa 138.45)
Taking up his sacred thread (yajñopavīta), he cut it and let out a roar; then,
once the one named Tāraka had been slain, the lords of the Gaṇas produced there a terrible lion-like cry and a fearsome sound of conch shells.
Hearing the roar of the Pramathas as well as the sound of musical instruments, Maya, standing nearby, spoke to Sumahāpārśva and Vidyunmālin: *matsyapurāṇa 138.47*
"Is this sound being heard, resembling the roar of a shattered ocean, from those with many mouths crying out?
Speak, O Taḍinmālin! What is this? Are the Gaṇapālas fighting, or have the lordly elephants gone forth?"
Thus goaded by the hook of my words, like the sun garlanded with rays amidst a garland of lightning,
that subduer of enemies arrived at the forefront of the battle against the gods and spoke this out of great joy.
O wise one, that storehouse of your fame known as Tāraka possesses the prowess of Yama, Varuṇa, Mahendra, and Rudra;
he is the lord of all the mountain-peaks at the head of battle, for having fought with the leaders of the Gaṇas, he indeed blazes like Tāraka.
Having beheld the one named Tāraka— who had crushed his enemies and possessed long eyes as terrifying as the fire blazing from the sun—
the Pramathas, their every eye and hair bristling with excitement, roared like clouds pouring rain.
Having heard those words of his friend, Maya, who wore a golden garland and resembled a mountain of black collyrium,
spoke these words to Taḍitmālin, who was adorned with a wreath of new moons, at the forefront of the battle.
"O Vidyunmālin, this is no time for us to achieve our goal through negligence;
by means of my prowess, I shall make this city free from calamity."
Then Vidyunmālin and Maya, the lord of Tripura, being enraged,
together with those great asuras, struck down the Gaṇas in great numbers.
Wherever Māyāmaya, garlanded with lightning, went from there,
that very place was made empty by the Pramathas who were struck down.
Then, having worshipped Bhava with the sounds of the *yama*, *varuṇa*, and *mṛdaṅga* drums, with the loud clamor of *paṇavas*, *ḍiṇḍimas*, and bowstrings,
and with lion-roars accompanied by the clapping of palms, the gods stood there.
Being worshipped by the high-souled sons of Diti, who possessed splendor equal to the thousand-rayed sun,
the Lord was praised by those devoted to truth whose wealth was their asceticism, like the sun reaching the western mountain peaks.
Matsya Purāṇa 139: Sūta said:
When Tāraka had been slain in battle, Maya, having driven away the Pramathas, spoke.
He spoke again and again to the Dānavas, who were overwhelmed by fear.
O lords of the asuras, all of you now listen to what has been spoken:
that which must be done by me and also by you, who possess great strength.
O you whose faces resemble the moon, at the proper time the moon will enter the Puṣya asterism,
when all three cities shall become one for a single moment.
"Act without fear at the proper time, signaled by the song of the cuckoo;
for that time of the conjunction with Puṣya has been ordained for the city by me."
At that time, whoever in that city shall provide the necessary assembly,
that god shall cause him to prepare this powder with a single powerful arrow.
O Asuras, whatever vital breath, strength, and enmity you possess,
keep that within your hearts and protect this city.
With all your might, turn back Maheśvara’s single, terrifying chariot so thoroughly that he does not discharge his arrow.
Therefore, when we have thus secured the protection of Tripura,
the inhabitants of heaven will wait helplessly for the conjunction of Puṣya.
Having heard that, the Dānavas residing in Tripura,
who were like Yama himself, repeatedly let out lion-like roars and spoke to Maya, who was thus absorbed in his task.
With all our effort, we shall carry out everything you have commanded;
we will act in such a way that Rudra shall not release his arrow upon the city.
"Today we shall go to battle, desiring to slay that Rudra," so the sons of Diti say, joyful and their hair standing on end. (Matsya Purāṇa 139.11)
Either Tripura, remaining in the sky, shall endure for an eon as eternal and fixed;
or else it shall become devoid of demons, [merely] the three steps of Nārāyaṇa.
"We shall not abandon the Dharma in which you will engage us;
men shall behold a world that is neither godless nor devoid of Daityas."
Having thus deliberated, those enemies of the gods, filled with joy within the city, became delighted at nightfall and moved about like the god of love himself.
Rising again and again, the great jewel of the Lord Moon,
having dispelled the darkness, wanders toward the eastern peak and expands across the sky.
Like a swan upon a vast lake adorned with white water-lilies, or like a great lion seated upon a peak of beryl. (Matsya Purāṇa 139.16)
Just as Viṣṇu’s necklace rests upon his broad chest,
so too does the moon, born from the eye of Atri, shine in the deep sky,
illuminating the worlds and forcibly creating the essence of moonlight.
When the cool-rayed moon had risen and the city was filled with moonlight, the Asuras performed graceful acts at twilight, both within their homes and upon themselves.
In the streets, on the royal highways, and in the palaces and houses,
there were lamps with the luster of campaka flowers, ignited by no small amount of oil.
Then, those lamps filled with oil were ignited in the monasteries;
and their wealthy houses, composed of all kinds of jewels,
shone as the lamps blazed, like the planets at the rising of the moon.
The darkness in Tripura, though shining with moonbeams and brilliantly illuminated by interior lamps,
is swallowed up as if by a family beset by calamities.
In that city, during the youthful evening when the moon was laughing loudly, the sons of Danu,
seeking pleasure, sported for a long time with their women in their homes.
But those five arrows of the bull-bannered god, which had been diverted by the dolphin-bannered one,
caused the wives of the foremost among the Asuras to break out in sweat there.
While the lamentations of the *dānavīs* and the melodies of the lutes reached a crescendo,
and amidst the intoxicated warbling of the cuckoos, Madana, armed with his bow and arrows, churned [her] with passion.
Having swiftly dispelled the nocturnal darkness and spread a canopy of moonlight over the world,
the Moon, having united with his beloved Rohiṇī in the sky, exercises sovereign rule through his radiance.
Standing right at the foot of her beloved, a certain excellent woman applies a most beautiful decorative mark upon the base of her own cheek, thereby adorning her face.

Seeing her face reflected in the mirror of the mandala, the noble-limbed woman, reciting "The great radiance is from my mouth," and remembering the words of her lover, attained pleasure through that very state of being.
Others, their excellent limbs bristling with horripilation due to their passion for lovemaking,
go of their own accord to their lovers swiftly, overcome by intoxication, like nights at the end of the sun's day.
Some drank deeply, permeated by intense passion; others, having sought out their beloved, were clear-minded and joyful.
Some, having been pleased with their beloved after a very long time, remained perfectly serene throughout their amorous chatter.
Adorned with gośīrṣa and yellow sandalwood, their eyes marked with cosmetic paste,
those excellent asuras became beautiful and lovely to behold, like golden jars filled with nectar.
With their lower lips wounded and stained with the blood of swiftly flowing wounds, the Daityas dally with their beloveds;
they are devoted to the lute-like lamentations in the three cities, yet they are utterly dispassionate toward the actual cries of women.
In some places, sweet singing has begun—a well-crafted repository for the arrows of Kama;
and in the drinking grounds, they perform songs that are easily measured by pleasure.
Then, as the song began, some there purified their beloveds, while others brought them to perfection;
some awakened their beloveds at that moment, and having awakened them again and again, they delighted them.
When the sun had set upon Tripura, there arose a beautiful fragrance born of shaken blossoms;
the sound of anklets and girdles rang out, surpassing even the song of the cuckoos.
A certain woman, embraced by her beloved and with her hair standing on end,
was like the earth sprinkled with fresh rain, covered with the sprouts and shoots of beautiful tears.
In the magnificent palaces adorned by the rays of the moon,
the great sounds of the excellent women— whose very sweetness served as their ornament— became equal to the arrows of Love.
"Why do you, exhausted by drinking, excessively smell my cheek?
Climb upon these broad, full, and elevated hips of mine, adorned with a golden girdle."
In the streets illuminated by the rising moon and upon the broad paths of the Lord of the Gods,
the Daitya women gathered in groups shone like the stars of the moon at the end of the day.

And as the chowries on the watchtowers and the swings were swaying due to the state of their intoxicated restlessness, Kāñcī, with her subtle sound like the thread of a girdle, spoke these playful words: aṭṭāṭṭahāseṣu ca cāmareṣu preṅkhāsu cānyā madalolabhāvāt / saṃdolayante kalasamprahāsāḥ provāca kāñcī guṇasūkṣmanādā // MatsP_139.39 //
This is the turn of the joyful beauties adorned with unfading garlands;
their voices, like the sound of refined gold, are heard alongside the calls of other ruddy geese in the ponds.
The girdles with their waistbands and body-unguents, as well as the emotional states produced by the passion for those swings,
cut through the dwellings of the beloveds of those demonesses, who are themselves the arrows of the God of Love.
Clad in variegated garments and with his mass of hair disheveled, he shone as he was being swung about by the Asura women;
endowed with most beautiful attire and ornaments, he was like the moon among the hosts of stars.

The ground of the swing shines with wonderful splendor, variegated by those gems that have fallen from their girdles as the threads snapped during the swaying, scattered about like the stars approaching the side of the moon.
At nightfall, in the moonlit grove where flocks of cuckoos were singing,
Madana, having exhausted his arrows by reaching the city of the Asuras, wandered about with his shafts depleted.
Thus, in that city, there was then for the enemies of the gods a final moonlight festival;
for the enemies were utterly destroyed by the steeds of Bhava upon the field of battle.
Then the moon—possessing the hue of jasmine flowers, pearl necklaces, and the autumnal sky, yet devoid of its canopy of moonlight—assumed a color like that of a cloud.
For just as a tree loses its luster when it has become shorn of its foliage, so too does a lord of wealth appear pale and lacking in splendor when his fortune is exhausted.
Having overcome the moonlight with his crimson charioteer, his orb resembling a wheel of refined gold,
the sun stands upon the crest-ornament of the eastern mountain and shines intensely in the sky, as if desiring to cross over the waters of darkness.
Matsya Purāṇa 140. Sūta said:
When the thousand-rayed sun, the maker of light, had risen upon Mount Meru;
He roared with his entire divine army, like the ocean at the end of a cosmic age.
Then the thousand-eyed god Śakra, the destroyer of cities, along with Savitṛ,
Varuṇa, and Hara, set out for Tripura.
Those various forms of Pramathas and Atipramathas went forth with terrible lion-roars and the sounds of musical instruments.
Then, with the sounding of musical instruments and great trees serving as parasols,
that divine army became like a forest in motion.
Beholding that great and fierce army of Rudra as it descended,
a tumult among the lords of the Dānavas arose, resembling the agitation of the ocean.
And they [hurled] swords, spears, javelins, tridents,
staffs, axes, bows, thunderbolts, and heavy maces.
With eyes red with rage,
they seized [their weapons] like winged mountains and struck at the mountain-slayer, like clouds at the end of the summer heat.
Those sons of Diti, adorned with garlands of lightning,
being joyful, approached the enemies of the gods together with the gods of gods according to their covenant.
The army of those who had resolved to die, whose minds were set on victory yet remained undecided,
and who were powerless, appeared like a woman with weak limbs.
Roaring like clouds and possessing a luster resembling that of the clouds,
those skilled in combat fought one another after having committed offenses against each other.
Smoking with their blazing weapons that possess the luster of the moon,
they strike one another out of anger or because they are greedy for battle.
Some fall, struck by thunderbolts; others are torn apart by arrows;
still others, mangled by discuses, fall indeed into the waters of the ocean.
With their garlands, necklaces, and large strings of pearls broken, and their garments and ornaments rubbed away,
the Pramathas and the gods fall into the swarms of whales and crocodiles.
From all sides there was a rain of maces, clubs, javelins, battle-axes, thunderbolts, spears, lances, and sharp-edged pattiśas.
A great torrent of mountain peaks and stones hurled by the enraged [demons],
along with the swift-moving Dānavas, smoke-filled [fires],
and weapons possessing the brilliance of the sun, fell even as the flood of the ocean surged.
There, by those weapons of increased velocity, wielded by the hands of gods and asuras,
a great destruction is wrought, in which the stars tremble with fear.
Just as there is destruction among small creatures in a battle between two elephants,
so too did the destruction of the *timi* and *nakra* fish occur at the hands of the hosts of gods and asuras.
And Vidyunmālī, like a cloud garlanded with lightning,
rushed impetuously toward Nandīśvara, roaring with a sound as deep as a mass of lightning-charged clouds.
That best of speakers, the Dānava whose voice resounded like the ocean, spoke while roaring at Śailādi, whose face was like the darkness of night. *Matsya Purāṇa* 140.19.

"Desiring battle, O powerful one, I, Vidyunmālin, have come here. If you escape from me alive now, O Nandikeśvara, then the slaying of Vidyunmālin shall not be accomplished by words alone in this war, O Dānava! (Matsya Purāṇa 140.20)
To that Daitya who was speaking thus, Nandīśa, the best among those who perform austerities and skilled in the ornamentation of speech, spoke while striking him there.
"O Dānavas who desire righteousness, this is not the proper occasion;
why do you, though capable of killing, increase your own self-destruction through the fault of your birth? (Matsya Purāṇa 140.22)
If you were previously slain by me like a sacrificial animal,
how indeed could I not now destroy this defiler of the sacrifice?
Even one who could cross the ocean with his two arms or bring down the sun from the sky would not be able to look upon me even with his eyes.
To Nandin, who was speaking thus there, that Daitya, equal to him in strength,
pierced with a single arrow, as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays.
From his chest, that arrow drank his excellent blood,
just as the sun, by its own power, drinks the waters of rivers and oceans.
By that excellent blow, he was first deeply pierced;
then, uprooting a tree with his hand, he hurled it like a king of elephants.
And that tree, shaken by the wind, its flowers withered and making a great roar,
was severed by the arrows of Vidyunmālin and fell like the lord of birds.
Beholding that tree severed by the Dānava with his excellent arrows,
Nandīśvara, possessed of a beautiful form, summoned a fierce rage.
Raising his hand, which possessed the radiance of the rays of the sun and Indra’s thunderbolt,
he rushed toward the cruel buffalo to slay him, like a king of elephants.
As he was rushing forward with great speed,
the powerful Vidyunmālin forcefully and violently overwhelmed Nandin with hundreds of arrows.
With his body bristling with arrows, Śailādi seized the chariot of that great enemy and fled away with speed.
With his horses stalled and his head severed, the chariot whirled in battle and fell by the sage’s curse, like the sun-chariot with its sun fallen.
Having emerged from within by means of his illusory power, that son of Diti then struck Śailādi, who was standing there, with a spear.
But having drawn forth that very spear, which was smeared with blood,
the leader of the Pramathas hurled it at Vidyunmālin.
With his armor shattered by her and his heart torn asunder,
he fell to the ground like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, though he was adorned with a garland of lightning.
When Vidyunmālin was slain, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kiṃnaras exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and honored the Lord of Umā.
When the Daitya Nandin had been slain and Vidyunmālin killed,
Maya set fire to the army of the Pramathas like a fierce conflagration consuming a forest.
With chests torn open by spears, heads crushed by maces,
and deeply pierced by arrows, they fall into the ocean of the Pramathas.
Then Vajradhara, Yama, Arthada, Nandin, and the six-faced Guha—
having slain their enemies with excellent weapons— overcame Maya, who had been engaged by the heroic Asuras.
But Maya swiftly pierced Śatākṣa, the lord of the Nāgas, with an excellent arrow.
Having pierced both Yama and Vaiśravaṇa, the lord of wealth, she then roared like a thundering cloud in rut.
