Then, struck firmly by Śiva’s arrows and the hosts of Pramathas, the Dānavas— though possessing supreme speed and prowess—
were deeply pierced and driven back into Tripura, just as Śiva was joined by Cakradhara in the battle.
Then, conchs, kettledrums, bherīs, and mṛdaṅgas, accompanied by lion-roars that shattered the sons of Danu,
resounded on all sides within Kapardin’s army as they were struck down in battle like thunderbolts.
Then, upon the destruction of the Daityas' cities, the conjunction with Puṣya occurred;
and indeed, those three cities became joined with that conjunction.
Then the three-eyed Hara, the lord of the three paths, swiftly released an arrow composed of the three deities in three parts toward Tripura.
By that released arrow, which possessed a luster like the *bāṇa* flower,
the sky was made to resemble gold and was colored by the sun.
Having released the arrow consisting of the three deities at Tripura, the god of the thirty-three cried out, "Fie, fie upon me! Alas, alas! Matsya Purāṇa 140.47.
Seeing the absence of the deity, Śailādi approached like an elephant and asked Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, "What is this? (Matsya Purāṇa 140.48).
Then Śaśāṅkatilaka Kapardin, like one deeply distressed, spoke to Nandin out of devotion: "This Maya shall perish this very day."
Then Nandīśvara, powerful as the mind and the wind,
swiftly approached Tripura with his arrow and entered it.
Having seen me, that leader of the Gaṇas, who resembled gold in complexion, said:
"O Maya, this most terrible destruction of Tripura has arrived;
I tell you, depart from this very house."
Having heard those words of Nandi, he who was firm in his devotion to Maheśvara was led away from Tripura by that very leader of the household.
That arrow, having consumed those three cities like a fire in a leaf-cup,
was like the sacrificial fire, the moon, and Nārāyaṇa— each being threefold.
O best of the twice-born, cities enveloped by the heat of autumnal arrows—
meaning the heat of the king's wrath— are consumed just as families are burnt from above due to the fault of a wicked son.
Resembling Mount Meru and Kailāsa, and resembling the peaks of Mount Mandara,
they were provided with doors and windows and adorned by powerful beings.
They were delightful with palaces, towering with gabled chambers, provided with water, well-proclaimed, and equipped with viewing galleries.
In that city of Tripura, during the affliction of the Dānavas, houses made of gold and silver, adorned with fixed banners and flags,
were burned by the fire in their thousands, blazing like flames themselves.
Some were on the delightful tops of palaces, in groves and pleasure gardens;
others were at the windows, and still others beneath the open sky.
And those women, though embraced by their lovers and sporting with them,
were burned by the fire of the lords of the Dānavas.
A certain woman, unable to depart elsewhere while leaving her beloved behind,
met her death before her lover, perishing like fire in his mouth.
With eyes like lotus petals and hands joined in reverence, she spoke as if with tearful eyes:
"O Havyavāhana, burner of enemies, I am the wife of another;
you, the witness of the dharma of the three worlds, ought not to touch me here."
"O God, O Śivaprabha, I and Śivā have already slept;
depart by another way, leaving this house, for it is indeed dear to me. (Matsya Purāṇa 140.62)
A certain Dānava woman, taking her young son with her, stood near the fire and spoke thus to the fire-god: MatsP_140.63.
"O Agni, this child was obtained by me with great difficulty;
O beloved son of the Six-faced One, you ought not to take him away."
Some distressed wives of the Dānavas, having abandoned their beloveds,
fall into the waters of the ocean with their ornaments jingling.
"O father! O son! O mother! O maternal uncle!"—thus did the women in Tripura cry out in distress, trembling from the flames of the fire.
Just as a mountain fire consumes a lake together with its lotuses,
so did the fire burn the lotus-faces of the women in Tripura.
Just as a mass of frost destroys the lotuses in the beds of water during the cold season,
even so did that fire consume the lotus-like faces and eyes of the women of Tripura.
As the exceedingly delicate women there were pursued by the falling arrows and fire,
the sound of their girdles, anklets, and their cries became indistinguishably blended together.
There, burnt-out houses— half-moons with their altars destroyed, their palaces shattered, and their gateways ruined—
fell one after another into the flood of the ocean as if for the sake of protection.
With houses falling down, consumed by tongues of fire, the water in the ocean became heated,
just as the family of a wealthy man falls into ruin when struck and pierced by the faults of a wicked son.
The water in that ocean, heated on all sides by the heat of the houses and surging with great force,
terrified the *timi*, *śiṃśumāra*, and *timiṅgila* fish, as well as other creatures, as they were boiled therein.
Then that excellent rampart of Tripura, resembling Mount Mandara with its gate-towers,
fell together with those very palaces into the ocean, producing a great roar.
When Tripura— resembling the lord of mountains with its thousand peaks—
was reduced to a mere name, it became food for the fire, offered as a sacrificial oblation.
As that city was being consumed by fire, the entire world, including the subterranean realm of Pātāla and the heavens, was scorched;
and having encountered great suffering, it sank into the waters where Maya’s magnificent palace stood.
Having heard those words, Indra, the lord of the gods and wielder of the thunderbolt,
son of Aditi, then cursed that house of Maya as well.
The house of Māyā will be unapproachable, without foundation, and enveloped in fear;
it shall be eternally like a blazing fire.
In whichever region there shall be defeat,
people who have met their destruction will see this fragment of Tripura;
even today, this very house of Maya remains free from disease.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, O Camasodbhava, tell us the fate of that house by which Maya fled."
Sūta said:
"Wherever Dhruva was seen, there my abode was seen;
therefore, Maya, the enemy of the gods, became distressed in mind."
Having descended from there, he indeed acted for the sake of protection in this other world.
There too dwell the deities, the Āptoryāmas, the best of gods;
yet he was unable to go from there to that one supreme city.
Having created a house, Śiva gave it to Maya, who was seeking a dwelling;
the thousand-eyed Indra then desisted and worshipped the Lord.
And as the Lord of Beings was being worshipped, all praised the Supreme Lord.
Beholding the Lord of the Gaṇas, the foremost leader, being worshipped by the gods and the hosts,
the deities leaped for joy, laughed, and, with arms entwined, went about roaring aloud.

Then, having paid homage to the Grandfather and to Maheśa, and having taken up his bow and wiped it over all beings, he leaped down from the chariot; and that city, consumed by Hara’s arrow, was cast into the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters.
To him who recites this *Rudravijaya*, which brings about victory,
the bull-bannered Lord grants victory in all his undertakings.
Whoever shall cause this to be heard during the Śrāddha rites for the ancestors,
his merit shall be infinite, bestowing the fruit of all sacrifices.
This is a meritorious means of securing well-being; this is a great rite for procreating male offspring.
Having heard and recited this, people attain the same world as Rudra.
Matsya Purāṇa 141. The sages said: "O King, how does the monarch go to heaven every month on the new moon day?"
O Sūta, how did Aila Purūravas satisfy the ancestors?
We wish to hear about this, as well as the power of that wise man.
Sūta said:
Manu indeed questioned Madhusūdana about this very matter;
listen to me as I relate how he spoke it to the son of the Sun. *Matsya Purāṇa* 141.2.
The Fish said:
I shall, moreover, describe to you in detail the power of that wise Aila and his union with Soma in heaven. *Matsya Purāṇa* 141.3.
From Soma, moreover, comes the attainment of immortality as well as the gratification of the ancestors;
these are the Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, the Kāvyas, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas.
And when the moon and the sun, together with the constellations, meet and dwell upon a single orb on the day of the new moon (amāvāsyā). MatsP_141.5 //
Then, on every new moon day, he goes to visit his maternal grandfather and paternal grandfather, who are like the sun and the moon.
Having saluted them there, he remained waiting for the proper time;
then, having worshipped Soma, he leaped down from his exhaustion.
The learned Purūravas, son of Ilā, desiring to perform the monthly Śrāddha,
then indeed approached Soma in heaven as well as the ancestors.
Having established both of those for two lava-periods and the duration of the *kuhū* [new moon],
he [performs] the vow at the rising of the *sinīvālī* and the slight *kuhū* duration.
Having understood that the Pitṛs reside in the new moon (kuhū), they worship the new moon;
having worshipped it, one who awaits the lunar digit then looks toward Soma.
Indeed, the nectar of *svadhā* flows from the moon for their satisfaction;
through ten and five streams of that *svadhā*-nectar, the supreme delight of those who feast during the dark fortnight is nourished by the highest rays. (Matsya Purāṇa 141.11)
Then, as the funeral offerings were presented according to the ancestral rite, he was [honored] with that gentle honey which flowed forth immediately.
He indeed gratified the ancestors with the sweet nectar of *svadhā*:
the Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, the Kāvyas, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas.
The sages have declared that Agni is the *ṛtu* (season); they know the *ṛtu* to be the year (*saṃvatsara*).
From him the seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*) were born, and from the seasons the seasonal periods (*ārtavāḥ*) came into being. (Matsya Purāṇa 141.14)
The Pitṛs are to be known as the seasons (ṛtu), and the sons of the seasons are the half-months (ardhamāsa).
The Grandfathers (pitāmaha) are indeed the seasons, for they are the sons of the year (abda).
The Great-grandfathers (prapitāmaha) are remembered as the gods; they are the five years, the sons of Brahmā.
"The Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, the Kāvyas, and the Agniṣvāttas—these are the three classes.

Those householders who are performers of sacrifices, and those who offer oblations at the seasonal sacrifices, are declared in the Purāṇa to be the Barhiṣads; this is the settled conclusion. (Matsya Purāṇa 141.16)
The householders who perform sacrifices are known as the Agniṣvātta Ṛtus; the Kāvyas are the lords of the Aṣṭakā rites. Now, learn of those who have five years [of life]. MatsP_141.17 //
Among them, Agni is indeed Saṃvatsara, Sūrya is Parivatsara,
Soma is Iḍvatsara, and Vāyu is Anuvatsara.
Rudra is the year for those five-year periods that constitute the Yugas;
presided over by Time, the Moon sheds nectar upon them.
These are remembered as the divine rites for those who drink the Soma and those who drink the steam;
with that [offering], he gratified them until the time of Purūravas.
Since Soma is produced from it month after month in particular,
therefore that which sustains the *svadhā* of the Soma-drinking ancestors is indeed this nectar;
for it is both Soma and honey.
Then, with a single ray called Suṣumna, that very Sun causes the Moon, who has drunk the nectar, to swell;
indeed, [he swells] the Moon who drinks the Soma.
In the past, while being nourished by the *suṣumnā*, he simultaneously pervaded all the preceding digits (*kalā*) in their entirety,
part by part, according to the sequence of the days.
The dark digits wane, and the bright ones indeed wax;
thus is the body of the moon nourished by the power of the sun.
On the full moon day, he is seen white with a perfectly full orb;
thus, having been replenished during the bright fortnight by the sequence of days,
the gods drink the nectar-like Soma first, and afterwards the Sun drinks it.
For fifteen days, the Sun, by means of a single ray through the Suṣumṇa, nourishes [the moon] part by part in the sequence of the days.
As he is nourished by the Suṣumnā, the white digits indeed increase;
therefore, the black digits wane, for it is the white digits that nourish him.
In this way, Soma waxes and wanes again and again;
such is the prosperity of Soma during the two fortnights, the bright and the dark.
Thus, this Soma is remembered as possessing the Pitṛs;
he is composed of that very essence, beautiful with the fifteen [digits] together with the flowing streams of nectar.
Hereafter I shall explain the junctions of the cosmic cycles (parvan),
and how these cycles are joined together like the joints of a reed stalk that has been twisted back.
Likewise, the years, months, and fortnights are remembered as being both bright (śukla) and dark (kṛṣṇa);
so too are the distinctions of the full moon (paurṇamāsī), as well as the knots (granthi) and the junctions (saṃdhi).
Since the rites for establishing the sacred fires are performed at the junctions of the lunar phases (parvan), the parvans of the half-month begin from the second day.
Therefore, at the beginning of the lunar festival (parvan), at the junctions of the first day (pratipad) and so forth,
during the evening, two lava-measures of time are prescribed for Anumati;
likewise, two lava-measures of the full moon (rākā) are to be known as the afternoon time.
When the time of the dark fortnight has passed in the afternoon,
this very time at evening is the moment for the full-moon ritual.
When the sun is situated in Vyatīpāta and has risen above the horizon, and when the moon has risen in another *yuga* (division of time) and is likewise situated above the horizon— MatsP 141.35.
When one observes the Full Moon and the Vyatīpāta yoga occurring in mutual conjunction,
they both remain established at that time until the arrival of the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad).
At that time, having observed the sun, you should count [the duration];
that indeed is the time for the performance of rites, and it is designated as the sixth period.
The full moon is indeed in the bright fortnight at the junctions of the nights;
therefore, on the night of the full moon (paurṇamāsī), the maker of the night is replenished.
When the moon and the sun are seen during the day at midday on the full moon day, they fall into each other's domain;
because of this fullness in the afternoon, it is known as the full moon (pūrṇimā).
Because the ancestors together with the deities give their approval on that day, it is called Anumati; and because of its fullness, it is known as Pūrṇimā.
Because the moon shines exceedingly on the night of the full moon,
and because it delights [all beings], the poets know that night as Rākā.
When the moon and the sun dwell together in the same constellation,
that single fifteenth night is traditionally known as Amāvāsyā.
When the moon and the sun come together on that new-moon day (amāvāsyā), they are called "darśa" because of their mutual sighting (darśana) of one another.
Two *lava*s each at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)—that is the time during the junctions of the lunar phases (*parvasaṃdhi*).
It consists of two syllables and lasts for the duration of a *kuhū*; that is traditionally remembered as the time of the *parvan*.
Indeed, from midday onwards here, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is one during which the moon is visible;
thereafter, during the day, when the sun has reached the night [meridian],
the moon would suddenly rise together with the sun, and thus it is indeed at dawn.
At midday, when two lava-s have elapsed, the sun sets;
then, on the first day of the bright fortnight, the moon emerges from the solar disc.
Between those two mandalas as they are being released,
that indeed is the time for the subsequent oblation (anvāhuti) and the vaṣaṭ-calls of the new moon;
this should be known as the beginning of the season, while the full-moon rite belongs to the new moon (amāvāsyā).
The day of the full moon is the festival, while the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs when the moon has waned; however, it is indeed during the bright fortnight that the new moon falls on a day.
Therefore, the new moon is observed during the day by the one who is the maker of the day (the Sun).
"Kuhū," so it was said by the cuckoo; because it is completed from that [specific] time, this new moon day (amāvāsyā) is known by that name and is remembered as Kuhū.
When the moon, with only a small remnant remaining, has reached the size of Sinīvālī, it enters the sun on the new moon day; that is traditionally known as Sinīvālī.
Anumati, Rākā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū—of these, the time consists of two lavas; Kuhū is said to be of the measure of a single lava.
Thus, this time of the junctions of the lunar phases (parvan-sandhi) is indeed remembered as lasting for two lavas;
the duration of the phases is equal, as are the offerings and the utterances of vaṣaṭ.

On the two full-moon days when the moon and Jupiter are in conjunction and there is no vyatīpāta yoga, as well as on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) following such a conjunction, the period of the festival (parvakāla) lasts for two measures.
The interval between the *kuhū* and *sinīvālī* phases is known as the *samuddha*, consisting of two *lava*s;
when the moon is within the solar disc, that time of the lunar node (*parvakāla*) is said to consist of *kalā*s.
For this reason, the moon is filled on the fifteenth day of the full moon by means of ten and five digits respectively, through the progression of the days.
Therefore, in the fifteenth lunar day of the moon, there is indeed no sixteenth digit;
for this reason, O Brahmin, the waning of the moon was declared by me to occur on the fifteenth day.
Thus these Pitṛs are gods who drink Soma and cause Soma to increase;
they are the seasonal ones, the seasons, and the years, for they indeed nourish those gods.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim who those ancestors are that partake of the śrāddha,
as well as their destiny, their true nature, and indeed the attainment of the śrāddha itself.
The destination of the dead, or their return once more, cannot be known even by one perfected through ascetic penance; how much less so by the eye of flesh?
In this regard, these worldly ancestors (pitaras) are traditionally held to be both gods and pitṛs;
by the power of their merit, they are said by the twice-born to attain union (sāyujya) with them.
Or if, by means of the duties of their respective stages of life, they remain established in wisdom,
others here will find favor in those actions endowed with faith.
By celibacy, austerity, sacrifice, progeny on earth,
ancestral rites, knowledge, and the gift of food— thus in seven ways.

Those who remain attached to these rites until the fall of their bodies rejoice in heaven, having gone there with the gods, the *ūṣmapas*, and the *somapas*; they, possessing their ancestors, attend upon them.

This is indeed well-known among those with offspring and those who perform the Śrāddha rites; for what is given in their funeral offering by kinsmen born of the same lineage [yields great fruit]. (Matsya Purāṇa 141.64)
For those who eat the monthly śrāddha offerings pass beyond to the world of Soma;
these human ancestors are indeed the ones who consume the monthly śrāddha.
But others besides them, who are of mixed origin from wombs of action,
have fallen away from the duties of their stages of life and are devoid of the utterances *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
When the body is shattered, those who have fallen into misfortune become ghosts in the abode of Yama;
having reached the place of torment, they grieve over their own past deeds.
Tall, exceedingly emaciated, bearded,
and naked, overcome by hunger and thirst, they flee hither and thither.
Desiring the food of others, they will be driven hither and thither to every river, lake, pond, and lotus-pool.
Those who are cast down into those various places of torment—
namely, upon the Śālmali tree, in the Vaitaraṇī river, in the Kumbhīpāka hell, and in the hell of burning sand— [suffer there].
And indeed, being cast down into the Forest of Sword-leaves by their own past actions,
those who remain there, suffering and unable to lie down, [experience great pain].
When those who have departed to other worlds receive three rice-balls (piṇḍas) offered on the ground upon Darbha grass by their kinsmen, using their names and lineages,
they certainly satisfy them as they remain presiding over the realms of the deceased.

Those who have not reached the places of torment, and those who have fallen away in five ways, and those who afterwards, by their own actions, belong to the host of beings ending with the stationary ones; MatsP_141.73.
In various forms among the species of the animal realm,
whatever food these beings consume in those respective wombs, [that is described here].

Whatever food is given with faith at various times, acquired by righteous means, and offered according to rule into a worthy recipient, reaches the one who has taken it wherever he may abide. (Matsya Purāṇa 141.75)
Just as a calf finds its mother when the cows have been lost,
so too does the mantra, seen in the ancestral rites (śrāddha), cause that [deceased] to reach [the ancestors].
For thus Manu declared that a gift given with faith is complete;
and Sanatkumāra spoke thus, seeing with his divine eye. (Matsya Purāṇa 141.77)
He knows the coming and going of the pretas and the attainment of the śrāddha;
for them, the dark fortnight is their hand, while the bright fortnight is for sleep during the night.
Thus these are both the Pitṛs and the Devas; indeed, the Devas are the Pitṛs and the Pitṛs are the Devas. For these Devas and Pitṛs are fathers to one another in heaven.
These indeed are the divine ancestors and those who are human ancestors—
the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
Thus has this domain of the Soma-drinking ancestors been declared;
for this greatness of the ancestors is established as certain in the Purāṇa.
Thus ends this account of the meeting between Soma, Sūrya, and Aila,
as well as the attainment [of progeny] through faith and the propitiation of the ancestors.
The time of the lunar phases and the very place of torment have been described to you in brief; this is the eternal creation.
The diversity [of these] has been described by him as merely partial;
it is impossible to enumerate them all completely, yet they must be accepted with faith by one who desires prosperity.
This creation of the divine Svāyambhuva has been recounted by me in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I tell you?
Matsya Purāṇa 142.
The sages said:
"Regarding those four yugas that occurred previously in the Svāyambhuva interval..."
We wish to hear in detail their natural number as well.
Sūta said:
"In connection with the earth and the sky, I have previously described this cycle of four yugas; now listen as I speak of it further."
Having fully calculated its dimensions in detail and in their entirety, [one should know it].
The human year, however, is to be established by worldly means of measurement;
having calculated even by that [standard] here, I shall describe the four ages (caturyuga),
as well as the syllables obtained through the measures of time equal to the duration of a blink of an eye.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and one should count thirty *kāṣṭhās* as one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and thirty of those make up a day and night combined.
In the human world, the sun divides day and night:
night is for the sleep of beings, and day is for the performance of actions.
For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night; furthermore, their division is as follows:
the dark fortnight is their day, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep.
Thirty human months are said to constitute one month of the ancestors (pitrya).
Three hundred and sixty such human months are understood to be one year of the ancestors. (Matsya Purāṇa 142.7)
That which constitutes one hundred years by human measurement is indeed reckoned as three hundred years and twelve months by the measurement of the ancestors (pitṛs) here. MatsP_142.8 //
That which is known as a human year by worldly means is a single day and night of the gods; such is the Vedic revelation.
A divine day and night constitute a year; their further division is as follows:
that which is the northern course (of the sun) is the day, and that which is the southern course is the night.
These are reckoned as the divine day and night. MatsP_142.10.
Thirty human years are known as one divine month; three hundred human years indeed constitute three divine months. This is recorded as the rule for calculating divine time.
Three hundred and sixty such years are proclaimed as one divine year by human reckoning.
Three thousand years by human measure,
plus another thirty years, is recorded as one year of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
Nine thousand human years and ninety years are recorded as one Dhruva-year.
Thirty-six thousand human years,
along with sixty thousand more when calculated by number,
are said by those who know calculation to constitute one divine thousand-year period. (Matsya Purāṇa 142.15)
O twice-born ones, this has been sung by the seers according to divine calculation;
the number of the yugas has been determined by that very same divine measure.
The sages have declared that there are four ages in the land of Bhārata:
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali; such is the cycle of the four ages.
First is that which is called the Kṛta Yuga, then that designated as Tretā;
one should likewise reckon the Dvāpara and Kali as the [remaining] ages.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn and its twilight are each of the same duration.
In the other three ages, along with their twilights and twilight-portions,
thousands and hundreds of years elapse when only one quarter remains.
Those who know the calculation of the yugas understand that the Tretā consists of three thousand years;
its morning twilight is three hundred years, and its evening twilight is equal to the morning twilight.
The Dvāpara age consists of two thousand years, while its dawn and twilight periods each consist of four hundred years;
the Kali age alone is proclaimed to be one thousand years,
and its dawn and twilight periods are recorded as being two hundred years each.
This period of twelve thousand years is designated as the number of a Yuga;
it consists of the fourfold division known as Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
In that regard, learn from me of the years created for human beings:
ten and two and five *niyutas* in number, plus twenty-eight thousand; this is called the Kṛta Yuga. (Matsya Purāṇa 142.24)
One full prayuta, two additional niyutas,
and ninety-six thousand—
this is the calculated number of the Tretā Yuga as designated by human reckoning.
Eight hundred thousand years of human beings constitute the Dvāpara Yuga,
which consists of sixty-four thousand years.
The Kali Yuga shall consist of four million and thirty-two thousand years by human calculation; this is declared to be the measure of the Kali Yuga.
This state of the four yugas has been proclaimed according to human reckoning;
the total number of the four yugas, together with their junctions (saṃdhyās) and their constituent parts (saṃdhyāṃśakas), has thus been calculated.
This period known as the four yugas, consisting of seventy-one such cycles with an additional portion,
joined with the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, is called an interval of a Manu (manvantara).
Now learn the number of a Manvantara according to human reckoning:
it has been calculated by the twice-born as thirty-one crores.
Likewise, there are one hundred and ten thousand parts,
and thirty-two thousand and eight hundred more.
Eighty years and six additional months—
this is proclaimed as the measure of a Manvantara according to the human reckoning.
And by divine measure, I shall declare the interval of a Manu;
they say that, by calculation, it consists of one hundred thousand [years].
Forty thousand [years] are called a Manvantara;
the duration of a Manvantara, together with its associated Yugas, is thus proclaimed.
This period, known as the four yugas, consisting of seventy-one [cycles] plus a surplus,
revolving in succession, is called an *antara* of Manu.
Those who know this declare that fourteen such kalpas constitute one [Mahākalpa];
thereafter follows the total dissolution, which is indeed the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya).
The duration of a Kalpa is explained as being twice the number [of years] previously stated;
thus are the ages known as Kṛta and Tretā described within the cycle of four Yugas.
I shall describe the Tretā, the Dvāpara, and the Kali as well;
it is impossible to speak of these two [latter ages] separately when they are joined together simultaneously.

This succession of two ages, which has come down to me in due order, was not told by me to you because of my preoccupation with the lineage of the sages and because of the sequential nature of the account.

The remainder that was not stated regarding the Tretā Yuga, I shall now declare; listen to it. Now, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, Manu and the Seven Sages, urged by Brahmā, proclaimed the Dharma consisting of the Śruti and the Smṛti.

The seven seers proclaimed the extensive Vedic dharma, beginning with the union of wife and the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and the collections of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas. (Matsya Purāṇa 142.41)

Manu Svāyambhuva has proclaimed the tradition of Dharma handed down through succession, characterized by the Smṛtis and defined by conduct, which is joined with the practices of the social classes and stages of life.
Through truth, celibacy, sacred learning, and likewise through austerity,
those who had performed intense penance [attained their status] according to the traditional succession of the sages.
Then, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, for the sake of the Seven Sages and Manu,
it occurred first without conscious intent and subsequently with conscious intent.
Those mantras were indeed augmented by the appearances of Tāraka and others;
however, in the first kalpa, they manifested spontaneously among the gods.
Then, for those who have attained perfection through the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), as well as for others,
the application of mantras proceeds; indeed, throughout thousands of past kalpas,
those mantras have repeatedly appeared in their respective images.
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and those mantras belonging to the Atharvans,
as well as those proclaimed by the Seven Seers— Manu declared these to be the Smārta (tradition-based) Veda.
In the beginning of the Tretā age, the Vedas were unified and served solely as the bridges of dharma;
however, due to the decline of the lifespan, they are divided during the Dvāpara age.
During that time, the sages study the Vedas day and night through the power of their ascetic penance.
The divine [Vedas], which are without beginning or end, were proclaimed of old by the Self-Existent One;
enveloped in their own dharma and complete with their auxiliary limbs, they are modified according to the dharma in each successive age,
for the declarations of the Vedas undergo transformation according to the age and their own inherent nature.
The Kṣatriyas are said to have sacrifices involving physical exertion; the Vaiśyas, oblation sacrifices;
the Śūdras, sacrifices of service; and the Brāhmaṇas, sacrifices of silent recitation.
Then, during the Tretā age, the social orders (varṇas) arose together, devoted to righteousness,
performing their duties, possessing progeny, prosperous, and indeed happy.
The Kṣatriyas are ordained by the Brāhmaṇas, and the Vaiśyas by the Kṣatriyas;
the Śūdras follow the Vaiśyas, through mutual favor toward one another.
Their virtuous natures consist of those duties based on caste and stage of life;
for in the undegenerated Tretā Yuga, the undertaking of ritual action succeeds through the intended mind, speech, or manual labor.
Longevity, physical form, strength, intelligence, health, and virtuous conduct—
indeed, all these were common to everyone during the Tretā Yuga.
Brahmā likewise established for them the system of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama),
as well as the Saṃhitās, the Mantras, health, and a virtuous character.
Likewise, the Saṃhitās and the Mantras were composed by the sages, the sons of Brahmā;
and at that very time, the sacrifice was set in motion by the deities.

In the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, those sacrifices were first set in motion by the gods, together with the Yāmas, the Śukras, the Jayas— all who provide all means of accomplishment— as well as Viśvasṛj and the highly powerful Indra, the lord of the gods.
Truthfulness, recitation, austerity, and charity are said to be the ancient dharma;
yet when that dharma declines, the dharma of the branches increases.
And at that time, heroes are born who are long-lived and possessed of great strength;
they lay aside the rod of punishment, are great yogis, performers of sacrifice, and exponents of the Veda.
With eyes as broad as lotus petals, large faces, and well-knit frames;
with lion-like chests and great strength, they moved with the gait of elephants in rut.
And in the Tretā age, there were universal monarchs who were great archers;
they were endowed with all the auspicious marks and had bodies as well-proportioned as the banyan tree.

The two arms are known as *nyagrodha*; when the span of the outstretched arms (*vyāma*) is equal to the height, one is called *nyagrodha*. For that embodied being whose height is equal to his circumference, he is described as having the proportions of a *nyagrodha* tree.
The wheel, the chariot, the jewel, the wife, the treasure, the horse, and likewise the elephant—
these were declared to be the seven jewels in the former Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
By a portion of Viṣṇu, universal monarchs are born upon the earth throughout all past and future Manvantaras.
Among those *tretā* ages that have passed, those yet to come, and those occurring in the present here, it is in these that universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) are born.
And these four most wonderful blessings— strength, righteousness, happiness, and wealth— are clearly perceived in those rulers of the earth.
O King, wealth, virtue, pleasure, fame, and victory itself are all attained together, without mutual conflict.
Endowed with the power and strength of lordship, such as the faculty of atomization (aṇimā) and others,
they indeed surpass the ṛṣis through their learning and asceticism.
By their strength they overcome both Dānavas and Mānavas,
and they are born with superhuman marks residing upon their bodies.
Their hair rests upon their foreheads, and their tongues serve as cleansing brushes;
they possess a dark radiance, four fangs, noble lineages, and their vital energies are directed upward.

Their arms reached down to their knees, their hands were as long as palm trees, and they had the form of bulls; they possessed the girth and proportions [of lions], lion-like shoulders, and were endowed with intelligence.
On their feet are wheels and fish, and on their hands are conchs and lotuses;
indeed, eighty-five thousand [of them] live free from old age and disease.
The four unimpeded movements of those wheel-turning monarchs extend through the atmosphere,
the oceans, the netherworld, and the mountains.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, and truth are indeed remembered as the duties of the Tretā age.
At that time, Dharma proceeds according to the divisions of caste and stage of life,
and the science of government (daṇḍanīti) is set in motion for the purpose of establishing the boundaries of conduct.
All people were joyful, well-nourished, free from disease, and full of heart's content.
In the Tretā age, the Veda is recorded as having four quarters;
there, those subjects lived for three thousand years.
Surrounded by sons and grandsons, they die one after another;
such is the condition in the Tretā Yuga—learn now the calculation of the Tretā.

It proceeds by means of the transitional quarter (saṃdhyā-pāda) characterized by the nature of the Tretā Yuga; and that portion which, by its own nature, remains by means of a quarter is the transitional quarter.
Matsya Purāṇa 143.
The sages said:
"How did the commencement of sacrifice take place at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga?"
Tell us correctly, as it happened, about the previous creation of Svāyambhuva.
When the twilight period had vanished along with the Kṛta Yuga,
and the age called Kāla had begun, the Tretā Yuga then arrived.
When the medicinal herbs had grown, when the release of rain had begun,
and when the means of livelihood were established in both villages and cities.
"Having established the system of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) by means of those mantras, and having properly compiled the Saṃhitās, how was the sacrifice set in motion?
Having heard this, Sūta said: 'Listen to that which was proclaimed.'"
Sūta said:
Having indeed applied the mantras to his rites for this world and the next,
the lord Indra, the enjoyer of all, thus set the sacrifice in motion.
Having gathered together with the deities and being surrounded by all means of accomplishment,
the great seers arrived when his horse sacrifice had been set forth.
Then, at the beginning of the sacrificial rite, the officiating priests engaged in their duties as various kinds of oblations were being offered into the fire by the divine Hotṛ priest.
While the gods were listening attentively and the chanters of the *Sāmaveda* were singing in beautiful voices,
and while the swift *adhvaryu* priests were moving about.
And while the groups of sacrificial animals were being immolated,
and the gods who partake of the sacrifice had been summoned at that time, MatsP 143.9.
Those gods who consist of the senses and partake in the sacrificial portions,
those gods who exist during the Kalya and other ages, then worship them.

But at the time of the Adhvaryu’s summons, the sages and great seers arose; seeing those herds of animals distressed, they then asked Viśvabhuj: "How is your sacrificial rite proceeding? (Matsya Purāṇa 143.11)

"O best of gods, this unrighteousness of yours—this practice of violence in the desire for dharma—is indeed powerful; moreover, O supreme deity, a new animal sacrifice has been favored by you in your rite."
"Unrighteousness has been undertaken by you and the animals for the destruction of righteousness.
This is not dharma; this is adharma, for violence is not said to be dharma.
If you so desire, let your dharma be practiced in accordance with the sacred tradition (āgama)."
O best of gods, [one should worship] with sacrifices prescribed by rule, performed according to dharma without addiction, using sacrificial seeds gathered for the sake of the three goals of life.

"This great sacrifice is Indra himself, ordained by the Self-Existent in ancient times. Though addressed thus by the seers who perceive the truth, Indra, the consumer of the universe, did not accept it, being possessed by pride and delusion.
A very great dispute arose among those great ṛṣis regarding Indra, concerning whether the sacrifice should be performed with moving beings or with stationary ones. Thus it was said.
But those great ṛṣis, exhausted by their dispute yet endowed with power,
made an alliance with Indra and questioned the sky-faring Vasu.
The sages said:
"O highly wise one, O King, how was the ritual of sacrifice seen by you?
O son of Uttānapāda, tell us; O Lord, dispel our doubt. (Matsya Purāṇa 143.18)
Sūta said:
Having heard their words, Vasu, without deliberating upon their relative strengths and weaknesses,
recalled the Vedic scriptures and spoke concerning the true nature of sacrifice.
"The sacrifice must be performed with whatever has been brought forth," so said the king;
"the sacrifice may be performed with pure animals, or even with roots and fruits."
"It is my traditional teaching and vision that the very nature of sacrifice is violence;
likewise, these mantras have been composed by the great seers as having the characteristic mark of violence."
That measure has been declared by me for those endowed with long austerity who can point out the stars and other celestial bodies; therefore, you ought to pacify yourselves.
O twice-born ones, if your own mantra-texts are indeed authoritative for you, then let the sacrifice proceed accordingly; otherwise, it would be a false statement.
Having thus received this reply, they then applied their minds with wisdom;
seeing that [fall] was inevitable, they then cursed him downward.
As soon as these words were spoken, the king entered the subterranean realm;
having been a wanderer above the earth, the king became a dweller of Rasātala.
By those words, King Vasu, the dispeller of doubts regarding all dharmas, descended to the subterranean realm and became a wanderer upon the surface of the earth.
Therefore, even by one who is highly learned, a doubt regarding the dharma—which has many streams—should not be voiced; for its course is subtle and difficult to follow.
Therefore, no one— beginning with the gods and the ṛṣis— is able to declare the Dharma with absolute certainty, except for Manu, the son of the Self-Existent One.
Therefore, there should be no violence in sacrifice, as was stated by the seers of old:
"Thousands of millions of seers have gone to heaven by means of their own austerities."
Therefore, the great seers whose wealth is austerity do not praise the sacrifice involving violence;
rather, they praise the gathering of gleaned grains, roots, fruits, vegetables, and a vessel of water.
Having given this according to their means, they are established in the heavenly world;
likewise, freedom from malice, freedom from greed, self-restraint, compassion for all beings, and tranquility.
Celibacy, austerity, purity, compassion, forgiveness,
and fortitude are indeed the unassailable roots of the eternal dharma.
Sacrifice consists of material substances and mantras, while austerity is characterized by equanimity;
through sacrifices one attains the gods, and through austerity, moreover, the state of Vairāja.

Through the renunciation of action one attains the state of Brahmā; through dispassion, dissolution into Prakṛti; and through knowledge, absolute liberation (kaivalya). These five are recorded as the destinies.
Thus, in the former Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there was a very great dispute between the sages and the deities regarding the performance of the sacrifice.
Then those sages, seeing that dharma had been forcibly taken away and disregarding the words of Vasiṣṭha, departed indeed by the way they had come.
When the hosts of sages have departed, the gods shall obtain the sacrifice;
for it is heard that kings such as those of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes were perfected through asceticism.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, Dhruva, Medhātithi, Vasu,
Sudhāmā, Viraja, and likewise Śaṅkhapāda were the sons of Rājasa.
Prācīnabarhis, Parjanya, Havidhāna, and other kings—
these and many others attained heaven through their ascetic penances.
The great-souled royal sages whose fame is firmly established—
for all these reasons, austerity is superior to sacrifice.
In ancient times, this entire universe was created by Brahmā through austerity;
therefore, one does not attain that [result] from sacrifice alone, for this is remembered as having its root in austerity.
For such was the commencement of sacrifice during the Svāyambhuva interval;
from that time forward, this sacrifice has proceeded along with the ages (yugas).
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall again proclaim the rules for the Dvāpara age.
There, when the Tretā Yuga has declined, the Dvāpara Yuga begins.
That success which belongs to living beings in the Tretā Yuga perishes indeed when that Yuga has passed into the Dvāpara and subsequent ages.
Then, when the Dvāpara age had again begun for those subjects,
greed, persistence, trade, warfare, and uncertainty regarding the principles of truth arose.
There will be the destruction of the social classes and the perversion of their duties;
their livelihood will be slaughter, and their supreme punishment will be pride, arrogance, intolerance, and brute force.
Likewise, when the Dvāpara age has again begun with an abundance of rajas and tamas, there is no unrighteousness in the first Kṛta age; that [unrighteousness] was introduced during the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, having become confused, it perishes;
and in the Kali age, the duties of the social classes as well as those of the stages of life are further mixed together.
In that age, a twofold division arises regarding the Śruti and the Smṛti;
both the Śruti and the Smṛti become split in two, and no certain conclusion can be reached.
Because there is no certain comprehension, the true nature of phenomena does not exist;
for when the true nature of phenomena is not understood, a divergence of opinions arises.
They were mutually divided by the delusion of their various views;
therefore, this world was rendered utterly chaotic by those whose perspectives were so diverse.
The single Veda, which consists of four quarters, is repeatedly condensed;
here in this world, it is divided again during the Dvāpara ages due to the brevity of the lifespan.
The single Veda is divided into four at the beginning of the Dvāpara age and subsequent ages;
furthermore, the Vedas are split by the sons of the sages due to the confusion of their vision.
But those collections of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas] were compiled by those great seers through the arrangement of Brahmins and by means of variations in accent and sequence.
Due to both commonality and modification, and because of differences in perspective here and there,
the Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpasūtras, and likewise the sciences of the commentaries [arose].
But others have set out against them, and some have stood in opposition;
in the Dvāpara ages, they proceed with their own philosophical systems that have divergent aims.
Originally, there was only one office of the Adhvaryu priest, but that was later split into two;
this scripture has thus become confused by matters that contradict its general principles.
The duties of the Adhvaryu priest were thrown into great confusion by various ritual procedures (*prasthāna*),
and likewise those of the Atharvans by the divergent options (*vikalpa*) and the omissions of their own *Sāman* chants.
In the Dvāpara age, the meaning [of the Vedas] is made confused by those with divergent views;
when the Dvāpara has passed away, those Vedas indeed perish in the Kali age.
In the Dvāpara age, however, their opposites arise:
lack of vision, death, and likewise the afflictions of disease.
From the sufferings caused by the actions of speech and mind, world-weariness arises;
from that world-weariness, there arises in them a contemplation on liberation from suffering.
From investigation comes detachment; from detachment comes the perception of faults;
and from the perception of faults, the arising of knowledge indeed occurs.
Formerly, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara in the mortal world, there arose among those intelligent men adversaries of the scriptures in the Dvāpara age.
There were also various branches of Āyurveda, as well as those of the auxiliary sciences and Jyotiṣa;
there were various branches of Arthaśāstra and the classification of Hetuśāstra.
The ritual procedures of the Kalpasūtras, the various interpretations of the commentaries,
and the different divisions of the Smṛti scriptures— these are the distinct systems.
In the Dvāpara ages, the divergences of men's minds increase;
through thought, deed, and speech, even their livelihood is accomplished only with great difficulty.
In the Dvāpara age, it is taught that for all beings, time is characterized by excessive affliction;
there is greed, lack of fortitude, strife among merchants, and a failure to ascertain the true principles.
The composition of Vedic scriptures, the confusion of dharmas, the destruction of the system of castes and stages of life, as well as desire and hatred; MatsP_144.26 //
At that time, the maximum lifespan of humans was two thousand years;
when that Dvāpara age had reached its end, its twilight period lasted for one quarter of that duration.
But those devoid of qualities remain during the Dvāpara age;
likewise, its Sandhyā remains for one quarter, and a portion of it is established therein.
Now learn of the transition from the Dvāpara age to the Puṣya [Yuga];
for when a portion of the Dvāpara remains, then the commencement of the Kali age occurs.
Violence, theft, falsehood, deceit, and hypocrisy—
these are the inherent natures of the ascetics among the Puṣyas, and they bring these traits to fruition for their offspring.
This entire dharma has been declared, yet dharma is being lost;
whether through mind, action, or speech, worldly livelihoods may or may not succeed.
The Kali age shall be a destroyer, with constant disease and the perpetual fear of hunger;
there will be the dread of drought and the upheaval of nations.
Indeed, there is no stability in the Puṣya or Ghora ages during the Kali Yuga;
some die while still in the womb, and others do so while in their youth.
In the Kali age, living beings die in old age, middle age, or childhood;
they possess little luster or strength, are sinful, highly irascible, and indeed unrighteous.
And during the Puṣya age, the subjects will abide in falsehood, broken vows, and greed, due to ill-performed sacrifices,
poorly studied texts, wicked conduct, and false scriptures.
Through those defects of action by the Brahmins, fear arises among the subjects;
likewise, violence, pride, envy, anger, malice, intolerance, and lack of fortitude [arise]. (Matsya Purāṇa 144.36)
During the Puṣya age, greed and delusion arise among living beings in every respect;
indeed, upon reaching the Kali Yuga, extreme agitation comes into being.
The twice-born do not study the Vedas nor perform sacrifices;
likewise, the Kṣatriyas perish along with the Vaiśyas.
In that Kali age, the connection of Śūdras with Brāhmaṇas arises from the source of mantras, as well as through sharing beds, seats, and food.
Kings will consist mostly of Śūdras; there will be the proliferation of heretics, as well as those wearing saffron robes who go about naked, and likewise the Kāpālikas.

And those others who observe the vows of the gods, as well as those who corrupt the Dharma, and whoever among them follow a divine mode of life merely for the sake of a livelihood while wearing the signs of the Vedas; 144.41.
And whoever such as these there may be here in the Kali age— Śūdras learned in dharma and artha— they will then study the Vedas.
For kings born of the Śūdra caste will perform Aśvamedha sacrifices after having committed the slaughter of women, children, and cows, and after having killed one another. (Matsya Purāṇa 144.43)
Having thus harmed one another, the people then bring about their own destruction;
there will be an abundance of suffering, short lifespans, the ruin of countries, and the prevalence of disease.
In the Kali age, it is taught that the adherence to unrighteousness is characterized by darkness;
for the killing of embryos among people does not proceed in such a manner [as it did before].
Therefore, in the Kali age, lifespan, strength, and beauty decline;
for men overwhelmed by suffering, the maximum lifespan is one hundred years.
Having existed, all the Vedas cease to exist here in the Kali Yuga;
likewise, the sacrifices that are the sole causes of dharma perish.
This is the condition of the Kali Yuga; now understand its two transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśau).
In each successive age, the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) diminish by three-quarters each.
The natures of the Yugas persist during the Sandhyās for one quarter;
the natures of the Sandhyās likewise persist within their own portions for one quarter.
Thus, when the twilight period at the end of the age had arrived,
he who was established in the lineage of the Bhṛgus became the teacher of those unrighteous ones.
By lineage he belongs to the Moon, and by name he is called Pramati;
he appears during the Kali-saṃdhyāṃśa periods within the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Wandering indeed over the earth for a full thirty years,
Aśvakarman [ruled] that army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then, surrounded by hundreds and thousands of Brahmins with uplifted weapons,
he slaughtered all the Mlecchas.
Having slain all those kings of Śūdra origin,
that lord, the sovereign, forever rendered all heretics utterly extinct.
And he destroys in every way all those who are unrighteous,
including those from the north, the middle country, and likewise the mountain dwellers.
[He conquered] those of the east and the west, as well as those from the back of the Vindhya mountains and the western regions;
likewise, those of the south, the Dravidians, along with the Siṃhalas.
The Gāndhāras, Pāradas, Pahlavas, Yavanas, Śakas,
Tuṣāras, Barbaras, Śvetas, Halikas, Daradas, and Khaśas.
With his wheel set in motion, the powerful king shone as the destroyer of the Lampakas, the Āndhras, and likewise the tribes of thieves and Śūdras.
Having put all beings to flight, he wandered over this earth;
and in the lineage of Manu, he was born here as a god among men.
In a previous birth, the powerful Viṣṇu was named Pramati;
he was indeed the son of Candra, the lord in the former Kali age.
When he had reached his thirty-second year, he set out and for twenty years slaughtered all human beings everywhere.
Having reduced that earth to nothing but seeds through cruel deeds— caused by mutual conflict as well as by sudden time— MatsP_144.62.
That army which had suddenly halted with Pramati attained perfection through meditative absorption (samādhi) in the middle of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Then, when those of cruel deeds had perished at the time of twilight,
and after all the kings had been exterminated and they had passed away, (Matsya Purāṇa 144.64).
Then, when the time of twilight had arrived, like that at the end of a Yuga, and when the creatures remaining here in various places were few in number; MatsP_144.65.
Then, indeed, being possessed by greed and refusing to give their own wealth,
they will in groups injure one another and plunder each other.
When the portion of the Yuga devoid of a king had arrived and destruction was imminent,
all those subjects were indeed afflicted by fear of one another.
Agitated, they turned back and abandoned the god for their own homes;
looking only toward their own lives, they were utterly miserable due to their lack of compassion.
When the dharma of the Śruti and Smṛti has perished, people will follow the sway of desire and anger;
they will be devoid of moral boundaries, joyless, lacking affection, and shameless.
When the Dharma has perished, the people will be obstructed, short-lived, and twenty-five years of age; abandoning their wives and sons, their progeny will be agitated by despair.
Stricken by drought and abandoned by their means of livelihood, those people, filled with suffering, left their own provinces and took refuge in the borderlands.
Wearing rags and black antelope skins, devoid of ritual action and free from possessions, they frequent rivers, the coastal marshlands of the ocean, and even the mountains.
Having fallen away from their castes and stages of life, and having entered into a terrible state of social confusion,
the subjects then reached such a miserable condition that only a small remnant remained.
And living beings, overcome by hunger, fell into despair because of their suffering;
they wandered about like a wheel, taking refuge in various regions.
Then all those creatures indeed became meat-eaters—
deer, boars, bulls, and whatever other forest-dwellers there were.
Those creatures which have taken refuge in the ocean and the rivers eat all things, both those that are fit to be eaten and those that are unfit to be eaten. (Matsya Purāṇa 144.76)
They too will carry off fish here for the sake of food in every way;
through the fault of consuming food that is unfit to be eaten, all beings will become of a single caste.
Just as in former times during the Kṛta Yuga there was indeed but a single caste,
so too at the end of the Kali Yuga all subjects will have become Śūdras.
In this manner, a full hundred divine years passed for them,
which indeed corresponds to thirty-six thousand human years.
Then, after a long time, birds, beasts,
and even fish were all killed by everyone who was overcome with hunger from every side.
Then, when all the fish, birds, and animals had been completely destroyed,
and the period of twilight had arrived, they were then rendered entirely extinct.
Then the subjects, having gathered together, dug up tubers and roots;
they all subsisted on fruits and roots and likewise remained without dwellings.
They possess bark garments, clothes, and beds upon the ground in every respect;
they have no sense of ownership, and thus they attain purity of wealth.
In this way, indeed, the remaining few creatures will then go to their destruction;
for those who remain in such small numbers, prosperity is desired through food.
In this manner, his twilight period (saṃdhyāṃśa) lasts for a hundred divine years;
then, at the end of those hundred years, women and sons remain in small numbers.
All those pairs indeed procreated with one another;
thereafter, those beings who had been born previously began to die.
Then, as soon as offspring were born, Kṛta-yuga prevailed,
just as it does for embodied beings in heaven and likewise in hell.
In this way, [the objects] were capable of being enjoyed during the Kṛtayuga and other ages;
likewise, there was a continuity of the Kṛta age, and similarly, the decay of the Kali age.
From reflection comes detachment, and likewise through the state of equanimity;
from that arises self-awakening, and from awakening comes the nature of righteousness.
When only those remnants of the Kali age remained, offspring were born from them as before;
then, by the power of the destiny yet to come, the Kṛta age began once more.
Those [characteristics] which have occurred and will occur here in the past and future Manvantaras—
these natures of the Yugas have been described by me in brief.
Having paid homage to the Self-Existent One in detail and in due order,
that Kṛta Yuga then indeed set in once more.
Beings born during the remnants of the Kali age are like those of the Kṛta age;
likewise, those perfected ones (*siddha*) who remain here move about unseen.
Those who were there together with the Seven Sages, and those established there— the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are remembered here as being for the sake of the seed—
then became indistinguishable from those born in the Kṛta Yuga.
Among them, the Seven Sages discourse upon the Dharma here in this world.
In this way, during the Kṛta age, those engaged in ritual acts proceed here, endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti.
But for those established in the dharma shown by the seven seers according to the Śruti and Smṛti,
they remain here in the Kṛta Yuga for the sake of maintaining the order of dharma.
Those sages remain during the periods of the Manvantaras,
just as new grass grows again among the grasses consumed by a forest fire.
Just as the first rain causes the growth of forests at their roots,
so indeed does one Yuga give rise to the succession of subsequent Yugas.
For it proceeds without interruption until the end of the manvantara,
[granting] happiness, long life, strength, beauty, dharma, artha, and even kāma.
"In each age, these three quarters diminish in succession;
thus, O twice-born ones, has this transition been described by me to you. (Matsya Purāṇa 144.101)
This alone is the means of calculation for all the sets of four yugas;
indeed, seventy-one such sets of four yugas constitute one *manvantara*.
When these [ages] have gradually revolved, it is called the interval of Manu;
and whatever occurs here during all those periods known as Yugas, [that is described].
And that very same [principle] applies again to those other [ages], in their respective order;
for in each creation, the various distinctions arise in exactly that manner.
In the fourteen Manvantaras here, there are as many [types of women] to be known:
the Āsurī, the Yātudhānī, the Paiśācī, and the Yakṣa-Rākṣasī.
Listen now to how, in age after age and at that time, those creatures are born;
according to the kalpa, they come to possess characteristics identical to those of the ages.
Thus has the characteristic of the ages been declared in due order. (Matsya Purāṇa 144.106)
The revolutions of the Manvantaras have been proceeding for a long time due to the inherent nature of the Yugas;
the world of living beings does not remain still for even a moment, revolving through decline and rise.
These natures of the yugas have been described to you in their proper order;
now I shall also speak of those Manvantaras that belong to this Kalpa.
Matsya Purāṇa 145: Sūta said:
"In every Kalpa, there are fourteen Manvantaras."
Those which have passed and those yet to come within the Manvantaras here on this earth.
I shall describe in detail and in due order their establishment in each age, as well as their origin in that age and the duration of their lives.
They live for a period of two yugas, or less by two;
it should be known that there are as many such [Manus] here in the fourteen Manvantaras.
The lifespan of humans, beasts, birds,
and stationary beings has been fully set forth in its entirety according to the characteristics of the ages (yugas).
In the same way, the lifespan has completely passed away across all the ages (yugas);
indeed, having observed the instability of beings and of life itself in the Kali age.
In the Kali age, the maximum lifespan of human beings is recorded as one hundred years;
this applies to gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas.
In the Kṛta Yuga, those born of the eight divine origins are equal in both circumference and height; indeed, their elevation is ninety-six finger-breadths.
Likewise, when it is completed with a measurement of nine finger-breadths, there are eight;
this is the natural measurement for those who undertake [the practice].
But humans existing here during the transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśaka) of the ages have a stature equal to that of the gods and asuras, increasing by seven times seven finger-breadths respectively.
It is recorded that one who measures nine tālas from the soles of the feet to the top of the head consists of eighty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) according to the kali-standard.
With his arms reaching down to his knees, he is honored by the gods;
[he is also honored] by cows, elephants, buffaloes, and all things possessing a stationary nature.
In this sequence, the decrease and increase [of stature] are to be understood in each successive age;
in the Kṛta age, a beast would be sixty-seven finger-breadths in height, including its hump.
The height of elephants is recorded as eight hundred finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
while [the height of] horses is one thousand and forty-two finger-breadths.
The maximum height of trees is fifty finger-breadths;
such is the configuration of the human body.
The tall characteristic is seen among the gods because it is observed in their lineage;
the body of the gods is said to be endowed with an excellence of intellect.
Likewise, a human body is said to possess no excellence whatsoever;
thus indeed are all things, whether divine or human, fully encompassed.
Among all animals, birds, and stationary beings alike,
cows, goats, horses, elephants, birds, and wild beasts are to be understood [as the primary examples].
These are all fit for sacrificial rites here, as they serve in rituals;
moreover, these animal-forms are the sequential objects of enjoyment for the gods.
There, those beings— both stationary and moving— were endowed with delightful enjoyments corresponding in form and size to themselves,
and they indeed attained happiness.
Now I shall describe the refined ones, and then indeed the virtuous ones:
the Brāhmaṇas, who are the very words of the Śruti and the animal-forms of the gods;
for because they are united with Brahman within, they are called "the good" (santaḥ).
And likewise, among the common castes and the Vaiśyas,
the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are engaged in their duties according to the Śruti and Smṛti.

The dharma consisting of the Śruti and Smṛti, which is practiced by one engaged in the [four] castes and [four] stages of life, which results in happiness and leads to heaven— that is called the dharma of knowledge (jñānadharmas).
A celibate student (brahmacārī) is called virtuous because he accomplishes divine goals and is devoted to his teacher;
likewise, a householder is said to be virtuous because of his causes and his accomplishments.
Likewise, the virtuous Vaikhānasa is remembered as one who practices austerity in the forest;
the virtuous Yati is remembered as one who strives through the practice of yoga.
Dharma is declared to be the course of dharma; for this word is of the nature of action.
The Lord spoke of both dharma and adharma as being wholesome and unwholesome.
Then the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and even human beings, though appearing in the form of silence, would say, "This is indeed dharma; this is not. (MatsP 145.26)
The verbal root *dhr* is said to mean "to hold" (*dhāraṇa*) and also "greatness" (*mahattva*). Whether it be in the sense of holding or in the sense of greatness, that is defined as *dharma*.
In this regard, the teachers teach that dharma is that which procures what is desired;
and they do not teach that adharma is that which results in what is undesired.
Those who are aged, free from greed, self-possessed, devoid of hypocrisy,
well-disciplined, and gentle— they are declared to be true teachers (ācāryas).
The dharma consisting of the Śruti and Smṛti has been ordained for the twice-born by those who know the Dharma.
The characteristic of Śrauta [dharma] is the performance of sacrifice involving the wife and the Agnihotra fire.

The seven seers, having first taught here the Vedic [dharma], declared that the conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramācāra), joined with restraints and observances, is based on tradition (smārta). MatsP_145.31.
The Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda are indeed the limbs of Brahman according to the Śruti;
having remembered them from a past Manvantara, Manu proclaimed them. (Matsya Purāṇa 145.32)
Therefore, the dharma remembered by tradition (smārta) pertains to the divisions of caste and stage of life;
thus, indeed, dharma is twofold, and that which is called the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is also included therein.
They declare the word *śiṣṭa* to be derived from the verbal root *śās* with the suffix *niṣṭhā*;
those righteous ones who remain here during the various Manvantaras are called *śiṣṭas*.
Manu and the seven ṛṣis, who ensure the continuity of the world, remain here for the sake of dharma; they are designated as the śiṣṭas (the cultured).
By those remaining learned ones, the Dharma that has been disturbed is indeed established in age after age—
the three Vedas, the means of livelihood, and the science of government— out of a desire for the welfare of the subjects according to their castes and stages of life.
Because it is practiced by the learned,
and because it is observed by each successive predecessor at the end of a Manu-period, that conduct of the learned is eternal.
Charity, truthfulness, austerity, sacred knowledge, sacrifice, worship, self-restraint, and control—
these eight are the practices that characterize the conduct of the cultured.
Because the learned (śiṣṭas), as well as Manu and the seven ṛṣis,
practice this in all the Manvantaras, it is therefore known as "the conduct of the learned" (śiṣṭācāra).
That which is to be known through hearing is called *śrauta*, and that which is known through recollection is called *smārta*.
The *śrauta* consists of sacrifice and the Vedas; the *smārta* consists of the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).
Now, I shall here declare the characteristics of Dharma, including its individual limbs.
And he who, when questioned, does not conceal an object seen or experienced—
speaking exactly as it is— this is the characteristic of truth.
Celibacy, austerity, silence, and even fasting—
this is the nature of austerity, which is most formidable and difficult to attain.
The conjunction of sacrificial animals, material offerings, the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses,
as well as the officiating priests and the priestly fee, is called a sacrifice.
He who always acts for the welfare and the auspiciousness of all beings as if they were himself, remaining ever joyful—this supreme action is remembered as compassion. (Matsya Purāṇa 145.44)
When reviled or struck, he who does not revile in return nor strike back,
remaining free from malice in speech, mind, and body, and enduring it— that is remembered as forbearance (kṣamā).
The non-appropriation of others' property, whether it be guarded by its owner or left unattended during a state of confusion, is designated as non-greed (*alobha*). (Matsya Purāṇa 145.46)
Abstaining from sexual intercourse through speech as well as thought, and the cessation thereof, is celibacy (brahmacarya); this is the characteristic of tranquility (śama).
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, that state in which the senses do not engage with their objects here is indeed the characteristic of self-control.
He who does not become angry when struck by an object consisting of the five elements or by the eightfold causes will be one who has conquered his self.
Whatever object is most beloved and has been acquired through righteous means—that very thing should be given to one possessed of virtues; this is the defining characteristic of giving.
Dharma, consisting of the system of castes and stages of life, is ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti;
this dharma, augmented by the conduct of the learned, is esteemed by the virtuous.
For there is no aversion toward what is undesirable, nor does one rejoice in what is desired;
the cessation of joy, suffering, and despondency is detachment.
Renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is the abandonment of actions, both those performed and those unperformed;
indeed, the relinquishing of both the auspicious and the inauspicious is called renunciation.
When this modification, beginning with the unmanifest and ending with the specific elements,
ceases, one who knows both the conscious and the unconscious is called a knower in the context of knowledge.
Furthermore, the ancillary limbs of Dharma— this is the definition recorded by the ancient seers who knew the true essence of Dharma during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
In this regard, I shall describe to you the ordinance concerning the Manvantara,
as well as that of the Cāturhotra and the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya).
And at the beginning of every Manvantara, another Śruti is ordained—
Ṛks, Yajus, and Sāmans— accordingly for each respective deity.
The ritual praise (vidhi-stotra), as well as the priestly office (hautra), proceed as before;
likewise the praise of substances (dravya-stotra), the praise of qualities (guṇa-stotra), and the praise of actions (karma-stotra).
In the same way, there is the praise of his lineage; thus, the hymn of praise is fourfold, according to the various divisions that indeed occur throughout all the Manvantaras.
They indeed chant the hymn of praise to Brahmā for them again and again;
such is the fourfold origin of the qualities of the mantras.
Then, among those sages performing most difficult penance here within the Vedas—the Atharva, Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman—each separately, [the Lord appeared]. (Matsya Purāṇa 145.61)
In the beginning of the previous Manvantara, the mantras appeared in five ways: due to dissatisfaction, fear, suffering, delusion, and grief.
I shall here describe that characteristic by which the sages are stars, and according to which they possess their nature as sages, even by chance.
The *ārṣa* [style] is indeed remembered as fivefold regarding the past and the future;
likewise, I shall here describe the origin of the *ārṣa* of the sages.
Then, at the universal dissolution, all things exist in the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas),
undifferentiated within the gods, in the indefinable state composed of darkness (tamas).
That which is not preceded by conscious intent proceeds for the sake of consciousness;
however, that which is revealed by the seers (*ārṣa*) is preceded by conscious intent and is likewise presided over by consciousness.
It proceeds in such a way that both [the fish and the water] exist together;
everything presided over by consciousness, consisting of the qualities (guṇas), proceeded forth.
Thus it proceeds through the relationship of cause and effect.
At that time, the object and the state of being the subject consist of the meaning and the word;
and by means of the time to be reached, the distinctions consist of the nature of the cause.
Then the primordial dispositions (vṛttis) of Mahat and the others arose spontaneously;
from Mahat came this Ahaṃkāra, and from that, the elements and the sense organs.
And the various modifications of the elements arose from the elements themselves through mutual interaction;
the effect, which is the cause of their perfection, manifests instantaneously.
Just as branches indeed emerge from a single firebrand at one and the same time,
so too do the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) proceed forth from a single cause by means of Time alone.
Just as a firefly suddenly becomes visible in the darkness,
so too does the unmanifest, having returned, blaze forth like a firefly.
That Great-Souled One, remaining within the body, proceeds right here;
yet, because he stands beyond the great darkness, he is perceived through his distinct nature.
It is heard that while the wise one remained right there at the conclusion of his ascetic penance,
a fourfold awakening manifested and his intellect flourished.
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue—
these four are innate to him and are indeed not acquired through practice.
The accomplishment of the Great Self (mahātman) is said to arise from consciousness;
for it is called the "Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña) because it formerly lay within the city (puri). (Matsya Purāṇa 145.76)
A person is called a *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) because of pure consciousness;
and because he is indeed born from dharma, he is therefore truly a righteous man (*dhārmika*).
In the spontaneously arisen body, the conscious one is indeed unmanifest through the intellect;
thus the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is revealed, for the Field (kṣetra) is without intentionality.

But at the very moment of its cessation, that ancient, insentient [nature], having been fully known by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), thinks: "This is the object to be enjoyed by me. (MatsP 145.79)
The root *ṛṣ* indeed signifies "to go" or "to move"; since he is the abode of knowledge, truth, austerity, and sacred learning, he is therefore called an *ṛṣi*, a Brāhmaṇa.
And because this seer perceives the Unmanifest through his intellect at the very moment of its cessation,
he is therefore remembered as the Supreme Seer (Paramarṣi).
Because he is self-born, the cause for the formation of his name is derived from the root *ṛṣ*, meaning "to go"; therefore, his status as a seer (*ṛṣi*) is recognized.
The sons of Brahmā, born of his mind, were themselves possessed of a lord;
by them, as they turned back with their intellects, the supreme Mahat was fully comprehended.
Because they were devoted to the vision [of the Lord], therefore those great sages were indeed the sons of the lords— both those born of their mind and those born of their bodies.
The Ṛṣi is superior to him; from him come the Bhūtādi-Ṛṣis;
the sons of the Ṛṣis are the Ṛṣīkas, who are born from the womb through sexual union.
Because they indeed perceive the Bhūtas and others as being beyond [them], they are therefore called Ṛṣikas;
those who are the sons of the Ṛṣikas are to be known as the Ṛṣiputrakas.
Because they heard of the Ṛṣis as being supreme, they are therefore called Śrutarṣis;
likewise, there are those whose self is the Unmanifest (Avyaktātman), the Great Self (Mahātman), and the Self of Ego (Ahaṃkārātman).
"The elemental self (bhūtātmā) and the sensory self (indriyātmā)—the knowledge of these is called their [knowledge].
Thus, the lineage of sages is renowned by five names."
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
Manu, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, and Pulastya— these are the ten.
For these were born from the mind of Brahmā as self-ruling lords;
because they are considered to be superior even to the ṛṣis, they are therefore called maharṣis (great seers).
Now learn of the sons of these lords, who are the sages:
Kāvya, Bṛhaspati, Kaśyapa, and likewise Cyavana.
Utathya, Vāmadeva, Agastya, Kauśika,
Kardama, the Vālakhilyas, Viśravas, and Śaktivardhana.
Thus have these sages been described, who attained the status of sages through austerity;
now learn of their sons, the secondary sages (ṛṣīkas), who were born from the womb.
Vatsara, Nagnahu, the powerful Bharadvāja, the seer Dīrghatamas, and Bṛhadvakṣas, the son of Śaradvat; ||| MatsP_145.94 |||
Vājiśravas, Sucintya, Śāva along with Parāśara,
Śṛṅgin, Śaṅkhapāda, and likewise King Vaiśravaṇa.
Thus all these Ṛṣikas attained the status of sages through truth;
they were indeed lords and seers, as well as those renowned as Ṛṣīkas.
In this manner, learn all those who were creators of mantras in their entirety:
Bhṛgu, Kāśyapa, Pracetas, and the self-possessed Dadhīca.
Ūrva, Jamadagni, Veda, Sārasvata, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Cyavana, and Vītahavya were all possessed of wisdom.
Vainya, Pṛthu, Divodāsa, Brahmavān, Gṛtsa, and Śaunaka—
these nineteen were indeed the Bhṛgus who were the most eminent composers of mantras.
Aṅgiras, Trita, Bharadvāja, and Lakṣmaṇa; Kṛtavāk, as well as Garga, Smṛti, and Saṃkṛti.
Guruvīta, Māndhātṛ, and likewise Ambarīṣa;
Yuvanāśva, Purukutsa, Svaśravas, and Sadasyavat.
Ajamīḍha, Aśvahārya, Utkala, Kavi,
Pṛṣadaśva, Virūpa, Kāvya, and Mudgala.
Utathya, Śaradvat, as well as Vājiśravas,
Apasyu, Oṣas, Sucitti, and likewise Vāmadeva.
Ṛṣija, Bṛhacchukla, the sage Dīrghatamas,
and Kakṣīvān— these thirty-three are remembered as the foremost among the Aṅgirases.
All these were makers of mantras; now learn of the Kāśyapas:
Kāśyapa, Sahavatsara, Naidhruva, and Nitya.
Asita, Devala, Atri, Ardhasvana, Śāvāsya, and Gaviṣṭhira—these six were exponents of the Veda. MatsP_145.106 //
And the seer Karṇaka was perfected, as was he who was Pūrvātithi.
Thus these three great ṛṣis, the authors of mantras, have been declared:
Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and the third, Parāśara.
Then the fifth was Bharadvāja, equal to Indra;
the sixth was the most excellent Mitrāvaruṇa, as well as Kuṇḍina.
Thus these seven should be known as the Vasiṣṭhas, exponents of the Veda:
Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, Devarāta, and likewise Bala.
Likewise, the learned Madhucchandas, the seer Aghamarṣaṇa, Aṣṭaka, Lohita, Bhṛtakīla, and Māmbudhi; MatsP_145.111 //
Devashravas, Devarata, Purana, Dhananjaya, the highly resplendent Shishira, and Shalankayana as well. (Matsya Purāṇa 145.112)
These thirteen should be known as the foremost Kauśikas, most devoted to Brahman:
Agastya, Dṛḍhadyumna, and likewise Indrabāhu; MatsP_145.113 //
