For these three— Brahmiṣṭha, Agastya, and Vaivasvata Manu— are of supreme renown,
as is King Purūravas, the son of Ilā.
These three—Bhalandaka, Vāsāśva, and Saṃkīla—are to be known as the foremost among the Kṣatriyas who are practitioners of mantra. (Matsya Purāṇa 145.115)
These are to be known as the mantra-makers, the perpetual preeminent lineages (pravara) of the Vaiśyas;
thus ninety-two have been declared, along with those excluded from the mantras.
O Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, learn from me concerning the sons of the sages;
for these sons of the sages, whose seership is heard of, are indeed the offspring of the Ṛṣīkas.
Matsya Purāṇa 146. The sages said: "How was the great slaying of Tāraka described by the Fish?"
O son of Sūta, at what time did this story take place?

This story, arising from the milk-ocean of your face and consisting of nectar, does not produce satiety for us as we drink it with our ears. O Sage of great intellect, explain this which dwells in our minds. (Matsya Purāṇa 146.2)
Sūta said:
Being questioned by Manu, the Lord Janārdana in the form of a fish [said]:
"O All-pervading One, how was the six-faced God born in the forest of reeds?"
Having heard these words of the king of immeasurable luster,
the blessed son of Brahmā, being pleased, spoke to the high-minded one.
The Fish said:
There was a Daitya named Vajrāṅga, and his son was Tāraka; that one of great strength drove the gods out from their cities.
Then, oppressed by fear, they went into the presence of Brahmā;
and seeing the gods terrified, Brahmā spoke to them.
"O gods, cast away your fear; the infant son of Śaṅkara, the grandson of the Snowy Mountain, shall slay that Dānava."
Then, at a certain time, having beheld the daughter of the mountain, Śiva discharged his own semen into the mouth of Agni for a specific reason.
That semen, having entered the mouth of Agni, satisfied the gods;
O Sage, it emerged undigested after tearing through their bellies.
It fell from there into that best of rivers, and then into a forest of Śara reeds;
from that, Guha was born, possessing the radiance of the sun.
That boy slew the demon Tāraka on the seventh day;
having heard these words, the best of sages then spoke to him.
The sages said:
This story is most wonderful, delightful, and destructive of sins;
tell it to us in detail, exactly as it happened, for we are listening.
From whose lineage did the lord of the Daityas named Vajrāṅga originate in ancient times,
who had a powerful son, Tāraka, the crusher of the gods?
Who was it that brought about the death of that lord of the Daityas?
O giver of honor, tell us in full how Guha’s birth occurred.
Sūta said:
The mind-born son of Brahmā was the Prajāpati named Dakṣa;
we have heard that he begot sixty daughters by Vairiṇī alone.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
The powerful Lord Prajāpati gave two [daughters] to Bāhukaputra, two to Aṅgiras,
and two to the learned Kṛśāśva.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Viśvā, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, as well as Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, and Irā. (Matsya Purāṇa 146.18)
Kadrū, Muni, and the Mothers of the World are the mothers of cows;
from them [come] the worlds of all beings, both moving and stationary.
Other embodied beings are known to have various kinds of births;
Devendra, Upendra, Pūṣan, and all others like them are considered to be born of Diti.
From Diti were born the worlds, Hiraṇyakaśipu and others;
from Danu came the sons of Danu, the Dānavas; and from Surabhi came the cows.
The birds with Vinatā as their mother are known to have Garuḍa at their head;
the Nāgas are to be understood as the sons of Kadrū, as are all other living beings.
The immensely powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu, having conquered Śakra— the lord of the three worlds and sovereign of all the hosts of immortals— ruled the kingdom.
Then, after some time, Hiraṇyakaśipu and the others were slain by Viṣṇu in battle, while the remaining Dānavas were slain by Indra.
Then Diti, whose sons had been slain, requested a boon from her husband, the divine Kaśyapa: another son of great strength.
The Lord gave her a slayer of Śakra in battle.
"O Goddess, remain steadfast in your observance with a pure mind for a thousand years, and you shall obtain a son. Having been told this, she did exactly so.
While she was engaged in her religious observance, the thousand-eyed Indra, being composed in mind, waited upon her; and she, in turn, gave him her consent.
When ten years remained of the thousand-year period, Diti,
established in asceticism and ready to grant a boon, spoke very joyfully to Śakra.
Diti said: "O Pākaśāsana, know me as one whose vow is nearly completed because of my son;
and you shall have a brother, with whom you shall share this prosperity."
"O child, enjoy the three worlds as you desire, with all its thorns removed.
Having spoken thus, she was overcome by sleep, her hair being trampled by his feet. (Matsya Purāṇa 146.31)
Out of respect for the destined future, she herself fell into an irregular sleep;
and having found that vulnerability, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, entered her womb.
The king of the gods split the embryo into seven parts with his thunderbolt;
then Maghavan further divided each fragment into one more part.
Then Diti, having been awakened seven times over from her anger, woke up and said:
"O Śakra, do not cause the destruction of my offspring!"

Having heard that, Śakra emerged and stood before him with palms joined in reverence; trembling, he spoke these words at his mother’s bidding: matsyapurāṇe pratisargaparvaṇi manvantarānukīrtane ṣaṭcatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ // 146 // Chapter One Hundred and Forty-Six of the Matsya Purāṇa, in the Section on Secondary Creation, concerning the Narration of the Manvantaras.
Śakra said:
"O Mother, you were intent on sleeping during the day, with your hair trodden upon by my feet;
therefore, your embryo has been fashioned by me from seven times seven [semen]."
"O you who are worshipped by the gods, those sons of yours shall be divided into forty-nine portions by Vajra;
I shall grant them their stations in heaven."
Thus addressed, the goddess then replied, "So be it.
And again, the dark-eyed goddess spoke to her husband: *matsya-purāṇa* 146.38.
"O Prajāpati, grant me a son who is powerful and a conqueror of Śakra,
one who cannot be slain by the missiles or weapons of the inhabitants of the triple heaven."
Thus addressed, he spoke to his deeply distressed wife:
"After performing austerities for ten thousand years, you shall indeed obtain [your desire]."
"O you who are affectionate toward your children, your son shall be named Vajrāṅga, possessing limbs made of the essence of diamond— unbreakable, iron-like, and firm."
Having obtained the boon, that goddess went to the forest for asceticism;
for ten thousand years she practiced severe penance.
At the conclusion of her ascetic penance, the Blessed One gave birth to an invincible son, whose deeds were beyond compare, unconquerable, and difficult even for the thunderbolt to pierce.
As soon as he was born, he became a master of all weapons and missiles;
with devotion, he said to his mother, "O Mother, what shall I do?"
Then Diti, being delighted, spoke to that lord of the Daityas:
"O dear son, many of my sons have been slain by the thousand-eyed one."
"You must indeed go to retaliate against them and to slay Śakra.
Having said "So be it" to her, the powerful one went to the third heaven.
Then, having bound the thousand-eyed one with a noose of unfailing power,
he went before his mother like a tiger toward a small deer.
In the meantime, Brahmā and Kaśyapa of great asceticism arrived at that place where the mother and son, who were free from fear, were staying.
Having seen them, Brahmā and Kaśyapa said this:
"Release this son, O Lord of the Gods; what need have you for him?"
"O son, for one who is highly esteemed, dishonor is said to be equivalent to death;
know that he who is released by my word is as good as dead."
Freed from the burden of others, he shall instead bear the weight of his enemies;
O child, though living, he is dead day by day.
"When one has fallen under the power of the great, there is no enmity at all toward an enemy.
Having heard this, Vajrāṅga bowed and spoke these words: [Matsya Purāṇa 146.52]
"I have no further business with him; I have fulfilled my mother's command.
You are the lord of gods and asuras, and you are my great-grandfather."
"O God, I shall carry out your word; here is Śatakratu released.
O God, may I find delight in my asceticism, and may it be free from obstacles for me."
"By your grace, O Blessed One," having said this, he became silent;
while that Daitya remained thus, the Grandfather spoke as follows.
Brahmā said:
"You have indeed undertaken this severe austerity while remaining established in our command;
by this purity of heart, the fruit of your birth has been fully attained."
Having spoken thus, the lotus-born god,
the source from the lotus, created a large-eyed maiden and bestowed her upon him as a wife.
Having given her the name Varāṅgī, the Grandfather departed;
Vajrāṅga also went to the forest with her to practice austerities.
With his arms raised, that lord of the Daityas,
whose eyes were like lotus petals, possessed of pure intellect and great austerity, practiced [penance] for a thousand years.
For that long he remained with his face turned downward, for that long he stayed amidst five fires;
abstaining from food and performing terrible penance, he became a mass of ascetic merit.
Then he spent a thousand years within the water;
while he had entered the depths of the water, his wife remained firm in her great vows.
On the very bank of that lake, out of love for him,
she of great splendor undertook severe penance, observing silence and abstaining from food.
While she was engaged in ascetic penance, Indra,
having become a great monkey, created a terrifying spectacle there at her hermitage.
He completely overturned his wobbly basket of gourds and jars;
then, in the guise of a cloud, the Great One caused him to tremble.
Then, having bound her two feet with his form as a serpent,
he dragged her far away from there, making her wander this earth.
Rich in the power of asceticism, she did not fall victim to his slaughter;
thereafter, in the form of a jackal, she defiled his hermitage.
Then, assuming the form of a cloud and moistening her hermitage,
the subduer of Pāka tormented her with many terrifying apparitions.
When the queen of Vajrāṅga did not cease speaking in this manner, she,
perceiving the wickedness of the mountain, prepared to pronounce a curse.
Seeing her facing the curse, the mountain, who had assumed a human form,
spoke to that beautiful woman of excellent limbs, his heart filled with fear.
"O beautiful woman, I am not wicked; I am to be served by all embodied beings.
It is this Indra, the subduer of Pāka, who, being enraged, creates this delusion."
In the meantime, a period of a thousand years passed.
When that time had elapsed, the Blessed One, born from the lotus,
being pleased, approached that reservoir of water and spoke to Vajrāṅga.
Brahmā said:
"I grant you all your desires; arise, O son of Diti!
Thus addressed, the lord of the Daityas, a treasury of austerities, then rose up.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to the Grandfather of all the worlds.
Vajrāṅga said:
"May I have no asuric disposition; may my worlds be imperishable;
may my delight be in austerity alone, and may my body be sustained by it."
Saying "So be it," the god departed for his own abode;
and Vajrāṅga, firm in his self-restraint, remained once his penance was completed.
Desiring food, he did not see his own wife in his hermitage;
overcome by hunger, he entered the thicket of the mountain.
And as he was looking about there to gather fruits and roots, he beheld his beloved wife, miserable and weeping, her face partially covered by her thin garment;
seeing her, the lord of the Daityas spoke, consoling her: matsya-purāṇa 146.76.
Vajrāṅga said:
"O timid one, who has done you wrong that you wish to go to the world of Yama?
Or what desire shall I grant you? Tell me quickly, O beautiful lady. (Matsya Purāṇa 146.77)
Matsya Purāṇa 147.
Varāṅgī said:
"I have been terrified, cast aside, struck, and even tormented."
By the fierce king of the gods, she was repeatedly treated like one who has lost her protector.
Seeing no further shore to her suffering, she resolved to give up her life:
"Give me a son who will deliver me from this great ocean of misery and grief. (Matsya Purāṇa 147.2)
Thus addressed, that lord of the Daityas, his eyes agitated with anger, though capable of retaliating against the king of the gods, [remained silent]. (Matsya Purāṇa 147.3)
The exceedingly powerful Daitya again resolved to perform austerities;
but Brahmā, having understood his even more cruel intention once more, [acted].
Then the Lord, the Master, arrived at the place where that son of Diti was,
and spoke to him with a sweet voice.
Brahmā said:
"O son, for what purpose do you again desire such a cruel restraint?
O Daitya of great vows, tell us that, as you are intent upon food."
Whatever fruit is obtained by one who remains without food for a thousand years,
that is attained in a single moment by one who has renounced food and remained steadfast.
O lotus-eyed one, the renunciation of unattained desires is not as weighty as the abandonment of a desire already attained.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, the Daitya, reflecting upon what had issued from the mouth of Brahmā and intent on penance, spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Vajrāṅga said:
"Having risen at your command, I beheld through my meditative concentration the queen, terrified, distressed, and weeping at the foot of a tree. (Matsya Purāṇa 147.10)
With a grieving heart, I spoke to that slender-limbed woman:
"O timid one, why do you behave thus? Tell me, what is it that you wish to do?"
Having been addressed thus by me, O Lord, that slender-limbed woman, frightened, spoke these words with faltering syllables, providing a reasoned explanation. *Matsya Purāṇa* 147.12.
The beautiful woman said:
"I have been terrified, cast aside, dragged away,
and tormented many times by the fierce King of the Gods, like one who has lost her protector."
Seeing no end to my suffering, I am resolved to give up my life;
grant me a son who will deliver me from this great ocean of misery. (Matsya Purāṇa 147.14)
Thus addressed, he became agitated and, intent on obtaining a son from her, resolved:
"I shall perform severe penance for the sake of conquering the inhabitants of heaven."
Having heard these words, the four-faced god born from the interior of the lotus then spoke to the king of the Daityas, being well-pleased.
Brahmā said:
"Enough of your asceticism, my child; do not enter into further insurmountable suffering.
A son named Tāraka, possessed of great strength, shall be born to you."
"Regarding the loosening of the braided hair of the celestial women"—
having been addressed thus, the lord of the Daityas prostrated before the Grandfather.
Having arrived with a joyful countenance, he gladdened his queen;
then the couple, having achieved their purpose, went to their own hermitage with delight. (Matsya Purāṇa 147.19)
The noble-limbed woman of excellent complexion bore that embryo, deposited by Vajrāṅga,
within her very womb for a full thousand years.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Varāṅgī gave birth to a son;
indeed, as that lord of the Daityas was being born, he caused fear among the worlds.
The entire earth trembled, the oceans shook, all the mountains moved, and terrifying winds blew. (Matsya Purāṇa 147.22)
The best of sages chanted their prayers, and even the beasts of prey and wild animals cried out;
the moon and sun lost their luster, and the quarters of the sky became shrouded in mist.
When that great Asura was born, all the great Asuras and likewise the Asura women arrived there, filled with joy.
Overcome with joy, the Asura women sang and danced;
then, O best of the twice-born, a great festival arose among the Dānavas.
Then the gods, including Indra, became despondent in mind;
yet Varāṅgī, seeing her own son, was then filled with joy.
But she did not consider even the victory over the Lord of the Gods as much;
meanwhile, the lord of the Daityas, Tāraka, possessed of fierce prowess, was born. (Matsya Purāṇa 147.27)
He was consecrated by all the asuras, beginning with Kujambha and Mahiṣa,
who were capable of rivaling the earth itself, into the great sovereignty over all the asuras.

O best of sages, having obtained the great sovereignty, Tāraka spoke these well-reasoned words to the foremost of the Dānavas: matsyapurāṇe saptacatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ // 147 // Chapter 147 of the Matsya Purāṇa. The one hundred and forty-seventh chapter of the Matsya Purāṇa.
Matsya Purāṇa 148:
Tāraka said:
"Listen, all you mighty Asuras, to my words."
Let everyone apply their intellect toward the accomplishment of what is beneficial for the sake of their own welfare.
"O gods, all the Dānavas are destroyers of our lineage;
indeed, it is our innate nature that enmity has taken root and remains inexhaustible."
"Today we shall all go forth to subdue the gods, relying solely on the strength of our own arms; of this there is no doubt."
"But I do not believe that an encounter with the gods can occur without being joined by asceticism;
therefore, O sons of Diti, I shall first perform severe penance. (Matsya Purāṇa 148.4)
"Then we shall conquer the gods and enjoy the three worlds;
for a man who possesses stable means becomes one whose prosperity is likewise stable."
"One who is fickle is not at all able to protect riches that are themselves fickle.
Having heard those words of that asura, all the dānavas [acted accordingly].
"Excellent! Excellent! said those Daityas there in amazement;
he then went to an excellent cave of Mount Pāriyātra.
It was strewn with flowers of every season, illuminated by various medicinal herbs,
variegated by the flow of juices from diverse minerals, and possessed many cave-dwellings.
It was concealed on all sides by thickets, providing refuge for wish-fulfilling trees of variegated forms; it abounded in many shapes and was teeming with various flocks of birds.
Having reached that cave, which was endowed with various springs and possessed diverse bodies of water, the Daitya performed extensive ascetic penance.
Without food, performing the penance of five fires, subsisting on leaves, or consuming only water,
he performed these various austerities for a hundred, then another hundred, years.
Then, cutting off piece after piece from his own body day by day, he offered a karṣa of flesh into the fire; consequently, he became devoid of flesh.
When he had become fleshless and attained the state of a mass of ascetic heat,
all living beings blazed on every side with his splendor.
All the gods were agitated and terrified by his ascetic power;
meanwhile, Brahmā attained supreme satisfaction.
To grant a boon to Tāraka, the god departed from the abode of the thirty deities;
having reached that king of mountains where he resided in a mountain cave,
the god spoke to Tāraka with sweet words.
Brahmā said:
"O son, enough with your asceticism; there is nothing now that is unattainable for you.
Choose a desirable boon, whatever dwells in your mind."
Thus addressed, the Daitya Tāraka, of vast prowess, bowed down to the omnipresent Lord, the Self-born, and having joined his palms in reverence, spoke with humility.
Tāraka said:
"O abode of the minds of gods and beings, you know the conduct of living creatures;
for most people desire retaliation for what has been done and are intent on victory."
"By our very nature of birth, we have been made enemies with the immortals;
by those cruel ones, who have abandoned righteousness, the Daityas have been utterly destroyed.
It is my resolve that I shall be their deliverer. (Matsya Purāṇa 148.19)
"May I be invulnerable to all beings and to weapons of great power; for this is the supreme boon that has resided in my heart. (Matsya Purāṇa 148.20)
"O Lord of Gods, grant this to me; no other boon pleases me.
Then Viriñci, the leader of the gods, spoke to that Daitya.
"O best of Daityas, it is not possible for embodied beings to exist without death;
therefore, choose as your death that from which you do not fear. (Matsya Purāṇa 148.22)
Then, having reflected, that lord of the Daityas, a great asura deluded by arrogance, chose death from the child after seven days.
And Brahmā, having granted him whatever boon was desired by his mind,
the god went to the third heaven and the Daitya also to his own abode.
When that Daitya had emerged from his ascetic penance, the lords of the Daityas surrounded him,
just as the hosts of gods surround the thousand-eyed Indra in heaven.
While that Tāraka, the delighter of the Daityas, was established in his great sovereignty,
the seasons appeared in embodied form, augmented by the specific qualities of their own times.
The world-protectors (lokapālas) in their entirety became his servants;
and Kānti, Dyuti, Dhṛti, Medhā, and Śrī, having beheld the Dānava, likewise [became his attendants].
Indeed, all those who were filled with virtues and free from flaws surrounded him,
whose limbs were anointed with black aloe-wood and who was adorned with a magnificent crown.
The most excellent apsarases stand fanning him, whose limbs are adorned with beautiful armlets, as he sits upon the great lion-throne; they do not cease their service at all.
The moon and sun became his lamps on the paths, the wind served as his fan,
and the Best of Sages, Kṛtānta, went before him, O best of munis.
As time thus passed away, the Daitya Tārakāsura,
arrogant due to the many boons he had received, spoke to his ministers.
Tāraka said:
"What use have I for a kingdom without having assailed the triple heaven?
Without avenging my enmity against the gods, what peace can there be in my heart?"
Even today, the immortals indeed enjoy their shares of the sacrifice in the celestial realm;
Viṣṇu does not abandon Śrī, and he remains free from all delusion.
In the pleasure gardens of heaven, those beloved by the immortals are attended by healthy celestial women who carry lotuses and the fragrance of wine.
If any man, having obtained birth, does not exert human effort, his birth has been in vain;
indeed, one who is unborn is superior.

That man who does not fulfill the desires of his parents, nor brings freedom from grief to his kinsmen, nor acquires a fame as bright as snow, is in my view dead even though he has been born. (Matsya Purāṇa 148.36)

Therefore, for the sake of victory over the foremost of the immortals and for the swift seizure of the Fortune of the three worlds, let my eight-wheeled chariot be yoked; let my army, that circle of Daityas difficult to conquer, be assembled;
and let my banner, bound with bands of gold, and my parasol, adorned with nets of pearls, be prepared.
Having heard the words of Tāraka, the powerful Dānava named Grasana,
the commander-in-chief of the Daitya king, acted accordingly.
Having struck the deep-sounding drum and swiftly summoned the Daityas,
he [mounted] a chariot adorned with eight wheels and drawn by a thousand horses.
Adorned with white garments and extending four yojanas in width,
it was filled with various pleasure-houses and enchanting with songs and instrumental music.
Like the celestial chariot of the lord of the gods, Śatakratu,
the Daityas— lords of ten crores and possessed of fierce prowess— [ascended].
Jambha was their leader, followed immediately by Kujambha;
then Mahiṣa, Kuñjara, Megha, Kālanemi, and likewise Nimi.
Mathana, Jambhaka, and Śumbha were the ten leaders of the Daityas;
there were also hundreds of others capable of shattering the earth.
The lords of the Daityas are of mountainous stature and possess fierce prowess;
they wield various weapons and missiles, and have mastered diverse arms and astras.
Tāraka’s banner was fierce and adorned with gold;
likewise, the army commander Grasana, the slayer of enemies, had a banner in the form of a crocodile.
The face of Jambha was that of a Piśāca,
and the banner of Kujambha featured an iron tail lashed by a donkey.
At that time, a jackal was the banner of Mahiṣa, while a golden one belonged to Ketu;
on the banner of Śumbha, there was a raised black crow made of iron.
Furthermore, there were other banners arranged in many different forms,
along with a hundred tigers of swift speed adorned with golden garlands.
The chariot of Grasana was yoked [to horses] adorned with garlands of networks of small bells;
and the invincible chariot of Jambha was likewise drawn by a hundred lions.
Kujambha’s chariot was yoked with donkeys having the faces of Piśācas;
Mahiṣa’s chariot was drawn by camels, while Gaja’s was drawn by horses.
Nimi was mounted upon intoxicated great elephants resembling mountains— elephants belonging to Meṣa, Bhīma, Kuñjara, and Kālanemi.
With four-tusked, fragrant, well-trained elephants as formidable as clouds, and with black horses a hundred cubits long adorned with golden ornaments; (Matsya Purāṇa 148.52)
Adorned with a network of white yak-tail whisks toward the southern direction,
his limbs were beautiful with white sandalwood paste, and he was radiant with garlands of various flowers.
The lord of the Daityas named Mathana shone forth with a noose in his hand;
Jambhaka, for his part, was mounted upon a camel adorned with a garland of networks of small bells.
The Dānava Śumbha was mounted upon a great black-and-white ram;
other heroic Dānavas also proceeded, riding various mounts.
Performing fierce and wondrous deeds, adorned with earrings and turbans,
they wear various upper garments and are decorated with diverse garlands.
Rich with the scents of various fragrant perfumes, praised by various bands of musicians,
accompanied by the resonance of various musical instruments, they were preceded by great chariot-warriors.
The great asuras in that army were intent on various tales of heroism;
thus, the force of that lion among Daityas assumed a terrifying form.
Crowded with intoxicated and fierce elephants, horses, and chariots,
and featuring many foot soldiers and banners, that army set out for battle with the immortals.
In the meantime, Vāyu, the messenger of the gods,
having seen the army of the Dānavas in the celestial realm, went to announce it to Indra.
Having gone to the divine assembly hall of the high-souled Mahendra,
he reported that urgent matter which had arisen in the midst of the gods.
Having heard that, the mighty-armed king of the gods, with his eyes closed,
spoke these words to Bṛhaspati at that time.
Indra said:
"This great conflict between the gods and the Dānavas has arrived.
Tell me what must be done here, provided with the means of political strategy."
Having heard these words of Mahendra,
the highly fortunate Bṛhaspati, the lord of speech and possessor of noble intellect, spoke as follows.
O best of gods, for those desiring victory, policy preceded by conciliation is said to be an army of four divisions with a banner; this is the eternal way of abiding.
Conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force are the four limbs of policy;
in statecraft, these are applied in sequence according to the requirements of place, time, the enemy, and other such factors.
One who is greedy for the domain of peace, cruel, and has found a secure refuge—
that wicked person, once tormented, reaches a state of being subdued, his doubts cast aside.
Conciliation has no place among the Daityas, since they have found refuge [with us];
nor can they be divided by the nature of their own kind, and what is the use of giving to one who has already attained prosperity?
If it pleases you, punishment is the only means in this matter;
for conciliation shown toward the wicked becomes utterly fruitless.
The cruel consider conciliation toward great-souled beings as arising from fear; they perceive it as straightforwardness, noble-mindedness, and a transgression of justice and policy.
The wicked always regard conciliation as arising from fear;
therefore, it is better to rely on manly prowess to overcome the wicked.
When one is attacked, it is proper for the virtuous to act; this is the great vow of the good.
A wicked person can never be transformed into a virtuous one.
"Even a virtuous person might at some time desire the abandonment of his own nature;
such is my mind's understanding in this matter—determine what you shall do."
Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed one said to him, "So be it.
Having reflected upon what must be done, he spoke in the assembly of the immortals.
Indra said:
"O dwellers of heaven, listen attentively to my words;
you are the enjoyers of the sacrifice, with contented souls and exceedingly pure."
"O lords of the Dānavas, you who are eternally established in your own majesty and are the protectors of the world, are being oppressed by us without cause."
"They possess neither conciliation nor other means; let punishment alone be ordained.
Let preparations for battle be made, and let my army be assembled. (Matsya Purāṇa 148.77)
Let the weapons be honored and let the deities of the missiles be worshipped;
and let the immortals yoke my mounts and vehicles.
"Having made Yama the commander-in-chief, let the dwellers of heaven act thus immediately. Thus addressed, those who were the foremost among the gods equipped themselves for battle.
In battle, a horse adorned with golden bells,
endowed with various wonderful qualities, and attended by all the gods arrived, accompanied by ten thousand steeds.
Yama, mounted upon his buffalo, took his place at the head of the army in the invincible chariot prepared by Mātali for the King of the Gods.
Surrounded on all sides by a host of fierce servants,
his eyes filled the sky with flames as violent as those at the end of an aeon.
The Fire-god stands mounted upon a goat, holding a spear in his hand;
the Wind-god, however, has a goad in his hand and possesses vast, expanded speed.
The Lord Jaleśa himself was mounted upon the king of serpents;
the god Rākṣaseśa, who moves through the sky, was in a chariot yoked with men.
The formidable god, who possesses a sharp sword, stands ready for battle;
he is the lord of wealth, possessing the roar of a great lion and wielding a mace as his weapon.
Candra, Āditya, and the Aśvins, accompanied by their fourfold armies,
stood there together with kings and Gandharvas adorned with golden ornaments.
Wearing upper garments of golden-yellow, with variegated armor, chariots, and weapons,
they possess crests reaching to the vault of heaven and banners bearing makaras made of beryl.
The Rākṣasas have crimson-red upper garments and red hair;
they possess great heroism, carry vultures as their banners, and are adorned with stainless iron ornaments.
With pestles, swords, and maces in their hands, wearing turbans and armor upon their chariots,
these elephants— whose roar was like that of great clouds— had terrifying firebrands and thunderbolts as their weapons.
The Yakṣas, clad in black garments, wielding terrible arrows and bows,
bearing banners of copper-colored owls, were fierce and adorned with gold and jewels.
The army of night-stalkers shone with upper garments of leopard skins,
mostly bearing banners with vulture feathers, and was adorned with ornaments made of bone.
Difficult to behold due to the club-weaponed [warriors], with the great roar of various living beings,
the Kinnaras there were dressed in white garments and bore white-feathered banners.
They mostly ride upon elephants in rut, armed with sharp lances and weapons;
their ornamentation consists of nets of pearls, and they possess swans fashioned from silver.
The fire of the Lord of the Ocean was a terrifying column of smoke and flame,
while that of Dhanada was a branch composed of great rubies.
The great banner of Yama, made of wood and iron, stood raised aloft like a flagpole, appearing as if it were about to ascend into the sky.
The face of the lord of the Rākṣasas shone like that of a corpse;
the two gods, the Sun and the Moon of immeasurable splendor, had banners of golden lions.
The banner of the Aśvins was a water-pot variegated with jewels,
fashioned from a golden elephant and adorned with various gems.
The banner of Śatakratu was adorned with white chowries;
it was attended by nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, mahoragas, and niśācaras.
That army of the king of the gods is invincible in the three worlds;
it consists of thirty-three crores of the hosts of gods and demigods.

With white chowries like the Himalayas, with beautiful garlands of pure golden lotuses, with bright sprouts of saffron applied as lovely cosmetics, and with swarms of bees sporting upon her cheeks; (Matsya Purāṇa 148.100)
Seated upon that elephant named Airāvata, the mighty Indra,

the subduer of Pāka, shone in heaven; adorned with variegated ornaments and garments, graced by a canopy of the rays from his expansive robes, his circle of forearms adorned with scattered armlets, and praised by thousands of bards, he appeared like the thousand-eyed one.
That army, crowded with floods of the strength of horses and elephants, resplendent with rows of white parasols and banners,
and filled with a multitude of invincible foot-soldiers, shone forth— difficult to cross due to its warriors and various weapons.
Matsya Purāṇa 149: Sūta said:
In that exceedingly terrible clash between the gods and the asuras, [the conflict raged].
A tumultuous and exceedingly great clamor arose from both armies alike.
With the roar of shouting gods and demons, the sound of conchs and kettledrums, the blare of trumpets, and the trumpeting of elephants; 149.2 //
A tumultuous and exceedingly great clamor arose from the neighing of the herds of horses, the sound of chariot rims, and the twanging of the bowstrings of the heroes.
The two armies, having encountered one another— those who desired victory over each other,
who were completely overcome by rage, and whose minds had renounced all regard for life— [clashed].
Having encountered one another in succession, yet in reverse order,
the chariot [encountered] the infantry, and the chariot [encountered] the horse.

An elephant was joined by foot-soldiers, and in some places a chariot-warrior was joined by another chariot-warrior; one elephant was joined by another elephant-driver, and an elephant was joined by many horses.
A single foot soldier is joined by many rutting elephants,
and then by spears, thunderbolts, clubs, slings, and battle-axes.
With spears, sharp-edged axes, tridents, mallets, clubs, and maces;
with discuses, spikes, and white javelins and goads.
With *karṇins*, *nālīkas*, *nārācas*, *vatsadantas*, and *ardhacandras*;
with *bhallas*, *śatapatras*, and stainless *śukatuṇḍas*.
An exceedingly wondrous rain was seen in the sky,
completely shrouding all directions and making them appear as if filled with darkness.
In that dense darkness, they could not recognize one another;
discharging their uplifted volleys of weapons blindly, they remained unobserved.
They gazed at one another as they fell in the midst of the two armies,
[covered] by banners, arms, umbrellas, and heads adorned with earrings.
The earth was strewn with elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers— both those falling and those already fallen—
like lotuses dropped from the celestial lake.
With their tusks broken, their temples split, and their long, great trunks severed,
the elephants fell upon the earth like mountains, streaming with blood.
Chariots with their poles, shafts, wheels, and axles shattered were reduced to fragments,
and thousands of horses fell, likewise broken into pieces.
Then the earth became difficult to traverse due to the flowing blood;
the rivers had whirlpools of gore, bringing joy to the flesh-eaters,
and that chaotic battlefield became a playground for *vetālas*.
Matsya Purāṇa 150: Sūta said:
Then, beholding Grasana, Yama was overwhelmed with rage.
He rained down a shower of arrows, especially those possessing the brilliance of fire.
Pierced by many arrows, that highly valiant Grasana,
desiring to retaliate for what had been done to him, bent his formidable bow.
With five hundred extremely fierce arrows, he oppressed Yama;
then Yama, reflecting upon the extreme prowess of Grasana with those shafts, [acted].
With fierce showers of arrows, Yama crushed Grasana;
he [Grasana] then repelled that rain of Kṛtānta’s shafts as it advanced through the sky.
Grasana, the lord of the Dānavas, cut that continuous stream of arrows to pieces with a rain of his own shafts;
seeing that volley rendered fruitless, Yama [acted].
Reflecting thus, Antaka (the Destroyer) swiftly hurled a terrible mallet toward Grasana’s chariot amidst his volley of arrows.
Leaping up into the sky as that mallet approached,
the joy of the Dānavas seized it with his left hand, O descendant of the Yamī line.
Seizing that very mallet, he furiously hurled it with great force at Yama’s buffalo; it fell down upon the surface of the earth.
Then Yama, leaping from his buffalo as it was about to spring forward,
struck Grasana firmly in the mouth with a spear.
But he, having fainted from the blow of the spear, fell to the ground;
seeing Grasana fallen, Jambha, of terrible prowess, [advanced].
With a slingshot, he struck Yama in the heart;
from that blow, blood flowed from Yama’s mouth.
Seeing Kṛtānta crushed, the Lord of Wealth,
mace in hand and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Yakṣas, advanced in fury against Jambha.
Jambha, surrounded by the host of Dānavas, spoke these words with affection to him as he approached in a state of wrath. ||| MatsP_150.13 |||
Then Grasana, having regained consciousness, dispatched to Yama a heavy mace adorned with jewels and gold, which was capable of crushing enemies.
Beholding that inconceivable mace, the one whose vehicle is the buffalo [Mahiṣa] produced a mace for the purpose of countering it—
one as terrifying as the destruction of the world.
In his fury, he released a staff wreathed in garlands of flames;
having reached the sky with that mace, it roared like a rain-cloud.
A collision occurred between those two that was as unbearable as that between two mountains;
the quarters of the sky were numbed by the roar produced by their crushing impact.
The world fell into agitation, fearing the onset of universal dissolution;
in an instant, its roar was stilled as it became strewn with blazing meteors.
In their crushing struggle, a terrible conflict took place in the realm of the sky;
then, having struck down his mace, Daṇḍa brought it down upon the head of Grasana.
Like misfortune seizing away prosperity, that heavy blow fell upon the wicked man;
yet, by that stroke, he saw the quarters of the sky shrouded in darkness.
He fell unconscious upon the ground, adorned by the dust of the earth;
then a terrible cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from both armies.
Then, after only a moment, Grasana regained consciousness and saw his own body ruined, with its ornaments and garments in disarray.
And he too reflected upon how to repay the master for the humiliation that had arisen toward a man such as himself.
The armies have taken refuge in me; once I am conquered, they shall be destroyed.
Let people who act according to their own whims never again be trusted.
But a man whose wealth is merely boasted of in hundreds of useless words does not;
having reflected thus, the mighty one rose up with speed. (Matsya Purāṇa 150.25)
Resembling a mountain, Grasana— whose resolve was terrible— seized a mallet that shone like the staff of Time (Yama),
his lips bitten together.
Traveling swiftly by chariot, Grasana encountered Antaka in battle;
having reached Yama in the fight, he whirled his mace.
With great force, he hurled the terrible mallet at the head of Yama;
beholding that blazing mallet, Yama’s eyes became bewildered with alarm.
That one of great strength deceived the invincible mallet;
when it had retreated far away, [he encountered] those of fierce deeds who were violent.
He crushed a thousand of Yama’s servants;
then, seeing that formidable army of servants slain, [he was filled with joy].
But Grasana, having beheld that army consisting of servants, became extremely agitated and raised various weapons.
Grasana, discharging showers of weapons, perceived thousands of Yamas created by the illusory power of Yama, whom he was subduing as he devoured the army.
Intoxicated with rage, he became as terrible as the end of an eon;
he pierced some with his trident and others with straight-flying arrows.
He crushed some with his mace and others with showers of mallets;
then some were struck by terrible blows from spears.
Others hung many times upon his circle of arms;
others struck him with rocks, and still others with other trees of great height.
Others, moreover, bit his limbs with their teeth,
while other servants struck his back with their fists.
Thus pursued by those terrible beings, Grasana, frantic with rage,
cast his body upon the surface of the earth and crushed it in a thousand ways.
Rising up, he struck some of those who relied on the *kiṃkaras* with his fists;
however, through that battle with the *kiṃkaras*, Grasana became exhausted.
Seeing him exhausted and his own army slain, Yama,
whose vehicle is a buffalo, approached brandishing his staff.
But as Grasana was approaching, the enemy-slayer Antaka struck him on the chest with his mace;
yet Grasana took no account of that deed of Antaka.
The wrathful one struck the tigers at the front of the chariot with his staff;
that chariot was then dragged by those half-tigers who had been mangled by the staff.
As doubt arose in the mind of the Daitya Puruṣa, he abandoned that chariot;
leaving the vehicle, the Daitya went to the earth on foot.
Seizing Yama with both arms, the Dānava fought him;
Yama, too, casting aside his weapons, engaged in a hand-to-hand struggle.
Seizing Yama by his loincloth with great force, Grasana whirled him around with speed, just as confusion whirls about a distracted mind.
Yama, seizing the Daitya by the neck with his two arms,
lifted him up from the surface of the earth and whirled him around with great force.
Then, with their fists, those two mercilessly struck one another;
because of the Daitya lord’s immense body, Yama’s arms subsequently grew weary.
Placing his face upon the shoulder of the Daitya, he desired rest;
then, perceiving that Antaka was exhausted by his own vigor, the Daitya [acted].
He trampled the surface of the earth many times with his heels and hands,
until much blood flowed from the mouth of Yama.
Seeing Yama lifeless, the Dānava then abandoned him;
having achieved victory, the Daitya, possessing a great voice, let out a haughty roar.
Having reached his own army, he stood as immovable as a mountain,
[pierced] by Jambha’s vital-organ-piercing arrows from the Lord of Wealth.
The quarters were obstructed by the enraged one, and his army was cut to pieces;
then Dhaneśa, overcome with anger, [attacked] the Dānava Jambha.
In the battle, he pierced him in the heart with a thousand arrows blazing like fire,
his charioteer with a hundred, and his banner with ten.
And his two hands were struck with seventy-five arrows, and his bow with ten straight-flying shafts,
fletched with peacock feathers and cleansed with oil.
With one arrow he struck that lion, piercing it with ten sharp shafts;
Jambha, however, beheld that deed of the Lord of Wealth, which was exceedingly difficult to accomplish.
Taking courage to heart, though his mind was somewhat terrified,
he grasped sharpened arrows capable of piercing the vital organs of the enemy.
Then the Dānava Jambha, his bow drawn back to his ear and overflowing with rage, pierced the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in the chest with sharp arrows.
The Dānava struck his charioteer in the heart with a firm arrow,
and with another, polished with oil, he severed the bowstring.
Then, that performer of cruel deeds pierced the Lord of Wealth in the chest with ten sharp, dreadful arrows capable of piercing the vital organs.
Falling into utter delusion, the lord of wealth was indeed pierced deeply;
yet in an instant, summoning his fortitude, he drew his formidable bow.
The Lord of Wealth showered thousands of sharpened arrows upon the quarters,
the sky, the intermediate directions, the earth, and the armies of the asura.
Jambha also, in that battle, swiftly filled the sky by covering the solar disc with many supreme arrows, one after another.
Because of the great prowess of the Lord of Wealth, he who was swift in aiming cut [the arrow];
thereupon, the Lord of Wealth became enraged by the deed of the lord of the Dānavas.
He scattered his armies with showers of various arrows;
seeing that difficult feat of the Lord of Wealth, the Dānavas [were amazed].
Seizing a formidable iron mallet adorned with gold,
he crushed thousands of yakṣas who were followers of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
Being struck by the Daitya and uttering terrible cries,
they all stood surrounding the chariot of the Lord of Wealth.
Seeing them being tormented, the god seized a terrible trident;
with it, he swiftly slaughtered thousands of Daityas.
As the Daityas were being destroyed, the Dānava, overwhelmed with rage,
seized his axe, the crusher of the enemies of the Daityas.
With that sharp-edged [weapon], the Daitya cut the great chariot of the Lord of Wealth into hundreds of pieces, just as a rat gnaws through a piece of soft cloth.
The lord of wealth, on foot, took up his terrible mace,
which destroys proud enemies in the crushes of great battles.
Unassailable by all beings, honored for many groups of years,
her limbs smeared with various sandalwoods and perfumed with divine flowers.
Enraged, the Lord of Wealth hurled at the head of Jambha a heavy, unerring iron spear, pure and adorned with gold.
Beholding her approaching, adorned with a mass of lightning,
the Daitya released a shower of weapons for the purpose of striking her with his mace.
With arms adorned with golden armlets, he of fierce prowess [wielded] wheels, corpses, spears, *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, and even *paṭṭiśa* weapons.
Having rendered all those weapons useless against the chest of the Daitya, the fierce goddess fell quivering like a great meteor into a mountain cave. (Matsya Purāṇa 150.74)
Struck deeply by her, he fell upon the pole of his chariot;
and from the apertures of his unconscious body, blood flowed forth.
Thinking that Jambha had been slain, Kujambha, who possessed a terrifying voice,
became enraged at the Lord of Wealth and was further provoked by his words.
He created a net of arrows in all directions against the lord of the Yakṣas;
then, with sharp crescent-shaped shafts, he cut through that web of arrows.
The powerful lord of the Yakṣas released a shower of arrows at him,
but that Daitya cut down that multitude of arrows with his own sharp shafts.
Seeing that shower of arrows rendered futile,
the Lord of Wealth seized a formidable spear, which resounded with the laughter of golden bells.
Having gazed upon her with his arm, which shone with the continuous radiance of jeweled bracelets,
he released it with great force at Kujambha.
It tore open the cruel heart of Kujambha,
just as worldly desire, when cultivated, tears the heart of a man of little strength.
Then, having pierced his heart, it entered the surface of the earth;
thereupon, after a moment, the Dānava of terrible form became unwell.
The Daitya seized a long spear with a sharp stone-tipped blade;
with that spear, he struck the chest of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in the battle.
With words of a piercing nature that spread through his very vitals,
he pierced the heart of the noble-born man, just as a wicked person does.
By that blow from the spear, Dhaneśa was rendered unconscious and fell upon the seat of his chariot like a shattered draft animal.
But seeing that Tathāgata, the Lord of Wealth Naravāhana,
the god Nirṛti, armed with a sword and followed by the forces of night-stalkers, [approached].
He rushed with speed toward Kujambha of terrible prowess;
then, seeing that invincible lord of the Rākṣasas, Kujambha [stood his ground].
He urged his armies toward the slaughter of the lord of the Rākṣasas;
he, seeing the army thus incited and terrifying with various weapons and broad-headed arrows, [proceeded].
Leaping swiftly from his chariot, radiant with the luster of his ornaments,
he [struck] with his unsheathed sword, which possessed the brilliance of the sky, as if [cutting] lotuses.
With his great sword, he whose arms were long cut off the various faces of his enemies on all sides— across, behind, below, and above.
With his face made formidable by the contraction of his bitten lips and knitted brows,
and with eyes bloodshot from fierce anger, he cut down the Dānavas in battle.
Then, seeing his own army almost entirely destroyed,
Kujambha abandoned the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) and rushed toward the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
Then Jambha, having regained consciousness, seized by the throat thousands of followers of the Lord of Wealth, binding them with nooses.
But the various jewels were personified, as were the Dānavas;
there were also divine mounts and celestial chariots by the thousands.
Then Dhaneśa, having regained consciousness and beholding that state,
sighed long and hot, his eyes copper-red with rage.
Having meditated upon the divine Gāruḍa weapon and fixed an arrow to his bow,
he released that foe-crushing shaft into the army of the Dānavas.
First, lines of smoke issued forth from his bow,
and immediately thereafter, millions of sparks of blazing radiance.
Then that weapon made the sky filled with flames on all sides;
thereafter, it gradually assumed various forms that were difficult to resist.
The world was formless and indeed enveloped in darkness;
then, in the intermediate space, they praised that refined radiance.
Having observed that, the exceedingly powerful Dānava Kujambha rushed impetuously on foot toward the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), roaring aloud.
Then, seeing the Daitya approaching toward him, the Lord of Wealth became overcome with agitation and intent on flight.
Then, as he was fleeing, his crown adorned with jewels fell upon the earth, blazing like the orb of the sun falling from the sky.
For brave and noble women, when their husband has fled from the battle, it is fitting to die at the forefront of the fray; that is their highest ornament.
Having thus resolved, those invincible yakṣas, with various weapons and missiles in their hands and eager for battle, stood surrounding that crown.
Seeing those heroes, whose wealth was their pride, following in the footsteps of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
the Dānava of fierce prowess looked upon them with indignation.
Then, seizing a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon that was terrifying in appearance and as heavy as a mountain,
he crushed the night-stalkers who were guarding the crown.
Then, having crushed them, the son of Danu, the enemy of the gods, defeated the Giver of Wealth in battle and placed his crown upon his own chariot.
Taking all his wealth, jewels, personified treasures, and embodied riches, Jambha, the Daitya and lion among the lords of the Danujas, departed with his own army; while the Lord of Wealth,
his hair disheveled, went dejected into the presence of the Lord of the Gods.
Then the son of the night-stalker,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, engaged with Kujambha, resorting to an unerring illusion of darkness.
He deluded the lord of the Daityas by enveloping the world in darkness;
consequently, the forces of the Dānavas had their eyes rendered useless.
At that time, they were unable to move even a single step from their place;
then, with a rain of various weapons, [they struck] the great army of the Dānavas.
While the Daityas were being slain and Kujambha’s mind was bewildered, he struck down his mount, which was distressed by the darkness of thick frost.
Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas, who resembled the ocean at the end of a kalpa,
discharged the Sāvitra weapon, adorned with a multitude of meteors.
Then, as that powerful and supreme weapon of Savitṛ began to expand,
the intense and terrible darkness immediately perished.
Then the weapon, marked by sparks, destroyed all that darkness,
just as a stainless lake in autumn [dispels gloom] with its mass of blossoming, ruddy lotuses.
Then, when the darkness had subsided and the lords of the Daityas regained their sight,
they acted with cruel intent against the hosts of gods in a most extraordinary manner.
Having dispelled the serpent-weapon with weapons released out of indignation,
he then took up a formidable bow and arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Kujambha rushed toward the army of the king of the Rākṣasas that had been hurled [at him].
Seeing him approaching, the lord of the Rākṣasas, along with his followers, [prepared for battle].
He pierced him with sharpened arrows, terrifying as cruel venomous serpents;
neither their taking up, nor their aiming, nor even their release could be perceived.
With extreme dexterity, he cut through the enemy's volleys of arrows with his own shafts;
then, with an exceedingly sharp arrow, that performer of wondrous deeds severed the banner of the foe of the gods.
And with a broad-headed arrow, Kujambha struck down his charioteer from the seat of the chariot;
having witnessed that feat of the lord of the Rākṣasas in the battle.
With eyes reddened by rage, the Dānava leaped from his chariot and swiftly seized a sword as stainless as the autumnal sky.
Adorned with ten crescent moons on his armor,
the Daitya rushed with vigor against the lord of the Rākṣasas in battle.
The lord of the Rākṣasas struck him in the heart with a mallet as he approached;
by that blow, however, he was weakened and his mind became bewildered.
The Danava stood motionless like a steadfast mountain;
that lord of the Danavas, exceedingly difficult to conquer, remained there for a moment, having regained his composure.
Having mounted his chariot, the Daitya seized Nirṛti by the hair with his left hand as he stood there, having been stepped upon by the demon's knee.
Then, filled with indignation, he desired to cut off his head with a sword;
in that interval, the god Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, arrived swiftly.
And with a noose, he bound the two arms of the lord of the Dānavas;
then the Daitya, his arms bound and his prowess rendered fruitless, [was subdued].
Casting aside all compassion, the wielder of the noose struck him with his mace;
from that blow, he vomited blood from his orifices.
He assumed the form of a cloud enveloped by a garland of lightning;
seeing Kujambha in that state, Mahiṣāsura—
With his mouth wide open and his fangs bared, he whose face was fierce sought to devour both gods, Nirṛti and Varuṇa, in that unfathomable abyss.
Perceiving that corrupted intention of the Daitya,
the two [gods], terrified, abandoned the path of their chariot and fled with extreme speed from Mahiṣa.
Greatly agitated by fear, both fled swiftly from the two directions;
Nirṛti quickly went for refuge to Pākaśāsana.
The Daitya Mahiṣa, enraged, rushed toward Varuṇa;
beholding him caught within the jaws of Death, [Varuṇa], who possessed the splendor of the Himalayas, [acted].
Candra employed the Vāyavya weapon as his second, which was incomparable and possessed thorns consisting of masses of snow, discharged from the Soma weapon.
By that wind, by the moon, and by the parched frost, all the Dānavas were afflicted; their manliness destroyed, they were overwhelmed by the cold.
They were unable to move on foot, nor even to take up their weapons,
due to the falling of great masses of snow and by the missiles discharged by Candra.
The limbs of the asura hosts were scorched on all sides;
Mahiṣa, however, became motionless, his face trembling from the cold.
Clasping their armpits with both hands and sitting with their faces cast downwards,
all those Daityas were defeated by the Moon and rendered powerless to retaliate.

Having abandoned their desire for battle from afar, they stood there seeking only to preserve their lives; then Kālanemi, inflamed with rage, spoke to the Daityas: mā bhaiṣṭa yūyaṃ saṃgrāme tyajadhvaṃ bhayamuttamam / yudhyadhvaṃ sarvaśo daityā na bhīrvo 'sti parājayaḥ // MatsP_150.141 // "Do not fear in this battle; cast away your supreme dread! Fight in every way, O Daityas; for those who are not cowards, there is no defeat."
O, O passionate arrows, all of you who have mastered every weapon and missile—
even each one of you individually is capable of lifting the entire world with your arms!
Each one of them alone is capable of devouring the entire world, including all that is moving and stationary;
even all the gods together are not a match for each one of them.
O you of exceeding prowess, why have you departed with such effort to fulfill the sixteenth digit? Stay in battle, you who have conquered even the immortals!
This is not fitting for heroes, especially for those born of the Daityas;
for our king Tāraka, the destroyer of the worlds, has been hidden from us.
Enraged, he will take away the lives of those who withdraw from this battle;
likewise, their hearing will be lost by the cold, and their eloquence of speech will fail.
Then the Daityas became mute, their rows of teeth chattering;
seeing those Daityas deprived of their senses and overcome by the cold, [the gods rejoiced].
Considering his task to be one that required time, the great asura Kālanemi resorted to the illusion of a dānava, expanding his own massive body.
The lord of the Dānavas filled the sky, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate quarters; he manifested ten thousand suns within his own body.
And with fierce fires produced by his illusory power, he filled the quarters;
then, in an instant, the entire three worlds became engulfed in flames.
By that mass of flames, the moon was reduced to a state of exhaustion;
thereafter, as it gradually faded away, a cold, overcast sky appeared.

Seeing that army of the lords of the Dānavas through the illusion of Kālanemi, and seeing that host of Dānavas having regained their senses, the Sun—the sole eye of the world—became agitated and spoke to Aruṇa out of anger: matsya-purāṇa 150.151.151.1–20: "Arise, O Aruṇa! Divākara said: "O Aruṇa, drive the chariot quickly toward where Kālanemi’s chariot is;
there a terrible clash will occur, resulting in the destruction of heroes."
"This moon has been conquered here, upon whose strength we rely," having said this,
the elder brother of Garuḍa urged on the chariot.
Then the Blessed One, the lamp of the world, took up his drawn bow, while horses restrained with great effort carried him along, accompanied by rows of white chowries.
The highly fortunate one, having aimed two divine arrows with the brilliance of venomous serpents using the *saṃcāra* weapon, discharged a single shaft.
He released a second [illusion] joined with the net of Indra;
by means of the "wandering" weapon (*saṃcārāstra*), he caused a transformation of forms in an instant.
Perceiving the demonic form of the gods and the divine form of the demons,
he slew his own kin, the gods, by means of the swiftness of his terrible weapons.
Kālanemi, possessed by rage like Kṛtānta at the time of universal destruction,
struck some with a sharp sword, some with showers of iron arrows,
some with terrible maces, and others with fearsome battle-axes.
With fierce speed, he struck off the heads of some, as well as their arms, chariots, and charioteers;
then, by the momentum of his chariot, he crushed some, while others he slew with wrathful blows of his upraised fists.
Seeing his own [followers] struck down in battle, Nemi, the lord of the Dānavas,
[observed that] the Asuras who had been overwhelmed by the gods were indeed regaining their own forms.
Overcome with rage, Kālanemi did not perceive their forms;
however, the Daitya Nemi, seeing them, spoke to Kālanemi.
"I am Nemi, not Sura; know me, O Kālanemi!
It was by you, deluded in battle, that those of great prowess were slain."
"Ten hundred-thousand Daityas here are invincible even by the gods;
discharge with haste the Brahma-weapon, which wards off all missiles."
Awakened by him, the Daitya, his mind agitated with alarm,
fixed an arrow charged with the Brahmāstra.
Then that lord of the Daityas himself, the thorn of the gods, released [the weapon];
thereupon, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were pervaded by the splendor of that missile.
The entire army of the gods became filled with fear;
their discharged weapons were pacified, and the battlefield itself shone forth spontaneously.
When that weapon was repelled, the sun, its splendor diminished,
resorted to Mahendra’s net and assumed ten million forms of his own.
With the impact of his flashing arms, he overwhelmed the three worlds;
the army of the Dānavas was scorched, with its blood flowing like a flood of molten lead.
Then the Lord rained down fire from all sides in a dense mass,
and he rendered the eyes of the lords of the Dānavas blind.
The fat of the elephants oozed out and their cries fell upon the earth;
the horses, afflicted by heat, were panting, as were the chariot-warriors.
Afflicted by thirst, they wandered here and there seeking water,
as well as the shady branches of trees and the mountain caves.
While they were longing for coolness as it spread through the spaces between the trees,
a forest fire blazed up with terrible flames, burning the trees;
yet those seeking water saw before them water garlanded with waves.
Though standing right before them, they were unable to reach it, being crushed down;
failing to obtain water on the ground, they lay with gaping mouths, deprived of their senses.
Here and there, the lords of the Daityas were seen lying dead upon the earth;
chariots and elephants had fallen, and horses were brought to their end.
Thousands of dead Dānavas were seen standing, vomiting, and running, with blood, fat, and gore trickling from them.
When that great destruction of the lords of the Dānavas had taken place,
Kālanemi, his eyes copper-red with fury and afflicted by rage, [arose].
He appeared like a cloud at the end of an eon, flashing with many hundreds of lightning bolts,
his deep, crashing roar shaking the very heart of the world.
Having covered the expanse of the sky, he destroyed the sun's illusory power and rained down cool water toward the army of the lord of the Dānavas.
Having encountered that rain, the Daityas were then gradually restored,
like seeds and sprouts on the surface of the earth that have withered but flourish upon receiving rain.
Then that great asura Kālanemi, assuming the form of a cloud,
rained down a fierce and invincible shower of weapons upon the divine armies.
Afflicted by that rain and unable to find any refuge, the cows of the mighty lords of the Daityas were like those tormented by the cold.
With weapons in hand, they pressed against one another on their backs;
when hard-pressed, they sought refuge among their own elephants and horses.
Terrified by the host of gods, some hid here and there among the chariots;
others, with their bodies hunched, covered their faces with their own hands.
Confused and agitated, they wandered here and there through the ten directions during such a tumultuous battle that caused the destruction of the gods.
They were seen fallen upon the ground, their joints and limbs pierced by weapons;
with arms broken, heads split open, and likewise thighs and knees severed.
With chariots overturned and obstructed, rows of banners crushed to pieces, and horses with mangled limbs alongside elephants resembling mountains; MatsP_150.186 //
With pools of flowing blood, the ground appeared both transformed and untransformed;
thus did the powerful Daitya, the great Asura Kālanemi, fare in battle.
In a mere moment, he slew ten thousand Gandharvas,
five hundred thousand Yakṣas, and sixty thousand Rākṣasas.
He slew three hundred thousand powerful kinnaras;
fearless, he also slew seven hundred thousand leaders of the piśācas.
Enraged and skilled in the use of weapons, he slew tens of millions of others belonging to countless classes of divine beings with various missiles.
Thus, during that terrible humiliation and the destruction of the immortals,
the two divine Aśvins became enraged, resplendent with variegated weapons and armor.
Having encountered that terrible Daitya, who resembled the fire of Death (Kṛtānta), each of them struck him in battle with sixty arrows. (MatsP 150.192)
He struck the fearsome-looking Asura in his vital organs with sharp-pointed arrows;
by those blows from their shafts, the demon’s consciousness became somewhat distressed.
He seized an eight-spoked wheel, polished with oil and destined to bring an end to the battle;
with that wheel, he severed the chariot-pole of the two Aśvins.
Then the Daitya took up his bow and arrows resembling venomous serpents;
he rained them down upon the head of Bhiṣaja, completely covering the expanse of the sky.
The two of them also cut down those sharp arrows of the Daitya with their own weapons;
seeing that feat of theirs, he was struck with amazement and overcome by anger.
With great rage,
he seized a formidable mallet made entirely of iron, as terrifying as the staff of Death.
Then, having whirled it with great speed, he hurled it toward the chariot of Aśvin;
and seeing that mallet approaching through the sky, [he took action].
Having abandoned their chariots, those two Aśvins leaped away with speed and force;
meanwhile, that mallet, resembling a mountain, crushed those two chariots.
Adorned with a golden net, he split the earth;
seeing his feat, the Aśvins, who were skilled physicians and versatile warriors, [were amazed].
They then unleashed the Vajrāstra weapon to ward off the lord of the Dānavas;
thereupon, an exceedingly terrible rain consisting of thunderbolts began to fall.
Struck by those terrible vajra-blows, the lord of the Daityas was overwhelmed;
his chariot, banner, bow, discus, and even his golden armor were shattered.
In an instant, while the entire army looked on, he was reduced to pieces as small as sesame seeds;
seeing that difficult feat performed by the two Aśvins, he of terrible prowess [acted].
The powerful one released the Nārāyaṇa weapon at the head of the battle,
but the lord of the Dānavas neutralized the Vajra weapon with the fiery power of his own weapon.
When that adamantine weapon had been quelled,
Kālanemi immediately proceeded to capture the two Aśvins alive.
Then the two Aśvins, terrified of the battle, fled toward the chariot of the Thousand-Eyed One,
trembling and on foot, devoid of weapons.
Following those two was the exceedingly powerful Daitya Kālanemi;
accompanied by the host of Daityas, the cruel one reached Indra’s chariot.
Seeing him, all beings were terrified and agitated;
beholding that cruelty of the Daitya, all beings reflected upon it.
At the defeat of Mahendra, which brought about the destruction of all the worlds,
the principal mountain peaks shook and meteors fell from the vault of heaven.
The clouds thundered in all directions and the great oceans surged;
seeing that transformation of the elements, the Blessed One whose banner is Garuḍa [appeared].
He awoke from his yogic sleep upon the serpent-couch,
his lotus-feet being perpetually caressed by the pair of hands of Lakṣmī.
The Lord possesses the splendor of a body as beautiful as an autumnal blue lotus;
his chest is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and he shines with lovely armlets.
Having reflected upon the agitation of the gods, he summoned Vainateya;
and when he had been summoned and stood there, possessing the massive body of a serpent.
Mounting his divine chariot, which emitted the sharp flames of various celestial weapons, he himself came to the gods;
there he saw the Lord of the Gods being pursued by those who had leaped forward.
Just as a man is [overwhelmed] by terrible and unfortunate kinsmen who are arrogant in their prowess, so was he by the lords of the Dānavas, who possessed the luster of fresh clouds.
For the sake of protection, a stainless deed was swiftly performed in that fertile field;
then the Daityas beheld a circle of light in the sky.
Desiring to know the power of his splendor, the Dānavas were like those wishing to test the sun with its hot rays as it stands upon the mountain of sunrise, quivering with light.
They beheld Garuḍa, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon,
seated upon that inexhaustible and infallible one who possesses the splendor of a mass of clouds.
Beholding him, the lords of the Asuras, their minds filled with joy, thought:
"This indeed is the very essence of the gods; once he is conquered, the gods are defeated."
This Keśava, the slayer of enemies, is the very Death for the hosts of Daityas;
by relying upon him, the immortals enjoy their shares of the sacrifices in the worlds.
Having spoken thus, all the Dānavas surrounded him on all sides and struck him with various weapons as he advanced in the battle. *Matsya Purāṇa* 150.221.
Ten great chariot-warriors among the Daityas, headed by Kālanemi, [attacked];
Kālanemi pierced Janārdana with sixty arrows.
Nimi struck him with a hundred arrows, Mathana with eighty shafts,
Jambhaka with seventy, and Śumbha with ten.
All the remaining lords of the Daityas,
exerting themselves, each struck Viṣṇu with ten arrows in the battle, along with Garuḍa.
Unable to endure that deed of theirs, Viṣṇu, the slayer of the Dānavas,
struck each individual Dānava with six straight-flying arrows.
Then Kālanemi, his eyes red with rage, drew [his bow] back to his ear and pierced Viṣṇu in the heart with three arrows.
Those arrows of refined gold shone upon his heart like the radiant rays of the brilliantly lustrous Kaustubha gem.
Slightly distressed by those arrows, Hari seized a mallet;
whirling it incessantly with great speed, he hurled it at the Dānava.

The enraged lord of the Dānavas, displaying his lightness of hand, cut that [missile] into pieces as small as sesame seeds with hundreds of arrows while it was still in the sky before it had reached him.
Then Viṣṇu, enraged,
seized a terrible spear and struck the heart of the Daitya with it most forcefully.
In an instant, having regained consciousness, the great asura Kālanemi seized a sharp-pointed spear that resounded with the laughter of golden bells.
With that [spear], the son of Diti pierced the left arm of Viṣṇu;
his arm, pierced by the spear and streaming with blood, shone brightly.
Adorned as if with an armlet made of rubies,
Viṣṇu, becoming enraged, then seized a massive bow.
And with seventeen sharp iron arrows that pierce the vital organs,
he struck the heart of the Daitya with six and pierced it further with three shafts.
With four arrows he struck his charioteer, with one feathered shaft his banner,
with two more his bowstring and bow, and with another feathered arrow his left arm.
Deeply pierced in the heart by Hari’s arrows, the Daitya’s tall form was crimson with flowing blood, and his mind was overwhelmed with agony.
He trembled like a *kiṃśuka* tree stirred by the wind;
observing him thus shaken, Keśava seized his mace.
And Kālanemi hurled it with great force toward his chariot;
that massive and fierce weapon fell upon the head of Kālanemi.
With his head crushed and his crown ground to powder, the asura,
with streams of blood flowing from his wounds, resembled a mountain from which mineral ores have been extracted.
When his chariot was shattered, he fell unconscious, with only a remnant of life remaining;
as the Dānava lay fallen upon the seat of the chariot, Acyuta, the slayer of enemies, [approached].
Preceded by a smile, the Lord whose weapon is the discus spoke these words:
"Go, O Asura; you are now released. Live free from fear."
"Then, in a very short time, I myself shall be your end.
Having heard these words of his, the charioteer drove Kālanemi’s chariot far away.
Matsya-Purāṇa 151: Sūta said:
Having seen him, the enraged Dānavas, surrounded by their respective armies, set out.
Like bees flying in every direction to gather honey,
[they flocked] to that place rich with nets of black yak-tail fans, its pillars fashioned from plaster,
adorned with five-colored banners, and featuring elephants with temples flowing with rut.
Mounting a formidable, mountain-like elephant that was difficult to restrain and flowing with rut,
the powerful Daitya Nimi advanced against Hari in battle.
His foot-guards were the fierce Dānavas,
twenty-seven thousand in number, resplendent with crowns and armor.
Mathana was mounted on a horse, Jambhaka rode upon a camel,
and Śumbha also advanced to the battle mounted upon a massive ram.
Other lords of the Dānavas, however, alert and with various weapons in their hands, angrily struck Viṣṇu, the one whose actions are effortless, in the battle.
The Daitya Nimi was struck by a club, Mathana by a mallet,
Śumbha by a sharp trident, and likewise Grasana by a spear.
In that great battle, the enraged Mahiṣa struck with a discus,
Jambha with a spear, and all the remaining [demons] struck Nārāyaṇa with sharp arrows.
Those weapons, once discharged, entered the body of Hari,
just as the words spoken by a guru enter the ears of a good disciple when they are taught.
Then Viṣṇu, unperturbed in battle,
took up his bow and arrows that were like venomous serpents, cleansed with oil, and straight-flying.
Then, aiming at those Daityas with his bow drawn back to his ear,
he rushed furiously against the Daitya host in battle through his prowess.
He pierced Nimi with twenty arrows possessing the brilliance of fire,
Mathana with ten arrows, and Śumbha with five.
Enraged, he pierced Mahiṣa in the chest with a feathered arrow,
Jambha with twelve sharp shafts, and each of the others with eight.
Seeing that agility of his, the Dānavas, frantic with rage,
roared and waged an exceedingly wonderful battle with great effort.
Then the Dānava Nimi cut Viṣṇu’s bow with a crescent-headed arrow (bhalla),
and Mahiṣāsura cut the arrow being aimed in his hand.
Jambha afflicted Garuḍa with sharp arrows,
while Śumbha, who resembled a mountain, struck his arm forcefully.
When his bow was severed, Govinda seized a terrifying mace;
in that great battle, he hurled it with great force at Mathana.
Before it could reach her, Nimi cut that [missile] into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his arrows in battle;
seeing it destroyed like a prayer rendered futile by one who has already lost the cause, he was struck with wonder.
He seized a terrible mallet adorned with divine jewels and then hurled it with great force toward the Dānava Nimi.
As he was approaching through the sky, three Daityas intercepted him:
the Daitya Jambha with a mace, and Grasana with a paṭṭiśa.
And the Daitya Mahiṣa, out of a desire for victory for his own side, [fought] with his power;
having observed him thus repulsed, as if one observes affection shown toward a wicked person.
He seized a spear with a fierce tip and the loud resonance of eight bells;
aiming it at Jambha, he who was terrifying in battle hurled it forth.
The elephant, the delighter of the Dānavas, seized her as she stood in the sky, just as the wise seize instruction once it has been grasped. *Matsya Purāṇa* 151.23.
Taking up another firm, strong, and essential bow,
and aiming a fierce weapon, he released an arrow at him.
Then the entire world, including all moving and stationary beings, was pervaded by the splendor of his weapons;
consequently, the whole sky appeared as consisting entirely of arrows.
The earth, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate quarters appeared as if composed of a web of arrows;
having witnessed the majesty of that weapon, the Asura general Grasana [was overcome].
He discharged the Brahma-weapon, which wards off all other weapons;
by it, that fierce weapon, the devourer of the worlds, was brought to subdual.
When that weapon had been repelled, Viṣṇu, the slayer of the Dānavas,
unleashed the Kāladaṇḍa weapon, which strikes fear into all the worlds.
As that [union] was being joined, a harsh wind blew,
the divine earth trembled, and the Daityas became distraught in mind.
Then, beholding that fierce weapon, the Dānavas, intoxicated with the pride of battle,
discharged various kinds of divine weapons in the conflict.
Grasana took up the Nārāyaṇa weapon, while Nimi released his own excellent discus;
and Jambha employed the Aiṣīka weapon to ward off the Kāladaṇḍa weapon.
Before the twilight arrived and before the lords of the Daityas could reach their state of employing weapons for defense,
he, in that very instant, slew ten million lords of the Daityas along with their elephants and horses.
Immediately thereafter, that Kāladaṇḍa weapon was neutralized by the application of the Daitya’s own weapon;
seeing his own weapon thus pacified, Hari, his form filled with wrath, [prepared] his own weapon according to his own prowess.
He seized a discus, radiant as ten thousand suns, with a fierce rim like a second self;
aiming at the general, he hurled that terrible weapon, as hard as a thunderbolt, at his throat.
Beholding that discus situated in the sky, the foremost Daityas, despite their own prowess and with all their might,
were unable to ward it off— just as one cannot thwart fierce destiny when it has overtaken one's actions in vain.
Producing that inconceivable and invincible discus, it fell upon the throat of Grasana;
having split Grasana’s throat in two, with its terrible hub reddened by the stream of his blood,
it returned once more to the hand of Janārdana, blazing like a swelling fire.
When that Daitya Grasana, the leader of the worlds, had been slain, the Dānavas fought with Hari without restraint. (Matsya Purāṇa 152.1)
With spears, clubs, nooses, maces, and even corpses; with sharp-pointed iron arrows, discuses, and likewise with javelins.
Janārdana, the versatile warrior, split each of those weapons released by the Dānavas into hundreds of pieces with arrows resembling tongues of fire.
Then, when their weapons and strength were exhausted and their minds were bewildered,
the Dānavas became incapable of taking up missiles in the battle.
Then, with dead elephants and horses, the Daityas fought Janārdana from all sides; by the millions, they assailed him from every direction.
Having assumed many forms, Viṣṇu, with his arms somewhat calmed,
spoke to Garuḍa in that most tumultuous battle.
"O Garuḍa, are you indeed still unwearied even now?
If you are unwearied, then go toward the chariot of the churning."
"You are weary; now withdraw from the battle for a moment.
Thus was Garuḍa addressed by that powerful Viṣṇu.
In battle, he encountered the Daitya Mathana, who was terrible to behold;
but the Daitya, seeing the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace facing him, [fled].
In that great battle, Viṣṇu struck him in the chest with a sharp arrow from his *bhindipāla* weapon, remaining entirely unperturbed by that blow.
He struck him with five arrows, polished and sharpened on stone,
and again he struck him in the middle of the chest with ten drawn shafts.
Pierced in his vital organs by Hari’s arrows, the lord of the Daityas trembled;
having recovered for a moment, he then seized a club.
He also struck Janārdana with an iron club blazing like fire;
by that blow, Viṣṇu was slightly reeled about.
Then Mādhava, his eyes rolling with rage, seized his mace and, out of fury,
crushed Mathana along with his chariot.
Then that lord of the Daityas fell like a mountain at the time of universal destruction;
when that powerful Dānava had fallen upon the earth, [the world was shaken].
The Daityas fell into despondency like elephants in the mud;
then, when those exceedingly arrogant Dānavas had been defeated, [the gods prevailed].
With eyes red with rage, the fierce Mahiṣa, lord of the Dānavas,
