advanced against Hari, relying on the strength of his own arms.
The heroic Mahiṣa, crushing Hari with a sharp-edged spear and striking Garuḍa in the chest with a javelin, assailed them both.
Then, turning his face, which resembled a cave in a great mountain,
the Daitya desired to devour the infallible Garuḍa in battle.
Then Acyuta, the one of great strength, having understood what the Dānava intended to do, filled his mouth with divine weapons.
Then the one whose banner bears Garuḍa discharged a flood of arrows at Mahiṣa,
covering his face with divine shafts consecrated by divine weapons.
Struck by those arrows, the buffalo, who resembled a mountain,
turned his body and fell down, yet he did not die.
Seeing Mahiṣa fallen upon the ground, Keśava said:
"O Mahiṣāsura, you do not deserve death at my hands by means of weapons."
"You were previously declared by the Lotus-born himself to be one who must be slain by a woman;
arise, save your life, and depart quickly from this battle. (Matsya Purāṇa 152.24)
When that Daitya Mahiṣa had turned his back, the Dānava Śumbha,
biting his lips in rage, his face contorted by a frown, [attacked].
Rubbing his hand against his hand, he took up a formidable bow and made it ready with a string,
as well as arrows resembling venomous serpents.

Then that Daitya, a versatile warrior with a firm grip, assailed Viṣṇu and Garuḍa with countless discharged arrows resembling the flames of a blazing fire, which were yet devoid of the impact of a mace.
And Viṣṇu, though struck by the arrows of the lord of the Daityas, took up a *bhuśuṇḍi* weapon equal to the God of Death;
with that *bhuśuṇḍi*, he crushed Śumbha’s ram, which resembled a mountain peak.
Then, having leaped down from that slain ram, the lord of the Daityas stood on the ground as a foot-soldier;
thereupon, Hari released showers of arrows, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction, at him who was standing upon the earth.
With three arrows Viṣṇu pierced his arm, with six his head, and with ten his banner;
drawing them back as far as his ears, he, whose eyes were rolling, struck the Daitya.
Pierced by that [arrow], the lord of the Daityas became distressed, with a profuse flow of blood;
then, as he wavered slightly from his fortitude, the one who holds the conch, lotus, and Śārṅga bow spoke to him.
"You are to be slain by a maiden; O Asura Śumbha, abandon the battle!
You do not deserve death at my hands here, O fool; why are you so eager for war in vain? (Matsya Purāṇa 152.32)
Having heard these words from the mouth of Viṣṇu, Jambha and Nimi both desired to crush Viṣṇu;
raising a fierce mace, Nimi struck Garuḍa violently upon the head.
Śumbha also struck Viṣṇu on the head with his iron club, which was variegated with the brilliance of a multitude of polished gems;
those two, resembling clouds and fire, fell upon the earth along with the two Dānavas due to their uneven blows.
Seeing that deed, all the sons of Diti roared loudly with lion-like cries;
brandishing their bows, those fierce ones tore up the earth with blows against the gods,
while others shook their garments and blew forth multitudes of conchs, *ānakas*, and *gomukhas*.
Then, having quickly regained consciousness, Garuḍa, together with Keśava,
turned his back on that battle and fled with great speed.
The Sūta said: Having beheld him fleeing with his banner and bow fallen, the Matsya-Purāṇa 153...
The thousand-eyed god Indra considered Hari to have been defeated in that difficult battle.
Seeing the Daityas rejoicing, he could not determine what ought to be done;
then the Lord of the Gods, Pākaśāsana, approached the presence of Viṣṇu.
And he spoke these sweet words to him, which were full of encouragement:
"O Lord, why do you play with these Dānavas of wicked minds? (Matsya Purāṇa 153.3)
For a man who has been exploited by wicked people for an opening, how can there be any effective action? A base person, when ignored by one who is capable, considers it to be his own strength.
Therefore, a wise man should not abandon a low-lying place that is devoid of fortifications;
for by means of superior strategic positioning, chariot-warriors may achieve victory.
O Lord, in ancient times, during the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa, there was a powerful Daitya named Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was arrogant with pride. He became his friend. (Matsya Purāṇa 153.6)
Having encountered you, the Asura experienced a terrible confusion of memory;
so too did those former lords of the Daityas, the enemies of the gods, who were possessed of exceeding strength.
Having encountered destruction like moths reaching a fire,
you alone, O Hari, are the bringer of end to the Daityas in age after age.
"O Viṣṇu, refuge of the gods, become likewise a support for those who are submerged here today.
Being thus addressed, the mighty-armed Viṣṇu then grew in size.
Endowed with supreme supernatural power, the refuge of all beings and the slayer of enemies,
Adhokṣaja then spoke to the thousand-eyed Indra, who was enduring the time of his trial.
Indeed, the lords of the Daityas can be slain by their own specific means of destruction and not otherwise;
the Daitya Tāraka is invincible, except for a seven-day-old infant.
Someone who had incurred the penalty of being slain by a woman was killed instead by a maiden;
likewise, the Dānava Jambha, of cruel prowess, incurred the penalty of being slain.
Therefore, with divine vigor, slay Jambha, the bestower of [boons] upon the world;
for that Dānava cannot be slain by any living beings except you.
"Protected by me, uproot Jambha, who is a thorn to the world, in battle.
Having heard those words of Vaikuṇṭha, the thousand-eyed one, the slayer of the enemies of the immortals, [acted].
He commanded all the gods regarding the arrangement of the army:
"Whatever is the essence of valor and of ascetic power in all the worlds [is to be gathered here]."
Then Hari made the eleven Rudras his precursors;
they were powerful, blue-throated, and their limbs were bound by the coils of serpents.
Their broad crests were adorned with rows of human heads and crescent moons;
their limbs were smeared with the flames of tridents, and they were terrifying with their circle of arms.
The Rudras, led by Kapālīśa, who have dispelled the great asuras, possess tawny, lofty masses of matted hair and are draped in lion skins.
Kapālī, Piṅgala, Bhīma, Virūpākṣa, Vilohita,
Ajeśa, Śāsana, Śāstṛ, Śambhu, Caṇḍa, and Dhruva.
These eleven Rudras, possessed of infinite power and majesty,
stood at the forefront of the army, protecting it and rending asunder the Dānavas.
Strengthening the thirty gods like thundering clouds,
they stood upon a great chariot resembling the Himalayas and adorned with a garland of golden lotuses.
Upon Airāvata, the four-tusked elephant, who stands as immovable as a mountain and is adorned with clusters of golden bells and waving chowries; *Matsya Purāṇa* 153.22.
At Kāmarūpa, which flows with the waters of great intoxication,
Śatakratu stood upon a peak of the Himavat mountain, radiant like the sun.
Māruta, of immeasurable prowess, protected his left foot,
while Agni, filling the quarters of the sky with his flames, guarded the other.
Viṣṇu became the rear-guard of Śatakratu along with his army;
so too did the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the two Aśvins.
Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, along with Kinnaras and Mahoragas,
bearing various and wonderful weapons and adorned with golden ornaments.
Forming groups by the millions upon millions, distinguished by their respective emblems,
and preceded by throngs of bards proclaiming their own glory,
the classes of gods, together with Indra, wandered about joyful at the destruction of the Daityas.
Protected by the hosts of immortals under Śatakratu, that army— resounding with hundreds of elephants and horses,
adorned with the tips of white, lofty banners and cloth streamers— became the increaser of the grief of the sons of Diti.
Then, beholding the celestial army approaching, Gajāsura,
in the form of an elephant, appeared as formidable as a mass of great clouds.
Armed with a battle-axe and wearing armor, his lips compressed in a snarl,
the Daitya crushed the gods in battle and hurled others away with his hand.
The lord of the Daityas, of fierce prowess, struck down his enemies with an axe;
as he was felling the army, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras [fled].
All of them together released a multitude of various weapons and missiles:
nooses, battle-axes, discuses, slings, and mallets.
Spears, javelins, sharp swords, and even unbearable mallets—
all those he swallowed up like a leader of a herd swallows mouthfuls of food.
Striking with his long-tipped trunk, which he brandished in anger,
the demon Gaja moved through the battle, felling the gods while remaining difficult to behold.
Wherever Gajāsura fell upon the host of gods, there a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Then, seeing that army fleeing in every direction,
the Rudras, whose flames arose from their own ego-sense, spoke to one another.
"O, seize the lord of the Daityas! Crush him, for his refuge is destroyed!
Drag him away with sharp spears and break him at his vital points! (Matsya Purāṇa 153.37)
Having heard these words, Kapālī wiped the trident with its sharp-pointed tip with his left hand, his eyes wide open in fury.
With his face contorted by a frown, he rushed toward the lord of the Daityas in battle,
firmly gripping a stainless trident with a tight fist.
Kapālī struck the Dānava Gaja in the region of the frontal globes;
then all ten Rudras [struck him] in battle with stainless iron [weapons].
In the battle, they struck the lord of the Daityas, who possessed the stature of a mountain, with spears;
his wounds bled profusely as he was tormented by the points of the sharp spears.
The Daitya, dark-complexioned as Krishna, shone like a stainless lake in autumn,
with clusters of fully blossomed red and blue lotuses spread in every direction.
Then the Daitya, his body pale like ash, surrounded by Rudras as if by swans,
approached with distress, his leaf-like ears trembling.
Gajāsura pierced Śambhu in the region of the navel with his tusks;
seeing him thus engaged by the two Rudras, the nine Rudras then performed a marvel.
Standing firm on the battlefield, powerful and fearless in combat, they hacked at the body of the enemy of the gods with various weapons.
Just as jackals approach a dead buffalo in the forest,
so too did that bull among the Asuras depart, abandoning the wearer of the skull.
Enraged with speed, the Daitya rushed toward the nine Rudras;
he crushed them with blows from his feet, with his teeth, and also with his trunk.
When he had become exhausted by that tumultuous battle,
Kapālī then seized the hand of that enemy of the gods.
He whirled the elephant-demon with extreme force,
seeing that the Daitya was overcome by exhaustion and his life was barely flickering.
Then, while he was falling in that battle, devoid of energy and with his enthusiasm for the festival of war gone,
[the other] tore away his shield with a terrifying roar.
Seeing the Daitya slain, the mighty lords of the Dānavas made their own garments dark red by the flood of blood flowing from all his limbs.
Upon seeing the form of Kapālin, clothed in an elephant hide, thousands fled, ran away, and fell down. (Matsya Purāṇa 153.52)
In every direction on the ground, the Daityas beheld that very same fierce Rudra;
while that mighty lord of the Dānavas was thus being overwhelmed.
Then the lord of the Daityas, that Dānava, mounted upon his elephant, was struck by Dundubhi,
who resembled a cloud at the end of an aeon and was difficult even for the most powerful to withstand.
Nimi rushed forward swiftly, agitating the armies of the gods.
Whichever direction the elephant Nimi went,
the gods, afflicted by fear and having cast away their weapons, fled from it, abandoning their mounts;
even the celestial elephants fled from the scent of that elephant.
When the armies of the gods had fled, Indra, the subduer of Pāka,
stood firm together with the eight guardians of the quarters and Keśava.
Just as Nimimātaṅga reached toward the elephant of Śakra,
the elephant of Śakra let out a terrifying roar and departed.
Even though it was being held with great effort, the elephant did not remain in the battle;
when that elephant had fled, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, dismounted.
Turning his face away, he fought against the host of the lord of the Dānavas;
but Śatakratu struck Nimi in the chest with his thunderbolt.
With his mace, he struck the elephant firmly on the temple;
yet Nimi, whose valor was fearless, disregarded that blow entirely.
He struck Airāvaṇa on the hip with a mallet;
thus was Śakra’s elephant struck by the mallet in the battle.
Then that great celestial elephant, possessing the form of a mountain, moved along the earth on his hind legs; thereafter, rising quickly with agility, he departed.
Terrified by the elephant Nimi, they quickly retreated from the battlefield;
then a harsh wind blew, filled with much grit and dust.
Facing him, the elephant Nimi, who shook the swift-moving mountains,
shone with flowing blood like a mountain whose mineral veins and hollows have been exposed.
The Lord of Wealth, the lord of the Daityas, also hurled a heavy mace with great force at that Dānava-elephant; it fell upon its head.
Stunned by that blow from the mace, the elephant,
resembling a mountain, struck the earth with its tusks and fell down with great force.
When that elephant had fallen, a great lion-roar arose from all sides among the celestial armies, amplified by the trumpeting of elephants.
Seeing that elephant slain and Nimi also turning his back, there arose the neighing of horses and the twanging of bowstrings by the archers.
And having heard the lion’s roar of the gods, Jambha, who was exceedingly prone to anger,
blazed with rage like a fire fed with clarified butter.
With eyes bloodshot with anger, he fixed an arrow upon his bow, said "Stay! to them, and urged on his charioteer.
As that chariot moved with great speed,
its brilliance was like that of a thousand suns risen upon the mountain of sunrise.
With that chariot, which was adorned with banners, garlanded with networks of tiny bells,
and possessed a moon-white parasol, he [advanced] in battle.
Striking the hearts of the celestial armies, he was seen approaching;
beholding him thus, [Indra] fixed an arrow upon his bow.
Śatakratu, undaunted in spirit, firmly took up his bow and an arrow with a straight flight,
its tip cleansed with oil, shaped like a half-moon.
With that [arrow], the slayer of Vṛtra cut his bow along with the shaft in battle;
Jambha, the delighter of the Dānavas, quickly cast aside that bow.
Taking up another bow, powerful and capable of bearing a great strain,
he also took arrows shaped like venomous serpents, polished with oil and straight-flying.
He pierced Śakra with ten feathered arrows in the region of the collarbone,
with three in the heart, and with two in each of the two shoulders.
Śakra also [discharged] such a web of arrows at the lord of the Dānavas;
however, the lord of the Dānavas [warded off] those arrows released from Śakra’s arms before they could reach him.
Then, with arrows resembling tongues of fire, he cut [the bow] into ten pieces in the sky;
thereafter, Devendra [covered] the lord of the Dānavas with a net of arrows.
"Cover him with effort, as the clouds cover the sky during the rains!
Even the Daitya dispersed that web of arrows with his own sharp shafts.
Just as the wind, having surrounded a mass of clouds at the face of the quarters,
Śakra then does not distinguish them due to his impetuous rage.
Then he discharged the most wonderful Gandharva weapon at the lord of the Dānavas;
the entire range of his movement became pervaded by the splendor arising from it.
And with cities of the Gandharvas, featuring various ramparts and gateways,
emitting a rain of weapons of wondrous form from every side.
Then, the great army of the Daityas, being struck by the rain of missiles,
sought refuge with Jambha, whose prowess was immeasurable.
Though himself agitated and tormented by the weapon of the thousand-eyed Indra, the Daitya,
remembering the conduct of the virtuous, became intent on protecting those who were afraid.
Then the son of Diti released the weapon named Mausala;
thereupon, the entire world became filled with iron clubs.
Within them were Gandharva cities, created by the weapons of the Gandharvas, which were invincible from all sides and capable of delivering a single decisive blow.
Having aimed the Gāndharva weapon at the celestial armies,
with each single blow he struck down elephants, horses, and great chariot-warriors.
He swiftly struck down chariots and horses by the hundreds and thousands;
then the lord of the gods invoked the Tvaṣṭṛ weapon.
Then, as the weapon of Tvaṣṭṛ was being joined together, flames of fire issued forth,
followed by divine, unassailable weapons composed of mechanical contrivances.
By those machines, a canopy was formed in the sky;
and by that canopy, when the club-fight had subsided, [the dust was laid].
Jambha discharged the mountain-weapon, which struck like a multitude of machines; from that, a rain of stones measuring a fathom in size began to fall.
Immediately thereafter, the mechanical engines constructed by the son of Tvaṣṭṛ were reduced to pieces as small as sesame seeds by that falling of stones.
Having reduced the machines to pieces as small as sesame seeds, the mountain-weapon fell with extreme velocity upon their heads and then tore asunder the earth.
Then the thousand-eyed Purandara discharged the vajra-weapon;
thereupon, that great rain of stones was shattered on all sides.
Then, when the mountain-weapon had been neutralized, Jambha— who resembled a mountain and possessed exceeding prowess—
fearlessly discharged the reed-weapon (*aiṣīka-astra*).
By means of the Aiṣīka weapon, he brought to ruin the Vajra-weapon, the favorite of Śakra;
then, while that supreme Aiṣīka weapon was expanding, it became exceedingly difficult to withstand.
The divine armies, together with their chariots and elephants,
blazed up as the best of gods scorched the ranks with his splendor.
The powerful Indra, the subduer of Pāka, discharged the Āgneya weapon;
by that weapon, the other weapon was instantly brought down.
When that weapon was repelled, the fire-weapon (pāvakāstra) manifested;
it blazed forth, engulfing the body of Jambha along with his chariot and his charioteer.
Then, having been repelled, that brilliant lord of the Daityas released the Vāruṇa weapon, which extinguishes the flames of fire.
Then the sky was filled with clouds crowded with flickering streaks of lightning,
as if the atmosphere were pervaded by the deep resonance of kettledrums.
With torrents of water falling from the sky like the trunks of lordly elephants,
the entire world appeared in an instant to be completely filled.
Seeing that fiery weapon pacified,
the lord of the gods discharged the Vāyavya weapon, which destroys masses of clouds.
Then, when the circle of clouds had been blown away by the power of the Vāyavya weapon,
the sky became stainless, possessing the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
Shaken by that most terrible wind, those Dānavas,
even though they were exceedingly powerful, were unable to remain there in the battle.
Then Jambha became a mountain ten yojanas in extent,
intended to obstruct the wind and to dispel the fear of the Dānavas.
Then, when the wind had been stilled by the lord of the Daityas, who was mountain-like in form, the trees blazed with the fierce splendor of various weapons hurled [at him].
Śatakratu quickly released a great thunderbolt made of diamond;
by that falling thunderbolt, the Daitya, who was like a mountain, [was struck].
The caves crumbled and the waterfalls on all sides collapsed;
then that mountain-illusion of the lord of the Dānavas vanished.
Then the lord of the Dānavas, having cast off his illusory form as a mountain and being intoxicated with pride,
became a fearsome elephant with the appearance of a massive mountain.
That Dānava crushed the host of gods, struck the gods with his tusks,
and broke others on their backs by encircling them with his trunk.
Then, as he was destroying the armies of the gods,
the slayer of Vṛtra released the Narasiṃha weapon, which is invincible throughout the three worlds.
Then, by the power of the mantra, thousands of lions emerged,
with black fangs and loud laughter, and claws resembling saws.
With his body torn apart by them, he crushed the illusory elephant;
thereafter, he became a terrible venomous serpent, crowded with a hundred hoods.
Then the great chariot-warrior Śakra, with his beautiful arms, employed the Gāruḍa weapon against the host of gods who had been scorched by the poisonous breath [of the serpent].
Then, thousands [of beings] issued forth from that Garuḍa;
having been encountered by those Garuḍas, Jambha, who had assumed the form of a serpent,
was cut into pieces, and his illusion vanished.
When his illusion had vanished, the great asura Jambha then assumed an incomparable form that followed the paths of the moon and the sun;
with his mouth wide open, he desired to swallow the foremost of the gods.
Then the divine army, along with its great chariots and elephants, entered his terrifying mouth, which had its palate extended down to the netherworld (pātāla).
While the armies were being devoured by the powerful Dānava,
Śakra fell into a state of dejection, his arms and his mount exhausted.
Having understood his duty, he spoke thus to Janārdana: "What remains here that must be done next? *Matsya Purāṇa* 153.122.
"Since we have relied upon him as we strive against this Dānava, desiring to fight,
the noble-minded Hari then spoke these words to the wielder of the thunderbolt."
"You must not now abandon the battle out of cowardly fear;
O Purandara, quickly increase your great illusion against the enemy."
"I have perceived this Daitya; he has been empowered and has attained prowess.
O Śakra, do not fall into delusion; O Lord, quickly recall your weapon! ||| MatsP_153.125 |||
Then Śakra, the king of the gods, enraged at the Dānava,
prepared and released the Nārāyaṇa weapon at the chest of the Asura.
In the meantime, the Daitya, with his mouth wide open,
instantly devoured three hundred thousand Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Then that Nārāyaṇa weapon fell upon the chest of the Asura;
his heart pierced by that great weapon, he bled profusely.
The delighter of the Asuras vomited forth what was like a battle-chamber;
by the splendor of that weapon, the form of the Daitya was destroyed.
Then the Daitya vanished into the sky, unperceived;
remaining in the heavens, that lord of the Daityas drew his weapon, which was beyond the reach of the senses.
He released the supreme instruments for the destruction of the divine armies:
spears, battle-axes, discuses, arrows, thunderbolts, and mallets.
The fierce Dānava rained down axes along with swords, slings, and iron balls— missiles that were indeed never-failing and inexhaustible.
By those terrifying weapons discharged by the Dānavas upon the divine hosts,
the earth was covered with arms and with heads adorned with earrings.

With thighs resembling the trunks of elephants, like lordly elephants or mountains, [the earth was covered] with chariots—along with their charioteers—whose poles, axles, wheels, and hubs were shattered. *Matsya Purāṇa* 153.133.
The earth became impassable, a mire of flesh and blood,
with whirlpools and pools of flowing streams of gore, and heaps of mountain-like piles of corpses.

In that chaos of dancing headless trunks, amidst the mire of flowing fat and blood, when the three worlds were being destroyed and all embodied beings were equalized, the jackals, vultures, and crows experienced supreme joy; in one place, a crow, its eyes drawn wide, shrieks at a corpse.
In some places jackals go about with their long, bloated entrails dragged out; in others stands a most terrifying crane, pecked at by the beaks of dogs.
While scavenging for the flesh of the dead, various species of dogs remain stationed there; in another spot, a wolf drank the elephant's blood as it hid within its entrails.

In some places a troop of horses is dragged away by packs of dogs; in other places, it is devoured by various classes of *piśācas* who have drunk their fill of the wine of blood, accompanied by their own beloveds, rushing about in the frantic agitation of intoxication. "May this mouth of mine bring this to them; may this hoof of mine be dear to them! *Matsya Purāṇa* 153.137.

"May this hand of mine, resembling a lotus, become an ear-ornament for him," she thought; yet another woman, seeing her beloved looking on with wrath, then tore off the skin from a corpse—its dense foliage still attached—and offered it, while the other beloved received the warm blood and vital breaths of a victim.
The Yakṣa’s beloved woman cut down a tree with an axe and took the elephant’s tusk as her own son;
having split open the frontal globes of the elephant, she extracted the finest pearls while seeking the favor of her lover, and the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas drank his flesh, blood, and vital essence.

Taking in his hand the liquor flavored with the hair of a dead horse, he brought that blood-wine which had been tasted by his beloved while she was still clinging to life; yet that wine, having reached the domain of the cemetery, does not become wholesome for me, for it causes him to abandon the praiseworthy face of a Kinnara.
"This is that Naga; he causes us fear. His life has been spared, and it is not possible for me to kill the Danava alone.
Thus spoke the beloved Yaksha women to their lover, while other Pisacas, Yakshas, and Rakshasas stood by with skull-bowls in their hands.

"Give! Give to me! so cry out others who subsist on excessive meat-eating; having descended into the rivers of blood with their bodies washed clean, they satiate the ancestors and worship the deities with flesh offerings, and remaining firmly seated upon elephant-islands, they cross over the lake of blood.
Thus, in that most intense and perilous battle between gods and asuras, the proud warriors, casting off fear, burst forth as they were difficult to conquer.
Then Śakra, the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada), Varuṇa, Pavana, Anala,
Yama, and Nirṛti— those of great strength— [bestowed] divine weapons.
Aiming at the Dānavas, they all released [their weapons] into the sky;
yet the missiles of the gods proved useless against the Dānavas.
Though they fought with fury and in a tumultuous mass,
the gods, being exhausted, could not discern the Daitya's course of action.
With all their limbs pierced by the weapons of the Daityas,
they became utterly powerless and huddled together, like cows afflicted by the cold.
Seeing the gods in that state, Hari said to Śakra:
"O Lord of the Gods, remember the Brahmāstra, by means of which there is no one who cannot be slain.
Urged by Viṣṇu, Śakra remembered that weapon of great power.
Having fixed upon his invincible bow that arrow— which was constantly worshipped, which destroys enemies,
and which is concentrated for the slaying of foes— the wise one then became absorbed in the meditative concentration of the mantra.
Having uttered the mantra with his inner intent restrained, and having resolved in his mind upon the slaughter of the Daitya,
he drew back the arrow of unimpeded luster to his ear and released it, gazing upward toward the path of the sky.
Then the Asura, beholding the great weapon discharged, abandoned his illusion and stood upon the ground,
overwhelmed with agitation, his mouth trembling, his face parched, and his limbs failing him.
Then, in that great battle, an arrow consecrated with the most excellent of mantras, resembling a crescent moon and emulating the orb of the rising sun with its form,
attained the status of a companion to the seat of Purandara.

The head of Jambha, together with its earrings, fell down— its hair appearing like scattered smoke and flames, perfumed by various fragrant flowers, and crowded with the brilliant luster flashing from the tips of his crown.
When Jambha had been slain, the lords of the Dānavas turned their backs;
then, with their resolve shattered, they fled to where Tāraka was.
Beholding them terrified and hearing of it, he was filled with supreme rage upon learning that Jambha,
the lord of the Dānavas, had been slain by the gods at the front of the battle.
Tāraka entered into a state of being full of arrogance, fury, pride, and prowess;
it was manifest yet devoid of outward form.
Mounting his victorious chariot with a thousand Garuḍas,
the lord of the Dānavas went forth in fury to the front of the battle against the gods.
Equipped with all weapons and accoutrements, protected by all missiles,
endowed with the supernatural powers of the three worlds, and possessing a vast, great face.
Surrounded by a vast army, he swiftly rushed toward the battle,
leaving behind the elephant Airāvata, whose entire body had been mangled by the Jambha weapon.
The chariot of Indra, protected by Mātali and radiant with his splendor, was ready;
it was adorned with refined gold and equipped with great jewels.
Extending four yojanas in width, it was adorned by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas),
filled with the songs of gandharvas and kinnaras, and crowded with the dances of apsarases.
Surrounding that chariot of the king of the gods on all sides was a complete array of weapons, unobstructed and radiant with various artistic designs.
The world-protectors, clad in armor and accompanied by the one whose banner is Garuḍa, stood firm;
then the earth trembled, and a harsh wind blew.
From that, the oceans arose; from that, the radiance of the sun perished;
from that, darkness emerged, so that the stars were no longer visible.
Then the weapons blazed forth, and then the army trembled;
on one side was the Daitya Tāraka, and on the other side was the host of gods.
On one side was the destruction of the worlds, and on the other, the protection of the universe;
there were the moving and unmoving beings, distinguished as gods and demons.
Like spectators, they beheld those two as having attained oneness;
whatever object exists in the three worlds that possesses the nature of being,
all that was seen there with its power rendered barren.
By the power of his asceticism, he became a repository of the missiles, splendors, riches, fortitude, military strength, heroism, and prowess,
as well as the vital energy and vigor of both gods and demons.
Then, as he was approaching them face-to-face, they pierced Tāraka in the heart with nine arrows whose joints were bent and whose tips were like fire.
Disregarding those arrows that had struck his heart, that lord of the Daityas,
the Dānava, pierced the gods in return with nine arrows each.
Then, in that battle, the gods released an unceasing volley of arrows, which were like thorns produced for the purpose of supporting the world as they preceded them.

And immediately thereafter, the Dānava caused those [missiles], which had not yet reached their targets, to vanish in the sky itself, as if they were the incessant falling of tears from beloved women.

Just as a wicked son brings ruin to his own great lineage—which is renowned, of noble descent, supremely exalted, and perfectly pure—so too does one bring destruction through evil conduct. *Matsya Purāṇa* 153.173.
Then, having warded off that net of arrows discharged by the arms of the gods,
the Dānava filled the sky, the quarters, and the earth with his own shafts.
With swiftness, he severed [the arrows] at their feathered joints and at their own points with nets of extremely sharp-tipped shafts fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks.
With stainless arrows drawn back to his ear, shining with gold and silver,
he [pierced] those who had fallen into doubt regarding the meaning of the scriptures with well-reasoned arguments that were consistent with reality.
Then the Dānava pierced Śakra with a hundred arrows,
Nārāyaṇa with seventy, and Hutāśana with ninety.
With ten [arrows] he struck Māruta on the head, with ten likewise Yama,
with seventy Dhanada, and with eight Varuṇa.
The Daitya pierced Nirṛti with twenty arrows, and again with eight;
then he pierced each of them once more with ten arrows each.
And so the Daitya pierced Mātali with three swift arrows,
and he likewise pierced Garuḍa with ten feathered shafts.
Furthermore, with his joints bent, the Daitya reduced the armor of the gods to pieces as small as sesame seeds and cut their bows asunder;
thereupon the gods were rendered devoid of armor and stripped of their bows by his arrows.

Then, in that battle, the world-protectors, filled with wrath, took up other bows on all sides and mangled the lord of the Dānavas with inexhaustible arrows; at that time, the Dānava’s eyes were bloodshot with indignation.

Then, raining down arrows resembling fire, he took up an arrow possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction and swiftly struck Indra in the chest; Subāhu trembled even while remaining upon the seat of his chariot.

Beholding in the sky a thousand solar discs, the Dānava again sportively struck Viṣṇu, whose prowess had been aroused, at the base of his shoulders with two arrows; thereupon, Keśava’s Śārṅga bow fell before him.
Then Tāraka,

the invincible king of the Daityas, remembering Vasu’s former state of insignificance, afflicted the body of the Lord of Waters in battle with arrows resembling fire, while striking his left side with shafts.
With arrows resembling fire, the Daitya quickly struck the Rākṣasas so that they fled terrified in all directions;
and with harsh shafts, the lord of the Asuras effortlessly brought the wind, which had been unleashed as a portent, to a standstill.
In an instant, Viṣṇu, Śakra, Agni, and the others regained their composure;
uniting together, they engaged in a great battle with the fierce Daitya, which was like the devouring of the world at the end of an eon, using sharp arrows.
Then Hari, bending his bow, struck the heart of the charioteer of the Daitya king with sharp shafts.
Dhūmaketu gave him the banner, Mahendra the diadem, Dhaneśa the bow with its back covered in gold,
Yama the staff-like arms, Vāyu the wheels of the chariot, and even the Lord of Night-rangers the armor.
Having witnessed that battle performed by the immortals with unfeigned valor in the conflict,
the lord of the Daityas relied upon the kinship of his own pair of arms.
In the battle, he hurled a terrible mallet at the Thousand-eyed One;
then, seeing the mallet approaching unimpeded in the sky, [the god acted].
Leaping from the chariot, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) went to the earth;
the mallet too fell upon the seat of the chariot with a harsh sound.
He crushed the chariot, yet Mātali did not die;
seizing a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), the Daitya struck Keśava in the chest.
He too, rendered unconscious, sat upon the shoulder of Garuḍa,
and with his sword he cut down the mount of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
And the Daitya struck Yama down to the ground with a *bhuśuṇḍi* weapon,
and he struck Vahni on the head with a *bhindipāla*.
Lifting Vāyu up with his two arms, he threw him down upon the ground;
and the wrathful one struck Dhaneśa with the tip of his bow.
Then, in that battle, the lord of the Daityas, possessed of immeasurable prowess, struck each of the hosts of gods individually with countless weapons.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, Viṣṇu seized his irresistible discus,
which was smeared with the blood of the lord of the Dānavas and eager to devour flesh.
Keśava struck the firm chest of the lord of the Dānavas;
the discus, radiant as the sun, fell upon the heart of the Daitya.
Then it shattered against his body like a blue lotus against a stone;
thereupon Mahendra released the thunderbolt, which had been worshipped for a long time.
It was upon obtaining the body of the heroic Tāraka that Śakra conceived the hope of victory over the lord of the Dānavas in battle.
Released upon the chest of the Asura by the wind, it shattered into a hundred fragments, its flames scattered, and met its destruction.
Seeing the goad, blazing with the luster of fire like a thunderbolt,
brought to destruction by Vāyu in the battle, Matsya Purāṇa 153.202.
Enraged, he uprooted a lordly mountain whose caves were filled with flowering trees—
measuring five yojanas in width— and hurled it at the lord of the Dānavas.
Then the Daitya, with a smiling face,
seized that approaching mountain with his left hand as easily as one would play with a child's ball.
Then, raising his staff, the invincible Kṛtānta, overwhelmed with rage,
whirled it with great force and hurled it at the head of the lord of the Daityas.
Then that fire, possessing the brilliance of the conflagration at the end of an aeon and being invincible, fell upon the head of the Asura; yet the Daitya did not perceive it.
He hurled an invincible spear at the lord of the Dānavas in the battle;
it shone upon his chest like a fresh garland of śirīṣa flowers.
Then Nirṛti, the guardian of the world, drew from its scabbard a sword as stainless as the sky, which illuminated the dark quarters of the horizon.
He hurled it at the lord of the Dānavas, and it fell upon his head;
having fallen, that sword quickly shattered into a hundred fragments.
The Lord of Waters, desiring to bind the Daitya’s arm, released his noose, which was fierce, difficult to withstand, and as terrifying as poison and fire.
Having reached the arm of the Daitya, that serpent,
with its row of teeth as cruel as a cracked saw and possessing great jaws, instantly perished.
Then the Aśvins, along with the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the great serpents (Uragas),
as well as the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas, held various divine weapons in their hands.
All those of great strength united and struck the lord of the Daityas,
yet their weapons did not take hold upon his body, which was like a mountain of adamant.
Then, leaping down from his chariot, Tāraka, the lord of the Dānavas,
struck the gods by the millions with his very palms and heels.
The remnants of the gods' armies,
terrified, fled in all directions, abandoning their equipment for battle.
Then the Daitya bound the world-protectors, headed by Indra,
along with Keśava, in battle with firm nooses, like a butcher slaughtering animals.
Mounting his chariot once more, he went to his own abode,
which was situated upon the vast summit of a mountain resounded by hosts of Siddhas and Gandharvas.
Being praised by the sons of Diti and entertained by the Apsarases,
the Fortune of the Three Worlds entered that place as if it were his own city.
He sat down upon a seat fashioned from ruby gems;
then, being entertained for a moment by the diversions of Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Nāgas, and women,
his jeweled earrings swayed.
Matsya Purāṇa 154: Sūta said:
A doorkeeper appeared, his garments being white and blue like lotuses.
Having knelt upon the earth, he covered his mouth with his own hand.
He spoke words that were unclouded, concise, and perfectly clear to the lord of the Daityas, who possessed a radiant body like a multitude of suns. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.2)
Kālanemi, having seized the bound gods, stands at the gate;
he requests, "O Lord, where should these bards remain? (MatsP 154.3)
Having heard those words of the doorkeeper, the Daitya said:
"Stay as you please; these three worlds are my home."
When they were thus freed from their bonds without delay,
the gods, with hearts burning with grief, acted accordingly.
They went to seek refuge with the Lotus-born One, the Teacher of the World;
having prostrated their heads upon the earth, Śakra and the others praised the Lotus-seated Lord with words of clear syllables and meaning.
The gods said:

"You are the syllable Oṃ, produced at the beginning for the sake of the sprout of this universe of infinite variety, the Self of all that has come into being; thereafter, O you whose form is existence, who desire the withdrawal [of the world], salutations to you, O you whose form is Rudra! (Matsya Purāṇa 154.7)
Having manifested your own body by your own majesty from that egg which possesses a name, you, the inconceivable one,
effect a division of this egg into the upper portion, heaven, and the lower portion, earth.
It is evident that on Mount Meru your lifespan was such as it is; we know this clearly, for the world shines forth as guided by you.
It is manifest that the gods are your offspring of eternal birth; heaven is your head, and the moon and sun are your eyes.
Your hair is serpents, the cavities of your ears are the directions, your feet are the earth, and the oceans are within the cavity of your navel;
you are the renowned magician who is the cause, peaceful through the Vedas, and liberated by light.
Having realized that you, the Ancient One, are seated within the lotus of the heart, they explain the meanings of the Vedas through you;
those who have attained yoga praise you as the Self—that which is the seven subtle principles set forth by the Sāṃkhyas.
The eighth [verse] is also sung as their cause; in each of those [verses], you indeed are sung at the end.
Having seen the form, both gross and subtle, the gods fashioned it; thus have the entities been described by certain authorities.
They were born from you alone at the first creation, and they subsequently acquired their various latent impressions (vāsanās).
Time, which is measured by your resolve and hidden until its end is reached, is beyond the conceptualization of number.
You are the cause of the manifestation and withdrawal of existence and non-existence; you are that infinite one, O Self, and the creator of it.
You are celebrated as being subtler than those other subtle elements that exist, and yet you are the gross entities and their veilers.
Through those ancient and gross forms, You are perceived as both the past and the future of all things subject to manifestation;
in every state of being, You—having been meditated upon—join the devotee who is ever-yoked, casting off each successive manifestation.
Thus, O Lord of infinite form, You are our refuge, protector, and guardian for those who possess devotion. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.15)
Having praised the immutable Brahmā, the immortals took their leave;
thereafter, they stood with their minds intent on praying for the attainment of their desired objects.
Thus praised, Viriñci attained supreme grace;
pointing with his left hand, he spoke to the immortals as a granter of boons: *matsyapurāṇa* 154.17.
Brahmā said: "O Śakra,
why is this woman, whose husband is gone, with her body stripped of ornaments,
not shining as she once did, with her face and hair so withered?"
Though released from the fire, you do not shine forth from the smoke;
like a forest fire long extinguished, you are merely covered by ashes.
You do not shine at all upon this body composed of the elements of Yama, for you are like one who,
by leaning on a staff, finds no difficulty at every step.
O Lord of the night-rangers, why do you speak as if afraid? O King of Rākṣasas, enemy of the Kṣatriyas, you appear like one wounded by an adversary.
Your body was parched by Varuṇa as if it had been encircled by fire;
you gazed upon the noose from which the blood had been released, while serpents coiled around it.
O Vāyu, you have become bewildered, as if overcome by those who are affectionate;
O Kubera, why do you fear, having seemingly renounced the status of the Lord of Wealth?
"O Rudras, being trident-bearers yourselves, explain why you possess so many spears; by whom was that splendor of yours cast down? MatsP_154.24 //
"O Madhusūdana, your hand has become useless and does not shine;
enough with this discus that resembles a blue lotus."
O Viśvatomukha, why do you, with eyes fixed and motionless, gaze upon the entire world as it lies hidden within your belly? (Matsya Purāṇa 154.26)
Thus addressed by Brahmā, whose form is Brahman,
the gods urged that Māruta, because he was the primary element of speech.
Then Śvasana, having been awakened by the gods headed by Viṣṇu,
spoke to the four-faced Lord, the teacher of all things moving and unmoving.
Yet you do not perceive the nature of existence residing within all moving and unmoving beings, for you are exceedingly great, exalted, and the source of all;

you have been made to feel a curiosity that expands like an ear hearing the words of a petitioner. O Infinite One, you create the world of living beings, differentiated by qualities and containing both the mobile and the immobile.
O wonder, this entire host of gods and asuras is equal to you, since you are their progenitor.

Nevertheless, my father’s mind remains disturbed; for the son of the wielder of the thunderbolt—the exceedingly powerful son of Diti—is possessed of qualities, yet devoid of merit, strong, yet weak, and his fears have been dispelled by the boon he received from you.
Why, O Lord, have you made this rogue [the world] subject to the churning of the moving and the unmoving?
Indeed, it was by you that the great, wondrous, variegated, and diverse qualities were ordained for the stability of the worlds.
Moreover, O leader of the twice-born, the hosts of gods were made contented and granted the fruits of their desire for sacred learning;
indeed, by the power of your constant command, even heaven itself became the eternal domain of those who enjoy the sacrificial offerings.
Having had the multitude of celestial chariots carried away by that son of Diti, he made it resemble a vast desert;
yet you have rendered it superior in every excellence by being the sovereign of all the mountains.
That mountain, whose methods for discerning gestures and internal states were equal [to his own], has indeed attained eternal loftiness through the sky;
it was the fitting place for the practice of dwelling and meditation, its peaks and slopes scarred by the thunderbolt of the son of Diti.
O King of the Gods, that multitude of caves whose jewels had been plundered was made to serve as the assembly hall for many Daityas;
thus, even his departure from here in an incorporeal form due to fear of him was in vain.

This collection of divine weapons, which was manifested for utility long ago and filled the faces of the quarters with stainless luster, was created by you alone and remains unextinguished even in the first age.
Having reached the body of the son of Diti, it shattered into a hundred pieces like the wavering mind of a person of small intellect.
With our limbs covered in dust from the storm, we stood dejected at the gate;
only with great difficulty did we gain entrance to that enemy of the gods.
O God, even the immortals were seated in the assembly hall in a lowly position;
remaining silent while holding staffs in their hands, they were then mocked by those [others].
O immortals, you who possess great purpose and have accomplished all your aims speak very little; yet for this act involving flattery, you speak much.
"Tell us the agreement made with the lion among the Daityas, even with Śakra himself," they said;
and thus the messengers of the Daitya laughed at them profusely.
The seasons, personified, wait upon him day and night;
even when he has committed an offense, they are never afraid and never abandon him.
In his palaces, the celestial music, accompanied by the triple rhythm of the lute and performed by Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, is sung constantly.
Alas! He has abandoned his friends without regard for their services or the gravity of the situation;
he has forsaken those who sought refuge in him and cast aside the shelter of truth.
Thus, it is impossible to describe his misconduct in its entirety;
the Creator alone is the ultimate authority in that regard.
Thus addressed by the gods regarding the activities of the Daityas, the Lord, the self-born one, spoke to the deities with a lotus-like face smiling. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.46)
Brahmā said:
"The Daitya Tāraka is incapable of being slain by any gods or asuras;
that man who could slay him has not yet appeared anywhere in the three worlds."
Having enticed him with the granting of a boon,
I have now turned the king away from his asceticism, which was capable of consuming the three worlds.
And that Daitya chose his death at the hands of an infant no more than seven days old—
one who would arise from Śaṅkara on the seventh day.
He, who possesses the splendor of the sun, shall become the slayer of Tāraka;
for at present, the blessed Lord Śaṅkara is without a wife.
And as for what I said—
that her hand is always turned upward— this hand of the goddess is indeed forever turned upward, granting boons.
That goddess, the daughter of Himācala, shall become his wife;
from her, Śarva shall arise like fire from the friction-sticks in the forest.
"Having obtained him, Tāraka will overcome [the gods];
I too have devised this means so that it shall indeed come to pass."
Furthermore, his remaining power shall perish immediately thereafter;
wait for a short time with a mind free from doubt.
Thus addressed by the Lotus-born One in person, the thirty gods,
the inhabitants of heaven, bowed down to that Lord and departed as was appropriate for each.
Then, after the gods had departed, the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
recalled the night that had previously given birth to his own body.
Then the blessed Night approached the Grandfather;
beholding her in a secluded place, Brahmā spoke to Vibhāvarī.
Brahmā said:
"O Vibhāvarī, a great task has presented itself for the gods;
O Goddess, you must perform it—listen to the determination of this duty."
The lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, who has not been conquered by the celestial host, will be destroyed; for his destruction, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Controller, shall bring forth a son.
It has been heard that he will be the one who brings about the end of that Tāraka;
she who was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, became the wife of Śaṅkara.
That goddess, having died in anger due to some particular cause,
shall become the world-creating daughter of the Himālaya mountain.
In her absence, Hara, perceiving the three worlds as empty,
performed austerities in a cave of the Snowy Mountain frequented by the Siddhas.
Waiting for that birth, he will dwell there for some time;
he shall be the one of great strength born from those two who have performed intense austerities.
She will be the destroyer of the Daitya Tāraka;
and as soon as she is born, that beautiful goddess shall possess but little consciousness.

"O lady of auspicious countenance, there shall be a reunion for those two who have performed intense austerities— she, longing intensely from the pain of separation, and he, yearning for union with Hara."
Then a slight verbal quarrel will arise between those two;
from that, moreover, a great uncertainty regarding Tāraka is foreseen.
Therefore, when those two are united for the purpose of engaging in sexual pleasure, you must create an obstacle for them; listen now to how that shall be done by you.
And in the place of her womb, delight her with your own form;
then, O Śarva, having left her after sporting, you rested with playful jests.
He will revile that goddess, and then, becoming enraged, she will depart to perform ascetic penance; therefore, [you must prevent her] from that penance once again.
The one whom Śarva shall bring forth, adorned with a luster like that of his beloved,
will undoubtedly be the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
O Goddess, you too must slay the Dānavas who are difficult for the world to conquer,
as long as Satī has not transferred the accumulation of her virtues into her body.
"Until you have united with him, you will not be able to slay the Daityas;
once this is done, having performed penance, you shall be the one who effects the creation and destruction of the world. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.72)
When the goddess Umā has completed her vow and becomes full-grown,
then the daughter of the mountain will regain her own original form.
A portion of you, innate and consisting of a single part, shall come into being;
joined with a portion of your form, you shall exist within Umā.
O giver of boons, the world shall worship you as Ekānaṃśā;
you who are omnipresent and the fulfiller of desires through manifold and diverse forms.
"You are Gāyatrī, whose mouth is the syllable Oṃ," so you were addressed by the exponents of the Veda;
and you are the powerful stride of great-armed kings.
"You are the Earth, the mother of the people; you are worshipped as Śaivī by the Śūdras;
you are the unshakeable patience of the sages, and the compassion of those who observe self-restraint."
You are the collection of great expedients, the policy for those who spread through statesmanship;
you are the discernment of all objects, and you are the desire dwelling within the hearts of living beings.
You are the liberation of all beings; you are the refuge of all embodied ones.
You are the fame of those who possess fame; you are the embodiment of all embodied beings.
You are the delight of those with passionate hearts; you are the joy of those who look upon you with gladness;
you are the splendor of those adorned with ornaments; and you are the peace for those whose karma is suffering.
You are the delusion of all cognitions; you are the goal of those who perform sacrifices;
you are the great tide of the oceans; and you are the playful grace of the amorous.
You are the origin of all things; you are the stability that protects the worlds;
you are the Night of Time that destroys the entire succession of universes.
"O Goddess, you grant the joy of embracing the neck of one's beloved;
thus, O Goddess, you are worshipped in the world through these and many other forms. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.83)
O Giver of Boons, those who shall praise you or even those who worship you will obtain all their desires; this is certain, there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus addressed, the goddess Niśā, saying "So be it" with palms joined in reverence,
went quickly and swiftly to the supreme home of Himagiri.
There, in a great palace resting against jeweled walls,
he beheld Menā seated, her lotus-like face pale in complexion.
She was slightly bent by the weight of her breasts, which had dark nipples;
she was attended by the king of mantras bound with clusters of great medicinal herbs.
In that place illuminated by the great light of the radiance from clusters of jewel-lamps, [he saw] a great serpent (mahoraga) wearing a life-protecting amulet fastened with gold.

In that place where many perfected beings (siddhas) were gathered, which was filled with mind-born attendants, and which was radiant with pure silken cloths spread over the ground as a bed-covering; MatsP_154.89.
Then, as the day gradually passed away into the distant night, which was delightful with the fragrance of incense and permeated by the scent of *sarja* resin; MatsP_154.90 //
Then, in that great palace where the attendants were overcome by sleep and the men were mostly fast asleep, Menā yawned, heralding the onset of happiness.
When the moon was clearly visible, the nocturnal birds were bewildered;
meanwhile, the courtyards were filled with throngs of night-roaming spirits.
Then, as her beloved was clinging to her with a firm embrace of the neck,
Menā’s two lotus-eyes became somewhat agitated.
Night entered her mouth after a long and clear union, and then,
in due course, it entered the interior of the womb of the world-mother who gives birth to all beings.
Perceiving it as her own rebirth, the night indeed entered within;
in the cave-forest, the dark night made the complexion of the goddess radiant.
Then, at the auspicious hour of Brahmā (brāhma-muhūrta), the beloved of the Himavat mountain— the cause of the life-force of the Lord of the World— gave birth to Guhāraṇi.
While she was being born, all living beings— both stationary and moving— who dwell in all the worlds, became happy.
At that time, even for the hell-beings and for those cruel creatures, there arose a great happiness equal to that of heaven,
and the minds of all embodied beings became tranquil.
Even among the luminaries, there was brilliance; the celestial trees were exalted;
and the herbs dwelling in the forests bore sweet fruits.
The flower garlands were fragrant, the sky became stainless,
the wind was pleasant to the touch, and the quarters of the sky were most enchanting.
And by that [virtue], the goddess Earth became radiant with the qualities of sprouting, flowering, and ripening, and was also filled with rows of rice plants.
The austerities long practiced by the sages of purified soul and stainless mind attained their fruition at that time.
Forgotten weapons reappeared,
and at that time, the power of the foremost sacred fords became most meritorious.
In the intermediate space, there were thousands of gods in celestial chariots,
led by Indra, Hari, Brahmā, Vāyu, and Agni.
Upon that mountain of snow, they released a rain of flowers;
the chief Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
And Meru and the others, possessing physical forms and great strength,
arrived at that great festival with their hands filled with divine offerings.
The rivers and the oceans likewise gathered from all sides;
thus Himavat became the center of the world for all things mobile and immobile.
That best of immovable mountains is worthy of service and worthy of being approached; it is most auspicious.
Having experienced the festival, the gods returned joyfully to their own abodes.
Then, by virtue of her qualities of character being like those of the gods, Gandharvas, lords of Nāgas, mountains, and forests,
the goddess Himavat’s daughter herself took precedence.
Gradually brought to increase by wise men free from sloth,
she [Lakṣmī] gradually [filled] the three worlds with beauty, fortune, and awakening.
The daughter of the mountain adorned herself with peerless ornaments;
meanwhile, Śakra addressed Nārada, who is honored by the gods.
Then the Blessed One, having understood that Śakra had formed the thought of quickly accomplishing his task, remembered the celestial sage.
Filled with joy, he arrived at the residence of Mahendra;
seeing him, the thousand-eyed one rose from his great throne.
Vāsava honored him with water for the feet as was appropriate;
having accepted that worship offered by Śakra according to the prescribed rite, [the sage] received it.
Nārada inquired after the welfare of the god Pākaśāsana;
and when his welfare had been asked, the lord Śakra spoke these words.
Indra said:
"O Sage, now that the sprout of merit has emerged throughout the three worlds, you must remain unwearied in bringing about the perfection of its fruit."
"You know all this, yet you inquire;
by reporting the matter to a friend, one attains supreme peace. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.117)
"Just as the goddess Śailajā might enter into union with the wielder of the Pināka bow,
let all those on our side swiftly exert themselves toward that end."
Having understood the entire matter and then taken leave of Śakra, the venerable Nārada departed for his residence on the Himālaya mountains.
At that gate, crowded with variegated cane-staffs,
that lord of sages was saluted by the Himālaya mountain as he came forth before him.
Having entered together with him into the palace, which had become an ornament of the earth,
he was personally informed that the vast golden Himālaya mountain was there.
The excellent sage of incomparable splendor sat upon the great seat;
and Śaila offered him the guest-offering and water for his feet according to his merit.
The sage then accepted that guest-offering according to the prescribed rites;
having received the offering, he questioned the best of sages with gentle words.
Then the sage Śaila, whose lotus-face was slowly blooming with joy at his own ascetic merit,
likewise inquired after the welfare of the King of Mountains.
Nārada said: "O great mountain, how wonderful! All [the gods] have been brought down into your abode;
the extent of your caves is indeed equal to the vastness of the mind."
The weight of your multitude of virtues exceeds that of the mountains;
and your clarity surpasses even that of the water, as does your serenity exceed even that of the mind.
O Lord of Mountains, we do not perceive anything remaining from the interior of the cave,
nor does such splendor exist anywhere in heaven as it stands here in its excellence.

It is constantly sanctified by various sages who have taken refuge in your caves— sages whose splendor is equal to fire and the sun, and who are themselves purifying through their diverse ascetic penances.
Disregarding their celestial chariots and indifferent to dwelling in heaven,
the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras remained close by as if in the house of their father.
O Lord of Mountains, oh, how fortunate you are, since Hara,
the Lord of the World himself, dwells in your cave, entirely devoted to meditative absorption!
When the celestial sage Nārada had thus spoken with respectful words,
Menā, the queen of the Himālaya mountain, [prepared] out of a desire to see the sage.
Followed by her daughter and a very small retinue of attendants,
she entered her residence with her limbs bowed low in modesty and bashfulness.
While the self-controlled and excellent sage was staying there together with Śaila,
the beloved wife of Śaila then beheld that sage, who was a mass of splendor.
With her face hidden and her lotus-like hands joined in *añjali*, she paid homage;
and beholding her, the illustrious great seer of immeasurable luster [spoke].
He caused her to grow with blessings that were like the outpouring of nectar;
thereupon, the daughter of the Himavat mountain was struck with wonder in her heart.
The goddess gazed upon the sage Nārada of wondrous form;
and she was addressed by the ṛṣi with an affectionate voice, saying, "Come, my child! (Matsya Purāṇa 154.136).
Taking her father by the neck, she sat upon his lap;
then her mother said to that goddess, "Pay homage, my daughter."
"Then you shall obtain as a husband a blessed one, esteemed by all.
Having been addressed thus by her mother, she then covered her face with the edge of her garment.
With her head slightly trembling, she did not say anything at all;
then the mother spoke these words again to her daughter: *matsyapurāṇa* 154.139.
"Child, salute the celestial sage; then I shall give you a beautiful jewel toy, which has been kept by me for a long time. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.140)
Having been addressed thus, she then quickly raised her feet and,
joining her lotus-bud hands above her head, paid homage at his feet.
When her salutation had been performed, her mother, through the mouth of a female friend,
gently urged her to speak words indicative of her good fortune.
Out of curiosity to discern the characteristics of her body,
he bore in his heart the thought that she was of female nature because of his daughter.
Having understood that intention through his wife's heart-signs, the Mountain, though not speaking aloud, thought within his heart:
"This delightful thing has arrived, unharmed."
Then, urged by the friend of the mountain’s queen,
the illustrious and great sage Nārada, with a smiling face, spoke these words.

"O blessed lady, her husband has not yet been born; she is devoid of auspicious marks, with palms constantly turned upward and feet that are unsteady. She will be abandoned even by her own shadow—what more need be said? (Matsya Purāṇa 154.146)
Having heard this, the mighty Mahāgiri, overcome with agitation and his composure shattered, replied to Nārada with a throat choked by tears. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.147)
Himavat said:
"Since the course of this world, which is fraught with extreme defects, is difficult to comprehend,
[it must proceed] through some being of a transcendent nature during creation, which is an inevitable occurrence."
This law established by the Creator stands for those in the cycle of existence:
for whatever seed one is born from, that [seed] indeed belongs to the progenitor and not to another.
And since it is evident that there is no one who is the progenitor of what has been born,
the various classes of beings are produced solely by their own karma.
For a human born from an egg-born creature may be born again as an egg-born one;
and from a human, one is born among the reptiles, yet through the human state, one is born again as a human.
Even there, among those born in the highest caste, it is through the excellence of their dharma that they stand out;
all other living beings remain as those born without sons.
Human beings are born there because they are not householders;
for them, the attainment of the stages of life proceeds in sequence following the vow of the student (brahmacārin).
By whose command was this cycle of existence increased by that creator?
From where did the increase of the cycle of existence come, since all things are its grasping agents?
Therefore, the author [of the scriptures] has praised the attainment of a son in the treatises for the purpose of deluding living beings, by providing them with refuge and protection from hell.
The creation of living beings is not possible without women;
yet the female species is by its very nature wretched and speaks with a tone of dejection;
the Creator has deprived them of the capacity for the study of the scriptures.
It is stated unequivocally and repeatedly in the scriptures that a daughter who is not devoid of virtuous conduct is equal to ten sons and yields great fruit. *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.157.
This speech, which fails to yield its fruit, brings extreme despondency to a man;
for a maiden is indeed wretched and pitiable, increasing her father's sorrow.
This applies even to one who may be fully endowed with a husband, sons, wealth, and so forth;
how much more so for one who is unfortunate and destitute of a husband, sons, wealth, and the like?
"And you have described the collection of defects in my daughter's body;
alas, O Nārada, I am bewildered, I am withering away, I am exhausted, and I am sinking."
O Sage, even if it be improper or unattainable at this time, please out of favor sever for me the suffering rooted in my daughter.
Even when an object is clearly defined and beyond doubt, the unwholesome craving that relies on the desire for its fruits— being deeply rooted and based on contempt for the mind— steals it away.
For women, the supreme birth for both families is said to be that which is characterized by attaining a virtuous husband, leading to happiness in this world and the next.

A good husband is difficult for women to find; indeed, even a husband devoid of virtues is hard to obtain without merit; a husband is never attained by a woman except through her own religious merits.
For from that [source] arises the Dharma that requires no means, delight free from all measure,
and wealth sufficient for life, which is established in the husband for a woman.
Whether he be poor, unfortunate, foolish, or devoid of all auspicious marks,
the husband is indeed always declared to be the supreme deity of a woman.
For you have said, O divine sage, that her husband has indeed not been born;
this is an incomparable, countless, heavy, and unbearable misfortune.
O Sage, because you say that even today, within this creation of moving and unmoving beings,
he has not yet been born, my mind is deeply perplexed.
It is said that the characteristics on the hands, feet, and other parts indicate the auspicious and inauspicious destinies of human and divine births through the specific marks established therein.
O bull among sages, this "upturned hand" of which you spoke is said to belong eternally only to those who beg. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.170)
"By you, the feet of this woman— who is the source of auspiciousness for the fortunate and who never fails those who seek her favor— were declared to be unerring, yet they have proven otherwise."
Even in that regard, O Sage, hope for the highest good does not appear to us;
for there are other bodily characteristics that indicate various distinct results.
"O bull among sages, you have described the blessings of good fortune, wealth, sons, long life, and the attainment of a husband; yet she is now bereft of all these."
"You know everything about me, and you are also a speaker of truth;
therefore, O tiger among sages, I am bewildered, and my heart seems to be breaking."
Having spoken thus, the Mountain ceased his reflection on his great sorrow;
and having heard all this from the lotus-like mouth of that king of mountains, Nārada, impelled by the gods, spoke these words with a smile: MatsP_154.175.
Nārada said:
"O great mountain, even when there is a cause for great joy, you manifest sorrow;
you fall into delusion because you have not fully grasped the meaning of my words."
O Great Mountain, listen with a concentrated mind to these words from me, which are established in the secret doctrine, as I explain them for your consideration.
"O Himācala, as for what I said— that the husband of this goddess has not been born—
that Great God, the source of the past, the future, and the present, the refuge, the eternal, the teacher, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, has not been born. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.178)
O Mountain, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the sages— all of whom are afflicted by birth, death, and old age—
are but playthings of that Supreme Lord.
By his will, Brahmā remains, the lord of the world who has come into being;
Viṣṇu, of great body and manifold births, is born age after age.
O upholder of the earth, you think that Viṣṇu is born through illusion age after age;
yet for yourself there is no destruction, even at the end of all stationary things.
For the embodied being who is born and dies within saṃsāra, it is only the body that perishes here; the destruction of the self is not spoken of.
This cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is proclaimed to extend from Brahmā down to the stationary beings,
revolves helplessly, afflicted by the suffering of birth and death.
Mahādeva— the immovable, the pillar-like, the unborn, the progenitor, the ageless—
He, the Lord of the World, free from all affliction, shall become her husband.
And as for what was said by me, "O Goddess, you are devoid of auspicious marks," listen now to a thorough investigation of those words as well.
For a divine mark (*daivika-aṅka*) is a characteristic residing in the limbs of the body, which reveals the extent of one's lifespan, wealth, and good fortune. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.186)
O Supporter of the Earth, no mark in the form of a physical characteristic is ever produced upon the body of this one who possesses infinite and immeasurable good fortune.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, there is no mark upon her body such as I have described, for she always has her palms turned upward.
This hand of the Goddess, ever turned upward as a bestower of boons,
shall grant boons to the hosts of gods, asuras, and sages.
Just as it was previously stated that her feet never deviate from their own shadow,
O best of mountains, hear now my reasoned argument regarding this matter as well.
Her two feet, resembling lotuses and radiant with clear nails,
were illuminated by the luster of the jewels in the crowns of the gods and demons bowing before her.
O Mountain, this wife of the Preceptor of the World, whose emblem is the bull, shines with various colors, her reflection mirrored in her own clear form.
The mother of the world’s dharma, the source of all beings,
this auspicious one, possessing the brilliance of fire, has appeared in your field solely for the sake of purification.
"O best of mountain lords, O Himavat, you must duly arrange it so that they may quickly enter into union with the wielder of the Pināka bow;
for this is an exceedingly great task for the gods."
Sūta said: Having heard all this from Nārada, the lord of mountains,
the husband of Menā, then considered himself as if born again.
Having paid homage to the wise god who bears the bull upon his banner,
Himācala, being greatly delighted, then spoke to Nārada.
Himavat said: "O Sage, I have been raised up by you from the terrible hell so difficult to cross;
having been lifted from Pātāla, I have been made the sovereign of the seven worlds."
"O best of sages, I am now renowned by you as Himācala;
through you, I have attained the lofty eminence of the name Himācala, endowed with the quality of immovability."
O Sage, my heart, which steals away the very day of bliss,
can no longer determine the deliberation of the distinctions between duties;
for even if I were the Lord of Speech, I would be unable to fully describe your virtues.
O Sage, the sight of those such as you is invariably fruitful;
yet, O Great Sage, my fickleness toward you is evident.

I am to be served by you alone for the sake of providing dwellings for the sages and deities who possess forms identical to your own; even though I am the self-acting creator, I am subject to defilement.
"Nevertheless, let my command be granted regarding this single matter," said the Lord of Mountains at that time, overflowing with joy.
And so, O Lord, Nārada spoke these words: "Everything has been accomplished;
whatever purpose was for the sake of the gods is indeed even greater for you as well."
Having spoken thus, Nārada quickly departed toward the third heaven;
having gone there to the abode of Śakra, he beheld the Lord of the Immortals.
Then, having sat upon that great throne in that beautiful place, the Sage,
being questioned by Śakra, related the story concerning the Himālayas.
Nārada said:
Whatever ought to be done after gathering [the materials] has indeed already been performed by me;
however, this very time for the five-arrowed one (Kāma) has now arrived.
Thus addressed by the sage who perceived what was to be done, the lordly King of the Gods,
Pākaśāsana, called to mind the mango-sprout weapon.
Then, being quickly summoned by the wise thousand-eyed one, the god whose banner bears the fish appeared, accompanied by Rati and full of amorous grace.
Seeing him manifest, Śakra addressed him with respect: *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.208.
Śakra said:
What is the use of much instruction? I shall speak what is pleasing to you: you are the one born of the mind (Manobhava); therefore, you know the thoughts within the hearts of all beings.
Therefore, O Mind-born One, do exactly what is right and pleasing to the inhabitants of heaven; quickly unite Śaṅkara with the Daughter of the Mountain,
along with Madhu, the invincible king of seasons.
Thus addressed by Śakra for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose,
the five-arrowed Madana, being afraid, then spoke these words to the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
Kāma said:
"O Lord of the World, do you not know that with this divine assembly, which strikes fear into sages and Dānavas, the god Śaṅkara is difficult to overcome? *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.212.
"You know the imperishable cause of that god;
for generally, both the favor and the anger of the great are all indeed great."
For these Sundarīs, born in heaven, are the very essence of all enjoyments;
and as for the pleasure you have relied upon, your efforts have been in vain.
If, however, one should fall away through negligence, let one reflect upon the Lord;
for even here, the accomplishment of the goals of living beings is seen to occur primarily through Him.
"O Śakra, for those who desire excellence, the fruit is a fall from their common state.
Having heard these words, Śakra, accompanied by the immortals, spoke to him.
Śakra said:
"O Ratikānta, we are indeed your authority in this matter; there is no doubt about it.
However, without a message, the power to cause harm is not permitted."
And the capacity of any one thing is observed in some specific place, but not everywhere.
Thus addressed, Kāma, accompanied by his friend Madhu and joined by Rati,
quickly went to the plateau of the snowy mountain.
There he reflected upon the means for accomplishing his task;
for the minds of those who possess great purpose and remain unshakable are exceedingly difficult to overcome.
Therefore, having first agitated [the mind], victory will certainly be easy to attain;
indeed, they shall achieve complete perfection only after first purifying the mind.
And how, through various states of being, can anger— without following after hatred—
through its most cruel attachment, [give rise to] its terrifying great companion, envy?
I shall employ against him that supreme corruption of the mind, which is exceedingly powerful and has destroyed the very foundation of his steadfastness through its restlessness.
Having closed the doors of fortitude and having cast aside contentment,
indeed, no one there— not even the most learned— would be able to recognize me.
If one remains in a state of mere conceptual construction, a deformity of the mind will arise;
thereafter, it becomes difficult to cross due to the deep whirlpools of the commencement of fundamental activities.
Providing myself with delightful means for practice, I shall obstruct the collection of his senses and destroy the asceticism of that firm-minded Hara.
Having thought thus, Madana went to the hermitage of the Lord of Beings,
which was the essence of the world and featured an altar made of *sarala* trees.
It was filled with peaceful beings and crowded with steady creatures;
it possessed a network of various flowering creepers, and its lord of hosts stood in the sky.
There he beheld a certain second [abode] of the Three-eyed One, situated on a delightful blue meadow-plateau inhabited by the bull Nīlagrīva.
Vīraka, the lord of the world's heroes, possessed a splendor like that of Īśāna;
his mass of matted hair was tawny, resembling a heap of saffron filaments from the yakṣa-tree.
Then [he saw him] with a cane in his hand, composed, adorned by fierce lords of serpents,
and with eyes resembling the petals of a lotus that were closed yet seemed open.
He gazes straight ahead with beautiful eyes fixed on the tip of his nose;
he wears a flowing upper garment made of the skin of a bull, a swift horse, or a lordly lion.
Tawny with the fire of the sighs released by the serpent Śravaṇa,
his mass of matted hair hung down to his knees, bordered by dangling skulls.
He has Kṛta and Vāsuki as his two side-pillars, with their heads placed at his navel;
he is adorned by serpents whose tails are bound together and held in the *brahmāñjali* gesture.
Kāma slowly beheld Śaṅkara, who had gradually approached his presence;
he was seated upon a mountain peak where the trees were swaying with the humming of bees.
Madana entered the mind of Bhava through the opening of his ear;
then Śaṅkara, having heard that sweet sound concerning Madana, [was moved].
With his heart filled with passion, he remembered his beloved daughter of Dakṣa;
then she, being exceedingly pure, gradually vanished from his sight.
The cultivation of meditative absorption remained there, taking the form of direct perception of the objective;
then, having attained identity with that, his inner disposition was veiled by obstacles.
Through his sovereign power, the Lord Dhūrjaṭi perceived the transformation consisting of passion;
though slightly overcome by anger, he maintained his composure.
Having cast aside his composure through the presence of Madana,
and being completely enveloped by that illusory power (yogamāyā), he then blazed up with passion.
Having a body of desire, difficult to comprehend, and the great abode of the fault of anger,
he then emerged from the heart, consisting of the addiction of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Taking his stand upon the outer ground, he whose banner is the fish presented himself,
followed by his beloved friend Madhu.
Seeing a beautiful cluster of blossoms on a mango tree shaken by a gentle breeze, Madana quickly [placed it] upon the chest of Hara.
