The one whose banner is the sea-monster discharged an arrow called Mohana,
a great shaft capable of destruction, into Śiva’s pure heart.
Then the harsh, tall, and deluding Flower-Arrowed One fell;
thus Bhava was pierced in the heart, causing a confusion of the senses.
Although he possessed a fortitude comparable to that of a mountain, he became intent upon passion;
yet, due to the power of his inner dispositions, he did not succumb to total possession by it.
Having encountered many external obstacles consisting of the production of impediments,
[he entered] that place which was terrifying with the fierce *huṃ* sounds arising from the fire of his wrath.
In the face of Rudra, whose form was fierce, there appeared a third eye, filled with fire and terrifying to the world at the time of its destruction.
While Madana stood near him, Dhūrjaṭi opened his eye,
and by the spark from that eye, the inhabitants of heaven cried out.
Kandarpa, who inflates the pride of lovers, was swiftly reduced to ashes;
and that fire, born from the eye of Hara, having reduced him to ashes, [remained].
Then Bhava, voracious with flames and the sound of "hum," yawned in order to consume the world;
for the sake of the world, he brought forth the fire.
In the mango tree, in the springtime, in the moon, in flowers, in others as well,
in bees, and in the mouths of cuckoos— [he perceived] the fire of love distributed among these.
By Hara, who had pierced both the external and the internal, the arrow of Smara—
blazing with the fire of intense passion within, fueled by attachment and affection— was driven away.
Causing agitation in the divided worlds, with its irresistible expansion,
it indeed reaches the hearts of the lustful, which are saturated with affection.
Beholding Smara reduced to ashes by the flame of Hara’s *huṃkāra*, that terrible one, whose nature is a mouth difficult to cure, blazes day and night.
Rati lamented piteously together with her kinsman Madhu;
then, after lamenting profusely, she was consoled by Madhu.
Taking with her a flowering mango blossom followed by bees, she went for refuge to the three-eyed god who bears the moon upon his crest.
Having bound a creeper— her female friend— the *parabhṛtā*, around her hand in place of the sacred thread,
Rati tied up her mass of matted hair with her curling locks.
Having smeared his body with the bright and heart-pleasing ashes of Smara,
he knelt upon the ground and addressed the one adorned by the moon.
Rati said:
"Homage be to Śiva, who is free from all affliction; homage be to Śiva, who consists of mind.
Homage be to you, Śiva, who are worshipped by the gods and who are ever intent on showing compassion to your devotees."
Homage be to you, the source of worldly existence; homage be to you who have destroyed the mind-born god of love.
Homage be to you whose great vows are hidden; homage be to you who take refuge in the thicket of illusion.
Homage be to Śarva, homage to Śiva; homage be to the Siddha, the ancient one.
Homage be to Kāla, homage to Kalā; homage be to you, the bestower of the boon of knowledge.
Homage be to you who transcend the divisions of time; homage to you whose natural ornament is purity!
Homage be to you, the crusher of immeasurable darkness; homage to the refuge, homage to the one beyond attributes!
Homage be to you, who are followed by formidable hosts; homage be to you, the creator of various worlds and the like;
homage be to the ordainer of diverse living beings; homage be to you, the dispenser of manifold fruits.
Salutations indeed to the one whose eyes are indestructible at the end of all things; salutations to the enjoyer of the portions of the various sacrifices;
salutations to the bestower of desired objects upon devotees; salutations always to you, the remover of attachment to worldly existence.
Salutations always to you of infinite forms; salutations to you whose anger is irresistible;
salutations always to you who bear the mark of the moon; salutations to the immeasurable one who is praised. *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.265.
Homage to the one who rides upon the king of bulls, the destroyer of the cities; homage to the renowned one, the great medicine.
Homage be to you who grants desired objects through devotion; homage be to you, the remover of all suffering.

We have taken refuge in you, O moon-crested one, the preceptor who excels in discerning the conduct of all that moves and is stationary, who envisioned the creation of living beings, the beloved and immeasurable Great Lord of the great.
"O Lord, grant me the fulfillment of my desire for fame; let Kāmadeva live again!
Among those who cherish life, who else in these worlds besides you is dearer than you?"
The Lord is the source of all that is dear to His beloved, the one who has realized the ultimate and relative meanings of all things;
thus, You alone are the sole Protector of the world, compassionate and the eradicator of the fear of Your devotees.
Sūta said:
Thus praised by the beloved of Manmatha, the adorable Lord Śaṅkara, the Bull-bannered One who bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, was pleased;
and looking at her, he spoke these sweet words.
Śaṃkara said: "This desire shall indeed come to pass; in a short time, he will become beloved even by Kālī.
He shall attain fame throughout the worlds as 'Anaṅga' (the Bodiless One)."
Having been addressed thus, Rati, the beloved of Kāma, bowed her head to Giriśa and departed for the lovely grove of the Lord of Snow.
And she wept many times, distressed, upon that lovely spot;
yet, by the command of Hara, she desisted from her resolve to die.
Then, urged by the words of Nārada, the Mountain of Snow [Himavat] [prepared his daughter],
who had been adorned with ornaments and consecrated with auspicious marriage rites.
Then the Mountain, having taken his daughter— who wore a head-ornament made of celestial flowers, was clothed in garments of white Chinese silk, and was equipped with two arrows— [departed].
Then, with his heart’s desire fulfilled, he proceeded by an auspicious path,
approaching forests, groves, and pleasure gardens together with their surrounding woods.
On the delightful mountain ridges of the forest, he beheld a weeping woman of inconceivable and great majesty, whose beauty was peerless in the world.
Having touched her out of curiosity and seeing her weeping,
the Mountain approached her and questioned her from nearby.
Himavat said:
"Who are you, whose are you, O auspicious one, and for what reason do you weep?
O beauty of the world, I do not consider this cause to be a trivial one."
Having heard his words, she spoke with Madhu,
weeping piteously and sighing in a manner that produced sorrow and increased her wretchedness.
Rati said: "O you of noble vows, know me to be Rati, the beloved wife of Kāma.
O highly fortunate one, on this mountain, Giriśa is established in ascetic penance. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.281)
Enraged by that interruption, he widened his eyes and looked out;
"That fish-bannered one has been burnt—he who was my beloved, my most cherished. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.282)
Overwhelmed by fear, I then sought refuge in that god and praised him with hymns; having been thus extolled, Giriśa then spoke to me.
"I am pleased, O beloved of Kāma; this desire shall be yours.
Furthermore, a man who, taking refuge in me, recites your hymn of praise with devotion, shall obtain his desired wish, having turned back death and other such calamities."
And awaiting his word, O one of great luster, I shall preserve my body for some time through the force of hope and other such means. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.285)
Thus addressed by Rati at that time, the mountain, terrified with agitation,
took his daughter by the hand and desired to go to his own city.
Because that which is destined must necessarily come to pass, Bhavitrī— the one who brings about what was and will be—
shamefully spoke to her father, the Mountain, through the mouths of her friends.
The daughter of the mountain said:
"What use have I for this unfortunate body?
How may I obtain such happiness—that he may become my husband? (Matsya Purāṇa 154.288)
Through austerities, one's desired goal is attained; for indeed, nothing is unattainable for one who practices penance.
It is in vain that people endure misfortune when the means to remedy it exist.
"For one who does not practice austerity, death is indeed better than a miserable life;
I shall become so, there is no doubt—I will wither my body through religious observances."
My doubts having been dispelled by asceticism, I shall now exert myself with the desire to attain my goal;
I will perform such penance that I shall become difficult for anyone else to obtain.
Thus addressed by his daughter, the king of mountains, overwhelmed with affection,
spoke these words, O lord of mountains, in a voice faltering with love.
Himavat said:
"O Umā, O fickle one, O daughter of lovely appearance, your body is not capable of enduring asceticism,
which is by its very nature full of hardship."
Indeed, future objects of experience are always to be investigated;
for destined events inevitably come to pass, even by force, whether one desires them or not.
Therefore, O girl, there is no purpose for you in asceticism;
let us go back to our home, and there indeed I shall reflect upon it.
When the daughter of the mountain, having been addressed thus, did not enter the cave at all,
he was overcome with anxiety and praised his daughter.
Then, from the sky, a divine voice arose upon the surface of the earth:
"O fickle daughter, you have called her 'Umā'; therefore, she shall henceforth be known as Tanayā."
Because of this, her name shall be "Umā" throughout the worlds;
and she shall accomplish every desired perfection in embodied form.
Having heard these words from the sky, the mountain, white as a kāśa flower,
took leave of his daughter and quickly departed for his own abode.
Sūta said:
The daughter of the mountain king also went to the mountain, though it was inaccessible even to the gods,
followed by her two companions and remaining self-restrained.
The sacred peak of the Himavat, adorned with various minerals,
strewn with divine flowers and creepers, and frequented by siddhas and gandharvas.
It was filled with various herds of wild animals, its trees resounded with the humming of bees,
it was endowed with divine springs, and adorned with long ponds.
It was crowded with flocks of various birds and graced by ruddy geese;
it was further adorned with blossoming flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial.
It has the appearance of a variegated cave, a charming dwelling within a cavern,
frequented by flocks of birds, and densely filled with wish-fulfilling trees.
There he saw a tree with great branches and green foliage,
endowed with flowers of every season and radiant with hundreds of desires.
It was strewn with various flowers and endowed with many kinds of fruits;
its leaves were bent by the rays of the sun and alternately opened and closed.
There, having cast off her garments and ornaments, the daughter of the mountain was clothed in divine bark garments and wore a girdle fashioned from *darbha* grass.
For a hundred autumns she bathed three times a day and subsisted on *pāṭala* flowers; then, for another hundred years, she sustained herself with a single withered leaf.
That treasure-house of asceticism remained without food for a hundred years;
then all living beings were distressed by the fire of her austerity.
Then the Blessed One, Śatakratu, remembered the seven sages;
those sages, having all assembled together, arrived there.
Honored by Mahendra, they asked him about his purpose:
"O best of gods, for what reason have we been remembered by you?"
Śakra said: "May the Blessed Ones hear the purpose:
the daughter of the Mountain King is performing severe penance on the Himālaya;
you ought to fulfill her desired wish."
Then, saying "So be it," they rushed toward the lord of mountains, which is frequented by hosts of Siddhas, driven by haste for the sake of the world and the Goddess.
Then the sages, having approached her, spoke these sweet words:
"O daughter, O lotus-eyed one, what desire have you resolved upon?"
Then the goddess, feeling bashful out of respect for those sages who were performing austerities and observing a vow of silence, spoke to them, O highly fortunate ones: *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.315.
The intellect applied to salutation purifies that which is free from conceptual construction;
because you are intent on inquiry, it is fitting for you to take your seat at the outset.
"Once you have sat down and are freed from fatigue, you shall then question me. Having said this, she then prepared seats for them to occupy.
Having duly honored those venerable ones according to the prescribed rites,
that virtuous woman spoke slowly to the seven sages, who were as radiant as the sun.
Abandoning the silence consisting of his vows, he adopted a silence born of modesty; for her feelings reached their climax at the end of his silence, just as those of the Seven Sages did toward her.
Overcome by a sense of reverence, they questioned her once again;
she too, possessing a beautiful smile, with a mind full of respect, [replied].
Seeing the sages, whose speech was hushed in tranquility and who were observing a vow of silence, he spoke:
"The Blessed Ones understand the mental welfare of living beings."
For embodied beings are excessively tormented by the movements of their own minds;
yet some who are skillful apply themselves there with the efforts of the wise.
For those who are untiring, they attain through skillful means even those states that are difficult to reach;
whereas others, being limited, employ various different methods.
People undertake beneficial undertakings for the sake of another body;
but for me, it is adorned with a garland of flowers born from the sky.
Desirous of obtaining the son of a barren woman, her mind wanders repeatedly:
"I am indeed prepared to obtain the divine Bhava as my husband. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.325)
By his very nature, he is invincible; now engaged in ascetic penance, he is unassailable by gods or asuras, and he is the refuge for the performance of the highest goal.
And now, how could one such as I propitiate that Lord Śiva, who has burnt away passion and is free from desire? *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.327.
Having been addressed thus, those sages, in order to ascertain the stability of her mind, spoke these words relevant to the matter at hand in accordance with the context.
The sages said:
"O daughter, two kinds of happiness are indeed experienced in the worlds:
that which arises from the enjoyments of this body, and the tranquility of the mind."
By nature he is clothed in the directions (naked), formidable, dwelling in the cremation ground;
he carries a skull-bowl, is a mendicant, naked, three-eyed, and firm in his actions.
Appearing like one intoxicated or insane, having embraced loathsome deeds—
what purpose do you seek from that ascetic, who is an embodied misfortune?
If you indeed desire enjoyment for this body at present,
then how can you [be so] terrified of Mahādeva, who is [to you] loathsome?
From him who is adorned with skulls smeared with trickling blood and fat, and who is terrifying with ornaments made from hissing, fierce lordly serpents; MatsP_154.333.
O virtuous one, the slayer of enemies has his feet rubbed by the multitude of crowns of the lords of gods, even as he dwells in cremation grounds followed by fierce Pramathas.
Hari is the sustainer of the world, the beloved of Śrī, possessing infinite forms;
likewise, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, is the lord of those who enjoy the sacrificial offerings.
Fire is the treasure of the deities, the fulfiller of all desires;
and Vāyu is the sustainer of the world, who is the vital breath of all embodied beings.
Likewise, King Vaiśravaṇa is all-pervading and possesses the intelligence to achieve every goal;
why do you not wish to attain even one of these?
Furthermore, by attaining another body, the happiness desired by your mind will be yours;
for in this very way, you too shall have mastery over the splendors of heaven,
and in this world alone, all your supreme attainments of auspiciousness shall be realized.
All that which is not found among the gods belongs only to your father;
therefore, the hardship you endure here to attain it is likewise fruitless for you.
O blessed lady, that which is generally sought after is indeed very small and exceedingly difficult to obtain;
for here, the Ordainer (dhātṛ) is truly the maker of this conjunction of fate for you.
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, the daughter of the mountain, enraged at the best of sages, spoke with her eyes red with anger and her lips quivering. *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.341.
The Goddess said:
What joy is there in a false attachment, and where is the restraint for one's own ruin?
By what means can those who perceive things perversely be joined to the path of the virtuous?
Thus you know me to be of poor intellect, for I am fond of grasping at what is unreal and misplaced;
I have no power of discernment regarding that wherein false attachment arises.
"You are all equal to Prajāpati and possessors of all-seeing wisdom;
surely you do not know that eternal God, the Lord of the world."
The unborn Lord, unmanifest, whose arising is immeasurable in its majesty.
Let alone that wonderful awakening to the true nature of Dharma,
which indeed the lords of the gods, headed by Hari and Brahmā, do not know.
Do you not also know that which, arising from his own power, manifested throughout the worlds and became manifest to all beings? MatsP_154.347 //
To whom does this vast sky belong? To whom belongs fire, and to whom the wind?
To whom belongs the earth, and to whom Varuṇa? Who is he whose eyes are the moon and the sun?
Whose liṅga do the gods and asuras in the worlds worship with devotion—
He whom the gods, the great sages, and those beginning with Brahmā and Indra call the Lord?
Do you not even know their power and their origin?
Whose mother is this Aditi, and from whom was Janārdana born?
The gods, beginning with Nārāyaṇa, were born from Aditi and Kaśyapa;
for Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, and Aditi was the daughter of Dakṣa.
Marīci and Dakṣa were indeed the two sons of Brahmā;
Brahmā [emerged] from the golden egg, possessing divine perfection and majesty. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.352)
From whose meditation did the agitated portions of primordial nature (prakṛti) emerge?
And within the third primordial nature, the act of generating the Slayer of Madhu took place.
Once born, he emitted the six groups [of sons] produced by his own actions and preceded by intelligence;
then the Creator, whose birth is unmanifest, became unborn once again.
He who, by means of his own yoga, having agitated primordial nature (prakṛti),
brought about this sovereignty of Brahmā— which accomplishes all aims and constitutes the state of being the creator of the worlds.
Viṣṇu and the others always know this by their own majesty;
indeed, having assumed another body and another appearance, Hari again makes it just as it was before.
Just as it performs the tasks of the world— whether superior, inferior, or middling—
so too does this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which consists of birth and death.
For this fruit of action arises in manifold forms;
then the god Nārāyaṇa took refuge in his own shadow.
Impelled by that [ignorance], one undergoes birth in various forms;
that impulsion, too, is said to arise solely from the karma of those whose selves are powerless.
For just as the mind of one possessed by madness and the like becomes such that he perceives even desired objects as being contrary to reality.
In the worldly transactions that have been created,
Viṣṇu alone is ordained as the one who always presides over the attainment of the fruits of both dharma and adharma.
Now, although this [universe] has no beginning, it exists through its identity with the universal;
for its life is never seen to be long within any body whatsoever.
"Or perhaps you have not seen the inner core of this;
for embodied beings, this is simply the nature of things: that one is born in one place and dies in another."
In one case, he may perish while still in the womb; in another, he may live afflicted by old age;
in some cases he may live for a hundred years, while in others he meets his end in childhood.
A man who lives for a hundred years is infinite compared to one of very short life;
since he does not die before his time has come, he is called immortal.
For Viṣṇu and the others are considered to be such that their birth and death are unseen;
who in this world could obtain such pure sovereignty within saṃsāra?
In that [state], which possesses the nature of various wonders due to its connection with destruction and so forth,
all those who move by day are therefore defiled and possessed of meager prosperity.
"O auspicious ones, I do not desire anything except from Śarva, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
for this supreme state among living beings is established according to gradation. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.368)
The greatness of the great is measured by their wisdom, power, sovereignty, deeds, and so forth;
for there is nothing else besides them, and from whom everything proceeds.
I have gone for refuge to Him whose sovereignty is without beginning or end;
yet this resolve of mine has been long-standing and profoundly mistaken.
"Either go or stay, O sages who act on my behalf. Having heard these words of the goddess at that time, the best of sages [replied].
With eyes overflowing with tears of joy, they embraced that ascetic woman;

and being exceedingly delighted, they spoke these sweet words to the daughter of the mountain: matsyapurāṇe caturdaśottaraśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ // MatsP_154.372 // (The 114th chapter of the Matsya Purāṇa)
The sages said:
"O daughter, you are truly most wonderful! Pure as if the very embodiment of knowledge, you gladden our hearts by providing refuge from the nature of worldly existence."
"Indeed, we know the wonderful sovereignty of that god;
we have come here to test the firmness of your resolve."
"O slender-limbed one, this desire of yours shall be fulfilled before long;
for where can the radiance of the sun go apart from its gems? (Matsya Purāṇa 154.375)
What is the purpose of these indistinct syllables? O Girīśa, how can we go to him without you to entreat him with many approaches?
That very purpose indeed dwells even more deeply in our hearts;
therefore, you alone are that wisdom, for you alone are indeed statesmanship.
"Therefore, Śaṅkara will undoubtedly restore the body.
Having spoken thus, the sages, honored by the Daughter of the Mountain, departed.
They set out to see Giriśa on the great plateau of the Himavat,
his body bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā and his tawny matted locks tied up like a mane.
Having reached a plateau of the mountain, they beheld the hermitage of Śaṅkara, where a garland of mandāra flowers rested in his hand, followed by bees.
The entire flood of living beings was completely stilled, the forest became motionless as if new,
and in every direction the waterfalls were silent and undisturbed.
There, at the gate, they saw Vīraka with a cane in his hand;
those seven sages, humble due to the gravity of their mission, paid him homage.
Those best among eloquent speakers spoke with sweet voices:
"We have come here to behold the Lord of the Gaṇas, who is the refuge of all."
Know him as Trilocana; impelled by the task of the gods, you alone are our refuge, so that there may be no transgression of the appointed time.
"This is merely a request; generally, the master consists of his gatekeepers," he was told by the sages, and then, out of respect, he spoke to them.
O Brahmins, at the time of the evening twilight following the sacrifice, you shall bathe in the waters of the Mandākinī;
in an instant, you will behold the wielder of the trident there.
Thus addressed, the sages remained waiting for that time,
like thirsty cātaka birds awaiting a deep rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
Then, in an instant, having completed the ritual of meditative concentration,
the Lord assumed the heroic posture (vīrāsana) and was clothed in a deer skin.
Then Vinīta, supporting himself on his knees upon the ground,
spoke to the god Vīraka, taking refuge solely in prostration.

"O Lord, seven sages of blazing splendor have arrived to see you; you ought to grant them an audience and allow them to understand [the truth] here. They replied, "We are eager for a vision of you on account of a task for the gods."
Thus addressed by that high-souled Vīraka, Dhūrjaṭi then gave the command for their entrance with a sign of his knitted brows.
By a movement of his head, Vīraka also summoned all those great sages,
who were standing nearby, to behold the wielder of the Pināka bow.
With their topknots half-bound in haste and wearing hanging deerskins as garments,
those perfected ones (siddhas) entered the altar-platform adorned with the ashes of Śiva.
Then, with handfuls of celestial flowers cast from their cupped palms,
they paid homage to the pair of feet of the wielder of the Pināka bow, which are worthy of worship by the inhabitants of heaven.
Then, gazed upon affectionately by the wielder of the trident, the peaceful sages,
being joyful and full of respect, together praised the enemy of Manmatha.
The sages said:
"Aha! We have now truly achieved our purpose; even the Lord of the Gods shall become our bridegroom here.
By the sprinkling of the pure water of your grace, some fruit of our asceticism is being brought to fruition."
Victorious is that most blessed Himācala, whose sheltering daughter performs penance;
and even that king of the Daityas, Tāraka, who has indeed uprooted all the gods, is destined for a great fruition.
Indeed, he who beholds your portion shall be liberated from his own body through its defilement;
for he is the blessed-minded one, the four-faced Brahmā, the father of the worlds, and Hari himself, who is inflamed by the fire of his agitation.

Those who bear your pair of feet within their hearts as the sole cause for quelling great affliction are nevertheless addressed by the distressed with words such as, "You alone are indeed the one who performs various fabricated deeds. *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.399.
Now today you have spoken thus, and not otherwise; otherwise, the world would perceive you as being devoid of compassion.
Or perhaps you do not understand this suffering inherent in all living beings; indeed, your activity is being obstructed on every side.

If you disregard the calamities of the world, by what means can your compassionate nature be described? For one who dwells in the cave of the majesty of his own yogic power, there exists no weight of pure worldly prosperity.
And we are more blessed among embodied beings than others, since we behold you in such a manner;
for by that sight, the longing within our minds attains fulfillment, just as a wish reaches its end upon being seen.
"Since you will act as the sole ordainer of the world's creation at the very beginning of the universe, we shall therefore wander as mendicants.
Having uttered these words in the presence of the earth where the Lord of Mountains was listening, the sages bowed down.
Just as farmers sow a handful of good seed in an excellent field upon the surface of the earth for the sake of a bountiful harvest.
Having heard their delightful speech concerning the sequence of their preliminary efforts,
Vācaspati, being pleased, spoke these words beautiful with a smile.
Śarva said:
"I know that this daughter of the Mountain of Snow, born for the sake of the highest duty toward the world's creation, has been designated as the place of our meeting."
"It is true that all of you are longing and striving for the sake of the gods' mission;
their minds are in haste, yet what is the task you intend to speak of?"
The course of worldly affairs must be followed especially by the wise;
for they practice dharma because others abide by its authority.
Having been addressed thus, the sages departed quickly for the Himālaya.
There, they were respectfully honored by that Lord of Snow Mountains;
the excellent sages, being pleased, spoke with brief words in great haste.
The sages said:
"The Lord Pinākin himself seeks your daughter;
therefore, quickly purify yourself by offering her to him, as one offers an oblation into the fire."
And this task of the gods has persisted for a very long time;
let this effort indeed be made for the sake of uplifting the world.
Thus addressed by them, the mountain, overcome with joy, spoke to the sages;
yet he became unable to speak further, seeking refuge in Śiva.
Then Menā, seeing the sages, spoke, overwhelmed with affection;
she, who understood her purpose, sought refuge at the feet of both her daughter and those sages.
Manu said: "That very purpose for which they do not desire the birth of a daughter, even though it yields great fruit—
that has now arrived in its entirety through the natural course of events."
Even if he is endowed with noble birth, age, beauty, prosperity, and supernatural power,
a daughter should indeed be given to such a suitor after inviting him, even if he does not ask for her.
"How will my daughter endure all that terrible asceticism?
Whatever must be done here at the command of my daughter's words, let that be performed."
Thus addressed by the beloved of the Lord of Snows, those sages spoke again words of noble meaning that gladden the hearts of women.
The sages said:
"Understand the sovereignty of Śaṅkara, whose pair of lotus feet are being worshipped by the gods and asuras who have attained perfect peace."
Whatever form is useful to someone, and for the sake of attaining that,
a young woman performs severe penance for a long time— for her, liberation is found in that very form.
She who shall lead those divine vows to their completion will remain there with full attention;
therefore, she alone shall become [the queen].
Having spoken thus, they went together with the mountain to where the daughter of the mountain resided—
Umā, who was composed of the splendor of her asceticism and had surpassed the blazing flames of the sun and fire.
O sages, having affectionately honored me who has come upon your path—
my form which is beautiful, dear, and captivating— do not consume it with your ascetic heat.
"Tomorrow, O daughter, this Śaṅkara will take your hand;
we have come here first to request him from your father. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.423)
"Go home with your father; we shall go to our own abode."
Having been told this, she reflected that the fruit of asceticism truly exists,
and in great haste, she went to her father’s palace, which was adorned with divine objects.
There, the daughter of the Himālaya, filled with great longing born from the sight of Hara, considered that night to be equal to ten thousand years.
Then, during the Brahma-muhūrta, the celestial women performed for her a multitude of various auspicious rites according to the proper sequence and order.
In that temple of manifold auspiciousness, where the limbs [of the deity] were adorned with divine ornaments,
the personified Seasons, granting all desires, waited upon the Mountain.
The winds and the rain-givers attended to the task of sweeping the mountain;
and in the palaces, the goddess Śrī herself appeared, having adorned herself with various ornaments.
Beauty was present in all things, and prosperity became abundant;
the wish-fulfilling gem and other such jewels were found everywhere on the mountain.
The mountains also appeared, as did the great wish-fulfilling trees of the Kalpa age;
and the medicinal herbs, endowed with divine medicines, stood there in embodied form.
The juices and the mineral ores were all servants of that mountain;
they were the servants of that mountain, busily following its commands.
All the rivers, the oceans, and whatever is stationary or moving—
all that increased the majesty of the Snowy Mountain.
Sages, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras,
as well as the gods of Śaṅkara, were present on Mount Gandhamādana.
All the articles of adornment stood there with spotless forms;
even upon the matted locks of Śarva, the Grandfather [Brahmā] placed a fragment of the moon.
With eyes wide open in noble affection, he bound [it];
Cāmuṇḍā bound a massive garland of skulls upon his head.
And he spoke these words to his son: "O Śaṅkara, procreate one who, having destroyed the lineage of the lords of the Daityas, shall satiate me with their blood. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.437)
Taking up his crown of blazing crest-jewels and his fierce fire-weapon,
as well as his serpent ornaments, Sauri stood ready before Śambhu.
Śakra eagerly took up his elephant hide, its tips smeared with fat;
his broad lotus-face was covered in perspiration.
And Vāyu adorned the bull of great splendor, which was his vehicle, possessing vast and sharp horns and the luster of the snowy mountains.
The Sun, Fire, and Moon, residing within the corners of Śambhu’s eyes,
displayed their own radiance for the Lord of the World, the witness of the deeds of the universe.
Having placed funeral ashes, shining like silver,
upon his skull, he fastened a garland made of human bones with his hand.
The lord of the pretas stood at the eastern gate with a mace in hand,
adorned with various forms of great jewels bestowed by the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
Leaving aside his own hand, which was like the coil of the great serpent king,
the Lord himself made Vāsuki and Takṣaka his ear-ornaments.
Then those lords of the Gaṇas, having separately brought the one who was carried away by the lord of the waters and surrounded by stationary flowers, approached Vīraka there with humility.
O Procūri, with a focused mind, announce to the trident-bearer that the god has completed his ornaments; having adorned the Lord with these finery, inform him.
The seven oceans stood there to create the illusion of mirrors;
then he beheld his own self within the depths of the waters of the great ocean.
Embracing the earth with his knees, Keśava said to Sthāṇu:
"O Lord, you shine with a form that bestows joy upon the world."
The Mothers incited Kāma’s bride, who was marked by widowhood,
perceiving that "this is the time" through various gestures and signs.
Then, thus urged, they spoke to the god with smiling faces:
"Rati, having arrived before you, does not shine, being bereft of Madana."
Then, having calmed her with a gesture from the tip of his left hand,
he set out, his mind eager to behold the face of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Then Hara, with his eyes fixed upon the tumultuous host of his attendants, urged on the great white bull— whose form resembled a cave in the snowy mountain— with gentle strokes of the goad,
shaking the mountains like a thunderbolt.

Then Hari, his footprints swift as he moved forward, spoke to the attendants ahead who were taking refuge among the clusters of trees: "Move aside; do not make the path narrow for him, whose ornaments are dusted with the pollen of the earth."
Reinforcing his master’s primary command, Vīraka, though with a frowning face, spoke:
"O sky-travelers, what enemy is there in the sky? Depart from us, staying not far from the mountain."
"O great oceans, turn your waters into something like stone, for the arrival of the enemies of the gods will create a vast mire.
O lords of the Gaṇas, do not move out of fickleness; you are being watched by the lords of the gods, who possess steady minds."
Bhṛṅgin does not carry his own body before the broad-faced Maṇḍa of the wielder of the Pināka;
in vain, O Yama, do you bear your weapon with its hollowed-out fangs displayed, casting aside all fear.
The ground, crowded with many mothers, was not easily traversed by the chariots and horses of the Enemy of the Cities;
these gods, the beloved attendants of Hara, followed on foot, surrounded by their respective followers along double paths.
"O gods, why do you, traveling on your own vehicles with chowries fanned by the wind, banners fluttering,
and appearing graceful as you go, contemplate your own passionate and exalted state in accordance with the three fixed rhythms?"
Indeed, the sound arising from the multitude of ornaments cannot be surpassed even by the Kinnaras;
for why should those born of no birth not produce the Ṣaḍja and Madhyama notes? Here, many sounds that are neither broad nor thin shall be described.
Having reached a state of being bowed down, bent, stretched, and tossed about, and having attained a distinctness created by their own conventions,
these Gaudas— full of suspicion and habituated to extreme divisiveness— depart with rapid steps indeed.

Why do the *ṣāḍgava* and other musical instruments not play before the Lord with their own songs produced from the application of graceful words? For that which has arisen as a complete meaning is understood to remain unimpaired in his presence.

These various classes of serpents employ the *prakīrṇaka* dance, which spreads the fame of Śiva, featuring separately arranged beautiful rhythmic movements (*rāsaka*) and possessing a nature full of manifold gestures (*gamaka*).
How is it that these various musical instruments, mingled with the sounds of many women, resound in every direction at every moment?
Why are they not born from drums and pipes, and why are they not merely resonant, yet possess the nature of melodic modulations (*mūrchanā*)?
"Why was the drum not sounded by Tumburu, which is the means for achieving the various distinctions of melody, rhythm, and tempo?
Why is this grand display of many kinds of musical instruments—not to mention the scattered lutes, drums, and so forth—not being struck?
Thus spoke the gods and asuras, who were attentive, at which point they immediately [acted] by the command of Vīraka.
Restrained by their vows, they set forth exceedingly joyful, filling the entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Thus, as the great ocean roared with a thundering sound and the clouds thundered while the mountain caves were rent asunder,
the mountain— agitated by the Pināka-wielder moving with swift strides— became like a tumultuous world in upheaval.
In some places it had gateways of blazing gold thousands of spans high; in some places its courtyards and altars were made of emeralds joined together;
in various spots there were altars of pure lapis lazuli, and in others, lovely waterfalls with falling streams.
Adorned with thousands of excellent fluttering banners, its courtyards strewn with clusters of blossoms from the celestial trees;
variegated with the colors of white, black, and crimson minerals, it was radiant with splendor, featuring wide, extended pathways and gate-towers.

Hara, praised by the most excellent gods and asuras, reached the great mountain city— which was enchanting with fragrant city-breezes and possessed clouds of incomparable thundering sounds— as if in a mere moment. Upon seeing him entering, the city of the Lord of Mountains fell into a state of agitation.
The city was filled with agitated women crying out for victory, and its streets were crowded with people running along the roads.
A certain woman was clearly seen, veiled by the canopy of light from her own ornaments, like a garland of blue lotuses formed by the eyes of celestial women gazing from the windows of the palace.
One woman, her ornaments and decorations left unfinished, abandoned the affection of her friends and gazed at Hara;
another, her pride gone, spoke in a sweet voice: "O friend, do not be despondent, you fool! *Matsya Purāṇa* 154.472.
Only the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose own mind-born passion has been consumed, desires to sport by himself;
thus did a certain woman, herself falling [into his arms], speak to another whose limbs were failing due to the pangs of separation.
"O fickle one, do not speak of your transgression against Śaṅkara through your infatuation with me;
for this Lord of the Mountain spoke thus by way of reasoning, having seen no one else intervening. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.474)

This is he, at whom the lords of the sky-dwellers, beginning with those who have performed a thousand sacrifices, bow down with their own names uttered for the sake of the fruit obtained through their service to him whose matted locks contain the moon; let them strive [to worship him].
This is not he; this is indeed he who, with his body covered in skin and the moon upon his crest, runs ahead as the wielder of the thunderbolt, the king of the immortals, to clear this path.

This is that very Padmabhava; having approached, concealed by his tall matted hair and deer-skin, he pressed his face against [his son's] hand with affection and spoke a few measured words at the root of the ear.
Thus, due to their deep passion, the minds of the hosts of celestial women became agitated;
yet they said, "This is indeed the supreme fruit of the birth of Girijā, resulting from her taking refuge in Śaṅkara."
Then [he entered] the palace of Himavat, which had been designed by Viśvakarman,
featuring pillars made of sapphire and a floor of shining gold.
Adorned with networks of pearls, illuminated by blazing medicinal herbs,
rich with thousands of pleasure gardens, and possessing long ponds filled with golden lotuses.
Having seen that wonder, all the gods, headed by Mahendra, thought:
"Today our eyes have become fruitful, as have our minds. Thus they reflected.
Their armlets crushed by the friction, the inhabitants of heaven were blocked at the gate by lions;
with great difficulty, they entered there at the head of the procession.
Then the four-faced one, honored by the king of mountains who had bowed down,
performed everything according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the ritual formulas and mantras.
The taking of Śarva’s hand in marriage was witnessed by the fire and remained inviolate;
the giver was the lord of the mountains, and the officiating priest was the four-faced god.
Paśupati himself was the bridegroom, and Viśvāraṇī was the bride;
so too were all beings, both moving and unmoving, as well as the foremost among the gods and asuras.
There too, these [beings], whose forms were indeed agitated, necessarily came into being;
he released all the newly arisen grains of rice and flavorful medicinal herbs.
But the goddess Earth, who is delightful in all her states, was distressed;
meanwhile, Varuṇa took all the jewels and ornaments.
Meritorious and purifying, consisting of various jewels,
the god stood there adorned with ornaments, bestowing joy upon all embodied beings.
And Dhanada, being self-restrained, presented divine golden ornaments and various objects fashioned from refined gold.
A pervasive wind blew, fragrant and pleasant to the touch;
and Śatakratu held a brilliant white umbrella that shone like moonbeams.
Wearing garlands and adorned with many ornaments, he joyfully grasped [the child] with his arms;
the chief Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Playing their instruments, the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang most sweetly;
and the personified Seasons there indeed sang and danced.
And the fickle hosts stood there, shaking the Himalaya mountain;
and then Viśvabhuj, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, gradually rose up.
He performed the marriage rites with his wife as was appropriate;
having been presented with the guest-offering by the King of Mountains, he was entertained by the hosts of gods.
The Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) spent that night there together with his wife,
[entertained] by the singing of Gandharvas and even the dancing of Apsarases.
Awakened by the praises of the gods and the Daityas,
the Lord of the Gods took leave of the King of the Snowy Mountains at dawn, and together with Umā,
he went to Mount Mandara on the horned bull that moved with the speed of the wind.
Then, when the Lord Nīlalohita had departed with Umā, the Mountain did not find pleasure;
for whose mind, indeed, does it not become agitated in this world when it concerns the father of a daughter, along with his kinsmen?

Then Hara, having dismissed the host of immortals, entered his own city on the mountain— a city with crystal gate-towers of brilliant luster, magnificent with blazing jewels, crystals, and gold— which had been prepared there for a long time.
Accompanied by Umā, the Lord, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes,
sported in the delightful city gardens and in secluded forests.
With his heart deeply enamored of the goddess, preceded by the dolphin-bannered god,
the daughter of the mountain then, after a long period of time, desired a son.
Accompanied by her friends, she played with artificial dolls;
on one occasion, Śailajā anointed her body with scented oil.
He rubbed her body, which was covered with filth, with powders;
taking that powder for rubbing, he turned the man into an elephant-faced one.
The goddess was playing with her little son and cast him into the waters of the Jāhnavī, the friend of Śivā; thereupon, he became possessed of a massive body.
Then, with his exceedingly vast body, he filled the world;
the goddess said, "O son! and Jāhnavī also cried out, "O son!"
The elephant-faced one was honored by the gods as "Gāṅgeya," and the Grandfather (Brahmā) granted him the lordship over the Vināyakas.
Furthermore, for the sake of a son, that woman of excellent complexion and auspicious countenance played with a charming,
sprouted shoot of an aśoka tree.
And she, having performed the auspicious rites of purification,
caused him to be nourished by Brahmins led by Bṛhaspati, who were preceded by the Lord of Heaven.
Then the gods and the sages spoke these words to the Goddess:
"O Bhavānī, you have become auspicious, having been born for the welfare of the world."
Generally, people obtain the fruit of their existence through sons and grandsons;
yet, offspring are often seen to be childless due to the power of destiny.
"Now that the path has been shown, you ought to establish its boundaries.
O Goddess, what fruit will come from these fashioned tree-sons?
Thus addressed, Umā, her limbs filled with joy, spoke these auspicious words.
Likewise, the wise man who causes a well to be constructed in a waterless region shall dwell in heaven for as many years as there are drops of water in that well.
A large oblong pond is equal to ten wells; a square lake is equal to ten such ponds;
a son is equal to ten lakes; and a tree is equal to ten sons.
This is my established rule, which brings prosperity to the world.
Having been addressed thus, the brahmins, led by Bṛhaspati,
paid their respects to Bhavānī with reverence and returned to their own abodes.
When they had departed, Lord Śaṅkara also took the auspicious daughter of the Mountain by his left hand and slowly led her inside.
It generates clarity of mind; it is a palace with gate-towers, adorned with hanging strings of pearls, and its altars are crowded with garlands.
It was like a pleasure-cave made of polished gold,
enchanting, filled with the fragrance of scattered flowers and the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees.
Its walls were concealed by the music of the songs sung by kinnaras;
it was filled with masses of fragrant incense, desirable to the mind, yet remained unobserved.
It was surrounded by women sporting with peacocks and by stringed instruments,
resounded by flocks of swans, and featured altars supported by crystal pillars.
There, amidst the many kinnaras, the waters are clear and undisturbed;
there, parrots strike at objects fashioned from ruby.
The walls, with pearls reflected upon them, were mistaken for pomegranate seeds;
there the Goddess began to sport at a game of dice.
Established there in play upon a region of pure sapphire ground,
they attained companionship with their own bodies, finding fulfillment in the essence of sport.
While Devī and Śaṅkara were thus sporting there at that time,
a great sound arose, pervading the interior of their dwelling.
Having heard that, the goddess of auspicious form, out of curiosity and with a sense of wonder, asked Śaṅkara Hara, "What is this? (Matsya Purāṇa 154.523)
He said to the goddess, "O greatly amazed one, this has never been seen by you before;
these lords of the Gaṇas, who are always dear to me, are playing on this mountain."
Those best of men by whom I was formerly gratified through austerity, celibacy, observances, and the service of sacred sites— they are these very ones.
"O lady of auspicious countenance, those who have come into my presence are dear to my heart;
they can assume any form at will, possess great energy, and are endowed with the qualities of magnificent beauty."
I am filled with wonder at the deeds of those who possess such power,
for they are capable of creating and destroying the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
Though I am constantly surrounded by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and great serpents, I do not take delight when separated from these [devotees].
"O lovely one, with every limb beautiful, these were my playmates on the mountain," said the goddess,
and having spoken thus, she then departed, overwhelmed by wonder.
Having reached the lattice-window, she gazes out with a face full of wonder at all those who are thin,
tall, short, stout, or pot-bellied.
Some had the faces of tigers and elephants, some had the forms of rams and goats;
they possessed the forms of various creatures, with flaming mouths, and were dark brown in color.
Gentle yet fierce, with smiling faces and blackish-brown matted hair and manes,
they have the faces of various birds and the faces of various wild animals.
Some were clothed in silk and skins, while others were naked and deformed;
they had ears like those of cows or elephants, and possessed many mouths, eyes, and bellies.
They had many feet and many arms, holding various divine weapons in their hands;
they wore many flower garlands and were adorned with various serpents.
Bearing wolf-like faces and weapons, adorned with various types of armor,
mounted upon diverse vehicles, they possess divine forms and roam through the sky.

Seeing those lords of the Gaṇas, who were accompanied by the sound of lute-playing proclaimed from their mouths and who were dancing in various postures, the Goddess spoke to Śaṅkara. (Matsya Purāṇa 154.536)
The Goddess said:
"How many Gaṇeśas are enumerated? What are their names and what is their nature?
Tell me of each one individually who are stationed separately."
Śaṅkara said: "Indeed, numbering in the tens of millions and beyond count, with various renowned heroic powers,

O Daughter of the Mountain, whose neck is adorned with a circle of fire, who possesses the luster of a vast golden mountain,
and who is embellished by the girdle of venomous serpents— I take refuge in you.
In this world, who has ever granted the desires of those who bow before them as swiftly as you do when praised by the Siddhas?
And whom in this world does Śaṅkara not desire, even though he supports the universe, as much as he desires you, O daughter of the Earth?
In the maṇḍala of Maheśvara, which was fashioned by the stainless yoga and equal to your own invincible body,
you were first praised by the foremost gods, who had shattered the host of the kinsmen of Andhaka.
Seated upon the great chariot of the king of beasts, her neck raised high with a mass of white manes;
she has crushed the great asuras with the flood of her long arms, which are tawny like the fire issuing from the mouth of her stainless spear.
Thus is Caṇḍikā proclaimed by the worlds, O Mother, the slayer of Śumbha and Niśumbha;
she who, on earth, swiftly delights solely in the crushing of the Dānavas and Danavas who think [only] of those who bow before her.

O Goddess, I bow to that form of yours which exists in the sky along the path of the wind, blazing with fire, and upon the surface of the earth— O unconquered and peerless one, O source of all worlds, beloved of Bhava!
The oceans with their gracefully surging waves, the fires with the brilliance of the sacrificial flame,
and the serpents bearing a thousand hoods— all these shall grant me fearlessness when you address them.
O Blessed One, refuge for those whose devotion is steadfast, having come to take shelter at Your feet,
may my collection of sense organs here remain unshakable, due to the motive of the desire to attain even a minute fraction of Your praise as its fruit.
O you who are affectionate toward your own children, come to my side; homage be to you, the refuge of the three worlds!
May my mind be ever fixed upon you, the auspicious one; I have come to you for refuge, I bow before you—homage be to you!

Then the goddess, the daughter of the Mountain, being thus praised by Vīraka, became pleased and entered the auspicious palace of her husband.
Then Rudra, beholding the beautiful Mahāgaurī— Gaurī, whose form was enchanting to the mind and whose gait was like that of a rutting lordly elephant— [was struck with wonder].
She had a face like the full moon, was slender, with heavy hips, thighs, and breasts; she was thin at the waist, yet possessed inexhaustible nectar-like beauty that rained down grace.
Adorned with all ornaments, her upper body languid with intoxication, she was made by him who acts with mildness;
[the audience perceives her as] full of desire, apprehensive, dejected, fierce, heroic, and terrifying.
Filled with compassion, laughter, and disgust, and bearing various expressions,
he assumed a terrifying form out of a desire to slay [the demon] at the word of the gods.
And she too became as formidable as the god himself;
the dweller of the mountains beheld thousands of her forms.
When she had swallowed the thousand forms and displayed the form of a star,
Śaṅkara then became free from fear once more.
Having beheld her who was composed of the entire universe, he who is fond of amorous play took delight once more with his wife,
the daughter of Himavat, who had been longing for him during their separation.
For as long as a thousand years, while the two remained in seclusion,
their continuous play, characterized by various forms of union, persisted.
Standing at the gate, Vīraka respectfully sent back the gods who desired a sight of Hara to their own respective homes.
"O gods, there is no opportunity here; Vṛṣākapi is sporting secretly with the goddess," they said, and they departed as they had come. (Matsya Purāṇa 158.30)
When a thousand years had passed, the gods, with minds in haste,
urged Agni to learn of Śaṅkara’s actions.
Having entered through a lattice opening in the form of a parrot,
the Fire-god beheld Śarva on his bed engaged in dalliance with the Daughter of the Mountain.
And the Lord of Gods beheld that Agni in the form of a boar;
Mahādeva, filled with a touch of anger, spoke to him.
Śarva said:
"O you of radiant form, half of my semen has been infused into the Goddess;
since she has ceased out of shame, you, O Pāvaka, drink the other half."
"Since this obstacle was created by you, it therefore falls upon you.
Thus addressed, Vahni, with palms joined in reverence, drank the deposited semen.
Then, by bursting open their bellies according to the various distinctions of their bodies, that seed of Maheśvara filled those gods.
When he had departed, a great, pure lake, shining like molten gold and extending for many yojanas, appeared in the hermitage of Śaṅkara.
Having heard that [place]— a great body of water with golden trees, filled with blooming golden lotuses and resounded by the songs of various birds— the goddess then [proceeded].
Filled with curiosity, she went to that lake of golden lotuses;
having played in the water there, she made a crest-ornament from those lotuses.
Then the goddess, accompanied by her companions, sat down on its bank,
desiring to drink that sweet water which was pure and filled with lotuses.
He saw the six Kṛttikās, who resembled the brilliance of the sun, having bathed;
they stood before him at home, holding that water in a lotus leaf.
Out of joy, she said, "I see water resting upon a lotus leaf.
Then those Kṛttikās told everything to the daughter of the Snowy Mountain.

"If we give you our child when it has been conceived,
let him be our son as well, and let him live by our name."
O lady of auspicious countenance, he shall become renowned throughout all the worlds.
Thus addressed, Girijā said: "How can a son born from my body, endowed with all limbs, arise from you all?"
Then the Kṛttikās said to her: "We shall indeed provide him with excellent heads, provided that this shall come to pass."
The blameless Śailajā said,
"So be it," and then those women, filled with joy, [took] the water resting upon lotus leaves.
They gave it to her, and she drank that water gradually;
once that water had been drunk in that lake, [the following occurred].
Then, having split open the right side of the goddess's womb,
a wondrous child emerged, shining forth throughout all the worlds.
He whose form is the radiance of the sun, possessing the luster of shining gold, holding a pure and lofty trident as his weapon, and having six faces; MatsP_158.49.
Blazing with a golden luster to slay the contemptible Daityas,
for this reason he became the divine Kumāra as well.

Precisely from the union with Kṛttikā, they became known as the Śākhās (Branches) due to their specific branches;

Because of this, he became known in the worlds as Viśākha and Ṣaṇmukha;
Skanda, Viśākha, Ṣaḍvaktra, and the renowned Kārttikeya.
In the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, on the fifteenth day, two beings of great strength,
resembling the sun, were born in a vast forest of reeds.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Indra,
considering it for the welfare of the two boys, fashioned a single chowrie.
Then, on that very sixth day, the lord Guha was consecrated by all the hosts of immortals, including Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Bhāskara.

Having been duly consecrated according to the prescribed rites,

Then Viṣṇu gave that weapon to the God of gods for the sake of his wife,
and the Lord of Wealth gave ten lakhs of Yakṣas to him.
Agni bestowed his splendor, Vāyu gave him a vehicle,
and Tvaṣṭṛ gave him a cock as a plaything that could assume any form at will;
thus all those gods provided him with an unsurpassed retinue.
With joyful hearts, they gave [it] to Skanda, who possessed the splendor of the sun.
Standing upon the ground on their knees, the hosts of gods,
the foremost of deities, praised the boon-granting Ṣaṇmukha with this hymn.
The gods said:

"Homage to Kumāra of great splendor, and to Skanda, who has routed the Dānavas; homage be to you who possess the radiance of the rising sun and lightning; homage be to you, O six-faced one, who can assume any form at will! *Matsya Purāṇa* 159.13.
Homage to the husband adorned with various ornaments, who tears asunder the Dānavas in battle;
homage be to you whose splendor is like the sun; homage be to you, the secret one, the cave-dweller.
Homage be to you, the remover of fear from the three worlds; homage be to you, O child, who are devoted to compassion.
Homage to the one with large, stainless eyes; homage to Viśākha, the observer of the great vow.
Homage, homage be to you, O Manohara; homage, homage be to you, O Raṇotkaṭa.
Homage to you whose vehicle is radiant with peacocks; homage be to you, the wearer of armlets.
Homage to you who hold aloft the lofty banner; homage be to you, who are bowed down by your own majesty.
Homage to you, homage to you, O possessor of supreme heroism; be intent on us with compassion, O you whose form is auspicious!

Having praised the Lord of Sacrifice and being intent on their ritual duties, the lords of the gods and others thus bowed down. Then Guha, the six-faced one, being pleased, looked at those lords of the gods with his stainless eyes and said to them: "I shall slay the enemies; you may now be free from anxiety."
The youth said:
"O deities, speak with confidence; what desire of yours shall I grant? Even if it be something unattainable, yet cherished and deeply contemplated in your hearts."
Thus addressed by him, all the gods, with their heads bowed in prostration and their minds fixed upon Guha, spoke to that Great-Souled One.
"The lord of the Daityas named Tāraka is the destroyer of all the hosts of immortals;
he is powerful, invincible, wicked, of evil conduct, and exceedingly wrathful.
Slay him alone! This is our heart's desire, which removes our fear. (Matsya Purāṇa 159.21)
Thus addressed, saying "So be it," the Lord of the worlds, followed by all the immortals and being praised by the lords of the gods, departed.
Then Śakra, having found a refuge, dispatched him for the sake of slaying Tāraka, who was indeed a thorn to the world.
Having gone there, that messenger of the lion among the Dānavas— fearless despite his terrifying appearance and speaking with harsh words— addressed the Daitya.
The messenger said:
"O banner of the Daityas, Śakra, the lord of the gods and ruler of heaven, says this to you:

"O Dānava, whatever sin you have incurred by the destruction of the world, I am its punisher today; I am the king of the three worlds."

Having heard these words of the messenger, the evil-minded one, whose splendor was nearly destroyed and whose eyes were bloodshot with anger, spoke to the messenger: matsya uvāca: śrutvaitad dūtavacanaṃ kopasaṃraktalocanaḥ / uvāca dūtaṃ duṣṭātmā naṣṭaprāyavibhūtikaḥ // MatsP_159.27 // Matsya said: Having heard this speech of the messenger, his eyes reddened with rage, that evil-souled one, whose power was almost gone, addressed the messenger.

"O Śakra, I have witnessed your prowess in battles hundreds of times;
yet, O evil-minded Śakra, you possess no shame because of your lack of modesty."
When the messenger had spoken thus and departed, the Dānava reflected:
"Śakra, having found no refuge, would certainly not deserve to speak in such a manner."
That Śakra has been conquered; he who is the refuge of those seeking shelter does not arise without cause.
And that one of wicked conduct beheld ill-omened portents.
A rain of dust and a fall of blood from the sky onto the surface of the earth, as well as trembling of the arms and eyes, parching of the mouth, and confusion of the mind. (Matsya Purāṇa 159.31)
He observed the fading of the lotus-like faces of his beloved women,
and he beheld fierce, wicked creatures who were aware of their own malice.
Thinking thus, the son of Diti instantly cast aside his anxiety,
while [the army] became fierce with the loud ringing sound of the bells on the herds of elephants.
Likewise, it was turned tawny by the dust of the earth trampled by the throngs of horses,
and it shone with rows of lofty banners on the swaying chariots.
With celestial chariots of wondrous form, their divine yak-tail fans waving,
that city was adorned with ornaments and resounded with the rising songs of kinnaras.
She wore a head-ornament of various blossoming flowers from many trees;
her weapons were unsheathed and ready for use, and her armor appeared spotlessly bright.
Standing upon his palace, the Daitya gazed upon the army of the celestial dwellers, which resounded with the noise of various musical instruments and the sounds of praises proclaimed by bards.
Then, with his mind somewhat bewildered, he reflected:
"Who could this unprecedented warrior be, who has not been conquered by me?"

Then the Daitya, agitated by anxiety, heard these heart-rending, bitter words proclaimed by the Siddhas and bards: matsya uvāca: tataścintākulo daityaḥ śuśrāva kaṭukākṣaram / siddhabandibhirudghuṣṭam idaṃ hṛdayadāraṇam // MatsP_159.39 // Matsya said: Then the Daitya, overwhelmed with anxiety, heard these piercing words of bitter syllables proclaimed by the Siddhas and bards, which were as if tearing his very heart.
Victory to you, O Youth, whose staff-like arms are tawny with the radiance of incomparable and victorious power;
victory to you, the moon that causes the lotus-thicket of the faces of the gods to bloom; victory to you, the submarine fire for the great ocean of the race of the Daityas!
O Six-faced One, whose peacock-chariot possesses a sweet sound, whose sprout-like toenails are touched by the tips of the crowns of the gods, and who occupies the great throne;
victory to You, O Beloved of the fresh, stainless-petaled lotus upon Your graceful crest-lock, the unbearable forest-fire for the lineage of the Daityas! (Matsya Purāṇa 159.41)
Victory, O Lord Viśākha! Victory, O savior of all the worlds! Victory, O leader of the divine army!

Skanda, victory! O son of Gaurī, lover of the bell, dear one, O Lord Viśākha! You who hold a multitude of fluttering banners, you whose golden ornaments possess the brilliance of the blazing sun! *Matsya Purāṇa* 159.42.

Victory to you, who cause agitation [in your enemies] and have sportively cut down all your foes! Victory to you, the savior of all the worlds and the slayer of Tāraka, the chief of the Daityas and Asuras! O Skanda, victory to you, the seven-day-old child; victory to you, the destroyer of the sorrow of the succession of worlds!
Matsya Purāṇa 160: Sūta said:
Having heard all this proclaimed by the bards of the gods, Tāraka...
He recalled the words of Brahmā regarding the slaughter that was imminent from the boy.
Remembering this, with all his limbs drenched in sweat,

Then the Daityas, headed by Kālanemi, their minds bewildered by fury, were filled with haste and amazement within their respective divisions; the warriors cried out, "Run! Seize [your weapons]! Array the army! (Matsya Purāṇa 160.3).
Seeing the prince, Tāraka, who was of terrifying appearance, spoke:
"O child, do you wish to fight? Play instead with the sport of a ball! (MatsP 160.4)
"Because you have not seen the Dānavas who strike terror into battle,
your intellect, due to your youth, perceives only such a limited purpose."
The prince also spoke to him as he stood before him, gladdening the gods:
"Listen, Tāraka, the meaning of the scripture is being explained to you."
"Objects are not perceived by means of scriptures; they are seen by fearless warriors in battle.
Do not despise my childhood; even as a child, I am the serpent of Time."
The young sun is difficult to behold, and likewise I, a child, am hard to conquer;
yet a mantra consisting of few syllables—O Daitya—is it not seen to be most radiant?
As soon as Kumāra had spoken thus, the Daitya hurled a mallet;
Kumāra, having warded it off, then [struck him] with his thunderbolt of unfailing luster.
Then the lord of the Daityas hurled an iron bhindipāla;
Kārttikeya, the slayer of the enemies of the immortals, seized it with his hand.
The six-faced one hurled a mace of supreme sound at the Daitya;
struck by it, the Daitya then trembled like the king of mountains.
Then the Daitya considered the six-faced one difficult to conquer in battle;
he reflected with his intellect that, without a doubt, the time [for his end] had arrived.
Beholding him enraged, all the lords of the Daityas, led by Kālanemi, struck Kumāra, who was fierce in battle.
Unaffected by those blows and their futile afflictions, the immensely radiant one [remained firm];
however, the lords of the Daityas, skilled in combat, again assailed him with spears and arrows.
The powerful thorns of the gods struck the prince along with the deities;
yet, though struck by the weapons of the Daityas, the prince felt no pain.
The battle between the gods and the Dānavas became life-ending;
seeing the gods oppressed, Kumāra was seized with wrath.
Then he warded off the army of the Dānavas with his missiles;
thereupon, those thorns of the gods were struck by them, for which no counter-measure could be found.
All those headed by Kālanemi turned their backs and fled from the battle;
then, when the Daityas had been slain on all sides and had scattered, [the gods prevailed].
Then the great Daitya Tāraka, the leader of the Asuras, being enraged,
seized a divine mace adorned with a network of gold.
He whose armlets were like refined gold struck Kumāra with his mace and,
with arrows fletched with peacock feathers, turned the gods away from the field.
Likewise, the enraged Tāraka, the leader of the asuras, pierced Guha’s vehicle, the peacock, with great broad-headed arrows in the midst of the army.
Seeing the gods turning their backs and his own mount shedding blood,
he seized a spotless spear adorned with gold in the battle.
Then Mahāsena, the six-faced one, with his arm beautiful with its golden bracelet,
swiftly [struck] Tāraka, the lord of the Dānavas.
"Stay, stay, O you of evil intellect! Behold the world of the living!
You are slain today by me with this spear; remember your well-practiced weaponry! (Matsya Purāṇa 160.24)
Having spoken thus, he then released a spear toward the son of Diti;
discharged by Kumāra’s arm, followed by the sound of his armlets,
it pierced the heart of the Daitya, as hard as a mountain peak of diamond.
With his life departed, he fell upon the earth like a mountain at the time of universal dissolution;
his crown and turban were scattered, and all his ornaments were cast aside.
When that Daitya had been slain and there was a great festival for the gods,
not a single person— even a wrongdoer in the hells— was then sorrowful.
Praising the six-faced god and sporting with tens of thousands of women, the gods,
possessing great splendor, returned eagerly to their own abodes.
And all the gods, together with the Siddhas and those whose wealth is austerity, being satisfied and having attained all their desires, also granted a boon to Skanda’s face.
The gods said:
"That mortal of great intelligence who reads this story connected with Skanda,
or listens to it, or causes it to be heard, shall become a man of renown."
He shall be long-lived, fortunate, illustrious, radiant, and of auspicious appearance;
he shall be fearless toward all beings and free from all suffering.
He who, having performed the morning twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*), recites the life-story of Skanda,
shall be liberated from all sins and become a great lord of wealth.
For children afflicted by disease and for those who serve at the king’s gate,
this is that supreme, divine [mantra] which always grants all desires;
and upon the dissolution of the body, a man shall attain union with the Six-faced One.
Matsya Purāṇa 161.
The sages said: "Now we wish to hear about the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu."
Likewise, the majesty of Narasiṃha, which destroys all sins.
Sūta said:
O brahmins, in former times, during the Kṛta-yuga, the lord Hiraṇyakaśipu,
the first among the Daityas, performed great ascetic penance.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
he lived in the water, observing the vows of ritual bathing and silence.
Then, indeed, Brahmā became pleased with him because of his tranquility and self-restraint, his celibacy, and his austerity and disciplined observance.
Then the Blessed Lord Svayambhū himself arrived there,
traveling in a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans.
[He was honored] by the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, and likewise by the deities;
by the Rudras together with the Viśvedevas, and by the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas.
And by the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, by the rivers as well as the oceans,
by the lunar mansions, the muhūrtas, and the great planets moving through the sky.
Together with the gods, the brahmin-sages, the perfected ones (siddhas), the seven seers (saptarṣis),
the meritorious royal sages (rājarṣis), and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases.

The illustrious Brahmā, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, surrounded by all the inhabitants of heaven and the foremost among those who know Brahman, spoke these words to the Daitya: matsyapurāṇe ekasaptatyuttaraśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ // 161 // Chapter One Hundred and Sixty-One of the Matsya Purāṇa.
"I am pleased with this austerity of yours, O observer of noble vows;
choose a boon—blessings upon you—and obtain whatever desire you wish. (Matsya Purāṇa 161.10)
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Neither gods, asuras, nor gandharvas; neither yakṣas, uragas, nor rākṣasas; nor humans or piśācas, O best of gods, shall be able to slay me."
"O Great-Grandfather, if the Blessed One is pleased with me, this is the boon chosen by me: that the sages should not curse me with their curses. (Matsya Purāṇa 161.12)
Neither with a missile nor with a weapon, neither with a mountain nor with a tree,
neither with something dry nor with something moist, neither by day nor by night.
May I alone become the sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire; may I become the water, the atmosphere, the stars, and the ten directions. (Matsya Purāṇa 161.14)
I am Wrath and Desire, Varuṇa, Vāsava, and Yama; I am Dhanada, the lord of wealth, the Yakṣa, and the sovereign of the Kimpuruṣas.
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, these divine and wonderful boons have been granted to you by me;
O child, you shall always obtain all your desires—of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One indeed departed through the sky itself to the Vairāja abode of Brahmā, which is frequented by hosts of brahminical sages.
Then the gods, the nāgas, and the gandharvas, together with the ṛṣis,
having heard of the granting of the boon, approached the Grandfather.
"O Blessed One, because of the granting of that boon, that asura will destroy us.
Therefore, may you be gracious quickly, O Blessed One; let even his slaughter be considered."
O Blessed One, you are the primordial creator of all beings, the self-sovereign lord;
you are the wise one, the unmanifested source-nature, and the creator of the offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
Having heard those words for the welfare of the entire world, the divine Lord of Creatures consoled the gods with the cool waters of his speech.
The gods must inevitably receive the fruit of his asceticism;
at the conclusion of his penance, the Blessed Viṣṇu will bring about his destruction.
Having heard those words of the lotus-born one, all the gods,
filled with joy, departed for their own divine abodes.
Then, as soon as the boon was obtained,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, emboldened by the granting of that boon, oppressed all living beings.
In the hermitages, that Dānava assailed the highly fortunate sages of praised vows, who were self-restrained and devoted to truth and righteousness.
Having defeated the gods dwelling in the three worlds and brought the triple world under his control, the great Asura, the Dānava, dwells in heaven.
When, intoxicated by the pride of his boon and impelled by the law of time,
he made the Daityas worthy of sacrifice and the deities unworthy of sacrifice.
Then the Ādityas, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Vasus—
the hosts of gods along with Indra, the Yakṣas, the Siddhas, the twice-born, and the great ṛṣis— [gathered there].
They approached Viṣṇu, the refuge and protector, the one of great strength,
the God of gods, whose essence is sacrifice, Vāsudeva, the eternal.
The gods said:
"O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, the gods have come to you for refuge;
protect us! O Lord, slay Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas."
For you are our supreme creator; for you are our supreme teacher;
for you are our supreme deity, O best of gods among Brahmā and the others.
Viṣṇu said:
"O immortals, cast away your fear; I grant you fearlessness.
In that same manner, O gods, regain your celestial realm without delay."
"Here I am; I shall slay this lord of the Dānavas, the Daitya who, arrogant because of the granting of a boon, is unslayable by the lords of the gods, together with his host."
Having spoken thus and dismissed the lords of the thirty gods, the Blessed Lord,
the Sovereign, resolved upon the slaughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
And the mighty-armed one, quickly taking up the syllable *oṃ* as his aid—
then the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*, [proceeded].
The Lord Hari, appearing like the sun in his splendor and like another moon in his radiance, went to the abode of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Having assumed a body that was half-man and half-lion, with his human form and likewise his lion form,
he touched his hand with his hand in the Nārasiṃha incarnation.
Then he beheld the vast, divine, delightful, and enchanting,
bright assembly hall of Hiraṇyakaśipu, which was endowed with all objects of desire.
It was a hundred yojanas wide and one hundred and fifty yojanas long;
it moved through the air at will and was five yojanas in breadth.
Free from old age, grief, and fatigue, it was unshakable, auspicious, and blissful;
adorned with mansions and palaces, it was delightful and seemed to blaze with splendor.
It was situated within the waters, fashioned by Viśvakarman,
and endowed with divine trees made of jewels that yield both fruit and flowers.
With blue, yellow, white, dark green, black, and even red creepers and shrubs bearing hundreds of flower clusters; MatsP_161.42 //
Resembling a dense mass of white clouds, she appeared as if floating;
radiant with rays of light, she was brilliant and delightful with divine fragrance.
It is exceedingly pleasant and not painful; it is neither cold nor heat-giving.
Having reached that state, they do not experience hunger, thirst, or exhaustion.
That eternal and imperishable [city] is indeed never supported by pillars, though it is adorned with various forms that are diverse and exceedingly radiant.
Exceeding the moon, the sun, and the fire,
she who is self-luminous shines while stationed upon the vault of heaven, as if illuminating even the sun itself.
And all desires, both divine and human, shall be abundant;
there shall be an endless supply of food and drink, rich in flavor and plentiful.
There are garlands of meritorious fragrance and trees that perpetually bear flowers and fruit;
there are also cool waters in the heat and warm waters in the cold.
With flowering tops and great branches bearing young shoots and sprouts,
they were covered by canopies of creepers along the rivers and lakes.
There the powerful lord of beasts beheld various kinds of trees,
as well as fragrant flowers and succulent fruits.
In that assembly hall, the Lord beheld lakes that were neither too cold nor too hot, as well as various sacred fords (tīrthas) located here and there.
And they were covered with lotuses, white lotuses, fragrant hundred-petaled flowers,
red water-lilies, blue lilies, and night-blooming lilies.
It was graced by beautiful ruddy geese, beloved royal swans,
kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds, cranes, and ospreys as well.
With birds that were stainless, resembling crystal, and possessing white plumage,
the lakes resounded with the songs of many swans and the cries of cranes.
There, upon the mountain peaks, he beheld fragrant and beautiful creepers bearing lush clusters of blossoms and wearing various flowers.
The ketakī, aśoka, sarala, puṃnāga, tilaka, arjuna,
mango trees, nīpa, prasthapuṣpa, kadamba, bakula, and dhava trees [were there].
Priyaṅgu trees, pāṭala trees, śālmali trees along with haridraka trees, sāla trees, tāla trees, tamāla trees, and delightful campaka trees; MatsP_161.57 //
In that same way, other trees in the assembly hall shone brightly—
coral trees and ordinary trees alike, possessing a radiance like a blazing fire.
There were many citraka trees with thick trunks and beautiful branches, reaching as high as many palm trees, and possessing the dark hue of añjana and aśoka flowers.
Varuṇa, vatsanābha, panasa along with candana, nīpa, sumanas, nimba, aśvattha, and tinduka; MatsP_161.60.
There were *pārijāta* trees, *lodhra* trees, *mallikā* jasmine, and *bhadradāru* deodar;
likewise, there were *āmalaka*, *jambu*, *lakuca*, and *śailavāluka* trees.
There are date palms and coconuts, myrobalans and vibhītaka trees, kālīyaka and drukāla trees, as well as hiṅgu and pāriyātraka trees.
Mandāra flowers, kunda, lac-dye, pataṅgas, and likewise kuṭajas;
red kuraṇṭakas, as well as blue ones together with agaru.
There were kadamba trees, bhavya trees, pomegranates, citron trees,
saptaparṇas, and bilvas, all likewise covered with honeybees.
