There were aśoka and tamāla trees covered with various shrubs and creepers,
as well as many madhūka and saptaparṇa trees, and numerous kṣīraka trees.
And there were creepers of various forms, laden with leaves, flowers, and fruits;
these and many other forest-born trees were found there.
Adorned with various flowers and fruits, they shone brilliantly on all sides;
there were *cakora* birds, *śatapatra* birds, intoxicated cuckoos, and *sārikā* birds.
Great trees with flowering tops are falling,
and there, birds of red, yellow, and crimson hues are perched upon the branches of the trees.
In that assembly hall, the jīvajīvaka birds gazed at one another with great joy,
while Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas, was then present.
Surrounded by thousands of women, adorned with various ornaments and garments,
his earrings blazed with crests of light from priceless jewels and diamonds.
And he was seated upon a wonderful throne measuring ten nalvas,
divine and resembling the sun, spread with celestial coverings.
There the wind blew most pleasantly, carrying divine fragrances;
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu sat there, adorned with flaming earrings.
Then the best of the Gandharvas approached the great Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu and sang songs with divine melodies.
Viśvācī, Sahajanyā, the one renowned as Pramlocā,
Divyā, Saurabheyī, Samīcī, and Puñjikasthalī.
Miśrakeśī, Rambhā, Citralekhā, Śucismitā,
Cārukeśī, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and likewise Urvaśī.
Thousands of others, skilled in dance and song,
wait upon the lord King Hiraṇyakaśipu.
There, all the sons of Diti, having likewise obtained boons, waited upon their lord, the mighty-armed Hiraṇyakaśipu, as he sat.
There, Bali, Virocana, Naraka the son of the Earth, and others of incomparable deeds [worshipped him] by the hundreds and thousands.
Prahlāda, Vipracitti, and the great asura Gaviṣṭha;
Surahantṛ, Sunāman, Pramati, and the excellent Sumati.
Ghaṭodara, Mahāpārśva, Krathana, Piṭhara,
Viśvarūpa, Surūpa, Svabala, and Mahābala.
Daśagrīva, Vālī, the great asura Meghavāsas,
Ghaṭāsya, Akampana, Prajana, and Indratāpana.
All those hosts of Daityas and Dānavas wore blazing earrings;
they were all adorned with garlands, eloquent in speech, and always constant in their observance of vows.
All were heroes who had obtained boons, and all were free from death;
these and many others [served] their lord Hiraṇyakaśipu.
All, with their divine retinues, wait upon that Great-Souled One from celestial chariots of various forms, which shine like blazing fires.
All the sons of Diti, possessing bodies like those of Mahendra and arms adorned with variegated armlets, waited upon him from all sides, their limbs beautifully decorated.
In that divine assembly hall, all the Asuras were like mountains,
with bodies of gold and a radiance equal to the sun.
Indeed, neither has it been heard nor seen how the sovereignty of that great-souled lion among Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu, was such as his was.
In that assembly hall, adorned with well-fashioned jeweled windows, he— the lord of beasts— beheld a dais variegated with gold and silver and a walkway strewn with diverse precious gems.
That lord of beasts beheld the son of Diti, his body adorned with a necklace of pure gold,
blazing with a great splendor like that of the sun, and being attended by hundreds of thousands of the sons of Diti.
Matsya-Purāṇa 162: Sūta said:
Then, having seen that high-souled one approaching like the wheel of time, [the sages spoke].
He was concealed by the body of a man-lion, like a fire covered by ashes.
The powerful son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, named Prahlāda,
beheld with his divine eye the lion-god as he approached.
Seeing him who had assumed an unprecedented body with the luster of a mountain of gold,
all the Dānavas and Hiraṇyakaśipu were struck with wonder.
Prahlāda said:
"O mighty-armed one, O great king, first progenitor of the Daityas,
this form of Nṛsiṃha has neither been heard of nor seen by us."
"What is this divine form that has appeared, originating from the unmanifest?
It is terrible, bringing an end to the Daityas, and my mind is as if filled with doubt."
The gods reside within his body, as do the oceans and the rivers;
likewise, Himavat, Pāriyātra, and all the other principal mountain ranges.
And the Moon, together with the constellations, the Ādityas, and the Vasus;
as well as Dhanada, Varuṇa, Yama, and Śakra, the lord of Śacī.
The Maruts, the divine Gandharvas, and the sages whose wealth is asceticism;
the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess.
The god Brahmā and Paśupati indeed wander about, stationed upon the forehead,
as do all things both stationary and moving.
And may you, accompanied by us and surrounded by all the hosts of Daityas,
likewise have an assembly hall crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots.
O King, the entire three worlds and the eternal laws of the universe are seen within this Narasimha, as is this whole world.
And here were the high-souled Prajāpati Manu, the planets, the yogas, and the trees;
as well as the time of portents, fortitude, intellect, pleasure, truth, austerity, and self-restraint.
The high-souled Sanatkumāra, all the Viśvedevas, and all the ṛṣis;
as well as Krodha, Kāma, and likewise Harṣa, Dharma, Moha, and all the Pitṛs.
Having heard the words of Prahlāda, the lord Hiraṇyakaśipu,
that leader of the hosts, spoke to all the Dānavas and their attendants.
"Let this lord of beasts be captured, for he has assumed an unprecedented form;
or, if there is any doubt, let this forest-dweller be slain."
All those hosts of Dānavas, surrounding the lion-king of terrible prowess,
joyfully terrified him with their might.
Then, having let out a lion’s roar, the immensely powerful lion among men shattered that divine assembly hall like Death with his jaws wide open.
While the assembly hall was being shattered, Hiraṇyakaśipu himself,
his eyes agitated with rage, hurled weapons at the lion.
Then [he taught] the most excellent among all weapons, the extremely terrible mantra of the staff (daṇḍa),
as well as the Kālacakra, the Aghora, and the supreme Viṣṇucakra.
Likewise, the great and most fierce thunderbolt of the Grandfather (Brahmā), which can burn the three worlds;
the variegated lightning-bolt; and the two types of thunderbolts, the dry and the moist.
Raudra, Ugra, Śūla, Kaṅkāla, and likewise Musala;
as well as Mohana, Śoṣaṇa, Saṃtāpana, and Vilāpana.
The Vāyavya, the Mathana, the Kāpāla, and the Kaiṅkara;
likewise the irresistible Śakti, and similarly the Krauñca weapon.
The Brahmaśiras missile, as well as the Soma missile and the Śiśira;
the Kampana, the Śātana, and the most terrifying Tvaṣṭra missile.
Kālamudgara, Akṣobhya, Tapanas, and Mahābala;
Saṃvartana, Mohana, and likewise the supreme Māyādhara.
He possesses the beloved Gāndharva weapon and the jewel among swords, Nandaka;
the Prasvāpana, the Pramathana, and the supreme Vāruṇa weapon;
and indeed the Pāśupata weapon, the range of which is unimpeded.
The Hayashiras weapon, the Brahma weapon,
as well as the Narayana weapon, the Aindra weapon, and the wonderful Sarpa weapon.
The Paiśāca weapon is unconquered, as well as emaciating and pacifying;
it is of great power, conducive to meditation, and brings about departure and trembling.
Then Hiraṇyakaśipu discharged these divine weapons at Narasiṃha, like an oblation into a blazing fire.
The best of asuras covered the lion with blazing missiles,
just as Vivasvat covers the Himavat with his rays at the time of the summer heat.
For that ocean of the Daityas' army, stirred up by the wind of their indignation,
submerged [the host] in an instant, just as the ocean submerges Mount Maināka.
With spears, nooses, swords, maces, and likewise with clubs,
with thunderbolts, lightning bolts, and great trees ablaze with fire.
With mallets and javelins, with rocks, mortars, and mountains, with blazing *śataghnīs* and most dreadful clubs; ||| MatsP_162.32 |||
Those Dānavas, with nooses held in their hands, possessing the speed of the thunderbolt and lightning of great Indra,
stood with their arms and bodies raised on all sides like three-headed serpent-nooses.
With their limbs adorned with clusters of golden garlands and their bodies made radiant by the expanse of yellow silken garments,
they shine like swans with broad wings, their flanks graced by strings of pearl necklaces.
The heads of those whose vigor was like that of the wind, and who were adorned with armlets, crowns,
and bracelets, shone brilliantly on all sides with a luster equal to the rays of the morning sun.
Surrounded by those fierce, blazing, and mighty multitudes of great weapons hurled at him,
he shone like a mountain whose caves are filled with darkness by clouds raining incessantly and by trees.
Even while being struck by those hosts of Daityas of great strength gathered together with their vast arrays of great weapons, [he remained unshaken].

Established in his majesty, the Blessed One did not waver in battle, remaining as immovable by nature as the Himalayas. Terrified by him in his form as a Man-Lion, whose splendor was equal to fire, the sons of Diti trembled with fear like waves born from the waters of the ocean tossed by the wind.
Matsya Purāṇa 163: Sūta said:
"There were those with the faces of donkeys, those with the faces of donkeys and horses, and those with the faces of crocodiles and venomous serpents."
Others have the faces of leaping deer, while others are situated with the faces of boars.
Others have faces like the rising sun, or faces like comets;
some have half-moon or half-faces, and others have faces blazing with fire.
Some have the faces of swans and cocks, with gaping mouths that inspire terror;
others have the faces of lions, licking their lips, as well as those with the faces of crows and vultures.
Some had two tongues and crooked heads, while others stood with faces like flaming meteors;
still others were Dānavas with the mouths of great sea-monsters, arrogant in their strength.
Despite the showers of arrows in battle, they could not cause any pain to the body of that lion among men, who was like a mountain in stature and incapable of being slain.
Thus the lords of the Dānavas, enraged like hissing serpents, created many other even more terrible beings upon the lion.
Those terrible arrows of the Dānavas, discharged by the lord of the Dānavas,
met their destruction in the sky like fireflies against a mountain.
Then the Daityas, filled with rage, swiftly hurled blazing divine discuses at the king of beasts from all sides.
The sky was filled with those wheels falling here and there,
shining like the moon, the sun, and the planets at the end of a cosmic age.
Then all those uplifted wheels, which were indeed like the flames of a fire, were swallowed by the high-souled lord of beasts.
Those wheels, entering his mouth,
truly shone like the moon, the sun, and the planets within the cavernous bellies of clouds.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu again hurled a powerful,
blazing, and terrible spear, which possessed the luster of polished weapons and lightning.
Beholding that blazing spear as it came rushing toward him, the Lord, the king of beasts,
then shattered it with a fierce roar of "Hum."
Shattered by the lion,
that spear blazed upon the earth like a great meteor fallen from the sky, flaming and emitting sparks.
A row of iron arrows reached the lion from nearby and shone brilliantly,
appearing like a garland of blue lotus petals.
Having roared according to custom and displayed his prowess as he pleased,
he drove that army away like the wind scattering the tips of blades of grass.
Then the lords of the Daityas, stationed in the sky, unleashed a rain of stones consisting of mountain-sized fragments of rock and highly lustrous mountain peaks.
Then a shower of stones was dropped upon the great head of the lion;
scattered in the ten directions, they were like clusters of fireflies.
Then the hosts of Daityas again covered that lion, the subduer of enemies, with showers of stones,
just as clouds cover a mountain with torrents of rain.
And the hosts of Daityas could not shake that best of gods,
just as the ocean cannot move Mandara, the king of mountains, despite its terrible force.
Then, when that shower of stones had been warded off, immediately thereafter a shower of water appeared on all sides with streams as thick as axles.
Streams falling from the sky with fierce velocity,
having completely enveloped the firmament on all sides, as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The streams [of rain] everywhere in heaven and on the earth in every direction do not touch the god, even as they fall incessantly upon the ground.
They rained down from the outside, but they did not rain down from above,
as he stood in battle assuming the form of the king of beasts through his illusory power.
When that tumultuous shower of stones and shower of water had been dried up by him,
the Dānava unleashed an illusion impelled by fire and wind.
The thousand-eyed Mahendra, of great splendor, together with the clouds,
extinguished the fire with a mighty downpour of water.
When that illusion had been thwarted in battle, the Dānava created a fierce and intense darkness on all sides, appearing most terrible.
When the world was shrouded in darkness and the Daityas had taken up their weapons,
he shone like the sun, surrounded by his own splendor.
In the battle, the Dānavas beheld his three-pronged frown upon his forehead,
marked with the sign of a trident like the triple-pathed Gaṅgā.
Then, when all their illusions had been destroyed, the sons of Diti,
turning pale, sought refuge with the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Then, blazing with rage as if consuming everything with his splendor,
when that lord of the Daityas became enraged, the world was enveloped in darkness.
Āvaha, Pravaha, Vivaha, Udāvaha,
Parāvaha, and Saṃvaha, all possessed of great strength and prowess.
Likewise, the glorious Parivaha; thus were the seven Maruts, who roam the sky, agitated, foretelling the fear of portents.
Those planets that indeed appear at the time of the destruction of the entire world were all seen in the sky, moving about as they pleased.
And at night,
O subduer of enemies, the night-walker (Rāhu), the lord of the sky, together with the planets and the constellations, followed the path improperly while wandering.
The sun in the sky has turned pale, and likewise, a vast black headless trunk (kabandha) is seen in the heavens. (Matsya Purāṇa 163.36)
The fire, though resting upon the earth, emitted a multitude of flames,
and the Lord, while remaining in the sky, was frequently seen.
Seven terrible suns, resembling smoke, have arisen in the sky;
they stand like horns upon the moon as it dwells in the firmament.
Śukra and Bṛhaspati are stationed on the left and the right respectively;
Śanaiścara and Lohitāṅga possess a radiance equal to that of the blazing fire.
All those sky-dwellers ascended simultaneously upon the peaks,
as slowly and dreadfully as the planets that revolve at the end of an eon.
And the moon, the dispeller of darkness, together with the stars and planets,
did not rejoice in Rohiṇī for the destruction of all that is moving and unmoving.
The moon, seized by Rāhu, is struck by meteors;
blazing meteors roam across the moon as they please.
Even he who is the god of the gods rained down blood;
meteors in the form of lightning, accompanied by great thunder, fell from the sky.
At that time, all the trees blossomed and bore fruit out of season;
all the creepers were laden with fruit—those very signs which the Daityas had said would signal their destruction.
Fruits were produced from fruits, and likewise flowers from flowers;
they opened and closed their eyes, and they laughed and wept.
The statues of all the gods cry out, emit smoke, and blaze; they portend a great terror.
The domestic animals and birds, mingling with those of the forest,
raised a most terrifying clamor as the great battle drew near.
The rivers flow with contrary currents and turbid waters;
and the quarters of the sky do not shine, being filled with red dust.
Those trees worthy of worship are not honored in any way;
they are struck down by the force of the wind, broken, and made to bow. (Matsya Purāṇa 163.49)
And when the shadow of all beings does not shift, even as the sun has reached its afternoon course at the dissolution of the world-ages; (Matsya Purāṇa 163.50)
Then, within the treasury and the armory of the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu’s palace, honey was deposited.
For the destruction of the Asuras and for the victory of the Suras,
various portents appear— terrible and of fearsome appearance.
These and many other terrible portents have arisen;
fashioned by Time, they are seen for the destruction of the lord of the Daityas.
While the earth was trembling, the great-souled lord of the Daityas caused the mountains and hosts of Nāgas of immeasurable power to fall.
With mouths filled with the flames of poison, emitting fire,
there were serpents with four heads, five heads, and seven heads.
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Dhanañjaya,
Elāmukha, Kāliya, and the powerful Mahāpadma.
The lord Śeṣa, the infinitely fortunate Ananta, that serpent with a thousand heads whose banner is a golden palm tree, who is otherwise unshakable, was indeed shaken.
Then, by that great and enraged one, the blazing mountains situated within the waters were shaken on all sides.
The Nāgas, who possess fiery splendor and roam the depths of Pātāla,
as well as the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, then touched the earth.
With his lips bitten together in rage like the Primordial Boar,
[he beheld] the river Bhāgīrathī, as well as the Sarayū and the Kauśikī.
Then there are the Yamunā, the Kāverī, the river Kṛṣṇaveṇā,
the highly blessed Suveṇā, and likewise the river Godāvarī.
The Carmaṇvatī and the Sindhu, as well as the lord of rivers and streams,
the Kamalaprabhava, and the Śoṇa with its jewel-like water.
The Narmadā with its auspicious waters, as well as the river Vetravatī,
the Gomatī abounding in herds of cows, and likewise the eastern Sarasvatī.
Mahī, Kālamahī, Tamasā, and Puṣpavāhinī [flow there],
as does Jambūdvīpa, with its jeweled grove adorned with every kind of gem.
Suvarṇaprakaṭa, adorned with the mines of gold,
and the great Lauhitya river, beautified by mountains and forests.
Pattana, Kośakaraṇa, and the source of sages and heroes;
the great villages of Māgadha, as well as the Muṇḍas and Śuṅgas.
The Suhmas, Mallas, Videhas, Mālavas, Kāśis, and Kosalas,
as well as the abode of Vainateya, were all shaken by the lord of the Daityas.
The ocean named Lohitya, which was fashioned by Viśvakarman into the shape of a peak of Mount Kailāsa, possesses terrifyingly red waters.
And the great mountain Udaya rises a hundred yojanas high;
it is glorious, with golden altars, and frequented by rows of clouds.
It was radiant with trees made of gold resembling the sun,
and with flowering *śāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *karṇikāra* trees.
And there is the famous mountain Ayomukha, adorned with minerals;
and the auspicious Malaya mountain, which possesses the fragrance of tamāla groves.
The Surāṣṭras along with the Bāhlīkas, as well as the Śūras and Ābhīras;
the Bhojas, Pāṇḍyas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Tāmraliptakas.
In that very same way, the Auṇḍras, Pauṇḍras, Vāmacūḍas,
and Keralas— along with the gods and the hosts of Apsarases— were agitated by that Daitya.
And there is the abode of Agastya, which was formerly made inaccessible;
it is enchanting, with throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas scattered throughout.
It was filled with various kinds of colorful birds and great trees in full bloom,
possessing peaks made of gold and resounded by throngs of celestial nymphs.
Giripuṣpitaka, Lakṣmīvat, and Priyadarśana—
having risen up, piercing the ocean, and serving as a resting place for the moon and the sun—
shone with their immense peaks as if they were scraping the sky. (Matsya Purāṇa 163.76)
Resembling the rays of the moon and sun, surrounded by the waters of the ocean,
the glorious Vidyutvat was a hundred yojanas in length on all sides.
Where the collisions of lightnings are cast down upon that best of mountains,
there is the mountain Ṛṣabha, the glorious one known by the name Vṛṣabha.
There is the majestic mountain Kuñjara, where the auspicious home of Agastya is located;
and there is the invincible city Viśālākṣa, the abode of serpents.
Likewise, Bhogavatī was also shaken by the lord of the Daityas,
as were Mahāsena, Giri, and the Pāriyātra mountain.
And Cakravān, the best of mountains, as well as the mountain Vārāha,
and also the auspicious city of Prāgjyotiṣa, which is made of gold.
In that [place] dwells the evil-minded Dānava named Naraka,
as well as Megha, the best of mountains, whose roar is as deep as a thundercloud.
O best of the twice-born, there are sixty thousand mountains there;
among them is the great mountain Meru, which resembles the rising sun.
The great mountain Hemagarbha, whose caves are constantly frequented by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas, as well as the mountain Hemasakha; MatsP_163.84.
Kailāsa, the king of mountains, was shaken by the lord of the Dānavas,
as was the Vaikhānasa lake covered with golden lotuses by him.
The mind was indeed agitated, filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks;
likewise, Mount Triśṛṅga and Kumārī, the best of rivers.
Mount Mandara is also covered with masses of snow,
as are Mount Uśīrabindu, Mount Candraprastha, and the king of mountains.
And likewise the mountain Prajāpati, as well as the Puṣkara mountain;
the Devābhra mountain and indeed the Reṇuka mountain.
Krauñca, Saptarṣiśaila, and the mountain Dhūmravarṇa—these and other mountains, as well as countries and provinces. (Matsya Purāṇa 163.89)
That Dānava caused all the rivers, along with the oceans, to tremble;
and Kapila, the son of the Earth, as well as Vyāghravat, were shaken.
The Khecaras, the sons of Satī, and those dwelling in the depths of Pātāla;
likewise, there is another fierce Gaṇa named Megha, whose weapon is a goad.
Moving upward with terrifying speed, all were trembling;
then Hiraṇyakaśipu appeared, wielding a mace and a trident, looking truly formidable.
Resembling a dense mass of clouds, with a voice like the thundering of clouds,
with a resonance like the roar of clouds, he was as impetuous as a cloud itself.
The heroic son of Diti, the enemy of the gods, rushed toward Nṛsiṃha;
then, springing up, he was torn apart and slain in battle by the lion with his sharp, great claws, while Oṃkāra acted as his companion.
The earth and time, the moon and the sky, the planets and the sun, and all the directions;
the rivers, the mountains, and the great oceans—all attained serenity through the destruction of the sons of Diti.
Then the gods and the sages, whose wealth is their austerity, being greatly delighted,
praised the eternal Primordial God with divine names.
O Lord, those people who know the higher and the lower shall worship this very Narasimha form which has been assumed by you.
The gods said:
"You are Brahmā and Rudra, and Mahendra, the best of gods;
you are the creator and the transformer, the inexhaustible source of the worlds."
They call you the supreme accomplishment, the supreme deity, the supreme mantra, and the highest oblation;
the supreme Dharma, the supreme universe, the foremost Puruṣa, the ancient one.
They call you the supreme body, the highest Brahman, the supreme Yoga, and the most excellent speech;
they call you the supreme secret, the highest goal, and the foremost ancient Puruṣa.
Thus they call you the supreme goal even of the Supreme, the highest deity even of the Highest,
and the most excellent being even of the Most Excellent— the foremost, ancient Puruṣa.
The supreme secret even beyond the supreme,
the supreme greatness even beyond the supreme— that which they call you, the foremost, ancient Puruṣa, is the greatest of all.

They call you the supreme treasure even beyond the supreme, the supreme purity even beyond the supreme, and the supreme self-controlled one even beyond the supreme; you are called the foremost, ancient Puruṣa.
Having spoken thus and having praised the god Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the Grandfather of all the worlds, departed for the world of Brahmā.
Then, while the musical instruments resounded and the apsarases danced,
Hari, the Lord, went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Having established his exceedingly radiant Narasiṃha form, the Lord,
whose banner is Garuḍa, assumed his ancient form and departed.
By means of a radiant vehicle with eight wheels, accompanied by the elements,
the Lord, the God whose nature is the unmanifest, went to his own abode.
Matsya Purāṇa 164:
The Sages said:
"The majesty of Narasiṃha has been described by you in detail."
Furthermore, speak again of his majesty in detail.
How did this world come to have the form of a lotus made of gold?
And how did the creation of Viṣṇu arise in the midst of that lotus in ancient times?
Sūta said:
Having heard the majesty of Narasiṃha, the son of the Sun,
his eyes wide with wonder, questioned Keśava once again.
Manu said: O Janārdana, how did your lotus-made world arise here in the navel of you who were situated in the ocean of water during the great Padma Kalpa?
Through the power of Padmanābha as he slept upon the waters of the ocean,
how did the gods together with the hosts of sages come into being in the past at Puṣkara?
O Lord of those who know yoga, explain this yoga in its entirety;
as I listen to your glory, no satiety arises within me.
For how long a time does the Supreme Person indeed sleep,
or for how long does he slumber, and what is the nature of that period of time?
After how much time does the one of great renown arise?
And having arisen, O Blessed One, how does he create the entire world?
O great sage, who were the Prajāpatis in the beginning,
and how did he create this manifold, eternal world?
How [did it happen] when the world was a single ocean, empty, with all things moving and stationary destroyed,
when gods, asuras, and humans were burnt away, and serpents and rākṣasas had perished?
When wind and fire have perished in the world, when space and the surface of the earth have vanished,
and when the great elements have undergone their reversal, the world becomes nothing but a vast abyss.
The all-pervading lord of the great elements, possessed of great splendor and great form,
the most excellent among the best of gods, remains established in his method, a knower of yoga.
O Brahman, O most righteous one, you ought to speak in its entirety this glory whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, so that I may hear it with supreme devotion. (Matsya Purāṇa 164.13)
O Blessed One, you ought to speak to those who are seated here with faith.
The Fish said:
"O bull of the solar race, this desire of yours to hear the glory of Nārāyaṇa is fitting for one who is born of his own lineage."
Listen to what has been heard from the ancient Purāṇas and from the Vedas, having heard it indeed from the mouths of great-souled Brāhmaṇas as they were speaking. (Matsya Purāṇa 164.16)
And just as the illustrious preceptor Dvaipāyana, the son of Parāśara, who possesses splendor equal to Bṛhaspati, spoke after having seen [the truth] through ascetic penance; MatsP_164.17.
O most excellent ones, I shall relate that to you according to my ability and according to what I have heard—
whatever was possible for me to understand as a mere seer.
Who is capable of knowing the Supreme, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa,
whom even Brahmā, the progenitor of the universe, does not know in its true reality?
That is the karma of the all-knowing ones; that is the secret of the great seers;
He is the Lord of all sacrifices, the reality of all-seers;
He is the object of contemplation for those who know the inner self, and hell for those who perform no righteous deeds.
That which is the deity with respect to the divine, well-known as the deity with respect to sacrifice, that is the being with respect to beings;
it is the supreme state of the great seers.
That sacrifice is declared in the Vedas; the wise know that to be true austerity:
he who is the agent, the doer, the intellect, the mind, and indeed the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
The Praṇava is the Puruṣa, the Teacher, and is conceived as the One;
it is also the fivefold Prāṇa, the Fixed, and the Imperishable.
Time, ripening, the ripener, the seer, and even sacred study—
it is said by various gods that this very thing is all that, and nothing beyond it.
That very Blessed One performs and transforms everything;
he causes us all to act, and he transcends those who have been thrown into confusion.
We worship that very one today; we desire that very one, being at peace—he who is the speaker, that which is to be spoken, and I myself whom I speak of to you.
Whatever is heard, whatever is worth hearing, and whatever else is conversed about; whatever discourses exist, or those devoted to the Vedas—
the universe and its Lord are remembered as that Nārāyaṇa.
That which is truth, that which is immortal and imperishable, that which is supreme; that which has been, this which is present, and that which will be;
whatever is moving and unmoving, and whatever else exists—all that is the ancient Lord, the foremost of persons.
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 165:
The Fish said:
"They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years."
O son of the Sun, its twilight period lasts for as many hundreds of years, doubled.
Where Dharma has four feet and Adharma has its limbs severed, and where virtuous men are born devoted to their own duty; (Matsya Purāṇa 165.2)
The Brahmins remained devoted to dharma, the kings remained established in the conduct of rulers,
the Vaiśyas were intent on agriculture, and the Śūdras remained dedicated to service.
Then truth, purity, and righteousness indeed increase;
the deeds practiced by the virtuous are performed and truly proclaimed. (Matsya Purāṇa 165.4)
O King, this is the conduct of the Kṛta Yuga that has occurred for all living beings, even for those of low birth who are devoted to righteousness.
Three thousand years here are called the Tretā Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) is proclaimed to be as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (dviguṇā) is twice that.
Adharma is established upon two feet, while Dharma stands upon three;
where truth and goodness prevail, the Dharma of the Tretā age is ordained.
In the Tretā age, these social classes undergo transformation; of this there is no doubt.
Due to the corruption of the fourfold order of classes, the stages of life fall into weakness.
This is the wonderful course of the Tretā Yuga ordained by the gods;
you should now also hear of the activities of the Dvāpara Yuga.

The Dvāpara age consists of two thousand years, O son of the Sun; its morning twilight is said to be as many hundreds of years, and its evening twilight is twice that amount. Thus, the entire Yuga is described.
And there, O son of the Sun, all living beings will be intent on material gain, struck by passion;
they will all be born as deceitful and base men.
In two ways Dharma stands firm, while Adharma rises up on three;
conversely, through the opposite course, Dharma gradually goes to ruin in the Kali age.
Consequently, the zeal for the state of being a Brahmin then dissolves; in the transition of the Dvāpara Yuga, vows and fasts are abandoned. *Matsya Purāṇa* 165.13.
Likewise, the cruel Kali Yuga is reckoned to consist of one thousand and two hundred years, together with its transitional periods (saṃdhyā). MatsP_165.14 //
Where unrighteousness has four feet and righteousness exists with only one foot,
there men are born as seekers of pleasure, devoid of austerity.
No man there is born who is exceedingly virtuous, nor one who is truly righteous, nor one who speaks the truth; for the men there are either atheists or devotees of Brahmā.
In the Kali age, all brahmins will be gripped by egoism, their bonds of affection will be destroyed, and they will adopt the conduct of śūdras.
O son of the Sun, in the Kali age there occurs a reversal of the stages of life (āśramas),
and at the end of the Yuga, there is even uncertainty regarding the social classes (varṇas).
One should know that the period called a Yuga, consisting of twelve thousand years as previously established,
repeated a thousand times, is termed a single day of Brahmā.
Then, when that day had passed, seeing the cessation of the bodies of all living beings, he conceived the thought of destroying the world.
And of all the deities, O lord of the earth, beginning with Brahmā, as well as of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and birds; (Matsya Purāṇa 165.21)
O King, O best of beings, [this applies] to the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, and the Bhujaṅgas; to the mountains, the rivers, and the beasts;
and likewise to the creatures born of animal wombs and to the worms.
The Lord of the Great Elements, the creator of beings, having withdrawn the five elements,
brings about a great destruction for the purpose of dissolving the world.
Becoming the sun, he took away the eyes; becoming the wind, he seized the life-force of living beings;
becoming fire, he consumed all the worlds; and becoming a cloud, though fierce, he rained down once more.
The Fish Purāṇa, Chapter 166:
The Fish said:
"Having become the yogi Nārāyaṇa, the fire-god Vibhāvasu, whose form is composed of pure being (sattva)..."
With his blazing rays, he dries up the oceans.
Then, having drunk all the oceans, rivers, and wells from every side, and having taken up all the water of the mountains with his rays; *Matsya Purāṇa* 166.2.
Having pierced the earth with his rays and gone down to the subterranean realm (rasātala),
he takes up the waters of Pātāla and drinks that supreme essence.
Whatever else there is among living beings that is certainly composed of urine, blood, and moisture—
all that the lotus-eyed Puruṣottama takes up.
And Hari, becoming the powerful wind and shaking the entire universe,
draws forth the vital breaths, such as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and the others.
Then all the hosts of gods and whatever beings there are—
the sense of smell, the nose, and the body— these qualities are dependent upon the earth.
The tongue, taste, and moisture—these qualities are dependent upon water;
form, the eye, and digestion—these qualities are dependent upon light alone.
Tactile sensation, vital breath, and movement—these qualities are dependent upon the wind;
sound, the sense of hearing, and the cavities of space—these qualities are dependent upon the ether.
In an instant, the Blessed One destroyed the world-illusion (lokamāyā),
as well as the mind, the intellect, and that which is heard of as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of all beings.
Parameṣṭhin took refuge in that venerable Hṛṣīkeśa;
thereafter, he was surrounded by the rays of that Blessed One.
As the branches of the trees were being struck by the wind, he took refuge among them;
then, a fire produced by their friction blazed forth in a hundred ways.
Then the fire of universal destruction (saṃvartaka), having enveloped everything, burned all mountains, trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and grasses.
And he burnt all those divine palaces, various cities, and whatever else was worthy of being inhabited.
Then, having reduced all the worlds to ashes, Hari, the teacher of the world,
extinguished them once more by means of his activity at the end of the eon.
Having become a hundredfold with a thousand showers, the mighty Kṛṣṇa gratified the earth with divine water as an oblation.
Then, by means of that mass of milk— a most excellent, sweet, auspicious, and meritorious water— the earth attained supreme nirvāṇa.
Enveloped by that flood and covered by the raining waters,
the earth became a single ocean, devoid of all living beings.
Even the great beings entered the all-pervading Lord of immeasurable luster,
while the world— subtle, enveloped, and devoid of sun, wind, and space— had come to an end.
Having himself caused even the oceans to dry up,
and having likewise burnt and then flooded all embodied beings, the eternal One sleeps alone.
Assuming his ancient form, the one of immeasurable prowess,
a yogi who has taken recourse to yoga, lies sleeping, pervading the waters of the single ocean.
For many thousands of yugas within the waters of the single ocean,
no one is able to know this unmanifest as manifest.
Who indeed is that which is called "the Person" (puruṣa), what is its connection, and who is the possessor of yoga?
And for how long a time does that Lord abide in the state of the single ocean?
"No one understands that the Blessed One will act [in this way]."
There is no seer, no goer, no knower, and no one standing by his side;
nothing whatsoever is known apart from that best of gods.
Having pacified the sky, the earth, the wind, the waters, the illuminator, Prajāpati, the supporter of the world, the Lord of the gods,
the Grandfather, the abode of the Vedas, and the Great Sage, he again desired to lie down.
The Fish Purāṇa, Chapter 167:
The Fish said:
"In this manner, when the world has become a single ocean, the one of great splendor lies [therein]."
Then the swan Nārāyaṇa covered the earth with water.
In the midst of the great dust, indeed within the lakes of the great ocean,
they know that stainless, mighty-armed, and imperishable Brahman.
Enveloped by darkness through the manifestation of his own form,
the Lord established a sattvic mind and remained there in that which is Truth.
That supreme knowledge which is reality as it truly is, which is real, was declared of old by Brahmā;
it is what is designated in the *Rahasyas* and *Āraṇyakas*, and is remembered as the *Upaniṣadic* teaching.
That which is proclaimed as the Supreme Puruṣa, the sacrifice,
and he who is otherwise known as Puruṣa— he is indeed Puruṣottama.
And those Brahmins who perform sacrifices and are known as officiating priests (ṛtvij) were likewise born from this very sacrifice in ancient times; let that be heard.
From his mouth, the Lord created first Brahmā and the Udgātṛ who chants the Sāman;
from his two arms, he created the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu.
From Brahmā, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and the Prastotṛ were produced in their entirety;
from Mitra and Varuṇa, the Pratiprasthātṛ likewise arose.
O King, from his belly [he created] the Pratihartṛ and the Potṛ;
and from his thighs, O King, the Acchāvāka and the Neṣṭṛ.
Then, with his two hands [he touched] the Āgnīdhra, and with his knees the Subrahmaṇya;
with his feet the Grāvastut, and the Unnetṛ who belongs to the Yajurveda.
In this very manner, this Blessed One, the Lord of the World, created sixteen supreme officiating priests (ṛtvij) who are the expounders of all sacrifices.
Thus, this person consisting of the Vedas is designated as the sacrifice;
and all the Vedas, together with their auxiliary limbs, Upaniṣads, and ritual actions, consist of this very [sacrifice].
O Brahmins, hear now that wonder which occurred in the past when [the Lord] slept upon the single ocean—the marvel of Mārkaṇḍeya. MatsP_167.13.
Swallowed by that Blessed One, the great sage remained within his very belly,
possessing a lifespan of many thousands of years through the power of that very being's splendor.
Wandering over the earth, which is the domain of sacred fords, on account of his visits to holy sites,
he frequented meritorious hermitages and temples of the deities.
Devoted to recitation and burnt offerings, peaceful, he undertook severe austerity while traveling through various regions, kingdoms, and diverse cities.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya slowly emerged from his mouth;
as he was coming out, he did not recognize himself due to the divine illusion.
Then, having emerged from his mouth, Mārkaṇḍeya beheld the world as a single ocean, shrouded on all sides by darkness.
A sharp fear arose within him, along with doubt for his own life;
yet, thrilled by the sight of the god, he was filled with supreme wonder.
Standing in the midst of the water with palms joined, Mārkaṇḍeya, filled with apprehension, reflected:
"What indeed could this thought of mine be? Is it delusion, or is a dream being experienced?"
"Clearly, one of those states has been brought about for me;
for such an affliction of the world as this does not deserve to be real. (Matsya Purāṇa 167.21)
When the moon, the sun, and the wind had perished, and the earth and its mountains had vanished,
he remained lost in thought, wondering, "What indeed has become of this world?"
And he also beheld a man sleeping, resembling a mountain,
half-submerged in the water like a cloud in the ocean.
Blazing as if with splendors, like the sun yoked with its rays,
shining by his own brilliance as if awake during the night.
Out of wonder, [the king] asked, "Who are you that have come here to see the god?
and in that very same manner, the sage was made to enter the womb once again.
Mārkaṇḍeya, filled with great wonder, entered the womb once again,
perceiving it yet again as if it were a dream.
He wandered over the earth exactly as he had done before,
visiting various hermitages and sacred fords endowed with holy waters.
And she saw hundreds of twice-born priests performing sacrifices within the womb of the goddess, having completed their offerings with excellent sacrificial fees.
All four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, have remained established in virtuous conduct,
as have the four stages of life (āśramas) exactly as they were described by me to you.
Thus, for more than a full hundred years, as the wise Mārkaṇḍeya wandered over the entire earth, he did not see the end of his belly.
Then, at one time, having again emerged from his mouth,
he beheld a single sleeping boy upon the branch of a banyan tree.
In that very same way, he sports undisturbed in the world consisting of a single ocean, when the sky is shrouded in mist and all beings have vanished.
Overcome with wonder and filled with curiosity,
that sage was unable to gaze upon the boy who resembled the sun.
Reflecting thus and standing alone by the water’s edge,
he thought that what he saw was previously perceived, yet he was filled with doubt due to divine illusion.
In those deep waters, Mārkaṇḍeya, filled with wonder,
was tossed about and experienced great distress, his eyes wide with terror.
To him the Blessed One said, "Welcome, O youth practitioner of yoga," and Puruṣottama spoke with a voice like that of a cloud.
"Do not fear, child; you must not be afraid. Come right here into my presence," said the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to that boy, who was afflicted by fatigue.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Who is this that proclaims my name, seeking to diminish my ascetic power,
as if challenging my age which has lasted for a thousand divine years?"
Indeed, this conduct of yours is not appropriate even for the gods, let alone for me;
for even Brahmā, the lord of the gods, addresses me as "Long-lived One."
Having encountered this most terrible calamity today, having cast off his life,
he must surely face death after addressing me as "Mārkaṇḍeya."
Sūta said: Having thus addressed him in anger, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya spoke;
likewise, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana spoke once more.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O child, I am your father; Hṛṣīkeśa is your father and your preceptor. I am the ancient bestower of life; why do you not approach me?"
Desiring a son, your father, the sage Aṅgiras, first propitiated me by resorting to intense austerity.
Then, through his terrible asceticism, he chose you, who possess immeasurable splendor;
I spoke thus to that great seer of boundless power who was established within my own self.
And who else, other than one whose self is not composed of the elements,
would venture to behold him sporting by way of yoga while situated within the single ocean?
Then, with a joyful countenance and eyes wide with wonder,
Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism placed his joined palms upon his head.
Then, having uttered his name and lineage, saying, "May you live long and be honored by the world," he performed a salutation with devotion to that Blessed One.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O sinless one, I desire to know this illusion (*māyā*) of yours in its true essence—
why you, while situated in the midst of the single ocean, lie down in the form of a child."
"By what name, O Lord, are you known in the world, O Master?
I consider you to be a Great Soul (Mahātman); for who else could possibly exist [in such a state]?"
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, I am Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all beings;
I am he who is known as Sahasraśīrṣa (the Thousand-headed), who is designated by [my] steps."
The Person of solar hue is the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is composed of Brahman;
I am Agni, the bearer of oblations, the imperishable Lord of aquatic creatures.
I am Śakra in the position of Indra for a full year;
I am the yogin of the age known as the Yuga, and indeed the one who revolves at the end of the Yuga.
I am all beings indeed, as well as all the deities;
among serpents I am Śeṣa, and Tārkṣya am indeed among all birds.
I am the end-maker of all beings, known as Time for the universe; I am the dharma and the austerity of those dwelling in all stages of life.
I am indeed the divine river and the great ocean Kṣīroda;
I am that which is the supreme truth, and I alone am Prajāpati.
I am Sāṃkhya, I am Yoga, and I am that supreme state;
I am sacrifice and ritual action, and I am remembered as the Lord of Knowledge.
I am light, I am wind, I am earth, and I am the sky;
I am the waters and the oceans, the stars, and the ten directions.
I am the rain, I am the Soma, I am Parjanya, and I am the Sun;
I am in the Ocean of Milk, and I am the submarine fire in the sea.
Becoming the Saṃvartaka fire, I drink the oblation consisting of water;
I am the ancient one, the supreme, and likewise the ultimate refuge.
"I am the source of all that has been, all that is to be, and all that exists now;
whatever you see, O Brahmin, and whatever you hear."
Whatever you experience in the world, remember all that as being me;
behold me, who previously created the universe, and who even now am the one to be created.
"And in age after age, I shall create the entire world through Mārkaṇḍeya;
therefore, O Mārkaṇḍeya, comprehend all of this in its entirety."
Desirous of hearing my teachings and my duties, move happily within my womb;
for Brahmā, together with the gods and the sages, resides within my body.
"Understand me, the enemy of the Asuras, as the union of the manifest and the unmanifest;
I am the single-syllable mantra and also the three-syllabled *tāraka*."
"Beyond the three goals of human life is the syllable Om, which demonstrates the purpose of those three goals.
Speaking thus, the high-minded Lord of the Purāṇas, the Great Intellect, continued his discourse.
He quickly drew the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya into his mouth;
thereafter, that best of sages entered the belly of the Blessed One.
In that solitary bliss, he was intent on hearing of the imperishable Haṃsa;
he who, having assumed various bodies within the great ocean where the moon and sun have vanished,
moves slowly as the Lord known by the name Haṃsa, creates the world and sports therein as time passes.
The Fish Purāṇa, Chapter 168:
The Fish said:
Having become Āpava, that all-pervading Lord indeed performed austerities.
Having covered his own body, which was born from the race of aquatic creatures.
Then the Great-Souled One, possessed of supreme power, whose mind is directed toward the creation of the world,
Viśva, contemplated the universe consisting of the five great elements.
As he was thus reflecting, the ocean became windless;
the world, subtle and profound, consisting of water, was without space. (Matsya Purāṇa 168.3)
That ocean-dweller slightly agitated the sea;
then, by means of his continuous waves, a subtle opening was previously produced.
Then, regarding that sound, the wind arising from the apertures emerged;
having found an opening, that unshakeable air increased in strength.
As it grew powerful, the ocean was violently agitated by its force;
from that turbulent ocean, as its waters were churned,
the great lord Vaiśvānara, whose path is black, came into being.
Then the Fire-god dried up much water;
due to the depletion of the ocean, the sky became a vast expanse.
The meritorious waters, which are like the essence of nectar, arise from the splendor of the Self;
space is produced from apertures, and wind is born from space.
Seeing the fire produced by their friction, born from the wind, Mahādeva— the creator of the great elements— was filled with joy.
Having seen the beings, the Blessed One, assuming many forms, reflected upon the supreme purpose of the world's creation along with the birth of Brahmā.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas,
the Soul of the Universe, having indeed passed through many births, is called the sacrificial oblation of Brahmā.

That knowledge which has been showered upon the foremost of the twice-born on earth— whose souls are purified by austerity— and which serves the purpose of the universe, attains preeminence among yogins.
Recognizing him as one possessed of yoga and endowed with supreme, perfect sovereignty,
the knower of yoga established that Lord of the Universe in the state of Brahman.
Then, in those great waters, Hari Acyuta, the creator of all worlds, the lord of the earth, sports according to the prescribed rites and rejoices.
Then he produced a single lotus arising from his navel,
with a thousand petals, stainless, radiant as the sun, and made of gold.
Resplendent with a brilliance like the blazing crest of a sacrificial fire, possessing the splendor of the stainless autumn sun,
the lotus of the Great-Souled One shines forth with noble luster, its appearance made beautiful by the hair of his body.
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 169:
The Fish said:
Then he created the foremost of those possessed of yoga, one of immense splendor.
The creator of all worlds, Brahmā, whose face is turned in every direction.
Upon which golden lotus, extending for many yojanas, consisting of all qualities of splendor and endowed with the characteristics of the earthly realm; MatsP_169.2 //
And those great sages who know the Purāṇas declare that this lotus, which is the supreme form of the Earth, was produced from Nārāyaṇa.
She who is Padmā is the goddess Rasā, known as the Earth;
those who are the heavy essences of the lotus are known as the divine mountains.
The Himavat, Meru, Nīla, and Niṣadha;
Kailāsa, Muñjavant, and likewise the other, Gandhamādana.
Puṇya, Triśikhara, the lovely Mandara,
Udaya, Piñjara, and the Vindhya mountain as well.
These are the abodes of the hosts of gods, of the great-souled Siddhas, and of those of virtuous conduct; they bestow the fruits of all desires.
The region situated between these is known as Jambūdvīpa;
it is the shape of Jambūdvīpa wherein sacrificial rites are indeed performed.
The water that flows from these, resembling the taste of divine nectar,
is known as the delightful rivers that are the source of hundreds of divine tirthas.
Those innumerable filaments of the lotus that are known to be all around it are indeed all the mountains of the elements upon the earth.
O lord of men, those many lotus petals are conceived as the Mleccha countries, which are difficult to traverse and strewn with mountains.
O King, let those leaves which are on the lower part be, respectively,
the dwellings of the Daityas, the Uragas, and the Pataṅgas.
Among them is the great ocean known as Tadrasa,
wherein men who have committed heinous crimes (mahāpātaka) sink.
Within the interior of that lotus is the earth situated in a single ocean;
furthermore, it is said that in all directions there are four reservoirs of water.
Thus, for the sake of Nārāyaṇa, the earth was produced from a lotus;
therefore, this manifestation is known by the name Puṣkara.
For this reason, the ancient supreme sages who were experts in that knowledge and performers of sacrifice have prescribed the lotus-rite in the sacrifice, using the Vedas as their authority.
In this manner, the Blessed One established by him the method of retention for all mountains, rivers, and lakes.
Then the omnipresent Lord, of incomparable power, radiant like the sun and possessing white splendor like Varuṇa,
the self-existent one, slowly created that bed in the great ocean— a lotus consisting of the entire world, according to the ordinance.
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 170:
The Fish said:
"A great Asura named Madhu was born as an obstacle to his ascetic penance."
And with him, indeed, was born simultaneously the Asura named Kaiṭabha.
Those two, Rajas and Tamas, were born from Viṣṇu as two hosts of darkness;
possessed of great strength, they agitated the entire world within the single ocean.
Wearing divine red garments, possessing white, radiant, and formidable fangs,
they were majestic with their crowns and earrings, and resplendent with their armlets and bracelets.
With large, wide-open, copper-hued eyes, broad chests, and mighty arms,
they were like two moving mountains with the sturdy build of great peaks.
Resembling fresh clouds, with faces like the sun,
they were most terrifying with their hands, which held maces and flashed like lightning.
By the placement of their feet, they seemed as if lifting up the ocean,
and making Hari, the slayer of Madhu, who was lying there, tremble.
Wandering there at Puṣkara,
they then beheld that radiant one, the best of yogins, who faces every direction.
Recognized as Nārāyaṇa, he was creating all subjects,
all the deities, and the mind-born Asuras and Ṛṣis.
Then those two foremost of Asuras, blazing with fury, desirous of death, and their eyes agitated by rage, spoke there to Brahmā.

"Who are you, standing in the middle of the lotus, wearing a white turban and having four arms; why do you sit here, free from all distress, having undertaken a vow out of delusion? (Matsya Purāṇa 170.10)
"Come, come! O lotus-born one, give us battle.
You are powerless against us two supreme lords here in this ocean."
In this regard, what is your origin, or by whom have you not been joined [to existence]?
Who is your creator and who is your protector? By what name are you designated?
Brahmā said:
"He is called 'the One' by the worlds; he is inconceivable and possesses a thousand eyes.
Through union with him, may you two come to understand your own actions and names."
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"O Great-minded One, there is nothing superior to us in this world;
indeed, the entire universe is covered by us through our qualities of darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas). (Matsya Purāṇa 170.14)
We two, consisting of passion and darkness, have transgressed the sages; we, whose conduct is contrary to dharma, obscure [the truth] and are difficult for all embodied beings to cross over.
By us two, who are difficult to overcome, the world is carried along in age after age;
we two are wealth and desire, sacrifice and the attainment of heaven.
Wherever there is happiness joined with joy, wherever there is prosperity and fame, and whatever is desired by whomsoever—consider all that for us two. (Matsya Purāṇa 170.17)
Brahmā said:
"Through effort and by means of the vision of one possessed of yoga, yoga was previously acquired by me;
having concentrated upon that, I have taken refuge in the quality of goodness (sattva)."
He who is the supreme one possessing the intellect of yoga, who is called Yoga itself and pure Sattva; he who is the creator of Rajas and Tamas, and the source of the universe.
From that, beings are born, both those characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and others;
for he alone, the Lord who is self-controlled, shall slay you two as a portion of himself.
Then, while still sleeping, the glorious Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, by means of his own creative power (māyā), made his arm extend for many yojanas.
Then, being dragged by the arm of that powerful-armed one, the two of them moved about like two fat birds that had been released.
Then, having gone there, the two of them bowed down to the eternal god Padmanābha Hṛṣīkeśa and both stood before him.
We know you as the source of the universe, the one supreme Puruṣa;
protect us both for the sake of our purpose, for this is the cause of our intellect.
Since you are of unfailing vision and we know you to be eternal,
we have therefore come here to behold you from every side.
Therefore, O God, subduer of enemies, we desire an extraordinary boon from you;
for your vision is never in vain. Homage to you, O victor in battle!
The Blessed One said:
"O best of asuras, tell me quickly for what purpose you desire to live again in secret, having been granted your life once more."
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"O Lord, O Master of great vows, we desire our death at your hands in that place where no one has ever died. *Matsya Purāṇa* 170.28.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Indeed, you two shall become preeminent when the future time arrives;
there is no doubt that you will become so. I tell you this truth."
Then, having granted a boon to the two great Asuras, the eternal one, the best of the gods and supreme lord of the universe,
the Lord rubbed those twin sons born of the qualities of rajas and tamas with the sole of his foot.
The Fish Purāṇa, Chapter 171:
The Fish said:
And having remained upon that lotus, Brahmā, the best among those who know Brahman, [proceeded].
With arms raised, the one of great splendor resorted to severe austerity.
Blazing, as it were, with splendors and his own radiance, the dispeller of darkness shone while established in all dharmas, like the thousand-rayed sun with its beams.
Then, assuming another form, the imperishable Śambhu Nārāyaṇa,
possessed of great splendor, the teacher of yoga and of great fame, arrived.
For the wise Kapila was a preeminent brahmin teacher of Sāṃkhya;
both of these great souls were devoted to the field (kṣetra) and offered their praise.
Having arrived there, those two— who were experts in the distinctions between the higher and the lower and were honored by the great ṛṣis— spoke to Brahmā of immeasurable splendor.
Brahmā is firmly bound to the Self, vast, and established in the world;
he is the leader of all beings and is worshipped by the three worlds.
Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the knower of yoga who had brought them forth,
created these three worlds, according to this Vedic revelation of Brahmā.
And the Ṛṣi produced a single son for Śambhu;
before him stood Brahmā, restrained in speech, dark and imperishable.
As soon as he was born, the mind-born son spoke to Brahmā:
"What assistance may we provide for you? Let the blessed Ṛṣi speak."
Brahmā said:
"O high-minded one, that which this Kapila— who is Brahman and composed of Nārāyaṇa— declares as the truth, do that."
Then, for that purpose, he rose up once more before Brahmā and said with palms joined in reverence: "I am here to serve you both; what shall I do?"
The Blessed One said: That which is the true, imperishable Brahman is indeed eighteenfold;
remember that which is the truth, that which is the reality, for that is the supreme state. (Matsya Purāṇa 171.12)
Upon hearing these words, he departed for the northern direction;
having gone there, he attained the state of Brahmā through the splendor of his knowledge.
Then the powerful Lord Brahmā, the great-minded one, having formed it in his mind, created a second [world] named Bhuva.
Then he spoke these words: "O Grandfather, what shall I do?
Commanded by the Grandfather, I have approached Brahmā."
Having practiced the meditation on Brahman, he descended to the earth;
having attained the supreme station, he came into the presence of those two.
When that son had also departed, the Lord created a third,
the all-pervading one named Bhūrbhuva, who was skilled in the practice of liberation.
Having attained the status of a protector of cattle (gopati), he reached the very same destination as those two.
Thus have these three sons of the high-souled Śambhu been described.
Having taken those sons of his, the Lord Nārāyaṇa and Kapila, the lord of ascetics, departed for the destination they had earned for themselves.
At the very moment those two had departed and were liberated, Brahmā indeed then once again resorted to a most formidable and supreme vow.
Then Brahmā, the Lord, performing austerities alone, found no delight;
thereupon, he brought forth from half of his own body an auspicious wife.
By means of austerity, splendor, luster, and self-restraint,
he sought a goddess equal to himself and capable of creating the worlds.
Concentrated by her, Brahmā took delight there while performing austerities;
then he recited the three-footed Gāyatrī, which is honored by the Vedas.
Creating the lords of creatures, the omnipresent Lord also created the oceans and the other four Vedas, which originated from Gāyatrī.
The Grandfather indeed created sons equal to himself—
the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) from whom the worlds issued forth.
First, Viśveśa created his son Mahātāpasa,
the meritorious Dharma by name, who is beneficial for all mantras.
Dakṣa, Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Manu.
Now, these great ṛṣis known as the Adbhutas and the Paitāmahas were to be understood;
those great ṛṣis attained a dharma consisting of thirteen qualities.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyuḥ, Siṃhikā, Muni, Tāmrā, Krodhā, Suratā, Vinatā, and Kadrū. (Matsya Purāṇa 171.29)
O King, these twelve daughters were indeed the offspring of Dakṣa;
and Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, who was said to have been produced through ascetic penance.
Then Dakṣa gave him twelve other daughters;
likewise, the Ṛṣi then gave the Nakṣatras to Soma.
O son of the Sun, all the asterisms beginning with Rohiṇī are meritorious;
Lakṣmī, Marutvatī, Sādhyā, and Viśveśā are also considered auspicious.
And the goddess Sarasvatī herself was created by Brahmā in the past;
these five, O King, are indeed the most excellent among the best of the gods.
She who was the beautiful wife of Brahmā, capable of assuming any form at will, was given by Brahmā, whose deeds are witnessed, to Bhadra for the sake of Dharma.
Having become Surabhi and being well-disposed, she approached Brahmā;
then Brahmā, who is worshipped by the worlds, united with her in sexual intercourse.
The best of beings, who knew the cause for the creation of the world, was born for the sake of the cattle;
and from him were born sons resembling smoke in appearance, who were exceedingly numerous.
Resembling evening clouds at night and possessing fierce brilliance,
they burned [the world] while weeping, running about, and censuring the Grandfather.
Because of weeping (*rodana*) and running away (*dravaṇa*), they are therefore remembered as the Rudras;
Nirṛti, Śambhu, and the third, Aparājita.
Mṛgavyādha, Kapardin, Dahana, Īśvara, the venerable Ahirbudhnya, Kapālin, and Piṅgala; MatsP_171.39 //
The general was Mahātejas; these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
And from that very Surabhi came the cows and the lords of sacrifice.
Furthermore, there are excellent illusions, fragrant animals that do not decay,
goats, swans, and likewise the supreme nectar.
From Surasā, the most excellent medicinal herbs arose;
likewise, from Dharma, Lakṣmī was born, and Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas.
Bhava, Prabhava, Hīśa, and likewise Asuraha;
Aruṇa and Aruṇi, as well as Viśvāvasu, Bala, and Dhruva.
Haviṣya, Vitāna, Vidhāna, Śamitā, Vatsara, Bhūti, and Sarvāsuraniṣūdana; // MatsP_171.44 //
The goddess of great splendor, honored by the worlds, gave birth to the Sādhyas, who were gods with beautiful joints, following after Vāsava.
The first god is indeed Vara, the second is Dhruva the immutable,
the third is Viśvāvasu, and the fourth is Soma the Lord.
Then Yama was born as his suitable portion immediately after him;
likewise, Vāyu was the seventh, and Nirṛti the eighth Vasu.
This offspring of Dharma was indeed born of Sudevi;
and it is heard in the sacred tradition that the Viśvedevas were born from Viśvā through Dharma.
And Dakṣa of mighty arms, Puṣkarasvana,
Cākṣuṣa Manu, as well as Madhu and the great serpent [Kaiṭabha].
The child Viśrāntaka, the highly illustrious Viṣkambha, Garuḍa of exceeding strength and vigor, and Bhāskarapratimadyuti; MatsP_171.50 //
Devamātā gave birth to all the gods as her sons, the lords of the universe;
Marutvatī gave birth to the Marutvats, the gods, as her sons.
Agni, Cakṣu, Ravi, Jyotis, Sāvitra, Mitra,
Amara, Śaravṛṣṭi, and the long-armed Sukarṣa.
And Virāja, Vāc, Viśvāvasumatī, Aśvamitra, Citrarasmi, and Niṣadhana, O King. (Matsya Purāṇa 171.53)
Hūyanta, Vāḍava, Cāritra, Mandapannaga,
Bṛhanta, Bṛhadrūpa, and likewise Pūtanānuga.
In ancient times, Marutvatī gave birth to these hosts of Maruts;
Aditi gave birth to Kaśyapa as the twelve Ādityas indeed.
Indra, Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Ravi, Pūṣan, Mitra, Dhaneśa, Dhātṛ, and Parjanya; MatsP_171.56 //
Thus these were the twelve Ādityas, the most excellent dwellers of the third heaven;
and two excellent sons were born to Āditya by Sarasvatī.
Supreme in austerity and supreme in virtue, they were honored even by the inhabitants of heaven;
Danu gave birth to the Dānavas, and Diti gave birth to the Daityas.
Kālā indeed bore the Kālakeyas, while Surasā bore the Asuras;
and the sons of Anāyuṣā were the diseases of great power.
Siṃhikā was indeed the mother of the grahas, Muni the mother of the gandharvas,
and Tāmrā, O descendant of Bharata, was the mother of the meritorious apsarases.
O King, lord of the people, from Krodhā were born all the bhūtas, the piśācas,
as well as the hosts of yakṣas and the rākṣasas.
Vinatā gave birth to four-footed creatures, as well as cows of the Surabhi breed,
and to the birds known as Suparṇas.
The goddess Kadrū gave birth to all the mountains and all the nāgas;
in this way, O scorcher of foes, all the worlds attained growth.
Then indeed, O King, occurred the manifestation of the Great-Souled One;
that manifestation of Puṣkara has been recounted by me as proclaimed by Dvaipāyana.
The ancient Puruṣa, Viṣṇu, Hari, the Lord,
has been described by me to you in due order, as he has been praised by the supreme ṛṣis.
And that man who, with reverence, should always listen to this foremost Purāṇa on the sacred festival days,
having attained the worlds of those free from passion, enjoys the fruits of heaven in the hereafter.
He who propitiates Kṛṣṇa in four ways— with his eyes, his mind, his speech, and his actions— Kṛṣṇa, in turn, becomes gracious toward him.
A king obtains a kingdom, and one who is destitute obtains supreme wealth;
likewise, one whose life is exhausted gains long life, and one desiring a son obtains a son.
A devotee of Viṣṇu attains sacrifices, the Vedas, as well as desires, various forms of austerity, manifold merit, and riches. (Matsya Purāṇa 171.69)
Whatever one desires, all that shall be obtained from the Lord of the World;
provided that, having renounced everything else, one recites this *Pauṣkaraka* of Hari.
O best of kings, there shall indeed be no inauspiciousness for him who hears of this manifestation.
O illustrious one, this manifestation of the Great-Souled One, named Pauṣkaraka,
has been recounted to you according to the Vedic revelation of Vyāsa.
The Fish Purāṇa, Chapter 172:
The Fish said:
"Listen to the nature of Viṣṇu and his state as Hari in the Kṛta Yuga."
He possesses the nature of Vaikuṇṭha among the gods and the nature of Kṛṣṇa among human beings.
For such is the profound course of the deeds of that Lord;
now hear, O King, concerning those of the past and those yet to come, exactly as they are.
This Lord and Master, Nārāyaṇa, who is himself unmanifest yet dwells within manifest forms, is indeed infinite in essence, the source of all, and immutable.
Having become Nārāyaṇa, this eternal Hari was Brahmā,
Vāyu, Soma, Dharma, Śakra, and Bṛhaspati.
In age after age, he attains even the status of being the son of Aditi;
this all-pervading one is known as Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra.
For this was born from the grace of the Lord Aditi for the sake of having a son,
in order to slay the enemies of the gods— the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
In the past, this Lord, whose self is Pradhāna, created Brahmā;
he, the Primeval Person, created the Prajāpatis in the ancient kalpa.
There he created human beings of unsurpassed Brahman lineages;
from those great-souled ones, the eternal Brahman manifested in many ways.
Learn from me this proclamation of the deeds of Viṣṇu, who is a source of wonder, as they are being recited—He who is worthy of praise throughout the worlds. (Matsya Purāṇa 172.9)
When the slaying of Vṛtra had been accomplished and the Kṛta Yuga was prevailing,
there occurred the battle known throughout the three worlds as the Tārakāmaya.
There, all those terrible Dānavas, invincible in battle,
were slaying all the hosts of gods, along with the Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Being slaughtered in battle, turned away from the fight, and with their weapons exhausted,
they sought in their minds a protector— the Lord, the divine Nārāyaṇa.
In the meantime,
clouds with the luster of extinguished charcoal covered the expanse of the sky, along with the sun, moon, and the host of planets.
Fierce winds, accompanied by masses of lightning and producing terrible roars,
blew forth, striking one another with great force.
The sky seemed as if it were being consumed by fires of terrible portents— flashes of lightning, thunderbolts, the force of thunderclaps, and fierce winds— amidst most horrific sounds.
Then thousands of meteors fell even as they moved through the sky,
and divine celestial chariots were seen both descending and ascending.
At the end of the cycle of the four ages, whatever fear may arise for the worlds, during that time characterized by portents, forms appear that are formless.
Everything that had come into being became lusterless, and nothing could be discerned;
enveloped by a mass of darkness, the ten directions did not shine.
Kālī entered in embodied form, shrouded by dark clouds;
like the sky obscured by a terrible darkness when the sun has been overwhelmed, she did not shine.
Having warded off those masses of darkness with his two arms,
that Lord Hari, whose body is dark, revealed his divine form.
Resembling a dark cloud in hue, with body-hair like a cloud,
he was black in both splendor and form, like a black mountain.
Wearing blazing yellow garments and adorned with ornaments of refined gold,
his body was like the darkness of smoke, appearing like the fire risen at the end of an eon.
With shoulders broad and thick, doubled fourfold, and hair covered by a diadem,
he shone, adorned with weapons that resembled gold.
Resplendent with the rays of the moon and sun, as lofty as a mountain peak,
gladdening the hands of Nandaka, and bearing arrows like venomous serpents.
Exalted by the diverse power of his energies, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace,
he is the Viṣṇu-mountain with forbearance as its root, the sacred tree possessing the Śārṅga bow as its peak.
Bestowing noble fruits upon the thirty [gods], possessing the beautiful sprouts of celestial women,
it is beloved by the minds of all the worlds and enchanting to the hearts of all beings.
The branches of this tree are the celestial mansions, which drip with the honey of rainwater;
it is enriched by the essence of knowledge and ego, and it is the place where the great elements sprout forth.
It was covered with special leaves, blossomed with the planets and constellations,
possessed the great trunk of the world of the Daityas, and was illuminated by the world of mortals.
It resounded with the roar of the ocean, had the great netherworld as its foundation,
was spread wide with the snares of the king of beasts, and was inhabited by winged creatures.
It is a great tree for all the world, rich with the beautiful fragrance of the purpose of moral conduct;
it has the unmanifest as its infinite waters and the manifest ego as its foaming waves.
It is a vast flood of waves consisting of the great elements, with planets and stars as its bubbles;
it is filled with celestial chariots as its birds and agitated by the tumultuous roar of clouds.
It is teeming with swarms of living beings and fish, filled with multitudes of mountains and shells,
possessing whirlpools that are the objects of the three qualities (guṇas), and having all the worlds as its timingila fish.
It has trees, creepers, and shrubs as its heroes; the serpents are its preeminent moss;
it possesses twelve suns as its great islands and eleven Rudras as its cities.
It was endowed with the eight treasures and mountains, a great ocean for the waters of the three worlds,
its waters possessing waves as numerous as the twilight periods, and it was frequented by the wind-like Suparṇa.
It had hosts of Daityas and Rākṣasas for its crocodiles, was teeming with Yakṣas and Uragas as its fish,
possessed the Grandfather (Brahmā) of great prowess, and was adorned by the jewels of all women.
It is adorned by rivers of glory, fame, splendor, and fortune;
it possesses the force of dissolution and creation during the great festival of the conjunction of time.
But him who has reached the great further shore of yoga, the great ocean that is Nārāyaṇa,
the God of gods, the giver of boons, who is affectionate toward his devotees— MatsP_172.37.
To the god who bestows grace, who brings about peace, and who is auspicious;
[to him] who is mounted upon a chariot yoked with bay horses and attended by the banner of Garuḍa.
In the vast cavern of Mount Meru, fashioned by the planets, moon, and sun, surrounded by the excellent Mandara and Akṣa trees, and endowed with countless rays of light; MatsP_172.39.
In the sky, variegated with the flowers of stars and beautiful with the ornaments of planets and constellations,
the gods, defeated by the Daityas, found refuge from fear in Him who grants fearlessness.
They beheld the God stationed upon a divine chariot consisting of the worlds;
all those gods, led by Śakra, stood with palms joined in reverence.
Placing the cry of "Victory! at their head, they sought refuge in him who is the worthy refuge;
and Viṣṇu, the god of gods, heard those words of theirs.
Viṣṇu, stationed in the sky and assuming his supreme form, set his mind upon the destruction of the Dānavas in the great battle.
He spoke these words with a solemn promise to all the deities:
"Attain peace; may it be well with you; do not fear, O hosts of Maruts."
"All the Dānavas have been conquered by me; let the three worlds be taken possession of.
They were gratified by those words of Viṣṇu, who was true to his promise.
The gods attained great joy, as if having consumed the most excellent nectar;
then that darkness was withdrawn and the clouds vanished.
Auspicious winds blew and the ten directions became tranquil;
the luminaries shone with pure radiance, and the moon moved in a clockwise direction.
The planets did not engage in conflict, the rivers became tranquil, the three realms beginning with the celestial sphere became free from dust, and the paths were cleared of all impurity.
The rivers flowed according to their true nature and the oceans were not agitated;
the sense organs within the inner selves of men became tranquil.
The great sages, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud,
and the purifying fire brought the sacrificial oblations to auspicious completion.
The worlds became engaged in their duties with joyful minds upon hearing the words of Viṣṇu, who had given his promise regarding the destruction of his enemies.
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 173:
The Fish said: Then, having heard the words of Viṣṇu granting them fearlessness, the Daityas and Dānavas—
They made vast preparations for battle and for victory.
But Maya [created] an inexhaustible chariot made of gold, three *nalva*s in length,
with four wheels, very spacious, and equipped with well-fashioned great yokes.
Resounding with the tinkling of networks of small bells, adorned with leopard skins,
and beautified by lovely lattices of jewels and gold.
It was crowded with herds of wild beasts, adorned with rows of birds,
bearing divine weapons and quivers, and resounded with the thundering of clouds.
It was a noble and excellent chariot, with a comfortable seat, resembling the sky,
filled with maces and iron clubs, like the ocean personified.
Adorned with golden armlets and bracelets, with a golden orb as its pole and equipped with banners and flags, it was like Mount Mandara accompanied by the sun.
In one place, he had a body with the expansive form of a lordly elephant, possessing the splendor of a lion,
joined by a thousand bears, and resounding like a full-grown cloud.
Desiring battle, he ascended a blazing, divine chariot that traveled through the sky and crushed the chariots of his enemies, like the radiant sun ascending Mount Meru.
A chariot made entirely of gold, as wide as a loud cry,
mountain-like in form, spacious, and resembling a mass of blue collyrium.
It was divine, made of black iron, with its pole-bound yoke-fastenings of metal,
emitting rays like a mass of darkness, and thundering like a rain-cloud.
It was fortified with a great iron lattice provided with latticed windows,
and filled with iron bars and mallets intended for hurling.
It was adorned with spears and outstretched nooses, with unattached thorns,
and with terrifying javelins and battle-axes.
He mounted that excellent chariot, which was yoked to a thousand donkeys and rose up for the sake of his enemies like a second Mount Mandara.
But Virocana, enraged, stood with mace in hand at the head of that army, like a mountain with blazing peaks.
The Dānava Hayagrīva,
the crusher of enemy armies, drove his chariot yoked with a thousand horses.
Stretching his great bow a thousand *kiṣkus* in length,
Varāha stood at the front like a mountain covered in new growth.
But Khara, dripping with pride and shedding tears born of rage from his eyes, with his teeth, lips, and eyes quivering, longed for battle. (Matsya Purāṇa 173.17)
Tvaṣṭṛ, the powerful Dānava, mounting a formidable eight-elephant vehicle,
moved about to arrange the Dānava battle formation.
The son of Vipracitti was Śveta, adorned with white earrings;
resembling a white mountain, he stood facing the battle.
Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, most excellent and armed with mountain rocks,
stood facing the battle, making the mountains tremble.
But Kiśora, out of extreme joy, was addressed as "Kiśora," and the Dānavas,
along with Bala, prepared for battle in due order.
He appeared in the midst of the Daitya army like the risen sun;
Lamba, however, had the luster of a fresh cloud and was adorned with flowing garments as his ornaments.
Stationed within the array of the Daityas, he shone like the sun amidst the mist;
Svarbhānu, however, fought with his mouth, using his teeth, lips, and eyes as weapons.
That great planet stood laughing in the presence of the Daityas;
others there were mounted on horses, while still others were upon the shoulders of elephants.
Others have mounted lions and tigers, while others are on boars and bears;
some ride donkeys and camels, and some have beasts of prey as their vehicles.
But other Daityas, footless, terrifying, and with deformed faces—
some with only one leg and others with half a leg— danced, longing for battle.
Clapping their hands and likewise roaring with cries of defiance,
many of those preeminent Dānavas bellowed with the roar of joyful tigers.
Holding rocks and clubs in their hands,
they threatened the deities with fierce maces and iron bludgeons, their arms resembling iron bars.
They sported with nooses, spears, iron clubs, javelins, hooks, and sharp-edged spears; with *śataghnīs* and mallets possessing a hundred edges.
With boulders from mountain slopes, with crags, with iron clubs,
and with discs, the foremost of the Daityas made their army joyful.
That entire army of the Dānavas, fierce with the intoxication of battle,
stood facing the gods like a surging mass of clouds.
