That wondrous army, dense with thousands of Daityas and resembling wind, fire, mountains, clouds, and water,
surged forth at the onset of the flood of battle and appeared as if intoxicated with the desire to fight.
The Fish Purāṇa, Chapter 174:
The Fish said:
"O son of the Sun, you have heard the detailed account of the Daitya army."
Now hear concerning the vast extent of the Vaiṣṇava army of the gods as well.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins of great strength,
together with their armies and followers, equipped themselves for battle in due order.
Then Puruhūta, the thousand-eyed guardian of the world and leader of all the gods,
mounted the celestial elephant.
And in its center is a chariot with haṃsas—the best of all birds—as its steeds;
it has most beautiful wheels for feet and is adorned with gold and diamonds.
He was followed by thousands of hosts of gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas,
and was praised by radiant members of the assembly and celestial rishis.
He was accompanied by hosts of clouds that moved at will like mountains, produced by the flashing of vajras and arising from lightning and rainbows.
Mounted upon which the Blessed One traverses the entire world,
the Brahmins standing at the commencement of the sacrifice sing [of it] within the *havirdhāna* sheds.
In heaven, as Śakra follows after them amidst the sounding of celestial instruments,
hundreds of beautiful throngs of Apsarases dance around.
Shining like the sun with Ketu as its royal banner,
it was yoked to a thousand horses possessing the speed of thought and the wind.
Then that excellent chariot, protected by Mātali,
shone like the entire Mount Meru enveloped by the splendor of the sun.
Yama, however, raising his staff and his mallet appropriate for the occasion,
stood within the host of the gods' hosts, terrifying the Daityas with a roar.
Joined by the four oceans and by licking serpents,
wearing armlets of conch-shell and pearls, he bears a body composed of water.
Striking down the snares of Time with horses resembling moonbeams—
horses tossed by the wind and appearing like water— he performed thousands of playful maneuvers.
Clad in white, fluttering garments, with armlets as beautiful as coral,
his excellent body darkened by jewels, the noble one bore the burden of Hari.
Varuṇa, the wielder of the noose, stood in the midst of the host of gods,
longing for the time of battle like the ocean whose shores have been breached.
Accompanied by an army of yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as hosts of guhyakas,
he is the sovereign lord of treasures, joined by the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma.
The glorious lord of the lords of kings was seen with mace in hand; Dhanada, who fights from his celestial chariot, stood upon the Puṣpaka vimāna.
Seeking battle, that king of kings, who is carried by men, shone resplendent as he mounted his bull in the fray,
like Śiva himself in person.
The eastern wing is Sahasrākṣa, the southern is Pitṛrāja,
Varuṇa the western wing, and Naravāhana the northern.
The four world-protectors, endowed with great strength, were stationed at the four quarters,
guarding their respective directions for that divine army.
The Sun, with his chariot yoked to seven horses that travel immeasurable distances,
blazes with splendor and shines with radiant rays.
With its wheel of rising and setting, traversing Mount Meru and serving as the gateway to the third heaven, it shines upon the imperishable world.
Endowed with a thousand rays and blazing with splendor,
the twelve-fold Lord of Day moved through the midst of the worlds.
Soma shines upon the white-horsed chariot like the cool-rayed moon,
gladdening the world with his beams filled with water like the Himavat.
He was like the moon, the lord of the twice-born, followed by a multitude of stars,
his body marked by the shadow of the hare, and the destroyer of the nocturnal darkness.
The lord of the luminaries in the sky, the bestower of flavor upon tastes, the master,
and the repository of thousands of medicinal herbs and of nectar.
The Dānavas beheld Soma standing there, the first portion of the world, gentle, consisting of truth, a chariot, with snow as his weapon.
That vital breath (prāṇa) which, existing in all beings among men, is divided fivefold and pervades the seven constituent elements, sustains and moves through the three worlds.
They call him the creator of fire, the source of all, the Lord;
he who is eternally extolled with songs consisting of the seven musical notes.
That which they call the supreme being, that which they call bodiless, that which they say moves through space, travels swiftly, and is joined with sound; // MatsP_174.30 //
That wind, the life-force of all beings, having arisen by its own power,
blew in a contrary direction along with clouds, causing great distress to the Daityas.
The Maruts, together with divine gandharvas and hosts of vidyādharas,
sported with their bright swords that resembled snakes just released from their sloughs.
Creating poison consisting of fierce water,
those lords of serpents moved through the sky with their mouths wide open, having become arrows for the Indras in heaven.
With mountains, rocky peaks, and hundreds of trees,
the hosts of gods stood ready to strike the Dānava army.
He who is that god Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Trivikrama;
he who resembles the black path at the end of the age, the Lord of the entire universe.
He is the source of all wombs, the slayer of Madhu, the consumer of oblations established in sacrifice;
he is the soul of earth, water, and ether, dark-hued, the bestower of peace, and the destroyer of enemies.
Taking up his discus, the destroyer of the enemies of the immortals,
Gadādhara raised it with his supreme splendor, like the sun rising from the serpent-king.
Grasping with his left hand the great mace that destroys all asuras— a mace black in form that brings death to enemies— MatsP_174.38.
With his other arms, the mighty Lord, whose banner bears the enemy of serpents, held various kinds of weapons, such as the Śārṅga bow and others.
He was the self-born son of Kaśyapa, a twice-born one who feeds upon serpents,
a bird of prey whose flight exceeds that of the wind and who agitates the sky.
It shone with the lord of serpents coiled within its mouth,
appearing like the towering Mount Mandara when it was released after the churning for the nectar of immortality.
His prowess had been witnessed many times in the battles between the gods and the asuras;
and for the sake of the nectar, Mahendra had marked him with his thunderbolt.
He had a crest and was powerful, adorned with glowing earrings;
clad in garments of variegated feathers, he resembled a mountain rich in minerals.
With a radiant jewel-gem hanging from his broad chest, possessing a luster equal to the cool-rayed moon and resting upon the coils of a serpent.
And with his two beautiful-winged arms, he playfully covered the sky in heaven,
as if with two clouds bearing rainbows at the end of a cosmic age.
Adorned with blue, red, and yellow banners,
that great abode of a massive body was concealed by the guise of a banner.
The glorious and powerful Lord, having mounted his younger brother Aruṇa in battle—
Suparṇa, the best of sky-travelers, whose body was golden-hued.
The hosts of gods and the composed sages followed him,
and they praised Janārdana with words consisting of supreme mantras.
It was indeed embraced by Vaiśravaṇa, preceded by Vaivasvata,
encircled by the Moon, and adorned by the King of the Gods.
With moon-like splendors, he engaged in a vast battle that possessed the roar of wind-swept clouds and was ablaze with kindled fire.
The powerful and surging force of Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, and Bhrājiṣṇu, shrouded in darkness by their own splendor,
assembled for battle.
"May there be well-being for the gods," Bṛhaspati declared;
"May there be well-being for the host of Dānavas," Uśanas took up the speech. (Matsya Purāṇa 174.52)
The Matsya Purāṇa, Chapter 175:
The Fish said:
Then, from those two forces, a tumultuous conflict arose.
Of the gods and the asuras, who were each desirous of victory over the other.
The Dānavas, together with the gods, with various weapons raised,
encountered one another in combat like mountains clashing against mountains.
That battle, joined by gods and asuras, appeared most wonderful;
it was characterized by both righteousness and unrighteousness, and by both pride and humility.
Then, with chariots detached from their teams and elephants urged forward,
men with swords in hand leaped into the sky from all sides.
With clubs being hurled, with arrows falling, with bows being drawn, and with mallets being brought down; ||| MatsP_175.5 |||
That battle became terrible, crowded with gods and dānavas,
generating terror for the world and resembling the destruction at the end of a yuga.
With iron clubs hurled by hand and with mountains cast down,
the Dānavas struck the gods led by Indra in battle.
Being slaughtered by the powerful Dānavas who appeared triumphant,
the gods, with dejected faces, suffered extreme distress in the battle.
Mangled by missiles and spears, their heads split by iron clubs,
and their chests pierced by the sons of Diti, they vomited much blood from their wounds.
Enveloped by nets of arrows and rendered powerless by the asuras,
they entered the illusion of the dānavas and were unable to move.
The army of the gods, rendered effortless by the asuras and deprived of its weapons, appeared like something that had set, resembling a lifeless form.
Having severed with his thunderbolt those terrible arrows discharged from the bows of the Daityas,
the thousand-eyed Śakra entered the formidable army of the Daityas.
Having slain the leaders of the Daityas and that great army of Dānavas,
he then rendered them into darkness with a net of *tāmasa* weapons.
Overcome by that terrible darkness through the splendor of Indra, they did not recognize one another nor the vehicles of the gods.
Freed from the snares of illusion and exerting themselves,
those best of gods cast down the bodies of the lion-like Daityas, which had become like darkness.
Overwhelmed and deprived of consciousness by that dark-blue radiance,
the hosts of Dānavas fell like mountains whose wings had been clipped.
With that lord of the Daityas having become solidified like darkness in the ocean,
the Dānava, who was the destroyer of the gods, became as if turned into pure gloom.
Then Maya, burning with a dark passion, created that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā),
which produced a brilliance like that at the end of an eon and was fashioned by the submarine fire (Āurva).
Then she burned all those Daityas who had been fashioned by Māyā,
and they immediately rose up in the battle with bodies like the sun.
Having encountered the illusory bowstring, the inhabitants of heaven, being scorched,
took refuge in the domain of the moon, which provides cool water.
Being consumed by the Aurva fire, those gods, their minds bewildered and tormented, sought refuge with the wielder of the thunderbolt, imploring him for protection.
While the army was being harassed by the Dānavas through illusion, Varuṇa, urged by the king of the gods, spoke these words: *matsya-purāṇa* 175.22.
In ancient times, O Śakra, the son of a Brahmarṣi named Ūrva— formerly possessed of great splendor and equal to Brahmā in his qualities— performed most rigorous penance.
The hosts of sages, together with the divine seers, approached that imperishable world which, through its ascetic power, was like the scorching sun.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Dānava and lord of the Dānavas,
together with others, once petitioned the seer of supreme splendor.
The brahmin-sages spoke these words to him, consistent with dharma:
"O Blessed One, this status has its root severed within the lineages of the sages."
"You alone are childless, and no other kinsman of your lineage remains;
having undertaken a vow of lifelong celibacy, you pursue nothing but hardship."
Many lineages of Brahmins, consisting of sages of purified souls,
remain as single bodies, secluded and without offspring.
"Since our sons have thus been cut off at the root, we have no cause for concern;
you, however, are preeminent in asceticism and possess a splendor equal to that of Prajāpati."
Abide there for the sake of your lineage; increase yourself by means of your own self.
Through you, dharma has been earned; with that, indeed, produce a second body.
Thus addressed by the sages, the sage, feeling as if struck in his vital organs, rebuked those hosts of ṛṣis and spoke these words: matsyapurāṇa 175.31.
Just as this eternal law of the sages was ordained of old,
so too is the rishi-like duty for one who subsists on forest roots and fruits.
For a Brāhmaṇa born from the womb of Brahman who perceives the Self,
well-practiced celibacy can move even Brahmā himself.
There are three modes of life for people who dwell in the householder stage;
however, for us, the mode of life of those dwelling in the forest hermitage is superior.

Those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, those who use their teeth as a mortar, those who grind with stones, those who eat only what comes spontaneously, and those who endure the five fires; MatsP_175.35 //
These remain established in austerity through vows that are exceedingly difficult to perform;
placing celibacy at the forefront, they seek the supreme goal.
"The status of a Brāhmaṇa is ordained for a Brāhmaṇa through celibacy (brahmacarya); thus say the people who know celibacy in the other world. (Matsya Purāṇa 175.37)
Truth is established in celibacy; austerity is established in celibacy.
Those Brahmins who are established in celibacy abide in heaven.
There is no accomplishment without yoga, nor is there fame without accomplishment;
in this world, there is no root of fame, nor any austerity superior to the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Whoever restrains the collection of the senses and the group of five elements and practices celibacy— what austerity could be greater than this?
Wearing matted hair without spiritual discipline, performing vows and rituals without a firm resolve,
and practicing conduct that is not celibate— these three are known as hypocrisy.
Where are wives, where is union, and where is the reversal of states? Indeed, this progeny was created by Brahmā through his mind as a mental creation.
If you who have realized the Self possess the power of asceticism,
then create mental sons through the rite pertaining to Prajāpati.
The womb fashioned by the mind must be established by ascetics;
for those practicing austerities, neither union with a woman nor seed is said to be the vow.
That which has been spoken here by you—though you are virtuous and fearless—for the sake of a lost cause, appears to me to be exceedingly like the speech of the wicked. (Matsya Purāṇa 175.45)
Having made this mind-made body with an inner self that is radiant,
I shall create a son born from my own body, even without union with a woman.
"In this manner, my self shall generate a second self by means of this forest rite, as if desiring to consume all creatures. (Matsya Purāṇa 175.47)
But Ūrva, possessed by ascetic fervor, having cast his thigh into the sacrificial fire,
churned with a single blade of *darbha* grass the kindling-stick from which his son was to be born.
Suddenly piercing his thigh, Agni,
wreathed in flames and devoid of fuel, was born as the son [of the sage], desiring to consume the world.
Having burst forth from the thigh of Urva, the fire named Aurva was born,
exceedingly wrathful, as if desiring to consume the three worlds.
As soon as he was born, he spoke to his father with a feeble voice:
"O father, hunger oppresses me; I shall devour the world—release me! (Matsya Purāṇa 175.51)
Yawning with flames that ascended to the third heaven and burning all living beings, that fire of destruction increased, pervading the ten directions.
In the meantime, Brahmā, honoring the sage Urva, said:
"Let your son be restrained; have compassion for the world."
"O Brahmin, I shall provide an excellent place for this child of yours;
hear these truthful words, O son, best among speakers. (Matsya Purāṇa 175.54)
Ūrva said:
"I am blessed, I am favored, since the Blessed One today bestows this wisdom upon my child here for the sake of supreme grace."
When the time of dawn has arrived, at the longed-for moment of reunion,
O Blessed One, with what offerings will the son, once satisfied, attain happiness?
Where shall his dwelling be, and of what nature shall be the food of this Blessed One, who possesses great majesty and power equal to his own valor? (Matsya Purāṇa 175.57)
Brahmā said: "O Brahmin, his dwelling shall indeed be in the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha) in the ocean;
for him who has drunk my source, the water, there will be happiness."
"Wherever I was, constantly drinking the water-offering as my oblation—
that oblation and its very abode I now relinquish to your son."
Then, at the end of the age, O son, this one and I shall wander together, removing the debts of those who are childless.
At the time of the end, this fire has been made by me to consume water;
it shall burn all beings, including gods, asuras, and rakshasas.
"So be it," said Agni; with his circle of flames withdrawn, he cast forth his radiance upon his father and entered the mouth of the ocean.
Then Brahmā and all the great sages departed;
having recognized the power of Aurva’s fire, they each returned to their own respective abodes.
Then, having witnessed that great marvel, Hiraṇyakaśipu, with all his limbs bowed low, spoke these words aloud: Matsya Purāṇa 175.64.
O Blessed One, this wonderful event has occurred before the eyes of the world:
O best of sages, the Grandfather has been thoroughly pleased by your ascetic penance.
"But I, O observer of great vows, must be understood as the servant of both your son and yourself, to be accomplished here through my actions."
Therefore, behold me, who have attained this state and am devoted solely to your propitiation;
O best of sages, if I should fail, it would be your own defeat.
Aurva said:
"I am blessed, I am favored, since you stand here as my preceptor;
O observer of noble vows, by this penance of mine, I have no fear today."
"Accept that very illusion created by my son—
an illusion consisting of fire, devoid of fuel, and invincible even to fires."
This [weapon] of yours, when brought under control, will subdue enemies within your own lineage;
it shall protect your own side and utterly consume your adversaries.
Saying "So be it," the lord of the Dānavas took her leave, bowed to that bull among sages, and departed for heaven, joyful and having achieved his purpose.
This unbearable illusion, difficult even for the gods to overcome,
was created in the past by Aurva, the son of Urva, the fire-god.
But when that Daitya has risen up, she will undoubtedly be rendered powerless;
for this curse was previously pronounced upon her by the very same splendor that created her.
If this [obstacle] is to be warded off, O Blessed One, you should act so that I may be happy;
let my friend Śakra, the moon born from the waters, be given to me.
Therefore, having joined with him and surrounded by aquatic creatures, I shall destroy this illusion through your grace; of this there is no doubt.
The Fish Purāṇa, Chapter 176:
The Fish said:
"So be it," replied Śakra, the enhancer of the thirty gods, filled with joy.
He commanded Soma, whose weapon is the cold, to go to the forefront for battle.
"Go, O Soma, and provide assistance to the wielder of the noose (Varuṇa) for the destruction of the Asuras and for the victory of the dwellers of heaven."
You are more powerful than I, the Lord of the lords of light;
those who know the essence perceive the essence consisting of you throughout all the worlds.
In you, O Manifest One, there is waning and waxing like the circle of the ocean;
you revolve day and night, joining time to the world.
O Moon, even the gods and those whose origin is the stars do not know that your mark, which resembles a hare, is merely a shadow of the world reflected upon you.
Situated above the path of the sun and above the luminaries,
you dispel the darkness with your splendor and illuminate the entire world.
Śvetabhānu, Himatanu, Jyotiṣām-adhipa, Śaśin, Adhikṛt, Kālayogātman, Iṣṭa, Yajñarasa, and Avyaya. (Matsya Purāṇa 176.7)
Lord of herbs, source of ritual action, and likewise the one who bears the crescent on his crest;
the cool-rayed moon, the repository of nectar, the fickle one, and the one whose vehicle is white.
You are the splendor of those with radiant bodies; you are the moon for the drinkers of Soma;
you are the gentle one of all beings; you are the king of the stars, the destroyer of darkness.
Therefore go, O Mahāsena, together with Varuṇa and his protective host;
subdue the demonic illusion by which we are being consumed in battle.
Soma said:
"O King of the Gods, granter of boons, as you tell me to do for the sake of battle,
I shall now rain down the cold that dispels the illusions of the Daityas."
Behold these lions among the Daityas in the great battle, scorched by my glance, enveloped in frost, deprived of their magic powers, and stripped of their pride.
Having spoken thus, the lord of the stars, together with the lord of the waters,
drenched the armies of the gods with the waters of Śiva for the increase of their peace.
The terrible snow-showers released by Himakara, accompanied by nooses,
enveloped those Daityas like masses of clouds.
